name: 2-methylacyl-CoA racemase deficiency
formal: Autosomal recessive peroxisomal disorder of branched-chain fatty acid and bile acid metabolism (AMACR) causing adult sensorimotor neuropathy, retinopathy, seizures, encephalopathy and pristanic acid accumulation.
simple: A rare inherited metabolic disease in which the body cannot process certain fats, causing nerve damage, vision problems and sometimes seizures or confusion.

name: 3-methylglutaconic aciduria
formal: Heterogeneous group of inherited disorders with raised urinary 3-methylglutaconic acid, linked to mitochondrial dysfunction; neurological forms feature optic atrophy, dystonia, spasticity and developmental delay.
simple: A group of rare inherited conditions where a chemical builds up in the urine because of faulty energy production in cells, often causing movement problems and developmental delay.

name: 4-hydroxybutyric acidaemia
formal: Autosomal recessive succinic semialdehyde dehydrogenase deficiency causing GABA and gamma-hydroxybutyrate accumulation; presents with developmental delay, hypotonia, ataxia, seizures and behavioural problems.
simple: A rare inherited disorder where brain chemicals are not broken down properly, leading to delayed development, poor muscle tone, unsteadiness and seizures.

name: 5-MTHF deficiency
formal: Disorder of cerebral folate transport or metabolism (e.g. FOLR1 or MTHFR defects) with low CSF 5-methyltetrahydrofolate, causing irritability, ataxia, seizures, developmental regression; folinic acid responsive.
simple: A shortage of an active form of folate in the brain that can cause developmental problems, unsteadiness and seizures, and may improve with folinic acid treatment.

name: Abducens (VIth) nerve palsy
formal: Lesion of the sixth cranial nerve causing impaired ipsilateral abduction and horizontal diplopia; causes include raised intracranial pressure (false localising), microvascular ischaemia, trauma and pontine lesions.
simple: Weakness of the nerve that moves the eye outward, so the eye cannot turn sideways properly and the person sees double.
aN: vith | abducens nerve palsy

name: Abetalipoproteinemia (Bassen-Kornzweig disease)
formal: Autosomal recessive MTTP defect abolishing apoB-lipoprotein assembly, causing fat malabsorption, acanthocytosis, retinitis pigmentosa, and spinocerebellar ataxia with large-fibre neuropathy from vitamin E deficiency.
simple: A rare inherited problem absorbing fats and vitamin E, leading to unsteady walking, weak nerves, and vision loss if untreated.
more: Very low cholesterol and absent apoB; acanthocytes on smear. High-dose vitamin E with fat-soluble vitamin supplements and a low-fat diet slow or prevent neurological decline when started early.
th: โรคยีนด้อยที่สร้าง lipoprotein ชนิด apoB ไม่ได้ — ท้องเสียไขมันตั้งแต่ทารก cholesterol ต่ำมาก acanthocyte และขาด vitamin E จนเกิด ataxia กับจอตาเสื่อม
tempoNote: Gut symptoms from infancy; neurological and retinal signs appear in childhood or adolescence if vitamin E is not replaced
feat: Fatty, foul stools, vomiting and poor weight gain from early infancy
Later sensory ataxia, areflexia with impaired vibration and proprioception
Night blindness and pigmentary retinopathy
Acanthocytes on the blood film; possible bleeding tendency from vitamin K deficiency
Myopathy or ophthalmoplegia in long-standing untreated cases
inv: Very low total cholesterol and near-absent triglycerides; apoB and LDL undetectable
Blood smear: acanthocytes; low vitamins E, A, D and K (prolonged INR)
Parents have normal lipid levels (contrast familial hypobetalipoproteinaemia)
MTTP genetic testing; ophthalmology and NCS baseline

case.story: Greasy diarrhoea since infancy and small for age; now stumbles in the dark and her legs feel 'asleep'.
case.exam: Thin, short; wide-based gait worse with eyes closed, absent ankle jerks, reduced vibration to the knees; fundi show peripheral pigment clumps.
case.tests: Cholesterol 0.9 mmol/L, triglycerides 0.1 mmol/L, apoB undetectable; acanthocytes; vitamin E unmeasurably low; parents' lipids normal.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and the key long-term treatment?
case.a: Abetalipoproteinaemia (MTTP); low-fat diet with very high-dose vitamin E plus vitamins A, K and D, and monitored essential fatty acids.

read.where: Review: Autosomal recessive cerebellar ataxias for which treatment is available; Table 3

det.patho: Loss of microsomal triglyceride transfer protein (MTTP) prevents assembly of apoB-containing lipoproteins in gut and liver, so chylomicrons, VLDL and LDL are absent. Fat and fat-soluble vitamin absorption fail; the neurological and retinal disease results mainly from severe vitamin E deficiency, with vitamin A deficiency adding to retinopathy. Red cell membranes become spiky (acanthocytes) because of abnormal lipid composition.
det.clinical: Infants present with steatorrhoea and failure to thrive. Without replacement, the first decade brings loss of reflexes and proprioception, then a spinocerebellar syndrome, neuropathy and retinitis pigmentosa leading to visual loss. Coagulopathy, liver steatosis and occasionally myopathy or cardiomyopathy occur.
det.diagnosis: Strikingly low cholesterol and triglycerides with absent apoB, acanthocytes and very low vitamin E make the diagnosis; MTTP sequencing confirms it. Normal parental lipids separate it from homozygous familial hypobetalipoproteinaemia (APOB). Track vitamin levels, INR, liver ultrasound and retinal function.
det.treatment: A low-long-chain-fat diet controls diarrhoea, with essential fatty acid supplements. High-dose vitamin E (on the order of 100–300 IU/kg/day) is the key neuroprotective measure, together with vitamin A, K and D replacement adjusted to levels. Early, sustained therapy prevents or limits neurological and retinal disease; late treatment stabilises but rarely reverses deficits.
det.prognosis: Good if treatment begins in infancy or early childhood; untreated, disabling ataxia and blindness develop by early adulthood.
pearls: Ataxia + retinitis pigmentosa + acanthocytes + near-zero cholesterol: abetalipoproteinaemia.
Serum vitamin E is low partly because carrier lipoproteins are absent; adipose or red-cell levels are better guides on treatment.
Treatable — begin vitamin E on suspicion, without waiting for confirmation.
det.thd: Abetalipoproteinemia เกิดจากยีน MTTP ร่างกายสร้าง lipoprotein ที่มี apoB ไม่ได้ ทารกจึงถ่ายเป็นไขมันและโตช้า ต่อมาขาด vitamin E อย่างรุนแรงทำให้เดินเซ reflex หาย และจอตาเสื่อม เลือดพบ acanthocyte cholesterol และ triglyceride ต่ำมาก รักษาด้วยอาหารไขมันต่ำร่วมกับ vitamin E ขนาดสูงมากและวิตามิน A, K, D

ddx.pt: Normal lipids and no malabsorption or acanthocytes
Normal lipids and vitamin E; cardiomyopathy; FXN repeat expansion
Also retinopathy and neuropathy, but phytanic acid high and lipids normal

aN: bassen kornzweig disease | abetalipoproteinemia | abl | bassen kornzweig syndrome | mttp deficiency | microsomal triglyceride transfer protein deficiency | acanthocytosis with ataxia

name: Abversive seizures
formal: Focal seizures with forced, sustained turning of the eyes and head away from the epileptic focus (contraversive), often arising from frontal eye field or adjacent frontal regions.
simple: Seizures in which the eyes and head are forced to turn to one side without the person controlling it.

name: Acanthocytes/acanthocytosis
formal: Presence of spiny, irregularly contracted red cells on blood film, characteristic of neuroacanthocytosis syndromes (chorea-acanthocytosis, McLeod) and abetalipoproteinaemia, with chorea, orofacial dyskinesia and myopathy.
simple: Red blood cells with spiky edges, seen in some rare inherited diseases that cause abnormal movements, muscle disease and nerve problems.

name: Acetazolamide benign paroxysmal tonic upgaze and ataxia of childhood
formal: Childhood-onset episodic tonic upward gaze deviation with ataxia, linked to CACNA1A variants, tending to resolve with age and sometimes improving with acetazolamide or levodopa.
simple: A childhood condition with repeated episodes where the eyes drift upward and balance is poor; it usually settles with age.
nN: acetazolamide benign paroxysmal tonic upgaze and ataxia of childhood

name: Achoreic Huntington’s disease (Huntington sine chorea)
formal: Huntington disease presenting without chorea, with cognitive-psychiatric decline, bradykinesia, rigidity or dystonia, but with a pathological CAG repeat expansion in HTT; seen with juvenile or late-stage disease.
simple: Huntington disease that appears without the typical jerky dance-like movements, showing instead as stiffness, slowness, or changes in thinking and mood.
nN: achoreic huntington disease huntington sine chorea
aN: huntington sine chorea | achoreic huntington disease

name: Acid maltase deficiency
formal: Glycogen storage disease type II (Pompe disease) from lysosomal alpha-glucosidase deficiency; causes proximal and respiratory muscle weakness, with infantile cardiomyopathy or adult limb-girdle pattern.
simple: An inherited disease in which muscles cannot clear stored sugar, causing progressive weakness and breathing difficulty.
more: Diagnose by low acid alpha-glucosidase activity in dried blood spot or leucocytes plus GAA gene testing; EMG shows myopathic changes with myotonic discharges in paraspinals. Alglucosidase or avalglucosidase enzyme replacement slows decline.

name: Acid-base disorders
formal: Disturbances of systemic pH balance (metabolic or respiratory acidosis or alkalosis) that can cause encephalopathy, seizures, tetany, hyperventilation and altered consciousness depending on severity and rate of change.
simple: Imbalances of acid and alkali levels in the blood that can cause confusion, seizures, muscle cramps and drowsiness.

name: Acoustic trauma
formal: Cochlear injury from loud noise or blast producing sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus and sometimes hyperacusis, due to hair cell damage particularly at 3 to 6 kHz.
simple: Hearing damage caused by very loud noise, leading to hearing loss and ringing in the ears.

name: Acquired ataxia syndromes
formal: Ataxias of non-hereditary origin including alcohol, vitamin deficiency, immune-mediated, paraneoplastic, toxic, vascular and infectious causes; subacute progressive cerebellar syndrome needs urgent aetiological work-up.
simple: Unsteadiness and poor coordination that develops from causes such as alcohol, vitamin lack, immune reactions, cancer or infection rather than being inherited.

name: Acquired cardiac disease
formal: Cardiac conditions arising after birth (valvular disease, arrhythmia, cardiomyopathy, endocarditis) that are major sources of cardioembolic stroke and cerebral hypoperfusion.
simple: Heart problems developed during life, such as valve disease or irregular rhythm, that can send clots to the brain and cause stroke.

name: Acquired immune deficiency syndrome
formal: Infection with HIV causing severe CD4 depletion and opportunistic neurological disease including toxoplasmosis, cryptococcal meningitis, PML, CNS lymphoma, HIV dementia and neuropathy.
simple: Advanced HIV infection in which the immune system is badly weakened, leading to brain infections, memory problems and nerve damage.

name: Acquired metabolic disorders
formal: Non-genetic metabolic derangements (hypoglycaemia, uraemia, hepatic failure, electrolyte disturbance, thyroid disease, vitamin deficiency) producing encephalopathy, neuropathy, myopathy or movement disorders.
simple: Body chemistry problems such as low sugar, kidney or liver failure or vitamin shortage that can affect the brain, nerves or muscles.

name: Acquired muscle diseases
formal: Non-hereditary myopathies such as inflammatory, toxic, endocrine, metabolic and critical illness muscle disease, presenting with proximal weakness, myalgia and raised creatine kinase.
simple: Muscle diseases that develop during life from inflammation, drugs, hormone problems or illness, causing weakness and sometimes pain.

name: Acquired peripheral nerve diseases
formal: Neuropathies from non-genetic causes including diabetes, immune-mediated, toxic, nutritional, infectious, paraproteinaemic and vasculitic mechanisms, causing sensory loss, weakness and pain.
simple: Nerve damage in the arms and legs from causes such as diabetes, immune attack, toxins, infection or poor nutrition.

name: Acquired prion diseases
formal: Transmissible spongiform encephalopathies acquired by exposure, including kuru, iatrogenic Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease and variant CJD from bovine spongiform encephalopathy, with rapid dementia and myoclonus.
simple: Fatal brain diseases caused by abnormal proteins passed on through contaminated tissue, medical procedures or food, causing rapid memory loss and jerking.

name: Acquired retro-cochlear (central) hearing disorders
formal: Central auditory disorders from lesions beyond the cochlea (auditory nerve, brainstem, cortex) causing impaired speech discrimination and processing out of proportion to pure-tone loss.
simple: Hearing problems caused by damage to the nerve or brain pathways rather than the ear, so sounds are heard but speech is hard to understand.
nN: acquired retro cochlear central hearing disorders
aN: central | acquired retro cochlear hearing disorders

name: Acquired retrocochlear hearing disorders
formal: Hearing loss from lesions of the auditory nerve or central auditory pathways, such as vestibular schwannoma, demyelination or stroke, with poor speech discrimination and abnormal brainstem responses.
simple: Hearing loss caused by a problem in the hearing nerve or brain rather than the ear itself, often making speech hard to follow.

name: Acquired symptomatic parkinsonian syndromes
formal: Parkinsonism due to an identifiable cause such as drugs, vascular disease, toxins, infection, trauma or structural lesions, as opposed to idiopathic Parkinson disease.
simple: Parkinson-like symptoms such as slowness, stiffness and tremor that are caused by a drug, stroke, toxin or other identifiable problem.

name: Action dystonia
formal: Dystonia that appears or worsens during voluntary movement, as in task-specific dystonias such as writer's cramp, and is typically absent at rest.
simple: Abnormal muscle twisting or posturing that happens only when moving or doing a specific action, and not when resting.

name: Action myoclonus
formal: Brief shock-like jerks triggered or aggravated by voluntary movement, typical of cortical myoclonus, posthypoxic Lance-Adams syndrome and progressive myoclonic epilepsies.
simple: Sudden muscle jerks that are set off by trying to move, making it hard to perform everyday tasks.

name: Action myoclonus renal failure syndrome
formal: Progressive myoclonic epilepsy with action myoclonus, tremor, ataxia and later renal failure with proteinuria, caused by SCARB2 mutations affecting lysosomal function.
simple: A rare inherited disease causing movement-triggered jerking, tremor and unsteadiness along with kidney failure.

name: Action myotonia
formal: A non-dystrophic myotonia phenotype where muscle stiffness is provoked by voluntary action, usually from chloride or sodium channel dysfunction, without a prominent warm-up effect or weakness.
simple: Muscles stiffen and are slow to relax when you try to use them, for example when gripping something firmly.
more: EMG shows myotonic discharges; genetic testing of CLCN1 or SCN4A helps. Mexiletine is the usual first-line drug; the course is generally benign.

name: Action tremor
formal: Tremor occurring during voluntary muscle activation, including postural, kinetic and intention subtypes, as in essential tremor, cerebellar disease or enhanced physiological tremor.
simple: A shaking that appears when the person holds a position or moves, rather than when the limb is resting.

name: Acute akathisia
formal: Subjective inner restlessness with an urge to move and objective pacing or shifting, appearing hours to days after starting a dopamine blocker such as an antipsychotic or antiemetic.
simple: A distressing feeling that you cannot sit still, usually brought on by a medicine, making a person pace or fidget.
more: Diagnosis is clinical. Reduce or change the drug, and treat with propranolol, benzodiazepines, mirtazapine or anticholinergics; it usually resolves when the cause is removed.

name: Acute brachial neuritis
formal: Idiopathic inflammatory brachial plexopathy (Parsonage-Turner syndrome) with abrupt severe shoulder pain followed by patchy upper limb weakness and wasting, often after infection or vaccination.
simple: Sudden severe shoulder pain followed by weakness of the arm and shoulder muscles due to inflammation of the nerves, usually improving slowly.

name: Acute cerebellar ataxia of childhood
formal: Self-limited post-infectious cerebellar syndrome in young children with abrupt gait ataxia, with or without nystagmus or tremor, usually recovering over weeks to months.
simple: A sudden unsteadiness in young children, usually after a viral illness, that normally gets better by itself over weeks.

name: Acute cervical cord disorders
formal: Acute myelopathies of the cervical spinal cord from trauma, compression, infarction, inflammation or infection producing quadriparesis, sensory level and sphincter dysfunction.
simple: Sudden damage to the spinal cord in the neck causing weakness or paralysis of the arms and legs, numbness and bladder problems.

name: Acute chorea
formal: Abrupt onset of irregular, flowing involuntary movements due to causes such as Sydenham chorea, stroke affecting basal ganglia, drugs, metabolic disease, lupus or hyperthyroidism.
simple: Sudden onset of irregular dance-like jerky movements that the person cannot control.

name: Acute disseminated encephalomyelitis (ADEM)
formal: Monophasic immune-mediated inflammatory demyelination of brain and spinal cord, often post-infectious in children, with encephalopathy, multifocal deficits and widespread MRI white matter lesions.
simple: An immune reaction, usually after an infection, causing brain and spinal cord swelling with confusion, weakness and vision or balance problems.
th: สมองและไขสันหลังอักเสบแบบกระจายเฉียบพลัน มักตามหลังการติดเชื้อในเด็ก มีซึมหรือสับสนร่วมกับอาการทางประสาทหลายตำแหน่ง
tempoNote: Polyfocal deficits and encephalopathy evolve over days, peaking within about 3 months; usually monophasic
feat: Encephalopathy (drowsiness, irritability or altered behaviour) not explained by fever
Multifocal deficits: weakness, ataxia, cranial nerve palsies, optic neuritis, myelitis
Commonly 1–3 weeks after a viral illness or, rarely, vaccination
Mostly children under 10; fever, headache, vomiting and meningism may occur
Seizures in a minority; can deteriorate rapidly to need ventilation
inv: MRI: large, bilateral, poorly marginated T2/FLAIR lesions in white matter, deep grey matter (thalami, basal ganglia), brainstem and cord, mostly of similar age
CSF: lymphocytic pleocytosis and raised protein; oligoclonal bands usually absent
MOG IgG and AQP4 IgG in serum; infectious screen (PCR, cultures) to exclude encephalitis
Repeat MRI at 3 months and later to confirm monophasic course

case.story: Ten days after a febrile rash illness she becomes sleepy and irritable, then cannot walk steadily and her speech is slurred.
case.exam: GCS 12, bilateral extensor plantars, truncal ataxia, left sixth nerve palsy, mild neck stiffness.
case.tests: MRI: multiple fluffy FLAIR lesions in both hemispheres, both thalami and the pons. CSF: 40 lymphocytes, protein 80 mg/dL, OCB negative, viral PCR negative. MOG IgG positive.
case.q: What diagnosis best fits, and what does the MOG result add?
case.a: ADEM; MOG positivity places it within the MOGAD spectrum and identifies a risk of further demyelinating events, so follow-up imaging and clinical review are needed.

read.where: Chapter 10 ADEM and MOG antibody-associated disease

det.patho: ADEM is an immune-mediated, typically monophasic inflammatory demyelination of the CNS, thought to follow molecular mimicry or bystander activation after infection. Perivenous demyelination with lymphocyte and macrophage cuffs is the pathological hallmark, distinguishing it from confluent MS plaques. A large share of paediatric cases carry MOG antibodies.
det.clinical: Onset usually follows a prodrome of fever, malaise and headache, then encephalopathy with multifocal neurological signs develops over days. Brainstem involvement can compromise breathing, and concurrent myelitis causes paraparesis and bladder retention. Adults can be affected, often with more severe illness. A new event after 3 months suggests multiphasic ADEM, MOGAD, NMOSD or MS.
det.diagnosis: Paediatric consensus criteria require a first polyfocal CNS event of presumed inflammatory cause, encephalopathy, compatible MRI and no new features after 3 months. Infective encephalitis must be excluded before steroids where possible, but acyclovir can be started in parallel. Check MOG and AQP4 antibodies, and consider mitochondrial, metabolic, vasculitic and neoplastic mimics such as CNS lymphoma or HLH.
det.treatment: First line is IV methylprednisolone for 3–5 days followed by an oral taper over several weeks. IVIG or plasma exchange is used for steroid-refractory or severe disease. Supportive care includes airway protection, seizure control and treatment of raised intracranial pressure; decompressive surgery is rarely needed in fulminant forms.
det.prognosis: Most children recover fully or nearly so, though subtle cognitive or behavioural sequelae occur; adults and haemorrhagic variants fare worse.
pearls: Encephalopathy is required for ADEM; multifocal lesions without it suggest MS or MOGAD.
Deep grey matter involvement favours ADEM over MS.
Check MOG IgG in every case because it predicts relapse risk.
det.thd: ADEM เป็นการอักเสบและทำลายปลอกประสาทแบบกระจายในสมองและไขสันหลัง มักเกิดหลังติดเชื้อไวรัสในเด็ก ผู้ป่วยซึม สับสน ร่วมกับอาการทางระบบประสาทหลายตำแหน่ง MRI พบรอยโรคใหญ่ขอบไม่ชัดทั้งเนื้อขาวและ thalamus ต้องแยกการติดเชื้อสมองและตรวจ MOG IgG รักษาด้วย IV methylprednisolone ตามด้วยการลด steroid ช้า ๆ ถ้าไม่ดีขึ้นให้ IVIG หรือ PLEX ส่วนใหญ่หายดี

ddx.pt: No encephalopathy, well-defined ovoid lesions of differing age, oligoclonal bands and further relapses
MOG IgG positive; may follow ADEM with recurrent optic neuritis or myelitis
Fulminant hyperacute variant with petechial haemorrhage, oedema, neutrophilic CSF and high mortality

aN: adem | acute disseminated encephalomyelitis | post infectious encephalomyelitis | postvaccinal encephalomyelitis | acute demyelinating encephalomyelitis

name: Acute dystonia
formal: Sudden sustained muscle spasms of face, neck or trunk (oculogyric crisis, torticollis) shortly after starting dopamine-blocking drugs, responding to anticholinergics.
simple: Sudden painful muscle spasms of the face, neck or eyes that can happen soon after taking certain medicines such as anti-sickness or antipsychotic drugs.
more: Treat with IV or IM benztropine or diphenhydramine, usually relieving symptoms within minutes. More common in young men on high-potency antipsychotics or metoclopramide; consider laryngeal dystonia as an emergency, and switch or reduce the offending drug.

name: Acute flaccid paralysis
formal: Syndrome of rapid-onset limb weakness with hypotonia and areflexia, caused by poliovirus, enteroviruses, Guillain-Barre syndrome, myelitis or other anterior horn cell, nerve or muscle disease.
simple: Sudden floppy weakness of one or more limbs, often in children, with a range of possible causes including viral infections.

name: Acute haemorrhagic leukoencephalitis (AHL)
formal: Hyperacute fulminant, usually post-infectious, haemorrhagic demyelinating encephalitis (Hurst disease) with fever, rapid coma and cerebral oedema; considered a severe variant of ADEM.
simple: A rare, very severe brain inflammation with bleeding and swelling that comes on quickly, usually after an infection.
aN: ahl | acute hemorrhagic leukencephalitis

name: Acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (AIDP)
formal: Most common form of Guillain-Barre syndrome: immune-mediated demyelination causing ascending areflexic weakness with albuminocytological dissociation and slowed nerve conduction.
simple: The common type of Guillain-Barre syndrome in which the immune system attacks nerve coverings, causing weakness that spreads upward from the legs.
more: Nerve conduction shows prolonged distal latencies, conduction block and absent F waves or H reflexes; CSF protein rises after the first week. IVIG or plasma exchange speeds recovery; ventilatory and autonomic monitoring are essential.
aN: aidp | acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy

name: Acute inflammatory myopathy
formal: Acute onset immune-mediated or infectious muscle inflammation (e.g. polymyositis, viral or bacterial myositis) producing myalgia, proximal weakness and elevated creatine kinase.
simple: Sudden inflammation of muscles causing pain and weakness, usually in the shoulders and hips.

name: Acute intermittent porphyria (AIP)
formal: Autosomal dominant hepatic porphyria from porphobilinogen deaminase deficiency causing attacks of abdominal pain, autonomic instability, psychosis, seizures and motor neuropathy, triggered by drugs, fasting or hormones.
simple: An inherited disorder causing attacks of severe belly pain, confusion, seizures and nerve weakness that can be triggered by certain drugs or fasting.
th: โรคพอร์ไฟเรียเฉียบพลัน — ปวดท้องรุนแรง อาการทางจิต ระบบประสาทอัตโนมัติผิดปกติ แล้วแขนขาอ่อนแรงแบบแอกซอน
tempoNote: Attacks over days, often triggered by drugs, fasting, alcohol or the menstrual cycle
feat: Severe abdominal pain without peritonism, vomiting, constipation
Tachycardia, hypertension, hyponatraemia (SIADH), seizures, confusion or psychosis
Rapid motor axonal neuropathy, often proximal and arm-predominant; may need ventilation
Dark or reddish urine that darkens further on standing in light
inv: Urine porphobilinogen (PBG) and ALA markedly raised during the attack
Sodium, magnesium; NCS: motor axonal pattern
HMBS gene testing and family screening

case.story: After starting a new anticonvulsant and dieting, 4 days of colicky abdominal pain, then agitation and arm weakness.
case.exam: Pulse 130, BP 170/100, proximal arm weakness MRC 3/5, reduced reflexes, soft abdomen.
case.tests: Sodium 122 mmol/L; urine PBG markedly raised; urine turned port-wine colour on the window sill.
case.q: What are the first treatment steps?
case.a: Stop porphyrinogenic drugs, give IV glucose and haem arginate (hemin), treat pain and seizures with porphyria-safe drugs, monitor breathing.

ddx.pt: No abdominal pain or psychiatric features; CSF albuminocytological dissociation; PBG normal
Wrist drop, anaemia with basophilic stippling, high blood lead
Low potassium, no abdominal or mental symptoms, hours not days

aN: aip | acute intermittent porphyria | acute porphyria | porphyric neuropathy | hepatic porphyria

det.patho: AIP is an autosomal dominant deficiency of hydroxymethylbilane synthase (HMBS, also called PBG deaminase) in haem synthesis, with low penetrance. Triggers that induce hepatic ALAS1 — cytochrome P450-inducing drugs, fasting, alcohol, progesterone, infection and stress — cause accumulation of ALA and PBG. ALA is thought to be directly neurotoxic, causing the visceral, autonomic, central and peripheral nerve manifestations. Attacks are most common in women of reproductive age.
det.clinical: Attacks begin with severe, poorly localised abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting and constipation, with tachycardia and hypertension. Anxiety, insomnia, confusion, hallucinations, seizures and hyponatraemia from SIADH may follow; PRES can occur. A motor-predominant axonal neuropathy may develop over days, often proximal and arm-first, sometimes with cranial nerve and respiratory involvement. Recurrent attacks can lead to chronic pain, hypertension, kidney disease and an increased risk of liver cancer.
det.diagnosis: A spot urine PBG (with creatinine) that is markedly elevated during symptoms establishes an acute porphyria attack and should be sent urgently, not deferred. ALA is also raised. Plasma fluorescence, faecal porphyrins and enzyme or HMBS gene testing distinguish AIP from other acute porphyrias and allow family screening. NCS shows a motor axonal pattern. Check sodium, magnesium and liver function.
det.treatment: Stop all unsafe drugs, treat pain with opioids, control nausea, and correct electrolytes. Give intravenous haem (hemin or haem arginate, usually a 4-day course at 3–4 mg/kg per day) as early as possible; glucose loading is only a holding measure for mild attacks. Treat seizures with porphyria-safe drugs and monitor vital capacity. For frequent recurrent attacks, givosiran (an siRNA silencing hepatic ALAS1) reduces attack rates; liver transplantation is a last resort.
det.prognosis: Most attacks resolve with early haem therapy, but established neuropathy recovers slowly over months and may be incomplete.
pearls: Abdominal pain + hyponatraemia + psychiatric change + new weakness: send a urine PBG.
Many antiepileptic drugs trigger attacks; check a porphyria drug database before prescribing.
AIP has no skin photosensitivity, unlike variegate porphyria and hereditary coproporphyria.
det.thd: AIP เป็นโรคพันธุกรรมจากการขาดเอนไซม์ HMBS ในการสร้างฮีม เมื่อมีตัวกระตุ้น เช่น ยาบางชนิด การอดอาหาร แอลกอฮอล์ หรือฮอร์โมน จะเกิดการสะสมของ ALA และ PBG ซึ่งเป็นพิษต่อระบบประสาท ผู้ป่วยมีอาการปวดท้องรุนแรง ใจสั่น ความดันสูง สับสน ชัก โซเดียมต่ำ และแขนขาอ่อนแรงแบบแอกซอน การวินิจฉัยคือพบ PBG ในปัสสาวะสูงมากขณะมีอาการ การรักษาคือหยุดยาที่กระตุ้น ให้ hemin ทางหลอดเลือดดำโดยเร็ว และใช้ givosiran ป้องกันในรายที่เป็นซ้ำบ่อย

name: Acute ischaemic stroke
formal: Sudden focal neurological deficit due to arterial occlusion and cerebral infarction, treated with thrombolysis or thrombectomy within defined time windows.
simple: A stroke caused by a blocked blood vessel in the brain, leading to sudden weakness, speech or vision problems.

case.who: 68-year-old man with hypertension and atrial fibrillation (not anticoagulated)
case.story: Found by his wife at breakfast unable to speak; he was normal when he went to the toilet 50 minutes earlier.
case.exam: Global aphasia, left gaze preference, right face-and-arm weakness worse than leg, right hemianopia.
case.tests: CT brain: no blood, hyperdense left MCA; CTA: left M1 occlusion; glucose 6.1 mmol/L.
case.q: Which vessel is occluded and what two reperfusion options should be considered now?
case.a: Left middle cerebral artery (M1). Within the window he is a candidate for IV thrombolysis and mechanical thrombectomy; AF is the likely embolic source.

det.patho: Sudden arterial occlusion starves a region of brain; a densely ischaemic core dies within minutes while a surrounding penumbra stays salvageable for hours if flow returns, and how fast the core grows depends largely on collateral supply. The usual TOAST-style mechanisms are cardioembolism (AF above all), large-artery atherosclerosis (extracranial carotid in Western series, intracranial stenosis much more often in Asian patients), small vessel (lacunar) occlusion, other determined causes such as dissection or vasculitis, and cryptogenic or embolic stroke of undetermined source. After occlusion, energy failure, excitotoxicity and cytotoxic oedema evolve over hours, while blood–brain barrier breakdown later drives vasogenic swelling and haemorrhagic transformation. Stroke remains a leading cause of death and adult disability worldwide, with a rising burden in Asia, Thailand included.
det.clinical: Deficits appear abruptly and map onto one arterial territory: MCA strokes give contralateral face-arm weakness, aphasia (dominant) or neglect (non-dominant) and gaze deviation toward the lesion, while ACA strokes favour the leg and PCA strokes give a homonymous hemianopia. Lacunar syndromes (pure motor, pure sensory, ataxic hemiparesis, dysarthria–clumsy hand, sensorimotor) lack cortical signs and may fluctuate over the first day as a capsular warning syndrome. Posterior circulation strokes are easily missed when they present as vertigo, imbalance, diplopia or dysarthria; basilar occlusion may announce itself with stuttering symptoms before coma or locked-in state. Early worsening comes from clot propagation, failing collaterals, malignant oedema (large MCA infarcts peak at days 2–4) or haemorrhagic transformation. Examiners like the NIHSS, territory localisation, the time-last-known-well logic and recognition of a large-vessel occlusion at the bedside (forced gaze, aphasia or neglect plus dense hemiplegia).
det.diagnosis: The first goal is to exclude haemorrhage and mimics within minutes: non-contrast CT plus capillary glucose, then CT angiography from arch to vertex to find a large-vessel occlusion, without waiting for creatinine. ASPECTS on CT estimates early ischaemic change in the MCA territory, and CT perfusion (core–penumbra mismatch) or MRI (DWI–FLAIR mismatch) selects patients who wake up with symptoms, have unknown onset or arrive beyond the standard windows. DWI is the most sensitive test but can miss very small brainstem infarcts in the first hours, so a negative scan does not overrule a convincing posterior circulation syndrome. Mimics include seizure with Todd paresis, hypoglycaemia, migraine aura, functional weakness, tumour, subdural haematoma and sepsis unmasking an old deficit. Once stable, define the mechanism with prolonged rhythm monitoring (including implantable loop recorders for cryptogenic stroke), echocardiography, vessel imaging, lipids, HbA1c and, in the young, tests for dissection, PFO, thrombophilia and vasculitis.
det.treatment: IV thrombolysis is given within 4.5 hours of last known well, using tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg as a single bolus (maximum 25 mg) or alteplase 0.9 mg/kg (maximum 90 mg, 10% as bolus); beyond 4.5 hours or for wake-up stroke it remains an option up to 9 hours when perfusion or DWI–FLAIR imaging shows salvageable tissue, but it adds little for minor non-disabling deficits, where dual antiplatelet therapy is preferred. Mechanical thrombectomy is standard for ICA or proximal MCA occlusion up to 24 hours with imaging selection, recent trials extend benefit to large established cores (ASPECTS roughly 3–5), and basilar occlusion with moderate–severe deficit also benefits up to about 24 hours; routine thrombectomy for medium or distal vessel occlusions has not shown benefit. Keep BP at or below 185/110 before and 180/105 for 24 hours after reperfusion, and avoid driving systolic pressure well below 140 after successful thrombectomy, since intensive targets worsened outcome. Admit to a stroke unit, screen swallowing, treat fever and hyperglycaemia, prevent aspiration, DVT (intermittent pneumatic compression) and falls, and start early rehabilitation; decompressive hemicraniectomy within 48 hours saves lives in malignant MCA infarction. Secondary prevention follows mechanism: 21 days of aspirin plus clopidogrel after minor stroke or high-risk TIA, a DOAC for AF started early (within about 2 days for minor and 6–7 days for severe strokes per recent trials), high-intensity statin with LDL target below 70 mg/dL, BP control and carotid revascularisation when indicated.
det.prognosis: Outcome depends on infarct size, age, collateral status and speed of reperfusion; roughly a third of survivors remain dependent. Recurrence risk is highest in the first weeks, especially with large-artery disease.
pearls: Time is brain: always record the time last seen well, not the time found.
Check glucose before calling a stroke — hypoglycaemia is the classic reversible mimic.
A dizzy patient with a normal CT can still have a cerebellar stroke; look for gait ataxia and use HINTS.
A large core is no longer an automatic exclusion for thrombectomy, and basilar occlusion is treated up to about 24 hours.

name: Acute lymphocytic leukaemia (ALL)
formal: Malignancy of lymphoid precursor cells that can involve the CNS with leukaemic meningitis, cranial neuropathies and treatment-related neurotoxicity such as leukoencephalopathy and neuropathy.
simple: A fast-growing blood cancer that can spread to the brain coverings or cause nerve problems, including from its treatment.
aN: all | acute lymphocytic leukemia

name: Acute motor and sensory axonal neuropathies (AMSAN)
formal: Severe axonal form of Guillain-Barre syndrome with motor and sensory involvement, rapid progression, marked axonal degeneration and poor, slow recovery.
simple: A severe form of Guillain-Barre syndrome that damages the nerve fibres themselves, causing weakness and numbness with slow recovery.
more: Nerve conduction shows low motor and sensory amplitudes with relatively preserved velocities; sural response often lost. Treat with IVIG or plasma exchange as in other GBS forms; mechanical ventilation is frequently needed and long-term disability is common.
ab: Acute motor and sensory axonal neuropathies
nN: acute motor and sensory axonal neuropathies amsan
aN: amsan | acute motor and sensory axonal neuropathies

name: Acute motor axonal neuropathy (AMAN)
formal: Axonal Guillain-Barre variant, often following Campylobacter infection, with anti-GM1 or GD1a antibodies, pure motor weakness and reduced motor amplitudes on nerve conduction.
simple: A type of Guillain-Barre syndrome causing sudden weakness without numbness, often after a stomach infection.
more: Anti-ganglioside antibodies (GM1, GD1a) support diagnosis; electrodiagnosis may show reversible conduction failure mimicking demyelination. Treat with IVIG or plasma exchange; recovery is often good, though some patients stay with residual weakness.
th: GBS ชนิดแอกซอนสั่งการ — หลังท้องเสีย (Campylobacter) อ่อนแรงล้วน ไม่ชา แอนติบอดี GM1/GD1a
feat: Pure motor, rapidly ascending weakness after a diarrhoeal illness
Sensory nerve studies normal
Reflexes may be preserved or even brisk in some patients
Two recovery patterns: fast (reversible nodal conduction failure) or slow (axonal degeneration)
inv: IgG antibodies to GM1, GM1b, GD1a; Campylobacter serology/stool
Serial NCS: low CMAPs; conduction block that recovers without temporal dispersion indicates nodal, not demyelinating, block

case.story: Ten days after bloody diarrhoea, he developed leg then arm weakness over 4 days with no numbness.
case.exam: Symmetric weakness MRC 2–3/5, reduced reflexes, normal sensation, no facial weakness.
case.tests: NCS day 5: low CMAPs with apparent conduction block, normal sensory potentials; anti-GD1a IgG positive. Repeat NCS at 3 weeks: CMAPs recovered without dispersion.
case.q: On day 5 the study suggested demyelination. Why was this misleading?
case.a: The block was at the node (reversible conduction failure) — it resolved without temporal dispersion, which is typical of AMAN rather than demyelinating GBS. Serial studies are needed to classify GBS correctly.

Sensory potentials also lost; slower, poorer recovery

det.patho: Most cases follow Campylobacter jejuni enteritis: lipo-oligosaccharide on the bacterium mimics GM1 and GD1a gangliosides of motor axons. Cross-reacting IgG binds the nodal axolemma, activates complement and disrupts sodium channels. Mild injury causes reversible nodal conduction failure; heavier injury leads to Wallerian-like axonal degeneration. AMAN is proportionally more frequent in East and South Asia and Latin America, and in younger patients.
det.clinical: Weakness ascends over days without sensory symptoms, often with deep tendon reflexes that are preserved or briefly brisk. Cranial nerves are less often affected than in AIDP, but respiratory failure still occurs. Recovery follows one of two tracks: rapid improvement within weeks (reversible conduction failure) or slow recovery over many months (axonal degeneration, sometimes with permanent distal weakness). Pain and dysautonomia are generally milder than in AIDP.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis rests on the GBS clinical criteria plus electrophysiology showing reduced CMAPs, normal sensory responses and no persistent demyelinating features. Early studies may mimic demyelination; repeat at 3–6 weeks to classify correctly. CSF protein may be normal in the first week. IgG anti-GM1/GD1a supports the diagnosis and Campylobacter can be sought in stool or serology. Exclude poliomyelitis and other acute flaccid myelitis, hypokalaemia, botulism and porphyria.
det.treatment: Management is the same as GBS: IVIG (total 2 g/kg, split across 5 days) or plasma exchange, ideally within the first two weeks. Corticosteroids are not effective. Monitor vital capacity, swallowing and autonomic function and anticipate ventilation. Thromboprophylaxis, pain control and early rehabilitation are part of standard care.
det.prognosis: Most patients walk again; those with reversible conduction failure recover quickly, while extensive axonal loss predicts slow and incomplete recovery. The modified Erasmus GBS outcome score helps estimate prognosis.
pearls: Preserved or brisk reflexes do not exclude GBS — this is classic for AMAN.
One early NCS can mislabel AMAN as demyelinating; serial studies are needed.
Normal sensory potentials in an acute flaccid paralysis point to AMAN, poliomyelitis-like illness or NMJ disease.
det.thd: AMAN เป็น GBS ชนิดที่ทำลายแอกซอนของเส้นประสาทสั่งการ มักเกิดหลังท้องเสียจาก Campylobacter ซึ่งทำให้ร่างกายสร้างแอนติบอดีต่อ GM1/GD1a ผู้ป่วยอ่อนแรงขึ้นจากขาไปแขนภายในไม่กี่วัน แต่ไม่มีอาการชา และรีเฟล็กซ์อาจยังปกติ การตรวจไฟฟ้าพบ CMAP ต่ำโดย sensory ปกติ ควรตรวจซ้ำเพื่อแยกจาก AIDP การรักษาเหมือน GBS คือ IVIG หรือ plasma exchange และเฝ้าระวังการหายใจ

name: Acute necrotising encephalopathy
formal: Rapidly progressive post-infectious encephalopathy with symmetric multifocal brain lesions involving thalami, brainstem and cerebellum, associated with RANBP2 mutations in familial recurrent cases.
simple: A rare severe brain illness in children after a viral infection, causing fever, seizures and coma with damage in deep brain areas.

name: Acute necrotising myopathy
formal: Rapid muscle fibre necrosis with markedly elevated creatine kinase, caused by statins, immune-mediated disease, cancer, infection or toxins, presenting with severe proximal weakness.
simple: Sudden breakdown of muscle fibres causing marked weakness and pain, with a very high muscle enzyme level in blood.

name: Acute necrotising myopathy of intensive care
formal: Critical illness myopathy variant with acute rhabdomyolysis and muscle fibre necrosis, associated with sepsis, high-dose steroids and neuromuscular blockers, causing flaccid quadriparesis and ventilator weaning difficulty.
simple: Severe muscle damage in very ill patients in intensive care that causes generalised weakness and makes it hard to come off the ventilator.
nN: acute necrotising myopathy of intensive care

name: Acute necrotizing myopathy
formal: Rapid-onset myopathy with myofibre necrosis and marked CK elevation, seen with rhabdomyolysis, toxins, drugs, infection, or paraneoplastic and autoimmune causes, often with myoglobinuria.
simple: A sudden illness where muscle fibres break down, causing pain, weakness, and dark urine.
more: Check CK, renal function, potassium, and drug or toxin history; biopsy shows necrosis with little inflammation. Treat the cause, give fluids, and protect the kidneys; recovery is often good.

name: Acute otitis media
formal: Infection of the middle ear that may cause neurological complications such as mastoiditis, lateral sinus thrombosis, meningitis, brain abscess and facial palsy.
simple: A middle ear infection that can sometimes spread to cause facial weakness, meningitis or brain abscess.

name: Acute parkinsonism
formal: Subacute-onset rigid-akinetic syndrome from drugs, toxins, encephalitis, basal ganglia stroke or metabolic causes, differing from slowly evolving idiopathic Parkinson disease.
simple: Parkinson-like stiffness and slowness that starts suddenly, often caused by a medicine, toxin, infection or stroke.

name: Acute quadriplegic myopathy (AQM)/critical illness myopathy
formal: Acute flaccid weakness with selective myosin loss in ICU patients, linked to steroids, neuromuscular blockers, and sepsis, with low-amplitude CMAPs, normal sensory studies, and mildly raised CK.
simple: Severe weakness of arms and legs that develops in very sick patients on intensive care, making it hard to wean from a ventilator.
more: Direct muscle stimulation and biopsy showing thick-filament loss confirm it. Treatment is supportive with early mobilisation; most survivors recover over weeks to months.
nN: acute quadriplegic myopathy aqm critical illness myopathy
aN: aqm | acute quadriplegic myopathy critical illness myopathy

name: Acute reversible hyperglycaemic neuropathy
formal: Transient painful or sensory neuropathy occurring with severe hyperglycaemia and resolving once glucose is normalised, distinct from chronic diabetic polyneuropathy.
simple: Nerve pain or numbness that appears with very high blood sugar and goes away once the sugar is brought under control.

name: Acute small fiber sensory neuropathy
formal: Abrupt-onset neuropathy of thinly myelinated and unmyelinated fibres presenting with burning pain and autonomic symptoms with preserved strength and reflexes and normal nerve conduction studies.
simple: A sudden nerve problem causing burning pain and odd skin sensations, usually without weakness.
more: Skin biopsy shows reduced intra-epidermal nerve fibre density; look for diabetes, post-infectious, and drug causes. Treat pain symptomatically; some cases improve spontaneously or with immunotherapy.

name: Acute stroke
formal: Abrupt focal neurological deficit from cerebral infarction or haemorrhage, requiring urgent imaging and reperfusion or haemorrhage management.
simple: Sudden loss of brain function, such as weakness or speech trouble, caused by a blocked or bleeding blood vessel in the brain.

name: Acute vestibular syndrome
formal: Acute onset of vertigo, nausea, nystagmus and gait imbalance lasting days, caused by vestibular neuritis or posterior circulation stroke; HINTS examination helps distinguish them.
simple: Sudden spinning dizziness with nausea and unsteadiness lasting days, caused by an inner ear nerve problem or sometimes a stroke.

name: Acute viral infections
formal: Systemic viral illnesses that can involve the nervous system as meningitis, encephalitis, myelitis or post-infectious immune syndromes.
simple: Short-lived virus infections that can sometimes spread to the brain, spinal cord or nerves.

name: Acute viral myositis
formal: Self-limited inflammatory muscle injury after viral infection, commonly influenza B, with severe myalgia, tender calves, raised CK, and occasionally rhabdomyolysis.
simple: Sudden muscle pain and weakness, often in the calves, that follows a viral illness such as flu.
more: CK is elevated and biopsy, if done, shows necrosis with inflammation. Rest, fluids, and analgesia; most children and adults recover within days to weeks.

name: ADA2 deficiency
formal: Autosomal recessive autoinflammatory vasculopathy (DADA2) from CECR1 mutations causing recurrent fever, livedo, early-onset ischaemic and haemorrhagic strokes and polyarteritis nodosa-like disease.
simple: A rare inherited condition causing fevers, skin rash and strokes at a young age due to inflamed blood vessels.

name: Addison’s disease
formal: Primary adrenal insufficiency, usually autoimmune, causing fatigue, hypotension, hyponatraemia and hyperpigmentation; may cause neurological symptoms such as weakness, confusion and myopathy.
simple: A condition where the adrenal glands do not make enough hormones, causing tiredness, low blood pressure and weakness.

name: Adenosine deaminase (ADA2) deficiency
formal: Autosomal recessive vasculopathy from CECR1 mutation causing deficient adenosine deaminase 2, with fevers, livedoid rash, recurrent lacunar strokes and immunodeficiency features.
simple: A rare inherited enzyme deficiency that inflames blood vessels, causing fevers, rashes and strokes in young people.
aN: ada2 | adenosine deaminase deficiency

name: Adhesive arachnoiditis
formal: Chronic inflammation of the arachnoid membrane following surgery, infection, haemorrhage or contrast, leading to scarring and tethering of nerve roots with chronic pain and neurological deficits.
simple: Scarring of the spinal cord coverings that makes nerve roots stick together and causes long-lasting pain, numbness and weakness.

name: Adrenal insufficiency
formal: Inadequate cortisol production causing fatigue, hypotension, hyponatraemia and hypoglycaemia; may present with confusion, myopathy or encephalopathy, and occurs in adrenoleukodystrophy.
simple: The adrenal glands do not produce enough hormones, leading to weakness, tiredness, low blood pressure and sometimes confusion.
more: Confirm with morning cortisol, ACTH and a short synacthen stimulation test; primary disease shows high ACTH and autoantibodies to 21-hydroxylase. Treat with hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone; adrenal crisis needs urgent IV hydrocortisone and saline.

name: Adrenal-induced myopathy
formal: Proximal muscle weakness resulting from excess or deficient adrenal corticosteroids, including Cushing syndrome and chronic steroid therapy, with normal creatine kinase.
simple: Muscle weakness, mainly of the thighs and shoulders, caused by too much or too little steroid hormone.

name: Adrenoleukodystrophy (ALD)
formal: X-linked peroxisomal disorder from ABCD1 mutation with very long chain fatty acid accumulation, causing childhood cerebral demyelination, adrenal insufficiency or adult adrenomyeloneuropathy.
simple: An inherited disease in which fatty substances build up and damage the brain's white matter, spinal cord and adrenal glands.
more: Screen with plasma very long chain fatty acids (raised C26:0); MRI shows posterior-predominant symmetric white matter change with rim enhancement. Early cerebral disease is treated by stem cell transplant; steroid replacement for adrenal failure.
aN: ald | adrenoleukodystrophy

name: Adrenomyelodystrophy
formal: Adult-onset X-linked ABCD1 disorder (adrenomyeloneuropathy) with progressive spastic paraparesis, sensory and sphincter disturbance and adrenal insufficiency, due to distal axonopathy of long tracts.
simple: A slowly progressive form of an inherited fat-storage disease causing stiff weak legs, bladder problems and adrenal gland failure in adults.

name: Adrenomyeloneuropathy (AMN)
formal: X-linked ABCD1-related adult phenotype of adrenoleukodystrophy with very-long-chain fatty acid accumulation causing spastic paraparesis, mild axonal neuropathy, and adrenal insufficiency.
simple: An inherited disorder, mainly in men, causing slowly worsening leg stiffness and weakness, along with adrenal gland problems.
more: Elevated plasma very-long-chain fatty acids and ABCD1 mutation confirm it. Replace adrenal hormones; Lorenzo's oil is of limited benefit; progression is slow over decades.
aN: amn | adrenomyeloneuropathy

name: Adult neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis (Kufs’ disease)
formal: Rare autosomal dominant or recessive lysosomal storage disorder (Kufs disease) with adult-onset dementia, myoclonic epilepsy, ataxia and movement disorders without visual loss.
simple: A rare inherited brain disease starting in adulthood, causing dementia, jerks, seizures and movement problems.
nN: adult neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis kufs disease
aN: kufs disease | adult neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis

name: Adult onset SMA
formal: Late-onset 5q SMN1-related spinal muscular atrophy (type 4) with slowly progressive proximal weakness from anterior horn cell loss, normal sensation, and usually mild disability.
simple: A genetic condition where nerve cells controlling muscles slowly die, causing gradual weakness of the hips and shoulders in adulthood.
more: Diagnosed by SMN1 deletion testing; CK mildly raised and EMG neurogenic. Nusinersen, risdiplam, and gene therapy exist; adult course is slow with normal lifespan.

name: Adult polyglucosan body disease
formal: Adult-onset GBE1-related glycogen branching enzyme deficiency with progressive upper and lower motor neuron signs, neurogenic bladder, sensory neuropathy and leukoencephalopathy.
simple: A rare inherited disorder where abnormal sugar deposits build up in nerves, causing stiff weak legs, numbness and bladder problems.

name: Adult-onset inherited leukodystrophies
formal: Group of genetic white matter diseases manifesting in adulthood, including X-linked ALD, CSF1R-related leukoencephalopathy, Alexander disease, CADASIL and metachromatic leukodystrophy, with cognitive, psychiatric, motor decline.
simple: A set of inherited diseases damaging the brain's white matter in adults, causing memory loss, mood changes, stiffness and walking problems.

name: Adult-onset Niemann–Pick disease type C
formal: Lysosomal cholesterol transport disorder from NPC1 or NPC2 mutation presenting in adulthood with psychiatric symptoms, cognitive decline, ataxia, vertical supranuclear gaze palsy and dystonia.
simple: An inherited disease affecting how cells handle cholesterol, causing psychiatric symptoms, memory trouble, clumsiness and difficulty moving the eyes up and down.
nN: adult onset niemann pick disease type c

name: Advanced sleep–wake phase disorder
formal: Circadian rhythm disorder with sleep onset and waking much earlier than desired, due to an advanced circadian phase; some familial cases involve PER2 mutations.
simple: A body-clock problem in which a person gets sleepy very early in the evening and wakes up far too early in the morning.

name: Affective disorders
formal: Psychiatric conditions of mood, such as depression and bipolar disorder, that frequently coexist with and complicate neurological disease including stroke, Parkinson disease and epilepsy.
simple: Mood conditions such as depression and bipolar disorder, which often occur alongside brain and nerve diseases.

name: Agnosia
formal: Inability to recognise objects, faces or sounds despite intact primary sensation and intellect, due to lesions in modality-specific association cortex such as occipitotemporal regions.
simple: Being unable to recognise things such as objects, faces or sounds even though the eyes or ears work normally.

name: Aicardi–Goutieres syndrome
formal: Inherited type I interferonopathy (TREX1, RNASEH2A-C, SAMHD1 and others) with early-onset encephalopathy, intracranial calcification, leukodystrophy, raised CSF interferon and chilblain-like skin lesions.
simple: A rare inherited condition where the immune system attacks the brain, causing severe developmental problems and brain calcium deposits.

name: Aicardi–Goutières syndrome (AGS)
formal: Genetic interferon-driven encephalopathy (AGS) with basal ganglia calcification, white matter changes, CSF lymphocytosis and progressive microcephaly, often resembling congenital infection.
simple: A rare inherited illness in which the immune system is overactive in the brain, causing small head size, seizures and developmental delay.
aN: ags | aicardi goutieres syndrome

name: AIDS dementia complex
formal: HIV-associated dementia with subcortical cognitive slowing, motor impairment and behavioural change caused by HIV infection of the brain, usually in advanced untreated disease.
simple: Memory and thinking problems with slowness and clumsiness caused by HIV infection of the brain.

name: Akathisia
formal: Subjective inner restlessness with compulsion to move, with pacing and shifting of the legs, typically a side effect of dopamine-blocking drugs such as antipsychotics.
simple: An uncomfortable inner restlessness that makes a person feel they must keep moving, often caused by certain medicines.

name: Akinesia
formal: Poverty and slowness of spontaneous and voluntary movement with difficulty initiating motion, a cardinal feature of parkinsonism due to basal ganglia dysfunction.
simple: A reduced ability to start movements, so the person moves very little, as seen in Parkinson disease.

name: Akinesia paradoxica
formal: Sudden transient ability of severely akinetic parkinsonian patients to move normally in response to emotional or external stimuli, such as fire or visual cues.
simple: A surprising short burst of normal movement in a person with severe Parkinson disease when stimulated, for example by an emergency.

name: Akinetic mutism
formal: State of wakefulness with absent speech and voluntary movement but preserved eye tracking, caused by lesions of the medial frontal, diencephalic or reticular systems.
simple: A state in which a person is awake but does not speak or move, though the eyes may follow things.

name: Akinetic–abulic syndrome
formal: Frontal lobe syndrome with apathy, reduced spontaneous activity and speech and loss of initiative, due to damage to medial frontal, cingulate or frontal-subcortical circuits.
simple: A condition of marked lack of drive, in which a person barely moves, speaks or shows interest after frontal brain damage.

name: Akinetic–rigid syndromes
formal: Disorders such as Parkinson disease, MSA, PSP and CBD that combine slowness of movement with rigidity, due to basal ganglia or nigrostriatal dysfunction.
simple: Conditions in which slow movement is combined with muscle stiffness, as in Parkinson disease and related disorders.

name: Alarm clock headache
formal: Rare primary headache that wakes patients from sleep at a fixed time, similar to hypnic headache, usually in older adults and often responsive to caffeine or lithium.
simple: A headache that wakes a person at the same time every night, as if triggered by an alarm clock.

name: Alcohol-induced cramps
formal: Painful muscle cramps related to alcohol intake or withdrawal, due to electrolyte disturbance, myopathy or neuropathy.
simple: Painful muscle cramps linked to heavy drinking or stopping alcohol.

name: Alcoholic myopathy
formal: Muscle disease from chronic heavy alcohol use, either acute necrotising with rhabdomyolysis or chronic proximal atrophy with type II fibre loss, partly reflecting nutritional deficiency.
simple: Muscle damage and weakness caused by heavy long-term drinking.
more: CK may be high in the acute form; biopsy shows type II fibre atrophy. Stopping alcohol and improving nutrition usually brings recovery over months.

name: Alcoholic neuropathy
formal: Length-dependent axonal sensorimotor polyneuropathy from chronic alcohol exposure and thiamine and other B-vitamin deficiency, with painful distal paraesthesia and sometimes autonomic features.
simple: Nerve damage in the feet and hands from long-term heavy drinking, causing burning pain, numbness, and weakness.
more: Nerve conduction studies show axonal loss; rule out other causes. Abstinence, thiamine and B-vitamin replacement, and neuropathic pain drugs help; recovery is slow and partial.

case.who: 52-year-old male rice farmer from Roi Et
case.story: Drinks local rice spirit daily for 20 years and eats little. Feet burn at night and he stumbles in the dark.
case.exam: Thin, tender calves, stocking loss of pinprick and vibration to mid-shin, absent ankle jerks, Romberg positive, mild ankle dorsiflexion weakness.
case.tests: NCS: absent sural responses and low peroneal CMAP; MCV 104 fL, GGT high, thiamine low.
case.q: Besides abstinence, what simple treatment is essential?
case.a: Thiamine (and multivitamin) replacement with a balanced diet; start thiamine before any glucose load to avoid precipitating Wernicke encephalopathy.

det.patho: Damage reflects both direct ethanol and acetaldehyde toxicity to axons and nutritional deficiency, especially thiamine. Pure alcohol toxicity tends to cause a slow, painful small-fibre-predominant neuropathy, while thiamine lack produces a quicker, more motor large-fibre form. Lifetime alcohol dose correlates with severity.
det.clinical: Usually affects people with many years of heavy drinking. Pain and burning are frequent and may be the main complaint. Weakness and wasting appear later, and sensory ataxia combined with cerebellar degeneration makes falls common. Look for coexisting Wernicke–Korsakoff, myopathy, compressive palsies (radial 'Saturday night' palsy) and liver disease.
det.diagnosis: A length-dependent axonal neuropathy in a heavy drinker with no other cause supports it. Check nutritional markers and screen for diabetes, B12 deficiency, thyroid disease and paraproteins. Rapid or asymmetric progression should prompt a broader work-up, including vasculitis or GBS.
det.treatment: Abstinence and nutrition are the core: thiamine, B-complex and a balanced diet, plus support for alcohol use disorder. Painful symptoms may respond to duloxetine, amitriptyline or gabapentinoids. Foot care, balance training and fall prevention help.
det.prognosis: Slow partial recovery over months to years after abstinence; established severe axonal loss may not fully reverse.
pearls: Always give thiamine before glucose in malnourished drinkers.
Burning feet plus ataxia: check both neuropathy and cerebellar vermis signs.
Recurrent radial or peroneal pressure palsies occur after intoxicated sleep.

name: Alexander disease
formal: Leukodystrophy from GFAP gain-of-function mutations with Rosenthal fibres, causing infantile macrocephaly and seizures or adult bulbar signs, ataxia and spasticity with periventricular or brainstem MRI changes.
simple: A rare inherited disease damaging the brain's white matter, causing a large head, seizures and developmental problems in babies or swallowing and walking trouble in adults.

name: Allergic angiitis
formal: Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Churg-Strauss), an ANCA-associated small-vessel vasculitis in asthmatic patients causing eosinophilia and mononeuritis multiplex.
simple: An inflammatory disease of small blood vessels in people with asthma, which can damage nerves and cause sudden foot or hand drop.
more: Blood eosinophilia, p-ANCA in about 40 percent, and nerve or muscle biopsy support it. Treat with corticosteroids with cyclophosphamide, or mepolizumab; relapses are common.

name: Allgrove syndrome
formal: Autosomal recessive triple A syndrome from AAAS mutations with achalasia, adrenal insufficiency, alacrima and progressive neuropathy, ataxia and autonomic features.
simple: A rare inherited disease causing swallowing difficulty, dry eyes, adrenal gland weakness and nerve problems.

name: Alpers–Huttenlocher syndrome
formal: Mitochondrial POLG-related disease with intractable seizures, psychomotor regression and liver failure, typically in early childhood; valproate may precipitate fatal hepatotoxicity.
simple: A severe inherited energy-production disorder in children causing hard-to-control seizures, loss of skills and liver failure.

name: ALS-like syndrome
formal: Motor neuron syndrome mimicking amyotrophic lateral sclerosis from other causes such as lead, hexosaminidase deficiency, paraneoplastic disease, lymphoma and hyperthyroidism, with mixed upper and lower motor neuron signs.
simple: A condition that resembles motor neuron disease but has another identifiable, sometimes treatable cause.
more: Search for reversible causes with metals, serology, thyroid and imaging. Treatment of the underlying cause may stabilise symptoms.

name: Altered mental status
formal: Acute change in awareness, attention or cognition, ranging from confusion to coma, with causes including metabolic, infective, toxic, structural and epileptic factors.
simple: A sudden change in how alert or clear-thinking a person is, such as confusion or unusual sleepiness.

name: Alternating hemiplegia of childhood
formal: Rare neurodevelopmental disorder, usually ATP1A3-related, with recurrent episodes of hemiplegia alternating sides from infancy, plus dystonia, nystagmus, seizures and cognitive impairment.
simple: A rare childhood condition with repeated episodes of weakness affecting one side of the body, sometimes switching sides.

name: Aluminium neurotoxicity
formal: Neurotoxicity from aluminium exposure, historically dialysis encephalopathy with speech disturbance, myoclonus, seizures and dementia, and associated with microcytic anaemia and bone disease.
simple: Brain damage caused by too much aluminium exposure, historically in kidney dialysis patients, leading to speech problems, jerks and confusion.

name: Alzheimer’s disease (AD)
formal: Most common neurodegenerative dementia with progressive amnestic cognitive decline, amyloid plaques and tau tangles, and early hippocampal and medial temporal atrophy.
simple: A brain disease that slowly destroys memory and thinking skills, and is the most common cause of dementia.
more: Diagnosis by clinical criteria plus CSF amyloid-beta 42 reduced with raised tau/phosphotau, or amyloid PET and FDG-PET temporoparietal hypometabolism. APOE e4 raises risk; autosomal dominant APP, PSEN1 and PSEN2 mutations cause early onset.

Atypical variants: posterior cortical atrophy, logopenic aphasia
inv: Cognitive testing; reversible causes (B12, thyroid, syphilis, depression)
MRI: medial temporal/hippocampal atrophy
CSF or plasma amyloid/tau, amyloid PET when disease-modifying therapy considered

det.patho: Extracellular amyloid-beta plaques and intraneuronal tau tangles accumulate over decades, spreading from the entorhinal cortex and hippocampus to association neocortex, with synaptic loss correlating best with cognition. APOE e4 is the major genetic risk factor; rare early-onset autosomal dominant forms result from APP, PSEN1 or PSEN2 mutations. Age is the strongest risk factor, and vascular risk factors, hearing loss, inactivity and low education add to risk.
det.clinical: The typical amnestic form begins with trouble learning and keeping new information: repeated questions, misplaced items and forgotten appointments, while remote memories are relatively intact. Word-finding problems, getting lost, and difficulty managing money or medication follow; insight is often poor. Behavioural symptoms such as apathy, depression, agitation and delusions increase in moderate stages. Atypical presentations include posterior cortical atrophy (visuospatial and reading difficulty), logopenic aphasia (slow speech with poor repetition of sentences) and a frontal variant. Early prominent parkinsonism, hallucinations or gait failure suggest another cause.
det.diagnosis: Assess cognition objectively (MoCA or MMSE, then neuropsychology if needed), obtain a collateral history, and screen for reversible contributors: B12, thyroid, syphilis, HIV where relevant, depression, sleep apnoea and anticholinergic drugs. MRI typically shows hippocampal and medial temporal atrophy, and helps exclude vascular disease, tumour or NPH. Biological confirmation uses CSF (low Aβ42 or Aβ42/40 ratio, raised p-tau), amyloid PET, or increasingly blood p-tau217, and is required before anti-amyloid therapy. Biomarkers indicate pathology, not necessarily the cause of symptoms in an older person with mixed disease.
det.treatment: Cholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine) give modest symptomatic benefit in mild to moderate disease; memantine is added or used in moderate to severe stages. Anti-amyloid monoclonal antibodies (lecanemab, donanemab) slow decline modestly in early, biomarker-confirmed disease but require MRI monitoring for ARIA, and APOE e4 homozygotes carry the highest risk. Non-drug care — exercise, cognitive and social engagement, hearing correction, caregiver support, safety and driving review, and advance care planning — matters as much as medication. Avoid antipsychotics where possible and minimise anticholinergic burden.
det.prognosis: Average survival after diagnosis is roughly 8–10 years, with wide variation; late stages bring dependence, dysphagia and infection.
pearls: A spouse who answers for the patient (head-turning sign) is a common clue to cognitive impairment with poor insight.
Normal neurological examination early is expected — focal signs should make you look for another cause.
Biomarker positivity is not dementia: interpret it alongside the clinical picture.

Blood p-tau217 is meant for people who already have cognitive complaints and are being assessed in a memory service — ideally early, at the mild stage — not for screening healthy people; a clearly positive or negative result can spare PET or lumbar puncture, while an intermediate result needs CSF or PET.

The 2025 Lancet series stresses that a molecular diagnosis (amyloid plus tau evidence) is now the entry ticket for anti-amyloid therapy, so access to biomarkers, MRI safety monitoring and specialist pathways must expand together.

name: Alzheimer’s disease and Parkinson’s disease
formal: Two most common neurodegenerative diseases, often overlapping clinically and pathologically, with cognitive decline in Alzheimer disease and dopaminergic motor disorder in Parkinson disease.
simple: Two common brain diseases of ageing: one mainly affects memory and thinking, the other mainly affects movement.

name: Amantadine akathisia
formal: Restlessness and urge to move as a rare adverse effect of amantadine, resolving after dose reduction or withdrawal.
simple: Inner restlessness that can occur as a side effect of the medicine amantadine.

name: Amino acid and organic acid metabolism disorders
formal: Inherited aminoacidopathies and organic acidurias (e.g. phenylketonuria, maple syrup urine disease, methylmalonic aciduria) causing encephalopathy, seizures, developmental delay and metabolic crises.
simple: A group of inherited conditions in which the body cannot break down certain protein parts, causing brain problems, seizures and developmental delay.
nN: amino acid and organic acid metabolism disorders

name: Amiodarone neuropathy
formal: Dose- and duration-related toxic neuropathy with demyelinating and axonal features, tremor, and ataxia, from the antiarrhythmic amiodarone.
simple: Nerve damage causing numbness, tingling, and weakness in people taking the heart rhythm drug amiodarone.
more: Nerve conduction studies show mixed demyelination and axonal loss; reducing or stopping the drug leads to slow improvement.

name: Amnesia
formal: Impaired ability to form new memories or recall past ones, due to lesions of the hippocampus, thalamus or basal forebrain, or to transient global amnesia, trauma or Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome.
simple: Loss of memory, either for recent events or for things from the past.

name: Amniotic fluid embolism
formal: Obstetric emergency with sudden hypoxia, shock, coagulopathy and seizures or coma, which may produce hypoxic-ischaemic brain injury in the mother.
simple: A rare, life-threatening childbirth complication where amniotic fluid enters the mother's blood, causing collapse and sometimes brain injury.

name: Amyloid myopathy
formal: Myopathy from amyloid deposition in muscle, usually AL type, causing progressive proximal weakness, macroglossia, and pseudohypertrophy with a raised or normal CK.
simple: Weakness of muscles caused by an abnormal protein called amyloid building up inside them.
more: Biopsy with Congo red staining shows amyloid; screen for plasma cell disorder with serum and urine immunofixation. Treat the underlying clone with chemotherapy; prognosis depends on cardiac involvement.

name: Amyloid neuropathy
formal: Neuropathy from extracellular amyloid deposition in nerves, as in hereditary transthyretin or AL amyloidosis, with painful small fibre loss, autonomic failure and carpal tunnel syndrome.
simple: Nerve damage caused by abnormal protein deposits, leading to pain, numbness, weakness and problems with blood pressure and digestion.

name: Amyloid polyneuropathy
formal: Length-dependent axonal sensorimotor and autonomic neuropathy caused by amyloid deposited in nerves, from hereditary transthyretin, AL, or rarer types, often with early pain and temperature loss.
simple: Nerve damage caused by amyloid protein deposits, leading to burning pain, numbness, weakness, and problems with blood pressure and digestion.
more: Diagnosed by tissue biopsy with typing and genetic or monoclonal testing. Treatments include TTR silencers and stabilisers, chemotherapy for AL, and liver transplantation in selected patients.

name: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS)
formal: Progressive neurodegeneration of upper and lower motor neurons causing weakness, wasting, fasciculations and bulbar involvement, leading to respiratory failure; some cases are familial and associated with frontotemporal dementia.
simple: A progressive disease destroying the nerve cells controlling muscles, causing weakness, muscle wasting, and eventually difficulty speaking, swallowing and breathing.

det.patho: Progressive degeneration of upper motor neurons in the motor cortex and lower motor neurons in the brainstem and anterior horn. Most cases show TDP-43 protein aggregates; around 10% are familial, and the commonest genes are C9orf72 repeat expansion, SOD1, TARDBP and FUS, which are also found in some apparently sporadic cases. Mechanisms include impaired protein handling, RNA processing defects, glutamate excitotoxicity and glial toxicity. ALS overlaps clinically and genetically with frontotemporal dementia.
det.clinical: Onset is usually focal and asymmetric — limb onset (hand wasting, foot drop) in about two-thirds, bulbar onset (dysarthria, dysphagia) in about a quarter — then spreads to contiguous regions. Mixed UMN and LMN signs coexist: wasting and fasciculations with brisk reflexes, spasticity and pseudobulbar affect. Eye movements, sensation and sphincters are typically spared. Cognitive or behavioural change occurs in up to half, with frank FTD in some. Respiratory muscle weakness causes orthopnoea, morning headache and disturbed sleep. Variants include progressive muscular atrophy, primary lateral sclerosis and flail-arm syndrome.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical, supported by EMG, using the Gold Coast criteria: progressive motor impairment with UMN and LMN dysfunction in one region or LMN dysfunction in two regions, after excluding other causes. EMG shows active denervation and chronic reinnervation, with fasciculation potentials, and normal sensory nerve studies. MRI of brain and spine excludes compressive myelopathy and other structural mimics. Bloods and targeted tests exclude MMN, Kennedy disease, IBM, paraproteinaemia and hyperparathyroidism; offer genetic testing, now relevant for SOD1-targeted therapy.
det.treatment: Riluzole modestly prolongs survival; edaravone is available in some countries, and tofersen is an antisense therapy for SOD1-ALS. Multidisciplinary clinic care improves survival and quality of life. Non-invasive ventilation for respiratory insufficiency extends survival, and gastrostomy should be placed before vital capacity falls too far. Manage sialorrhoea, cramps, spasticity, pseudobulbar affect and communication needs, and discuss advance care planning early.
det.prognosis: Median survival is about 2–4 years from symptom onset, mainly ending in respiratory failure; around one in ten live beyond 10 years.
pearls: UMN and LMN signs in the same limb with normal sensation = ALS until proven otherwise.
Always exclude cervical myelopathy and MMN — both are treatable mimics.
Split hand: thenar and first dorsal interosseous wasted more than hypothenar.

name: Anaemia
formal: Reduced haemoglobin with neurological consequences including fatigue, headache, tinnitus, stroke risk and, in B12 or iron deficiency, neuropathy and cognitive effects.
simple: A low level of red blood cells or haemoglobin, causing tiredness, headache and breathlessness.

name: Anaesthetic-induced myoclonus
formal: Involuntary myoclonic jerks occurring on induction or emergence from anaesthesia due to certain agents such as etomidate, propofol or opioids.
simple: Brief muscle jerks that can happen when certain anaesthetic drugs are given.

name: Anaplastic astrocytoma
formal: WHO grade 3 diffuse glioma with increased cellularity, mitotic activity and nuclear atypia, typically IDH-mutant in younger patients, treated with surgery, radiotherapy and chemotherapy.
simple: A fast-growing cancer of brain support cells that needs surgery, radiation and chemotherapy.

name: Andersen–Tawil syndrome
formal: Autosomal dominant KCNJ2 channelopathy with periodic paralysis, ventricular arrhythmia with prolonged QU interval and dysmorphic features such as low-set ears and small mandible.
simple: An inherited condition causing episodes of muscle weakness, heart rhythm problems and distinctive facial and skeletal features.

case.story: Episodes of leg weakness lasting hours since age 12, plus palpitations and a fainting episode at school.
case.exam: Short stature, small mandible, fifth-finger clinodactyly; strength normal between attacks.
case.tests: K 3.2 mmol/L in an attack; ECG shows large U waves and frequent bigeminy; Holter: runs of bidirectional VT; KCNJ2 variant.
case.q: What must be considered before giving potassium-lowering or QT-prolonging drugs?
case.a: Arrhythmia risk — check ECG, avoid QT/QU-prolonging drugs, refer to cardiology for beta-blocker or flecainide; carbonic anhydrase inhibitors reduce attacks.

det.patho: Most cases result from dominant-negative mutations in KCNJ2, encoding the inward-rectifier potassium channel Kir2.1 expressed in skeletal muscle, heart and bone. Reduced inward-rectifier current destabilises the resting potential in muscle, prolongs terminal repolarisation in the heart, and disturbs skeletal development. Inheritance is autosomal dominant with variable expressivity; de novo cases are frequent.
det.clinical: The full triad is present in only a portion of patients, so diagnosis is often delayed. Attacks of weakness resemble other periodic paralyses but can occur with any potassium level. Cardiac features range from asymptomatic ectopy to syncope; sudden death is uncommon but reported. Dysmorphic features are subtle and require deliberate inspection of face, hands and feet. A fixed proximal weakness may develop later.
det.diagnosis: Suspect ATS in any periodic paralysis with ventricular arrhythmia or characteristic ECG changes (enlarged U waves, long QU, ventricular ectopy). ECG and Holter are essential, together with potassium in attacks and a long exercise test. Genetic testing for KCNJ2 confirms most cases; first-degree relatives should be screened with ECG.
det.treatment: Neuromuscular attacks are reduced with carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (acetazolamide or dichlorphenamide) and careful potassium management, keeping in mind cardiac effects. Cardiology manages arrhythmia, often with beta-blockers or flecainide; ICD is considered for syncope or sustained VT. Avoid drugs that prolong repolarisation and severe hypokalaemia.
det.prognosis: Life expectancy is usually close to normal with treatment; disability comes from attacks and later fixed weakness.
pearls: Always do an ECG in periodic paralysis — U waves and bidirectional VT unmask ATS.
Look at the hands and jaw: clinodactyly and micrognathia are easy to miss.
Potassium may be low, normal or high in attacks.
