simple: Bleeding around the brain from a burst weak spot in a blood vessel, causing a sudden severe headache.

name: Aneurysms
formal: Focal dilations of arterial walls, in the brain usually saccular at arterial bifurcations, which can compress nerves such as the third cranial nerve or rupture causing subarachnoid haemorrhage.
simple: Bulges in weakened blood vessel walls that can press on nerves or burst and cause bleeding.

name: Angelman syndrome
formal: Neurodevelopmental disorder with severe intellectual disability, absent speech, ataxia, tremulous movements, epilepsy and a happy demeanour, due to loss of maternal UBE3A function on chromosome 15q11-13.
simple: A genetic condition causing developmental delay, no speech, unsteady walking, seizures and frequent smiling or laughter.
more: Confirmed by methylation testing and other chromosome 15 studies. Management includes antiseizure drugs, sleep and behavioural therapy; life expectancy is near normal.

name: Ankylosing spondylitis
formal: Chronic inflammatory spondyloarthropathy with sacroiliitis and spinal fusion, associated with HLA-B27 and neurological complications such as cauda equina syndrome and spinal fracture myelopathy.
simple: A long-term inflammatory disease that stiffens the spine and can occasionally damage the spinal cord or nerves.

name: Anoctamin-5-related muscular dystrophy (LGLD
formal: Limb-girdle muscular dystrophy (LGMD R12) from ANO5 mutations with asymmetric proximal or distal weakness, calf atrophy, myalgia and markedly raised creatine kinase.
simple: An inherited muscle disease causing weakness of the hips, shoulders or calves and very high muscle enzyme levels.

name: Anterior canal benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (a-BPPV)
formal: Rare form of BPPV in which displaced otoconia affect the anterior semicircular canal, causing brief positional vertigo with downbeating torsional nystagmus, treated with repositioning manoeuvres.
simple: A rare type of brief spinning dizziness triggered by head position, caused by tiny crystals in a part of the inner ear.
ab: Anterior canal benign paroxysmal positional vertigo
nN: anterior canal benign paroxysmal positional vertigo a bppv
aN: a bppv | anterior canal benign paroxysmal positional vertigo

name: Anterior cingulate syndrome
formal: Frontal syndrome from anterior cingulate damage causing apathy, akinetic mutism, reduced motivation and impaired error monitoring, as in stroke from anterior cerebral artery occlusion.
simple: Loss of drive, speech and emotion after damage to a front part of the brain.

name: Anterior cord syndrome
formal: Spinal cord infarction or injury in the anterior spinal artery territory with loss of motor function and pain and temperature sensation below the lesion, with preserved dorsal column function.
simple: Spinal cord damage causing paralysis and loss of pain and temperature sensing below the injury, while touch and position sense stay normal.

name: Anterior horn cell disease
formal: Disorders of spinal motor neuron cell bodies such as ALS, spinal muscular atrophy and poliomyelitis, causing lower motor neuron weakness, wasting and fasciculations without sensory loss.
simple: Diseases that damage the nerve cells in the spinal cord that control muscles, causing weakness and muscle wasting.

name: Anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy (AION)
formal: Optic nerve head infarction, non-arteritic from small vessel disease or arteritic in giant cell arteritis, causing sudden painless monocular vision loss with disc swelling.
simple: Sudden painless loss of vision in one eye from poor blood supply to the front of the optic nerve.
aN: aion | anterior ischemic optic neuropathy

name: Antibody-mediated neurological diseases
formal: Neurological diseases caused by antibodies against neuronal surface or synaptic antigens (e.g. NMDA receptor, LGI1, AQP4), producing encephalitis, seizures, psychiatric features or neuromuscular disease.
simple: Brain and nerve illnesses in which the body's antibodies wrongly attack the nervous system.

name: Anticholinergic syndrome
formal: Toxidrome from muscarinic receptor blockade with confusion, delirium, dry skin and mouth, mydriasis, tachycardia, urinary retention and hyperthermia.
simple: A reaction to certain drugs causing confusion, dry mouth, wide pupils, fast heartbeat and difficulty passing urine.

name: Anticholinergics akathisia
formal: Restlessness following anticholinergic drug use, which is unusual compared with the classic dopamine-blocker akathisia.
simple: Inner restlessness that can occasionally follow use of anticholinergic medicines.

name: Antimicrotubular myopathies
formal: Drug-induced vacuolar myopathy from colchicine or vincristine impairing microtubule function, producing proximal weakness with a modestly raised CK, often alongside neuropathy and renal impairment.
simple: Muscle weakness caused by drugs such as colchicine that interfere with the internal scaffolding of muscle cells.
more: EMG shows myopathic and neuropathic features; biopsy shows autophagic vacuoles. It usually resolves within weeks after stopping the drug.

name: Antiphospholipid antibody syndrome (APAS)
formal: Autoimmune prothrombotic disorder with persistent antiphospholipid antibodies causing arterial and venous thrombosis, recurrent pregnancy loss, and neurological events such as stroke, chorea or migraine.
simple: An immune condition that makes the blood clot too easily, leading to strokes, pregnancy losses and sometimes movement problems.
more: Diagnosed by lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin and anti-beta-2 glycoprotein antibodies on two occasions. Treated with long-term warfarin; direct oral anticoagulants are less effective.
aN: apas | antiphospholipid antibody syndrome

name: Antiphospholipid syndrome (APLS)
formal: Autoimmune thrombophilia with antiphospholipid antibodies causing arterial and venous thrombosis, stroke, recurrent miscarriage, livedo reticularis and sometimes cognitive dysfunction or migraine.
simple: An immune disorder that makes blood clot too easily, leading to strokes, clots in veins and pregnancy losses.

case.story: Sudden left face and arm weakness lasting 6 hours. She had two miscarriages at 9 and 11 weeks and a calf DVT after a long bus trip.
case.exam: Mild left hemiparesis; lacy purple mottling on both thighs.
case.tests: MRI: small right MCA infarct; aPTT prolonged, not corrected on mixing; lupus anticoagulant positive, aCL IgG 80 GPL, anti-β2GPI high; platelets 110,000.
case.q: Which anticoagulant is preferred and which should be avoided?
case.a: Warfarin (INR 2–3) after confirming persistent positivity at 12 weeks; avoid DOACs, especially rivaroxaban, which had more arterial events in triple-positive APS.

det.patho: Autoantibodies directed against phospholipid-binding proteins, mainly beta-2-glycoprotein I and prothrombin, activate endothelial cells, platelets, monocytes and complement, producing a prothrombotic state in arteries, veins and microvessels. Valve thickening and vegetations add an embolic route. It may be primary or accompany SLE and other autoimmune diseases; transient positivity also follows infections and some drugs.
det.clinical: Stroke and TIA are the commonest arterial events, typically in young adults and often recurrent. Other presentations include cerebral venous thrombosis, multi-infarct cognitive decline, migraine-like headache, seizures and chorea. Pregnancy morbidity and thrombocytopenia are clues. Catastrophic APS is a rare storm of microvascular thrombosis in three or more organs within a week, carrying high mortality.
det.diagnosis: Requires a clinical event plus persistent laboratory positivity (lupus anticoagulant, medium-high titre anticardiolipin or anti-β2GPI) on two occasions at least 12 weeks apart; the 2023 ACR/EULAR criteria weight the features. Lupus anticoagulant testing is unreliable during heparin, DOAC or warfarin therapy and in the acute phase. Low titres and isolated IgM are of uncertain significance. Screen for SLE and look for valve lesions on echocardiography.
det.treatment: Acute stroke follows standard pathways; thrombolysis is not contraindicated by the antibodies alone, but a prolonged aPTT must be interpreted carefully. For definite APS with arterial events, long-term warfarin at INR 2–3 is usual, with some experts adding aspirin or aiming higher in recurrent cases. DOACs are not recommended for arterial or triple-positive APS. Low-antibody profiles without a full syndrome may be managed with aspirin alone. Catastrophic APS needs anticoagulation, glucocorticoids and plasma exchange or IVIG.
det.prognosis: Recurrence is common without adequate anticoagulation; triple positivity and arterial events predict a worse course.
pearls: Prolonged aPTT that fails to correct with mixing in a young stroke patient = check for lupus anticoagulant.
One positive test is not APS: repeat after 12 weeks.
Arterial APS: warfarin, not rivaroxaban or apixaban.

name: Anton syndrome
formal: Cortical blindness with denial of visual loss and confabulation, usually due to bilateral occipital lesions.
simple: A condition in which a person is blind from brain damage but insists they can see.

name: Aortic disease
formal: Disorders of the aorta, including atherosclerosis, aneurysm and dissection, that can cause stroke, spinal cord ischaemia and peripheral embolism.
simple: Problems with the main artery from the heart that can cause strokes or spinal cord damage.

name: Aortic dissection
formal: Tear in the aortic intima that may extend into carotid or spinal arteries, producing stroke, spinal cord infarction, limb ischaemia and Horner syndrome with tearing chest pain.
simple: A tear in the wall of the main artery from the heart that can block blood flow to the brain or spinal cord and cause a stroke or paralysis.

name: Aphasia
formal: Acquired language impairment from dominant hemisphere lesions, affecting fluency, comprehension, repetition or naming, and classified as Broca, Wernicke, conduction, global or anomic types.
simple: Loss of the ability to speak, understand, read or write caused by brain damage, often from a stroke.

name: Apoceruloplasmin deficiency
formal: Rare disorder of absent or reduced ceruloplasmin (aceruloplasminaemia) causing brain iron accumulation with diabetes, retinal degeneration, ataxia, dystonia and cognitive decline.
simple: A rare inherited disease where iron builds up in the brain and organs, causing movement problems, memory loss and diabetes.

name: Apolipoprotein A1-related amyloidosis
formal: Rare autosomal dominant hereditary amyloidosis from APOA1 variants causing visceral deposition of amyloid and sometimes a sensory or autonomic neuropathy, with laryngeal or skin involvement in some families.
simple: An inherited disease in which an abnormal cholesterol-carrying protein forms deposits in organs, occasionally including nerves.
more: Diagnosed by biopsy with mass-spectrometry typing and APOA1 sequencing. Management is supportive; liver or kidney transplantation is considered in advanced organ failure.

name: Apperceptive visual agnosia
formal: Failure to perceive object form despite preserved elementary vision, due to bilateral occipitotemporal damage, often from carbon monoxide poisoning or hypoxia; patients cannot copy or match shapes.
simple: Inability to recognise objects because the brain cannot put what the eyes see together, even though vision is otherwise normal.

name: Apraxia
formal: Impaired execution of learned purposeful movements not explained by weakness, sensory loss or incoordination, often from left parietal or frontal lesions; includes ideomotor and ideational types.
simple: Difficulty carrying out skilled, purposeful movements on request, even though the muscles are strong and the person understands the task.

name: Arachnoiditis
formal: Inflammation of the arachnoid mater causing nerve root adhesions and chronic back pain, leg pain, sensory change and sphincter disturbance, following surgery, infection, haemorrhage or intrathecal agents.
simple: Inflammation of one of the membranes around the spinal cord and nerves, causing long-standing pain, numbness and weakness.

name: Arachnoiditis fibrosis
formal: Chronic stage of arachnoiditis with fibrotic scarring of the meninges and nerve roots, producing clumped roots on MRI, chronic radicular pain and cauda equina deficits.
simple: Scarring of the membranes around the spinal nerves that causes ongoing pain and nerve problems.

name: Arginase deficiency
formal: Urea cycle disorder from ARG1 mutation presenting with progressive spastic diplegia, developmental delay and seizures, with hyperargininaemia and sometimes hyperammonaemia.
simple: A rare inherited metabolic condition causing leg stiffness, delayed development and seizures because a waste-removing enzyme is missing.

name: Arginosuccinic aciduria
formal: Urea cycle disorder from argininosuccinate lyase deficiency causing hyperammonaemia, seizures, developmental delay and brittle hair, with citrulline and argininosuccinate elevation.
simple: An inherited condition where ammonia builds up in the blood, causing seizures, developmental problems and brittle hair.

name: Argyll Robertson syndrome
formal: Pupils that accommodate but do not react to light, with small irregular pupils, classically due to neurosyphilis involving the midbrain pretectal area.
simple: Small pupils that tighten when focusing on near objects but not in response to light, classically caused by late syphilis.

name: Argyrophilic grain disease (AGD)
formal: Late-onset tauopathy with 4-repeat tau argyrophilic grains in limbic regions, producing slowly progressive amnestic cognitive impairment and behavioural change.
simple: A slowly progressive brain disease of older people, causing gradual memory loss and personality change.
more: Usually diagnosed only at autopsy, often coexisting with Alzheimer or other tauopathies; there are no specific biomarkers. Management is symptomatic only.
aN: agd | argyrophilic grain disease

name: Arm tremor
formal: Rhythmic involuntary oscillation of the upper limb that may be rest, postural or kinetic, with causes including Parkinson disease, essential tremor, cerebellar lesions and drugs.
simple: Shaking of the arm that may occur at rest, while holding a position, or during movement.

name: Arrhythmic myoclonus
formal: Myoclonus with irregular, non-repetitive jerks, typical of cortical or subcortical myoclonus, unlike rhythmic myoclonus seen with focal brainstem or spinal lesions.
simple: Muscle jerks that happen at random, with no regular pattern.

name: Arsenic neurotoxicity
formal: Toxic exposure causing gastrointestinal illness, Mees lines, painful sensorimotor axonal polyneuropathy resembling Guillain-Barre, and encephalopathy, diagnosed by urine arsenic levels.
simple: Nerve and brain damage from arsenic poisoning, causing painful numbness, weakness, confusion and white lines on the nails.

name: Arteriolosclerosis
formal: Hyaline thickening and narrowing of small arterioles from chronic hypertension and ageing, underlying lacunar infarcts, white matter disease and vascular cognitive impairment.
simple: Hardening and narrowing of the smallest blood vessels, often from high blood pressure, which can cause small strokes and memory problems.

name: Arteriovenous malformation (AVM)
formal: Congenital tangle of dilated arteries and veins with direct shunting causing haemorrhage, seizures, headache or focal deficits.
simple: An abnormal tangle of blood vessels in the brain that can bleed or cause seizures.

det.patho: A brain AVM is a tangle of dysplastic vessels (nidus) through which arterial blood shunts directly into veins without a capillary bed. High flow and pressure cause venous dilatation, flow-related aneurysms on feeders and fragile walls prone to rupture. Most are sporadic, with somatic KRAS/BRAF mutations found in endothelial cells; multiple AVMs suggest HHT (ENG, ACVRL1). Prevalence is about 15–20 per 100,000, and AVMs cause a disproportionate share of haemorrhagic strokes in young adults.
det.clinical: About half present with haemorrhage, typically lobar or intraventricular, often less devastating than hypertensive bleeds. Seizures are the second commonest presentation; headache, progressive deficits and incidental discovery make up the rest. Risk factors for (re)bleeding include prior rupture, deep location, exclusively deep venous drainage, associated aneurysms and venous outflow stenosis.
det.diagnosis: CT/CTA in acute haemorrhage, MRI/MRA for unruptured lesions, and digital subtraction angiography to define architecture before treatment. Spetzler–Martin grade (I–V) predicts surgical risk; supplementary scores add age, prior haemorrhage and compactness. If an early angiogram is negative because of haematoma compression, repeat imaging after resorption.
det.treatment: Ruptured AVMs are generally treated to eliminate the nidus, as rebleeding risk is high in the first year. Options: microsurgical resection (low grade, accessible), stereotactic radiosurgery (small, deep or eloquent nidus; obliteration takes 2–3 years), and embolisation mainly as an adjunct or for feeder aneurysms. For unruptured AVMs, the ARUBA trial found medical management alone gave fewer strokes or deaths over several years than intervention, so many are observed with seizure and headache control, though selected low-grade lesions in young patients may still be treated. Anti-seizure medication for seizures; acute haemorrhage care as for ICH.
det.prognosis: Unruptured AVMs bleed at roughly 1–3% per year, rising to perhaps 5–15% in the first year after a rupture; mortality per haemorrhage is lower than for hypertensive ICH.
pearls: Lobar haemorrhage in a young normotensive adult: image for an AVM.
Spetzler–Martin = size + eloquence + deep venous drainage.
Unruptured AVMs: intervention is not automatically better (ARUBA).

det.patho: MOG is a minor component on the outermost surface of CNS myelin and oligodendrocytes. Antibodies to it, usually IgG1, together with T-cell and complement-mediated inflammation produce demyelination with relative axonal preservation, unlike the astrocytopathy of AQP4-NMOSD. It is now regarded as a separate disease from MS and NMOSD.
det.clinical: Children commonly present with ADEM or encephalitis, adults with optic neuritis or myelitis. Optic neuritis is frequently bilateral with severe swelling; myelitis tends to involve the conus and grey matter and may cause lasting sphincter problems even after motor recovery. Cortical encephalitis with seizures and headache, and brainstem syndromes, are characteristic additional phenotypes. Around a third to half of adults relapse, most often optic neuritis.
det.diagnosis: International criteria (2023) require a core demyelinating event plus MOG IgG on a cell-based assay, with supporting MRI or clinical features when titres are low or only CSF is positive. Serum should ideally be taken before treatment, since titres fall after steroids or plasma exchange. Always check AQP4 IgG and assess for MS. MOG positivity in a phenotype typical of MS should be interpreted with caution.
det.treatment: Treat attacks with IV methylprednisolone, adding plasma exchange or IVIG for severe or poor responses, followed by a slow steroid taper. Maintenance therapy is reserved for relapsing disease: options include maintenance IVIG, azathioprine, mycophenolate, rituximab or tocilizumab, with IVIG showing the strongest observational data. Several MS disease-modifying drugs are ineffective or harmful here.
det.prognosis: Recovery after each attack is often good, especially vision, but residual bladder, bowel and sexual dysfunction from myelitis is common; persistent seropositivity predicts relapse risk.
pearls: Bilateral swollen discs with long anterior optic nerve enhancement: test MOG before giving steroids.
Conus involvement and the spinal-cord H-sign point towards MOGAD.
Do not taper steroids too fast; early relapse is often withdrawal-related.

name: Astrocytoma
formal: Glial tumour arising from astrocytes, ranging from pilocytic (grade 1) to diffuse and anaplastic forms and glioblastoma, presenting with seizures, headache or focal deficits.
simple: A brain tumour that grows from star-shaped support cells in the brain, ranging from slow-growing to aggressive.

name: Asymptomatic alcoholic myopathy
formal: Subclinical muscle involvement in chronic drinkers, detected by raised CK, EMG, or biopsy showing type II fibre atrophy without overt weakness.
simple: Muscle changes from heavy drinking that show up on tests but cause no noticeable weakness.
more: Often an incidental finding; abstinence and adequate nutrition may reverse it, preventing progression to symptomatic myopathy.

name: Asymptomatic carotid stenosis
formal: Carotid narrowing found without prior stroke or TIA, carrying a modest annual stroke risk, managed with medical therapy and in selected cases endarterectomy or stenting.
simple: A narrowing of the neck artery to the brain found without having caused symptoms, which raises stroke risk.
th: ICA ตีบที่ตรวจพบโดยบังเอิญหรือจากการคัดกรอง โดยไม่มีอาการทางตาหรือสมองข้างเดียวกันใน 6 เดือน ความเสี่ยง stroke ต่ำ (< 1–2% ต่อปี) ภายใต้ยาที่ดี การผ่าตัดหรือใส่ stent พิจารณาเฉพาะราย
tempoNote: Clinically silent; found on screening, by a bruit or before cardiac surgery, and followed over years
feat: No ipsilateral TIA, amaurosis or stroke in the last 6 months (check carefully — vague symptoms are often missed)
Often discovered by a neck bruit, routine ultrasound or pre-operative screening
Commonly coexists with coronary and peripheral artery disease
Annual stroke risk with modern medical therapy is low, roughly 0.5–1%
inv: Carotid duplex with velocity criteria; repeat to watch for progression
CTA/MRA if intervention is being considered
Markers of higher risk: silent ipsilateral infarcts, rapid progression, intraplaque haemorrhage, microemboli on TCD
Global cardiovascular risk assessment (lipids, HbA1c, BP, renal function)

case.who: 71-year-old woman from Chon Buri awaiting coronary artery bypass surgery
case.story: Pre-operative duplex shows a left ICA stenosis; she denies any visual loss, weakness, numbness or speech trouble, now or ever.
case.exam: Left carotid bruit; neurological examination normal.
case.tests: Duplex peak systolic velocity 290 cm/s (≈ 75% stenosis); MRI brain: no infarcts; LDL 132 mg/dL.
case.q: What is the cornerstone of management?
case.a: Intensive medical therapy (antiplatelet, high-intensity statin, BP and diabetes control, stop smoking); revascularisation is reserved for selected higher-risk plaques in centres with very low complication rates.

read.where: Chapter 17 Preventing recurrent stroke and other serious vascular events

det.patho: The plaque biology is identical to symptomatic disease, but without evidence of recent embolisation. Most asymptomatic plaques remain stable; risk rises with greater degree, progression, lipid-rich necrotic cores, intraplaque haemorrhage and ulceration. Prevalence of ≥ 50% stenosis is around 2–5% in people over 65 and higher in those with coronary disease.
det.clinical: By definition there are no relevant symptoms, so a careful history is the key step: brief monocular dimming or transient hand weakness reclassifies the patient as symptomatic. Patients usually die of cardiac rather than cerebrovascular causes, so the stenosis is mainly a marker of systemic atherosclerosis. A bruit is a poor guide to severity.
det.diagnosis: Duplex grades the stenosis; screening the general population is not recommended. Imaging the brain may reveal silent ipsilateral infarcts, which increase future risk. Identify patients who may benefit from intervention by risk markers (progression on serial scans, intraplaque haemorrhage on MRI, microembolic signals, reduced cerebrovascular reserve) and estimate life expectancy, which should exceed about 5 years for intervention to make sense.
det.treatment: Best medical therapy is mandatory for everyone: antiplatelet, high-intensity statin (with ezetimibe or PCSK9 inhibitor as needed), BP and glucose control, exercise and smoking cessation. Older trials showed a small absolute benefit of endarterectomy for 60–99% stenosis, but medical therapy has improved since; recent randomised data comparing intensive medical care with and without revascularisation are mixed, with some benefit of stenting suggested in selected severe stenoses. Intervention is therefore individualised for severe stenosis with high-risk features, in centres whose procedural stroke/death rate is under 3%. Carotid screening before CABG does not routinely justify prophylactic surgery.
det.prognosis: Ipsilateral stroke risk is generally under 1% per year on modern therapy; cardiovascular events and death are considerably more frequent.
pearls: Ask about symptoms carefully — a missed amaurosis fugax changes the patient to symptomatic.
Treat the patient's whole vascular risk; the heart is the usual killer.
Intervene only when expected survival is long, risk markers are present and the centre's complication rate is very low.
det.thd: Asymptomatic carotid stenosis คือ ICA ตีบที่ไม่มีอาการทางสมองหรือตาข้างเดียวกันใน 6 เดือน มักพบจากการคัดกรองหรือได้ยิน bruit ความเสี่ยง stroke ต่ำมากภายใต้การรักษาด้วยยาเต็มที่ (antiplatelet, statin, คุมความดัน เบาหวาน เลิกบุหรี่) การผ่าตัดหรือ stent พิจารณาเฉพาะรายที่ตีบมากร่วมกับลักษณะเสี่ยงสูงและคาดว่ามีชีวิตยืนยาว และต้องซักประวัติให้แน่ใจว่าไม่เคยมีอาการ

name: Ataxia
formal: Incoordination of movement and gait from cerebellar or sensory pathway dysfunction, with dysmetria, intention tremor, dysarthria and wide-based gait; causes are genetic, toxic, autoimmune, vascular or nutritional.
simple: Poor balance and clumsy, uncoordinated movements, such as staggering walking and slurred speech.
more: MRI, vitamin and thyroid tests, antibodies and genetic panels identify causes. Treat reversible causes; otherwise physiotherapy, speech therapy and supportive care.

name: Ataxia with oculomotor apraxia (AOA1, AOA2)
formal: Autosomal recessive cerebellar ataxias (AOA1, AOA2, etc.) with oculomotor apraxia, peripheral neuropathy and hypoalbuminaemia or raised alpha-fetoprotein, caused by DNA repair gene defects such as APTX and SETX.
simple: Inherited conditions causing unsteadiness together with difficulty starting eye movements and nerve damage, usually starting in childhood.
th: ataxia ยีนด้อยกลุ่มซ่อมแซม DNA ที่มีกลอกตาเริ่มยาก ร่วมกับเส้นประสาทเสื่อมรุนแรง — AOA1 (APTX) albumin ต่ำ, AOA2 (SETX) AFP สูง
tempoNote: AOA1 usually starts in early-to-mid childhood; AOA2 in the teens; both progress over years to wheelchair use
feat: Progressive gait and limb ataxia with cerebellar dysarthria
Difficulty launching saccades, compensated by head turns or blinks (more consistent in AOA1 than AOA2)
Marked axonal sensorimotor neuropathy: areflexia, distal wasting, foot deformity
Chorea or dystonia, especially early in AOA1; head tremor in some
No telangiectasia, immunodeficiency or high cancer risk
inv: AOA1: low albumin and high LDL/total cholesterol that become clearer with disease duration
AOA2: AFP moderately raised (useful screening marker); CK sometimes up
NCS: axonal sensorimotor neuropathy; MRI: cerebellar atrophy
Gene testing: APTX (AOA1), SETX (AOA2), ideally within a recessive-ataxia panel

case.story: Since age 13 she trips more and her handwriting has become shaky; her parents are cousins.
case.exam: Gait and limb ataxia, absent reflexes, distal leg wasting with pes cavus, reduced vibration at the toes; saccades are slightly hypometric but she starts them normally.
case.tests: AFP 32 ng/mL (age norm < 10); albumin normal; NCS axonal sensorimotor neuropathy; MRI cerebellar atrophy.
case.q: Which subtype fits best, and which gene would you test first?
case.a: AOA2 — teenage onset, neuropathy, cerebellar atrophy and a modest AFP rise; test SETX.

read.where: Review: Ataxias with oculocephalic dissociation; Biomarkers; Table 3

det.patho: Both are recessive disorders of nucleic-acid processing. Aprataxin (APTX) repairs abortive DNA ligation intermediates at single-strand breaks; senataxin (SETX) is a helicase that resolves RNA–DNA hybrids during transcription. Cerebellar and peripheral sensory neurons seem especially vulnerable. AOA1 is frequent in Japan and Portugal, while AOA2 is among the commoner recessive ataxias after Friedreich's in Europe.
det.clinical: AOA1 typically begins before 10 with ataxia, choreic movements and later a severe neuropathy that can dominate the picture; cognitive slowing may occur. AOA2 starts in adolescence with ataxia and neuropathy, and oculomotor apraxia is present in only around half, so its absence should not deter testing. Both lack the immune and cancer features of A-T. Wheelchair dependence usually arrives within one to three decades.
det.diagnosis: Think of these after Friedreich's ataxia is excluded in a young patient with cerebellar atrophy and axonal neuropathy. AFP points towards AOA2 (or A-T), and low albumin with high cholesterol towards AOA1. Confirm with gene testing; a multigene ataxia panel or exome is efficient. Note that dominant SETX variants cause a juvenile ALS (ALS4), a different disease.
det.treatment: No disease-modifying therapy exists. Rehabilitation, foot orthoses, speech therapy and management of dyskinesia are the mainstays. Coenzyme Q10 has been tried because some AOA1 patients have low muscle levels, but evidence is weak. Genetic counselling is important for siblings.
det.prognosis: Slowly progressive; life expectancy is often reduced but many survive into middle age.
pearls: Ataxia + neuropathy + cerebellar atrophy + high AFP in a teenager: AOA2.
AOA1 biomarker pair: low albumin and high cholesterol.
Oculomotor apraxia is not required for the diagnosis of AOA2.
det.thd: AOA เป็น ataxia ยีนด้อยที่มีปัญหาเริ่มกลอกตา ร่วมกับเส้นประสาทส่วนปลายเสื่อมชนิด axonal และสมองน้อยฝ่อ AOA1 จากยีน APTX เริ่มในวัยเด็ก มี chorea และ albumin ต่ำ cholesterol สูง ส่วน AOA2 จากยีน SETX เริ่มวัยรุ่นและมี AFP สูงปานกลาง ต่างจาก AT ตรงที่ไม่มีภูมิคุ้มกันบกพร่องหรือมะเร็ง รักษาแบบประคับประคองและให้คำปรึกษาทางพันธุกรรม

name: Ataxia ataxia-telangiectasia
formal: Autosomal recessive DNA repair disorder from ATM mutation with progressive cerebellar ataxia, oculocutaneous telangiectasia, immunodeficiency, raised alpha-fetoprotein and cancer predisposition.
simple: An inherited disease causing unsteadiness in childhood, small red blood vessels in the eyes and skin, weak immunity and cancer risk.

name: Ataxia autosomal dominant hereditary
formal: Group of dominantly inherited progressive cerebellar ataxias (spinocerebellar ataxias), often from CAG repeat expansions, with gait ataxia, dysarthria and variable extrapyramidal or pyramidal features.
simple: Inherited conditions passed down in families that cause gradually worsening balance, clumsiness and slurred speech.
more: Genetic testing identifies subtypes such as SCA1, 2, 3 and 6, with anticipation seen in repeat disorders. No disease-modifying therapy exists; physiotherapy and symptomatic care are used.

name: Ataxia telangiectasia (AT)
formal: Autosomal recessive ATM disorder presenting in early childhood with progressive ataxia, oculomotor apraxia, telangiectasia, immunodeficiency, sensitivity to radiation and lymphoid malignancy risk.
simple: An inherited disease causing progressive clumsiness in children, visible tiny blood vessels, frequent infections and high cancer risk.
more: Raised serum alpha-fetoprotein is a key marker; MRI shows cerebellar atrophy. Cells are radiosensitive, so avoid unnecessary radiation; there is no cure, with care being supportive and many patients reaching adolescence or early adulthood.
th: ataxia แบบถ่ายทอดยีนด้อยที่เริ่มตั้งแต่เด็กเล็ก มีเส้นเลือดฝอยขยายที่ตาขาว กลอกตาเริ่มยาก ภูมิคุ้มกันบกพร่อง และเสี่ยงมะเร็งเม็ดเลือดสูง AFP สูง
tempoNote: Wobbly gait from the time the child starts walking (1–4 years), steady worsening; most need a wheelchair by about 10
feat: Toddler-onset truncal and gait ataxia that keeps worsening rather than improving with age
Head thrusts to shift gaze because saccades are hard to start (oculomotor apraxia); slurred speech and drooling
Dilated vessels on the bulbar conjunctiva and ears, usually appearing after ataxia (age 3–6)
Chorea, dystonia or myoclonus in later childhood; reflexes fade as an axonal neuropathy develops
Repeated sinus and chest infections, growth failure, early greying; lymphoma or leukaemia risk
inv: Serum alpha-fetoprotein: raised above the age norm in almost all patients after about 2 years old
Immunoglobulins (low IgA, IgG2, IgE) and lymphocyte subsets; karyotype may show 7;14 rearrangements
MRI: cerebellar atrophy becomes obvious with age; avoid unnecessary CT and X-rays (radiosensitivity)
ATM gene sequencing; ATM protein absent or reduced on immunoblot

case.story: Walked late and has always swayed; teachers notice he falls more each term. He has had pneumonia twice and constant runny ears.
case.exam: Broad-based gait, intention tremor, turns head before eyes when asked to look sideways, red thread-like vessels on both sclerae, depressed ankle jerks.
case.tests: AFP 180 ng/mL; IgA undetectable; MRI shows mild vermian atrophy.
case.q: Which gene is responsible, and what change in imaging practice follows?
case.a: ATM — ataxia telangiectasia; limit ionising radiation (prefer MRI and ultrasound) because cells are radiosensitive and cancer risk is high.

read.where: Review: Clinically common syndromes — Ataxia telangiectasia; Table 3

det.patho: Biallelic loss-of-function variants in ATM, a kinase that senses DNA double-strand breaks and triggers repair and cell-cycle arrest, cause genomic instability. Cerebellar Purkinje cells degenerate early, lymphocytes fail to rearrange antigen-receptor genes properly, and all cells are hypersensitive to ionising radiation. It is the second most common recessive ataxia in most populations; carriers have a modestly raised breast cancer risk.
det.clinical: The classic form begins in the second year with truncal sway, then oculomotor apraxia, dysarthria and dyskinesias; telangiectasia appear only later, so their absence early does not exclude it. Intellect is usually preserved at first but learning slows. Sinopulmonary infection, bronchiectasis and interstitial lung disease are leading causes of morbidity; lymphoid malignancy affects roughly a quarter. Milder 'variant' A-T with residual ATM activity presents in adolescence or adulthood with dystonia, tremor or neuropathy and less immune and cancer burden.
det.diagnosis: A progressive childhood ataxia with raised AFP is A-T until proved otherwise. Confirm with ATM sequencing (with deletion analysis) or absent ATM protein; radiosensitivity assays are supportive. Check immunoglobulins and vaccine responses, and screen lung function. Cerebellar atrophy is often absent in the first years, so a normal early MRI does not exclude it.
det.treatment: There is no disease-modifying therapy approved; dexamethasone delivered within autologous red cells has been studied in trials. Care is multidisciplinary: physio and speech therapy, nutrition and gastrostomy when swallowing fails, prophylactic antibiotics or immunoglobulin replacement for antibody deficiency, and vigilant cancer surveillance using non-ionising imaging. Oncologists must reduce radiotherapy and some chemotherapy doses. Offer genetic counselling and breast screening advice to carrier relatives.
det.prognosis: Most patients now survive into their 20s or 30s; death usually follows malignancy or chronic lung disease.
pearls: Ataxic toddler + head thrusts + high AFP: think A-T even before telangiectasia appear.
Avoid needless X-rays and CT; radiation tolerance is very low.
Normal AFP with an A-T picture suggests ATLD (MRE11) or another DNA-repair ataxia.
det.thd: Ataxia telangiectasia เกิดจากยีน ATM ซึ่งซ่อมแซม DNA ผิดปกติ เด็กเริ่มเดินเซตั้งแต่ขวบปีที่สองและแย่ลงเรื่อย ๆ กลอกตาเริ่มยากต้องหันศีรษะนำ มีเส้นเลือดฝอยขยายที่ตาขาวตามมา ติดเชื้อทางเดินหายใจบ่อยและเสี่ยงมะเร็งต่อมน้ำเหลือง ตรวจพบ AFP สูงและ IgA ต่ำ ยืนยันด้วยยีน ATM รักษาแบบประคับประคอง ป้องกันติดเชื้อ และหลีกเลี่ยงรังสีที่ไม่จำเป็น

MRE11 defect with similar neurology but normal AFP and no telangiectasia
Non-progressive deficit from early brain injury; AFP normal and no new signs over time

name: Ataxia-ocular motor apraxic syndrome
formal: Cerebellar ataxia with impaired voluntary horizontal gaze initiation due to saccade failure, seen in ataxia with oculomotor apraxia types 1 and 2 and ataxia-telangiectasia.
simple: Unsteadiness together with difficulty moving the eyes quickly to look at things, seen in some inherited ataxias.

name: Ataxia-telangiectasia-like disorder (ATLD)
formal: Ataxia-telangiectasia-like disorder from MRE11 mutations, causing slowly progressive cerebellar ataxia, dysarthria and oculomotor apraxia without telangiectasia or immunodeficiency.
simple: A rare inherited disorder similar to ataxia-telangiectasia causing slowly worsening unsteadiness and slurred speech.
aN: atld | ataxia telangiectasia like disorder

name: Atherosclerosis
formal: Chronic arterial disease with intimal lipid-laden plaques causing stenosis and thromboembolism, leading to ischaemic stroke, TIA and vascular dementia.
simple: Fatty build-up that hardens and narrows arteries, which can cause strokes and heart attacks.

name: Atherothrombotic stroke
formal: Ischaemic stroke due to rupture or stenosis of an atherosclerotic plaque in large extracranial or intracranial arteries with thrombosis or artery-to-artery embolism.
simple: A stroke caused by a blood clot forming on a fatty plaque in one of the major arteries to the brain.

name: Athetosis
formal: Slow, writhing involuntary movements of distal limbs, often combined with chorea, resulting from basal ganglia damage as in dyskinetic cerebral palsy.
simple: Slow, twisting, writhing movements of the fingers, hands and feet that the person cannot control.

name: Athetotic cerebral palsy
formal: Dyskinetic cerebral palsy with writhing involuntary movements and fluctuating tone, commonly following perinatal basal ganglia injury such as kernicterus or hypoxia.
simple: A type of cerebral palsy caused by early brain injury, with slow twisting uncontrolled movements and changing muscle tone.

name: Athetotic hemiplegia, hereditary
formal: Congenital or hereditary hemiplegia with unilateral slow writhing movements from contralateral basal ganglia or thalamic damage.
simple: Weakness of one side of the body combined with slow writhing movements, caused by damage to deep brain structures.
aN: athetotic hemiplegia | hereditary

name: Atonic seizure
formal: Brief generalised seizure with sudden loss of muscle tone causing head drops or falls, typical in Lennox-Gastaut syndrome, with EEG showing generalised slow spike-wave or electrodecrement.
simple: A seizure in which the muscles suddenly go limp, so the person drops their head or falls to the ground.

name: Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD)
formal: Neurodevelopmental disorder with persistent inattention, hyperactivity and impulsivity, linked to dopaminergic and noradrenergic dysfunction in frontostriatal circuits.
simple: A condition beginning in childhood that makes it hard to focus, sit still and control impulses.
aN: adhd | attention deficit hyperactivity disorder

name: Atypical absence seizure
formal: Generalised seizure with slower onset and offset of impaired awareness, often with tone changes, and slow 1.5 to 2.5 Hz spike-wave EEG, typical in Lennox-Gastaut syndrome and developmental epileptic encephalopathy.
simple: A type of seizure with staring and reduced awareness that starts and stops more slowly, usually in children with other developmental problems.

name: Atypical forms of parkinsonism
formal: Parkinsonian syndromes such as multiple system atrophy, progressive supranuclear palsy and corticobasal degeneration with early falls, poor levodopa response and additional neurological signs.
simple: Parkinson-like disorders that have extra features, such as early falls or poor drug response, and progress faster than Parkinson disease.

name: Atypical Parkinsonian disorders
formal: Neurodegenerative parkinsonian syndromes such as MSA, PSP, corticobasal syndrome and dementia with Lewy bodies, with poor levodopa response, early falls, autonomic failure or cognitive features.
simple: Parkinson-like diseases that progress faster and respond poorly to usual Parkinson drugs.
more: Diagnosed by clinical red flags and MRI patterns such as hot cross bun or hummingbird signs. Treatment is symptomatic with limited drug benefit, and prognosis is worse than Parkinson disease.

name: Atypical parkinsonism on Guadeloupe
formal: Cluster of parkinsonism with dementia and PSP-like features in Guadeloupe, associated with consumption of annonaceous fruits and herbal teas containing acetogenins, a probable environmental tauopathy.
simple: A form of parkinsonism seen in Guadeloupe with memory loss, linked to eating certain tropical fruits and teas.

name: Auditory agnosia
formal: Failure to recognise environmental sounds or speech despite intact hearing, from bilateral temporal lesions, including pure word deafness and cortical deafness.
simple: Inability to make sense of sounds or speech even though hearing is normal, from damage to hearing areas in the brain.

name: Auditory neuropathy
formal: Hearing disorder with preserved outer hair cell function (present otoacoustic emissions) but absent or abnormal auditory brainstem responses, causing poor speech understanding out of proportion to audiogram.
simple: A hearing problem in which the ear detects sound but the nerve sends it poorly to the brain, so speech is hard to understand.

name: Auditory processing disorder (APD)
formal: Impaired central processing of auditory information despite normal peripheral hearing, causing difficulty with speech in noise, localisation and temporal processing.
simple: Trouble understanding what is heard, especially in noisy places, even though hearing tests are normal.
aN: apd | auditory processing disorder

name: Autoimmune autonomic ganglionopathy (AAG)
formal: Autoimmune disorder with antibodies against ganglionic nicotinic acetylcholine receptors causing subacute pan-autonomic failure with orthostatic hypotension, anhidrosis, dry mouth and gut dysmotility.
simple: An immune attack on the nerve junctions of the autonomic system, causing dizziness on standing, dry mouth, constipation and abnormal sweating.
th: ระบบประสาทอัตโนมัติล้มเหลวทั่วไปจากแอนติบอดีต่อ ganglionic (α3) AChR — ความดันตกเมื่อยืน ตาแห้งปากแห้ง ลำไส้ไม่เคลื่อน รักษาได้
tempoNote: Often subacute over days to weeks, sometimes after infection; a slowly progressive form mimics pure autonomic failure
feat: Severe orthostatic hypotension with fainting on standing
Dry eyes and mouth, reduced sweating
Gut dysmotility: early satiety, vomiting, constipation or ileus
Urinary retention and erectile failure
Poorly reacting, dilated pupils; motor and sensory function largely preserved
inv: Ganglionic (α3) AChR antibody — higher titres are more specific
Autonomic testing: tilt with BP/HR, Valsalva, QSART or thermoregulatory sweat test, heart-rate variability
Low supine and standing noradrenaline; NCS to show sparing of large fibres
Cancer screening (CT chest/abdomen) because of paraneoplastic associations

case.story: Two weeks after a febrile illness she cannot stand without blacking out; she vomits after meals, passes little urine and her mouth is parched.
case.exam: BP 132/84 lying, 74/50 standing with HR unchanged at 84; pupils 6 mm sluggish to light; dry skin; normal strength, sensation and reflexes.
case.tests: α3-AChR antibody strongly positive; tilt test shows neurogenic OH; sweat test widespread anhidrosis; CT chest–abdomen unremarkable.
case.q: What treatment can be offered beyond symptomatic care?
case.a: Immunotherapy — IVIG, plasma exchange or steroids, with rituximab or mycophenolate for maintenance — alongside OH management (fluids, midodrine, droxidopa if available).

det.patho: Antibodies against the α3 subunit of the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor in autonomic ganglia block fast synaptic transmission in both sympathetic and parasympathetic ganglia and enteric neurons. Titres correlate with severity, and passive transfer reproduces the disorder in animals. Some cases are paraneoplastic (small-cell lung cancer, thymoma, others).
det.clinical: Two patterns exist: an acute-subacute onset with widespread failure, often after a viral prodrome, and a slow form closely resembling pure autonomic failure. Cholinergic failure (sicca, pupils, gut, bladder) is usually more prominent than in degenerative autonomic failure. Somatic nerves are largely spared, though mild sensory symptoms or cognitive complaints can occur.
det.diagnosis: Combine objective evidence of generalised autonomic failure with a positive ganglionic AChR antibody; low titres are seen in other disorders and must be interpreted cautiously. Seronegative cases exist and may still respond to immunotherapy. Rule out diabetes, amyloidosis (including TTR), Sjögren syndrome, porphyria, botulism and paraneoplastic anti-Hu disease.
det.treatment: Treat OH with fluids, salt, compression, midodrine, fludrocortisone or droxidopa, and manage gut motility and bladder. Immunotherapy is reasonable once diagnosed: IVIG 2 g/kg, plasma exchange or steroids, then maintenance with mycophenolate, azathioprine or rituximab. Search for and treat any tumour.
det.prognosis: About a third recover well spontaneously or with treatment; many have partial improvement, and the chronic form often needs long-term immunotherapy.
pearls: Prominent dry eyes/mouth, fixed pupils and gut failure in subacute autonomic collapse: test α3-AChR antibody.
Unlike MSA, the brain examination stays normal.
Pyridostigmine can help some patients by boosting ganglionic transmission.
det.thd: AAG เป็นโรคภูมิคุ้มกันที่สร้างแอนติบอดีต่อ α3 AChR ที่ปมประสาทอัตโนมัติ ทำให้ความดันตกเมื่อยืน ตาแห้ง ปากแห้ง เหงื่อไม่ออก ลำไส้ไม่เคลื่อน ปัสสาวะคั่ง และรูม่านตาขยาย โดยกล้ามเนื้อและความรู้สึกยังปกติ วินิจฉัยด้วยการตรวจระบบอัตโนมัติร่วมกับแอนติบอดี และควรค้นหามะเร็ง รักษาด้วย IVIG, PLEX, steroid หรือ rituximab ร่วมกับรักษาอาการความดันตก

name: Autoimmune autonomic neuropathy
formal: Antibody-mediated autonomic failure, often with ganglionic acetylcholine receptor antibodies, causing orthostatic hypotension, anhidrosis, dry eyes and mouth, gut dysmotility, and urinary retention.
simple: An immune attack on the nerves that control automatic body functions, causing dizziness on standing, dry mouth, and constipation.
more: Check anti-ganglionic AChR antibodies and autonomic tests; screen for cancer. Plasma exchange, IVIG, and immunosuppression help; many patients improve partially.

name: Autoimmune chorea
formal: Chorea arising from immune-mediated mechanisms, including Sydenham chorea, lupus, antiphospholipid syndrome and paraneoplastic or anti-CV2 and anti-LGI1 syndromes.
simple: Jerky, dance-like movements caused by the immune system attacking the brain.

name: Autoimmune disease
formal: Condition in which the immune system attacks self-tissues; neurological examples include multiple sclerosis, myasthenia gravis, Guillain-Barre syndrome and autoimmune encephalitis.
simple: A disease in which the body's immune system wrongly attacks its own tissues, including parts of the brain and nerves.

name: Autoimmune disorders
formal: Immune-mediated conditions that affect the nervous system via autoantibodies, T cells or vasculitis, including MS, neuromyelitis optica, myasthenia gravis and autoimmune encephalitis.

name: Autoimmune inner ear disease
formal: Progressive bilateral sensorineural hearing loss with vestibular symptoms from immune-mediated cochlear damage, responsive to corticosteroids and associated with systemic autoimmune disease.
simple: Hearing loss, sometimes with dizziness, caused by the immune system attacking the inner ear, which may improve with steroid treatment.

det.patho: The node of Ranvier and its flanking paranodes are held together by a protein complex: neurofascin-155 on the glial side binds contactin-1 and Caspr1 on the axon, while neurofascin-186 sits in the nodal gap. Antibodies against these proteins — most often of the IgG4 subclass — loosen the axo-glial junction and disperse sodium channels, so conduction fails without the macrophage-driven myelin stripping seen in classic CIDP. Because IgG4 barely activates complement, the disease is driven by functional blockade rather than inflammation. Since the 2021 EAN/PNS guideline these patients are classed as a separate entity, no longer as a CIDP subtype.
det.clinical: Many patients are first labelled GBS or CIDP; the clue is a course that keeps advancing past 8 weeks or a striking lack of response to IVIG. Each antibody carries a typical profile: NF155 in young adults with tremor, ataxia and huge roots; CNTN1 in older adults with rapid axonal loss and membranous nephropathy; Caspr1 with severe neuropathic pain; pan-neurofascin with a catastrophic GBS-like illness. Weakness is usually distal and motor-predominant and the nadir is deep. Cranial, respiratory and autonomic involvement mark the most aggressive cases.
det.diagnosis: Request a nodal–paranodal antibody panel by cell-based assay whenever a CIDP-like or GBS-like patient has atypical features: tremor, sensory ataxia, poor IVIG response, nephrotic syndrome or very high CSF protein. Report the IgG subclass, as IgG4 predicts IVIG resistance. Nerve conduction may look demyelinating (very long distal latencies) or show reversible conduction failure that recovers without dispersion. CSF protein is often above 1–2 g/L and MRI or ultrasound may show enlarged roots and plexuses. Check urine protein and immunofixation because renal and haematological associations change management.
det.treatment: Rituximab is the most effective long-term option for IgG4-mediated disease and often produces sustained remission after one or two cycles. Plasma exchange and high-dose corticosteroids are used for rapid control while rituximab takes effect. IVIG may help early or in IgG1/IgG3-predominant cases but rarely suffices alone. Associated membranous nephropathy or lymphoproliferative disease should be managed together with nephrology or haematology. Antibody titres can be followed as a rough marker of response.
det.prognosis: With timely rituximab most patients improve substantially, though axonal damage accumulated during a delayed diagnosis may leave residual weakness. Untreated or IVIG-only cases often progress to severe disability.
pearls: IVIG failure in 'CIDP' should prompt antibody testing before simply escalating IVIG.
IgG4 does not fix complement — this is why IVIG works poorly and B-cell depletion works well.
Conduction block that reverses without temporal dispersion points to a nodal, not myelin, problem.

name: Autoimmune polyendocrine syndromes

simple: Conditions in which the immune system attacks several hormone glands at once, sometimes also affecting nerves and muscles.
more: Diagnosed with organ-specific autoantibodies and hormone testing, plus AIRE testing in type 1. Treat with hormone replacement and monitor for new glands being affected.

name: Autoinflammatory disease
formal: Disorders of innate immune dysregulation with recurrent systemic inflammation, such as cryopyrin-associated syndromes, some causing aseptic meningitis, hearing loss and papilloedema.
simple: Conditions with repeated unprovoked inflammation, such as fevers and rashes, which can affect the brain coverings.

name: Autonomic disorders
formal: Conditions of impaired sympathetic, parasympathetic or enteric function, such as orthostatic hypotension, MSA, pure autonomic failure and autonomic neuropathy.
simple: Problems with the body's automatic functions such as blood pressure, heart rate, sweating and bladder control.

name: Autonomic failure
formal: Failure of autonomic regulation, causing orthostatic hypotension, anhidrosis, impaired heart rate control and gut and bladder dysfunction, in conditions such as MSA, Parkinson disease and diabetes.
simple: Loss of the body's automatic controls, causing dizziness on standing, abnormal sweating and bladder and bowel problems.

name: Autonomic neuropathies
formal: Damage to autonomic nerve fibres from diabetes, amyloidosis, autoimmune disease or toxins, producing orthostatic hypotension, gastroparesis, sweating abnormalities and bladder dysfunction.
simple: Damage to the nerves that control automatic body functions, causing blood pressure drops, digestive problems and abnormal sweating.

name: Autonomic neuropathy
formal: Damage to autonomic nerves causing orthostatic hypotension, anhidrosis, bladder, bowel and sexual dysfunction, caused by diabetes, amyloid, autoimmunity or toxins.
simple: Nerve damage affecting automatic functions like blood pressure, digestion and sweating.
more: Autonomic reflex testing; treat cause and symptoms such as with fludrocortisone and midodrine.

formal: Genetically heterogeneous group (spinocerebellar ataxias) with adult-onset progressive cerebellar syndrome, often from CAG repeat expansions and variable extracerebellar features.
simple: Inherited conditions passed down through families that cause slowly worsening balance, coordination and speech problems.

simple: An inherited eye nerve disease that slowly reduces central vision in both eyes, usually starting in childhood.

det.patho: ARSACS results from biallelic SACS variants encoding sacsin, a very large protein that interacts with chaperones and regulates mitochondrial and neurofilament organisation. First described in a founder population in the Charlevoix and Saguenay regions of Quebec, it is now found worldwide and is one of the more frequent recessive ataxias outside Friedreich's. Purkinje cell loss, corticospinal degeneration and peripheral demyelination combine to produce the phenotype. Sacsin is abundant in Purkinje cells and motor neurons, and its loss leaves intermediate filaments bundled abnormally and mitochondria poorly divided. The Quebec founder alleles account for nearly all French-Canadian patients, whereas patients elsewhere mostly carry private truncating or missense variants, which partly explains why the eye and nerve findings vary between populations.
det.clinical: Children are noted to be unsteady when they start to walk (usually between 1 and 5 years), then develop progressive leg spasticity, ataxia, dysarthria, nystagmus and distal amyotrophy. The mix of pyramidal signs (brisk knees, Babinski) with lost ankle reflexes is typical, and pes cavus, hammer toes, distal wasting and reduced vibration sense accumulate as the neuropathy advances. Urinary urgency, mitral valve prolapse and thinning of the cervical cord are additional reported features; cognition is usually normal, though some have mild learning difficulties. Hypermyelinated retinal fibres are common in Quebec but often absent in patients from Asia and elsewhere, and many such children are first labelled as spastic diplegic cerebral palsy. Later-onset forms may resemble spastic paraplegia or a pure neuropathy.
det.diagnosis: Look for the triad of early cerebellar ataxia, lower-limb spasticity and sensorimotor neuropathy, with retinal nerve fibre thickening as a bonus finding. Nerve conduction typically shows prolonged distal motor latencies and slowed motor velocities with absent or tiny sensory potentials; ARSACS and Refsum disease are the recessive ataxias in which a demyelinating component is prominent, unlike the axonal sensory neuropathy of Friedreich ataxia. MRI shows atrophy of the upper vermis with the lower vermis relatively spared, linear T2/FLAIR dark bands across the pons, thick middle cerebellar peduncles and later cervical cord thinning, while the cerebral white matter stays normal; OCT is a cheap bedside supplement. Screening tests that rule out mimics — AFP, albumin, cholesterol, vitamin E, echocardiography and frataxin repeat testing — are normal. Confirm with SACS testing, including copy-number analysis since deletions occur.
det.treatment: There is no disease-modifying therapy; management is supportive: physiotherapy, stretching, antispasticity drugs or botulinum toxin for focal spasticity, ankle–foot orthoses, and orthopaedic care for foot deformity. Muscle coenzyme Q10 may be secondarily reduced in ARSACS, but high-dose CoQ10 given to affected patients has not improved ataxia scores, so it should not be promised as treatment. Bladder symptoms, falls and fractures, and later swallowing need attention. Speech and swallowing assessment and genetic counselling of siblings and parents should be offered.
det.prognosis: Slowly progressive over decades; most patients need a wheelchair somewhere between their 30s and 50s, and survival into the sixth or seventh decade is typical.
pearls: Spastic + ataxic + absent ankle jerks + thick retinal fibres: ARSACS.
Pontine 'stripes' on T2 MRI are a strong clue.
OCT is an inexpensive screening test before genetic confirmation.
A normal fundus does not exclude ARSACS outside Quebec; low muscle CoQ10 here is secondary and does not predict a response to supplements.
