det.patho: Most adult infections start with colonisation of the nasopharynx; encapsulated strains then enter the blood, resist complement and slip across the choroid plexus or brain capillaries into CSF, a space with little antibody or complement defence. Bacterial lysis releases wall components that drive a cytokine- and complement-led inflammatory storm, and it is this host reaction that produces brain swelling, failed autoregulation, arteritis, cortical vein and sinus thrombosis and hydrocephalus. Pneumococcus and meningococcus account for most adult cases; Listeria monocytogenes becomes important beyond about 50, in pregnancy, alcohol misuse and impaired T-cell immunity, while staphylococci and Gram-negative rods dominate after neurosurgery or shunting. Across South-East Asia, including Thailand, Streptococcus suis caught from raw pork dishes or handling pigs is a major adult cause and very often leaves permanent deafness.
det.clinical: Illness usually builds over hours to a day or two, but older or immunosuppressed people can drift in over several days with confusion as the main sign. The full fever–stiff neck–altered mentation triad is present in fewer than half, yet almost everyone has at least two of fever, headache, meningism and reduced consciousness; Kernig and Brudzinski signs are seldom positive, so their absence reassures little. A petechial or purpuric rash points to meningococcus but is also seen with pneumococcus and S. suis. Seizures, cranial nerve palsies (especially VIII), arterial or venous infarcts, hydrocephalus, subdural effusion or empyema, ventriculitis and cord infarction can arise at any stage, even after antibiotics finish, so any fresh deterioration needs repeat imaging. Always ask about ear or sinus infection, CSF leak or skull fracture, splenectomy, alcohol, HIV and pork exposure.
det.diagnosis: Draw blood cultures and give antibiotics within the first hour; neither scanning nor LP should hold treatment up. CT before LP is needed only for a GCS below about 12 or falling, focal signs, papilloedema, recent seizures or severe immunosuppression, and LP is deferred in shock, coagulopathy, a fast-spreading rash or skin sepsis at the puncture site. The classic CSF is turbid under high pressure, with hundreds to tens of thousands of mainly neutrophils, CSF:blood glucose below about 0.4 and protein usually above 1 g/L; a CSF lactate near 4 mmol/L or higher, if sampled before antibiotics, strongly favours bacteria over viruses. Gram stain, culture (still needed for susceptibility) and species-specific or multiplex PCR on CSF and EDTA blood identify the organism, and PCR often stays positive for days after antibiotics have sterilised cultures. Partial treatment and Listeria can make the CSF look lymphocytic; offer an HIV test to everyone.
det.treatment: Adult empirical cover is ceftriaxone 2 g IV 12-hourly (or cefotaxime), with vancomycin added where penicillin-resistant pneumococci are a concern, high-dose IV amoxicillin or ampicillin for Listeria in older, pregnant or immunocompromised patients, and acyclovir until HSV encephalitis is excluded; after neurosurgery use vancomycin with an anti-pseudomonal agent such as meropenem or ceftazidime. Dexamethasone 10 mg IV 6-hourly is begun with or just before the first antibiotic and continued for 4 days when pneumococcus is proven or likely, but stopped if another organism is identified. Once the isolate is known, narrow therapy: roughly 5–7 days for meningococcus, 10–14 days for pneumococcus and about 21 days for Listeria. Manage sepsis, seizures, raised pressure, hyponatraemia and fluids in a monitored bed, with ventricular drainage for symptomatic hydrocephalus. Report to public health, give close contacts of meningococcal cases prophylaxis (single-dose ciprofloxacin or rifampicin) and book a hearing test before discharge.
det.prognosis: Adult case fatality is still about 15–20% overall, highest with pneumococcus, older age, coma, seizures and delayed antibiotics; up to half of survivors carry deafness, cognitive slowing or focal deficits.
pearls: Antibiotics first; scan and LP afterwards whenever they would cause delay.
Deafness after meningitis in someone who eats raw pork dishes (e.g. larb or koi): suspect Streptococcus suis.
Fever with a non-blanching rash is meningococcal sepsis until proved otherwise.
A lymphocytic CSF does not rule out bacteria — think Listeria or prior antibiotics.
det.thd: เยื่อหุ้มสมองอักเสบจากแบคทีเรียเป็นภาวะฉุกเฉินที่ต้องให้ยาภายในชั่วโมงแรก เชื้อหลักในผู้ใหญ่คือ pneumococcus และ meningococcus ผู้สูงอายุ หญิงตั้งครรภ์ และผู้ภูมิคุ้มกันต่ำต้องครอบคลุม Listeria ส่วนในไทยต้องนึกถึง Streptococcus suis จากการกินหมูดิบ ซึ่งมักทำให้หูหนวกถาวร อาการคือไข้ ปวดศีรษะ คอแข็ง ซึมสับสน แต่ไม่ครบทุกข้อเสมอ ให้เจาะเลือดเพาะเชื้อแล้วให้ ceftriaxone (± vancomycin, ampicillin, acyclovir) ร่วมกับ dexamethasone ทันที ทำ CT ก่อนเจาะหลังเฉพาะรายที่มีข้อบ่งชี้ น้ำไขสันหลังมี neutrophil สูง น้ำตาลต่ำ โปรตีนสูง ส่ง Gram stain เพาะเชื้อ และ PCR หลังหายควรตรวจการได้ยินและแจ้งควบคุมโรค

name: Bacterial spinal infection
formal: Infections of vertebrae, discs or epidural space (vertebral osteomyelitis, discitis, epidural abscess) causing back pain, fever and risk of cord compression.
simple: A bacterial infection in the spine that causes back pain and fever and can press on the spinal cord.

name: Balance disorders
formal: Disturbances of equilibrium from vestibular, cerebellar, proprioceptive or visual dysfunction, causing unsteadiness, dizziness and falls.
simple: Problems staying steady on the feet, causing dizziness, unsteadiness and falls.

name: Balint syndrome
formal: Triad of simultanagnosia, optic ataxia and oculomotor apraxia from bilateral parieto-occipital lesions, seen in posterior cortical atrophy and watershed infarcts.
simple: Damage to both sides of the back of the brain causing difficulty seeing more than one thing at a time, reaching for objects and directing gaze.

name: Ballism
formal: Violent, large-amplitude flinging movements of proximal limbs, usually unilateral (hemiballismus) from lesions of the contralateral subthalamic nucleus or its connections.
simple: Wild, flinging, uncontrolled movements of the arm or leg, often after damage to a deep brain area.

name: Ballism–chorea
formal: Spectrum of hyperkinetic movements from basal ganglia dysfunction, with ballism as proximal large-amplitude flinging and chorea as distal flowing jerks, often coexisting after subthalamic or striatal lesions.
simple: Uncontrolled flinging and dance-like movements that come from damage to deep brain structures.

name: Baltic myoclonus
formal: Unverricht-Lundborg disease, an autosomal recessive progressive myoclonic epilepsy from CSTB mutation, with stimulus-sensitive myoclonus, tonic-clonic seizures and mild ataxia.
simple: An inherited form of epilepsy with muscle jerks and seizures that starts in childhood and is common in Baltic and Mediterranean regions.

name: Barth syndrome
formal: X-linked mitochondrial disease from TAZ mutation with cardiomyopathy, skeletal myopathy, neutropenia and 3-methylglutaconic aciduria.
simple: An inherited condition in boys causing heart and muscle weakness and low white blood cell counts.

name: Basal cell naevus syndrome
formal: Gorlin syndrome, an autosomal dominant PTCH1 disorder with multiple basal cell carcinomas, jaw keratocysts, medulloblastoma risk, falx calcification and skeletal anomalies.
simple: An inherited condition causing many skin cancers, jaw cysts and an increased chance of a childhood brain tumour.

name: Basal ganglia calcification
formal: Mineral deposits in basal ganglia seen on imaging, either incidental or in Fahr disease (SLC20A2, PDGFRB, XPR1), hypoparathyroidism and infections, causing parkinsonism, dystonia, cognitive decline and psychiatric features.
simple: Calcium deposits in deep parts of the brain that may cause movement problems, memory decline or mood changes.

name: Bassen–Kornzweig syndrome
formal: Abetalipoproteinaemia from MTTP mutation with fat malabsorption, acanthocytosis, retinitis pigmentosa and progressive spinocerebellar degeneration due to vitamin E deficiency.
simple: An inherited disease in which fat and vitamin E cannot be absorbed properly, causing unsteadiness, nerve damage and vision loss.
more: Diagnosis by low or absent cholesterol, triglycerides and vitamin A/E/K with no apoB-containing lipoproteins; blood smear shows acanthocytes. Treat with a low-fat diet and high-dose vitamin E and A supplementation.

name: Batten disease
formal: Neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis, a group of inherited lysosomal storage disorders with progressive visual failure, seizures, dementia and motor deterioration, most often juvenile onset from CLN3 mutations.
simple: An inherited childhood disease causing gradual vision loss, seizures, loss of skills and movement difficulty.

name: Becker muscular dystrophy
formal: X-linked dystrophinopathy with partially functional dystrophin causing later-onset, slower progressive proximal limb weakness, calf hypertrophy and raised creatine kinase.
simple: An inherited muscle disease in males that causes slowly progressing weakness, milder than Duchenne muscular dystrophy.
more: Diagnosed by DMD gene deletion or duplication testing, with muscle biopsy showing reduced, truncated dystrophin on Western blot; reading frame is preserved. Cardiomyopathy surveillance is crucial; steroids are used less consistently than in Duchenne.
th: กล้ามเนื้อเสื่อมเบคเกอร์ — คล้ายดูเชนน์แต่ช้ากว่า เดินได้นาน แต่หัวใจอาจเสียมาก
feat: Males with proximal leg weakness from late childhood to adulthood; still walking after 16
Calf hypertrophy, exercise-induced cramps or myoglobinuria
Dilated cardiomyopathy may dominate and appear before weakness
inv: CK raised; DMD in-frame deletion; reduced (not absent) dystrophin on biopsy
Cardiac surveillance

case.story: Cramps in the calves after football since his teens; recently breathless on exertion.
case.exam: Mild hip weakness, calf hypertrophy.
case.tests: CK 3,200 U/L; echo: dilated left ventricle, EF 35%; in-frame DMD deletion.
case.q: Who else in the family should be offered cardiac screening?
case.a: Female carriers (mother, sisters) — they can develop cardiomyopathy even without weakness.

ddx.pt: Onset by 5, loss of walking by early teens, absent dystrophin
Normal dystrophin, other genes; either sex
Second wind phenomenon, flat lactate on exercise test

aN: bmd | becker dystrophy | becker dystrophinopathy

det.patho: Becker dystrophy results from dystrophin gene mutations, usually in-frame deletions, that permit production of a shortened, partly functional dystrophin. The amount and quality of residual protein broadly determine severity. Cardiac muscle may be disproportionately affected because it receives less protection from the residual protein and has a high workload.
det.clinical: Onset ranges from childhood to adulthood with exercise-induced myalgia, cramps or myoglobinuria, then proximal leg weakness and calf hypertrophy. Patients remain ambulant past 16 and often into adulthood, with a wide range of severity. Dilated cardiomyopathy may be the presenting or dominant problem, sometimes in men with little weakness. Some present only with an incidentally raised CK.
det.diagnosis: CK is raised (moderately to markedly). Genetic testing shows a DMD deletion or duplication that usually preserves the reading frame; muscle biopsy, if done, shows reduced or patchy dystrophin. Exclude LGMD (especially FKRP-related), which can look identical. Echocardiography or cardiac MRI and ECG are needed at diagnosis and periodically.
det.treatment: There is no approved disease-modifying drug; corticosteroids are not routinely used. Management centres on cardiac surveillance and early heart-failure therapy (ACE inhibitors or ARBs, beta blockers, mineralocorticoid antagonists), with heart transplantation for end-stage disease. Physiotherapy, avoidance of extreme eccentric exercise and anaesthetic precautions apply. Female carriers should be offered cardiac screening.
det.prognosis: Life expectancy is reduced mainly by cardiomyopathy, often in middle age; with good cardiac care many live into their 50s or beyond.
pearls: In Becker, the heart can be severely affected even when walking is good.
Exercise-induced cramps and myoglobinuria in a man can be the only early sign.
det.thd: Becker muscular dystrophy เกิดจากการกลายพันธุ์ของยีน dystrophin แบบที่ยังสร้างโปรตีนได้บางส่วน อาการจึงช้ากว่าและเบากว่า Duchenne ผู้ป่วยยังเดินได้หลังอายุ 16 ปี อาจมีปวดหรือเป็นตะคริวหลังออกกำลังกาย น่องโต และ CK สูง ปัญหาสำคัญคือกล้ามเนื้อหัวใจโตผิดปกติ ซึ่งอาจรุนแรงแม้แขนขาจะยังแข็งแรง จึงต้องตรวจหัวใจเป็นระยะ และให้ยารักษาหัวใจล้มเหลวตั้งแต่ระยะแรก รวมถึงตรวจหัวใจในพาหะผู้หญิงด้วย

name: Becker’s disease
formal: Recessive form of myotonia congenita from CLCN1 mutations causing muscle stiffness that eases with exercise, with transient weakness and mild hypertrophy.
simple: An inherited condition in which muscles are stiff after rest but loosen with repeated movement.

name: Behavioral disorders
formal: Abnormalities of conduct, mood or personality that may result from neurological disease such as frontal lobe damage, dementia or epilepsy.
simple: Problems with behaviour or emotions that can be caused by brain disease.

name: Behavioural variant frontotemporal dementia (bvFTD)
formal: Frontotemporal dementia with early personality change, disinhibition, apathy, loss of empathy, compulsive behaviours and executive dysfunction, with frontal or anterior temporal atrophy.
simple: A form of dementia that first changes personality and social behaviour, with apathy, poor judgement and loss of empathy, rather than memory loss.
th: สมองส่วนหน้าเสื่อม — บุคลิกและพฤติกรรมเปลี่ยน ไม่มียั้งคิด เฉยเมย กินมากผิดปกติ มักอายุน้อยกว่า 65
feat: Early disinhibition, apathy, loss of empathy
Compulsive or ritualistic behaviour, hyperorality/sweet craving
Executive dysfunction with relatively spared memory and visuospatial skills
May overlap with ALS (C9orf72)
inv: MRI frontal/anterior temporal atrophy; FDG-PET frontal hypometabolism
Genetics if familial (C9orf72, MAPT, GRN)

case.story: Over a year he has made rude comments to strangers, spent savings impulsively and eats whole jars of sweets.
case.exam: Poor verbal fluency and set-shifting, utilisation behaviour, normal recall.
case.tests: MRI: bilateral frontal and right anterior temporal atrophy.
case.q: Which feature argues against Alzheimer’s disease?
case.a: Prominent behavioural change with relatively preserved episodic memory early.

files.chapter: 9 - Atypical parkinsonism, parkinsonism-­plus syndromes and secondary parkinsonian disorders

ddx.pt: Memory-led onset
Look for fasciculations — FTD-ALS overlap

aN: bvftd | behavioural variant frontotemporal dementia | ftd | pick disease | frontotemporal dementia

det.patho: bvFTD reflects frontotemporal lobar degeneration, most often with TDP-43 or tau inclusions and less often FUS. Up to a third of patients have a family history; the main genes are C9orf72 (hexanucleotide expansion, also causing ALS), MAPT and GRN. It is a leading cause of dementia below 65.
det.clinical: Personality and social conduct change first: disinhibition, tactlessness, loss of sympathy, apathy, compulsive or ritualised routines and a change in eating, with sweet cravings and overeating. Insight is typically absent, so the history must come from family. Memory and visuospatial function are relatively intact early, which can mislead clinicians toward a psychiatric diagnosis. Some patients develop motor neuron disease or parkinsonism; C9orf72 carriers may present with psychosis. Overlap with semantic dementia and progressive non-fluent aphasia is common later.
det.diagnosis: International (Rascovsky) criteria require three of six features — disinhibition, apathy, loss of empathy, perseverative behaviour, hyperorality and a dysexecutive profile — for possible bvFTD, with imaging support for probable disease. MRI shows frontal and/or anterior temporal atrophy, often asymmetric; FDG-PET can reveal hypometabolism when MRI is still normal. Exclude primary psychiatric illness (late-onset bipolar disorder, depression), frontal tumours, AD with a frontal presentation and the bvFTD phenocopy syndrome, which does not progress. Examine for fasciculations and consider EMG and genetic testing.
det.treatment: There is no disease-modifying treatment. SSRIs or trazodone may reduce disinhibition, compulsions and eating changes; cholinesterase inhibitors are not helpful and may worsen behaviour. Antipsychotics are used sparingly for severe agitation. Key work is carer education, legal and financial protection, safety (driving, finances, impulsive spending) and planning support.
det.prognosis: Survival is about 6–11 years from onset and shorter when ALS coexists.
pearls: A middle-aged person with new socially inappropriate behaviour and no insight needs a neurological work-up, not only psychiatric care.
Always look for tongue and limb fasciculations — FTD and ALS lie on one spectrum.
Early MRI can be normal; FDG-PET or repeat imaging helps.
det.thd: bvFTD เป็นสมองเสื่อมจากการเสื่อมของสมองกลีบหน้าและขมับส่วนหน้า มักเริ่มก่อนอายุ 65 อาการเด่นคือบุคลิกเปลี่ยน ขาดการยั้งคิด เฉยเมย ไม่เห็นใจผู้อื่น ทำซ้ำ ๆ และกินหวานมาก ขณะที่ความจำยังดีในระยะแรก ผู้ป่วยมักไม่รู้ตัวจึงต้องซักประวัติจากญาติ MRI หรือ PET เห็นสมองส่วนหน้าฝ่อหรือทำงานลดลง ควรตรวจหา ALS ร่วมและพิจารณาตรวจยีน การรักษาเป็นการประคับประคอง เช่น SSRI และช่วยเหลือผู้ดูแล

name: Behcet’s disease
formal: Multisystem vasculitis with recurrent oral and genital ulcers, uveitis and skin lesions; neuro-Behcet causes brainstem encephalitis, venous sinus thrombosis and meningoencephalitis.
simple: An inflammatory disease causing repeated mouth and genital ulcers and eye inflammation, which can involve the brain.
more: MRI brain may show parenchymal lesions or cerebral venous thrombosis; CSF often shows pleocytosis with raised protein. Treat parenchymal disease with high-dose steroids, azathioprine or infliximab, and avoid ciclosporin, which can worsen neurological disease.

name: Behçet syndrome
formal: Multisystem vasculitis with recurrent oral and genital ulcers, uveitis and skin lesions; neuro-Behcet causes brainstem encephalitis, venous sinus thrombosis and meningoencephalitis.
simple: An inflammatory disease causing repeated mouth and genital ulcers and eye inflammation, which can involve the brain.

name: Behçet’s disease
formal: Multisystem vasculitis with recurrent oral and genital ulcers, uveitis and skin lesions; neuro-Behcet causes brainstem encephalitis, venous sinus thrombosis and meningoencephalitis.
simple: An inflammatory disease causing repeated mouth and genital ulcers and eye inflammation, which can involve the brain.

name: Belly dancer’s dyskinesia
formal: Rhythmic involuntary movements of the abdominal wall, associated with spinal or peripheral nerve lesions, abdominal surgery or radiculopathy, or idiopathic.
simple: Continuous wave-like twitching movements of the belly muscles that the person cannot control.

name: Bell’s palsy
formal: Acute idiopathic unilateral lower motor neuron facial nerve palsy, often with ear pain or taste change, thought to be post-viral, with usual recovery over weeks.
simple: Sudden weakness of one side of the face, often improving over weeks, thought to follow a viral nerve inflammation.
th: เส้นประสาทใบหน้าอ่อนแรงเฉียบพลันข้างเดียว — หน้าเบี้ยวทั้งซีกรวมหน้าผาก หลับตาไม่สนิท
tempoNote: Peaks within 72 hours
feat: Unilateral facial weakness involving the forehead (LMN pattern)
Postauricular pain, hyperacusis, altered taste
Incomplete eye closure with Bell phenomenon
Most recover; early prednisolone improves outcome
inv: Clinical diagnosis; check for vesicles (Ramsay Hunt), bilateral involvement, other cranial nerves
Glucose, BP; imaging if atypical or no recovery by 3–4 months

case.story: Woke up with drooling from the left side of her mouth and inability to close the left eye; ached behind the ear yesterday.
case.exam: Complete left facial weakness including forehead, eyeball rolls up on attempted closure, no ear vesicles, other cranial nerves normal.
case.tests: Glucose normal.
case.q: Why does forehead involvement localise the lesion to the nerve rather than the cortex?
case.a: The upper face receives bilateral cortical input; a cortical (UMN) lesion spares the forehead, whereas a nerve (LMN) lesion paralyses it.

files.chapter: 18. FOCAL NEUROPATHIES: NERVE INJURIES, ENTRAPMENTS, AND OTHER MONONEUROPATHIES

ddx.pt: Vesicles in the ear or palate, vertigo/hearing loss; VZV
Forehead spared, arm weakness or dysarthria
Bilateral facial weakness with limb areflexia
Travel/tick exposure, often bilateral

aN: bell palsy | idiopathic facial palsy | facial nerve palsy | lmn facial palsy | cn vii palsy

det.patho: Idiopathic acute lower motor neuron facial palsy, thought to result mainly from reactivation of herpes simplex virus in the geniculate ganglion, causing inflammation and swelling of the facial nerve within the narrow labyrinthine segment of the facial canal. Risk is higher in pregnancy (third trimester), diabetes and obesity. Annual incidence is roughly 20–30 per 100,000.
det.clinical: Unilateral weakness of upper and lower face develops over hours to 72 hours, often preceded by pain behind the ear. Patients cannot raise the eyebrow, close the eye fully or smile symmetrically, and the eye rolls upward on attempted closure (Bell phenomenon). Taste loss on the anterior tongue, hyperacusis and reduced tearing localise the lesion along the nerve. Red flags include gradual progression beyond 3 weeks, other cranial neuropathies, bilateral palsy, ear vesicles, a parotid mass, recurrent same-side palsy or no recovery by 3–4 months.
det.diagnosis: Bell palsy is a diagnosis of exclusion based on history and examination. Look carefully in the ear and mouth for vesicles (Ramsay Hunt), examine other cranial nerves and the parotid, and check glucose and BP. Laboratory tests and imaging are not routinely needed; MRI with contrast is indicated for atypical features. Electroneurography after the first week helps predict recovery in complete palsy. Bilateral palsy suggests GBS, Lyme disease, sarcoidosis, HIV or leukaemia.
det.treatment: Start oral corticosteroids within 72 hours, e.g. prednisolone 50 mg daily for 10 days or 60 mg daily for 5 days followed by a taper; this increases complete recovery. Adding an antiviral offers at most a small benefit and may be considered in severe palsy. Eye protection is vital: lubricating drops by day, ointment and taping at night, and urgent ophthalmology review if the eye becomes red or painful. Persistent severe weakness or synkinesis may benefit from physiotherapy, botulinum toxin and reanimation surgery.
det.prognosis: About 70% recover fully without treatment and over 80% with steroids; complete palsy, older age and absent early recovery predict incomplete recovery and synkinesis.
pearls: Forehead involved = LMN (nerve) lesion; forehead spared = UMN (central) lesion.
Always look in the ear for vesicles — Ramsay Hunt has a worse prognosis.
Protect the cornea; exposure keratopathy is the main early complication.
det.thd: Bell's palsy คือเส้นประสาทใบหน้า (CN VII) อ่อนแรงเฉียบพลันข้างเดียวโดยไม่ทราบสาเหตุ เชื่อว่าเกิดจากเชื้อ herpes simplex ทำให้เส้นประสาทบวมในช่องกระดูก อาการคือหน้าเบี้ยวทั้งซีกรวมหน้าผาก หลับตาไม่สนิท อาจปวดหลังหู รับรสผิดปกติ และได้ยินเสียงดังผิดปกติ วินิจฉัยโดยแยกสาเหตุอื่นออก เช่น ดูตุ่มน้ำในหู (Ramsay Hunt) และตรวจเส้นประสาทสมองเส้นอื่น รักษาด้วย prednisolone ภายใน 72 ชั่วโมงและปกป้องกระจกตา ส่วนใหญ่หายดี

name: Benedikt’s syndrome
formal: Midbrain tegmental lesion causing ipsilateral third nerve palsy with contralateral tremor, ataxia or involuntary movements from red nucleus involvement.
simple: A brainstem stroke syndrome with a drooping eye on one side and tremor or jerky movement of the opposite arm and leg.

name: Benign adult familial myoclonic epilepsy (BAFME)
formal: Autosomal dominant cortical tremor and myoclonic epilepsy (also FAME) with adult onset tremulous myoclonus, infrequent seizures and photosensitivity, linked to intronic repeat expansions.
simple: An inherited condition causing tremor-like jerks and occasional seizures that start in adulthood and progress slowly.
nN: benign adult familial myoclonic epilepsy bafme
aN: bafme | benign adult familial myoclonic epilepsy

name: Benign hereditary chorea (BHC)
formal: Autosomal dominant NKX2-1 disorder with early-onset non-progressive chorea, mild gait delay and sometimes thyroid and lung abnormalities.
simple: An inherited childhood condition with mild non-worsening jerky movements, sometimes with thyroid or lung problems.
aN: bhc | benign hereditary chorea

name: Benign hereditary myoclonus
formal: Familial myoclonus with early onset, non-progressive course, often alcohol-responsive, with normal cognition and EEG.
simple: An inherited condition of mild muscle jerks that begins in childhood and does not get worse.

name: Benign myoclonus of infancy
formal: Self-limited infantile condition with brief spasms of head and arms during feeding, mimicking infantile spasms but with normal EEG and development.
simple: Harmless brief jerks in a baby, especially during feeding, which stop by themselves.

name: Benign paraproteinaemic neuropathy
formal: Peripheral neuropathy associated with monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (often IgM anti-MAG) producing distal demyelinating sensory-predominant neuropathy with tremor and ataxia.
simple: Nerve damage associated with an abnormal blood protein that is not cancer, causing numbness, imbalance and tremor in the legs and hands.

name: Benign paroxysmal infantile torticollis
formal: Recurrent episodes of head tilt in infants, lasting hours to days, with pallor, irritability or vomiting, and linked to CACNA1A variants and later migraine or vertigo.
simple: Repeated episodes where a baby's head tilts to one side, with fussiness or vomiting, that settle with age.

name: Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV)
formal: Brief positional vertigo from displaced otoconia in the semicircular canals, causing characteristic torsional nystagmus on Dix-Hallpike testing, treated with the Epley manoeuvre.
simple: Short bouts of spinning dizziness when moving the head, caused by tiny crystals in the inner ear.
th: เวียนศีรษะบ้านหมุนเมื่อเปลี่ยนท่าศีรษะ เป็นไม่ถึงนาที — จากหินปูนในหูชั้นใน รักษาด้วยการจัดท่า
tempoNote: Spells of seconds (< 1 min) provoked by head position
feat: Brief rotatory vertigo turning in bed, looking up or bending down
Posterior canal most common
No hearing loss or neurological signs
inv: Dix–Hallpike: latent, torsional-upbeating, fatigable nystagmus
Supine roll test for horizontal canal

case.story: Spinning for 20 seconds whenever she rolls onto her right side in bed.
case.exam: Right Dix–Hallpike: after 3 s latency, upbeating torsional nystagmus toward the right ear lasting 20 s.
case.tests: None needed.
case.q: Treatment?
case.a: Epley canalith repositioning manoeuvre for right posterior canal BPPV.

files.chapter: 19 Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo: A guide to diagnosis and treatment
Chapter 23 Neuro-Otology: Dizziness, Balance and Hearing

ddx.pt: Continuous vertigo for days with spontaneous nystagmus
Minutes–hours of vertigo with migraine features
Attacks of 20 min–hours with fluctuating hearing loss and tinnitus
Central positional nystagmus without latency/fatigue; other brainstem/cerebellar signs

aN: bppv | benign paroxysmal positional vertigo | positional vertigo | canalithiasis

det.patho: Otoconia (calcium carbonate crystals) break loose from the utricular macula and drift into a semicircular canal, most often the posterior canal because it is the lowest part of the labyrinth when lying down. When the head moves in the plane of that canal the free particles sink under gravity and drag endolymph, deflecting the cupula and producing brief vertigo with canal-specific nystagmus (canalithiasis); less often the debris sticks to the cupula itself (cupulolithiasis), giving longer-lasting nystagmus. The posterior canal accounts for roughly 80–90% of cases, the horizontal canal for most of the rest, and the anterior canal is rarely affected. BPPV is the commonest cause of vertigo, with a lifetime prevalence of about 2–3%, a peak between 50 and 70 years and a female excess. Secondary BPPV follows head injury, vestibular neuritis, Ménière disease or prolonged bed rest, and low vitamin D and osteoporosis are associated.
det.clinical: Patients describe short bursts of spinning lasting under a minute, triggered by rolling over in bed, lying down, sitting up, looking up to a shelf or bending forward, often worst on first rising in the morning. Nausea and a lingering sense of unsteadiness may persist between spells, but there is no hearing loss, headache or neurological deficit. Horizontal canal BPPV causes violent vertigo on turning the head to either side while lying supine. Older patients may report only imbalance or falls rather than spinning, so BPPV is under-diagnosed in the elderly. Spells cluster over days to weeks and often relapse months or years later.
det.diagnosis: The Dix–Hallpike manoeuvre for posterior canal BPPV provokes, once a brief delay of seconds has passed, upbeating-torsional nystagmus whose fast phase twists the top of each eye toward the undermost ear, building and fading within a minute, reversing direction on sitting up and lessening with repetition. The supine roll test detects horizontal canal BPPV: geotropic nystagmus (beating toward the ground, from free particles) is stronger when the affected ear is down, whereas apogeotropic nystagmus (from cupular or anterior-arm debris) is stronger when the healthy ear is down. In typical cases neither imaging nor vestibular laboratory testing is needed. Atypical findings — no latency, nystagmus that does not fade, pure downbeat or direction not matching any canal, failure of repeated manoeuvres, or other neurological signs — require MRI to exclude central positional nystagmus from a cerebellar or fourth-ventricle lesion.
det.treatment: Canalith repositioning is curative in most patients: the Epley or Semont manoeuvre for posterior canal BPPV, each clearing about 80% after one or two sessions, and the Lempert (barbecue) roll or Gufoni manoeuvre for horizontal canal BPPV; apogeotropic forms may first need conversion to geotropic. Post-manoeuvre restrictions on posture are not required. Vestibular suppressants have no role beyond brief nausea control, and Brandt–Daroff exercises are less effective than repositioning. Patients with recurrences can be taught self-treatment, older patients should have a falls assessment, and vitamin D supplementation reduces recurrence in those who are deficient. Very rare intractable cases are considered for posterior canal occlusion surgery.
det.prognosis: Most cases resolve with one to three manoeuvres, but about a third to a half recur within a few years, sometimes in a different canal.
pearls: Vertigo lasting seconds on lying down or turning in bed = BPPV until proved otherwise.
Nystagmus without latency, without fatigue or in a non-canal direction is a central warning sign.
Repositioning beats medication — betahistine and antihistamines do not cure BPPV.
Look for BPPV after head injury or vestibular neuritis — it is a common secondary cause of positional vertigo.

name: Benign paroxysmal tonic upgaze and ataxia of childhood
formal: Childhood paroxysmal disorder with intermittent tonic upgaze deviation and ataxia, often CACNA1A related, typically self-limiting with normal development.
simple: A childhood condition where the eyes drift upward in episodes with unsteadiness, usually going away with age.
nN: benign paroxysmal tonic upgaze and ataxia of childhood

name: Benign sleep myoclonus of infancy
formal: Self-limiting repetitive myoclonic jerks during sleep in neonates and infants, with normal EEG and development, disappearing with arousal.
simple: Harmless jerking in a sleeping baby that stops when the baby wakes up.

name: Benign tremulous Parkinson’s disease
formal: Parkinson disease with prominent tremor, slow progression, mild bradykinesia and relatively preserved cognition and gait.
simple: A form of Parkinson disease with mainly tremor that progresses slowly and causes few other problems.

name: Bent spine syndrome (camptocormia)
formal: Marked forward flexion of the trunk when standing, which disappears when lying down, seen in Parkinson disease, axial myopathy, dystonia and ageing.
simple: A stooped forward bend of the upper body when standing or walking that disappears when lying flat.
aN: camptocormia | bent spine syndrome

name: Bent spine/dropped head syndrome
formal: Axial myopathy with weak paraspinal or neck extensor muscles causing camptocormia or head drop, seen in isolated forms, inflammatory myopathy, ALS, myasthenia, and Parkinson disease.
simple: A condition where back or neck muscles are too weak to hold the trunk or head upright, so the spine bends forward.
more: Investigate with EMG, MRI, CK, and biopsy to find the cause. Treat the underlying disease, and use bracing and physiotherapy; response varies by cause.

name: Bethlem myopathy
formal: Collagen VI-related autosomal dominant myopathy with slowly progressive proximal weakness, distal joint hyperlaxity and finger contractures.
simple: An inherited muscle disease causing slowly progressive weakness with stiff finger and elbow joints.
more: Diagnosed by COL6A1, COL6A2 or COL6A3 mutations or collagen VI immunostaining of muscle or skin fibroblasts; CK is normal or mildly raised. MRI shows a rim of fatty change in muscle; management is supportive with contracture care and respiratory monitoring.

name: Biballism
formal: Bilateral ballism with large proximal flinging movements on both sides, usually due to bilateral subthalamic nucleus lesions or metabolic causes.
simple: Wild, uncontrolled flinging movements of limbs on both sides of the body.

name: Bickerstaff brainstem encephalitis
formal: Autoimmune brainstem encephalitis with anti-GQ1b antibodies causing ophthalmoplegia, ataxia and impaired consciousness, belonging to the Miller Fisher-Guillain-Barre spectrum.
simple: An immune illness after infection causing drowsiness, unsteady walking and weakness of eye movements.

name: Bilateral optic neuritis
formal: Inflammation of both optic nerves causing subacute visual loss with pain on eye movement, seen in neuromyelitis optica, MOGAD, MS, ADEM and post-infectious syndromes.
simple: Inflammation of the nerves from both eyes, causing blurry vision, painful eye movement and reduced colour vision.

name: Bilateral vestibular failure (BVF)
formal: Loss of vestibular function on both sides, causing oscillopsia, unsteadiness worse in the dark and a positive head impulse test, from ototoxins, meningitis or idiopathic causes.
simple: Loss of balance function in both inner ears, causing unsteadiness and a bouncing view of the world when walking.
aN: bvf | bilateral vestibular failure

name: Bilateral vestibular schwannoma
formal: Hallmark of neurofibromatosis type 2 with bilateral eighth nerve tumours causing progressive hearing loss, tinnitus and imbalance, often with meningiomas and spinal ependymomas.
simple: Tumours on both hearing and balance nerves, typical of an inherited condition called neurofibromatosis type 2.

name: Bindearmchorea
formal: Historical term for the large proximal wing-beating tremor due to lesions of the superior cerebellar peduncle (brachium conjunctivum) or red nucleus.
simple: An old name for severe coarse, flinging tremor of the arms due to damage to a cerebellar pathway.

name: Binswanger’s disease
formal: Subcortical arteriosclerotic leukoencephalopathy with hypertensive small vessel disease, white matter lesions and lacunes causing slowly progressive dementia, gait disturbance and pseudobulbar signs.
simple: A form of dementia caused by long-term damage to small brain vessels, with slow thinking, trouble walking and mood changes.
more: MRI shows periventricular and deep white matter T2 hyperintensities sparing U-fibres, with lacunes and microbleeds; CADASIL and amyloid angiopathy should be considered. Control blood pressure and vascular risk factors; no specific therapy exists.

name: Biotin-responsive basal ganglia disease (BBGD)
formal: Autosomal recessive thiamine transporter-2 disorder (SLC19A3) with recurrent encephalopathy, confusion, dysarthria, dystonia and seizures with bilateral caudate and putamen necrosis on MRI.
simple: An inherited childhood brain disease with episodes of confusion, stiffness and seizures that improves with vitamins.
more: Treatment with high-dose biotin and thiamine given early can reverse episodes and prevent disability, and should be lifelong; delays in treatment risk permanent dystonia.
nN: biotin responsive basal ganglia disease bbgd
aN: bbgd | biotin responsive basal ganglia disease

name: Biotin-responsive encephalopathy
formal: Subacute encephalopathy with confusion, seizures, dysarthria and dystonia from SLC19A3 mutation with bilateral basal ganglia necrosis, responsive to biotin and thiamine.
simple: An inherited illness causing episodes of confusion, seizures and abnormal movements that improves with vitamin treatment.

name: Bismuth encephalopathy
formal: Reversible encephalopathy from chronic bismuth subsalicylate exposure with confusion, myoclonus, ataxia, tremor and speech disturbance.
simple: Confusion, jerking and balance problems caused by excess bismuth-containing medicines, usually reversible.

name: Bismuth toxicity
formal: Toxic accumulation from excessive bismuth compounds causing encephalopathy, myoclonus, tremor and renal impairment.
simple: Harmful effects of too much bismuth medicine, including confusion, tremor and muscle jerks.

name: Blepharospasm
formal: Focal dystonia of orbicularis oculi causing involuntary forceful eyelid closure, often idiopathic in middle-aged women and treated with botulinum toxin.
simple: Uncontrolled, forceful blinking and eyelid closing that can make the person functionally blind.

name: Bobble-head doll syndrome
formal: Rhythmic anteroposterior head nodding at 2 to 3 Hz, suppressed by voluntary effort or sleep, associated with third ventricle cysts, hydrocephalus and cerebellar lesions.
simple: A rare condition in children with slow, constant head nodding, sometimes linked to a fluid-filled cyst in the brain.

name: Bodily distress disorder
formal: Mental health condition with persistent distressing bodily symptoms and excessive attention to them, in the ICD-11 classification, often presenting to neurology as functional disorders.
simple: A condition where a person has ongoing physical symptoms that cause great worry, without a clear physical cause.

name: Border-zone infarction
formal: Ischaemic stroke in watershed territory between major arteries, usually from hypoperfusion or microembolism, causing proximal limb weakness (man-in-a-barrel) or visual deficits.
simple: A stroke in areas at the edge between two blood vessel regions, often caused by a drop in blood pressure.
th: สมองขาดเลือดบริเวณรอยต่อระหว่างเขตหลอดเลือดใหญ่ (cortical) หรือระหว่างแขนงลึกกับแขนงผิว (internal) มักเกิดเมื่อความดันเลือดตกร่วมกับหลอดเลือดแดงใหญ่ตีบ หรือจาก microemboli
tempoNote: Sudden, often on standing, after cardiac surgery, arrhythmia, dehydration or over-treatment of BP; may stutter with repeated hypotensive episodes
feat: Cortical (external) border zones: ACA–MCA gives proximal arm and shoulder weakness ('man-in-a-barrel' when bilateral); MCA–PCA gives visual and parieto-occipital deficits
Internal border zone: chain of small infarcts in centrum semiovale/corona radiata, often with fluctuating hemiparesis
Transcortical motor or sensory aphasia from anterior or posterior border-zone infarcts in the dominant hemisphere
Precipitant: hypotension, cardiac arrest, bypass surgery, haemodialysis, aggressive antihypertensives
Usually severe ipsilateral ICA stenosis/occlusion when unilateral
inv: MRI DWI: wedge-shaped cortical strips or a rosary-like row of deep lesions between territories
CTA/MRA/duplex for ipsilateral carotid or MCA stenosis/occlusion
CT or MR perfusion: prolonged transit time in the affected hemisphere

case.who: 74-year-old man from Lampang with known left ICA occlusion
case.story: Started on three new BP tablets last week; this morning he stood up quickly, felt faint, then noticed his right shoulder and hip were weak and his words came out slowly.
case.exam: BP 98/60 lying. Right proximal arm weakness more than hand, mild right leg weakness, sparse speech with preserved repetition.
case.tests: MRI DWI: string of small lesions in the left corona radiata and a cortical strip between ACA and MCA territories; CTA confirms left ICA occlusion.
case.q: What is the mechanism and the immediate management?
case.a: Haemodynamic border-zone infarction distal to an occluded ICA; stop excess antihypertensives, hydrate, keep the patient flat and allow higher BP.

det.patho: Distal fields between two arterial supplies sit at the end of each tree and receive the lowest perfusion pressure, so when systemic pressure falls or a proximal artery is severely narrowed or occluded with poor collaterals, these zones fail first. Cortical (external) border zones lie between the ACA, MCA and PCA surface territories; internal (deep) border zones lie in the corona radiata and centrum semiovale between lenticulostriate and medullary penetrators, which are themselves end arteries. Small emboli wash out poorly from low-flow regions, so reduced perfusion and microembolism (from carotid plaque, the heart or a valve) often act together — Caplan's 'impaired washout' concept — and cortical border-zone lesions are more often embolic while internal ones are more strongly tied to haemodynamic failure and early recurrence. Systemic disorders can produce the same pattern: cardiac arrest or bypass surgery, severe anaemia or sickle cell disease, hyperviscosity (polycythaemia, myeloproliferative disease), hypereosinophilic syndrome with microvascular thrombosis, and infective endocarditis with showers of tiny emboli.
det.clinical: Bilateral anterior (ACA–MCA) border-zone infarcts after cardiac arrest or bypass cause proximal arm and shoulder weakness with relatively spared face, hands and legs ('man-in-a-barrel'), sometimes with transcortical motor aphasia when dominant. Posterior (MCA–PCA) border-zone lesions cause visuospatial and visual disturbances such as Balint features, cortical blindness or transcortical sensory aphasia. Internal border-zone infarcts present with hemiparesis that fluctuates or progresses in steps over hours to days and are a warning of exhausted haemodynamic reserve. A unilateral pattern points to ipsilateral ICA or MCA stenosis or occlusion and may be heralded by orthostatic TIAs or limb-shaking TIAs; symptoms that appear on standing, after a meal, during dialysis or with a new antihypertensive and settle lying flat are a strong clue.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis rests on the DWI pattern plus a plausible haemodynamic trigger or vascular lesion: wedge-shaped cortical strips between territories, or a chain ('rosary') of lesions in the centrum semiovale parallel to the lateral ventricle. Map the territories carefully because individual anatomy and collateral supply shift the borders. Image the carotid and intracranial arteries with CTA, MRA or duplex, and use CT or MR perfusion (or cerebrovascular reactivity testing) to demonstrate delayed transit and impaired reserve. Check the blood pressure record and drug chart, fluid balance, haemoglobin and haematocrit, cardiac rhythm and output, and recent anaesthesia or procedures; scattered bilateral border-zone lesions without a large-artery cause should prompt echocardiography and a search for blood disorders such as hypereosinophilia or polycythaemia. Distinguish from global hypoxic-ischaemic injury, which also involves cortex, basal ganglia and hippocampi.
det.treatment: Restore perfusion first: correct hypotension and hypovolaemia, stop or reduce antihypertensives in the acute phase, keep the head flat early if tolerated, treat arrhythmia, anaemia or low cardiac output, and mobilise cautiously while watching for orthostatic worsening. Standard reperfusion treatment (thrombolysis or thrombectomy) applies when there is a qualifying occlusion. For the underlying lesion, offer endarterectomy or stenting for symptomatic carotid stenosis; for symptomatic intracranial stenosis, use intensive medical therapy (short-term dual antiplatelets, high-intensity statin, risk-factor control), since stenting has not beaten medicine and EC–IC bypass has not shown benefit for carotid occlusion in trials. Blood pressure should be lowered gradually over weeks: for symptomatic intracranial stenosis guidelines favour a systolic target below 140 rather than 130 mmHg, because patients with low distal flow did worse when pressure was pushed lower. Treat systemic causes such as hyperviscosity or hypereosinophilia specifically.
det.prognosis: Outcome depends on infarct size and the haemodynamic substrate; internal border-zone infarcts beyond a severe stenosis or occlusion carry a high early risk of progression and recurrence, whereas cortical border-zone infarcts after a single correctable hypotensive episode often have a good outlook.
pearls: Proximal arm and shoulder weakness with hand sparing = ACA–MCA border zone ('man-in-a-barrel' if bilateral).
A rosary of deep white matter infarcts points to haemodynamic failure beyond a carotid or MCA lesion — treat it as an unstable patient.
Check the drug chart and the lying–standing BP: new antihypertensives and dehydration are frequent, reversible triggers.
Bilateral scattered watershed infarcts with no large-artery disease: think microemboli (endocarditis, NBTE) or blood disorders (hyperviscosity, hypereosinophilia).

name: Borderline leprosy
formal: Unstable leprosy classification (BT, BB, BL) with variable nerve involvement, multiple asymmetric skin patches and risk of type 1 reactions with nerve palsy.
simple: An in-between form of leprosy with skin patches and nerve damage that can flare up into painful weakness.

name: Borderline personality disorder
formal: Psychiatric condition with unstable mood, relationships and self-image and impulsivity, commonly encountered in functional and neuropsychiatric presentations.
simple: A mental health condition with intense swings in emotions, unstable relationships and impulsive behaviour.

name: Borderzone infarcts
formal: Watershed infarcts at the junction of major arterial territories (cortical or internal), caused by haemodynamic compromise or microemboli, often with carotid stenosis.
simple: Small strokes in the brain areas at the edge of blood supply zones, often when blood pressure falls.

name: Bourneville’s disease
formal: Tuberous sclerosis complex, an autosomal dominant TSC1 or TSC2 disorder with cortical tubers, subependymal nodules, seizures including infantile spasms, intellectual disability and angiofibromas.
simple: An inherited condition causing benign tumours in the brain and skin, seizures and learning difficulties.

name: Bovine spongiform encephalopathy
formal: Prion disease of cattle caused by misfolded prion protein, transmissible to humans as variant Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease through contaminated beef.
simple: A fatal brain disease of cattle, commonly called mad cow disease, which can cause a similar disease in humans.

name: Boxers’ encephalopathy
formal: Chronic traumatic encephalopathy (dementia pugilistica) from repeated head blows, with cognitive decline, parkinsonism, dysarthria, ataxia and tau deposition.
simple: Long-term brain damage in boxers after repeated head blows, causing memory loss, slurred speech and slowness.

name: Brachial neuritis
formal: Immune-mediated inflammation of the brachial plexus (neuralgic amyotrophy) with sudden severe shoulder pain, then patchy weakness and wasting of upper limb muscles.
simple: Sudden shoulder pain followed by weakness of the arm because of inflammation of the nerves in the shoulder region.
th: เส้นประสาทแขนอักเสบเฉียบพลัน — ปวดไหล่รุนแรงเป็นวันแล้วตามด้วยอ่อนแรงลีบเป็นหย่อม ๆ สะบักยก
tempoNote: Severe pain for days to weeks, then patchy weakness; recovery over months to years
feat: Sudden severe shoulder/arm pain, often at night, sometimes after infection, surgery, vaccination or childbirth
As pain settles: patchy weakness and wasting — serratus anterior (winging), anterior interosseous, suprascapular, axillary
Mild sensory loss; can be bilateral or recurrent (hereditary form: SEPT9)
inv: EMG after 2–3 weeks: multifocal denervation outside a single root or nerve
MRI neurography/ultrasound: nerve hourglass constrictions

case.story: Woke with excruciating right shoulder pain a week after a viral illness; 10 days later the pain eased but he could not lift his arm or pinch.
case.exam: Medial scapular winging, weak shoulder abduction, weak flexion of the thumb tip and index fingertip (cannot make an 'OK' sign), minimal sensory loss.
case.tests: EMG: denervation in serratus anterior, deltoid and flexor pollicis longus; cervical MRI normal.
case.q: Why can't the patient make an 'OK' sign?
case.a: Anterior interosseous nerve involvement — a classic branch affected in neuralgic amyotrophy.

det.patho: Neuralgic amyotrophy is thought to be an immune-mediated inflammation of brachial plexus nerves and branches, triggered by infection, surgery, vaccination, childbirth or strenuous exercise in a genetically or mechanically susceptible person. Pathology shows perivascular inflammation, and imaging can reveal focal hourglass-like constrictions of nerve fascicles. A hereditary form linked to SEPT9 causes recurrent attacks. Incidence is higher than once thought, roughly 1 in 1,000 per year in some estimates.
det.clinical: The illness begins with sudden severe shoulder or arm pain, often at night, unrelieved by usual analgesia and lasting days to weeks. As pain subsides, patchy weakness and wasting appear, commonly affecting the long thoracic nerve (scapular winging), suprascapular, axillary and anterior interosseous nerves, sometimes the phrenic nerve with orthopnoea. Sensory loss is modest and patchy. Bilateral involvement occurs in a minority. A second phase of persistent fatigue and residual pain is common.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical, supported by EMG showing denervation in a patchy distribution that does not fit a single root or nerve, best performed after 2–3 weeks. MRI of the cervical spine excludes radiculopathy; MRI neurography or high-resolution ultrasound may show nerve swelling or constrictions. Check diaphragm movement if breathless lying flat. Exclude rotator cuff disease, cervical radiculopathy, ALS, MMN and Pancoast tumour.
det.treatment: Adequate pain relief is the immediate priority, often requiring a combination of NSAID and a long-acting opioid. A short course of oral corticosteroids in the first weeks may shorten pain and speed recovery, although evidence is limited. Rehabilitation focuses on scapular stability and compensatory movement patterns; surgery (neurolysis or nerve transfer) is considered for constrictions without recovery.
det.prognosis: Most patients improve over 1–3 years, but many have residual weakness, pain or fatigue. Recurrence is common in hereditary forms.
pearls: Severe pain then weakness as pain fades — the sequence is the clue.
Isolated anterior interosseous or long thoracic palsy without trauma: think neuralgic amyotrophy.
Ask about orthopnoea: phrenic nerve involvement is under-recognised.
