name: Brachial plexopathies
formal: Disorders of the brachial plexus from trauma, tumour infiltration, radiation, inflammation or thoracic outlet compression, causing arm weakness, sensory loss and pain.
simple: Damage to the network of nerves between the neck and arm causing arm weakness, numbness and pain.
more: Diagnose with EMG, nerve conduction and MRI plexus imaging; radiation plexopathy shows myokymia whereas tumour infiltration is painful. Treat the cause, with analgesia, physiotherapy and surgical repair for traumatic avulsions in the early months.

name: Brachial plexopathy
formal: Lesion of the brachial plexus from trauma, neuralgic amyotrophy, tumour, radiation, or other causes, with pattern of weakness and sensory loss matching trunk, cord, or branch involvement.
simple: Damage to the network of nerves in the shoulder that supply the arm, causing weakness, pain, and numbness.
more: MRI and EMG define the site and cause. Treatment depends on the cause: surgery for trauma, steroids for inflammatory forms, and rehabilitation.

name: Brain abscess
formal: Focal suppurative collection in brain parenchyma from contiguous infection, haematogenous spread or trauma, presenting with headache, fever, seizures and focal deficits, with ring-enhancing lesion on imaging.
simple: A pocket of pus in the brain due to infection, causing headache, fever, seizures and weakness.

name: Brain tumor
formal: Intracranial neoplasm, primary or metastatic, presenting with progressive headache, seizures, focal deficits or raised intracranial pressure.
simple: An abnormal growth of cells in or around the brain that may cause headache, seizures or weakness.

name: Brain tumour
formal: Intracranial neoplasm, primary or metastatic, presenting with progressive headache, seizures, focal deficits or raised intracranial pressure.
simple: An abnormal growth of cells in or around the brain that may cause headache, seizures or weakness.

name: Brainstem encephalitis
formal: Inflammation of the brainstem from infection (Listeria, enterovirus 71, herpes), autoimmune or paraneoplastic causes, with cranial neuropathies, ataxia and altered consciousness.
simple: Inflammation of the brainstem causing double vision, trouble swallowing, unsteadiness and drowsiness.

name: Brainstem encephalitis in adults
formal: Brainstem inflammation in adults from Listeria, viruses, Behcet disease, anti-GQ1b antibodies or paraneoplastic causes, with ophthalmoplegia, ataxia and long tract signs.
simple: Inflammation of the lower brain in adults, often from infection or immune disease, causing double vision, unsteadiness and weakness.

name: Brainstem meningoencephalitis
formal: Infectious inflammation of the brainstem and meninges, typically Listeria or viral, causing fever, cranial nerve palsies, ataxia and drowsiness.
simple: Infection of the lower brain and its coverings, causing fever, double vision, unsteady walking and drowsiness.

name: Brainstem myoclonus
formal: Myoclonus generated in the brainstem, including startle syndromes (hyperekplexia) and reticular reflex myoclonus, with generalised jerks propagating up and down the neuraxis.
simple: Sudden whole-body or facial jerks arising from the lower part of the brain, often provoked by sound or touch.

name: Brainstem reticular myoclonus
formal: Generalised myoclonus originating in the brainstem reticular formation, with jerks spreading caudally and rostrally, often provoked by action or stimuli after hypoxic injury.
simple: Sudden body jerks that start in the brainstem and spread, sometimes after oxygen deprivation to the brain.

name: Breughel’s syndrome
formal: Combination of blepharospasm and oromandibular dystonia, a segmental cranial dystonia named after a painting.
simple: Combined involuntary eyelid closing and jaw or mouth spasms.

name: Broca’s aphasia
formal: Non-fluent aphasia with effortful agrammatic speech and impaired repetition but relatively preserved comprehension, from left inferior frontal lesions.
simple: Difficulty producing speech, with slow effortful short phrases, though understanding is mostly preserved, after damage to the left frontal brain.

name: Brody disease
formal: Autosomal recessive exercise-induced muscle stiffness from ATP2A1 mutation affecting SERCA1 calcium pump, causing painless delayed relaxation with electrically silent cramp.
simple: An inherited problem where muscles become stiff and slow to relax after exercise, especially in the cold.
more: Diagnosed by ATP2A1 testing and reduced SERCA1 activity; EMG is silent during stiffness. Dantrolene may help; it is generally non-progressive.

name: Brown–Séquard syndrome
formal: Hemisection of the spinal cord with ipsilateral weakness and loss of proprioception and vibration, and contralateral loss of pain and temperature below the lesion.
simple: Damage to one half of the spinal cord, causing weakness and loss of position sense on one side and loss of pain and temperature sense on the other.

name: Brown–Vialetto–Van Laere syndrome
formal: Riboflavin transporter deficiency neuronopathy from SLC52A2 or SLC52A3 mutations with progressive bulbar palsy, sensorineural deafness, respiratory compromise and motor weakness; responsive to riboflavin.
simple: An inherited condition with hearing loss, weakness of face and throat muscles and breathing difficulty, which can improve with vitamin B2.
th: โรคพันธุกรรมขนส่งไรโบฟลาวิน — หูหนวก กลืนพูดลำบาก แขนลีบในเด็ก/วัยรุ่น รักษาได้ด้วยวิตามินบี 2 ขนาดสูง
feat: Childhood or adolescent onset of sensorineural deafness
Progressive bulbar palsy, facial weakness, tongue wasting; respiratory failure
Arm and neck weakness; some have sensory ataxia and optic atrophy
inv: SLC52A2 / SLC52A3 genetic testing; acylcarnitine profile may be abnormal
EMG: neurogenic change; audiometry

case.story: Gradual hearing loss from age 8, now nasal speech and difficulty swallowing; neck feels weak.
case.exam: Bilateral sensorineural deafness, facial weakness, wasted fasciculating tongue, weak neck flexors and shoulders.
case.tests: EMG: active denervation in bulbar and cervical muscles; SLC52A3 variants.
case.q: Why must treatment start before genetic confirmation?
case.a: High-dose riboflavin is safe and can halt or reverse the disease; delays allow irreversible respiratory and bulbar failure.

read.where: Chapter 27 Brown Vialetto Van Laere syndrome, pp. 391–402

files.chapter: Chapter 27: Brown Vialetto Van Laere [BVVL] Syndrome
Chapter 15 Disorders of the Motor Cells: The Motor Neuron Diseases
15: Approach to the Differential Diagnosis of Hypotonia in Infancy

ddx.pt: Adult, no deafness, UMN signs
Adult male, gynaecomastia, AR expansion
Fatigable bulbar weakness without wasting or deafness

aN: bvvl | riboflavin transporter deficiency | rtd | slc52a3 | slc52a2 | fazio londe

det.patho: BVVL is an autosomal recessive riboflavin transporter deficiency caused by mutations in SLC52A3 (RFVT3) or SLC52A2 (RFVT2). Reduced riboflavin uptake impairs flavin-dependent mitochondrial enzymes, including fatty acid oxidation and the respiratory chain. Cochlear neurons, cranial nerve motor nuclei, anterior horn cells, sensory neurons and optic nerves are especially vulnerable. Fazio–Londe disease, its counterpart without deafness, belongs to the same spectrum.
det.clinical: Progressive sensorineural hearing loss usually comes first in childhood or adolescence, followed by bulbar palsy with dysarthria, dysphagia, facial weakness and tongue fasciculations. Neck and shoulder weakness, often with a 'dropped head', and respiratory failure from diaphragmatic weakness may follow. SLC52A2 cases more often have sensory ataxia, optic atrophy, nystagmus and prominent upper limb weakness. Infantile forms can be rapidly fatal.
det.diagnosis: Genetic testing for SLC52A2 and SLC52A3 confirms the diagnosis. Plasma acylcarnitine and urine organic acid profiles may show a MADD-like pattern, though they can be normal. EMG shows neurogenic changes in bulbar and limb muscles, NCS may show a sensory neuronopathy, and audiometry documents hearing loss. Consider in any young patient with deafness and motor neuron disease features.
det.treatment: Start high-dose oral riboflavin immediately when the diagnosis is suspected, without waiting for genetic results; it is inexpensive and safe. Supportive care includes respiratory support, gastrostomy, hearing aids or cochlear implants, and physiotherapy. Families should be offered genetic counselling.
det.prognosis: Early riboflavin can stabilise or improve motor, bulbar and respiratory function; hearing loss responds less consistently. Untreated disease often leads to respiratory failure.
pearls: Childhood deafness + bulbar palsy + neck weakness = give riboflavin now.
This is one of the few treatable causes of motor neuron disease in the young.
det.thd: Brown–Vialetto–Van Laere syndrome เป็นโรคพันธุกรรมแบบยีนด้อยจากความผิดปกติของตัวขนส่งไรโบฟลาวิน (วิตามินบี 2) ทำให้เซลล์ประสาทหลายกลุ่มเสื่อม อาการเริ่มด้วยหูหนวกในเด็กหรือวัยรุ่น ตามด้วยพูดและกลืนลำบาก ลิ้นลีบ คอและไหล่อ่อนแรง และอาจหายใจไม่ได้ การวินิจฉัยใช้การตรวจยีน SLC52A2/SLC52A3 ส่วนการรักษาคือให้ riboflavin ขนาดสูงทางปากทันทีที่สงสัย โดยไม่ต้องรอผลยีน เพราะช่วยหยุดหรือฟื้นอาการได้

name: Bucco-linguo-masticatory (BLM)
formal: Repetitive involuntary chewing, tongue and lip movements, most often tardive dyskinesia after dopamine-blocking drugs or edentulous orofacial dyskinesia in older people.
simple: Repeated uncontrolled chewing, lip smacking and tongue movements, often from long-term use of certain medicines.
aN: blm | bucco linguo masticatory

name: Bulbar palsy
formal: Lower motor neuron weakness of cranial nerves IX to XII muscles causing dysarthria, dysphagia, tongue wasting and fasciculation, seen in ALS, brainstem lesions and myasthenia.
simple: Weakness of the muscles of the tongue, throat and mouth, causing slurred speech and trouble swallowing.

name: Burning mouth syndrome
formal: Chronic idiopathic intraoral burning pain with normal mucosa, usually in peri/postmenopausal women; thought to reflect small-fibre or central pain mechanisms; exclude secondary causes first.
simple: A long-lasting burning feeling in the mouth or tongue even though the mouth looks normal.

name: C5 radiculopathy
formal: Compression of the C5 nerve root, usually at C4-5, causing neck and shoulder pain with weakness of deltoid and biceps, reduced biceps reflex, and lateral shoulder sensory loss.
simple: A pinched nerve in the neck causing pain and weakness lifting the arm to the side.
more: MRI and EMG confirm it. Most improve with conservative care; surgery is used for severe or persistent deficits.

name: C6 radiculopathy
formal: Compression of the C6 root, commonly from C5-6 disc or spondylosis, causing weakness of biceps, brachioradialis, and wrist extensors, reduced biceps reflex, and thumb and index paraesthesia.
simple: A pinched nerve in the neck causing pain down the arm into the thumb, with weak elbow bending and wrist lifting.
more: Diagnosed by exam, MRI, and EMG. Usually settles with physiotherapy and analgesia; surgery for refractory pain or progressive weakness.

name: C7 radiculopathy
formal: Most common cervical radiculopathy from C6-7 disease, with triceps, wrist flexor, and finger extensor weakness, reduced triceps reflex, and middle finger paraesthesia.
simple: A pinched nerve in the neck causing pain and weakness when straightening the arm, with tingling in the middle finger.
more: MRI and EMG confirm it. Conservative treatment helps most; surgery if severe weakness or myelopathy occurs.

name: C8/T1 radiculopathy
formal: Lower cervical root compression causing weakness and wasting of finger flexors and hand intrinsics with medial forearm and hand sensory loss, requiring differentiation from ulnar neuropathy and thoracic outlet.
simple: A pinched nerve low in the neck causing a weak, numb hand and small hand muscle wasting along the little finger side.
more: EMG shows involvement outside ulnar-innervated muscles; MRI looks for disc, tumour, or Pancoast lesion. Treatment depends on the cause.

name: Caffeine-related headache
formal: Headache triggered by caffeine intake or by withdrawal after regular use, typically diffuse and pressing or migrainous, resolving after stable intake or abstinence.
simple: A headache caused by too much caffeine or by suddenly stopping usual caffeine.

name: Caisson disease
formal: Decompression sickness from nitrogen bubbles after rapid pressure drop; spinal cord (thoracolumbar) and inner ear are commonly involved, with pain, weakness and vertigo.
simple: Illness in divers or compressed-air workers when gas bubbles form in the body after surfacing too fast, which can affect nerves and the spinal cord.

name: Calcification of basal ganglia
formal: Symmetric calcium deposits in basal ganglia, dentate and cortex (primary familial brain calcification or secondary to hypoparathyroidism); presents with parkinsonism, dystonia, cognitive and psychiatric change.
simple: Calcium builds up in deep brain areas, which can cause movement problems, memory change and mood symptoms.

name: Calcium channelopathies
formal: Disorders of voltage-gated calcium channels such as CACNA1S hypokalaemic periodic paralysis, CACNA1A episodic ataxia type 2 and migraine, and malignant hyperthermia susceptibility.
simple: Inherited conditions where faulty calcium channels cause episodes of muscle weakness, unsteadiness, or other attacks.
more: Genetic testing identifies the variant. Acetazolamide helps periodic paralysis and episodic ataxia; avoid triggers and triggering anaesthetics when relevant.

name: Calcium deficiency
formal: Hypocalcaemia causing neuromuscular irritability: perioral paraesthesia, tetany, Chvostek and Trousseau signs, seizures and prolonged QT.
simple: Low blood calcium, causing tingling around the mouth, muscle spasms and sometimes seizures.

name: Calpainopathy (LGMD R1/2A)
formal: Autosomal recessive limb-girdle muscular dystrophy from CAPN3 mutations with proximal pelvic and shoulder girdle weakness, scapular winging, and contractures.
simple: An inherited muscle disease that slowly weakens muscles around the hips and shoulders.
aN: lgmd r1 | 2a | calpainopathy

name: Camptocormia (bent spine syndrome)
formal: Marked involuntary forward flexion of the trunk when standing or walking that disappears when lying; seen in parkinsonism, axial myopathy and idiopathic paraspinal myopathy.
simple: A stooped, bent-forward posture of the back that appears when standing or walking and eases when lying down.
aN: bent spine syndrome | camptocormia

name: CAP disease
formal: Rare congenital myopathy defined by peripheral caps of disorganised sarcomeres under the sarcolemma, caused by TPM2, TPM3, or ACTA1 mutations, with hypotonia, weakness, and respiratory problems.
simple: A rare inherited muscle disease present from early life, causing floppiness and weakness.
more: Biopsy shows subsarcolemmal caps lacking myofibrillar ATPase. Care is supportive, focusing on breathing, swallowing, and scoliosis; severity varies.

name: CAR T cell neurotoxicity
formal: Immune effector cell neurotoxicity after CAR T therapy with encephalopathy, aphasia, tremor and seizures, often following cytokine release syndrome; managed with steroids and supportive care.
simple: Confusion, speech trouble or seizures that can occur after a type of immune cell cancer treatment.

name: Carbamate poisoning
formal: Reversible acetylcholinesterase inhibition causing cholinergic crisis with miosis, salivation, bronchorrhoea, fasciculations and weakness; treated with atropine.
simple: Poisoning from certain insecticides that overstimulates nerves, causing small pupils, drooling, muscle twitching and weakness.

name: Carbamyl phosphate synthetase deficiency
formal: Urea cycle disorder causing hyperammonaemia with vomiting, lethargy, seizures and encephalopathy, mainly in neonates; low citrulline and absent orotic acid.
simple: An inherited problem in clearing ammonia from the blood, causing sleepiness, vomiting and seizures.

name: Carbohydrate metabolism disorders
formal: Inherited disorders of sugar metabolism such as galactosaemia and glycogen storage diseases, with hypoglycaemia, hepatomegaly, myopathy or encephalopathy.
simple: A group of inherited conditions in which the body cannot properly handle sugars, which can harm muscles, liver and brain.
more: Detect with newborn screening, urine reducing substances, red cell GALT activity, plasma lactate and muscle biopsy enzymology. Treatment depends on the defect, with galactose exclusion in galactosaemia and diet or enzyme therapy in glycogenoses.

name: Carbon disulphide poisoning
formal: Industrial solvent toxicity causing polyneuropathy, parkinsonism, psychosis and encephalopathy, with basal ganglia and optic nerve involvement.
simple: Poisoning by an industrial chemical that can damage nerves and brain, causing weakness, tremor and mood changes.

name: Carbon monoxide poisoning
formal: Hypoxic poisoning from carboxyhaemoglobin with headache, confusion and coma; delayed leukoencephalopathy and bilateral globus pallidus lesions may follow.
simple: Poisoning from breathing carbon monoxide gas, which causes headache, confusion and unconsciousness and can injure the brain.

name: Carbon monoxide toxicity
formal: Toxic brain injury from carbon monoxide exposure causing tissue hypoxia, with acute encephalopathy and possible delayed cognitive and parkinsonian sequelae.
simple: Brain harm caused by breathing carbon monoxide, which stops blood carrying oxygen properly.

name: Carbon tetrachloride poisoning
formal: Solvent poisoning causing hepatorenal toxicity plus headache, confusion, coma and sometimes peripheral neuropathy or optic neuritis.
simple: Poisoning by a cleaning solvent that damages the liver and kidneys and can cause confusion and nerve damage.

name: Cardioencephalomyopathy
formal: Multisystem mitochondrial disorder with heart, brain and muscle involvement, such as cytochrome oxidase deficiency from SCO2 variants, with infantile hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and lactic acidosis.
simple: A severe inherited energy disease affecting the heart, brain and muscles in infants.
more: Genetic testing and enzyme studies make the diagnosis. No cure and treatment is supportive; prognosis is poor.

name: Cardiomyopathies
formal: Primary heart muscle diseases that can cause cardioembolic stroke, syncope and arrhythmia; also associated with neuromuscular diseases such as dystrophies and Friedreich ataxia.
simple: Diseases of the heart muscle that can send clots to the brain or occur together with some muscle and nerve diseases.

name: Cardiomyopathy
formal: Primary disease of heart muscle, dilated, hypertrophic or restrictive, which is often present in neuromuscular disorders such as muscular dystrophies, Friedreich ataxia and mitochondrial disease.
simple: A disease of the heart muscle that weakens the heart, often seen alongside inherited muscle and nerve diseases.
more: Echocardiography, cardiac MRI and ECG monitor it. Treat with ACE inhibitors, beta-blockers and devices; screening is routine in dystrophies.

name: Cardiovascular autonomic failure
formal: Failure of autonomic cardiovascular regulation causing orthostatic hypotension and abnormal heart rate control; seen in MSA, pure autonomic failure and neuropathies.
simple: Failure of the nerves that control blood pressure and heart rate, causing dizziness or fainting on standing.

name: Carnitine palmitoyl transferase II (CPT-II) deficiency
formal: Autosomal recessive disorder of long-chain fatty acid oxidation causing exercise-, fasting- or illness-induced myalgia and rhabdomyolysis with myoglobinuria.
simple: An inherited problem burning fat for energy that causes muscle pain and breakdown after exercise or fasting.
th: สาเหตุพันธุกรรมที่พบบ่อยที่สุดของกล้ามเนื้อสลายซ้ำในผู้ใหญ่ — เกิดหลังออกกำลังนาน อดอาหาร หรือมีไข้
tempoNote: Attacks follow prolonged exertion, fasting, infection or cold; normal between episodes
feat: Recurrent myalgia and myoglobinuria after long-duration exercise rather than brief bursts
Provoked by fasting, fever, cold, general anaesthesia or certain drugs (valproate, ibuprofen in high doses)
Normal strength and usually normal CK between attacks
No second-wind phenomenon (unlike McArdle)
inv: CK and renal function during attacks
Plasma acylcarnitine profile (raised long-chain C16, C18:1) — may be normal between episodes
CPT2 gene sequencing (S113L common); enzyme assay in muscle or fibroblasts if needed

case.story: Third episode of dark urine: first after a marathon, second during dengue fever, now after skipping meals during a long hike.
case.exam: Tender calves and thighs, mild weakness; neurologically normal between episodes per old records.
case.tests: CK 62,000 U/L; acylcarnitines show raised C16 and C18:1; homozygous CPT2 S113L.
case.q: What practical advice prevents further attacks?
case.a: Avoid prolonged fasting and exhausting exercise, eat carbohydrates before and during exertion, treat fever early, and alert anaesthetists; some benefit from triheptanoin or a high-carbohydrate, lower-fat diet.

det.patho: CPT2 on the inner mitochondrial membrane converts long-chain acylcarnitines back into acyl-CoA for beta-oxidation. Partial deficiency, as in the adult myopathic form, limits fatty-acid fuel when muscle depends on it—during prolonged exercise, fasting or fever—so energy failure and fibre breakdown follow. Inheritance is autosomal recessive; the S113L variant is common in European populations, while other variants are found in Asia. Severe neonatal and infantile forms are multisystemic.
det.clinical: The adult form produces episodes of muscle pain, stiffness, weakness and myoglobinuria, typically starting in adolescence or early adulthood. Exercise tolerance for short bursts is normal; endurance activity is the problem. Some attacks occur with no clear trigger or with viral illness. Acute kidney injury is the main danger, and respiratory muscle involvement is occasionally reported.
det.diagnosis: Suspect CPT2 deficiency in recurrent rhabdomyolysis linked to prolonged activity, fasting or fever, with normal CK between attacks. Acylcarnitine profiling, ideally during or soon after an attack or after fasting, shows increased long-chain species. Genetic testing confirms; enzyme assay is used if only one variant is found. Muscle biopsy is often normal and may not show lipid storage.
det.treatment: Acute attacks are treated as rhabdomyolysis with IV fluids plus intravenous glucose to suppress fat oxidation. Prevention focuses on regular carbohydrate intake, avoiding prolonged fasting and exhausting exertion, early treatment of fever, and an emergency letter for hospitals. Triheptanoin or medium-chain triglycerides may help some patients; avoid valproate and prolonged fasting before surgery.
det.prognosis: The adult form has good long-term prognosis if renal failure is avoided; attacks often become less frequent with lifestyle adaptation.
pearls: Long exertion, fasting, fever = CPT2; short intense effort with second wind = McArdle.
Normal CK and biopsy between attacks do not exclude the diagnosis.
Give IV glucose during attacks and perioperatively to prevent fat-dependent energy crises.
det.thd: CPT II deficiency เป็นโรคพันธุกรรมแบบด้อยที่ทำให้กล้ามเนื้อใช้กรดไขมันเป็นพลังงานไม่ได้ จึงเกิดกล้ามเนื้อสลายซ้ำเมื่อออกกำลังเป็นเวลานาน อดอาหาร มีไข้ หรือหนาว ระหว่างอาการกำลังและ CK ปกติ วินิจฉัยด้วย acylcarnitine profile และตรวจยีน CPT2 การรักษาคือให้สารน้ำและกลูโคสขณะเกิดอาการ และป้องกันด้วยการกินคาร์โบไฮเดรตสม่ำเสมอ ไม่อดอาหาร และรักษาไข้เร็ว

ddx.pt: Symptoms within minutes of intense exercise, second wind, high baseline CK
Similar triggers but distinct acylcarnitine pattern (C14:1 elevation)
Triggered by volatile anaesthetics/suxamethonium with rigidity and hyperthermia; RYR1

nN: carnitine palmitoyl transferase ii cpt ii deficiency
aN: cpt ii | carnitine palmitoyl transferase ii deficiency | cpt2 deficiency | cpt ii deficiency | muscle cpt deficiency | myopathic cpt2

name: Carnitine transporter deficiency
formal: Autosomal recessive SLC22A5 defect causing primary systemic carnitine deficiency with hypoketotic hypoglycaemia, cardiomyopathy, and myopathy, due to impaired fatty acid transport.
simple: An inherited inability to move carnitine into cells, which weakens muscles and the heart and can cause low blood sugar.
more: Plasma carnitine is very low; confirm with gene testing. Lifelong oral L-carnitine is very effective at preventing complications.

name: Carpal tunnel syndrome (CTS)
formal: Median nerve entrapment at the wrist causing thumb-to-ring finger paraesthesia, nocturnal symptoms, thenar weakness; confirmed by slowed distal median conduction.
simple: Pressure on a nerve in the wrist that causes numbness, tingling and weakness in the thumb and first fingers.
more: Electrodiagnostic study shows prolonged median sensory and motor latencies with preserved ulnar responses across the wrist; ultrasound shows an enlarged median nerve. Treat with wrist splinting, steroid injection or surgical carpal tunnel release.
th: เส้นประสาท median ถูกกดที่ข้อมือ — ชานิ้วโป้งถึงนิ้วนางครึ่งนิ้ว ปวดชาตอนกลางคืน สะบัดมือแล้วดีขึ้น
feat: Nocturnal paraesthesia in the thumb to radial ring finger; relief by shaking the hand
Sensation over the thenar eminence spared (palmar cutaneous branch leaves before the tunnel)
Late thenar (APB) wasting
Associations: pregnancy, hypothyroidism, diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis, amyloidosis
inv: NCS: prolonged median distal latency, slowed sensory conduction across the wrist
Ultrasound: enlarged median nerve cross-sectional area

case.story: Wakes at night with numb right fingers and shakes her hand to relieve it.
case.exam: Reduced sensation on the thumb, index and middle fingers, normal palm sensation, Phalen positive, mild APB weakness.
case.tests: Median sensory latency prolonged; ulnar normal.
case.q: Why is palm sensation spared?
case.a: The palmar cutaneous branch arises proximal to the carpal tunnel.

files.chapter: 18. FOCAL NEUROPATHIES: NERVE INJURIES, ENTRAPMENTS, AND OTHER MONONEUROPATHIES
2. Entrapment Neuropathies of the Upper Extremity

ddx.pt: Neck pain, reflex change (biceps/triceps), sensory loss extends to forearm
Little and ulnar ring finger, intrinsic hand wasting, Froment sign
Medial forearm sensory loss and thenar wasting (true neurogenic TOS)

aN: cts | carpal tunnel syndrome | median neuropathy at the wrist | carpal tunnel

det.patho: Compression of the median nerve beneath the transverse carpal ligament raises local pressure, impairs epineurial blood flow and leads to focal demyelination, then axonal loss if prolonged. Contributing factors include female sex, obesity, pregnancy, diabetes, hypothyroidism, rheumatoid arthritis, acromegaly, wrist fractures, dialysis and transthyretin amyloidosis (bilateral CTS often predates amyloid cardiomyopathy). It is the most common entrapment neuropathy.
det.clinical: Numbness, tingling and pain affect the thumb, index, middle and radial half of the ring finger, typically waking the patient at night and relieved by shaking the hand (flick sign). Symptoms may be felt more diffusely or radiate to the forearm. Repetitive grip or wrist flexion aggravates them. Advanced cases show thenar wasting and weakness of thumb abduction. The palm over the thenar eminence is spared because its cutaneous branch bypasses the tunnel.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical, supported by provocative tests (Phalen, Tinel, carpal compression) that have moderate accuracy. Nerve conduction studies confirm focal slowing of median sensory and motor fibres across the wrist and grade severity; comparison techniques (median vs ulnar or radial) increase sensitivity. Ultrasound shows an enlarged median nerve cross-sectional area at the tunnel inlet. Consider C6–C7 radiculopathy, proximal median neuropathy, polyneuropathy and thoracic outlet syndrome, which can coexist (double crush).
det.treatment: Mild to moderate cases respond to neutral-position night splinting, activity modification and treatment of underlying conditions; local corticosteroid injection gives short- to medium-term relief. Surgical carpal tunnel release (open or endoscopic) is indicated for persistent symptoms, constant numbness, thenar weakness or wasting, or severe electrodiagnostic changes. Pregnancy-related CTS usually settles after delivery.
det.prognosis: Most improve with conservative care or surgery; advanced axonal loss may leave persistent numbness or weakness.
pearls: Spared palm sensation separates CTS from a more proximal median lesion.
Bilateral CTS in an older man: consider transthyretin amyloidosis.
Neck pain, reflex changes or forearm sensory loss suggest radiculopathy instead.
det.thd: CTS คือเส้นประสาท median ถูกกดที่อุโมงค์ข้อมือ พบบ่อยที่สุดในบรรดาโรคเส้นประสาทถูกกดทับ ปัจจัยเสี่ยงคือเพศหญิง อ้วน ตั้งครรภ์ เบาหวาน ไทรอยด์ต่ำ และ amyloidosis อาการคือชาและปวดนิ้วโป้งถึงครึ่งนิ้วนาง ตื่นกลางดึกแล้วสะบัดมือจึงดีขึ้น ระยะท้ายมีกล้ามเนื้อโคนนิ้วโป้งลีบ ฝ่ามือส่วน thenar ไม่ชาเพราะแขนงประสาทแยกก่อนเข้าอุโมงค์ วินิจฉัยจากอาการร่วมกับ NCS หรืออัลตราซาวด์ รักษาด้วยเฝือกอ่อนตอนกลางคืน ฉีดสเตียรอยด์ และผ่าตัดเมื่ออาการรุนแรงหรือกล้ามเนื้อลีบ

name: Castleman disease
formal: Lymphoproliferative disorder with angiofollicular lymph node hyperplasia, linked to POEMS syndrome with sensorimotor demyelinating neuropathy, high VEGF, and plasma cell dyscrasia.
simple: A rare disease causing enlarged lymph nodes, which can be linked with nerve damage in some patients.
more: Lymph node biopsy diagnoses it. Treatment includes surgery for localised disease and rituximab, siltuximab, or chemotherapy for multicentric disease.

name: Cat scratch disease
formal: Bartonella henselae infection after cat scratch or bite, with regional lymphadenopathy; neurological complications include encephalopathy, neuroretinitis and myelitis.
simple: An infection from a cat scratch causing swollen glands, and rarely brain or eye problems.

name: Cataplexy
formal: Sudden bilateral loss of muscle tone triggered by emotion with preserved consciousness, characteristic of narcolepsy type 1 due to hypocretin deficiency.
simple: Sudden muscle weakness or collapse triggered by strong emotions such as laughter, while staying awake.

name: Catatonia
formal: Psychomotor syndrome with stupor, mutism, posturing, negativism, waxy flexibility or excitement; occurs in psychiatric and medical disorders and responds to benzodiazepines or ECT.
simple: A state in which a person becomes unusually still and unresponsive, or sometimes agitated, and may hold odd postures.

name: Catheter-related infections
formal: Device-associated bloodstream or local infections, including intrathecal or ventricular catheter infection causing meningitis or ventriculitis.
simple: Infections that start from a tube placed in the body, which can sometimes spread to the brain coverings.

name: Cauda equina syndrome
formal: Compression of lumbosacral nerve roots causing saddle anaesthesia, sphincter dysfunction and lower limb weakness with areflexia; a surgical emergency.
simple: Pressure on the nerves at the bottom of the spine causing numbness in the groin and loss of bladder or bowel control.

name: Causalgia and dystonia
formal: Complex regional pain syndrome type 2 after nerve injury with burning pain, autonomic change, and sometimes fixed dystonic posture of the limb.
simple: Severe burning pain after nerve injury, sometimes with painful twisted muscle postures.

name: Cavernous malformation
formal: Cluster of dilated thin-walled vascular channels without intervening brain, causing seizures, haemorrhage or focal deficits; may be familial (CCM1-3).
simple: A cluster of abnormal blood vessels in the brain that can cause seizures or bleeding.
th: กลุ่มหลอดเลือดฝอยขยายผนังบางแบบมีลักษณะคล้ายลูกหม่อน ไม่มีเนื้อสมองคั่น เลือดไหลช้า มักมีเลือดซึมซ้ำ ๆ ทำให้ชักหรืออาการทางระบบประสาทเป็นพัก ๆ เห็นชัดใน MRI (popcorn + วงแหวน haemosiderin) แต่ไม่เห็นใน angiography
tempoNote: Often silent for years; symptomatic bleeds give acute or subacute deficits that improve over weeks, and may cluster
feat: Seizures from supratentorial cortical lesions (most common presentation)
Acute focal deficits from small haemorrhages, especially in brainstem lesions (diplopia, facial numbness, ataxia)
Headache; many lesions found incidentally on MRI
Familial form: multiple lesions, autosomal dominant inheritance
Often adjacent developmental venous anomaly in sporadic cases; may follow cranial radiotherapy
inv: MRI with SWI/GRE: mixed-signal 'popcorn' core with dark haemosiderin rim; SWI reveals additional small lesions
Catheter angiography is usually normal (low-flow lesion)
Genetic testing (KRIT1, CCM2, PDCD10) when multiple lesions or family history
EEG in patients with seizures

case.story: Two days of double vision and numbness of the left face, after a mild headache. A year ago she had similar but briefer symptoms that resolved.
case.exam: Right internuclear ophthalmoplegia, reduced left facial sensation, mild gait ataxia.
case.tests: MRI: 12-mm pontine lesion with mixed signal core, dark rim and fresh blood products; SWI shows three further tiny dark dots in both hemispheres; CTA normal.
case.q: What is the diagnosis and what genetic implication do the extra lesions carry?
case.a: Brainstem cavernous malformation with a recent bleed; multiple lesions suggest familial CCM — test KRIT1/CCM2/PDCD10 and screen relatives with MRI.

read.where: Chapter 12 Subarachnoid hemorrhage, aneurysms and vascular malformations

det.patho: Cavernous malformations are clusters of dilated, thin-walled sinusoidal channels lined by a single endothelial layer without intervening brain. Loss of function in the CCM protein complex (KRIT1/CCM1, CCM2, CCM3/PDCD10) disrupts endothelial junctions through MEKK3–KLF2/4 signalling; familial forms carry a germline mutation plus a second somatic hit, while sporadic lesions often carry somatic PIK3CA and MAP3K3 variants. Repeated low-pressure bleeding produces the haemosiderin rim and lesion growth. They occur in about 0.2–0.5% of people.
det.clinical: Supratentorial lesions present mainly with seizures; brainstem and spinal cord lesions with acute deficits after haemorrhage. Bleeds are small and rarely fatal, but brainstem bleeding causes cumulative disability. Haemorrhage tends to cluster in time, so a recent bleed raises short-term rebleed risk. Familial disease (common in Hispanic families of Mexican descent through a KRIT1 founder) gives multiple lesions, and CCM3 causes the most aggressive phenotype.
det.diagnosis: MRI is diagnostic: a reticulated popcorn lesion with mixed signal and a complete haemosiderin rim on T2, blooming on GRE/SWI. Angiography is normal unless an associated developmental venous anomaly is shown. The Zabramski classification describes MRI types. Multiple lesions prompt genetic testing and family screening; post-radiation cavernomas should be considered in patients treated for childhood tumours.
det.treatment: Asymptomatic lesions are observed. Seizures are treated with anti-seizure medicines; surgical resection, including the haemosiderin ring, is considered for drug-resistant epilepsy and offers good seizure control. Surgery is offered for accessible lesions after symptomatic haemorrhage, especially repeated brainstem bleeds reaching a pial surface. Radiosurgery is controversial. Propranolol and statins are under investigation; antithrombotic drugs are not contraindicated when needed for other reasons. Avoid unnecessary cranial irradiation in familial forms.
det.prognosis: Annual haemorrhage risk is under 1% for incidental lesions but can reach 5–30% for brainstem lesions in the first years after a bleed, falling thereafter.
pearls: Popcorn lesion with a black rim on MRI and a normal angiogram = cavernous malformation.
SWI is the best sequence for counting lesions in familial disease.
Brainstem cavernomas cause step-by-step deficits from repeated small bleeds.
det.thd: Cavernous malformation (cavernoma) คือกลุ่มหลอดเลือดขยายผนังบาง เลือดไหลช้า มักมีเลือดซึมซ้ำ ๆ ทำให้ชัก หรือเกิดอาการทางระบบประสาทเฉียบพลันโดยเฉพาะในก้านสมอง MRI เห็นเป็นรูปคล้ายข้าวโพดคั่วมีวงแหวนดำของ haemosiderin แต่ angiography ปกติ ถ้ามีหลายตำแหน่งให้นึกถึงชนิดถ่ายทอดทางพันธุกรรม (KRIT1, CCM2, PDCD10) รักษาโดยเฝ้าติดตาม ให้ยากันชัก และผ่าตัดในรายที่เลือดออกซ้ำหรือชักดื้อยา

name: Cavernous sinus syndrome
formal: Lesion of the cavernous sinus involving cranial nerves III, IV, V1, V2 and VI, with ophthalmoplegia and facial sensory loss; causes include tumour, thrombosis, aneurysm and Tolosa-Hunt.
simple: Damage near the base of the brain that affects eye movement and facial feeling nerves.

name: CD8+ encephalitis
formal: Rare T-cell mediated encephalitis in HIV with CD8 lymphocytic infiltration and viral escape, causing subacute cognitive decline and seizures.
simple: A brain inflammation in people with HIV caused by overactive immune cells.

name: Celiac disease
formal: Gluten-triggered autoimmune enteropathy with neurological associations including gluten ataxia, axonal neuropathy, myopathy, and epilepsy with occipital calcifications.
simple: An immune reaction to gluten in food that damages the gut and can also affect the nerves and balance.
more: Tissue transglutaminase antibodies and duodenal biopsy diagnose it. A strict gluten-free diet may stabilise neurological features.

name: Central cord syndrome
formal: Cervical cord injury with disproportionate weakness of the arms compared with legs, variable sensory loss and bladder dysfunction; typical after hyperextension in spondylosis.
simple: A neck spinal cord injury that weakens the arms more than the legs.

name: Central core disease (CCD)
formal: Congenital myopathy from RYR1 mutations with central cores lacking oxidative enzyme activity, hypotonia and malignant hyperthermia susceptibility.
simple: An inherited muscle disease with weak, floppy muscles from birth and risk of a dangerous reaction to some anaesthetics.
aN: ccd | central core disease

name: Central core myopathy
formal: Congenital myopathy from RYR1 mutations with hypotonia, proximal weakness, and well-defined cores lacking oxidative activity on biopsy, and association with malignant hyperthermia.
simple: An inherited muscle disease from early life with mild weakness and a risk of dangerous reactions to some anaesthetics.
more: Confirm with RYR1 sequencing and biopsy; avoid volatile anaesthetics and succinylcholine. Treatment is supportive; usually non-progressive.

name: Central neurocytomas
formal: Rare intraventricular neuroglial tumours near the foramen of Monro in young adults, causing hydrocephalus; low-grade with good prognosis after resection.
simple: A slow-growing brain tumour in the fluid spaces of the brain that can block fluid flow.

name: Central post-stroke pain (CPSP)
formal: Neuropathic pain from thalamic or other central somatosensory lesions after stroke, often burning or allodynic and delayed by weeks to months.
simple: Long-lasting burning or painful sensations that develop after a stroke damages pain pathways in the brain.
aN: cpsp | central post stroke pain

name: Centronuclear myopathy
formal: Congenital myopathy with centrally placed nuclei in fibres; X-linked myotubular (MTM1) and autosomal forms (DNM2, BIN1) cause hypotonia and weakness.
simple: An inherited muscle disease with weakness and low muscle tone starting early in life.
more: Muscle biopsy shows central nuclei with radial sarcoplasmic strands; CK is usually normal, and genetics identifies MTM1 in males with severe neonatal disease. Prognosis ranges from early ventilator dependence to milder adult forms, and care is supportive.

name: Cerebellar ataxia
formal: Syndrome of incoordination with gait ataxia, dysmetria and dysarthria from cerebellar dysfunction; causes include genetic, toxic, immune, paraneoplastic and degenerative.
simple: Poor balance and clumsy movement due to cerebellum problems.

name: Cerebellar atrophy and variants
formal: Progressive cerebellar degeneration with ataxia, dysarthria and nystagmus; may be hereditary, alcoholic, paraneoplastic or idiopathic.
simple: Shrinking of the balance centre of the brain, causing unsteady walking and slurred speech.

name: Cerebellar disease
formal: General term for processes affecting the cerebellum causing ataxia, nystagmus, hypotonia, and intention tremor; ipsilateral signs for hemisphere lesions.
simple: Any illness of the cerebellum, which causes unsteadiness and clumsy movements.

name: Cerebellar disorders
formal: Group of conditions affecting cerebellar function, including degenerative, vascular, toxic, immune and genetic causes, with ataxia as the core sign.
simple: Conditions that affect the cerebellum and cause balance and coordination problems.

name: Cerebellar haemorrhage
formal: Spontaneous bleeding in the cerebellum from hypertension or vascular lesions, causing headache, vomiting, ataxia and risk of brainstem compression and hydrocephalus.
simple: Bleeding in the cerebellum causing sudden headache, vomiting and imbalance, which can be an emergency.

name: Cerebellar tremor
formal: Slow 3-5 Hz intention tremor from lesions of the dentato-rubro-thalamic pathway, worsening on approach to target; seen in MS, stroke and degenerative ataxias.
simple: A shaking that gets worse as you reach for something, caused by cerebellum pathway damage.

name: Cerebellopontine angle syndrome
formal: Lesions of the cerebellopontine angle affecting cranial nerves VII, VIII (and V) with hearing loss, tinnitus, facial weakness and ipsilateral ataxia; vestibular schwannoma is typical.
simple: Pressure near the hearing and balance nerve causing hearing loss, ringing in the ear and imbalance.

name: Cerebellopontine angle tumours
formal: Mass lesions in the cerebellopontine angle, most commonly vestibular schwannoma, then meningioma and epidermoid cyst.
simple: Growths near the ear nerve and brainstem, often causing one-sided hearing loss.

name: Cerebral abscess
formal: Focal pyogenic infection of brain parenchyma from contiguous spread or bacteraemia, producing headache, fever, focal deficits; ring-enhancing lesion on MRI.
simple: A pocket of pus in the brain from infection, causing headache, fever and weakness.

name: Cerebral amyloid angiopathy (CAA)
formal: Deposition of amyloid-beta in cortical and leptomeningeal vessels causing lobar haemorrhages, microbleeds, cortical superficial siderosis and cognitive decline in older people.
simple: Protein build-up in brain blood vessels in older adults that makes them fragile and can cause bleeding and memory loss.
th: โปรตีนอะไมลอยด์สะสมในผนังหลอดเลือดสมองผู้สูงอายุ ทำให้เลือดออกบริเวณผิวสมองซ้ำ ๆ
tempoNote: Acute lobar bleeds on a background of chronic small vessel disease; transient focal episodes
feat: Lobar haemorrhage in people over 55
Recurrent brief spreading sensory episodes ('amyloid spells')
Cognitive decline; may coexist with Alzheimer pathology
Inflammatory variant presents subacutely with headache, confusion and seizures
inv: MRI SWI: strictly lobar microbleeds, cortical superficial siderosis
Grade probable or possible CAA with Boston v2.0

case.exam: Left homonymous hemianopia, mild memory impairment.
case.tests: CT: right occipital lobar haematoma; SWI: multiple cortical microbleeds and convexity siderosis.
case.q: Why should the spreading tingling not be labelled TIA and treated with antiplatelets?
case.a: These are CAA-related transient focal episodes from cortical siderosis; antithrombotics raise the risk of further lobar haemorrhage.

TIA symptoms are negative and do not march

aN: caa | cerebral amyloid angiopathy | amyloid angiopathy | congophilic angiopathy

det.patho: Beta-amyloid (mainly Aβ40) deposits in the walls of small cortical and leptomeningeal arteries replace smooth muscle and make them brittle, causing lobar haemorrhages, cortical microbleeds, convexity SAH and cortical superficial siderosis, while impaired perivascular drainage produces white matter injury and enlarged centrum semiovale perivascular spaces. Prevalence rises steeply with age, and APOE e4 (amyloid deposition) and e2 (vessel rupture) genotypes modify risk. Hereditary forms (e.g. Dutch type, APP mutations) start earlier, and iatrogenic CAA appears decades after childhood neurosurgery or cadaveric dura or pituitary hormone exposure, implying seeded transmission. An inflammatory variant (CAA-ri) reflects an immune reaction against vascular amyloid, closely resembling ARIA from anti-amyloid antibody drugs.
det.clinical: Presentations include spontaneous lobar haemorrhage in older adults, transient focal neurological episodes (spreading paraesthesia, weakness or visual symptoms lasting minutes, from convexity SAH or siderosis), progressive cognitive decline with slowed processing, and incidental microbleeds on MRI. Cerebellar superficial haemorrhages can occur, whereas deep basal ganglia or brainstem bleeds point elsewhere. CAA-related inflammation causes subacute headache, confusion, seizures and focal signs with asymmetric confluent white matter oedema. Recurrent bleeds are common, cumulative disability follows, and amyloid spells that herald convexity bleeding predict a high short-term risk of ICH.
det.diagnosis: The Boston criteria v2.0 apply to people aged 50 or older presenting with spontaneous ICH, transient focal episodes or cognitive impairment. Probable CAA requires at least two strictly lobar haemorrhagic lesions in any combination (ICH, microbleeds, foci of cortical superficial siderosis or convexity SAH), or one such lesion plus one white matter feature (severe centrum semiovale perivascular spaces or a multispot subcortical white matter hyperintensity pattern), with no deep haemorrhagic lesion; possible CAA needs only one of these. Cerebellar lesions are not counted as deep. On CT alone, the Edinburgh criteria use finger-like projections and subarachnoid extension of a lobar haematoma. Pathology remains definitive; exclude vascular malformation, tumour, venous thrombosis, coagulopathy and trauma, and support CAA-ri with CSF anti-amyloid antibodies or biopsy.
det.treatment: There is no disease-modifying therapy; management focuses on preventing bleeding: strict BP control (the single most effective measure) and minimising antithrombotic exposure. After ICH, restarting an antiplatelet for a firm indication is reasonable, but long-term anticoagulation carries a high rebleeding risk in CAA, especially with siderosis or convexity SAH, so left atrial appendage occlusion is preferred for AF where feasible. Statins are not contraindicated when indicated. Transient focal episodes should not be treated as TIA with antithrombotics; some clinicians use antiseizure drugs or simply observe. CAA-ri responds to corticosteroids, sometimes with steroid-sparing immunosuppressants, and patients with CAA markers face higher ARIA risk on lecanemab or donanemab, which is why SWI is checked before treatment.
det.prognosis: Recurrent lobar haemorrhage occurs at several percent per year, highest with disseminated cortical siderosis; cognitive impairment and dementia are frequent.
pearls: Lobar bleed + microbleeds + siderosis in the elderly = probable CAA.
Amyloid spells mimic TIA or migraine aura; antithrombotics may cause harm.
Check SWI before starting anti-amyloid monoclonal antibodies for Alzheimer disease.
Lobar bleeding before age 55 with remote childhood neurosurgery should raise iatrogenic CAA.

name: Cerebral autosomal dominant arteriopathy with subcortical infarcts and leukoencephalopathy (CADASIL)
formal: Hereditary NOTCH3 small-vessel disease with migraine with aura, recurrent subcortical strokes, mood disorder and dementia; MRI shows anterior temporal and external capsule hyperintensities.
simple: An inherited disease of small brain blood vessels causing migraine, strokes and dementia in mid-adult life.
ab: Cerebral autosomal dominant arteriopathy with subcortical infarcts and leukoencephalopathy
th: โรคหลอดเลือดเล็กในสมองถ่ายทอดแบบยีนเด่นจาก NOTCH3 มี migraine with aura ตั้งแต่วัยหนุ่มสาว ตามด้วย lacunar stroke ซ้ำ ๆ อารมณ์ผิดปกติ และสมองเสื่อม MRI มี WMH ที่ anterior temporal pole และ external capsule
tempoNote: Migraine with aura from the 20s–30s, recurrent lacunar strokes in the 40s–50s, progressive cognitive decline thereafter
feat: Migraine with aura (often prolonged or atypical aura) as the first symptom in a third or more
Recurrent lacunar TIAs and strokes in middle age without strong vascular risk factors
Mood disorder, marked apathy, executive dysfunction progressing to dementia
Rare 'CADASIL coma': reversible encephalopathy with confusion, seizures, fever
Autosomal dominant family history of stroke, dementia or migraine (may be unrecognised)
inv: MRI: symmetric WMH involving the anterior temporal poles and external capsules, lacunes, microbleeds
NOTCH3 sequencing (exons 2–24): cysteine-altering variant confirms
Skin biopsy electron microscopy: granular osmiophilic material in arteriolar walls when genetics is inconclusive
Standard stroke work-up to exclude other causes

case.story: Since university she has had migraine with long visual and sensory auras. Now she has had two episodes of sudden right-sided clumsiness this year; her father had 'several small strokes' and dementia in his 50s.
case.exam: Mild right ataxic hemiparesis; slowed processing speed on bedside testing; BP 124/78.
case.tests: MRI: confluent WMH in both anterior temporal poles and external capsules, old lacunes in the pons and thalamus; lipids and glucose normal.
case.q: Which gene test is indicated and what advice would you add?
case.a: NOTCH3 — CADASIL; control vascular risk, avoid smoking, use antiplatelet only after ischaemic events, and offer genetic counselling to relatives.

det.patho: Mutations in NOTCH3, almost all altering the number of cysteine residues in the extracellular EGF-like repeats, cause accumulation of the NOTCH3 ectodomain and granular osmiophilic deposits around degenerating vascular smooth muscle cells. Small penetrating arteries become thickened and fibrotic with narrowed lumens, leading to chronic hypoperfusion of white matter and lacunar infarcts. It is the most common monogenic cause of stroke; variants in EGFr 1–6 cause more severe disease than those in EGFr 7–34. An Asian variant spectrum (e.g. R544C in Taiwan) often gives later onset without the temporal pole sign.
det.clinical: Course typically runs: migraine with aura in young adulthood, then recurrent subcortical ischaemic events, mood disturbance (depression, bipolar features) and apathy, and finally subcortical dementia with gait failure and pseudobulbar palsy. Strokes are lacunar, not territorial. Intracerebral haemorrhage is uncommon but more frequent in Asian series. Phenotype varies greatly even within one family.
det.diagnosis: Suspect in young lacunar stroke, extensive WMH out of proportion to age and risk factors, or a family history. Anterior temporal pole involvement is highly suggestive in European patients but less consistent in East Asians. Genetic testing for cysteine-altering NOTCH3 variants is the reference standard; skin biopsy with electron microscopy showing GOM is highly specific. Differentials include other monogenic SVDs (HTRA1, COL4A1/2, Fabry), MS and leukodystrophies.
det.treatment: No disease-specific therapy. Manage vascular risk aggressively, stop smoking, and use antiplatelet after ischaemic events (avoid routine anticoagulation). Migraine: standard preventives are fine; triptans and ergots are generally avoided because of vasoconstriction concerns. IV thrombolysis has been given without clear excess harm but evidence is limited. Treat depression, provide rehabilitation, and offer genetic counselling with careful pre-symptomatic testing protocols.
det.prognosis: Most patients become dependent by their 60s; median age at death is around 65–70, earlier in men and in carriers of EGFr 1–6 variants.
pearls: Migraine with aura + young lacunar strokes + family history = CADASIL until NOTCH3 tested.
WMH in anterior temporal poles and external capsules is a classic MRI clue.
Patients are often normotensive — extensive WMH without risk factors should prompt testing.
det.thd: CADASIL เป็นโรคหลอดเลือดเล็กในสมองถ่ายทอดทางพันธุกรรมแบบยีนเด่นจากยีน NOTCH3 เริ่มด้วย migraine with aura ในวัยหนุ่มสาว ตามด้วย lacunar stroke ซ้ำ ๆ ในวัยกลางคน อารมณ์ซึมเศร้า เฉยเมย และสมองเสื่อม MRI มี white matter hyperintensities ที่ anterior temporal pole และ external capsule ยืนยันด้วยตรวจยีน NOTCH3 หรือ skin biopsy ยังไม่มียารักษาเฉพาะ เน้นคุมปัจจัยเสี่ยง งดบุหรี่ และให้คำปรึกษาทางพันธุกรรม

name: Cerebral folate deficiency
formal: Neurological syndrome with low CSF 5-methyltetrahydrofolate despite normal blood folate, causing irritability, ataxia, seizures and developmental delay; due to FOLR1 mutations or folate receptor antibodies.
simple: Low folate in the brain fluid despite normal blood levels, causing developmental problems and seizures.

name: Cerebral haemorrhage and infarction
formal: Collective term for ischaemic and haemorrhagic stroke, the two main types of acute cerebrovascular events.
simple: Strokes caused by either a blocked or a bleeding blood vessel in the brain.

name: Cerebral infarction or haemorrhage
formal: Collective term for acute stroke of ischaemic or haemorrhagic type, distinguished by neuroimaging.
simple: A stroke caused either by a blocked or by a burst blood vessel in the brain.

name: Cerebral infarction/haemorrhage
formal: Collective term for ischaemic or haemorrhagic stroke, distinguished by CT or MRI.
simple: A stroke from either a blocked or a bleeding brain blood vessel.

name: Cerebral palsy
formal: Non-progressive disorder of movement and posture from early brain injury, with spastic, dyskinetic or ataxic forms; often with epilepsy and cognitive impairment.
simple: A lasting movement and posture condition caused by brain injury before or soon after birth.

name: Cerebral small-vessel disease (cSVD)
formal: Disease of perforating arterioles, capillaries and venules causing lacunes, white matter hyperintensities, microbleeds and dilated perivascular spaces; leads to stroke, gait problems and dementia.
simple: Damage to the tiny blood vessels of the brain, causing small strokes, slowed thinking and walking problems.
aN: csvd | cerebral small vessel disease

name: Cerebral trauma and dystonia
formal: Post-traumatic dystonia after brain injury, often delayed by months to years, typically hemidystonia contralateral to basal ganglia or thalamic damage.
simple: Painful twisting muscle postures that develop after a head injury.

name: Cerebral tumours
formal: Primary or metastatic neoplasms of the brain causing headache, seizures, focal deficits and raised intracranial pressure; gliomas and metastases are most frequent.
simple: Growths in the brain that can cause headaches, seizures or weakness.

name: Cerebral vasculitis
formal: Inflammation of CNS vessels, primary or secondary to systemic disease or infection, causing stroke-like events, headache and encephalopathy.
simple: Inflammation of brain blood vessels, which can cause strokes and confusion.

Recurrent strokes in several territories, often of different ages on MRI
Seizures and encephalopathy; spinal cord involvement occasionally

case.story: Three months of dull daily headache, forgetfulness and slowing at work; two episodes of transient left arm numbness, then new word-finding difficulty.
case.exam: Mild expressive aphasia, right pronator drift, MoCA 21/30; no rash or joint signs.

det.patho: Inflammation of the vessel wall narrows or occludes arteries and causes ischaemia, sometimes haemorrhage. In PACNS the process is confined to the brain and spinal cord vessels and is granulomatous, lymphocytic or necrotising on histology; one subset is linked to amyloid deposition. Secondary CNS vasculitis complicates infections (VZV, TB, syphilis, fungi, HIV), systemic vasculitides, connective tissue diseases, drugs and lymphoma.
det.clinical: Primary angiitis has a median age around 50 and slightly more men. The common pattern is headache plus cognitive decline with or without multifocal strokes; seizures, cranial neuropathies and myelopathy occur less often. Large-to-medium vessel disease presents more like strokes, while small vessel disease looks like a progressive encephalopathy with enhancing lesions. Fever, weight loss and raised inflammatory markers should prompt a search for systemic or infectious causes.
det.diagnosis: There is no single blood marker. Combine MRI evidence of multifocal ischaemia or enhancement, inflammatory CSF and vessel imaging, then aim for biopsy because angiographic beading is non-specific and small-vessel disease can have normal angiograms. Rule out RCVS (normal CSF, reversibility), infection, lymphoma, atherosclerosis, moyamoya, CAA-ri and demyelination. Vessel-wall MRI showing concentric enhancement supports but does not prove inflammation.
det.treatment: Induction typically uses high-dose glucocorticoids (often an intravenous methylprednisolone pulse then oral prednisolone) together with cyclophosphamide or rituximab for more severe or biopsy-proven disease. Maintenance with azathioprine, mycophenolate or methotrexate for 1–2 years or more follows. Secondary vasculitis is managed by treating the cause (e.g. aciclovir for VZV, antituberculous therapy). Use antithrombotics cautiously and monitor with serial MRI.
det.prognosis: With treatment many patients stabilise or improve; relapse occurs in about a quarter and mortality is higher with large-vessel involvement, infarcts at presentation or delayed diagnosis.
pearls: Normal CSF and normal MRI argue strongly against PACNS.
An abnormal angiogram is not proof of vasculitis — think RCVS, atheroma and infection.
Always exclude VZV and TB before immunosuppression.
det.thd: Cerebral vasculitis คือการอักเสบของผนังหลอดเลือดสมอง ชนิดปฐมภูมิ (PACNS) เกิดเฉพาะในระบบประสาทส่วนกลาง ผู้ป่วยปวดศีรษะเรื้อรัง ความจำหรือพฤติกรรมเปลี่ยน และมี stroke หลายตำแหน่งต่างเวลา CSF มักมีเซลล์และโปรตีนสูง การวินิจฉัยแน่นอนต้องตัดชิ้นเนื้อสมอง และต้องแยกจาก RCVS การติดเชื้อ และ lymphoma รักษาด้วย steroid ร่วมกับ cyclophosphamide หรือ rituximab

ddx.pt: Thunderclap onset, normal CSF and reversible narrowing on repeat angiography
Intravascular or angiocentric lymphoma can mimic; avoid steroids before biopsy if lymphoma is possible
Older patient with lobar microbleeds; inflammatory CAA (CAA-ri) is a vasculitis-like variant with asymmetric white matter oedema

aN: pacns | primary angiitis of the cns | primary cns vasculitis | cns vasculitis | isolated angiitis of the cns | granulomatous angiitis | secondary cns vasculitis

name: Cerebral vasospasm
formal: Reversible narrowing of intracranial arteries, classically 4-14 days after subarachnoid haemorrhage, causing delayed cerebral ischaemia.
simple: Narrowing of brain arteries, often after bleeding around the brain, which can cause a stroke.

name: Cerebrovascular disease
formal: Umbrella term for diseases of cerebral blood supply, including ischaemic stroke, intracerebral haemorrhage, aneurysm and vascular malformations.
simple: Diseases of the blood vessels that supply the brain, including stroke.

name: Cervical degenerative disease
formal: Spondylotic degeneration of cervical discs and facets that causes neck pain, radiculopathy or myelopathy with spasticity and gait disturbance.
simple: Wear and tear of the neck spine that can pinch nerves or the spinal cord.

name: Cervical disk disease
formal: Herniation or degeneration of cervical discs compressing roots or cord, producing arm pain, sensory loss, weakness and sometimes myelopathy.
simple: A slipped or worn disc in the neck pressing on nerves, causing arm pain and weakness.

name: Cervical meningioma
formal: Benign dural tumour in the cervical canal, more often in women, causing slowly progressive cord compression with weakness, sensory loss and gait trouble.
simple: A slow-growing non-cancerous tumour pressing on the neck spinal cord.

name: Cervical myelopathy
formal: Compressive or ischaemic injury to the cervical cord, often from spondylosis, with spastic gait, hand clumsiness, hyperreflexia, Hoffmann sign and bladder disturbance.
simple: Pressure on the spinal cord in the neck causing clumsy hands, stiff legs and walking problems.

name: Cervical myelopathy with quadriplegia
formal: Severe cervical cord compression or injury with tetraparesis or tetraplegia, spasticity, sensory level and sphincter loss.
simple: Serious neck spinal cord damage causing weakness or paralysis of all four limbs.

name: Cervical radiculopathies
formal: Disorders of cervical nerve roots, usually from disc herniation or spondylosis, giving neck and arm pain with dermatomal sensory loss and myotomal weakness, most often C6 and C7.
simple: Pinched nerves in the neck causing pain, numbness, and weakness in the arm and hand.
more: MRI and EMG confirm it. Most cases improve in weeks to months with conservative care; surgery for progressive or severe deficits.

name: Cervical spine disease
formal: Degenerative, inflammatory, neoplastic or traumatic conditions of the neck spine that compress roots or cord and cause pain and neurological deficit.
simple: Problems of the neck spine that can pinch nerves or the spinal cord.

name: Chagas disease
formal: Trypanosoma cruzi infection with cardiomyopathy and megaviscera; neurological features include cardioembolic stroke, meningoencephalitis in immunosuppression and autonomic neuropathy.
simple: A parasite infection from insect bites that can damage the heart and gut and sometimes the brain.

name: Channelopathies
formal: Disorders of ion channel genes causing episodic phenotypes such as periodic paralysis, myotonia, epilepsy, ataxia, migraine and pain.
simple: Diseases caused by faulty electrical channels in cells, producing attacks of weakness, seizures or pain.

name: Charcoat-Marie-Tooth disease
formal: Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease, the commonest inherited neuropathy, with length-dependent distal weakness, pes cavus, and sensory loss, caused by mutations in genes such as PMP22 and MFN2.
simple: An inherited nerve disease that slowly weakens the feet and hands and causes high arched feet.
more: Nerve conduction studies and genetic testing define the type. Treatment is supportive with orthoses, physiotherapy, and surgery; avoid neurotoxic drugs such as vincristine.

name: Charcot–Marie–Tooth (CMT) disease
formal: Most common inherited neuropathy with distal weakness, pes cavus, foot drop and sensory loss; demyelinating or axonal forms from PMP22, MPZ, GJB1, MFN2 and others.
simple: An inherited nerve disease causing weakness and wasting in the feet and lower legs and high arches.
more: Diagnosed by nerve conduction (demyelinating below 38 m/s in median motor) and PMP22 duplication testing in CMT1A, the commonest form. No disease-modifying therapy exists; use ankle-foot orthoses and avoid neurotoxic drugs such as vincristine.
th: เส้นประสาทเสื่อมทางพันธุกรรม — เท้าโก่ง นิ้วเท้างอ ขาเรียวแบบขวดแชมเปญ เท้าตก
feat: Slowly progressive distal weakness and wasting from childhood/adolescence
Pes cavus, hammer toes, 'inverted champagne bottle' legs
Foot drop with steppage gait; few sensory symptoms despite signs
inv: NCS: uniform slowing (CMT1, < 38 m/s) or axonal (CMT2)
Genetic testing: PMP22 duplication first

case.story: Trips over kerbs and sprains ankles; his father has 'high-arched feet'.
case.exam: Pes cavus, bilateral foot drop, absent ankle jerks, thin calves, reduced distal vibration.
case.tests: Median motor conduction velocity 22 m/s, uniform without conduction block; PMP22 duplication.
case.q: Why does uniform slowing suggest an inherited rather than an acquired demyelinating neuropathy?
case.a: Inherited myelin defects affect all segments equally; acquired (e.g. CIDP) cause patchy slowing and conduction block.

read.where: Nagappa M, Sharma S, Taly AB. Charcot-Marie-Tooth Disease (updated 22 Jun 2024)
