feat: Symmetric distal-predominant flaccid weakness and wasting with reduced or absent reflexes
Distal loss of pain, temperature and vibration sense
Difficulty weaning due to phrenic nerve and diaphragm involvement
Facial muscles relatively spared; often combined with CIM
inv: NCS: reduced motor and sensory amplitudes with normal conduction velocity (axonal)
Needle EMG: fibrillations and positive sharp waves, later neurogenic units
CSF normal protein (helps exclude GBS) when the diagnosis is uncertain

case.story: Three weeks in ICU with leptospirosis, septic shock and renal failure; now alert but legs are floppy and she fails spontaneous breathing trials.
case.exam: Distal > proximal weakness, foot drop, absent ankle jerks, stocking sensory loss, grimaces normally.
case.tests: NCS: low CMAPs and absent sural SNAPs with preserved velocities; needle EMG: fibrillations in leg and diaphragm.
case.q: Why is GBS unlikely, and what is the prognosis?
case.a: Weakness began during critical illness, NCS show pure axonal loss without demyelination and CSF protein is normal. Recovery is slow over months and may be incomplete.

det.patho: Systemic inflammation in sepsis impairs nerve microcirculation, increases vascular permeability and causes bioenergetic failure of axons; sodium-channel inactivation produces early functional block before structural degeneration. The result is a length-dependent sensorimotor axonal neuropathy. Hyperglycaemia and multiorgan failure increase risk, and severity tracks with the duration of sepsis.
det.clinical: Most cases present as failure to wean or limp limbs once sedation is reduced. Weakness is distal-predominant with reduced reflexes and distal sensory loss, though examination is limited by encephalopathy. Phrenic neuropathy prolongs ventilation. CIP and CIM overlap in many patients and together form ICU-acquired weakness, a major cause of long-term disability after intensive care.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis combines a compatible setting with NCS showing reduced CMAP and SNAP amplitudes and normal velocities, and EMG showing denervation. Phrenic NCS and diaphragm EMG help explain ventilator dependence. Preserved SNAPs, inexcitable muscle on direct stimulation or a pure motor pattern suggest CIM instead. Exclude GBS, myasthenia, botulism, high cervical cord lesions and drug effects.
det.treatment: There is no proven specific therapy. Intensive insulin therapy reduces incidence but must be balanced against hypoglycaemia; current practice targets moderate glucose control. Treat sepsis aggressively, minimise sedation, mobilise early and provide physiotherapy, splints and long-term rehabilitation.
det.prognosis: Recovery takes months; many patients regain walking, but residual distal weakness, sensory loss and fatigue are common, more so than with CIM.
pearls: Absent sural SNAP plus low CMAP with normal velocities in a septic patient = CIP pattern.
Check phrenic nerve function in unexplained weaning failure.
CIP and CIM often coexist; electrophysiology defines the mix.
det.thd: CIP คือเส้นประสาทส่วนปลายเสื่อมชนิด axonal ที่เกิดระหว่างติดเชื้อรุนแรงหรืออวัยวะล้มเหลวหลายระบบ ผู้ป่วยอ่อนแรงส่วนปลาย reflex หาย ชาแบบถุงเท้า และถอดเครื่องช่วยหายใจยากเพราะเส้นประสาท phrenic เสีย NCS พบ amplitude ลดลงทั้ง motor และ sensory แต่ความเร็วปกติ ไม่มียารักษาเฉพาะ เน้นรักษาการติดเชื้อ คุมน้ำตาล เคลื่อนไหวเร็ว และฟื้นฟูยาวนานหลายเดือน

files.chapter: Chapter 28 Disorders of Consciousness and Intensive Care Neurology

ddx.pt: Sensory potentials preserved, proximal and facial weakness, myopathic EMG
Onset before ICU, CSF protein raised, demyelinating features
Fatigable ptosis and diplopia, decrement on RNS, positive AChR antibody

aN: cip | critical illness polyneuropathy | icu acquired neuropathy | sepsis associated polyneuropathy | critical illness neuromyopathy

name: CRMP-5 neuronal antibody-associated limbic encephalitis
formal: Paraneoplastic limbic or multifocal encephalitis with anti-CV2/CRMP5 antibodies, associated with small cell lung cancer and thymoma, often with neuropathy and chorea.
simple: Brain inflammation triggered by the immune system reacting to a hidden cancer, causing memory and mood changes.
nN: crmp 5 neuronal antibody associated limbic encephalitis

name: Crohn’s disease
formal: Inflammatory bowel disease with neurological complications including peripheral neuropathy, cerebral venous thrombosis, myelopathy and treatment-related effects.
simple: A bowel inflammatory disease that can also affect nerves and brain blood vessels.
more: Check for ulcerative thrombotic complications, B12 and folate deficiency, vitamin deficiency and anti-TNF-related demyelination; neuropathy and CNS involvement should be sought on imaging. Treat the bowel disease, anticoagulate venous thrombosis.

name: Cruciate paralysis
formal: Weakness of both arms with relative sparing of legs, caused by a lesion at the cervicomedullary junction affecting decussating pyramidal fibres.
simple: A weakness mostly in the arms, due to damage at the junction of brain and spinal cord.

name: Cryopyrin-associated periodic syndrome
formal: Autoinflammatory NLRP3 disease including CINCA/NOMID with chronic aseptic meningitis, hearing loss, papilloedema and rashes.
simple: An inherited inflammatory condition causing fever, rash, joint pain and brain-lining inflammation.

name: Cryptococcal meningitis
formal: Cryptococcus infection of meninges, mostly in immunosuppression with HIV, causing headache and raised intracranial pressure; India ink or antigen positive, treated with amphotericin and flucytosine.
simple: A fungal infection of the brain coverings in people with weak immunity, causing headache and confusion.

name: Cryptococcal meningoencephalitis
formal: Cryptococcal infection of meninges and brain parenchyma with encephalopathy, cryptococcomas and raised pressure, mainly in immunocompromised patients.
simple: A fungal infection of the brain and its coverings that mainly affects people with weak immunity.

name: Cryptogenic myoclonic epilepsy
formal: Myoclonic epilepsy without an identifiable cause, with seizures featuring brief myoclonic jerks.
simple: Epilepsy with sudden muscle jerks for which no cause is found.

name: Cuban epidemic neuropathy
formal: Epidemic optic and peripheral neuropathy and myeloneuropathy during 1990s in Cuba, linked to nutritional deficiency including B vitamins.
simple: A nutritional illness in Cuba that caused vision loss and numb, weak limbs.

name: Cushing syndrome
formal: Endogenous or exogenous glucocorticoid excess causing proximal myopathy, psychiatric symptoms, hypertension and stroke risk.
simple: A condition of too much cortisol hormone, which can cause muscle weakness and mood changes.
more: Confirm with 24-hour urinary free cortisol, late-night salivary cortisol and dexamethasone suppression test; CK is normal in steroid myopathy and EMG is often normal. Treat the underlying cause and reduce steroids.

name: Cutaneous neurofibromas
formal: Benign peripheral nerve sheath tumours in the skin, characteristic of neurofibromatosis type 1 and appearing from adolescence.
simple: Soft skin bumps made of nerve tissue, typical of neurofibromatosis.

name: Cyanide poisoning
formal: Cytochrome oxidase inhibition causing histotoxic hypoxia with headache, seizures, coma and lactic acidosis; delayed parkinsonism possible.
simple: Poisoning by cyanide that stops cells using oxygen, causing collapse, seizures and coma.

name: Cyanide toxicity
formal: Mitochondrial toxicity from cyanide exposure with histotoxic hypoxia and basal ganglia injury, including konzo from cassava.
simple: Harm to the body from cyanide, which stops cells using oxygen.

name: Cycad toxicity
formal: Neurotoxicity from cycad seed consumption (BMAA), linked to Guam ALS-parkinsonism-dementia complex.
simple: Brain harm from eating cycad seeds that has been linked to a disease similar to motor neuron disease and dementia.

name: Cyclothymic disorder
formal: Chronic mood instability with numerous hypomanic and depressive episodes insufficient for bipolar disorder.
simple: Ongoing mood swings between mild highs and lows.

name: Cystic fibrosis
formal: CFTR genetic disease with chronic lung and pancreatic disease; neurological aspects include vitamin E deficiency, stroke and ataxia.
simple: An inherited disease causing sticky mucus in lungs and gut, which can sometimes affect nerves.

name: Cytokine release encephalopathy syndrome (CRES)
formal: Reversible severe encephalopathy after CAR T therapy or T-cell engagers with cytokine release, aphasia, seizures and cerebral oedema.
simple: Confusion and brain swelling from an overactive immune response after some cancer immunotherapies.
aN: cres | cytokine release encephalopathy syndrome

name: Cytokine-driven neurological disease
formal: Neurological disease from excessive cytokine activity, such as in CRES, neuroinflammation and autoinflammatory conditions.
simple: Brain and nerve problems caused by too much immune signalling.

name: D-glyceric acidaemia
formal: Autosomal recessive organic aciduria from GLYCTK deficiency or related defect, with hypotonia, seizures and developmental delay.
simple: A rare inherited metabolic condition causing developmental delay and seizures.

name: DADS neuropathy
formal: Distal acquired demyelinating symmetric neuropathy, a sensory-predominant chronic demyelinating neuropathy often with IgM anti-MAG antibodies, causing distal numbness and ataxia.
simple: A chronic nerve disease with damage to the nerve insulation of the feet and hands, causing numbness and unsteadiness.
more: Search for anti-MAG IgM; rituximab for anti-MAG cases; IVIG for others.

name: Dancing eyes syndrome
formal: Opsoclonus-myoclonus syndrome: chaotic saccades with myoclonus and ataxia, in children with neuroblastoma or post-infectious, and in adults paraneoplastic.
simple: A condition of rapid, uncontrolled eye movements with jerky muscles and unsteadiness, often immune-related.

name: Dancing eyes–dancing feet syndrome (myoclonic encephalopathy of infancy)
formal: Opsoclonus-myoclonus syndrome in infancy with chaotic eye movements, myoclonus and ataxia, often paraneoplastic from neuroblastoma.
simple: Rapid uncontrolled eye movements and jerking in babies, often linked with a hidden tumour.
nN: dancing eyes dancing feet syndrome myoclonic encephalopathy of infancy
aN: myoclonic encephalopathy of infancy | dancing eyes dancing feet syndrome

name: Danon disease
formal: X-linked LAMP2 deficiency with vacuolar cardiomyopathy and skeletal myopathy, usually with intellectual disability, retinopathy, and Wolff-Parkinson-White pattern.
simple: An inherited disease causing thickened weak heart muscle, muscle weakness, and sometimes learning difficulties.
more: Biopsy shows autophagic vacuoles lacking LAMP2; confirm genetically. Heart transplant is often required; gene therapy is under study.

name: Davidenkow disease
formal: Scapuloperoneal syndrome with weakness of shoulder girdle and peroneal muscles, due to neurogenic or myopathic causes such as SPSMA or TRPV4.
simple: A rare condition in which weakness affects the shoulder and front leg muscles.
more: EMG and gene testing; supportive therapy with orthoses.

name: Deafness dystonia syndrome
formal: X-linked Mohr-Tranebjaerg syndrome from TIMM8A mutations, with progressive sensorineural deafness, dystonia, visual impairment and cognitive decline, with a mitochondrial import defect.
simple: An inherited condition in boys causing hearing loss in childhood followed by dystonia, vision loss and dementia.
more: Genetic testing of TIMM8A confirms it. Treatment is supportive with hearing aids or cochlear implants; dystonia and cognitive decline progress over years.

name: Degenerative spinal disease
formal: Age-related disc and facet degeneration with canal stenosis causing back pain, radiculopathy, neurogenic claudication or myelopathy.
simple: Wear and tear of the spine that can press on the spinal cord or nerves.

name: Degenerative vascular disease
formal: Atherosclerotic or small vessel degeneration causing cerebral ischaemia, white matter disease and vascular cognitive impairment.
simple: Age-related damage to blood vessels that supply the brain.

name: Degos’ disease
formal: Malignant atrophic papulosis, a thrombo-occlusive vasculopathy with porcelain-white skin papules, bowel infarction and cerebral infarcts and haemorrhage.
simple: A rare blood vessel disease with white skin spots that can cause strokes and bowel problems.

name: Dejerine–Roussy syndrome
formal: Thalamic pain syndrome after thalamic stroke with contralateral sensory loss, hemiataxia, burning pain and allodynia, later with choreoathetoid movements.
simple: One-sided burning pain and numbness that follow a stroke in the thalamus.

name: Dejerine–Sottas disease (DSD)
formal: Hereditary demyelinating neuropathy (CMT3) with severe early-onset weakness, hypertrophic nerves, marked conduction slowing and high CSF protein.
simple: An inherited nerve disease starting in childhood with severe weakness and thickened nerves.
aN: dsd | dejerine sottas disease

name: Dejerine–Thomas type of olivoponto-cerebellar atrophy
formal: Old term for late-onset cerebellar atrophy with olivopontocerebellar involvement, now part of multiple system atrophy-cerebellar type.
simple: An old name for a progressive balance disease that overlaps with multiple system atrophy.
nN: dejerine thomas type of olivoponto cerebellar atrophy

name: Delayed post-hypoxic encephalopathy
formal: Neurological deterioration days to weeks after apparent recovery from hypoxic injury such as carbon monoxide, with leukoencephalopathy and cognitive change.
simple: Brain problems appearing weeks after recovery from oxygen shortage such as carbon monoxide poisoning.

name: Delayed sleep–wake phase disorder
formal: Circadian disorder with persistent late sleep and wake times, causing difficulty falling asleep and waking for conventional hours.
simple: Being unable to fall asleep until very late and waking late, because the body clock runs behind.

name: Delayed-onset dystonia
formal: Dystonia appearing months or years after perinatal or acquired brain injury, such as hypoxic-ischaemic injury or kernicterus.
simple: Twisting muscle postures that develop long after a brain injury.

name: Delirium
formal: Acute fluctuating disturbance of attention and cognition from medical illness, drug or withdrawal; may be hyperactive, hypoactive or mixed.
simple: A sudden state of confusion and reduced awareness that fluctuates, often during illness.

name: Dementia
formal: Acquired decline in multiple cognitive domains interfering with independence, from Alzheimer, vascular, Lewy body, frontotemporal or other causes.
simple: A decline in memory and thinking that gets in the way of everyday life.

name: Dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB)
formal: Alpha-synucleinopathy with fluctuating cognition, visual hallucinations, parkinsonism, REM sleep behaviour disorder and neuroleptic sensitivity; dementia precedes parkinsonism by one year or less.
simple: A dementia with fluctuating thinking, vivid hallucinations and stiff slow movements.
more: Amyloid and tau biomarkers are usually negative; DAT-SPECT shows reduced striatal uptake and polysomnography confirms RBD. Cholinesterase inhibitors help cognition and hallucinations; avoid typical antipsychotics.
th: สมองเสื่อมจากโปรตีน Lewy — ความตื่นตัวขึ้นลง เห็นภาพหลอนชัดเจน มีอาการพาร์กินสัน แพ้ยาต้านโรคจิต
feat: Fluctuating attention and alertness
Well-formed visual hallucinations (people, animals)
REM sleep behaviour disorder
Parkinsonism; severe sensitivity to antipsychotics
inv: DAT SPECT reduced uptake; MIBG cardiac scintigraphy reduced
Polysomnography for REM sleep without atonia

case.story: Some days he is sharp, other days confused; he sees small children sitting in the living room. Gets worse rigid after haloperidol given in hospital.
case.exam: Poor attention and visuospatial copying, mild symmetric bradykinesia.
case.tests: DAT SPECT: reduced striatal uptake.
case.q: Why was haloperidol dangerous?
case.a: Neuroleptic sensitivity in DLB can cause severe rigidity, confusion and even death.

files.chapter: 9 - Atypical parkinsonism, parkinsonism-­plus syndromes and secondary parkinsonian disorders

ddx.pt: Parkinsonism precedes dementia by more than a year
Memory-led, no prominent fluctuations or hallucinations early
Acute onset with a precipitant; resolves

aN: dlb | dementia with lewy bodies | lewy body dementia | lbd | diffuse lewy body disease

det.patho: Alpha-synuclein Lewy bodies are widespread in limbic and neocortical regions as well as the brainstem, often with coexisting Alzheimer pathology. Profound cholinergic deficit from basal forebrain loss contributes to fluctuations and hallucinations and explains the good response to cholinesterase inhibitors. It is the second most common neurodegenerative dementia in older adults.
det.clinical: Cognitive decline affects attention, executive function and visuospatial skills earlier than memory. Core features are fluctuating cognition and alertness (staring spells, daytime drowsiness), recurrent detailed visual hallucinations, REM sleep behaviour disorder and parkinsonism. Supportive features include severe antipsychotic sensitivity, falls, syncope, autonomic dysfunction, hypersomnia, anosmia, delusions and depression. By convention, if dementia appears before or within a year of parkinsonism the label is DLB; if parkinsonism precedes dementia by more than a year it is PD dementia. Episodes of delirium-like confusion are common and may be the first presentation.
det.diagnosis: The 2017 consortium criteria classify probable DLB as dementia with two or more core features, or one core feature plus an indicative biomarker. Indicative biomarkers are reduced striatal DAT uptake on SPECT/PET, low cardiac MIBG uptake, and polysomnographic REM sleep without atonia. MRI shows relative preservation of the medial temporal lobes compared with AD; FDG-PET may show occipital hypometabolism with a cingulate island sign. CSF alpha-synuclein seed amplification is a promising test. Delirium, AD and vascular dementia are the main mimics.
det.treatment: Cholinesterase inhibitors (rivastigmine, donepezil) often help cognition, fluctuations and hallucinations. Levodopa can be tried cautiously for disabling parkinsonism but may worsen psychosis. For distressing psychosis use the lowest dose of quetiapine or clozapine; avoid haloperidol and other potent D2 blockers. Melatonin or clonazepam help RBD; manage orthostasis, constipation and falls. Educate carers and hospital staff about neuroleptic sensitivity.
det.prognosis: Decline is often faster than in AD, with survival of around 5–8 years from diagnosis.
pearls: Hallucinations of small people or animals in the room, often without distress, are typical.
Haloperidol in an agitated patient with DLB can trigger catastrophic rigidity — flag the notes.
Visuospatial failure (poor pentagon copy) with relatively better recall points to DLB over AD.
det.thd: DLB เป็นสมองเสื่อมจากโปรตีน alpha-synuclein กระจายในเปลือกสมอง อาการหลักคือ ความตื่นตัวและความคิดขึ้นลงเป็นวัน เห็นภาพหลอนชัดเจน ละเมอตามความฝัน และมีอาการพาร์กินสัน ผู้ป่วยไวต่อยาต้านโรคจิตมากจนอาจเกร็งรุนแรงหรือเสียชีวิต วินิจฉัยด้วยเกณฑ์ 2017 ร่วมกับ DAT scan, MIBG หรือ polysomnography รักษาด้วย rivastigmine หรือ donepezil ถ้าจำเป็นใช้ quetiapine ขนาดต่ำ หลีกเลี่ยง haloperidol

name: Dementia with Lewy Body
formal: Alpha-synuclein disease with fluctuating cognition, recurrent visual hallucinations, parkinsonism and REM sleep behaviour disorder; dementia precedes or occurs within a year of motor signs.
simple: A type of dementia with changing alertness, vivid hallucinations, stiffness and acting out dreams.
more: DaT scan, polysomnography and cognitive testing help; avoid neuroleptic drugs. Cholinesterase inhibitors help cognition and hallucinations, and survival averages about 8 years.

name: Demyelination, osmotic
formal: Central pontine or extrapontine myelinolysis from rapid sodium correction, causing quadriparesis, dysarthria, dysphagia and locked-in state.
simple: Brain damage caused by changing blood salt levels too fast, causing weakness and difficulty speaking and swallowing.
aN: demyelination | osmotic

name: Dental disease
formal: Dental conditions such as infection or abscess that may cause trigeminal pain or neurological complications including brain abscess.
simple: Tooth or gum problems that can cause facial pain or spread infection to the brain.

name: Dentatorubral pallidoluysian atrophy (DRPLA)
formal: Autosomal dominant CAG-repeat disease (ATN1) with ataxia, chorea, myoclonus, epilepsy and dementia; anticipation, juvenile and adult forms.
simple: An inherited brain disease causing clumsiness, jerking movements, seizures and dementia.
more: Diagnosis by genetic testing for ATN1 CAG expansion; MRI shows cerebellar and brainstem atrophy with white matter changes. Epilepsy is more frequent in juvenile onset, and chorea in adults; therapy is symptomatic and prevalence is higher in Japan.
aN: drpla | dentatorubral pallidoluysian atrophy

name: Dentatorubro-pallidoloysian atrophy
formal: Misspelled form of DRPLA, CAG-repeat ATN1 disease with ataxia, chorea, myoclonus, epilepsy and dementia.
simple: An inherited brain disease causing poor coordination, jerky movements, seizures and dementia.

name: Dentatorubro-pallidoluysian atrophy (DRPLA)
formal: Autosomal dominant CAG-repeat disease with ataxia, chorea, myoclonus, epilepsy and dementia, more common in Japan.
simple: An inherited brain disease causing clumsiness, jerky movements, seizures and memory loss.
aN: drpla | dentatorubro pallidoluysian atrophy

name: Dermatomyositis
formal: Idiopathic inflammatory myopathy with proximal weakness, heliotrope rash and Gottron papules; perifascicular atrophy on biopsy; associated with malignancy and anti-MDA5, Mi-2 or TIF1 antibodies.
simple: An immune disease causing muscle weakness and a typical skin rash.
more: Check CK and myositis-specific antibodies, and screen for malignancy with age-appropriate imaging; MRI shows muscle oedema and EMG shows irritability. First-line is corticosteroids with methotrexate, azathioprine or IVIG; skin disease needs sun protection.
th: กล้ามเนื้อและผิวหนังอักเสบจากภูมิคุ้มกัน — ต้นแขนต้นขาอ่อนแรง ผื่นม่วงรอบตา ผื่นที่ข้อนิ้ว ต้องหามะเร็งแฝง
feat: Symmetric proximal weakness over weeks
Heliotrope rash, Gottron papules, shawl sign, nailfold changes
Interstitial lung disease (anti-MDA5) and malignancy association (anti-TIF1γ)
inv: CK, myositis-specific antibodies
EMG myopathic with fibrillations; MRI STIR oedema
Biopsy: perifascicular atrophy
Cancer screening; HRCT chest

case.story: Six weeks of difficulty combing her hair and climbing stairs, with a purplish rash on the eyelids.
case.exam: Neck flexors and proximal limbs 4−/5, heliotrope rash, scaly papules over the knuckles.
case.tests: CK 5,800 U/L; anti-TIF1γ positive.
case.q: What must be searched for next?
case.a: An underlying malignancy (anti-TIF1γ carries a high cancer association).

read.where: บทที่ 6 หน้า 104–136 (MSA ตารางที่ 6.1 หน้า 107; แนวทางรักษา แผนภูมิ 6.2 หน้า 114); บทที่ 7 JDM หน้า 137–160 (แผนภูมิ 7.1 หน้า 141; Heliotrope/Gottron ภาคผนวก 7.1 หน้า 149)

ddx.pt: No skin signs; diagnosis of exclusion
Older, asymmetric finger flexor/quadriceps weakness, steroid unresponsive
Fatigable ocular weakness, normal CK

aN: dm | dermatomyositis | idiopathic inflammatory myopathy

det.patho: An immune-mediated myopathy driven largely by type I interferon, with complement-mediated injury to small vessels causing capillary loss and perifascicular fibre damage. Myositis-specific antibodies define clinical subsets: anti-Mi-2 (classic skin and muscle, good response), anti-TIF1γ and anti-NXP2 (cancer association in adults), anti-MDA5 (minimal myositis, rapidly progressive interstitial lung disease, notable in East Asia) and anti-SAE. Adult disease carries an increased risk of malignancy, especially within three years of diagnosis.
det.clinical: Symmetric proximal weakness evolves over weeks to months, often with myalgia, dysphagia and neck flexor weakness. Skin signs may precede weakness: heliotrope rash, Gottron papules over the knuckles, V-sign and shawl sign, nailfold capillary changes and mechanic's hands. Some patients have skin disease without weakness (amyopathic). Interstitial lung disease, arthritis, Raynaud phenomenon, calcinosis (especially in juvenile disease) and cardiac involvement occur. Ovarian, lung, gastric, nasopharyngeal and haematological cancers are typical associations.
det.diagnosis: The EULAR/ACR 2017 classification criteria combine age, weakness pattern, skin features, CK, anti-Jo-1 and biopsy findings. CK is often raised but may be normal. EMG shows an irritable myopathy and MRI STIR shows muscle and fascial oedema guiding biopsy. Biopsy features perifascicular atrophy, MxA expression and capillary loss. Screen all adults for cancer (CT chest/abdomen/pelvis, gynaecological and age-appropriate tests, PET in high-risk subsets) and for lung involvement with HRCT and lung function.
det.treatment: First-line treatment is corticosteroids (e.g. prednisolone around 1 mg/kg/day, with IV pulses in severe cases) combined early with methotrexate, azathioprine or mycophenolate to limit steroid exposure. IVIG is effective for refractory disease and dysphagia, and rituximab, calcineurin inhibitors and JAK inhibitors are further options. Anti-MDA5 ILD needs aggressive combined immunosuppression. Treat associated cancer, protect skin from sun, use hydroxychloroquine for skin disease, and give rehabilitation plus bone and infection prophylaxis.
det.prognosis: Most patients improve with treatment, though relapses are common; survival is reduced mainly by malignancy and rapidly progressive lung disease.
pearls: Rash plus proximal weakness in an adult = search for cancer.
Anti-MDA5: little weakness, ulcerating skin lesions, rapidly progressive lung disease.
Perifascicular atrophy on biopsy is the classic pathological clue.
det.thd: Dermatomyositis เป็นโรคภูมิคุ้มกันที่ทำให้กล้ามเนื้อและผิวหนังอักเสบ เกี่ยวข้องกับ interferon และการทำลายหลอดเลือดเล็กในกล้ามเนื้อ อาการคืออ่อนแรงต้นแขนต้นขาสองข้างเท่ากันภายในหลายสัปดาห์ ผื่นม่วงรอบตา (heliotrope) ผื่นที่ข้อนิ้ว (Gottron) และอาจมีปอดอักเสบ ในผู้ใหญ่ต้องค้นหามะเร็งแฝงโดยเฉพาะเมื่อพบ anti-TIF1γ วินิจฉัยด้วย CK, myositis antibodies, MRI และตัดชิ้นเนื้อพบ perifascicular atrophy รักษาด้วยสเตียรอยด์ร่วมกับยากดภูมิ เช่น methotrexate และให้ IVIG ในรายที่ดื้อยา

name: Developmental and epileptic encephalopathies (DEEs)
formal: Severe early-onset epilepsies in which epileptic activity and the underlying cause contribute to developmental slowing, e.g. West, Dravet and Lennox-Gastaut syndromes.
simple: Severe childhood epilepsies in which frequent seizures also hold back development.
aN: dees | developmental and epileptic encephalopathies

name: Devic’s disease
formal: Neuromyelitis optica, an antibody-mediated (AQP4-IgG) disease with optic neuritis and longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis, plus area postrema syndrome.
simple: An immune disease that attacks the eye nerves and spinal cord, causing vision loss and weakness.

name: Diabetic autonomic neuropathy
formal: Small-fibre autonomic neuropathy in diabetes causing orthostatic hypotension, gastroparesis, erectile dysfunction, bladder dysfunction, resting tachycardia, and hypoglycaemia unawareness.
simple: Damage to the nerves that run automatic body functions in people with diabetes, causing dizziness, stomach and bladder problems.
more: Autonomic reflex testing and tilt table assess it. Tight glucose control, fludrocortisone or midodrine, prokinetics, and symptomatic care are used.

name: Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA)
formal: Metabolic complication of insulin deficiency with hyperglycaemia and acidosis; may cause cerebral oedema, particularly in children, and altered consciousness.
simple: A dangerous complication of diabetes with very high blood sugar and acid build-up, causing drowsiness and sometimes brain swelling.
aN: dka | diabetic ketoacidosis

name: Diabetic mononeuropathies
formal: Focal nerve lesions in diabetes, including cranial nerve III and VI palsies, and median, ulnar, and peroneal neuropathies, mediated by ischaemia and entrapment.
simple: Damage to a single nerve in people with diabetes, such as a sudden eye-movement palsy.
more: Control glucose, treat entrapment; cranial palsies usually recover in 2 to 3 months.

name: Diabetic neuropathic cachexia
formal: Acute painful diabetic neuropathy with severe weight loss, burning pain, allodynia, and depression, often after starting insulin or glycaemic improvement.
simple: A rare form of painful diabetic nerve damage with marked weight loss, often after blood sugar is brought under control.
more: Pain control with neuropathic agents and good nutrition; it generally improves spontaneously within about a year.

name: Diabetic neuropathies
formal: Neuropathies due to diabetes: distal symmetric polyneuropathy, autonomic neuropathy, radiculoplexopathy, mononeuropathies and cranial neuropathies.
simple: Nerve damage caused by diabetes, causing numbness, pain, weakness or dizziness.

name: Diabetic neuropathy
formal: Most common form is length-dependent sensory polyneuropathy with painful feet, numbness and loss of ankle reflexes, from chronic hyperglycaemia and small-vessel disease.
simple: Nerve damage from diabetes, usually causing numb, tingling or painful feet.

name: Diabetic polyradiculopathy
formal: Diabetic lumbosacral or thoracic radiculoplexus syndrome with asymmetric severe pain, weight loss, and proximal leg weakness, thought to be microvasculitic and immune-mediated.
simple: Sudden severe pain and weakness in the thigh or trunk in people with diabetes, usually on one side.
more: MRI excludes compressive lesions; nerve biopsy may show microvasculitis. Treatment is pain control and rehabilitation, sometimes with immunotherapy; recovery is slow.

name: Diabetic radiculoplexus neuropathy
formal: Painful asymmetric lumbosacral or cervical radiculoplexus syndrome in diabetes, with proximal weakness and weight loss, linked to microvasculitis.
simple: A painful nerve disease in diabetes affecting the thigh or hip, with wasting and weight loss.
more: Pain control, glycaemic control, and sometimes immunotherapy such as IVIG or steroids; recovery over months to years.
th: เส้นประสาทเอว-ก้นอักเสบในผู้ป่วยเบาหวาน — ปวดต้นขารุนแรง น้ำหนักลด แล้วต้นขาลีบอ่อนแรง
tempoNote: Pain and weakness evolve over weeks to months; slow partial recovery
feat: Often type 2 diabetes with good control and recent weight loss
Severe thigh/hip pain, then asymmetric proximal leg weakness and wasting (quadriceps, hip flexors)
Absent knee jerk; often spreads to the other side; caused by microvasculitis
inv: EMG: denervation in multiple roots and plexus territories including paraspinals
MRI lumbar spine and plexus to exclude compression or tumour; CSF protein may be raised

case.story: Lost 8 kg over 2 months with burning pain in the right thigh keeping him awake; now his knee buckles.
case.exam: Wasted right quadriceps and weak hip flexion and adduction, absent right knee jerk, patchy anterior thigh numbness.
case.tests: EMG: denervation in L2–L4 muscles and paraspinals; MRI: no compression; HbA1c 7.0%.
case.q: What is the usual natural history?
case.a: Gradual improvement over months to years, often incomplete; pain control and rehabilitation are central (immunotherapy is debated).

ddx.pt: Back pain, single root, disc on MRI
Symmetric, demyelinating NCS, no weight loss
Systemic vasculitis markers, upper limb mononeuropathies

aN: diabetic amyotrophy | diabetic lumbosacral radiculoplexus neuropathy | dlrpn | bruns garland syndrome | proximal diabetic neuropathy

det.patho: Diabetic lumbosacral radiculoplexus neuropathy is caused by an immune-mediated microvasculitis of small epineurial and perineurial vessels, leading to ischaemic axonal injury across roots, plexus and peripheral nerves. It typically occurs in older people with type 2 diabetes, often with relatively mild or recently improved glycaemic control, so it is not simply a consequence of hyperglycaemia. Similar non-diabetic and cervical/thoracic forms exist.
det.clinical: Onset is usually with intense unilateral thigh, hip or buttock pain, followed within days to weeks by weakness of proximal leg muscles (quadriceps, iliopsoas, adductors) and sometimes distal muscles. Substantial unintentional weight loss is very common. The opposite leg is often involved weeks to months later. The knee jerk is lost on the affected side, and patients may need walking aids or a wheelchair at the nadir. Thoracic radiculopathy can coexist, causing abdominal pain or bulging.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis rests on the clinical picture plus EMG showing active denervation in multiple lumbosacral root and nerve territories, including paraspinals. MRI of the lumbar spine and plexus excludes compressive or neoplastic lesions and may show plexus enhancement. CSF protein is often raised. Consider malignancy, lymphoma infiltration, retroperitoneal haematoma, CIDP and vasculitis in the differential.
det.treatment: Management is largely supportive: aggressive neuropathic pain control, physiotherapy, falls prevention and maintaining diabetes control. Immunotherapy (IV methylprednisolone or IVIG) has been used, particularly for severe pain, but randomised evidence shows benefit mainly for pain and sensory symptoms rather than motor recovery, so use is individualised. Steroids worsen glycaemic control and require close monitoring.
det.prognosis: The illness is monophasic in most; pain improves first and strength recovers gradually over months to years, often incompletely. Recurrence is uncommon.
pearls: Painful thigh wasting with weight loss in a diabetic: DLRPN — exclude cancer and compression.
Often follows a period of improved or tight glucose control.
Contralateral spread is common; warn the patient.
det.thd: Diabetic radiculoplexus neuropathy (diabetic amyotrophy) เกิดจากหลอดเลือดเล็กที่เลี้ยงรากประสาทและ plexus อักเสบ มักในผู้สูงอายุเบาหวานชนิดที่ 2 ซึ่งคุมน้ำตาลได้ไม่แย่ เริ่มด้วยปวดต้นขาหรือสะโพกรุนแรงข้างเดียว น้ำหนักลด แล้วต้นขาลีบอ่อนแรง knee jerk หาย และมักลามไปอีกข้าง วินิจฉัยด้วย EMG และ MRI เพื่อแยกการกดทับหรือมะเร็ง รักษาหลักคือคุมปวด กายภาพ ส่วน steroid/IVIG พิจารณาเป็นราย ๆ และค่อย ๆ ฟื้นตัวเป็นเดือนถึงปี

name: Dialysis disequilibrium syndrome
formal: Cerebral oedema from rapid osmotic shifts during haemodialysis, causing headache, nausea, confusion and seizures.
simple: Headache, confusion or seizures during or after dialysis because of fast changes in body fluids.

name: Dialysis encephalopathy
formal: Progressive encephalopathy in long-term dialysis from aluminium toxicity, with speech arrest, myoclonus, seizures and dementia.
simple: A brain disorder in long-term dialysis patients, once from aluminium, with speech problems and seizures.

name: Diaphragmatic myoclonus
formal: Rhythmic or irregular involuntary contractions of the diaphragm, causing hiccup-like belly jerks, often from phrenic nerve irritation or drugs.
simple: Repeated jerks of the breathing muscle that cause belly movements like hiccups.

name: Diaphragmatic myoclonus/flutter
formal: Rhythmic involuntary diaphragm contractions, with 'belly dancer' movements, seen with phrenic nerve irritation or brainstem lesions.
simple: Repeated jerks or flutters of the breathing muscle.

name: Diazepam akathisia
formal: Akathisia-like restlessness related to diazepam, usually on withdrawal, with inability to sit still.
simple: A feeling of restlessness related to using or stopping diazepam.

name: Diffuse astrocytoma
formal: WHO grade 2 infiltrating glioma, often IDH mutated, in young adults presenting with seizures; slow growth with eventual malignant transformation.
simple: A slow-growing but spreading brain tumour, often first noticed through seizures.

name: Diffuse fasciitis with eosinophilia
formal: Eosinophilic fasciitis (Shulman syndrome) with sudden skin thickening and induration of limbs sparing hands, peripheral eosinophilia, and inflammation of fascia on MRI or biopsy.
simple: A rare condition where the tissue layer under the skin thickens and tightens the limbs, often after strenuous exercise.
more: Full-thickness biopsy including fascia is diagnostic; corticosteroids work well, with methotrexate as an adjunct.

name: Diffuse fasciitis with eosinophilia/Shulman syndrome
formal: Eosinophilic fasciitis with rapid skin and fascial induration, peripheral eosinophilia, groove sign, and responsiveness to corticosteroids.
simple: A rare disease where tissue under the skin thickens, tightening the limbs.
more: Deep biopsy and MRI; prednisolone with methotrexate for steroid sparing.
nN: diffuse fasciitis with eosinophilia shulman syndrome

name: Diffuse inflammatory lymphocytosis syndrome (DILS)
formal: HIV-related CD8 lymphocytosis with salivary gland swelling, sicca and extraglandular disease including peripheral neuropathy, meningitis and cranial neuropathies.
simple: A condition in HIV with dry mouth, swollen glands and sometimes nerve damage.
aN: dils | diffuse inflammatory lymphocytosis syndrome

name: Diffuse Lewy body disease (DLBD)
formal: Alpha-synucleinopathy with widespread cortical and subcortical Lewy bodies, causing dementia, parkinsonism and psychosis; synonym for dementia with Lewy bodies.
simple: A brain disease with protein deposits that causes dementia, hallucinations and stiffness.
more: Pathologically widespread Lewy bodies on alpha-synuclein staining, often with Alzheimer-type changes; DAT-SPECT is abnormal. Management follows DLB with cholinesterase inhibitors; avoid dopamine antagonists, since neuroleptic sensitivity is severe.
aN: dlbd | diffuse lewy body disease

name: Diffuse neurofibrillary tangles with calcification (DNTC)
formal: Rare tauopathy with neurofibrillary tangles and basal ganglia calcification without amyloid plaques, causing dementia and parkinsonism, mainly in Japan.
simple: A rare dementia with tangles and calcium deposits in the brain.
nN: diffuse neurofibrillary tangles with calcification dntc
aN: dntc | diffuse neurofibrillary tangles with calcification

name: Diffuse NFTs with calcification
formal: Rare tauopathy with neurofibrillary tangles and calcification without amyloid plaques, causing dementia and parkinsonism.
simple: A rare dementia with brain tangles and calcium deposits.

name: Diffuse non-necrotising cachectic myopathy
formal: Muscle wasting in cachexia from cancer or chronic disease with atrophic non-necrotic fibres, without inflammation.
simple: Muscle wasting and weakness in people who are severely underweight from long-term illness.

name: Diphasic dyskinesias
formal: Levodopa-induced dyskinesias occurring at onset and end of dose, with improvement during peak dose, mainly involving the legs.
simple: Involuntary movements in Parkinson disease that appear when levodopa starts and wears off.

name: Diphasic dystonia
formal: Levodopa-induced dystonia occurring when drug levels rise and fall, mostly in legs.
simple: Painful muscle twisting in Parkinson disease when levodopa starts to work or wear off.

name: Diphtheritic neuropathy
formal: Demyelinating neuropathy following diphtheria toxin, starting with palatal and accommodation paralysis, then generalised sensorimotor neuropathy.
simple: Nerve damage that follows infection with diphtheria bacteria, with throat and eye muscle weakness first.
more: Antitoxin and antibiotics for infection; prevention by vaccination; most patients recover fully.
th: เส้นประสาทเสื่อมจากพิษเชื้อคอตีบ — เริ่มที่เพดานอ่อนและคอ แล้วลามเป็น demyelinating neuropathy ทั่วตัวหลายสัปดาห์ต่อมา
tempoNote: Biphasic: bulbar/palatal palsy in weeks 1–4, then generalised neuropathy at weeks 5–8
feat: Recent membranous pharyngitis (grey adherent membrane) or skin diphtheria, often in unvaccinated people
Early palatal weakness: nasal speech and fluid regurgitating through the nose
Blurred near vision from accommodation paralysis with relatively preserved pupillary light reaction
Weeks later: ascending or generalised weakness, sensory loss and areflexia; may need ventilation
Myocarditis with arrhythmia, often in the same time window
inv: Throat swab culture and toxin PCR for Corynebacterium diphtheriae
NCS: demyelinating features with prolonged latencies and slowed conduction
CSF: raised protein, normal cells
ECG and troponin for myocarditis

case.who: 11-year-old boy from a remote northern village, incompletely vaccinated
case.story: Severe sore throat with a grey membrane three weeks ago; now his voice is nasal and water comes out of his nose when drinking. Two weeks later his legs become weak.
case.exam: Palatal palsy, impaired near focusing, symmetric limb weakness, global areflexia, distal sensory loss.
case.tests: Throat culture grew toxigenic C. diphtheriae; NCS shows marked slowing; CSF protein 1.2 g/L, cells 2; ECG first-degree AV block.
case.q: What does the time course tell you compared with GBS?
case.a: The biphasic course — bulbar palsy weeks after a throat infection followed later by limb neuropathy — reflects toxin action; GBS usually evolves to nadir within 4 weeks of a non-specific infection without the palatal-accommodation start.

det.patho: Diphtheria toxin, produced by toxigenic C. diphtheriae, is absorbed from the local infection and enters Schwann cells, where it blocks protein synthesis. This causes a non-inflammatory demyelination, first in nerves near the infection (palate, pharynx) and later in the peripheral nerves generally, with the dorsal root ganglia and roots also affected. Severity relates to the size of the membrane and delay in antitoxin.
det.clinical: Neurological complications occur in a sizeable minority of severe cases. Palatal paralysis appears in the first weeks, followed by cranial neuropathies including accommodation failure, then a generalised sensorimotor demyelinating neuropathy at about 5–8 weeks. Respiratory muscle weakness and cardiac involvement can be fatal. Cases still occur in under-vaccinated communities, including outbreaks in parts of Southeast Asia.
det.diagnosis: Key is the history of membranous pharyngitis or skin ulcer, the biphasic course and isolation of a toxin-producing strain. NCS shows demyelination that may lag behind the clinical course; CSF protein is raised. Distinguish from GBS, botulism and poliomyelitis.
det.treatment: Give diphtheria antitoxin as early as possible during the acute infection, plus antibiotics (penicillin or erythromycin) and isolation. Once neuropathy begins antitoxin has limited effect, so care is supportive: airway protection, ventilation, cardiac monitoring and rehabilitation. IVIG is not of proven benefit. Vaccinate after recovery and trace contacts.
det.prognosis: Survivors usually recover fully over weeks to months as remyelination occurs.
pearls: Nasal voice and nasal regurgitation weeks after a sore throat in an unvaccinated child: think diphtheria.
Accommodation paralysis with preserved light reflex is characteristic.
Watch the heart — myocarditis kills more often than neuropathy.
det.thd: Diphtheritic neuropathy เกิดจากพิษของเชื้อคอตีบที่ทำลาย Schwann cell อาการเป็นสองช่วง ช่วงแรกเพดานอ่อนอ่อนแรง เสียงขึ้นจมูก สำลักน้ำออกจมูก และมองใกล้ไม่ชัด ต่อมา 5–8 สัปดาห์มีแขนขาอ่อนแรงแบบ demyelinating neuropathy คล้าย GBS และอาจมีกล้ามเนื้อหัวใจอักเสบ การรักษาคือให้ antitoxin และยาปฏิชีวนะแต่เนิ่น ๆ ร่วมกับดูแลการหายใจและหัวใจ

name: Disequilibrium syndrome
formal: Imbalance and unsteadiness from vestibular, cerebellar or osmotic shifts, including dialysis disequilibrium; subjective unsteadiness without true vertigo.
simple: A feeling of being unsteady and off balance.

name: Disorders of glycosylation
formal: Congenital disorders of glycosylation: inherited defects of glycan synthesis causing hypotonia, ataxia, cerebellar hypoplasia, seizures, coagulopathy and liver disease; PMM2-CDG is commonest.
simple: Inherited problems in attaching sugar chains to proteins, causing developmental delay, poor balance and seizures.

name: Dissociative amnesia
formal: Reversible inability to recall autobiographical information, usually after stress or trauma, in the absence of structural brain disease.
simple: Sudden memory loss for personal information after stress, with no brain injury.

name: Dissociative disorders
formal: Disorders with disruption of consciousness, memory, identity or perception, including depersonalisation, dissociative amnesia and identity disorder.
simple: Conditions where a person feels detached from their memory, identity or surroundings.

name: Dissociative neurological symptom disorder
formal: Functional neurological disorder with symptoms such as weakness, tremor, gait disturbance or sensory loss, with positive clinical signs and no structural disease.
simple: Real neurological symptoms like weakness or shaking caused by how the brain functions, not by structural damage.

name: Dissociative seizure
formal: Functional seizure resembling epileptic events but without epileptiform EEG activity; often with eyes closed, long duration, and emotional triggers.
simple: A seizure-like attack that is not caused by abnormal electrical discharge in the brain.

name: Distal acquired demyelinating sensory neuropathy
formal: Slowly progressive sensory neuropathy with distal numbness, ataxia and demyelinating changes, with anti-MAG IgM in many.
simple: A nerve condition causing numbness in the hands and feet and unsteady walking.

name: Distal hereditary motor neuropathies (distal HMN)
formal: Inherited length-dependent motor axonal neuropathies with distal weakness and wasting without sensory loss, from HSPB1, GARS, BSCL2 and others.
simple: Inherited nerve diseases that weaken and thin the muscles in the hands and feet without numbness.
th: เส้นประสาทสั่งการปลายเสื่อมทางพันธุกรรม — เหมือน CMT แต่ไม่มีอาการชา
feat: Slowly progressive distal weakness and wasting, legs first; pes cavus
Clinically and electrically normal sensation
Subtype clues: hand-predominant (GARS, BSCL2), vocal cord palsy, pyramidal signs
inv: NCS: low motor amplitudes with normal sensory responses
Gene panel (HSPB1, HSPB8, GARS1, BSCL2, DYNC1H1 …)

case.story: Trips over steps since her teens; her father 'walked on high arches'.
case.exam: Bilateral foot drop, pes cavus, absent ankle jerks, normal sensation to all modalities.
case.tests: Low peroneal CMAPs, normal sural SNAPs; HSPB1 variant.
case.q: What single finding separates this from CMT2?
case.a: Preserved sensory nerve action potentials (pure motor neuropathy).

Proximal-predominant, SMN1 deletion

nN: distal hereditary motor neuropathies distal hmn
aN: distal hmn | distal hereditary motor neuropathies | dhmn | distal spinal muscular atrophy | dsma | hmn

det.patho: Distal HMNs are a genetically heterogeneous group of length-dependent degenerations of lower motor neurons and their axons, sparing sensory fibres. Genes involve protein folding (HSPB1, HSPB8), tRNA synthetases (GARS1), axonal transport (DYNC1H1, BICD2, DCTN1), RNA processing (SETX, IGHMBP2) and ion channels (TRPV4). Many genes overlap with CMT2, so the distinction from axonal CMT is a spectrum. Biallelic SORD variants have recently been recognised as a relatively common recessive cause.
det.clinical: Most patients develop slowly progressive distal leg weakness and wasting in childhood to early adulthood, with foot drop, pes cavus and reduced ankle reflexes. Specific features suggest genes: hand-first weakness (GARS1, BSCL2), pyramidal signs (BSCL2, SETX), vocal cord paresis (DCTN1, TRPV4), and infantile diaphragmatic paralysis (IGHMBP2, also called SMARD1). Sensory symptoms are absent or minimal.
det.diagnosis: Nerve conduction shows reduced motor amplitudes with normal sensory responses, and EMG shows chronic distal denervation. Next-generation sequencing panels for motor neuropathy and CMT genes are the main test; serum sorbitol helps when SORD neuropathy is suspected. Exclude MMN (conduction block), distal SMA variants, distal myopathies and acquired motor neuronopathies.
det.treatment: Most forms lack any disease-modifying drug; therapies targeting sorbitol accumulation in SORD neuropathy are in trials. Management involves ankle-foot orthoses, physiotherapy, orthopaedic foot surgery and hand therapy. Patients with SMARD1 need early respiratory support. Genetic counselling is recommended.
det.prognosis: Usually slowly progressive with preserved walking for decades, except for severe infantile forms such as SMARD1.
pearls: CMT picture with normal sensory potentials = distal HMN.
Hand weakness plus leg spasticity suggests BSCL2 (Silver syndrome).
det.thd: Distal HMN เป็นกลุ่มโรคพันธุกรรมที่ทำให้เซลล์ประสาทสั่งการและแอกซอนส่วนปลายเสื่อม โดยไม่มีผลต่อระบบรับความรู้สึก มีหลายยีน เช่น HSPB1, GARS1 และ SORD ผู้ป่วยมีขาอ่อนแรงปลายเท้า เท้าตก และอุ้งเท้าสูงคล้าย CMT แต่การรับความรู้สึกและ SNAP ปกติ บางชนิดเริ่มที่มือ มีสายเสียงอัมพาต หรือมีกล้ามเนื้อเกร็ง การวินิจฉัยใช้ NCS และตรวจยีนแบบ panel ส่วนการรักษาเน้นกายอุปกรณ์และกายภาพบำบัด

name: Distal limb dystonia
formal: Focal dystonia affecting the foot or hand, such as striatal toe, equinovarus foot or writer's cramp, arising from primary, drug-related, Parkinson-related or structural causes.
simple: Involuntary twisting or cramping of the hand or foot that interferes with writing or walking.
more: Examine for a secondary cause. Botulinum toxin is first-line, with anticholinergics, levodopa trial and sometimes deep brain stimulation for severe cases.

name: Distal myopathies
formal: Inherited or acquired myopathies with weakness starting in hands or feet, such as Welander, Miyoshi (dysferlin), GNE and titinopathy.
simple: Muscle diseases that weaken the hands, feet and lower legs first.
more: Diagnosis via CK (mild to markedly raised), muscle MRI patterns, biopsy with rimmed vacuoles or dystrophic change, and gene panels. Mostly slowly progressive with no specific cure; GNE myopathy spares the quadriceps, and dysferlin can be checked by immunoblot.
th: กล้ามเนื้อเสื่อมแบบเริ่มที่ปลายแขนปลายขา — แยกชนิดตามกล้ามเนื้อที่เป็นก่อน (หน้าแข้ง vs น่อง)
feat: Weakness starts distally with preserved reflexes and sensation
Anterior leg (foot drop) — GNE (quadriceps spared), Laing; posterior calf (cannot tiptoe) — dysferlin/Miyoshi; hands — Welander
Proximal spread later
inv: CK: very high in dysferlin, mild in GNE
EMG myopathic (excludes neuropathy); muscle MRI pattern
Biopsy: rimmed vacuoles in GNE; gene panel

case.story: Slapping feet for 5 years, now weak hips but strong thighs.
case.exam: Bilateral foot drop, weak hamstrings, strikingly preserved quadriceps, normal sensation and knee jerks.
case.tests: CK 600 U/L; biopsy: rimmed vacuoles; biallelic GNE variants.
case.q: Which muscle sparing is characteristic here?
case.a: Quadriceps sparing in GNE myopathy, despite marked anterior leg and hamstring weakness.

ddx.pt: Sensory loss, absent reflexes, neuropathic NCS
Older, finger flexors and quadriceps affected
Myotonia, ptosis, cataract

aN: distal myopathy | miyoshi myopathy | gne myopathy | nonaka myopathy | welander myopathy | udd myopathy

det.patho: Distal myopathies are genetic muscle diseases that begin in hand, foreleg or calf muscles. Causes include dysferlin (Miyoshi), GNE (sialic acid synthesis; Nonaka/GNE myopathy), titin (Udd tibial), MYH7 (Laing), TIA1 (Welander), ANO5, and myofibrillar myopathy genes such as desmin, myotilin and ZASP. Inheritance can be recessive or dominant depending on the gene. Several show rimmed vacuoles or protein aggregates on biopsy.
det.clinical: The first muscles involved help identify the type. Anterior leg weakness with foot drop occurs in GNE (quadriceps spared), Laing (early adulthood, toe extensors and neck flexors) and Udd (late onset, mild); posterior calf weakness with inability to stand on tiptoe occurs in dysferlin and ANO5 disease; finger and wrist extensor weakness occurs in Welander. Cardiomyopathy and arrhythmia are important in myofibrillar myopathies and some MYH7 cases. Reflexes and sensation are preserved early.
det.diagnosis: CK is very high in dysferlinopathy and normal to modestly raised in most others. EMG confirms a myopathic process and excludes neuropathy. Muscle MRI patterns are highly informative, and biopsy may show rimmed vacuoles (GNE, Welander), inflammation (dysferlin) or myofibrillar aggregates. Genetic panels confirm the subtype. Exclude CMT, distal HMN, inclusion body myositis and myotonic dystrophy.
det.treatment: No disease-modifying treatment is approved; sialic acid replacement for GNE myopathy has been studied without clear benefit. Management includes ankle-foot orthoses, hand splints, physiotherapy and, where relevant, cardiac surveillance with pacemaker or ICD. Steroids are not helpful.
det.prognosis: Most forms progress slowly and life expectancy is near normal, except when cardiac or respiratory involvement is significant.
pearls: Foot drop with preserved reflexes and normal sensation suggests a distal myopathy rather than neuropathy.
Quadriceps sparing is the signature of GNE myopathy.
Myofibrillar myopathies need cardiac screening.
det.thd: Distal myopathies เป็นกลุ่มโรคกล้ามเนื้อเสื่อมทางพันธุกรรมที่เริ่มอ่อนแรงจากปลายแขนหรือปลายขา แยกชนิดได้จากกล้ามเนื้อที่เป็นก่อน เช่น หน้าแข้งอ่อนแรงจนเท้าตกใน GNE myopathy ซึ่ง quadriceps ยังแข็งแรง หรือน่องอ่อนแรงจนเขย่งไม่ได้ใน Miyoshi (dysferlin) ซึ่ง CK สูงมาก รีเฟล็กซ์และการรับความรู้สึกยังปกติในระยะแรก ช่วยแยกจากโรคเส้นประสาท การวินิจฉัยใช้ EMG, MRI กล้ามเนื้อ ชิ้นเนื้อ และตรวจยีน การรักษาเป็นแบบประคับประคอง และบางชนิดต้องเฝ้าระวังหัวใจ

name: Distal myopathy
formal: Group of inherited or acquired myopathies with predominantly distal weakness, such as dysferlinopathy, GNE myopathy, Welander, Miyoshi, and ZASP types.
simple: Muscle diseases that mainly weaken the hands, feet, and lower legs.
more: CK, MRI, biopsy, and genetic panels determine type; supportive treatment; progression is usually slow.

name: Distal sensory peripheral neuropathy (DSPN)
formal: Common form of diabetic and other length-dependent neuropathy with distal numbness, tingling and burning pain in the feet and loss of ankle reflexes.
simple: Nerve damage causing numbness, tingling or pain in the feet and hands, often caused by diabetes.
more: Nerve conduction shows reduced sural amplitudes with preserved large-fibre velocities; skin biopsy nerve fibre density or QSART assess small-fibre involvement. Treat glycaemia, give foot care, and use duloxetine, pregabalin or amitriptyline for pain.
aN: dspn | distal sensory peripheral neuropathy

name: Distal SMA
formal: Distal hereditary motor neuropathy, with progressive distal weakness and wasting without sensory loss, from mutations in HSPB1, GARS, BSCL2, and others.
simple: An inherited nerve cell disease that slowly weakens the hands and feet without numbness.
more: EMG shows motor axonal loss; gene panels; supportive care.

name: Distal symmetric sensory neuropathy (DSSN)
formal: Length-dependent sensory axonal neuropathy with burning feet and numbness, often from diabetes and chemotherapy.
simple: Nerve damage causing numb and burning feet.
aN: dssn | distal symmetric sensory neuropathy

name: Dok-7 myasthenia
formal: Congenital myasthenic syndrome from DOK7 mutation causing limb-girdle weakness, ptosis, and fatigue, with endplate maldevelopment, and worsening with pyridostigmine.
simple: An inherited neuromuscular junction disorder with weakness of the hips and shoulders, presenting in childhood.
more: Salbutamol or ephedrine is effective; pyridostigmine can worsen symptoms.

name: Dominant intermediate CMT disease
formal: Group of CMT subtypes with intermediate conduction velocities of 25-45 m/s and dominant inheritance, e.g. DNM2, YARS, MPZ.
simple: An inherited nerve disease with mid-range nerve damage causing weakness and wasting in the feet and hands.
more: Nerve conduction velocity intermediate between demyelinating and axonal types, and nerve biopsy shows both features; genetics confirms the subtype. Management is supportive with foot care and orthoses; avoid neurotoxic drugs.

name: Doose syndrome (myoclonic-astatic epilepsy)
formal: Epilepsy syndrome with myoclonic-atonic seizures in early childhood, with drop attacks, mixed seizures, variable outcome; ketogenic diet helps.
simple: A childhood epilepsy with sudden jerks and drops that make the child fall.

name: Dopa-responsive dystonia (DRD)
formal: Dystonia due to GCH1 or TH deficiency with childhood onset, diurnal fluctuation and dramatic response to low-dose levodopa.
simple: A childhood movement disorder with twisting postures that worsens through the day and responds well to a small dose of levodopa.
more: Normal DAT-SPECT and no neurodegeneration; CSF biopterin and neopterin are low in GCH1 and a phenylalanine loading test is abnormal. Autosomal dominant with reduced penetrance.
ab: hereditary progressive dystonia with diurnal fluctuation
th: dystonia ในเด็กที่เริ่มจากขาและแย่ลงตอนเย็น ตอบสนองดีมากต่อ levodopa ขนาดต่ำ ส่วนใหญ่จากยีน GCH1
tempoNote: Childhood onset (often 5–8 years), slowly progressive, with marked worsening as the day goes on
feat: Foot or leg dystonia in a child causing toe-walking or an odd gait, often first noticed by teachers
Clear diurnal fluctuation: near-normal in the morning, worse in the evening or after exercise
Brisk reflexes and apparent extensor plantar responses that mimic spastic diplegia
Adult-onset cases may show mild parkinsonism or arm tremor
Dramatic and lasting response to small doses of levodopa without motor fluctuations
inv: Therapeutic levodopa trial — the key bedside test
Genetic testing: GCH1 (dominant, reduced penetrance); TH and SPR in recessive forms
CSF neurotransmitters: low HVA, low biopterin and neopterin in GCH1 deficiency; phenylalanine loading test where available
DAT-SPECT normal, which helps separate it from juvenile parkinsonism

case.story: Since age 7 she tiptoes and her right foot turns in, mainly after school; she runs well in the morning. Diagnosed as cerebral palsy at a district hospital, but birth and milestones were normal.
case.exam: Right foot inverted and plantar-flexed while walking, mild left-arm posturing at dusk, reflexes brisk, cognition normal.
case.tests: MRI brain normal. On carbidopa/levodopa at low dose, gait normal within two weeks. GCH1 heterozygous pathogenic variant.
case.q: Which feature of the history should have prompted a levodopa trial before labelling cerebral palsy?
case.a: Normal early development with later-onset gait problems and clear diurnal worsening — classic dopa-responsive dystonia.

det.patho: Most cases are autosomal dominant GCH1 mutations reducing GTP cyclohydrolase 1, the first step in tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4) synthesis. Low BH4 limits tyrosine hydroxylase, so striatal dopamine falls although nigral neurons survive. Penetrance is incomplete and higher in girls; recessive TH or SPR deficiency gives a more severe infantile phenotype.
det.clinical: Typical onset is around the first decade with leg dystonia that later spreads; symptoms fluctuate through the day and improve after sleep. Some develop parkinsonism in adulthood, and adult-onset relatives may present with tremor or mild parkinsonism alone. Recessive forms can show infantile hypotonia, oculogyric crises, developmental delay and autonomic features.
det.diagnosis: Every child or young adult with unexplained dystonia, or a spastic-diplegia picture without a clear cause, deserves a levodopa trial. Genetic testing confirms most cases, but a negative GCH1 result does not exclude DRD because some mutations are deletions or intronic. CSF pterins and amines and the phenylalanine loading test help when genetics are unhelpful. A normal DAT scan separates DRD from early-onset Parkinson disease.
det.treatment: Levodopa with a decarboxylase inhibitor, often only 50–300 mg/day of levodopa, yields near-complete and sustained benefit; start low and titrate. Long-term dyskinesia and wearing-off are uncommon. Severe recessive forms may need higher doses, 5-HTP or other neurotransmitter replacement.
det.prognosis: Excellent with treatment; most patients lead a normal life on stable low doses for decades.
pearls: Any childhood-onset dystonia: give a levodopa trial before investigations become exhausted.
Diurnal worsening is the historical clue.
DRD can masquerade as spastic diplegic cerebral palsy.
det.thd: DRD หรือ Segawa disease เกิดจากยีน GCH1 ทำให้สร้าง BH4 และ dopamine ได้น้อย เด็กมี dystonia ที่ขา เดินเขย่ง อาการแย่ช่วงเย็นและดีขึ้นหลังนอนหลับ มักถูกวินิจฉัยผิดเป็น cerebral palsy วินิจฉัยด้วยการลองให้ levodopa ขนาดต่ำซึ่งได้ผลดีมากและยั่งยืน ร่วมกับตรวจยีน

formal: Compulsive overuse of dopaminergic medication in Parkinson disease, causing hypomania, impulse control disorders, and dyskinesia.
simple: Compulsive over-use of Parkinson medicine, causing mood and behaviour changes.
more: Recognise by escalating levodopa dose despite motor control, with craving; treat by reducing levodopa and dopamine agonists, adding quetiapine or clozapine, and psychiatric support. Risk factors are young onset and prior substance use.

name: Dopamine β-hydroxylase (DβH) deficiency
formal: Congenital autonomic disorder causing noradrenaline deficiency with severe orthostatic hypotension, ptosis and low plasma noradrenaline.
simple: A rare inherited condition where the body cannot make noradrenaline, causing dizziness on standing and droopy eyelids.

name: Dorsal cord syndrome
formal: Posterior column spinal lesion with loss of proprioception and vibration, sensory ataxia and Romberg sign, with preserved motor function.
simple: Damage to the back part of the spinal cord that causes poor position sense and unsteady walking.

name: Dorsal root ganglionopathies
formal: Sensory neuronopathies with asymmetric non-length-dependent sensory loss, ataxia, and areflexia from paraneoplastic, Sjogren, toxic, or idiopathic causes.
simple: Damage to sensory nerve cell bodies, causing numbness and severe loss of position sense and balance.
more: Look for anti-Hu, Sjogren markers, and cisplatin or pyridoxine toxicity; treat the cause and immunotherapy where indicated.

feat: Asymmetric, non-length-dependent sensory loss — arms or face may be affected early
Severe proprioceptive loss: sensory ataxia, pseudoathetosis of outstretched fingers, Romberg
Areflexia with preserved strength
Causes: paraneoplastic (anti-Hu, small-cell lung cancer), Sjögren, cisplatin, B6 excess, idiopathic
inv: NCS: widespread reduced or absent SNAPs (including arms) with normal motor studies
Anti-Hu/CV2, anti-Ro/La, Schirmer test; CT/PET for cancer; B6 level; drug history
MRI spine: dorsal column T2 signal

case.story: Over 8 weeks her left hand became clumsy and numb, then both legs; she cannot find her keys in her bag without looking.
case.exam: Pseudoathetoid movements of the left hand with eyes closed, loss of joint position in all limbs, areflexia, normal power.
case.tests: Absent SNAPs in all four limbs, normal motor conduction; anti-Hu positive; CT: hilar mass.
case.q: Why is the asymmetric arm onset a clue?
case.a: Length-dependent neuropathies start in the feet; a ganglion (cell body) disorder can start anywhere, including the arms.

UMN signs, symmetric, low B12

aN: sensory neuronopathy | sensory ganglionopathy | ganglionopathy | sjogren neuronopathy | paraneoplastic sensory neuronopathy

det.patho: Sensory neuronopathy results from damage to the cell bodies of primary sensory neurons in the dorsal root ganglia, which lack a tight blood–nerve barrier and are exposed to circulating toxins and immune attack. Because the whole neuron degenerates, both the peripheral and central (dorsal column) processes are lost, independent of axon length. Main causes are paraneoplastic immunity (anti-Hu with small-cell lung cancer), Sjögren syndrome, platinum chemotherapy, pyridoxine toxicity, genetic causes such as RFC1 (CANVAS) and idiopathic cases.
det.clinical: Onset can be acute, subacute or chronic. Sensory loss is asymmetric and non-length-dependent, may begin in the hands, face or trunk, and is dominated by proprioceptive loss: clumsy hands, writhing pseudoathetoid fingers, an unsteady gait and Romberg positivity. Reflexes are diffusely lost while strength is preserved. Small-fibre forms cause pain and autonomic symptoms. Paraneoplastic cases may have associated encephalomyelitis, cerebellar or autonomic features, and the neuropathy can precede tumour discovery.
det.diagnosis: NCS show reduced or absent SNAPs in a non-length-dependent distribution (upper limb SNAPs as abnormal as lower) with normal motor studies. Validated diagnostic criteria weight asymmetric onset, upper limb involvement and SNAP pattern. Work-up includes onconeural antibodies (Hu, CV2/CRMP5), CT chest and PET when negative, anti-Ro/La with Schirmer test and salivary gland biopsy, vitamin B6, drug and toxin history, HIV, and RFC1 testing in chronic ataxia with cough or vestibular failure. MRI may show T2 hyperintensity in the dorsal columns.
det.treatment: Treat the underlying cause: tumour therapy for paraneoplastic disease (with immunotherapy, though response is usually modest), stopping pyridoxine or neurotoxic chemotherapy, and immunotherapy (IVIG, steroids, rituximab) in Sjögren-associated or idiopathic inflammatory cases. Early treatment is crucial because ganglion cells do not regenerate. Rehabilitation for ataxia and neuropathic pain management are supportive.
det.prognosis: Paraneoplastic forms usually leave severe disability; toxic forms may stabilise after removal of the cause. Established loss of ganglion neurons is generally permanent.
pearls: Absent arm SNAPs with normal motor studies and asymmetric onset = ganglionopathy.
Search for small-cell lung cancer in smokers, even if the CT is initially clear.
Pseudoathetosis of the outstretched hand with eyes closed is a bedside clue.

name: Dorsolateral prefrontal syndrome
formal: Frontal lobe syndrome from dorsolateral prefrontal damage with executive dysfunction, poor planning, perseveration and impaired working memory.
simple: Problems with planning, organising and flexible thinking from damage to the front of the brain.

name: Double athetosis
formal: Bilateral athetosis, slow writhing movements of limbs on both sides in cerebral palsy from perinatal basal ganglia injury.
simple: Slow twisting, writhing movements on both sides of the body, usually from early brain injury.

name: Down syndrome
formal: Trisomy 21 with intellectual disability, hypotonia, and neurological associations including early Alzheimer disease, epilepsy and atlantoaxial instability.
simple: A genetic condition from an extra chromosome 21, with learning difficulty, low muscle tone and distinctive features.

name: Down’s syndrome
formal: Trisomy 21 with intellectual disability, hypotonia, early Alzheimer pathology, epilepsy and atlantoaxial instability.
simple: A genetic condition from an extra copy of chromosome 21, causing learning disability and characteristic physical features.

name: Dravet syndrome
formal: SCN1A-related developmental epileptic encephalopathy beginning with febrile prolonged hemiclonic seizures at about six months, then multiple seizure types, ataxia and cognitive decline.
simple: A severe childhood epilepsy that starts in infancy with fever-triggered seizures and affects development.
th: ทารกปกติดีแต่มีชักนานร่วมกับไข้หรืออากาศร้อนตั้งแต่ขวบปีแรก ต่อมาชักหลายแบบและพัฒนาการช้า — SCN1A ห้ามใช้ sodium channel blocker
tempoNote: First seizure usually 4–8 months; frequent prolonged seizures in early childhood, developmental slowing from the second year
feat: Prolonged febrile or afebrile hemiclonic or generalised clonic seizures in the first year in a previously normal infant
Triggers: fever, warm baths, hot weather, exertion, vaccination-associated fever
From the second year: myoclonic jerks, atypical absences, focal seizures and repeated status epilepticus
Developmental plateau, behavioural problems, ataxia and later crouch gait
High risk of SUDEP
inv: SCN1A sequencing and deletion/duplication testing (positive in most), or epilepsy gene panel
EEG often normal at first, later generalised and multifocal discharges with photosensitivity in some
MRI usually normal; mainly used to exclude other causes

case.story: Three seizures since 5 months: a 40-minute left-sided clonic seizure with a mild fever after vaccination, then right-sided after a warm bath, then generalised during a cold. Development so far normal.
case.exam: Alert, normal tone and milestones.
case.tests: EEG normal between seizures; MRI normal. Gene panel: de novo truncating SCN1A variant.
case.q: Which common antiseizure drugs should be avoided, and what does the vaccine association mean for the family?
case.a: Avoid sodium-channel blockers (carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, phenytoin, lamotrigine) as they worsen seizures. The vaccine fever only unmasked an existing genetic disorder; it did not cause it, and vaccination should continue with fever prophylaxis.

read.where: Chapter 26 Infantile Epileptic Encephalopathies and De Novo Mutations
Chapter 18 Generalized Epilepsy Febrile Seizure Plus (GEFs+)

det.patho: About 80–90% carry a heterozygous loss-of-function SCN1A variant, usually de novo, reducing Nav1.1 sodium channel function mainly in inhibitory interneurons. Loss of inhibition makes the network hyperexcitable, which explains why further sodium channel blockade worsens seizures. Incidence is roughly 1 in 15,000–20,000; a few cases involve PCDH19 or other genes.
det.clinical: The first year features long hemiclonic seizures that switch side, triggered by fever or heat in an infant who is otherwise normal. Between ages 1 and 5 multiple seizure types emerge and development slows, with attention, language and motor problems; ataxia and a crouch gait appear later. Status epilepticus is frequent, and SUDEP risk is among the highest of all epilepsies. Milder SCN1A variants cause GEFS+ in families, a separate, less severe spectrum.
det.diagnosis: Suspect it with two or more prolonged or hemiclonic seizures before 1 year, especially with fever or heat, in a developmentally normal infant with normal MRI. Early EEG is often normal, so it cannot be used to exclude the diagnosis. Genetic testing confirms it and should be done early so that harmful drugs are avoided.
det.treatment: Valproate and clobazam are common first choices, with stiripentol, fenfluramine and cannabidiol as approved add-ons; topiramate and ketogenic diet also help. Avoid carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, phenytoin and lamotrigine. Each family needs a written rescue plan with buccal or intranasal midazolam, temperature control, avoidance of overheating, and SUDEP counselling. Antisense therapies targeting SCN1A expression are in clinical trials.
det.prognosis: Most have lasting intellectual disability and persistent seizures into adulthood; mortality is raised, chiefly from SUDEP and status.
pearls: Prolonged, side-switching febrile hemiclonic seizures in a normal infant: test SCN1A.
Sodium-channel blockers make Dravet worse.
Vaccines do not cause Dravet; they may unmask it via fever.
det.thd: Dravet syndrome เกิดจากยีน SCN1A ผิดปกติ (มักเกิดใหม่ ไม่ได้ถ่ายทอด) ทำให้เซลล์ประสาทยับยั้งทำงานลดลง ทารกที่ปกติดีจะชักนานร่วมกับไข้หรือความร้อนตั้งแต่ขวบปีแรก มักชักครึ่งซีกสลับข้าง ต่อมามีชักหลายแบบและพัฒนาการช้า ยืนยันด้วยการตรวจยีน รักษาด้วย valproate, clobazam, stiripentol, fenfluramine หรือ cannabidiol ห้ามใช้ยากลุ่ม sodium channel blocker เช่น carbamazepine ครอบครัวควรมียาฉุกเฉิน midazolam ติดบ้านและรับคำแนะนำเรื่อง SUDEP

name: Dropped head syndrome
formal: Severe neck extensor weakness with chin-on-chest posture, from myopathy, ALS, myasthenia, parkinsonism or isolated neck extensor myopathy.
simple: The head falls forward because the neck muscles are too weak to hold it up.

name: Drug-induced akathisia
formal: Akathisia from drugs like neuroleptics, with subjective inner restlessness and inability to stay still; treat by lowering dose, propranolol or anticholinergics.
simple: Inner restlessness and need to keep moving caused by a medicine.

name: Drug-induced choreas
formal: Chorea caused by medicines such as levodopa, neuroleptics, stimulants, antiepileptics and oral contraceptives; resolves after stopping.
simple: Dance-like involuntary movements caused by a medicine.

name: Drug-induced dystonias
formal: Dystonia from drugs, especially dopamine blockers and antiemetics, as acute reactions or tardive dystonia.
simple: Twisting muscle spasms caused by medicines, especially nausea or psychiatric drugs.
more: Withdraw the offending drug; acute dystonic reactions respond within minutes to anticholinergics such as benztropine. Tardive dystonia may persist and needs switching to clozapine or quetiapine, VMAT2 inhibitors, botulinum toxin or sometimes DBS.

name: Drug-induced movement disorders (DMID)
formal: Movement disorders caused by dopamine receptor blockers and other drugs, including acute dystonia, akathisia, parkinsonism, tardive dyskinesia and neuroleptic malignant syndrome.
simple: Movement problems such as stiffness, tremor, restlessness and twitching caused by medicines, especially antipsychotics.
more: Diagnosis relies on temporal link with the drug. Reduce or switch the agent; treat with anticholinergics, VMAT2 inhibitors for tardive dyskinesia or clozapine alternative.

name: Drug-induced myoclonus
formal: Myoclonus from drugs including opioids, antidepressants, lithium, antibiotics and levodopa, usually reversible after stopping.
simple: Sudden muscle jerks caused by a medicine.

name: Drug-induced parkinsonism (DIP)
formal: Parkinsonism from dopamine receptor blockers such as antipsychotics and metoclopramide, typically symmetric with bradykinesia and rigidity; usually resolves after stopping.
simple: Parkinson-like stiffness and slowness caused by certain medicines.

Postural/action tremor more than rest tremor; perioral 'rabbit' tremor is a clue
May coexist with akathisia or orofacial dyskinesia
Few non-motor prodromal features (normal smell, no REM sleep behaviour disorder)

Smell test can support unmasked PD if impaired

case.story: Taking flunarizine for 'vertigo' for 9 months from a private clinic; over 3 months he walks slowly and his voice softened.
case.exam: Symmetric bradykinesia and rigidity, mild postural tremor of both hands, reduced arm swing bilaterally, no gaze palsy.
case.tests: Routine blood tests normal; DAT-SPECT not available.
case.q: What should be done first, and when would you investigate for Parkinson disease?
case.a: Drug-induced parkinsonism from flunarizine: stop it and review over 3–6 months; if signs persist or progress beyond that, suspect unmasked PD and consider DAT imaging or a levodopa trial.

det.patho: Drugs that block striatal D2 receptors (typical and some atypical antipsychotics, antiemetics such as metoclopramide, the calcium-channel blockers flunarizine and cinnarizine) or deplete presynaptic dopamine (tetrabenazine, reserpine) reduce dopaminergic signalling. Risk rises with age, female sex, higher dose and pre-existing subclinical nigrostriatal loss. It is the commonest cause of secondary parkinsonism.
det.clinical: Symptoms often appear within three months of starting the drug and can be indistinguishable from PD, including asymmetry in some cases. Gait slowing and falls are common in older people and may be blamed on age. Some patients have a latent degenerative process; their signs improve on withdrawal then return later as PD.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is made by temporal association and resolution after withdrawal, which may take many months. A normal DAT scan supports pure DIP; an abnormal scan suggests unmasked degeneration. Remember that many patients do not report over-the-counter or clinic-dispensed drugs such as flunarizine or prochlorperazine.
det.treatment: Stop or reduce the causative drug where possible, or switch to an antipsychotic with lower D2 affinity (quetiapine or clozapine). Anticholinergics or amantadine can help while waiting, though anticholinergics are poorly tolerated in the elderly. Levodopa is reserved for disabling or persistent cases. Educate patients and prescribers to avoid re-exposure.
det.prognosis: Most recover within months of drug withdrawal; persistent or progressive signs after 6–12 months suggest underlying PD.
pearls: Ask specifically about flunarizine, cinnarizine and metoclopramide — common in Thai practice.
Recovery can lag drug withdrawal by months; do not label PD too early.
Normal DAT-SPECT favours pure drug-induced parkinsonism.

formal: X-linked dystrophin-deficiency myopathy with proximal weakness from early childhood, calf pseudohypertrophy, Gowers sign, very high CK, loss of ambulation by teens and cardiorespiratory failure.
simple: An inherited muscle disease in boys where muscles gradually weaken from early childhood, eventually affecting walking, breathing and the heart.
more: Diagnosis by CK, DMD gene deletion or duplication testing with MLPA, then sequencing; biopsy shows absent dystrophin. Corticosteroids (prednisolone, deflazacort) prolong ambulation; exon-skipping and gene therapy are available.

case.tests: CK 18,500 U/L; deletion of DMD exons 45–50 (out of frame).
case.q: Why does it matter whether the deletion is in frame or out of frame?
case.a: Out-of-frame deletions abolish dystrophin (Duchenne); in-frame deletions leave a shortened protein (milder Becker). It also guides exon-skipping eligibility.
