tempoNote: Onset usually after 50, slowly progressive over years to decades
feat: Action/intention tremor followed by gait ataxia in an older man
Executive dysfunction, memory problems, apathy or anxiety; later dementia
Mild parkinsonism, peripheral neuropathy and autonomic symptoms (bladder, erectile)
Family clue: grandchild with intellectual disability/autism (fragile X) or daughter with early menopause
inv: FMR1 CGG repeat analysis: premutation 55–200 repeats
MRI: T2 hyperintensity of the middle cerebellar peduncles (MCP sign), splenium change, cerebral and cerebellar atrophy
Nerve conduction for neuropathy; neuropsychology

case.story: Over 4 years his hands shake when drinking and he now walks with a broad base; he forgets appointments. His grandson has autism and developmental delay.
case.exam: Bilateral kinetic and intention tremor, gait ataxia, reduced ankle reflexes and distal vibration loss, mild bradykinesia.
case.tests: MRI: bilateral MCP T2 hyperintensity and mild atrophy; FMR1: 95 CGG repeats.
case.q: What genetic counselling issue arises for his family?
case.a: FXTAS; his daughters are obligate premutation carriers, at risk of primary ovarian insufficiency and of having children with full-mutation fragile X syndrome.

read.where: Chapter 27 Hereditary and Acquired Cerebellar Ataxias

det.patho: Premutation-sized CGG repeats (55–200) in FMR1 raise FMR1 mRNA levels, producing RNA toxicity, sequestration of RNA-binding proteins and repeat-associated non-AUG (FMRpolyG) translation. Pathology shows eosinophilic intranuclear inclusions in neurons and astrocytes. Penetrance increases with age and is much higher in men; carrier frequency is roughly 1 in 400–800 men.
det.clinical: Tremor usually precedes ataxia by a few years. Cognitive decline is frontal-executive in type and may progress to dementia, with apathy, disinhibition and depression. Neuropathy, autonomic dysfunction and mild parkinsonism are common. Women carriers develop FXTAS less often and more mildly, but have risks of ovarian insufficiency and mood disorders.
det.diagnosis: Consider FMR1 testing in anyone over 50 with unexplained late-onset cerebellar ataxia or action tremor plus cognitive change, especially with a relevant family history. Diagnostic criteria combine the premutation with clinical (tremor, ataxia) and radiological (MCP sign, white-matter change) features. Exclude MSA, SCAs, alcohol-related ataxia and vascular disease.
det.treatment: Management is symptomatic: propranolol or primidone for tremor, physiotherapy for gait and falls, treat neuropathy pain, mood and bladder problems, and cognitive support. Thalamic DBS has been used for disabling tremor but may worsen ataxia. Genetic counselling for the wider family is a central part of care.
det.prognosis: Slowly progressive; median survival after motor onset is around two decades, with increasing dependence.
pearls: Late-onset tremor plus ataxia in a man: ask about grandchildren with intellectual disability.
The MCP sign on T2 MRI is the radiological clue.
Premutation range is 55–200 CGG repeats; full mutation >200 causes fragile X syndrome.
det.thd: FXTAS เกิดในผู้ที่เป็นพาหะ FMR1 premutation (CGG 55–200 ซ้ำ) มักเป็นชายอายุเกิน 50 ปี มีมือสั่นขณะใช้งาน เดินเซ ความจำและการตัดสินใจถดถอย อาจมีปลายประสาทเสื่อม MRI พบ T2 hyperintensity ที่ middle cerebellar peduncle ประวัติครอบครัวมีหลานเป็น fragile X ช่วยมาก การรักษาเป็นการบรรเทาอาการและให้คำปรึกษาทางพันธุกรรมแก่ครอบครัว

Long-standing tremor without significant ataxia, cognitive decline or MCP sign

name: Fragile-X syndrome
formal: X-linked FMR1 full-mutation disorder (CGG greater than 200) with intellectual disability, autism spectrum features, macro-orchidism, long face and large ears; commonest inherited cause of intellectual disability.
simple: A common inherited condition causing learning difficulties and behaviour differences, with typical facial features.

name: Freezing
formal: Brief episodic inability to initiate or continue stepping, with feet feeling glued to the floor, in parkinsonism and related disorders; triggers include turning, doorways and cueing helps.
simple: Sudden moments when the feet seem stuck to the floor and walking cannot start or continue, common in Parkinson disease.

name: Friedreich’s ataxia
formal: Autosomal recessive GAA expansion in FXN with frataxin deficiency causing early-onset progressive gait and limb ataxia, areflexia, dorsal column loss, scoliosis, cardiomyopathy and diabetes.
simple: An inherited disease starting in childhood or teens causing worsening clumsiness, loss of balance and often heart disease.
more: Diagnose by FXN GAA repeat expansion testing; nerve conduction shows absent sensory responses and MRI shows cervical cord atrophy. Idebenone has uncertain benefit and omaveloxolone is approved; monitor for cardiomyopathy, diabetes and scoliosis.
th: โรคเดินเซทางพันธุกรรมแบบด้อยที่พบบ่อยที่สุด — เซ + reflex หาย + Babinski + cardiomyopathy เริ่มในวัยรุ่น
tempoNote: Usually starts before 25; steady progression over years; late-onset forms exist
feat: Progressive gait and limb ataxia beginning in childhood or adolescence
Absent ankle and knee jerks with extensor plantars; loss of vibration and position sense
Dysarthria, scoliosis, pes cavus, square-wave jerks
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and diabetes are common non-neurological features
inv: FXN gene test: biallelic GAA repeat expansion (rarely one expansion plus a point variant)
NCS: absent or reduced sensory potentials (sensory neuronopathy)
ECG and echocardiogram; HbA1c; spine X-ray for scoliosis

case.story: Clumsy in sport since age 11, now falls frequently and his handwriting has deteriorated; parents are first cousins.
case.exam: Broad-based ataxic gait, positive Romberg, absent reflexes in legs, bilateral Babinski, pes cavus, mild thoracic scoliosis.
case.tests: Sural SNAPs absent; ECG shows widespread T inversion and echo shows concentric LV hypertrophy.
case.q: Which genetic test confirms the diagnosis, and what drug is now approved?
case.a: GAA repeat expansion in FXN on both alleles. Omaveloxolone is approved for patients aged 16 and over; cardiac follow-up is lifelong.

det.patho: Most patients carry an expanded GAA trinucleotide repeat in intron 1 of FXN on both alleles, which silences the gene and reduces frataxin, a mitochondrial protein involved in iron–sulfur cluster assembly. Mitochondrial iron overload and oxidative stress damage dorsal root ganglia, spinocerebellar tracts, corticospinal tracts, dentate nucleus and heart. Shorter repeats on the smaller allele generally predict later onset and milder course.
det.clinical: Gait ataxia is the usual first sign, followed by limb ataxia, dysarthria and loss of proprioception, so Romberg is positive. Reflexes vanish early yet plantars become extensor, a classic combination. Scoliosis, pes cavus, optic atrophy, hearing loss and diabetes accumulate; many patients need a wheelchair 10–20 years after onset. Late-onset and retained-reflex variants occur and are easily missed.
det.diagnosis: Genetic testing for the FXN GAA expansion is diagnostic and should be requested in any young patient with progressive ataxia and areflexia. NCS show a sensory neuronopathy with preserved motor conduction. MRI often shows cervical cord thinning with relatively little cerebellar atrophy early on. Always measure vitamin E, and consider other recessive ataxias if testing is negative.
det.treatment: Omaveloxolone, an Nrf2 activator, has regulatory approval for patients 16 years and older and modestly slows decline; liver enzymes and lipids need monitoring. Supportive care includes physiotherapy, orthoses, scoliosis surgery when indicated, speech therapy and diabetes management. Regular cardiac review with ECG and echo is essential, treating heart failure and arrhythmia promptly.
det.prognosis: Disability progresses over decades; cardiomyopathy is the leading cause of death, often in middle age. Later onset generally means slower course.
pearls: Areflexia with upgoing toes in a teenager with ataxia = Friedreich until proven otherwise.
Cerebellar atrophy is usually mild early; the spinal cord is the thin structure on MRI.
Screen the heart at diagnosis even if the patient has no cardiac symptoms.
det.thd: Friedreich ataxia เกิดจาก GAA repeat expansion ในยีน FXN ทั้งสองข้าง ทำให้ frataxin ลดลงและไมโทคอนเดรียเสียหาย อาการเริ่มในวัยรุ่นด้วยการเดินเซ reflex หายแต่ Babinski บวก สูญเสีย proprioception ร่วมกับกระดูกสันหลังคด เท้าโก่ง เบาหวาน และหัวใจห้องล่างหนา วินิจฉัยด้วยการตรวจยีน ต้องตรวจหัวใจเป็นระยะ และมียา omaveloxolone สำหรับอายุ 16 ปีขึ้นไป

files.chapter: Chapter 23 Neuro-Otology: Dizziness, Balance and Hearing

ddx.pt: Same phenotype but low serum vitamin E; treatable with supplements — always check
Dominant inheritance, reflexes often preserved or brisk, cerebellar atrophy on MRI
Distal wasting and pes cavus but no cerebellar signs, cardiomyopathy or Babinski

aN: fa | frda | friedreich ataxia | frataxin deficiency

name: Friedrich’s ataxia
formal: Autosomal recessive spinocerebellar and sensory ataxia from GAA expansions in FXN, causing frataxin deficiency, areflexia, cardiomyopathy, scoliosis and diabetes.
simple: An inherited disease causing progressive loss of balance and coordination, with heart and spine problems, starting in childhood or teenage years.
more: Diagnosed by FXN repeat expansion testing; ECG and echo monitor the heart. Omaveloxolone is approved for treatment; otherwise supportive; typically wheelchair use within 10-15 years and cardiac cause of death.

name: Friedriech ataxia
formal: Autosomal recessive GAA expansion in FXN causing frataxin deficiency, with progressive gait and limb ataxia, areflexia, sensory neuronopathy, cardiomyopathy, and diabetes.
simple: An inherited disease causing progressive loss of balance and coordination from teenage years, with heart problems.
more: Diagnosed by FXN repeat testing; omaveloxolone is approved; treat cardiac disease and diabetes; wheelchair dependence is common within about 15 years.

name: Frontal lobe syndrome
formal: Constellation of executive dysfunction, apathy or disinhibition, personality change, perseveration and primitive reflexes with gait apraxia from frontal damage by tumour, trauma, stroke or degeneration.
simple: Changes in personality, motivation, judgement and behaviour after damage to the front of the brain.
more: MRI or functional imaging localises the lesion. Treatment targets the cause with behavioural management; recovery depends on the underlying disease.

name: Frontotemporal dementia (FTD)
formal: Neurodegenerative dementia with early behavioural change, disinhibition, apathy, or language impairment from frontal and temporal degeneration, often with tau, TDP-43 or FUS pathology and genetic forms (MAPT, GRN, C9orf72).
simple: A brain disease that mainly harms the front and sides of the brain, causing changes in personality, behaviour or language.
aN: ftd | frontotemporal dementia

name: Frontotemporal dementias
formal: Neurodegenerative dementia with early behavioural change, disinhibition, apathy, or language impairment from frontal and temporal degeneration, often with tau, TDP-43 or FUS pathology and genetic forms (MAPT, GRN, C9orf72).
simple: A group of brain diseases that mainly harm the front and sides of the brain, causing changes in personality, behaviour or language.

name: Frontotemporal lobar degeneration (FTLD)
formal: Pathological umbrella for frontotemporal dementia syndromes with selective frontal and temporal atrophy and tau, TDP-43 or FET protein inclusions, linked to behavioural, language and motor presentations.
simple: The brain-tissue changes underlying frontotemporal dementia, with shrinking of the front and side parts of the brain.
more: Subtypes include behavioural variant, semantic and nonfluent aphasia, and overlap with ALS or atypical parkinsonism; genes include MAPT, GRN and C9orf72. MRI or FDG-PET shows focal atrophy or hypometabolism; no disease-modifying therapy exists.
aN: ftld | frontotemporal lobar degeneration

name: Frontotemporal lobe dementia (FTD)
formal: Neurodegenerative dementia with early behavioural change, disinhibition, apathy, or language impairment from frontal and temporal degeneration, often with tau, TDP-43 or FUS pathology and genetic forms (MAPT, GRN, C9orf72).
simple: A brain disease that mainly harms the front and sides of the brain, causing changes in personality, behaviour or language.
aN: ftd | frontotemporal lobe dementia

name: FTD with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis
formal: Overlap syndrome of behavioural or language-variant FTD with upper and lower motor neuron disease, commonly from C9orf72 repeat expansion and TDP-43 proteinopathy.
simple: A combination of frontotemporal dementia and motor neuron disease, causing both behaviour or language changes and muscle weakness.

name: Functional dystonia
formal: Dystonic postures that are inconsistent with organic dystonia, often fixed, of sudden onset and with distractibility, painful and associated with other functional signs.
simple: Abnormal muscle spasms and twisted postures without a structural cause in the nervous system, real and treatable with rehabilitation.

name: Functional movement disorder (FMD)
formal: Abnormal movements such as tremor, dystonia, jerks or gait disturbance that are variable and distractible, with positive features such as entrainment, and arising from altered network function not structural disease.
simple: Real, involuntary movements such as shaking or odd walking that come from a problem in how the brain functions, not from damage.
aN: fmd | functional movement disorder

name: Functional myoclonus
formal: Jerks with a variable pattern, often with a long latency Bereitschaftspotential, distractibility and suggestibility, which are non-epileptic, and diagnosed from clinical and neurophysiology.
simple: Sudden jerks of the body that come from a change in how the brain functions rather than from structural damage.

name: Functional neurological disorder (FND)
formal: Neurological symptoms such as weakness, seizures or movement disorders, genuinely experienced and diagnosed by positive signs like Hoover sign, due to altered nervous system function rather than structural disease.
simple: Real nerve-related symptoms, such as weakness or shaking, caused by a problem with how the brain works rather than damage to it.
th: อาการทางระบบประสาทที่เกิดจากการทำงานของสมองผิดปกติ ไม่ใช่โครงสร้างเสียหาย — วินิจฉัยจากอาการแสดงเชิงบวก รักษาได้
feat: Diagnosis rests on positive signs, not only normal tests
Hoover sign and hip abductor sign in functional leg weakness
Tremor entrainment and distractibility; give-way weakness
Can coexist with structural disease
inv: Targeted tests to exclude what the history raises
Video-EEG for dissociative seizures

case.story: After a minor car accident, sudden heaviness of the left leg; drags it behind her.
case.exam: Left hip extension weak on direct testing but returns to normal when she flexes the right hip against resistance; dragging monoplegic gait, normal reflexes and plantars.
case.tests: MRI brain and spine normal.
case.q: Name the positive sign demonstrated.
case.a: Hoover sign — involuntary hip extension returns during contralateral hip flexion.

files.chapter: 27 - Functional (psychogenic) movement disorders: Phenomenology, diagnosis, and treatment

ddx.pt: UMN signs, MRI lesions
Weakness consistent in a vascular territory with reflex/plantar change
Axial rigidity and spasms with anti-GAD antibodies — often misdiagnosed as functional

aN: fnd | functional neurological disorder | functional weakness | conversion disorder | psychogenic | pnes | dissociative seizures

det.patho: FND reflects a problem of how the brain works, not of its structure: altered attention, prediction and sense of agency disrupt voluntary movement and perception, so symptoms are genuine and not feigned. Predisposing factors include anxiety, depression, prior adverse experiences and other functional disorders, but many patients have none; triggers such as injury, illness, pain or a panic attack are common. It ranks among the commonest reasons for neurology outpatient referral.
det.clinical: Presentations include functional limb weakness, tremor, dystonia, gait disorders, sensory loss, speech and swallowing symptoms, visual loss, cognitive complaints and dissociative (non-epileptic) seizures. Symptoms often start abruptly, fluctuate and are worse when the person is attending to them. Fatigue, pain, poor sleep and dissociation frequently coexist. Structural neurological disease may also be present, so careful assessment is needed in every case.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is made on positive clinical features, not by exclusion alone: Hoover sign and hip abductor sign for leg weakness, drift without pronation, entrainment and distractibility of tremor, a dragging monoplegic gait, and for dissociative seizures features like prolonged duration, eyes closed, fluctuating course and recall of the event. Video-EEG of a typical attack is the gold standard for dissociative seizures. Investigations should be guided by the history, and normal results should be presented as supportive, not as the basis of the diagnosis. Avoid labelling based on psychological history alone.
det.treatment: Explain the diagnosis clearly and confidently, naming it, describing the positive signs and emphasising that it is common, real and potentially reversible. Specialist physiotherapy using movement retraining and attention redirection is effective for motor symptoms; psychological therapy (e.g. CBT-based) helps dissociative seizures and coexisting anxiety or depression. Speech and occupational therapy address specific symptoms. Withdraw unnecessary antiseizure medication when seizures are confirmed as dissociative, and avoid repeated tests or invasive procedures.
det.prognosis: Outcomes vary; shorter symptom duration, acceptance of the diagnosis and early access to targeted therapy predict improvement, while long-standing symptoms are harder to reverse.
pearls: FND is a positive diagnosis — document the signs that show it.
Up to a fifth of patients with dissociative seizures also have epilepsy.
How the diagnosis is explained strongly influences the outcome.
det.thd: FND คือภาวะที่สมองทำงานผิดปกติในการควบคุมการเคลื่อนไหวและการรับรู้ โดยโครงสร้างสมองปกติ อาการจริงไม่ได้แกล้ง เช่น แขนขาอ่อนแรง สั่น เดินผิดปกติ หรือชักแบบ dissociative การวินิจฉัยใช้อาการแสดงเชิงบวก เช่น Hoover sign การสั่นที่เปลี่ยนตามจังหวะอื่น ส่วนการชักควรยืนยันด้วย video-EEG และต้องระวังว่าอาจมีโรคทางโครงสร้างร่วมด้วย การรักษาเริ่มจากอธิบายการวินิจฉัยอย่างชัดเจน ร่วมกับกายภาพบำบัดเฉพาะทาง และจิตบำบัด เช่น CBT

name: Functional seizures
formal: Episodes resembling epileptic seizures but without epileptiform EEG, with features such as long duration, eye closure and fluctuating course, linked to psychological stress; diagnosed with video-EEG.
simple: Seizure-like episodes that are not caused by abnormal electrical discharges in the brain, often related to stress, and treated with therapy.

name: Functional tics
formal: Tic-like movements or sounds with sudden adult or adolescent onset, complex and variable, without premonitory urge or typical suppressibility, often following social-media exposure or stress.
simple: Tic-like movements or sounds that start suddenly, usually in teenagers and young adults, and are linked to stress rather than classic tic disorder.

name: Fungal myositis
formal: Rare invasive muscle infection by fungi such as Candida or Aspergillus, usually in immunosuppressed patients, causing focal pain, swelling and abscess or necrosis.
simple: A rare muscle infection caused by fungi, mostly seen in people with weak immune systems.
more: Diagnosis by MRI, muscle biopsy and fungal culture. Treated with antifungal drugs and surgical drainage; prognosis depends on the underlying immune status.

name: Fungal neurological infections
formal: CNS infections by fungi such as Cryptococcus, Aspergillus, Candida, Mucorales and Histoplasma, causing chronic meningitis, abscess or vasculopathy, mostly in immunocompromised people.
simple: Infections of the brain or its coverings caused by fungi, usually in people with weakened immune systems.

name: Fungal spinal infections
formal: Spinal infections such as vertebral osteomyelitis or epidural abscess by Aspergillus, Candida or Coccidioides, often after surgery or in immunosuppression, causing back pain, radiculopathy or myelopathy.
simple: Infection of the spine or its coverings by a fungus, causing back pain and sometimes weakness or numbness in the legs.

name: Gait disorders
formal: Abnormalities of walking resulting from neurological, musculoskeletal or functional causes, classified by pattern such as spastic, ataxic, parkinsonian, steppage, or frontal gait.
simple: Problems with the way a person walks, which can come from the nerves, brain, muscles or bones.

name: Gangliocytomas
formal: Rare benign, well-differentiated tumours of mature ganglion cells, commonly in the temporal lobe, presenting with long-standing epilepsy in young people.
simple: Rare slow-growing non-cancerous brain tumours made of nerve cells, often causing seizures.

name: Gangliogliomas
formal: Low-grade glioneuronal tumours with neoplastic neurons and glia, typically temporal, causing drug-resistant epilepsy in children and young adults, with BRAF V600E mutation in many.
simple: Slow-growing brain tumours made of both nerve and support cells, usually causing seizures in young people.

name: Gardner’s syndrome
formal: Variant of familial adenomatous polyposis with colonic polyps, osteomas, soft tissue tumours and CNS tumours such as medulloblastoma, from APC mutations.
simple: An inherited condition with many bowel polyps, bone growths and a higher risk of some tumours, including in the brain.

name: Gaucher disease
formal: Autosomal recessive glucocerebrosidase deficiency; neuronopathic types (II, III) cause oculomotor apraxia, seizures, myoclonus and bulbar signs, with hepatosplenomegaly and bone disease.
simple: An inherited fat-storage disease causing an enlarged liver and spleen, and in some forms damaging the brain.
more: Diagnosis by low leukocyte beta-glucosidase activity and GBA1 gene sequencing; elevated chitotriosidase and lyso-Gb1. Enzyme replacement or substrate reduction treat visceral disease but do not cross the blood-brain barrier.

name: Gaucher’s disease
formal: Autosomal recessive glucocerebrosidase deficiency; neuronopathic types (II, III) cause oculomotor apraxia, seizures, myoclonus and bulbar signs, with hepatosplenomegaly and bone disease.
simple: An inherited fat-storage disease causing an enlarged liver and spleen, and in some forms damaging the brain.

name: Gelsolin-related amyloidosis
formal: Hereditary amyloidosis from gelsolin gene mutations (Finnish type), with corneal lattice dystrophy, progressive cranial neuropathy, cutis laxa and mild peripheral neuropathy.
simple: An inherited disease where abnormal protein builds up, causing facial nerve weakness, loose skin and eye changes.
more: Autosomal dominant (GSN, D187N/Y); first seen with corneal lattice dystrophy in adults. Management is supportive, including facial reanimation and eye care; life expectancy is near normal.

name: General paralysis
formal: Tertiary neurosyphilis (general paralysis of the insane) with progressive dementia, psychosis, tremor, dysarthria, Argyll Robertson pupils and frontal atrophy, treated with penicillin.
simple: A late brain infection from untreated syphilis causing memory loss, personality change and weakness.

name: Generalised convulsive status epilepticus
formal: Prolonged or repeated generalised tonic-clonic seizures without recovery, lasting over 5 minutes, a medical emergency needing benzodiazepines then second-line antiseizure drugs.
simple: A medical emergency where a convulsion lasts more than five minutes, or repeats without the person waking up in between.

name: Generalised seizure
formal: Seizure with rapid involvement of bilaterally distributed networks, including tonic-clonic, absence, myoclonic, atonic and tonic types, with impaired consciousness in most.
simple: A seizure that involves both sides of the brain from the start, often with loss of awareness.

name: Generalized cortical myoclonus
formal: Widespread myoclonic jerks of cortical origin, as in progressive myoclonic epilepsy, post-anoxic and metabolic states, with EEG spike correlate and giant SEPs.
simple: Widespread sudden jerks of the body arising from overactive brain surface, seen in some epilepsies and brain injuries.

name: Generalized myoclonus
formal: Widespread brief shock-like jerks of cortical, subcortical or spinal origin, found in epilepsy, metabolic encephalopathy, post-hypoxic states and neurodegeneration.
simple: Sudden, brief jerks affecting much of the body, with many possible causes.

name: Generalized primary dystonia
formal: Early-onset isolated dystonia that spreads to several body regions, often DYT1 (TOR1A) related, with onset in a limb in childhood and responses to deep brain stimulation.
simple: A dystonia that starts in childhood, often in a leg or arm, and spreads to much of the body, usually inherited.

name: Geniospasm
formal: Hereditary chin trembling with episodic, rapid quivering of the mentalis muscle, autosomal dominant, beginning in childhood, benign and triggered by stress.
simple: A harmless inherited condition in which the chin trembles in episodes, often when stressed.

name: Gerhardt’s syndrome
formal: Bilateral vocal cord paralysis due to recurrent laryngeal nerve dysfunction, with vocal cords in the median position, causing stridor and dyspnoea.
simple: Weakness of both vocal cords that can make breathing noisy and difficult.

name: Germ cell tumours (GCTs)
formal: Intracranial tumours from primordial germ cells in midline sites (pineal, suprasellar), including germinomas and non-germinomatous types, with raised AFP or beta-hCG, causing Parinaud syndrome, diabetes insipidus.
simple: Brain tumours in the middle of the head that start from early reproductive cells, often in children and teenagers.
aN: gcts | germ cell tumours

name: Germinomas
formal: Most common intracranial germ cell tumour, radiosensitive, in pineal or suprasellar regions, presenting with Parinaud syndrome, diabetes insipidus and hydrocephalus, with excellent prognosis.
simple: A type of brain tumour in the middle of the head, mostly in young people, that responds very well to treatment.

name: Gerstmann syndrome
formal: Dominant angular gyrus lesion syndrome of finger agnosia, left-right disorientation, agraphia and acalculia, typically from left parietal infarct or tumour.
simple: A set of four problems, finger recognition, telling left from right, writing and calculating, caused by damage in one part of the brain.

name: Gerstmann–Straussler–Scheinker syndrome
formal: Autosomal dominant prion disease (commonly P102L) with slowly progressive cerebellar ataxia, parkinsonism, and dementia, with multicentric amyloid plaques, lasting several years.
simple: A rare inherited brain disease causing slowly worsening unsteadiness, then memory loss, due to abnormal proteins in the brain.

name: Gerstmann–Sträussler–Scheinker (GSS) disease
formal: Autosomal dominant prion disease (commonly P102L) with slowly progressive cerebellar ataxia, parkinsonism, and dementia, with multicentric amyloid plaques, lasting several years.
simple: A rare inherited brain disease causing slowly worsening unsteadiness, then memory loss, due to abnormal proteins in the brain.
aN: gss | gerstmann straussler scheinker disease

name: Gerstmann–Sträussler–Scheinker syndrome (GSS)
formal: Autosomal dominant prion disease (commonly P102L) with slowly progressive cerebellar ataxia, parkinsonism, and dementia, with multicentric amyloid plaques, lasting several years.
simple: A rare inherited brain disease causing slowly worsening unsteadiness, then memory loss, due to abnormal proteins in the brain.
aN: gss | gerstmann straussler scheinker syndrome

name: Giant axonal neuropathy
formal: Autosomal recessive childhood sensorimotor neuropathy from GAN gene mutations, with enlarged axons filled by neurofilaments, kinky hair, ataxia and CNS involvement.
simple: An inherited disease where nerves swell with protein clumps, causing weak legs, clumsiness and tightly curled hair in children.
more: Diagnosis by nerve biopsy showing giant axons and GAN genetic testing; MRI shows white matter changes. No cure; supportive care, and death usually occurs in the second or third decade.

name: Giant cell vasculitis
formal: Granulomatous large-vessel vasculitis in people over 50 involving temporal and cranial arteries, with headache, jaw claudication, visual loss and raised inflammatory markers.
simple: Inflammation of arteries, often near the temples, causing headache, jaw pain and a risk of sudden blindness.
more: Diagnosis by ESR, CRP and temporal artery biopsy or ultrasound. Immediate high-dose steroids protect vision; tocilizumab is a steroid-sparing option; often associated with polymyalgia rheumatica.

name: Giant-cell arteritis (GCA)
formal: Large-vessel granulomatous vasculitis in people over 50 causing new headache, jaw claudication, scalp tenderness and visual loss from ischaemic optic neuropathy, with raised ESR; urgent steroids needed.
simple: Inflammation of blood vessels in older adults causing headache, jaw pain and a risk of sudden blindness if not treated quickly.
aN: gca | giant cell arteritis

name: Gilles de la Tourette’s syndrome
formal: Neurodevelopmental tic disorder with multiple motor and at least one vocal tic for over a year, onset in childhood, often with OCD and ADHD, involving cortico-striato-thalamic circuits.
simple: A condition starting in childhood with repeated movements and sounds, called tics, that the person cannot fully control.

name: Gillespie syndrome
formal: Rare disorder with partial aniridia, congenital hypotonia, cerebellar ataxia and intellectual disability, caused by ITPR1 mutations.
simple: A rare inherited condition with an abnormal iris in the eye, floppy muscles from birth, and balance and learning problems.

name: Glaucoma
formal: Optic neuropathy with raised intraocular pressure or vulnerability causing progressive optic disc cupping and peripheral visual field loss.
simple: An eye disease where pressure damages the optic nerve and gradually reduces side vision.

name: Glioblastomas
formal: Grade 4 IDH-wildtype diffuse astrocytic tumours, the commonest malignant primary brain tumour in adults, with necrosis, microvascular proliferation, ring enhancement and poor survival.
simple: The most common and aggressive brain cancer in adults, growing quickly and hard to treat.

name: Glomus tumours
formal: Paragangliomas of the glomus bodies in the jugular bulb or middle ear (glomus jugulare, tympanicum) causing pulsatile tinnitus, hearing loss and lower cranial neuropathies.
simple: Slow-growing tumours near the ear and base of the skull, causing hearing loss, a pulsing sound and sometimes swallowing problems.

name: Glossopharyngeal neuralgia
formal: Paroxysmal severe lancinating pain in the throat, tonsil and ear provoked by swallowing, often from vascular compression, sometimes with syncope; treated with carbamazepine.
simple: Sudden attacks of severe stabbing pain in the throat or ear, often set off by swallowing or talking.

name: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency
formal: X-linked enzyme deficiency causing haemolysis after oxidant drugs or fava beans; neurologically relevant for neonatal kernicterus and drug avoidance.
simple: An inherited enzyme shortage in which red blood cells break down after certain foods or medicines.

name: GLUT1 deficiency syndrome
formal: SLC2A1-related impaired glucose transport across the blood-brain barrier with infantile seizures, low CSF glucose, developmental delay, movement disorders and microcephaly, treated with ketogenic diet.
simple: An inherited condition where the brain cannot get enough sugar, causing seizures and developmental delay, helped by a special high-fat diet.
more: Diagnosis by CSF glucose below 40 mg/dL with low CSF-to-blood glucose ratio and normal blood glucose; confirm by SLC2A1 sequencing or erythrocyte 3-OMG uptake. Ketogenic diet should be started early; avoid phenobarbital and valproate.

name: Glutaric aciduria
formal: Autosomal recessive organic acidopathy (type 1, GCDH) with macrocephaly and acute striatal injury, causing dystonia after catabolic stress, and frontotemporal atrophy on MRI.
simple: An inherited metabolic disease in which a build-up of acids can damage the brain, causing stiffness and twisting movements in children.

name: Glutaric aciduria type I
formal: Autosomal recessive GCDH deficiency causing macrocephaly, acute striatal injury with dystonic-dyskinetic cerebral palsy after a febrile or catabolic crisis, with bilateral basal ganglia lesions.
simple: An inherited metabolic disease in which a crisis during infancy damages the brain and causes severe dystonia.
more: Urine glutaric and 3-hydroxyglutaric acid are raised; newborn screening exists. Low-lysine diet, carnitine and emergency treatment prevent damage if started early.

name: Glutaric aciduria type II
formal: Multiple acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency from ETF or ETFDH mutations causing lipid storage myopathy, metabolic crises and hypoglycaemia, some forms riboflavin-responsive.
simple: An inherited disorder of fat and protein use causing muscle weakness and sudden illness, often improved by vitamin B2.

name: Gluten encephalopathy
formal: Neurological manifestations of gluten sensitivity, including gluten ataxia, neuropathy and cognitive or white-matter involvement, with anti-gliadin antibodies, improving on a gluten-free diet.
simple: Nervous system problems such as unsteadiness or numbness linked to gluten sensitivity.

name: Glycerol kinase deficiency (GKD)
formal: X-linked recessive deficiency of glycerol kinase from Xp21 deletions, often a contiguous gene syndrome with DMD and adrenal hypoplasia, with hyperglyceroluria.
simple: An inherited enzyme deficiency that raises glycerol in blood and urine, sometimes coming with other genes missing next to it.
more: Isolated cases may be symptom-free; complex forms cause adrenal failure, developmental delay and dystrophinopathy. Diagnosed by urine organic acids and chromosomal microarray; treat any adrenal insufficiency.
aN: gkd | glycerol kinase deficiency

name: Glycogen and lipid storage disorders
formal: Inherited metabolic myopathies from defects in glycogen or fatty acid metabolism, causing exercise intolerance, rhabdomyolysis, or progressive weakness with variable cardiac involvement.
simple: Inherited conditions where the body cannot use stored sugar or fat properly, leading to muscle pain, weakness or tiredness.

name: Glycogen storage diseases (GSD)
formal: Inherited enzyme defects of glycogen metabolism, such as Pompe, McArdle and Cori diseases, causing exercise-induced cramps, myoglobinuria, or progressive proximal myopathy and cardiomyopathy.
simple: Inherited conditions where the body cannot use stored sugar properly, causing weakness, muscle cramps or heart problems.
aN: gsd | glycogen storage diseases

name: GM1-gangliosidosis
formal: Autosomal recessive beta-galactosidase deficiency with lysosomal ganglioside storage, causing infantile developmental regression, hepatosplenomegaly, cherry-red macula or later dystonia and ataxia.
simple: An inherited disease where a fatty substance builds up in brain cells, causing loss of skills in babies or movement problems later.
more: Diagnosis by reduced leukocyte beta-galactosidase and GLB1 sequencing; skeletal dysplasia and coarse features are common in infantile type. No disease-modifying therapy exists, with supportive care; juvenile and adult forms have slower progression.

name: GM2-gangliosidosis
formal: Hexosaminidase deficiency (Tay-Sachs, Sandhoff) with lysosomal GM2 storage, causing infantile regression, hyperacusis, cherry-red macula and seizures, with later-onset ataxia and motor neuron features.
simple: An inherited disease where a fatty substance builds up in brain cells, causing loss of skills, seizures and weakness.
more: Diagnosis by hexosaminidase A (Tay-Sachs) or A and B (Sandhoff) deficiency and HEXA or HEXB mutations; carrier screening in Ashkenazi Jewish communities reduces incidence. No proven therapy exists; infantile forms are fatal by early childhood.

name: Goodpasture syndrome
formal: Anti-glomerular basement membrane disease causing pulmonary haemorrhage and rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis; neurological involvement is uncommon, but it appears in differentials with vasculitis.
simple: An autoimmune disease in which antibodies attack the kidneys and lungs, causing blood in the urine and coughing blood.
more: Diagnosed with anti-GBM antibodies and kidney biopsy. Treated with plasma exchange, steroids and cyclophosphamide; early treatment is essential to save the kidneys.

name: Grade 3 oligodendrogliomas
formal: Anaplastic IDH-mutant, 1p/19q-codeleted gliomas with increased mitoses, vascular proliferation and a worse prognosis than grade 2, treated with surgery, radiotherapy and chemotherapy.
simple: A fast-growing type of brain tumour from support cells that responds fairly well to radiation and chemotherapy.

name: Gradenigo syndrome
formal: Petrous apicitis from otitis media causing the triad of retro-orbital pain, abducens palsy and ear discharge, with risk of meningitis and venous thrombosis.
simple: A complication of ear infection that causes pain behind the eye, double vision and ear discharge.

name: Graft versus host disease (GvHD)
formal: Immune complication of allogeneic stem cell transplant in which donor T cells attack host tissues, with neuromuscular manifestations such as myositis, myasthenia, neuropathy and cerebrovascular events.
simple: A complication of bone marrow transplants where the donor's immune cells attack the patient's body, sometimes causing muscle or nerve problems.
aN: gvhd | graft versus host disease

name: Gram-negative meningitis
formal: Bacterial meningitis due to Gram-negative bacilli such as E. coli, Klebsiella and Pseudomonas, in neonates, after neurosurgery, trauma or immunosuppression, with high mortality.
simple: A serious infection of the brain's coverings by a particular group of bacteria, mostly in newborns or after head surgery.

name: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA)
formal: ANCA-associated necrotising granulomatous vasculitis of upper airways, lungs and kidney, with cranial neuropathies, pachymeningitis and mononeuritis multiplex.
simple: An immune disease inflaming small blood vessels, usually in the nose, lungs and kidneys, and sometimes the nerves.
aN: gpa | granulomatosis with polyangiitis

name: Granulomatous hypophysitis
formal: Inflammation of the pituitary with granulomas, from sarcoidosis, GPA or idiopathic cause, presenting with headache, hypopituitarism, diabetes insipidus and visual disturbance.
simple: Inflammation of the pituitary gland that can cause headache, hormone shortages and eyesight problems.

name: Granulomatous myopathies
formal: Muscle inflammation with granulomas, most often from sarcoidosis, causing proximal weakness, nodules or pain, with corticosteroid-responsive course.
simple: Muscle inflammation with clumps of immune cells, most often from sarcoidosis, causing weakness and pain.

name: Granulomatous/giant cell myositis
formal: Inflammatory myopathy with noncaseating granulomas and multinucleated giant cells, usually in sarcoidosis or thymoma-associated myasthenia, causing proximal weakness or palpable nodules.
simple: A muscle inflammation where clusters of immune cells form small lumps in the muscle, causing weakness or pain.
more: Biopsy shows granulomas; look for sarcoidosis, thymoma or infection. Corticosteroids are the main treatment, with steroid-sparing agents if needed.

name: Graves’ disease
formal: Autoimmune hyperthyroidism with TSH receptor antibodies, causing thyroid eye disease, thyrotoxic periodic paralysis, myopathy, tremor and neuromuscular complications.
simple: An autoimmune condition making the thyroid overactive, which can cause tremor, muscle weakness and bulging eyes.
more: Confirm with low TSH, high free T4 and T3, and anti-TSH receptor antibodies; proptosis causes diplopia and ophthalmoplegia. Treat with antithyroid drugs, radioiodine or surgery, steroid and teprotumumab for eye disease, and propranolol.

name: Grisel’s syndrome
formal: Non-traumatic atlantoaxial subluxation after pharyngeal or head and neck infection or surgery, causing painful torticollis and risk of cord compression.
simple: A neck problem after a throat infection or surgery in which the top two neck bones slip, causing a painful tilted neck.

name: GTP cyclohydrolase I (GTPCH I) deficiency
formal: GCH1 deficiency causing dopa-responsive dystonia (Segawa disease) with childhood-onset limb dystonia with diurnal variation, parkinsonism and an excellent response to low-dose levodopa.
simple: An inherited condition in children causing stiff, twisted legs that are worse in the evening and respond very well to levodopa.
more: CSF biopterin and neopterin are low and genetics confirm it; dominant with reduced penetrance. Lifelong low-dose levodopa gives marked and sustained benefit.
nN: gtp cyclohydrolase i gtpch i deficiency
aN: gtpch i | gtp cyclohydrolase i deficiency

name: Guillain–Barré polyneuropathy
formal: Acute immune-mediated demyelinating or axonal polyneuropathy often after infection, with ascending weakness, areflexia, albuminocytologic dissociation, treated with IVIG or plasma exchange.
simple: A sudden immune illness, often after an infection, in which the nerves are attacked, causing weakness that spreads upward.

name: Guillain–Barré syndrome (GBS)
formal: Acute immune-mediated demyelinating or axonal polyneuropathy often after infection, with ascending weakness, areflexia, albuminocytologic dissociation, treated with IVIG or plasma exchange.
simple: A sudden immune illness, often after an infection, in which the nerves are attacked, causing weakness that spreads upward.
more: Use nerve conduction, CSF protein and, when needed, anti-ganglioside antibodies; monitor forced vital capacity and autonomic function. Recovery is typically good, with 5 to 10 percent mortality and some residual deficits, and relapses are rare.
th: เส้นประสาทอักเสบเฉียบพลันหลังติดเชื้อ — แขนขาอ่อนแรงลามขึ้นทั้งสองข้าง รีเฟล็กซ์หาย อาจหายใจไม่ไหว
tempoNote: Progresses to nadir within 4 weeks (usually 2)
feat: Symmetric ascending weakness with areflexia
Preceding diarrhoeal or respiratory infection 1–4 weeks earlier
Facial diplegia, dysautonomia, back or limb pain
Risk of respiratory failure — monitor vital capacity, not just SpO2
inv: Nerve conduction studies: demyelinating or axonal pattern (may be normal early)
CSF: albuminocytological dissociation (often after the first week)
Serial FVC/NIF; ECG and BP monitoring
Anti-ganglioside antibodies (e.g. GQ1b in Miller Fisher)

case.story: Diarrhoea 2 weeks ago; now 4 days of tingling feet and progressive leg then arm weakness; cannot climb stairs.
case.exam: Proximal and distal weakness MRC 3–4/5, absent reflexes, mild glove-and-stocking sensory loss, bilateral facial weakness.
case.tests: CSF protein 1.2 g/L, cells 2/µL; NCS: prolonged distal latencies and conduction block.
case.q: Which bedside measure decides ICU admission?
case.a: Serial forced vital capacity (e.g. < 20 mL/kg or falling quickly), plus bulbar weakness and autonomic instability; treat with IVIG or plasma exchange.

files.chapter: Chapter 16 Diseases of the Peripheral Nerves

ddx.pt: Progression beyond 8 weeks or ≥3 treatment-related fluctuations
Sensory level, sphincter involvement early, upgoing plantars
Fatigable ptosis/diplopia; reflexes and sensation preserved
Low potassium, hours not days, no sensory symptoms
Abdominal pain, psychiatric features, motor axonal neuropathy

aN: gbs | guillain barre syndrome | aidp | acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy | landry paralysis | ascending paralysis

det.patho: An acute immune-mediated polyradiculoneuropathy, frequently triggered by infection (Campylobacter jejuni, CMV, EBV, Mycoplasma, Zika, influenza) through molecular mimicry. In the demyelinating form (AIDP) macrophages strip myelin; in axonal forms (AMAN, AMSAN), antibodies against gangliosides such as GM1 and GD1a attack the nodal axolemma. Axonal variants are relatively more frequent in Asia, and anti-GQ1b antibodies define the Miller Fisher spectrum.
det.clinical: Weakness typically starts in the legs and ascends over days, with areflexia, distal paraesthesia and often back or limb pain; nadir is reached within 4 weeks, usually by 2. Facial and bulbar weakness, respiratory failure (in about a quarter) and autonomic dysfunction — arrhythmias, BP swings, ileus, urinary retention — cause most deaths. Variants include Miller Fisher syndrome (ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, areflexia), pharyngeal–cervical–brachial weakness, paraparetic GBS and Bickerstaff brainstem encephalitis. Reflexes may be preserved early or in AMAN.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical, supported by CSF albuminocytological dissociation (often normal in week one) and nerve conduction studies, which may need repeating to classify demyelinating or axonal subtype. CSF cell counts above 50/µL should prompt reconsideration (HIV, Lyme, lymphoma, polio-like infections). Anti-GQ1b supports Miller Fisher; other ganglioside antibodies are of limited routine value. Exclude spinal cord compression, myelitis, myasthenia, botulism, hypokalaemia, porphyria, tick paralysis and critical illness neuropathy.
det.treatment: IVIG 2 g/kg total, split over 5 days, or plasma exchange (about five exchanges) within 2–4 weeks of onset are equally effective for patients who cannot walk unaided; combining them adds nothing and corticosteroids alone are ineffective. Monitor FVC and NIF regularly, intubating early for FVC below 20 mL/kg, inability to lift the head or cough, or rapid decline; EGRIS helps predict ventilation need. Provide DVT prophylaxis, pain management (gabapentinoids, opioids cautiously), cardiac monitoring, bowel and bladder care and early rehabilitation. Treatment-related fluctuations within 8 weeks may justify re-treatment; a third deterioration raises the possibility of acute-onset CIDP.
det.prognosis: About four in five patients walk independently at 6 months, but mortality remains around 3–7% and many have residual fatigue or weakness; mEGOS estimates outcome.
pearls: Measure vital capacity, not oxygen saturation, to judge respiratory risk.
Normal CSF protein in the first week does not exclude GBS.
Three or more treatment-related fluctuations or deterioration after 8 weeks suggests acute-onset CIDP.
Dilated unreactive pupils point away from GBS toward botulism.
det.thd: GBS คือภาวะเส้นประสาทส่วนปลายและรากประสาทอักเสบเฉียบพลันจากภูมิคุ้มกัน มักเกิดหลังติดเชื้อ เช่น ท้องเสียจาก Campylobacter อาการคืออ่อนแรงลามขึ้นจากขาทั้งสองข้าง รีเฟล็กซ์หาย ปวดหลัง อาจมีหน้าอ่อนแรง กลืนลำบาก หายใจล้มเหลว และระบบประสาทอัตโนมัติแปรปรวน วินิจฉัยทางคลินิกร่วมกับน้ำไขสันหลังที่โปรตีนสูงแต่เซลล์ปกติ และการตรวจ NCS รักษาด้วย IVIG 2 g/kg แบ่งให้ 5 วัน หรือ plasma exchange และเฝ้าดู vital capacity อย่างใกล้ชิด

name: H-IBM with frontotemporal dementia
formal: Hereditary inclusion body myopathy with frontotemporal dementia, usually with Paget disease of bone, due to VCP gene variants (multisystem proteinopathy).
simple: An inherited disease causing muscle weakness along with memory and behaviour changes.
more: Autosomal dominant VCP; muscle biopsy shows rimmed vacuoles and TDP-43 pathology. No disease-modifying therapy; supportive and symptomatic management with family counselling.

name: H-IBM with Paget disease
formal: Autosomal dominant VCP-related multisystem proteinopathy combining inclusion body myopathy, early Paget disease of bone and sometimes frontotemporal dementia.
simple: An inherited condition where muscle weakness occurs together with bone disease called Paget disease.
more: VCP gene testing confirms it; high alkaline phosphatase indicates Paget. Bisphosphonates treat the bone disease, but the muscle and brain components have no cure.

name: Haemangioblastomas (HBO)
formal: Highly vascular benign tumours of the cerebellum, brainstem or spinal cord, sporadic or associated with von Hippel–Lindau disease, sometimes with polycythaemia and cystic changes.
simple: Slow-growing blood-vessel-rich tumours in the back of the brain or spinal cord, sometimes linked to an inherited syndrome.
aN: hbo | hemangioblastomas

name: Haematogenous osteomyelitis
formal: Bone infection spread via blood, in the spine causing vertebral osteomyelitis with back pain, fever and risk of epidural abscess and cord compression.
simple: A bone infection that has travelled through the blood, in the spine causing back pain and fever.

name: Haemolytic disease of the newborn
formal: Fetal or neonatal haemolysis from maternal alloantibodies such as anti-D, causing hyperbilirubinaemia; severe cases lead to kernicterus with athetosis, deafness and gaze palsy.
simple: Breakdown of a baby's red blood cells from the mother's antibodies, which can cause severe jaundice and brain damage.

name: Haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH)
formal: Life-threatening hyperinflammatory syndrome with fever, cytopenias, hepatosplenomegaly and high ferritin, with CNS involvement causing seizures, encephalopathy and cranial nerve palsies.
simple: A dangerous overreaction of the immune system causing fever, low blood counts and organ damage, sometimes involving the brain.
aN: hlh | hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis

name: Haemorrhage after thrombolysis
formal: Symptomatic intracerebral haemorrhage after intravenous thrombolysis for stroke, occurring in a small percentage, causing neurological worsening and requiring emergency CT.
simple: Bleeding in the brain as a complication of clot-busting treatment for stroke, which can worsen symptoms.

name: Haemorrhagic stroke
formal: Stroke due to intracerebral or subarachnoid haemorrhage, most often from hypertensive small-vessel disease, aneurysm or amyloid angiopathy, causing sudden deficits and high mortality.
simple: A stroke caused by bleeding in or around the brain, usually causing sudden headache and weakness.

name: Hallervorden–Spatz disease (HSD)
formal: Historic name for pantothenate kinase-associated neurodegeneration (PKAN), with iron accumulation in the globus pallidus, dystonia, parkinsonism, retinopathy and an eye-of-the-tiger MRI sign.
simple: An old name for an inherited brain disease with iron build-up, causing twisting movements, stiffness and vision loss.
more: Diagnosis by MRI and PANK2 mutation testing; autosomal recessive with early dystonia and retinitis pigmentosa, and acanthocytes may be seen. Treatment is symptomatic, with botulinum toxin, intrathecal baclofen and deep brain stimulation.
aN: hsd | hallervorden spatz disease

name: Haltia-Santavuori disease (infantile neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis)
formal: Infantile NCL (CLN1, PPT1 deficiency) with developmental regression at 6 to 24 months, microcephaly, myoclonus, visual failure, flat EEG and granular osmiophilic deposits.
simple: A rare inherited childhood brain disease that causes loss of skills, seizures and blindness, starting in infancy.
nN: haltia santavuori disease infantile neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis
aN: infantile neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis | haltia santavuori disease

name: Hansen’s disease
formal: Leprosy from Mycobacterium leprae causing hypoaesthetic skin lesions and thickened peripheral nerves with sensory loss, mononeuritis multiplex and deformity.
simple: A long-term bacterial infection of skin and nerves causing numb patches, weakness and deformities.

name: Harlequin syndrome
formal: Unilateral facial flushing and sweating with contralateral anhidrosis from sympathetic dysfunction, often with Horner or Adie pupil, and benign or following surgery or lesions.
simple: A rare condition where one side of the face flushes and sweats while the other stays pale and dry.

name: HARP syndrome
formal: Hypoprebetalipoproteinaemia, acanthocytosis, retinitis pigmentosa and pallidal degeneration, an allelic variant of PKAN due to PANK2 mutation.
simple: A rare inherited condition with abnormal blood fats and cells, vision loss and movement problems from deep brain damage.

name: Hartnup disease
formal: Autosomal recessive neutral amino acid transport defect (SLC6A19) causing pellagra-like rash, intermittent cerebellar ataxia, psychiatric symptoms and aminoaciduria; responds to nicotinamide.
simple: An inherited problem absorbing some amino acids, causing sun-sensitive rashes, unsteadiness and mood changes.

name: Hartnup’s disease
formal: Autosomal recessive neutral amino acid transport defect (SLC6A19) causing pellagra-like rash, intermittent cerebellar ataxia, psychiatric symptoms and aminoaciduria; responds to nicotinamide.
simple: An inherited problem absorbing some amino acids, causing sun-sensitive rashes, unsteadiness and mood changes.

name: Hashimoto’s encephalopathy
formal: Steroid-responsive encephalopathy associated with autoimmune thyroiditis (SREAT) and anti-thyroid antibodies, with seizures, myoclonus, stroke-like episodes and cognitive decline.
simple: A rare immune brain condition linked to thyroid antibodies, causing confusion, seizures and memory problems that improve with steroids.
ab: steroid-responsive encephalopathy associated with autoimmune thyroiditis
th: สมองเสื่อมหรือสับสนที่ตอบสนองต่อ steroid ในผู้ที่มีแอนติบอดีต่อต่อมไทรอยด์ (anti-TPO) — เป็นการวินิจฉัยแบบตัดโรคอื่นออก
tempoNote: Either relapsing stroke-like or seizure episodes, or a diffuse progressive course over weeks to months
feat: Fluctuating confusion, cognitive decline, psychosis or reduced consciousness
Tremor, myoclonus, ataxia and seizures are common
Stroke-like focal episodes in a relapsing form
Raised anti-TPO or anti-thyroglobulin antibodies; thyroid function may be normal
Marked improvement with corticosteroids
inv: Anti-TPO and anti-thyroglobulin antibodies, TSH and free T4
Comprehensive neuronal antibody panel (serum and CSF) to exclude a defined autoimmune encephalitis
CSF: raised protein, mild or no pleocytosis; EEG: diffuse slowing, sometimes triphasic or epileptiform discharges
MRI often normal or with nonspecific white matter change; DWI to exclude CJD

case.story: Six weeks of worsening forgetfulness, episodes of confusion and jerks of both hands; one generalised seizure.
case.exam: Inattentive, MMSE 19/30, multifocal myoclonus, postural tremor, unsteady tandem gait; no focal weakness.
case.tests: TSH 6.2, free T4 normal, anti-TPO 1450 IU/mL. CSF protein 78 mg/dL, 2 cells. Neuronal antibody panel negative. MRI DWI normal; EEG diffuse slowing. RT-QuIC negative.
case.q: Why is this label reached only after excluding other causes, and what response is expected?
case.a: Anti-TPO antibodies are common in healthy people and are not pathogenic in the brain, so prion disease, infections, metabolic causes and antibody-defined encephalitis must be ruled out first; SREAT typically improves strikingly with corticosteroids.

det.patho: The mechanism is uncertain; anti-thyroid antibodies are viewed as a marker of an autoimmune tendency rather than the cause, because they occur in up to 10–20% of healthy adults and do not bind the brain in a relevant way. Proposed mechanisms include cerebral vasculitis, immune-complex deposition or unidentified neuronal antibodies. Many historical cases would now be reclassified as defined antibody-mediated encephalitides.
det.clinical: Two patterns are described: a vasculitic type with recurrent stroke-like events and a diffuse progressive type with cognitive decline, psychiatric symptoms and confusion. Myoclonus, tremor, seizures and fluctuating consciousness are frequent across both. Women are affected more often, and thyroid status may be euthyroid, hypothyroid or occasionally hyperthyroid.
det.diagnosis: It is a diagnosis of exclusion: compatible encephalopathy, raised thyroid antibodies, no known neuronal antibodies and no alternative cause, plus steroid responsiveness. Mandatory exclusions include infection, prion disease, metabolic and toxic causes, non-convulsive status and defined autoimmune encephalitis. CSF protein rise and diffuse EEG slowing support but do not confirm it.
det.treatment: High-dose corticosteroids are the mainstay, often IV methylprednisolone followed by oral prednisolone tapered over months. IVIG or plasma exchange are used if steroids fail or are contraindicated, and azathioprine, mycophenolate or rituximab may be needed for relapse. Correct thyroid dysfunction, but thyroid hormone alone does not resolve the encephalopathy.
det.prognosis: Most patients improve substantially with steroids, but relapses occur, and lack of steroid response should prompt reconsideration of the diagnosis.
pearls: Anti-TPO alone is common and nonspecific; never stop the workup there.
Exclude CJD before giving the label to a patient with myoclonus and dementia.
Steroid responsiveness is part of the definition.
det.thd: Hashimoto encephalopathy หรือ SREAT คือภาวะสมองทำงานผิดปกติที่ตอบสนองต่อ steroid ในผู้ที่มี anti-TPO สูง ผู้ป่วยมีสับสน ความจำเสื่อม ชัก กระตุก มือสั่น หรืออาการคล้ายอัมพาตเป็นพัก ๆ แอนติบอดีไทรอยด์เป็นเพียงตัวบ่งชี้ ไม่ใช่ตัวก่อโรค จึงต้องแยก CJD การติดเชื้อ ภาวะเมตาบอลิก และ autoimmune encephalitis ชนิดอื่นก่อน รักษาด้วย steroid ขนาดสูงแล้วค่อย ๆ ลด
