ddx.pt: Cortical/striatal DWI restriction, periodic sharp waves and positive RT-QuIC; no steroid response
Slowing and confusion corrected by thyroid replacement; abnormal free T4 and TSH; no myoclonic encephalopathy
Continuous ictal EEG pattern that responds to antiseizure treatment

aN: sreat | steroid responsive encephalopathy associated with autoimmune thyroiditis | hashimoto encephalopathy | he

name: Hashimoto’s thyroiditis
formal: Autoimmune thyroiditis with anti-TPO antibodies causing hypothyroidism, with neuromuscular complications such as myopathy, carpal tunnel and neuropathy, and association with encephalopathy.
simple: An autoimmune thyroid disease causing an underactive thyroid, which can cause tiredness, weakness and slowed thinking.

name: Haw river syndrome
formal: Autosomal dominant dentatorubral-pallidoluysian atrophy variant (ATN1 CAG expansion) in African-American families with ataxia, chorea, dementia, seizures and basal ganglia calcification.
simple: A rare inherited brain disease with unsteadiness, jerky movements and memory loss, first described in one family.

name: Head tremor
formal: Rhythmic oscillation of the head, either yes-yes or no-no, from essential tremor, dystonic tremor or cervical dystonia, and sometimes from cerebellar lesions.
simple: A rhythmic shaking or nodding of the head that the person cannot control.

name: Headache
formal: Pain in the head, either primary (migraine, tension-type, cluster) or secondary to conditions such as haemorrhage, meningitis, giant-cell arteritis, tumour or raised pressure; red flags guide investigation.
simple: Pain felt anywhere in the head, most often harmless, but sometimes a sign of a serious illness.

name: Headache disorders
formal: Primary and secondary headache syndromes classified by the International Classification of Headache Disorders, including migraine, tension-type headache, trigeminal autonomic cephalalgias and secondary headaches.
simple: A group of conditions that cause repeated headaches, such as migraine and cluster headache.

name: Heart failure
formal: Cardiac pump failure leading to neurological issues such as cardioembolic stroke, cognitive impairment, hypoperfusion syncope and fatigue.
simple: A condition where the heart pumps poorly, which can cause fatigue, dizziness and raise the risk of stroke.

name: Heat stroke
formal: Hyperthermia above 40 C with CNS dysfunction, including delirium, seizures and coma, from environmental heat or exertion, and cerebellar injury in survivors.
simple: A life-threatening overheating of the body that causes confusion, seizures or collapse.

name: Heavy metal poisoning
formal: Toxicity from lead, mercury, arsenic, thallium or manganese, causing neuropathy, encephalopathy, ataxia, tremor or parkinsonism depending on the metal, treated by removal of source and chelation.
simple: Illness from exposure to metals such as lead or mercury, which can damage nerves and the brain.

name: Heller’s disease
formal: Childhood disintegrative disorder, with severe regression in language, social and motor skills after normal development for at least 2 years, often with seizures.
simple: A rare condition where a child who developed normally for years suddenly loses language, social and other skills.

name: Hemiathetosis
formal: Slow, writhing involuntary movements of one side of the body from contralateral basal ganglia lesions, often following stroke or perinatal injury.
simple: Slow, twisting involuntary movements on one side of the body, usually from damage in the brain.

name: Hemiballism
formal: Violent proximal flinging movements of one side of the body from contralateral subthalamic nucleus or connected lesions, classically stroke, often resolving with time.
simple: Wild flinging movements of an arm and leg on one side, usually after a small stroke deep in the brain.
th: การเหวี่ยงแขนขาข้างเดียวแรง ๆ อย่างควบคุมไม่ได้ มักเกิดเฉียบพลันจาก stroke ที่ subthalamic nucleus หรือ basal ganglia ด้านตรงข้าม หรือจากน้ำตาลสูง
tempoNote: Sudden onset with a stroke; usually lessens to hemichorea over weeks to months
feat: Large-amplitude, flinging, proximal movements of one arm and leg, continuous while awake
Sudden onset in an older person with vascular risk factors
Lesion contralateral: subthalamic nucleus, striatum, thalamus or their connections
Often merges with distal hemichorea; may cause injury, exhaustion and rhabdomyolysis
Little or no weakness in pure subthalamic strokes
inv: Capillary glucose and HbA1c at once — nonketotic hyperglycaemia is a key treatable cause
MRI with DWI (small STN or striatal infarct/haemorrhage); CT may miss small lesions
CT/MRI T1 striatal hyperintensity in diabetic striatopathy
Stroke work-up: ECG, lipids, vascular imaging

case.who: 73-year-old man with hypertension and diabetes from Phitsanulok
case.story: Woke up with his left arm and leg flinging wildly; he hit the bedside table repeatedly.
case.exam: Continuous large proximal throwing movements of left limbs, with distal writhing; strength near-normal; no visual field defect.
case.tests: Glucose 142 mg/dL; MRI DWI: small acute infarct in the right subthalamic nucleus.
case.q: Which drug class is most effective for the movements, and what is the expected course?
case.a: Vascular hemiballism from a right STN infarct: an antidopaminergic (haloperidol, risperidone or tetrabenazine) controls it; most improve over weeks, so taper later; plus secondary stroke prevention.

det.patho: Damage to the subthalamic nucleus or its pallidal connections reduces excitatory drive to the internal globus pallidus, releasing thalamocortical activity and producing large involuntary movements on the opposite side. Small-vessel ischaemia or haemorrhage is the main cause in older adults; non-ketotic hyperglycaemia, tumours, demyelination, infections (toxoplasmosis in HIV) and drugs are others. Most vascular lesions are actually in the striatum or thalamus rather than the STN itself.
det.clinical: Onset is abrupt, often on waking. Movements are violent and proximal, absent in sleep, and can lead to bruising, falls, fatigue and dehydration. Hemichorea and hemiballism lie on a continuum, and ballism tends to downgrade to distal chorea as the lesion matures. Rarely, it persists for months.
det.diagnosis: Check glucose first, then MRI with DWI and T1 sequences. Diabetic striatopathy shows T1 hyperintensity of the putamen with high glucose, usually in older Asian women. In younger patients consider HIV-related lesions, autoimmune disease and drugs. EEG if seizures are possible.
det.treatment: Protect the limbs and patient from injury and treat the cause (stroke prevention, glucose correction). Dopamine-receptor blockers (haloperidol, risperidone) or VMAT2 depleters (tetrabenazine) are effective; add clonazepam or topiramate if needed. Taper after weeks to months because of spontaneous improvement. Refractory persistent cases may benefit from GPi or thalamic surgery.
det.prognosis: Usually good — most vascular hemiballism improves substantially within weeks to a few months.
pearls: Acute one-sided flinging in an elderly diabetic: check glucose before ordering the MRI.
Lesion is contralateral, classically subthalamic nucleus, but striatal lesions are more common.
Many cases settle; avoid long-term dopamine blockers when possible.
det.thd: Hemiballism คือแขนขาข้างหนึ่งเหวี่ยงแรงและต่อเนื่อง มักเกิดเฉียบพลันจาก stroke ขนาดเล็กที่ subthalamic nucleus หรือ striatum ด้านตรงข้าม หรือจากน้ำตาลในเลือดสูงแบบ non-ketotic ต้องตรวจน้ำตาลทันทีและทำ MRI รักษาด้วยยาต้านโดปามีนเช่น haloperidol หรือ tetrabenazine ป้องกันบาดเจ็บ และป้องกัน stroke ซ้ำ ส่วนใหญ่อาการดีขึ้นในไม่กี่สัปดาห์

ddx.pt: Very high glucose, T1-bright contralateral putamen on CT/MRI; resolves with glucose control
Clonic rhythmic jerks with EEG correlate, possibly altered awareness; not continuous flinging
Variable, distractible movements without a corresponding lesion

aN: hemiballismus | ballism | hemiballism hemichorea | hb hc | subthalamic nucleus stroke | vascular hemiballism | post stroke hemichorea

name: Hemiballism-hemichorea syndrome
formal: Spectrum of unilateral hyperkinetic movements, from irregular flinging to chorea, due to lesions of the subthalamic nucleus or striatum, including non-ketotic hyperglycaemia.
simple: Unwanted flinging or dancing movements on one side of the body, usually from a stroke or high blood sugar.

name: Hemichorea
formal: Unilateral irregular, flowing involuntary movements from contralateral striatal or subthalamic lesion, often due to stroke, hyperglycaemia or lupus.
simple: Irregular, flowing involuntary movements on one side of the body.
more: MRI may show striatal hyperintensity on T1 with putaminal lesions in hyperglycaemic hemichorea; CT may be hyperdense. Treat the underlying cause (glucose control); dopamine blockers such as haloperidol or tetrabenazine are used and prognosis is usually good.

name: Hemicord syndrome
formal: Brown-Séquard syndrome of cord hemisection, with ipsilateral weakness and loss of proprioception and vibration, and contralateral loss of pain and temperature below the lesion.
simple: Damage to one half of the spinal cord causing weakness on one side and loss of pain sensation on the other.

name: Hemidystonia
formal: Dystonia affecting the arm and leg on one side, commonly secondary to a contralateral basal ganglia or thalamic lesion from stroke, trauma, perinatal injury or tumour.
simple: Twisting, abnormal postures of the arm and leg on one side of the body, usually from a brain injury on the opposite side.
more: MRI to look for contralateral lesions is essential. Treat with anticholinergics, baclofen, botulinum toxin or deep brain stimulation; onset may be delayed months after the injury.

name: Hemifacial spasm
formal: Unilateral involuntary twitching of facial muscles, usually from vascular compression of the facial nerve at the root exit zone, treated with botulinum toxin or microvascular decompression.
simple: Repeated twitching of the muscles on one side of the face, often caused by a blood vessel pressing on a nerve.
th: หน้ากระตุกข้างเดียวเป็นพัก ๆ เริ่มรอบตาแล้วลามลงมุมปาก ส่วนใหญ่จากหลอดเลือดกดเส้นประสาทที่ 7 รักษาด้วย botulinum toxin หรือ microvascular decompression
tempoNote: Brief twitches occurring in bursts many times a day; slowly worsens over years, persists in sleep
feat: One-sided clonic twitching beginning around the eye, spreading over years to cheek and mouth
Tonic contractions closing the eye and pulling the mouth; may continue during sleep
Babinski-2 (other Babinski) sign: eyebrow rises as the eye closes
Mild facial weakness or none; usually aged 40–60, more common in women and Asians
inv: MRI with high-resolution posterior fossa sequences (CISS/FIESTA) and MRA for vascular loop and to exclude tumour
EMG: lateral spread response (optional; useful intraoperatively)
Blood pressure check — association with hypertension

case.story: For 3 years her left eye twitches shut, and now the left corner of her mouth pulls up too; it continues when she sleeps according to her husband.
case.exam: Synchronous twitches of left orbicularis oculi and oris, left eyebrow rises as the eye closes; facial strength normal.
case.tests: MRI/MRA: left AICA loop touching the facial nerve root exit zone; no mass.
case.q: What are the two main treatment options?
case.a: Primary hemifacial spasm: botulinum toxin injections every 3–4 months, or microvascular decompression surgery for a durable cure.

det.patho: Most cases result from pulsatile compression of the facial nerve root exit zone by a vascular loop (AICA, PICA or vertebral artery). Ectopic excitation and ephaptic transmission at the damaged segment, plus facial nucleus hyperexcitability, produce synchronous contractions. Secondary causes include CPA tumours, AVMs, demyelination and previous facial nerve injury.
det.clinical: Typical HFS starts in the lower lid and spreads downward; atypical HFS starts in the lower face and spreads upward. Spasms are worsened by stress, fatigue and voluntary facial movements, and persist in sleep. It is usually unilateral; bilateral cases are rare and asynchronous. Social embarrassment and visual interference are the main burdens.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical. Every patient should have MRI with thin-slice cisternal sequences to identify the offending vessel and exclude a tumour. The other Babinski sign helps separate HFS from functional facial spasm. Differentiate from blepharospasm, facial myokymia, tics, focal seizures and synkinesis.
det.treatment: Botulinum toxin injection into orbicularis oculi (and lower face muscles if needed) helps the majority; repeat every 3–4 months. Carbamazepine, clonazepam or gabapentin give modest benefit. Microvascular decompression is curative in most, with risks of hearing loss and facial weakness; it suits younger, fit patients wanting a lasting solution.
det.prognosis: Spontaneous remission is rare; long-term control with toxin or surgery is good.
pearls: Spasms persisting during sleep favour HFS over blepharospasm or functional spasm.
Babinski-2 sign: frontalis rises while the eye closes.
Image every patient to look for a CPA lesion.
det.thd: Hemifacial spasm คือกล้ามเนื้อใบหน้าข้างเดียวกระตุก มักเริ่มที่เปลือกตาล่างแล้วลามลงมาที่ปาก และเป็นได้ขณะหลับ เกิดจากหลอดเลือดกดเส้นประสาทที่ 7 บริเวณที่ออกจากก้านสมอง ควรทำ MRI/MRA ทุกรายเพื่อแยกเนื้องอก รักษาด้วยฉีด botulinum toxin ทุก 3–4 เดือน หรือผ่าตัด microvascular decompression

ddx.pt: Bilateral eyelid closure, does not involve lower face, stops in sleep
Post-paralytic synkinesis: mouth moves with blinking after a previous facial palsy
Suppressible with premonitory urge, variable sites and younger onset

aN: hfs | hemifacial spasm | facial spasm | neurovascular compression of facial nerve | primary hemifacial spasm

name: Hemiparkinsonism
formal: Parkinsonian features limited to one side of the body, typically early Parkinson disease, but also from contralateral lesion or in hemiparkinsonism-hemiatrophy syndrome.
simple: Parkinson-like slowness and tremor affecting just one side of the body.

name: Hepatic encephalopathy
formal: Reversible neuropsychiatric syndrome of liver failure or portosystemic shunting, with asterixis, confusion, personality change and coma, linked to hyperammonaemia and treated with lactulose.
simple: Confusion, sleepiness and a flapping tremor caused by a failing liver that cannot clear toxins from the blood.
more: Diagnosis supported by raised blood ammonia, EEG triphasic waves, MRI pallidal T1 hyperintensity and psychometric tests; grade by West Haven criteria. Rifaximin is added to lactulose for recurrence, with precipitants (infection, bleeding.

name: Hepatitis C
formal: Chronic hepatitis C virus infection with neurological complications including cryoglobulinaemic neuropathy, mononeuritis multiplex, stroke, cognitive slowing and treatment-related neuropathy.
simple: A viral liver infection that can also affect nerves, causing numbness, weakness and tiredness.

name: Hepatopathy
formal: Liver disease within neurological or metabolic disorders, for example Wilson disease, POLG Alpers syndrome and mitochondrial depletion syndromes, with raised enzymes and hepatic failure.
simple: Liver damage that occurs together with certain inherited brain or muscle diseases.
more: Liver function tests and imaging with targeted genetic testing; treatment depends on cause, including chelation for Wilson disease.

name: Hereditary ataxias
formal: Genetically determined progressive cerebellar syndromes, either autosomal dominant (spinocerebellar ataxias), recessive (Friedreich, AT) or X-linked, with gait ataxia, dysarthria and variable extracerebellar signs.
simple: Inherited conditions that gradually cause problems with balance, coordination and speech.
more: Genetic panels cover repeat expansions and point mutations; MRI shows cerebellar atrophy, sometimes with pontine change. Care is mainly supportive rehabilitation, with specific therapy for treatable causes such as vitamin E and CoQ10 deficiency.

name: Hereditary essential myoclonus
formal: Autosomal dominant non-progressive myoclonus with onset in childhood or teens, often with dystonia, due to SGCE mutation and alcohol-responsive (myoclonus-dystonia).
simple: An inherited condition of sudden muscle jerks that begins early in life and may improve with alcohol.

name: Hereditary hyperekplexia
formal: Genetic startle disease (GLRA1, SLC6A5) with exaggerated startle, neonatal stiffness and falls; treated with clonazepam, and Vigevano manoeuvre for apnoea.
simple: An inherited condition in which a sudden noise or touch causes extreme startle and stiffening, sometimes causing falls.

name: Hereditary inclusion body myopathies
formal: Group of inherited vacuolar myopathies resembling inclusion body myositis but without inflammation, including GNE myopathy, sparing the quadriceps and presenting with distal weakness.
simple: A family of inherited muscle diseases with slowly worsening weakness and tiny holes seen in muscle fibres.
more: Most are autosomal recessive (GNE) or dominant (VCP, MYH2, desmin). Muscle biopsy shows rimmed vacuoles; no proven cure, with supportive care and physiotherapy.

name: Hereditary motor and sensory neuropathies (HMSN)
formal: Charcot–Marie–Tooth group of inherited neuropathies with distal weakness, pes cavus, areflexia and sensory loss, either demyelinating (PMP22 duplication) or axonal.
simple: A group of inherited nerve diseases causing weakness and wasting in the feet and hands, high arches and numbness.
nN: hereditary motor and sensory neuropathies hmsn
aN: hmsn | hereditary motor and sensory neuropathies

name: Hereditary motor and sensory neuropathy (HMSN)
formal: Charcot–Marie–Tooth group of inherited neuropathies with distal weakness, pes cavus, areflexia and sensory loss, either demyelinating (PMP22 duplication) or axonal.
simple: A group of inherited nerve diseases causing weakness and wasting in the feet and hands, high arches and numbness.
nN: hereditary motor and sensory neuropathy hmsn
aN: hmsn | hereditary motor and sensory neuropathy

name: Hereditary motor and sensory neuropathy type 1 (HMSN type 1)
formal: Demyelinating Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 1 with slow conduction velocities, distal weakness, pes cavus and enlarged nerves; most commonly from PMP22 duplication (CMT1A).
simple: An inherited nerve disease causing slowly worsening weakness and wasting in the feet and lower legs with high-arched feet.
more: Diagnosis by nerve conduction (below 38 m/s) and PMP22 testing; autosomal dominant. Treatment is orthoses, physiotherapy and surgery; lifespan is normal.
ab: Hereditary motor and sensory neuropathy type 1
nN: hereditary motor and sensory neuropathy type 1 hmsn type 1
aN: hmsn type 1 | hereditary motor and sensory neuropathy type 1

name: Hereditary motor neuropathies (HMNs)
formal: Inherited length-dependent motor axonopathies without clinically significant sensory loss, resembling Charcot–Marie–Tooth disease, with distal weakness and wasting.
simple: Inherited nerve diseases that mainly weaken and waste the muscles of the hands and feet, without much numbness.
aN: hmns | hereditary motor neuropathies

name: Hereditary motor neuropathy
formal: Length-dependent motor axonopathy without sensory loss, due to variants such as HSPB1, HSPB8, GARS or BSCL2, causing distal limb wasting and weakness.
simple: An inherited nerve condition that causes slowly progressive weakness and wasting of the feet and hands but not numbness.
more: Nerve conduction shows motor axonal loss with normal sensory responses. Genetic panel testing confirms it; management is supportive with orthoses and rehabilitation.

name: Hereditary neuropathy with liability to pressure palsies (HNPP)
formal: PMP22 deletion causing recurrent focal neuropathies at compression sites, such as peroneal and ulnar, after minor pressure, with tomaculous changes on nerve biopsy.
simple: An inherited condition in which nerves are very sensitive to pressure, causing episodes of numbness and weakness.
more: Diagnose by PMP22 deletion testing; nerve conduction shows diffuse mild slowing with prolonged distal latencies and conduction block at entrapment sites. Management is avoiding compression and splinting; most episodes resolve over weeks to months.
ab: Hereditary neuropathy with liability to pressure palsies
th: เส้นประสาทไวต่อการกดทับทางพันธุกรรม (PMP22 หาย) — ชา/อ่อนแรงซ้ำ ๆ หลังนั่งไขว่ห้างหรือนอนทับแขน หายเองได้
feat: Recurrent painless mononeuropathies at compression sites (peroneal, ulnar, radial, brachial plexus) after minor pressure
Most episodes recover over days to months
Autosomal dominant; relatives may have mild background neuropathy
inv: NCS: focal slowing at entrapment sites plus mild diffuse slowing even in unaffected nerves
PMP22 deletion (17p11.2)

case.story: Foot drop after kneeling on guard duty; last year a weak wrist after sleeping on his arm, which recovered. His mother has 'carpal tunnel' in both hands.
case.exam: Right peroneal palsy, reduced ankle jerks bilaterally.
case.tests: Conduction block at the fibular head plus prolonged distal latencies in median and ulnar nerves; PMP22 deletion.
case.q: What advice prevents further episodes?
case.a: Avoid prolonged pressure or stretching of nerves (crossing legs, kneeling, leaning on elbows) and take care during anaesthesia positioning.

files.chapter: Chapter 43: Hereditary Neuropathy with Pressure Palsy (HNPP)

ddx.pt: Progressive symmetric distal weakness; PMP22 duplication
Not related to pressure, raised CSF protein, steroid/IVIG responsive
Severe pain at onset

nN: hereditary neuropathy with liability to pressure palsies hnpp
aN: hnpp | hereditary neuropathy with liability to pressure palsies | tomaculous neuropathy | pmp22 deletion | pressure palsy neuropathy

det.patho: HNPP is usually caused by a heterozygous 1.4 Mb deletion of chromosome 17p11.2 that includes PMP22 — the reciprocal of the duplication in CMT1A; point mutations account for a minority. Reduced PMP22 dosage destabilises myelin and junctions, producing focal sausage-like myelin thickenings (tomacula) and nerves that tolerate pressure or stretch poorly. Inheritance is autosomal dominant with variable penetrance, and many carriers are unaware.
det.clinical: Typical patients have repeated painless focal palsies after trivial compression — peroneal palsy after crossing legs, ulnar palsy after leaning, radial palsy after sleeping on the arm, or brachial plexus palsy after carrying a backpack. Episodes usually recover over days to weeks, though recovery can be incomplete. Some develop a mild length-dependent polyneuropathy, recurrent carpal tunnel-like symptoms, or no symptoms at all. Pes cavus and reduced ankle reflexes may be found.
det.diagnosis: NCS characteristically show prolonged distal motor latencies, slowing at usual entrapment sites, and mild generalised sensory abnormalities even in clinically unaffected nerves — finding these in a patient with a single palsy is a strong clue. Genetic testing for the PMP22 deletion (MLPA or similar) confirms the diagnosis and avoids biopsy. Family members may need testing and counselling.
det.treatment: There is no specific therapy. Education is central: avoid prolonged leg crossing, kneeling, leaning on elbows, tight straps and repetitive wrist flexion, and use padding. Inform anaesthetists to pad and position limbs carefully. Orthoses and physiotherapy aid recovery from palsies, and surgical decompression of entrapments is generally avoided unless clearly indicated. Neurotoxic drugs such as vincristine should be used with caution.
det.prognosis: Life expectancy is normal and most episodes resolve, but accumulating residual deficits occur in some people over time.
pearls: Recurrent pressure palsies + diffuse NCS abnormalities = PMP22 deletion.
Deletion causes HNPP; duplication causes CMT1A.
Think HNPP before operating on a young patient with multiple entrapments.
det.thd: HNPP เป็นโรคเส้นประสาททางพันธุกรรม (PMP22 deletion) ทำให้เยื่อหุ้มเส้นประสาทไม่แข็งแรงและไวต่อการกดทับ ผู้ป่วยมีอ่อนแรง/ชาไม่ปวดซ้ำ ๆ หลังนั่งไขว่ห้าง นอนทับแขน หรือวางศอกนาน ส่วนใหญ่หายเองในไม่กี่สัปดาห์ NCS พบความผิดปกติกระจายทั่วไปแม้ในเส้นที่ไม่มีอาการ ยืนยันด้วยตรวจยีน ไม่มียารักษาเฉพาะ เน้นการหลีกเลี่ยงการกดทับและแจ้งวิสัญญีแพทย์เรื่องการจัดท่า

name: Hereditary optic neuropathy
formal: Inherited optic nerve disease, including Leber hereditary optic neuropathy (mitochondrial) and dominant optic atrophy (OPA1), causing painless visual loss and optic disc pallor.
simple: An inherited disease of the optic nerve that gradually causes loss of vision.

name: Hereditary sensory and autonomic neuropathies
formal: Heterogeneous inherited neuropathies marked by sensory loss, ulceration and autonomic failure, classified HSAN I to VIII based on genes such as SPTLC1 and RETREG1.
simple: Inherited nerve conditions where pain and temperature sense is lost and automatic body functions are impaired, causing painless injuries.
more: Diagnosis by genetic testing and nerve studies; inheritance mostly autosomal recessive except HSAN I. Care focuses on foot protection, wound care and managing autonomic symptoms.

name: Hereditary sensory and autonomic neuropathy
formal: Inherited neuropathies with predominant loss of pain and temperature sensation, ulcers, mutilation and autonomic dysfunction, such as HSAN types I to V.
simple: Inherited nerve diseases where people cannot feel pain or temperature properly, leading to injuries and sores.

name: Hereditary sensory neuropathy (HSN)
formal: Inherited neuropathies with predominant loss of pain and temperature sensation, ulcers, mutilation and autonomic dysfunction, such as HSAN types I to V.
simple: Inherited nerve diseases where people cannot feel pain or temperature properly, leading to injuries and sores.
aN: hsn | hereditary sensory neuropathy

name: Hereditary spastic ataxia
formal: Autosomal recessive disorder with spastic ataxia, such as ARSACS (SACS), with early-onset ataxia, spasticity, peripheral neuropathy and retinal striation.
simple: An inherited condition with both stiff legs and unsteady balance, usually starting in childhood.

name: Hereditary spastic paraplegia (HSP)
formal: Heritable upper motor neuron disorders with progressive lower limb spasticity and weakness from corticospinal tract axonopathy, pure or complicated, with many genes (SPG4 commonest).
simple: Inherited conditions that gradually make the legs stiff and weak because of damage to nerve fibres from the brain.
more: Diagnosis uses MRI to exclude structural causes, and a gene panel including SPG4 (SPAST), SPG3A and SPG11; thin corpus callosum is typical of SPG11. Treat symptomatically with baclofen, tizanidine, botulinum toxin and physiotherapy.
th: ขาเกร็งแข็งและเดินลำบากค่อยเป็นค่อยไปจากพันธุกรรม — corticospinal tract ยาวเสื่อม แขนมักปกติ
tempoNote: Any age from childhood to late adulthood; very slow progression over decades
feat: Spasticity in the legs out of proportion to weakness; scissoring, toe-walking gait
Brisk leg reflexes, extensor plantars, often mild vibration loss at the ankles
Urinary urgency is common; arms usually spared
'Complicated' forms add neuropathy, ataxia, cognitive decline, thin corpus callosum or epilepsy
inv: MRI brain and whole spine to exclude compression, demyelination and leukodystrophy
B12, copper, HTLV-1, VLCFA (adrenomyeloneuropathy) to exclude acquired or treatable mimics
Gene panel or exome (SPAST, ATL1, REEP1, SPG7, SPG11 and others)

case.story: Since his twenties he has tripped over curbs; legs feel stiff rather than weak. His mother walked with a stiff gait in later life.
case.exam: Spastic paraparesis with mild hip flexor weakness, ankle clonus, bilateral Babinski, reduced vibration at the toes; normal arms and speech.
case.tests: MRI brain and spine normal; B12, copper and HTLV-1 negative; SPAST pathogenic variant.
case.q: What is the role of spinal MRI when a family history is clear?
case.a: Still essential — structural lesions and treatable myelopathies must be excluded before attributing spastic paraparesis to HSP.

det.patho: HSP is a group of over 80 genetic disorders that cause length-dependent degeneration of the longest corticospinal axons and, to a lesser extent, the dorsal columns. Implicated genes affect axonal transport, membrane shaping of the endoplasmic reticulum, lipid metabolism and mitochondrial function. SPAST (SPG4) mutations are the most frequent dominant cause; SPG11 and SPG7 are common recessive causes.
det.clinical: Pure forms present with slowly progressive leg stiffness and gait difficulty; walking deteriorates more because of tone than weakness. Onset age varies widely even within a family. Complicated forms add features such as cerebellar ataxia, peripheral neuropathy, cognitive decline, optic atrophy, amyotrophy of the hands or a thin corpus callosum. Bladder urgency is common; rapid progression or sensory level should prompt a search for another cause.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis needs a compatible syndrome, family history or genetic confirmation, and exclusion of mimics. MRI of brain and spine is mandatory to rule out compressive myelopathy, MS, leukodystrophy and spinal dural fistula. Bloods for B12, copper, HTLV-1, VLCFA and syphilis address acquired and treatable causes. Next-generation sequencing panels identify a cause in perhaps half of familial cases.
det.treatment: There is no disease-modifying therapy. Management targets spasticity with stretching, physiotherapy, oral baclofen or tizanidine, botulinum toxin to selected muscles and intrathecal baclofen for severe cases. Ankle-foot orthoses, walking aids, bladder antimuscarinics and genetic counselling complete care.
det.prognosis: Pure forms usually allow independent walking for decades with normal lifespan; complicated forms carry more disability.
pearls: Stiffness greater than weakness in the legs is the HSP signature.
Thin corpus callosum on MRI suggests SPG11 or SPG15.
Always exclude B12, copper and adrenomyeloneuropathy — treatable or important mimics.
det.thd: HSP เป็นโรคพันธุกรรมที่ทำให้ corticospinal tract ส่วนที่ยาวที่สุดเสื่อม ผู้ป่วยมีขาเกร็งแข็ง เดินลากขา reflex ไว Babinski บวก แต่แขนมักปกติ แบ่งเป็นชนิด pure และ complicated ต้องทำ MRI สมองและไขสันหลัง และตรวจ B12, copper, HTLV-1, VLCFA เพื่อแยกโรคที่รักษาได้ ยืนยันด้วยการตรวจยีน การรักษาเน้นลดเกร็งและกายภาพบำบัด

X-linked; raised VLCFA, adrenal insufficiency, neuropathy

name: Herpes simplex encephalitis (HSE)
formal: Necrotising temporal and orbitofrontal encephalitis from HSV-1 with fever, seizures, aphasia and behavioural change; diagnosed by CSF PCR and MRI and treated promptly with aciclovir.
simple: A serious brain infection from the cold sore virus, causing fever, confusion and seizures, treated urgently with antiviral medicine.
th: สมองอักเสบจากเชื้อเริม — ไข้ สับสน พฤติกรรมเปลี่ยน ชัก กระทบสมองกลีบขมับ ให้ acyclovir ทันที
feat: Fever with confusion, behavioural change, dysphasia
Focal seizures, olfactory or gustatory hallucinations
Can trigger later anti-NMDAR encephalitis
inv: MRI: asymmetric medial temporal/insular/orbitofrontal T2 change
CSF lymphocytes, red cells; HSV PCR (repeat if early negative)
EEG: temporal periodic discharges

case.story: Two days of fever and headache, now talking nonsense and smelling burning rubber.
case.exam: Temp 38.7 °C, fluent dysphasia, no neck stiffness.
case.tests: MRI: left medial temporal FLAIR hyperintensity; CSF WBC 85 (lymphocytes), HSV-1 PCR positive.
case.q: When should acyclovir be started?
case.a: Immediately on suspicion — before results return.

files.chapter: Chapter 3 - Pathogenesis and Disease Mechanisms in Neuronal Antibody-Mediated Encephalitis
Chapter 12 Infection in the Nervous System
Part II: Viral Pathogens: Pathogenesis, Pathology, Diagnosis and Treatment

ddx.pt: Subacute psychiatric/seizure presentation, antibody positive, PCR negative
No fever or CSF inflammation
Meningism, neutrophilic CSF

aN: hse | herpes simplex encephalitis | hsv encephalitis | herpes encephalitis

det.patho: HSV-1, either from primary infection or reactivation in the trigeminal ganglion, reaches the orbitofrontal and medial temporal lobes and causes asymmetric haemorrhagic necrotising encephalitis. It is the most common sporadic fatal viral encephalitis worldwide, occurring at any age without seasonality. Defects in innate TLR3 signalling predispose some children; HSV-2 causes neonatal encephalitis and adult meningitis more often.
det.clinical: Most patients have fever and headache with altered behaviour, confusion, memory problems, dysphasia or personality change developing over days. Focal seizures, olfactory or taste hallucinations and hemiparesis may occur. Neck stiffness is often absent. About a quarter of patients develop anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis weeks after HSE, presenting as a relapse with movement disorders or psychiatric change and negative viral PCR.
det.diagnosis: CSF typically shows a lymphocytic pleocytosis with raised protein and often red cells; a normal early CSF does not exclude it. HSV PCR is highly sensitive and specific but can be falsely negative during the first three days, so repeat it if suspicion remains. MRI is the most sensitive imaging test, showing T2/FLAIR and diffusion change in the medial temporal lobe, insula and cingulate, often bilateral but asymmetric. EEG may show lateralised periodic discharges over the temporal lobe.
det.treatment: Start IV acyclovir 10 mg/kg every 8 hours (adjusted for renal function) as soon as encephalitis is suspected, and continue for 14–21 days in confirmed cases. Maintain hydration to avoid crystal nephropathy. Treat seizures and raised intracranial pressure; corticosteroids are not routinely recommended. Monitor for post-HSE autoimmune encephalitis and test NMDAR antibodies if new symptoms appear after initial improvement.
det.prognosis: Untreated mortality exceeds 70%; with acyclovir it falls to around 10–20%, but many survivors have memory, behavioural or language deficits, especially if treatment is delayed.
pearls: Fever plus confusion means acyclovir now — every hour of delay worsens outcome.
Early negative HSV PCR does not rule it out; repeat the LP.
New chorea or psychiatric change weeks after HSE suggests NMDAR encephalitis, not viral relapse.
det.thd: HSE เป็นสมองอักเสบจากเชื้อ HSV-1 ที่ทำลายสมองกลีบขมับด้านในและส่วนหน้าล่าง ผู้ป่วยมีไข้ ปวดศีรษะ สับสน พฤติกรรมเปลี่ยน พูดผิดปกติ หรือชัก บางรายได้กลิ่นแปลก ๆ MRI เห็นรอยโรคที่ medial temporal และ insula น้ำไขสันหลังมี lymphocyte และส่ง HSV PCR (ถ้าลบในช่วงแรกควรเจาะซ้ำ) ต้องให้ acyclovir ทางหลอดเลือดทันทีที่สงสัย 14–21 วัน หลังหายอาจเกิด anti-NMDAR encephalitis ตามมาได้

name: Herpes simplex virus 2 vasculitis
formal: HSV-2 related central nervous system infection that is associated with Mollaret meningitis and rare vasculopathy causing stroke or myelitis.
simple: A rare complication of the genital herpes virus that inflames blood vessels in the brain or spinal cord.

name: Hexosaminidase-A deficiency
formal: Deficiency of beta-hexosaminidase A causing GM2 gangliosidosis, with infantile Tay-Sachs or later-onset forms with ataxia, dystonia and motor neuron disease features.
simple: An inherited enzyme shortage causing a fatty substance to build up in nerve cells, causing loss of skills and weakness.

name: High-grade glioma
formal: Aggressive diffuse gliomas of WHO grade 3 or 4, including glioblastoma and anaplastic astrocytoma, with rapid growth, contrast enhancement and poor prognosis.
simple: Fast-growing brain tumours that spread into nearby tissue and are difficult to treat.

name: Hindbrain malformation
formal: Congenital cerebellar and brainstem malformations such as Chiari, Dandy-Walker and Joubert, with hydrocephalus, ataxia, developmental delay and respiratory irregularity.
simple: A birth defect of the back part of the brain that can cause balance problems, delay or fluid build-up.

name: Hippocampal sclerosis
formal: Neuronal loss and gliosis of hippocampus, the commonest pathology in drug-resistant temporal lobe epilepsy, with T2 hyperintensity and atrophy on MRI, treatable by temporal lobectomy.
simple: Scarring and shrinkage of a memory-related brain region, a common cause of seizures that do not respond to medicine.

name: Hirayama’s disease
formal: Juvenile asymmetric distal upper limb amyotrophy of the hand and forearm in young males, from forward displacement of the cervical dura on flexion, with benign self-limited course.
simple: A condition in young men causing slow wasting and weakness of one or both hands and forearms, usually stopping after a few years.
more: Diagnosis is usually clinical with MRI showing cervical flexion cord compression and forward displacement of the posterior dura; cervical collar is the mainstay. EMG shows chronic denervation in C7 to T1 myotomes and progression stops after 2 to 5 years.
ab: juvenile muscular atrophy of the distal upper extremity
th: กล้ามเนื้อปลายแขนลีบข้างเดียวในชายวัยรุ่น — จากไขสันหลังส่วนคอถูกกดเวลาก้มคอ มักหยุดลุกลามเอง
tempoNote: Insidious onset in teens/early 20s; progresses for a few years then usually plateaus
feat: Young man (often Asian) with unilateral or asymmetric hand and forearm wasting
Oblique amyotrophy: forearm wasted but brachioradialis preserved
Weakness worse in the cold (cold paresis); minipolymyoclonus of the fingers
No sensory loss, no UMN signs in the legs
inv: Cervical MRI in neutral AND full flexion with contrast: forward shift of the posterior dura with an enlarged epidural venous plexus; lower cervical cord atrophy
EMG: chronic denervation in C7–T1 myotomes, normal sensory studies

case.story: Over 18 months his right hand became weak and thin; it gets much worse in an air-conditioned room. Writing is now slow.
case.exam: Wasting of right intrinsic hand muscles and ulnar forearm with sparing of brachioradialis, fine finger tremor on extension, normal reflexes and sensation.
case.tests: Neutral MRI: mild cord flattening at C5–C6; flexion MRI: posterior dura moves forward with a crescent of epidural enhancement.
case.q: What simple measure is advised early?
case.a: A cervical collar to prevent neck flexion — it can halt progression; surgery is reserved for selected progressive cases.

Conduction block along individual nerves; responds to IVIG
Thenar-predominant wasting with medial forearm sensory loss and a cervical rib/band

aN: hirayama disease | monomelic amyotrophy | juvenile muscular atrophy of the distal upper extremity | benign focal amyotrophy

det.patho: During growth spurts, the dural sac may be relatively short compared with the vertebral column, so neck flexion pulls the posterior dura forward and compresses the lower cervical cord. Repeated flexion causes chronic ischaemic damage to the anterior horns at C7–T1, with an enlarged posterior epidural venous plexus visible on flexion. It predominantly affects young men and is reported most often in Asia.
det.clinical: Onset is between the mid-teens and early twenties with insidious weakness and wasting of the hand and ulnar forearm, usually on one side or asymmetric. Brachioradialis is typically spared, giving 'oblique amyotrophy'. Cold paresis, irregular finger tremor and mild contralateral involvement are common. There are no sensory or pyramidal signs, and the disease progresses for a few years before stabilising.
det.diagnosis: Cervical MRI in neutral position may show only lower cord atrophy or flattening; MRI in full flexion with contrast shows anterior shift of the posterior dura and an enhancing epidural crescent. EMG shows chronic denervation in C7–T1 myotomes with normal sensory studies. Exclude ALS, MMN, syringomyelia, spinal cord tumours and thoracic outlet syndrome.
det.treatment: Avoiding repeated neck flexion with a cervical collar during the active phase may stop progression. Surgery (duraplasty or anterior decompression and fusion) is reserved for progressive cases despite collar therapy. Hand therapy and occupational adaptation support function.
det.prognosis: The disease usually becomes self-limiting within about 5 years, leaving stable focal weakness.
pearls: Young man + unilateral hand/forearm wasting + spared brachioradialis + cold paresis = Hirayama.
A neutral-position MRI can be nearly normal — request flexion MRI.

name: Histone mutant gliomas
formal: Diffuse midline glioma H3 K27-altered and diffuse hemispheric glioma H3 G34-mutant, aggressive tumours of children and young adults, such as diffuse intrinsic pontine glioma.
simple: Aggressive brain tumours in children and young adults caused by a specific gene change, often in the brainstem.

name: HIV dementia
formal: HIV-associated neurocognitive disorder, ranging from asymptomatic to dementia, with subcortical features of slowed thinking, motor slowing, apathy and white-matter change, improved by antiretrovirals.
simple: Memory and thinking problems, with slowed movement, caused by HIV infection of the brain.

name: HIV infection
formal: Chronic retroviral infection of CD4 cells that causes progressive immunodeficiency and can directly injure brain, cord and nerve, or permit opportunistic CNS infections and lymphoma.
simple: A virus that weakens the immune system over time and can also affect the brain, spinal cord and nerves, directly or by allowing other infections.

name: HIV-1 (retrovirus)
formal: The human immunodeficiency virus type 1 retrovirus, the commonest cause of HIV disease, which infects CD4 T cells and microglia and enters the CNS early in infection.
simple: The main virus that causes HIV, which attacks the body's immune cells and can get into the brain early on.
aN: retrovirus | hiv 1

name: HIV-associated dementia (HAD)
formal: Severe subcortical dementia from advanced HIV, with psychomotor slowing, impaired attention and memory, and motor signs; reflects HIV-driven microglial and macrophage injury, now uncommon with antiretrovirals.
simple: A serious loss of thinking, memory and movement speed in advanced HIV infection, now rare because modern treatment protects the brain.
aN: had | hiv associated dementia

name: HIV-associated myopathy
formal: Muscle disease in HIV from the virus itself, an inflammatory polymyositis-like picture, or zidovudine toxicity, causing proximal weakness with raised creatine kinase.
simple: Muscle weakness in a person with HIV, caused by the virus, by inflammation, or by certain HIV drugs.

name: HIV-associated neurocognitive disorder (HAND)
formal: Spectrum of cognitive impairment in HIV, graded as asymptomatic, mild neurocognitive disorder or dementia, with attention, executive and motor slowing that persists despite viral suppression.
simple: Problems with thinking, concentration and memory that can occur in people with HIV, ranging from very mild to severe.
aN: hand | hiv associated neurocognitive disorder

name: HIV-related autonomic neuropathy
formal: Autonomic neuropathy in HIV infection, causing orthostatic hypotension, sweating abnormalities and gastrointestinal or bladder dysfunction, often with advanced disease.
simple: Nerve damage from HIV that disturbs automatic body functions such as blood pressure and digestion.
more: Assessed with autonomic function tests; antiretroviral therapy and symptomatic measures such as fluids and midodrine are used.

name: HIV-related inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy
formal: HIV-associated acute or chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy, often at seroconversion or with CD4 recovery, with CSF pleocytosis in contrast to typical GBS.
simple: An immune-driven nerve condition in people with HIV that causes weakness and loss of reflexes.
more: Nerve studies show demyelination; CSF has raised cells. Treated with IVIG or plasma exchange, with steroids in chronic forms, along with antiretroviral therapy.

name: HIV-related multiple mononeuropathies
formal: Vasculitic multiple mononeuropathy in HIV, either from immune reconstitution or CMV or other infection, producing stepwise multifocal nerve deficits.
simple: Several separate nerves become damaged in people with HIV, causing patchy weakness and numbness.
more: Nerve biopsy and CMV testing guide therapy; treatments include ganciclovir for CMV, immunotherapy for vasculitis and antiretroviral therapy.

name: HIV-related progressive polyradiculopathy
formal: CMV-related cauda equina syndrome in advanced HIV, with rapidly progressive flaccid paraparesis, sphincter dysfunction and neutrophilic CSF pleocytosis.
simple: A fast-worsening leg weakness and bladder problem from infection of lower spinal nerve roots in advanced HIV.
more: MRI shows root enhancement; CSF PCR confirms CMV. Prompt ganciclovir or foscarnet with antiretroviral therapy is needed to prevent permanent damage.

name: HIV-related sensory neuropathy
formal: Distal symmetric sensory polyneuropathy, the commonest HIV neurological complication, with painful burning feet from HIV itself or from antiretroviral toxicity.
simple: Burning, painful or numb feet and hands in people with HIV.
more: Diagnosed clinically with nerve studies or skin biopsy. Stopping neurotoxic drugs, antiretroviral therapy, and neuropathic pain agents such as gabapentin help.

name: HIV-related vacuolar myelopathy
formal: Spinal cord degeneration in advanced AIDS with vacuolation of the posterior and lateral columns, giving spastic paraparesis, sensory ataxia and bladder dysfunction, resembling B12 deficiency.
simple: Damage to the spinal cord in advanced HIV that causes stiff, weak legs, poor balance and bladder trouble.

name: HIV/AIDS
formal: Acquired immunodeficiency from HIV, with neurological disease from direct viral effects, opportunistic infections such as toxoplasmosis, cryptococcus and PML, lymphoma, and neuropathy.
simple: Late-stage HIV infection, when the weakened immune system lets many illnesses, including brain and nerve problems, develop.

name: HIV/AIDS basal ganglia calcification
formal: Bilateral basal ganglia calcification in children with HIV, often with encephalopathy, probably from vascular injury and mineral deposition, seen on CT as symmetric dense deposits.
simple: Calcium deposits in deep brain areas, seen on scans of some children with HIV, often linked to developmental problems.

name: Hodgkin’s disease
formal: Lymphoma with Reed-Sternberg cells; neurological involvement includes spinal cord compression, paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration, limbic encephalitis and neuropathy.
simple: A cancer of the lymph glands that can press on the spinal cord or trigger immune attacks on the brain and nerves.

name: Holmes tremor
formal: Rest, postural and kinetic tremor of low frequency (under 4.5 Hz) from midbrain lesions affecting the cerebello-thalamic and nigrostriatal pathways, often after stroke or trauma.
simple: A slow, large, shaking tremor of the arm, present at rest and with movement, usually after damage to the midbrain.

name: Holmes–Adie syndrome (HAS)
formal: Tonic pupil with absent or reduced tendon reflexes, from damage to ciliary ganglion and dorsal root ganglion neurons; usually young women, benign, with sectoral iris palsy and light-near dissociation.
simple: A harmless condition with one large, slowly reacting pupil and reduced knee and ankle reflexes.
aN: has | holmes adie syndrome

name: Horizontal gaze palsy
formal: Loss of conjugate eye movement to one side from a lesion of the PPRF or abducens nucleus in the pons, or the frontal eye field; may be isolated or part of a brainstem syndrome.
simple: Inability to move both eyes together toward one side, caused by damage in the brainstem or brain.

name: Horner syndrome
formal: Oculosympathetic palsy with ptosis, miosis and anhidrosis from a lesion along the three-neuron sympathetic pathway; causes include carotid dissection, Pancoast tumour and lateral medullary stroke.
simple: A drooping eyelid, small pupil and reduced sweating on one side of the face, from damage to nerves that run from brain to eye.

name: HTLV-1 associated myelopathy
formal: Chronic progressive spastic paraparesis from HTLV-1 infection with thoracic cord inflammation, causing leg weakness, bladder dysfunction and mild sensory loss; endemic in Japan, Caribbean and South America.
simple: Slowly worsening stiffness and weakness of the legs with bladder problems, caused by a virus infecting the spinal cord.

tempoNote: Insidious, slowly progressive over years; occasionally rapid in the first 2 years

Early bladder urgency, frequency and incontinence; constipation; erectile dysfunction
Low back pain and leg dysaesthesia with only mild sensory signs
Brisk reflexes and extensor plantars, sometimes with brisk jaw jerk
Associated: uveitis, infective dermatitis, Strongyloides, adult T-cell leukaemia
inv: HTLV-1 serology (ELISA) confirmed by western blot or PCR in blood and CSF

MRI spine: thoracic cord atrophy, occasionally T2 signal in active cases
Exclude compression, B12/copper deficiency, MS, HSP

case.who: 52-year-old woman who once received a blood transfusion abroad
case.story: Over 4 years her legs stiffened; she now walks with a stick and has urgency incontinence and low back ache.
case.exam: Spastic gait, mild hip flexor weakness, brisk knee and ankle reflexes with clonus, bilateral Babinski, vibration slightly reduced at toes; arms normal.
case.tests: MRI thoracic cord thin without compression; HTLV-1 antibody positive with western blot; CSF 12 lymphocytes, oligoclonal bands, high proviral load.
case.q: Which other condition must be screened for before giving steroids?
case.a: Strongyloides stercoralis infection — HTLV-1 predisposes to hyperinfection, which corticosteroids can make fatal; treat with ivermectin first if positive.

read.where: Chapter 12 Infection in the Nervous System (HTLV-1 associated myelopathy / tropical spastic paraparesis)
Chapter 8 Neurological illnesses involved in HIV and HTLV infections

det.patho: HTLV-1 is a deltaretrovirus that persists by clonal expansion of infected CD4 T cells rather than by free virions, so spread needs cell-rich fluids: prolonged breastfeeding, sex, transfused cellular blood products, shared needles and organ transplantation. Only about 1–4% of carriers ever develop HAM/TSP, and the main predictor is a high proviral load, with host HLA type and the vigour of the cytotoxic response also mattering. Infected T cells migrate into the cord, where viral protein (Tax) expression attracts virus-specific CD8 cells and a CXCL10-driven inflammatory loop; the bystander damage falls mostly on the lateral and posterior columns of the lower thoracic cord, which eventually atrophies. The same virus causes adult T-cell leukaemia/lymphoma, uveitis, infective dermatitis and a predisposition to Strongyloides hyperinfection.
det.clinical: Onset is usually in the fourth to sixth decade, after a latency of years, and women are affected more often. Stiff, heavy legs with slowly mounting spastic weakness (often more proximal), early urinary urgency, frequency or retention, constipation and erectile failure, and burning low back or leg pain dominate, while objective sensory loss is slight — perhaps reduced vibration at the ankles. Arms become involved late and mildly, and bulbar muscles are spared; a few develop cerebellar signs, peripheral neuropathy or a steroid-resistant inflammatory myositis. Most worsen steadily over decades, but about one in five progresses quickly over the first two years. Endemic regions include southern Japan, the Caribbean, South America, sub-Saharan Africa, Iran, Melanesia and central Australia; in Thailand the infection is rare, so ask about birthplace, migration, transfusion and partners.
det.diagnosis: Suspect it in any slowly progressive myelopathy with prominent bladder symptoms and few sensory signs. Screen serum and CSF with ELISA or chemiluminescence and confirm by western blot, line immunoassay or proviral DNA PCR (which also separates HTLV-1 from HTLV-2); the WHO and later graded criteria rank cases as definite, probable or possible depending on CSF evidence and exclusion of mimics. CSF typically shows a mild lymphocytosis, raised protein, intrathecal HTLV-1 antibody and specific oligoclonal bands, and a CSF/blood proviral load ratio above 1 together with high CSF neopterin or CXCL10 indicates active inflammation and a faster course. Spine MRI usually shows thoracic atrophy, sometimes swelling and T2 signal early, and brain MRI may show non-specific white matter lesions that can mislead toward MS. Exclude compression, B12 and copper deficiency, HIV and syphilis myelopathy, primary progressive MS and hereditary spastic paraplegia.
det.treatment: There is no proven antiviral therapy — zidovudine and lamivudine have not changed the course. Consensus favours corticosteroids for active or rapidly progressive disease (for example pulsed IV methylprednisolone followed by oral prednisolone tapering to a low maintenance dose) and low-dose oral prednisolone for slower progressors, always after excluding or treating Strongyloides with ivermectin. Interferon-alpha is licensed in Japan, and the anti-CCR4 antibody mogamulizumab is under evaluation as it reduces infected cell numbers. Symptomatic care is essential: baclofen, tizanidine or botulinum toxin for spasticity, antimuscarinics and intermittent catheterisation for the bladder, neuropathic pain treatment, physiotherapy and mobility aids. Counsel carriers about transmission (avoiding or shortening breastfeeding, barrier contraception, no blood or organ donation) and screen for adult T-cell leukaemia/lymphoma.
det.prognosis: The course is usually slowly progressive: many need a stick within about 10 years and a wheelchair after two decades, while rapid progressors may lose walking within a few years; life expectancy is mainly reduced by ATL, infections and immobility.
pearls: Spastic paraparesis with early bladder symptoms, back pain and few sensory signs: test HTLV-1 in serum and CSF.
Screen for Strongyloides before any steroid — hyperinfection can be fatal.
A CSF/blood proviral load ratio above 1 and high CSF CXCL10 or neopterin mark active disease likely to respond to steroids.
Check for adult T-cell leukaemia/lymphoma in carriers with lymphocytosis, flower cells, hypercalcaemia or skin lesions.

Family history, very slow course, bladder involvement later; normal CSF
Low B12 with prominent posterior column loss and neuropathy

name: HTLV-1 infection
formal: Infection with the human T-lymphotropic virus type 1 retrovirus, transmitted via breastfeeding, sex and blood; most carriers are asymptomatic, with risk of HAM and adult T-cell leukaemia.
simple: A long-term viral infection that usually causes no symptoms but can lead to spinal cord disease or a blood cancer in a few people.

name: Human herpesvirus and myelitis
formal: Spinal cord inflammation caused by herpesviruses such as VZV, HSV-2, CMV and EBV, producing acute or subacute myelopathy, often in immunocompromised patients, with CSF pleocytosis and PCR positivity.
simple: Inflammation of the spinal cord triggered by herpes-family viruses, causing weakness, numbness and bladder or bowel problems.

name: Human prion disease
formal: Group of transmissible neurodegenerative diseases from misfolded prion protein: sporadic, genetic, acquired or variant CJD, GSS and fatal familial insomnia, with rapid dementia and myoclonus.
simple: Rare, fatal brain diseases caused by abnormally folded proteins that destroy brain tissue and cause rapid dementia.

name: Human T-lymphocyte type 1 infection
formal: Retroviral infection causing HTLV-1-associated myelopathy (tropical spastic paraparesis), adult T-cell leukaemia, and sometimes myositis or neuropathy.
simple: A virus infection that can slowly damage the spinal cord and cause stiff, weak legs, or leukaemia in a few carriers.
more: Serology and CSF antibodies or PCR confirm it; myelopathy treated with steroids and symptomatic care. Most carriers stay symptom-free.

name: Hunter disease
formal: X-linked mucopolysaccharidosis II from iduronate-2-sulfatase deficiency, causing coarse features, hydrocephalus, cognitive decline, dysostosis multiplex and carpal tunnel syndrome.
simple: An inherited condition in boys where the body cannot break down certain sugars, leading to coarse features, skeletal problems and, in severe forms, brain damage.

name: Huntington sine chorea
formal: Genetically confirmed Huntington disease presenting with cognitive, psychiatric or hypokinetic-rigid features but without chorea, as in the juvenile Westphal variant or late disease.
simple: Huntington disease in which the typical jerky movements are absent, so it shows up as stiffness, slowness or thinking and mood changes.

name: Huntington’s disease
formal: Autosomal dominant CAG repeat disorder of huntingtin with progressive chorea, cognitive decline and psychiatric disturbance, due to striatal neuronal loss; onset usually in midlife.
simple: An inherited brain disease that gradually causes jerky involuntary movements, memory and thinking problems, and mood changes.
more: Diagnosis by HTT CAG repeats of 36 or more (full penetrance 40 or more) with caudate atrophy on MRI; genetic counselling and predictive testing protocols are crucial. Tetrabenazine or deutetrabenazine for chorea, antidepressants, and supportive care.
th: โรคพันธุกรรมยีนเด่น — การเคลื่อนไหวกระตุกไม่ตั้งใจ (chorea) บุคลิกเปลี่ยน ความคิดเสื่อม
feat: Chorea, motor impersistence (milkmaid grip), slow saccades
Psychiatric change: irritability, depression, obsessive behaviour
Subcortical dementia
Autosomal dominant with anticipation (paternal)
inv: HTT CAG repeat (≥40 full penetrance) with genetic counselling
MRI caudate atrophy

case.story: Family notice fidgeting and temper outbursts; his father died in a nursing home with 'dancing movements'.
case.exam: Flowing irregular movements of face and fingers, cannot keep tongue protruded, delayed saccade initiation.
case.tests: HTT CAG 44 repeats.
case.q: Name the inheritance pattern and the phenomenon seen in successive generations.
case.a: Autosomal dominant with anticipation — earlier onset, especially via paternal transmission.

HD phenocopy with JPH3 expansion, African ancestry
Childhood onset, non-progressive, no dementia

aN: hd | huntington chorea

det.patho: A CAG repeat expansion in HTT on chromosome 4 produces huntingtin with a long polyglutamine tract that is toxic to neurons, especially medium spiny neurons of the caudate and putamen. Inheritance is autosomal dominant; 36–39 repeats show reduced penetrance and 40 or more are fully penetrant. Larger repeats give earlier onset, and repeats tend to expand through the father, explaining anticipation and juvenile (Westphal) cases.
det.clinical: Onset is usually in the 30s–50s with a combination of motor, cognitive and psychiatric change, any of which may come first. Early motor signs are fidgety restlessness, slowed saccade initiation and motor impersistence, evolving to chorea, dystonia, dysarthria, dysphagia and gait instability. Psychiatric features include depression, irritability, apathy, obsessive behaviour and a high suicide risk. Cognitive decline affects speed, planning and multitasking before memory. Juvenile HD often presents with rigidity, bradykinesia and seizures rather than chorea.
det.diagnosis: Confirm with genetic testing for HTT CAG repeat length in a symptomatic person; predictive testing of at-risk relatives must follow a formal counselling protocol. MRI shows caudate atrophy with enlarged frontal horns, but this is supportive, not diagnostic. Where testing is negative, consider phenocopies: C9orf72 expansion, HDL2, SCA17, neuroacanthocytosis, Wilson disease, and acquired chorea from drugs, thyroid disease, lupus or polycythaemia.
det.treatment: No therapy slows the disease yet; antisense and other huntingtin-lowering strategies remain under study. Chorea that causes harm or distress can be treated with tetrabenazine or deutetrabenazine/valbenazine (watch for depression) or with antipsychotics, which also help agitation. Treat depression and irritability actively and screen for suicidality. Speech and swallow therapy, nutritional support (high calorie needs), physiotherapy, social care and genetic counselling for the family are essential.
det.prognosis: Death typically occurs 15–20 years after motor onset, usually from aspiration, falls or complications of immobility.
pearls: Motor impersistence — inability to sustain a grip or tongue protrusion — is often more reliable than chorea itself.
Always ask about suicidal thoughts; risk peaks around diagnosis and when independence is lost.
A negative family history does not exclude HD: misattributed paternity, early parental death or intermediate-allele expansion can hide it.
det.thd: Huntington's disease เป็นโรคพันธุกรรมแบบยีนเด่นจากการขยายของ CAG repeat ในยีน HTT ทำให้เซลล์ใน caudate และ putamen ตาย อาการมีสามด้านคือ การเคลื่อนไหวกระตุกแบบ chorea ความผิดปกติทางจิตใจ เช่น ซึมเศร้า หงุดหงิด และความคิดช้าลงจนสมองเสื่อม วินิจฉัยด้วยการตรวจยีน (40 repeats ขึ้นไปแสดงโรคแน่นอน) โดยต้องให้คำปรึกษาทางพันธุกรรม การรักษาเป็นการบรรเทาอาการ เช่น tetrabenazine และดูแลด้านจิตเวชและครอบครัว

name: Huntington’s disease look like-2 disease
formal: Phenocopy of Huntington disease with chorea, psychiatric and cognitive features but a negative huntingtin test; causes include HDL1 to 4 and other genetic disorders.
simple: A condition that looks like Huntington disease but is caused by a different gene or cause.

name: Huntington’s disease-like 2 (HDL2)
formal: Autosomal dominant triplet repeat disorder from a CTG/CAG expansion in JPH3, resembling Huntington disease with chorea, dementia and acanthocytes; almost exclusively in people of African ancestry.
simple: An inherited disease that closely mimics Huntington disease, with movement problems and dementia, mostly seen in people of African descent.
aN: hdl2 | huntington disease like 2

name: Huntington’s disese
formal: Misspelling of Huntington disease, an autosomal dominant CAG repeat disorder causing chorea, cognitive decline and psychiatric disturbance from striatal degeneration.
simple: An inherited brain disease that gradually causes jerky involuntary movements, memory and thinking problems, and mood changes.

name: Hurler-Scheie syndrome
formal: Intermediate form of mucopolysaccharidosis I from alpha-L-iduronidase deficiency, with corneal clouding, joint stiffness, valvular disease and carpal tunnel syndrome, but milder or absent intellectual impairment.
simple: An inherited enzyme disorder that causes joint stiffness, cloudy eyes and heart problems, milder than the severe infant form.

name: Hurst disease
formal: Acute haemorrhagic leukoencephalitis, a fulminant post-infectious demyelinating disease with perivascular haemorrhage and necrosis, causing rapid fever, coma and seizures; a hyperacute ADEM variant.
simple: A rare, very rapid and severe brain inflammation with bleeding, usually after an infection.

name: Hyaline body myopathy
formal: Congenital myopathy with subsarcolemmal hyaline inclusions of myosin, caused by MYH7, with slowly progressive scapuloperoneal or proximal weakness.
simple: A rare inherited muscle disease with glassy protein clumps seen in muscle biopsies, causing slowly progressive weakness.
more: Biopsy shows hyaline bodies reactive for slow myosin; MYH7 testing; supportive care.

name: Hydrocephalic parkinsonism
formal: Gait disorder with bradykinesia and rigidity predominantly in the legs in patients with hydrocephalus, due to ventricular enlargement compressing frontal-subcortical pathways; may improve after shunting.
simple: Slow, shuffling walking and stiffness caused by fluid build-up in the brain, which can improve after the fluid is drained.

name: Hydrocephalus
formal: Excess CSF within the ventricles from obstructed flow, impaired absorption or rarely overproduction, producing raised pressure, headache, vomiting and papilloedema, or gait and cognitive decline in normal pressure form.
simple: A build-up of fluid inside the brain that raises pressure and can cause headache, vomiting and problems with walking or thinking.

name: Hydrogen sulphide poisoning
formal: Toxic gas exposure inhibiting cytochrome oxidase, causing rapid loss of consciousness, seizures, respiratory failure and, in survivors, basal ganglia damage and parkinsonism or cognitive sequelae.
simple: Poisoning by a rotten-egg smelling gas that can cause sudden collapse, seizures and lasting brain damage.

name: Hyperacute stroke
formal: Earliest phase of ischaemic stroke, within roughly six hours of onset, when thrombolysis or thrombectomy can salvage penumbra; imaging may show early ischaemic change or a hyperdense vessel.
simple: The very first hours after a stroke begins, when urgent treatment can save the most brain tissue.

name: Hyperekplexias
formal: Startle disorders, usually hereditary from glycine receptor or transporter mutations, with exaggerated startle, stiffening and falls to unexpected stimuli, and neonatal stiffness; treated with clonazepam.
simple: Conditions in which a sudden noise or touch causes an exaggerated startle and stiffening, sometimes with falls.

name: Hypereosinophilic syndrome (HES)
formal: Persistent eosinophilia with end-organ damage, which can cause neuropathy, mononeuritis, myopathy, encephalopathy and cardiac thrombosis.
simple: A condition where very high levels of one type of white blood cell damage organs such as nerves and heart.
more: Diagnosed by sustained eosinophil count over 1500 with organ involvement after excluding other causes; treated with steroids, hydroxyurea or imatinib or mepolizumab.
aN: hes | hypereosinophilic syndrome

name: Hyperferritinemia-cataract syndrome (OMIM 600886)
formal: Autosomal dominant disorder from mutations in the iron-responsive element of the L-ferritin gene, causing high serum ferritin without iron overload and early bilateral cataracts.
simple: An inherited condition with very high blood ferritin without too much iron and cataracts at a young age.
more: Distinguished from iron overload by normal transferrin saturation; genetic test confirms. Treat cataracts surgically; venesection is not helpful and can cause anaemia.
aN: omim 600886 | hyperferritinemia cataract syndrome

name: Hyperkalaemic periodic paralysis (hyperPP)
formal: Autosomal dominant sodium or calcium channel muscle disease with episodes of flaccid weakness during raised serum potassium, often triggered by rest after exercise or potassium intake, with myotonia.
simple: An inherited condition causing attacks of muscle weakness when blood potassium rises, often after rest following exercise.
th: อ่อนแรงเป็นพัก ๆ สั้น ๆ เริ่มในวัยเด็ก กระตุ้นด้วยการพักหลังออกกำลังหรือกินอาหารโพแทสเซียมสูง — โรค SCN4A
tempoNote: Attacks last minutes to a few hours, often daily; onset in first decade
feat: Brief attacks of flaccid limb weakness, frequently in the morning or during rest after exercise
Provoked by potassium-rich food, fasting, cold, stress; eased by mild exercise or carbohydrate
Serum potassium high or high-normal in attacks (can be normal)
Mild myotonia or paramyotonia (eyelid lag), and later a fixed proximal myopathy in some
inv: Potassium during an attack; ECG
Long exercise test: post-exercise fall in CMAP amplitude; EMG may show myotonia
SCN4A genetic testing; exclude secondary hyperkalaemia (renal, adrenal, drugs)

case.story: Several times a week, after resting following football, his legs go weak for 30–60 minutes; eating bananas seems to bring attacks on. His father had similar episodes as a child.
case.exam: Between attacks strength is normal; lid lag after looking down; mild grip myotonia.
case.tests: K 5.6 mmol/L during an attack; long exercise test shows a 45% CMAP decline; SCN4A variant confirmed.
case.q: What are the first-line measures?
case.a: Frequent carbohydrate-rich low-potassium meals, avoiding fasting and cold, mild exercise at onset, inhaled salbutamol to abort attacks, and a thiazide or acetazolamide for prevention.

det.patho: Gain-of-function mutations in SCN4A, the skeletal-muscle sodium channel, impair inactivation so that a modest rise in extracellular potassium leaves the membrane persistently depolarised and inexcitable. Inheritance is autosomal dominant with high penetrance. The same gene causes paramyotonia congenita and some potassium-aggravated myotonias, and phenotypes overlap.
det.clinical: Attacks begin in infancy or childhood and are typically short and frequent. Weakness affects limbs more than face, rarely the respiratory muscles. Rest after exercise, fasting, cold, potassium intake and anaesthesia provoke attacks, while light activity can abort them. Myotonia, paramyotonia of the eyelids, and a slowly progressive fixed proximal weakness in middle age may accompany the disorder.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis rests on the clinical pattern, potassium during attacks (raised in many but not all), exclusion of secondary hyperkalaemia, and genetic confirmation of SCN4A. The long exercise test (prolonged exercise then serial CMAPs) shows a delayed decrement; EMG often reveals myotonic discharges between attacks. Provocative potassium loading is no longer recommended outside specialist settings.
det.treatment: Lifestyle: frequent carbohydrate-rich meals, avoid potassium-rich foods, fasting, cold and strenuous exercise followed by rest. Acute attacks may resolve with light exercise, glucose, or inhaled beta-agonist. Preventive therapy uses kaliuretic diuretics (thiazides) or carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (acetazolamide, dichlorphenamide). Anaesthetists must be informed—avoid potassium-containing fluids and depolarising relaxants and keep the patient warm.
det.prognosis: Attacks often lessen after middle age, but a permanent proximal myopathy can develop. Life expectancy is normal.
pearls: Short, frequent attacks in childhood favour hyperPP; long attacks in adolescence favour hypoPP.
Potassium can be normal in an attack — the name reflects sensitivity, not always the level.
Ask about anaesthesia: suxamethonium and potassium-rich fluids can provoke severe weakness.
det.thd: HyperPP เกิดจาก mutation ของยีน SCN4A (sodium channel ของกล้ามเนื้อ) ถ่ายทอดแบบเด่น ผู้ป่วยอ่อนแรงเป็นพัก ๆ สั้น ๆ ตั้งแต่เด็ก มักเกิดขณะพักหลังออกกำลังหรือหลังกินอาหารโพแทสเซียมสูง ระหว่างอาการโพแทสเซียมสูงหรือปกติ อาจมี myotonia ร่วม วินิจฉัยด้วย long exercise test และตรวจยีน รักษาโดยกินคาร์โบไฮเดรตบ่อย หลีกเลี่ยงโพแทสเซียม ใช้ thiazide หรือ acetazolamide ป้องกัน

ddx.pt: Longer attacks (hours–days), low K, carbohydrate provokes rather than relieves
Attacks with ventricular arrhythmia, long QU and dysmorphic features
Cold- and exercise-worsened stiffness dominates; weakness is secondary

aN: hyperpp | hyperkalemic periodic paralysis | hyperkpp | gamstorp disease | scn4a periodic paralysis | potassium sensitive periodic paralysis

name: Hyperkinetic syndromes
formal: Movement disorders with excess involuntary movement, including chorea, dystonia, tremor, tics, myoclonus and athetosis, from dysfunction of basal ganglia circuits.
simple: A group of conditions in which the body makes too many unwanted movements, such as jerks, twists, tremors or tics.

name: Hyperosmolar non-ketotic state (HONK)
formal: Hyperglycaemic emergency in type 2 diabetes with severe dehydration, serum osmolality above 320 and minimal ketosis, causing confusion, seizures, focal deficits and coma.
simple: A dangerous complication of diabetes with very high blood sugar and dehydration that can cause confusion, seizures and coma.
aN: honk | hyperosmolar non ketotic state

name: Hypertensive encephalopathy
formal: Acute encephalopathy from severe hypertension exceeding cerebral autoregulation, with headache, visual loss, seizures and confusion, and vasogenic oedema on MRI, as in PRES.
simple: Brain swelling caused by extremely high blood pressure, leading to headache, vision problems, seizures and confusion.
th: ภาวะสมองบวมทำงานผิดปกติจากความดันโลหิตสูงขึ้นเฉียบพลันเกินขีด autoregulation มีปวดศีรษะ สับสน ชัก ตามัว จอตามีเลือดออก/papilloedema อาการดีขึ้นเมื่อลดความดันลงอย่างควบคุม มักพบลักษณะ PRES บน MRI
tempoNote: Develops over hours to 1–2 days with a sharp BP surge; reversible within days if BP is lowered promptly
feat: Very high BP (typically > 180/120 mmHg, or a sharp rise from baseline in young or pregnant patients)
Severe headache, nausea, vomiting and progressive confusion or drowsiness
Visual blurring or cortical blindness; seizures
Grade III–IV hypertensive retinopathy: flame haemorrhages, cotton-wool spots, papilloedema
Other target organ damage: acute kidney injury, heart failure, microangiopathic haemolysis
inv: MRI FLAIR: symmetric parieto-occipital vasogenic oedema (PRES pattern); exclude haemorrhage and infarction
Fundoscopy for retinopathy and papilloedema
Renal function, urinalysis, troponin, ECG, blood film for schistocytes
Search for causes: renal disease, phaeochromocytoma, drug withdrawal, pre-eclampsia, stimulants

case.who: 39-year-old construction worker from Khon Kaen who stopped his BP pills 6 months ago
case.story: Two days of pounding headache and vomiting; this evening he became confused and had a generalised seizure at home.
case.exam: BP 230/140, drowsy but rousable, no focal weakness; fundi show flame haemorrhages, cotton-wool spots and bilateral disc swelling.
case.tests: Creatinine 2.6 mg/dL, proteinuria 3+; CT no haemorrhage; MRI FLAIR bilateral occipital subcortical oedema without diffusion restriction.
case.q: How fast should BP be lowered and with which drugs?
case.a: IV titratable agent (nicardipine or labetalol infusion) reducing mean arterial pressure by no more than about 20–25% in the first hour, then gradually toward 160/100 over the next 2–6 h.

read.where: Chapter 10 Hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy, cardiac arrests and cardiac encephalopathy

det.patho: Cerebral autoregulation keeps flow constant over a range of pressures; when BP rises abruptly above the upper limit (lower in previously normotensive people), forced dilatation of arterioles leads to hyperperfusion, endothelial injury and blood–brain barrier breakdown with vasogenic oedema, predominantly in the posterior circulation, which has less sympathetic innervation. Chronic hypertension shifts the curve rightwards, so long-standing hypertensives tolerate higher pressures — but also tolerate rapid reduction poorly.
det.clinical: Headache, vomiting and blurred vision progress over hours to confusion, lethargy, seizures and occasionally coma. Focal signs are usually mild; prominent focal deficits should raise suspicion of haemorrhage or infarction. Retinopathy with papilloedema confirms malignant-phase hypertension. In pregnancy, eclampsia is the obstetric counterpart and can occur at lower absolute BP levels.
det.diagnosis: It is a clinical diagnosis of encephalopathy with severe hypertension that improves after BP reduction. MRI usually shows the PRES pattern (parieto-occipital, sometimes frontal, cerebellar or brainstem oedema). Exclude stroke, CVT, infection, intoxication and metabolic encephalopathies. Investigate end-organ damage and secondary causes of hypertension, particularly in young patients.
det.treatment: Admit to a monitored bed and use IV titratable drugs (nicardipine, clevidipine, labetalol; avoid sublingual nifedipine). Lower the MAP by no more than about 20–25% in the first hour, then towards 160/100–110 over the next hours, and normalise over 24–48 h; overly rapid falls risk watershed infarction. Treat seizures with benzodiazepine then levetiracetam or similar. In eclampsia, give magnesium sulphate and plan delivery. Afterwards, establish a durable oral regimen and address adherence.
det.prognosis: Usually fully reversible with prompt treatment; delayed or excessive BP correction can leave infarction or haemorrhage.
pearls: Encephalopathy + very high BP + papilloedema/retinal haemorrhages = treat as hypertensive emergency.
Lower BP in a controlled way: about 25% in the first hour, not to normal.
Prominent focal deficits suggest stroke, not simple hypertensive encephalopathy.
det.thd: Hypertensive encephalopathy เกิดจากความดันโลหิตสูงขึ้นเฉียบพลันเกินความสามารถ autoregulation ของสมอง ทำให้เกิดสมองบวมแบบ vasogenic โดยเฉพาะบริเวณท้ายทอย ผู้ป่วยปวดศีรษะ อาเจียน สับสน ตามัว และชัก ตรวจพบ papilloedema และเลือดออกที่จอตา MRI มักเป็นแบบ PRES รักษาด้วยยาลดความดันทางหลอดเลือดดำ (nicardipine, labetalol) โดยลด MAP ไม่เกิน 20–25% ในชั่วโมงแรก แล้วค่อย ๆ ลดต่อ

Focal deficit with haematoma on CT; BP lowered to a different target (around 140 systolic)
Headache, seizures and papilloedema with venous infarcts; empty delta sign, abnormal venogram
