name: Hyperthermic catatonia
formal: Catatonia with fever and autonomic instability, overlapping with neuroleptic malignant syndrome and lethal catatonia; features stupor, rigidity and tachycardia and needs urgent benzodiazepines or ECT.
simple: A serious state of immobility or agitation with high fever and unstable vital signs, needing urgent hospital treatment.

name: Hypnic headache
formal: Rare primary headache of older adults that wakes patients from sleep at consistent times with moderate pain lasting 15 to 240 minutes; responds to caffeine or lithium.
simple: A rare headache in older people that wakes them from sleep at the same time each night.

name: Hypnogenic dyskinesias
formal: Abnormal involuntary movements arising from sleep, such as paroxysmal nocturnal dystonia, that are often frontal lobe seizures and appear in stereotyped episodes at night.
simple: Unusual movements that happen during sleep, sometimes caused by seizures in a part of the brain.

name: Hypnogenic paroxysmal dyskinesia
formal: Old term for paroxysmal dystonic or hyperkinetic attacks arising from sleep, now largely recognised as nocturnal frontal lobe epilepsy, often linked to CHRNA4 and related genes.
simple: Short, sudden episodes of abnormal movements during sleep that are usually due to frontal lobe seizures.
more: Video-EEG confirms an epileptic basis; carbamazepine often works. Differentiate from parasomnias and from true paroxysmal dyskinesias.

name: Hypokalaemic periodic paralysis (hypoPP)
formal: Channelopathy from calcium or sodium channel mutations causing episodes of flaccid weakness with low serum potassium, often after carbohydrate meals or rest following exercise; treated with potassium and acetazolamide.
simple: An inherited condition causing attacks of muscle weakness when blood potassium is low, often after carbohydrate-rich meals or rest after exercise.
th: อัมพาตเป็นพัก ๆ จากโพแทสเซียมต่ำ — ตื่นมาขยับแขนขาไม่ได้หลังมื้อแป้งหรือออกกำลังกาย หายในไม่กี่ชั่วโมง
tempoNote: Attacks last hours to a day, often on waking
feat: Flaccid weakness of limbs, sparing face and breathing, with low potassium during the attack
Triggers: carbohydrate-rich meals, rest after exercise, stress, cold
Primary form begins in the first two decades; adult first attacks suggest thyrotoxicosis or secondary causes
Late fixed proximal myopathy can develop
inv: Potassium during the attack; ECG (U waves, arrhythmia)
Thyroid function; urine potassium to exclude renal loss
Long exercise test on NCS; CACNA1S / SCN4A genetics

case.story: Woke at 5 a.m. unable to lift his arms or legs after a large rice-and-sweets dinner; normal the day before. Recent weight loss and tremor.
case.exam: Symmetric flaccid quadriparesis, absent reflexes, normal sensation and cranial nerves, fine tremor, tachycardia.
case.tests: K 1.9 mmol/L; ECG U waves; TSH suppressed, free T4 high.
case.q: How does this change long-term treatment?
case.a: Thyrotoxic periodic paralysis — attacks stop once the patient is euthyroid; beta-blockers help meanwhile. Give potassium cautiously to avoid rebound hyperkalaemia.

ddx.pt: Days not hours, sensory symptoms, normal potassium
Brief attacks with high or normal K, triggered by rest after exercise or fasting; myotonia
Ocular/bulbar fatigable weakness

aN: hypopp | hypokalemic periodic paralysis | hypokpp | cacna1s | thyrotoxic periodic paralysis

det.patho: Primary hypoPP is an autosomal dominant channelopathy, mostly from CACNA1S (calcium channel) and less often SCN4A (sodium channel) variants that create an abnormal leak current through the voltage-sensor region. When serum potassium falls, affected fibres depolarise paradoxically, sodium channels inactivate and the membrane becomes inexcitable. Thyrotoxic periodic paralysis, frequent in Asian men, reflects thyroid hormone driving Na/K-ATPase activity with a genetic susceptibility (e.g. KCNJ18), shifting potassium into cells.
det.clinical: Attacks of flaccid weakness usually begin on waking or after rest following exertion or a carbohydrate load, and may last from hours to a day or more. Proximal limbs are hit hardest; bulbar, ocular and respiratory muscles are generally spared, although severe hypokalaemia can threaten cardiac rhythm. Reflexes drop during the episode and sensation is normal. Primary forms start in childhood or adolescence, with attack frequency often waning after mid-life while a permanent proximal myopathy may emerge. A first attack in an adult man, especially with weight loss, tremor or palpitations, should prompt a thyroid screen.
det.diagnosis: Document a low potassium during an attack, since values between attacks are normal in primary disease. Check thyroid function, and measure urinary potassium and acid–base status to exclude renal or gastrointestinal loss (secondary hypokalaemic paralysis). The long exercise test on nerve conduction shows a delayed decline in CMAP amplitude in many patients, though a normal result does not exclude the diagnosis. Genetic testing of CACNA1S and SCN4A confirms primary disease; distinguish from Andersen–Tawil syndrome (KCNJ2) by looking for arrhythmia and dysmorphic features.
det.treatment: During an attack, give oral potassium chloride in modest repeated doses with ECG and potassium monitoring; reserve IV potassium for patients who cannot swallow or have arrhythmia, using non-glucose diluent. Overcorrection is common because potassium returns from cells as the attack resolves. Prevention includes avoiding high-carbohydrate meals and abrupt rest after strenuous exercise, plus carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (acetazolamide or dichlorphenamide) or potassium-sparing diuretics. In thyrotoxic paralysis, non-selective beta-blockade (propranolol) helps acutely and restoring euthyroidism stops attacks; acetazolamide is not useful there.
det.prognosis: Attacks are rarely fatal when potassium and rhythm are watched, but a fixed proximal myopathy can accumulate over decades. Thyrotoxic attacks cease once thyroid function is normal.
pearls: Normal potassium between attacks does not exclude hypoPP — test during the episode.
Adult Asian man with first attack: think thyrotoxicosis first.
Beware rebound hyperkalaemia after aggressive potassium replacement.
SCN4A-related hypoPP may worsen with acetazolamide; genotype guides choice.

name: Hypokalemia/Potassium disorders
formal: Disturbed serum potassium, with hypokalaemia causing weakness, cramps and rhabdomyolysis and hyperkalaemia causing weakness, arrhythmia and paralysis.
simple: Too low or too high potassium in the blood, which can cause muscle weakness, cramps and heart rhythm problems.
more: Investigate with ECG, renal function and drug history; correct the underlying cause and replace or lower potassium according to severity.

name: Hypokalemic myopathy
formal: Acquired proximal myopathy with severe hypokalaemia, from diuretics, licorice, renal tubular acidosis or hyperaldosteronism, with raised CK and sometimes rhabdomyolysis.
simple: Muscle weakness caused by a low level of potassium in the blood.
more: Corrected by potassium replacement and treating the cause; usually fully reversible.

name: Hypokalemic periodic paralysis type 2
formal: Autosomal dominant periodic paralysis from SCN4A mutations, with attacks of flaccid weakness with low potassium, often with tubular aggregates on biopsy.
simple: An inherited condition with attacks of muscle weakness linked to low potassium, caused by a sodium channel gene change.
more: Provoked by carbohydrate meals or rest after exercise; treat with potassium, acetazolamide or dichlorphenamide and trigger avoidance.

name: Hypokinetic (Parkinsonian) syndromes
formal: Syndromes with paucity of movement, bradykinesia and rigidity, mainly Parkinson disease, atypical parkinsonisms, drug-induced and vascular parkinsonism, from basal ganglia dopaminergic dysfunction.
simple: Conditions with slowed or reduced movement and stiffness, of which Parkinson disease is the commonest.
aN: parkinsonian | hypokinetic syndromes

name: Hypophysitis
formal: Inflammation of the pituitary, lymphocytic, granulomatous or secondary to checkpoint inhibitors, causing headache, visual disturbance and hypopituitarism, with an enlarged gland and stalk thickening on MRI.
simple: Swelling of the pituitary gland that can cause headache, vision trouble and low hormone levels.

name: Hypothyroid myopathy
formal: Proximal weakness, cramps, delayed reflex relaxation, and mounding with raised CK in hypothyroidism, from impaired glycogenolysis and mitochondrial function.
simple: Muscle weakness, cramps, and aching caused by an underactive thyroid.
more: Thyroid function tests confirm the cause; thyroxine replacement normalises strength over months.
th: กล้ามเนื้ออ่อนแรง ปวด ตะคริว และ CK สูงจากภาวะไทรอยด์ต่ำ — รักษาไทรอยด์แล้วดีขึ้น
tempoNote: Develops over weeks to months as hypothyroidism worsens
feat: Proximal weakness, muscle aches, cramps and stiffness, worse in cold
Slow relaxation phase of tendon reflexes ('hung-up' ankle jerk)
Muscle mounding (myoedema) when percussed
Occasional muscle enlargement (Hoffmann syndrome in adults)
Systemic signs: fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance, dry skin, bradycardia
inv: TSH and free T4
CK often raised, sometimes many times normal
EMG: normal or mildly myopathic; nerve studies may show coexisting carpal tunnel or neuropathy

case.who: 50-year-old woman with prior radioactive iodine for Graves
case.story: Missed follow-up; over 4 months tired, cold, gaining weight, with aching thighs and painful cramps climbing stairs.
case.exam: Puffy face, dry skin, HR 54; mild hip flexor weakness; ankle jerks contract briskly but relax very slowly; tapping the deltoid raises a ridge.
case.tests: TSH 86 mIU/L, free T4 low; CK 2,400 U/L.
case.q: Does she need a muscle biopsy?
case.a: Usually no — replace thyroid hormone and recheck CK and strength; biopsy is reserved for failure to improve once euthyroid.

det.patho: Thyroid hormone deficiency slows muscle metabolism: reduced mitochondrial oxidative capacity, impaired glycogen breakdown and slowed calcium reuptake by the sarcoplasmic reticulum. Slow calcium handling explains delayed relaxation of reflexes and myoedema. Membrane leakiness raises CK.
det.clinical: Most patients have aches, cramps, fatigue and mild proximal weakness rather than severe paralysis. Delayed reflex relaxation is a classic sign. Rarely there is marked muscle hypertrophy with stiffness (Hoffmann syndrome), or rhabdomyolysis, especially with exercise or statins. Carpal tunnel syndrome and a mild sensorimotor neuropathy may coexist.
det.diagnosis: High TSH with low free T4 explains the picture; CK may be strikingly high and can trigger an unnecessary myositis work-up. Always check TSH in any unexplained raised CK or myopathy. EMG and biopsy are needed only when weakness persists after correction.
det.treatment: Levothyroxine replacement, started cautiously in older patients or those with heart disease, resolves the myopathy. Hold or review statins until euthyroid. Symptoms and CK improve over weeks to months.
det.prognosis: Very good; weakness and CK normalise with adequate replacement, though recovery may take several months.
pearls: Check TSH before labelling a high CK as myositis.
Slow-relaxing ankle jerk is a bedside clue to hypothyroidism.
Hypothyroidism amplifies statin muscle toxicity.
det.thd: Hypothyroid myopathy เกิดจากภาวะไทรอยด์ต่ำ ทำให้ปวดกล้ามเนื้อ ตะคริว อ่อนแรงต้นขา และ CK สูงได้มาก ลักษณะเด่นคือ reflex คลายตัวช้า และเคาะกล้ามเนื้อแล้วนูน (myoedema) วินิจฉัยด้วย TSH สูงและ free T4 ต่ำ การรักษาคือให้ levothyroxine ซึ่งทำให้อาการและ CK กลับปกติในหลายสัปดาห์ถึงเดือน

Statin exposure; hypothyroidism itself raises statin myopathy risk
Myotonic discharges on EMG and CCTG expansion; thyroid normal

aN: myxedema myopathy | hypothyroid myopathy | hoffmann syndrome | kocher debre semelaigne syndrome

name: Hypothyroidism
formal: Thyroid hormone deficiency with neuromuscular manifestations including myopathy, carpal tunnel syndrome, polyneuropathy, myoedema, and delayed relaxation of reflexes.
simple: An underactive thyroid gland, which can cause tiredness, weakness, muscle pain, and nerve compression.
more: Diagnosed by high TSH with low free T4; levothyroxine replacement usually reverses neuromuscular complications.

name: Hypoxic ischaemic encephalopathy (HIE)
formal: Brain injury from inadequate oxygen and blood flow, classically after cardiac arrest or perinatal asphyxia, causing coma, seizures, myoclonus and watershed or deep grey matter infarction.
simple: Brain damage from a lack of oxygen and blood flow, for example after a cardiac arrest or a difficult birth.
aN: hie | hypoxic ischemic encephalopathy

name: Hysterical hyperekplexia
formal: Functional startle disorder with exaggerated, non-habituating startle responses and abnormal posturing that lack the features of genetic hyperekplexia and are inconsistent with distraction.
simple: A psychologically driven, exaggerated startle reaction to sudden stimuli that is not due to structural brain disease.

name: Hysterical tremor
formal: Functional tremor with variable frequency and amplitude, entrainment to voluntary rhythm, distractibility and co-contraction, often with a sudden onset and suggestibility.
simple: A tremor from a functional nervous system disorder that changes with attention and has no structural cause.

name: Iatrogenic Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease
formal: Prion disease transmitted by medical procedures, such as contaminated neurosurgical instruments, dura mater grafts or human growth hormone, with long incubation before progressive dementia and ataxia.
simple: A rare form of CJD passed on by contaminated medical equipment or tissue products, appearing years after exposure.

name: ICCA syndrome
formal: Familial syndrome linking infantile convulsions with later paroxysmal choreoathetosis, autosomal dominant, from PRRT2 mutation; benign infantile seizures respond well to carbamazepine.
simple: An inherited condition in which a baby has seizures and later in childhood or adulthood has episodes of writhing movements.

name: Ideational/conceptual apraxia
formal: Apraxia from failure of the concept of an action, so patients misuse objects and cannot sequence multi-step tasks, due to dominant parietal or diffuse lesions as in Alzheimer disease.
simple: Loss of understanding of how to use objects or plan a sequence of actions, even though muscles work normally.

name: Ideomotor apraxia
formal: Apraxia with impaired performance of skilled movements to command or imitation, with intact object use in context, due to dominant parietal or premotor lesions or the corpus callosum.
simple: Difficulty carrying out learned gestures, such as waving goodbye, on request even though the person understands and has normal strength.

name: IDH-mutant diffuse glioma
formal: WHO-defined astrocytoma or oligodendroglioma with IDH1 or IDH2 mutation, typically young adults, with favourable prognosis; oligodendroglioma also has 1p19q codeletion.
simple: A slow-growing type of brain tumour in younger adults that carries a particular genetic change and has a better outlook.

name: IDH-mutant gliomas
formal: Diffuse glioma family with IDH mutation, including astrocytomas with ATRX and TP53 changes and 1p19q-codeleted oligodendrogliomas, associated with longer survival than IDH-wildtype tumours.
simple: A group of brain tumours with a specific gene change that tend to grow more slowly and respond better to treatment.

name: IDH-wildtype glioblastoma
formal: The most aggressive primary adult brain tumour, with necrosis and microvascular proliferation and no IDH mutation; median survival about 15 months despite surgery, radiotherapy and temozolomide.
simple: The most common and aggressive primary brain cancer in adults, which is hard to treat.

name: Idiopathic axonal neuropathies
formal: Distal, mostly sensory length-dependent axonal polyneuropathy of unknown cause in older adults, slowly progressive, with normal evaluation for secondary causes.
simple: A slowly worsening nerve problem in the feet and hands of older people for which no cause can be found.

name: Idiopathic axonal neuropathy (IAN)
formal: Slowly progressive, mainly sensory distal axonal neuropathy in older people, with no identified cause after exhaustive work-up, diagnosed by exclusion.
simple: A slowly worsening nerve problem causing numbness and tingling in the feet, with no cause found.
aN: ian | idiopathic axonal neuropathy

name: Idiopathic basal ganglia calcification (IBGC)
formal: Familial or sporadic Fahr disease with bilateral calcification of basal ganglia, dentate and thalamus, causing parkinsonism, dementia and psychiatric features; genes include SLC20A2, PDGFB and XPR1.
simple: A condition in which calcium builds up in deep brain areas, leading to movement, thinking and mood problems.
aN: ibgc | idiopathic basal ganglia calcification

name: Idiopathic choreic syndromes
formal: Choreic disorders with no secondary cause, including benign hereditary chorea and senile chorea, as well as unexplained sporadic chorea, after genetic and metabolic exclusion.
simple: Jerky, dance-like movements for which doctors cannot find a clear cause.

name: Idiopathic copper toxicosis syndromes
formal: Copper overload disorders without a Wilson gene defect, such as Indian childhood cirrhosis and Tyrolean copper toxicosis, with hepatic copper accumulation and liver failure from environmental and genetic factors.
simple: Rare conditions in which too much copper builds up in the liver in children, causing liver damage.
more: Liver copper is high but ceruloplasmin is often normal. Treat with copper chelation like penicillamine and avoid copper-rich water and utensils.

name: Idiopathic cranial dystonias
formal: Primary focal dystonias of cranial muscles, such as blepharospasm, oromandibular dystonia and Meige syndrome, of unknown origin and usually in middle age.
simple: Involuntary muscle spasms of the eyes, face or jaw that start without a clear cause.

name: Idiopathic hypersomnia
formal: Chronic excessive daytime sleepiness with long unrefreshing sleep, sleep inertia and no cataplexy, with normal sleep apnoea testing and mean sleep latency below eight minutes.
simple: Constant, heavy daytime sleepiness despite long nights of sleep, without a clear cause.

name: Idiopathic inflammatory myopathies
formal: Heterogeneous autoimmune muscle diseases, including dermatomyositis, polymyositis, necrotising myopathy and inclusion body myositis, with proximal weakness and raised creatine kinase.
simple: A group of conditions in which the immune system attacks muscles, causing weakness and sometimes muscle pain.

name: Idiopathic inflammatory myopathy
formal: Autoimmune muscle diseases including dermatomyositis, polymyositis, necrotizing myopathy and inclusion body myositis, causing proximal weakness with raised CK.
simple: A group of conditions where the immune system attacks muscles, causing weakness and sometimes skin rashes.
more: Diagnosis by CK, EMG, MRI, antibodies and biopsy; treat with steroids, immunosuppressants or IVIG; screen for cancer in dermatomyositis.

name: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH)
formal: Raised intracranial pressure with normal imaging and CSF content, typical in overweight young women, causing headache, papilloedema and visual loss; treated with weight loss, acetazolamide or shunting.
simple: High pressure around the brain with no tumour, causing headaches and risk to vision, most often in young women with obesity.
th: ความดันในกะโหลกสูงโดยไม่มีก้อน — มักเป็นหญิงน้ำหนักเกิน ปวดศีรษะ ตามัวชั่วขณะ จอประสาทตาบวม
feat: Daily headache, transient visual obscurations, pulsatile tinnitus
Bilateral papilloedema; sixth nerve palsy may occur (false-localising)
Typically women of childbearing age with recent weight gain
Threat is permanent visual field loss
inv: MRI with MR venography to exclude mass and venous sinus thrombosis
Lumbar puncture in lateral decubitus: raised opening pressure, normal CSF contents
Formal visual fields and OCT

case.story: Three months of headache and brief greying of vision on standing; hears a whooshing in her ears.
case.exam: Bilateral papilloedema, enlarged blind spots, mild left abduction deficit.
case.tests: MRI/MRV normal apart from empty sella; LP opening pressure 38 cmH2O, normal cell count and protein.
case.q: What is the most important outcome to protect?
case.a: Vision — treat with weight loss and acetazolamide and monitor fields; escalate urgently if fields deteriorate.

read.where: Chapter 50 Headache attributed to non-vascular intracranial disorder

files.chapter: Chapter 50: Headache attributed to non-vascular intracranial disorder

ddx.pt: Venous filling defect on MRV
Disc drusen or crowded discs without true oedema; normal pressure
Normal fundi and pressure

aN: iih | idiopathic intracranial hypertension | pseudotumor cerebri | benign intracranial hypertension | pseudotumour cerebri

det.patho: IIH is raised intracranial pressure with normal brain parenchyma on imaging and normal CSF contents, diagnosed only after secondary causes such as cerebral venous thrombosis are excluded. Its mechanism is still debated; current models combine reduced CSF outflow, a self-sustaining loop in which high pressure narrows the transverse sinuses and the resulting venous hypertension further impairs drainage, and an obesity-linked metabolic state with androgen excess and heightened cortisol activation within fat tissue. The typical patient is a woman of child-bearing age with obesity, often after recent weight gain, and incidence is climbing with population obesity. A similar syndrome can follow tetracyclines, vitamin A derivatives, growth hormone, steroid withdrawal and some endocrine disorders. In men, children, older adults and slim patients, look harder for a secondary cause.
det.clinical: Headache is the commonest complaint and varies in pattern — often daily, sometimes worse lying flat or on straining, and frequently migraine-like. Brief visual obscurations on standing or bending, whooshing pulse-synchronous tinnitus, horizontal diplopia from abducens palsy and neck, back or radicular pain complete the picture. Papilloedema is usually bilateral but may be asymmetric; field loss begins with blind-spot enlargement and inferonasal defects while central acuity falls late, so a patient can read the chart well yet be losing field. Fulminant IIH, with rapid visual decline over less than about four weeks, is a neuro-ophthalmic emergency. Men and patients with untreated sleep apnoea carry a higher risk of visual loss, and headache often continues after the pressure is controlled.
det.diagnosis: Revised (Friedman) criteria require papilloedema, a normal neurological examination apart from cranial nerve palsy (usually the sixth), normal MRI parenchyma without hydrocephalus or mass, normal CSF composition, and lumbar opening pressure of at least 25 cmH2O in adults (28 in children) measured lying on the side with legs relaxed. Without papilloedema, the diagnosis needs a sixth nerve palsy, or at least three of four MRI signs (empty sella, flattened posterior globe, distended optic nerve sheath, transverse sinus stenosis). MRI with MR venography (or CT venography) is mandatory to exclude venous sinus thrombosis, and a single pressure reading can mislead in either direction. Record baseline perimetry, acuity, fundus photographs and OCT of the retinal nerve fibre layer to guide follow-up. Confirm true papilloedema and exclude disc drusen or other pseudopapilloedema with OCT, ultrasound or autofluorescence before committing the patient to the label.
det.treatment: Weight reduction is the only disease-modifying approach: loss of about 5–15% of body weight usually induces remission, bariatric surgery beat a community weight programme in a randomised trial, and GLP-1 receptor agonists are increasingly used. Acetazolamide, titrated as tolerated, is the usual first drug and improves papilloedema in mild visual loss; topiramate is an alternative that also helps weight and headache. Visual function dictates urgency — worsening fields or fulminant disease need prompt CSF shunting, optic nerve sheath fenestration or transverse sinus stenting in selected patients, with a lumbar drain as a temporary bridge. Serial lumbar punctures are not a long-term strategy. Manage headache as its own problem with migraine preventives and avoidance of medication overuse; opioids are unhelpful.
det.prognosis: With weight loss and close monitoring most patients stabilise, but permanent field loss affects a minority and relapse often follows weight regain; chronic headache frequently outlasts the papilloedema.
pearls: Always do MRI with MRV before calling it idiopathic.
Sixth nerve palsy in raised ICP is a false-localising sign.
Vision, not headache, is what you are protecting.
Field loss comes first — follow perimetry and OCT, not just Snellen acuity.
det.thd: ความดันในกะโหลกศีรษะสูงโดยไม่พบก้อน โพรงน้ำไม่ขยาย และไม่มีลิ่มเลือดในหลอดเลือดดำ พบบ่อยในหญิงวัยเจริญพันธุ์ที่น้ำหนักเกินหรือน้ำหนักเพิ่มเร็ว อาการคือปวดศีรษะ ตามัวชั่ววินาที ได้ยินเสียงฟู่ตามชีพจร และ papilloedema วินิจฉัยด้วย MRI+MRV ปกติ และเจาะหลังพบ opening pressure ≥25 cmH2O โดยน้ำไขสันหลังปกติ รักษาด้วยการลดน้ำหนักประมาณ 5–15% (อาจใช้ยากลุ่ม GLP-1 receptor agonist หรือผ่าตัดลดน้ำหนัก) ร่วมกับ acetazolamide หรือ topiramate เฝ้าติดตาม visual field และ OCT เป็นระยะเพราะลานสายตาเสียก่อนสายตาส่วนกลาง ถ้าการมองเห็นแย่ลงเร็วต้องผ่าตัดระบายน้ำไขสันหลัง ทำ optic nerve sheath fenestration หรือใส่ stent ที่ transverse sinus

name: Idiopathic late onset cerebellar ataxia (ILOCA)
formal: Sporadic progressive cerebellar ataxia starting after about age 40 with no family history and no identified cause, after excluding genetic, toxic, immune, vitamin and paraneoplastic causes.
simple: A balance and coordination problem beginning in later life with no known cause, in someone without a family history.
more: MRI shows cerebellar atrophy. Some cases are probable MSA-C or have genetic causes, so search carefully; treatment is supportive.
nN: idiopathic late onset cerebellar ataxia iloca
aN: iloca | idiopathic late onset cerebellar ataxia

name: Idiopathic late-onset ataxia
formal: Progressive cerebellar ataxia developing after age 40 with no identified genetic or acquired cause, often sporadic and including undiagnosed cases later classified as MSA-C.
simple: A balance and coordination problem that begins later in life without a known cause.

name: Idiopathic PD
formal: Sporadic Parkinson disease with bradykinesia, rest tremor, rigidity and postural instability from loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra with Lewy body pathology, responsive to levodopa.
simple: The usual form of Parkinson disease with slowness, tremor and stiffness, in which no single cause is found.
more: Diagnosis is clinical with levodopa response, and DaT scan if unclear. Treat with levodopa, dopamine agonists, MAO-B inhibitors and deep brain stimulation in selected patients.

name: Idiopathic perineuritis
formal: Rare inflammatory neuropathy affecting nerve perineurium, causing painful, patchy sensorimotor deficits, with perineurial inflammation on biopsy and no systemic cause.
simple: A rare inflammation of the nerve sheath that causes pain and patchy weakness without a clear cause.
more: Biopsy shows perineurial inflammation; corticosteroids are often effective.

name: Idiopathic recurring stupor
formal: Rare recurrent episodes of unexplained stupor with elevated endogenous benzodiazepine-like activity, reversed by flumazenil, with normal EEG and structural imaging.
simple: Repeated episodes of unexplained drowsiness and unresponsiveness that may be caused by natural sedative-like substances in the body.

name: Idiopathic scoliosis
formal: Lateral spinal curvature of unknown cause, usually in adolescent girls, defined by Cobb angle above 10 degrees; neurological screening is needed to exclude syringomyelia and other spinal causes.
simple: A sideways curve of the spine appearing in childhood or teens without a known cause.

name: Idiopathic sensory neuropathy
formal: Sensory polyneuropathy with no found cause after evaluation, causing distal numbness and tingling.
simple: Numbness or tingling in the feet and hands for which no cause can be found.
more: Exclude treatable causes; treat symptoms; the course is usually slowly progressive.

name: Idiopathic torsion dystonia
formal: Primary generalised dystonia, often DYT1 (TOR1A) mutation, with childhood onset limb dystonia that spreads, especially in Ashkenazi Jewish families, without other neurological features.
simple: An inherited condition in which muscles twist the body into abnormal postures, usually starting in childhood.
more: Normal MRI and DAT-SPECT; DYT1 is a GAG deletion in TOR1A with autosomal dominant inheritance and about 30 percent penetrance. Treat with anticholinergics such as trihexyphenidyl, botulinum toxin, and DBS of globus pallidus internus gives marked benefit.

name: Imipramine akathisia
formal: Akathisia induced by imipramine or other tricyclic antidepressants, with inner restlessness and inability to sit still, probably from altered dopaminergic and serotonergic transmission.
simple: Intense restlessness and inability to stay still caused by a tricyclic antidepressant medicine.

name: Immune cell associated neurotoxicity syndrome (ICANS)
formal: Neurotoxicity after CAR-T or bispecific T-cell therapy, with aphasia, encephalopathy, tremor, seizures and cerebral oedema, related to cytokine release and endothelial dysfunction; treated with steroids.
simple: Confusion, speech trouble and seizures that can occur after certain cancer immune cell treatments.
nN: immune cell associated neurotoxicity syndrome icans
aN: icans | immune cell associated neurotoxicity syndrome

name: Immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity
formal: Neurotoxicity following CAR-T or T-cell engager therapy, ranging from word-finding difficulty to seizures and fatal cerebral oedema, usually with cytokine release syndrome.
simple: Brain side effects such as confusion and speech problems after certain cell-based cancer treatments.

name: Immune mediated necrotising myopathy
formal: Autoimmune myopathy with anti-SRP or anti-HMGCR antibodies and necrotic muscle fibres with little inflammation, causing subacute proximal weakness and very high creatine kinase; may follow statin use.
simple: A muscle disease in which the immune system damages muscle, causing weakness and often linked to statin medicines.
th: กล้ามเนื้ออักเสบแบบเนื้อตายจากภูมิคุ้มกัน — อ่อนแรงต้นแขนต้นขารุนแรง CK สูงมาก สัมพันธ์ยาสแตติน (HMGCR) หรือ anti-SRP
feat: Weeks to months of severe symmetric proximal weakness; dysphagia common
No rash; weakness continues after stopping a statin (unlike toxic statin myopathy)
Anti-SRP: severe, cardiac involvement; anti-HMGCR: statin exposure, also in young statin-naive patients
inv: CK very high (often thousands to tens of thousands)
Anti-HMGCR and anti-SRP antibodies
Biopsy: scattered necrotic fibres with little inflammation; MRI oedema
Cancer screening

case.story: Three months of rising difficulty standing from a chair; the statin was stopped 6 weeks ago without improvement.
case.exam: Hip flexors and deltoids 3/5, neck flexors weak, no rash, reflexes normal.
case.tests: CK 9,800 U/L; anti-HMGCR positive; biopsy: necrotic fibres with minimal inflammation.
case.q: What treatment is usually needed?
case.a: Immunotherapy — steroids plus a steroid-sparing agent and often IVIG; stopping the statin alone is not enough.

ddx.pt: Endomysial inflammation around non-necrotic fibres; diagnosis of exclusion
Skin signs, perifascicular atrophy
Slow course from youth, family history, genetic variant

aN: imnm | necrotizing autoimmune myopathy | nam | anti hmgcr myopathy | anti srp myopathy | statin myopathy autoimmune

det.patho: IMNM is an autoimmune myopathy in which antibodies (anti-SRP or anti-HMGCR) and complement target muscle fibres, causing widespread necrosis with little lymphocytic infiltration. Anti-HMGCR disease is linked to statin exposure in older adults, although it also occurs in statin-naive younger patients; HLA-DRB1*11:01 increases risk. A seronegative form shows the strongest cancer association. It is classified alongside dermatomyositis, antisynthetase syndrome and inclusion body myositis.
det.clinical: Symmetric proximal weakness develops over weeks to months, often severe, with neck flexor weakness, dysphagia and myalgia. Extramuscular features are uncommon, though anti-SRP disease may involve the heart and lungs and is often more aggressive. Younger patients, especially children with anti-HMGCR disease, may present slowly and resemble limb-girdle dystrophy. Unlike self-limited statin myotoxicity, weakness and high CK persist after stopping the statin.
det.diagnosis: CK is typically very high. Test anti-SRP and anti-HMGCR antibodies; a positive HMGCR antibody with a typical picture may make biopsy unnecessary. Biopsy shows scattered necrotic and regenerating fibres, sparse inflammation and sarcolemmal complement deposition. Muscle MRI shows oedema and helps choose a biopsy site. Screen for cancer, especially in seronegative and anti-HMGCR cases, and assess cardiac and pulmonary function.
det.treatment: Start early, combined immunotherapy: corticosteroids plus a steroid-sparing agent (methotrexate, azathioprine or mycophenolate), with IVIG frequently added and effective, particularly for anti-HMGCR disease. Rituximab is used in refractory or anti-SRP disease. Stop the statin and avoid re-exposure; PCSK9 inhibitors or ezetimibe are lipid-lowering alternatives. Physiotherapy and swallowing therapy support recovery.
det.prognosis: Many patients improve, but relapses on tapering and residual weakness are common; younger patients and those with anti-SRP antibodies tend to do worse.
pearls: Persistent weakness with very high CK after stopping a statin = test anti-HMGCR.
Necrosis with little inflammation on biopsy does not mean non-immune.
Children with slow anti-HMGCR myopathy may be misdiagnosed as LGMD.
det.thd: IMNM เป็นโรคกล้ามเนื้ออักเสบจากภูมิคุ้มกันที่ทำให้เซลล์กล้ามเนื้อตายเป็นจำนวนมาก โดยมีเซลล์อักเสบน้อย สัมพันธ์กับแอนติบอดี anti-HMGCR (มักมีประวัติใช้ยาสแตติน) หรือ anti-SRP ผู้ป่วยอ่อนแรงต้นแขนต้นขารุนแรงภายในไม่กี่สัปดาห์ถึงเดือน CK สูงมาก และอาการไม่ดีขึ้นแม้หยุดยาสแตติน การวินิจฉัยใช้การตรวจแอนติบอดี MRI และชิ้นเนื้อ ร่วมกับตรวจคัดกรองมะเร็ง การรักษาคือสเตียรอยด์ร่วมกับยากดภูมิ และมักให้ IVIG ร่วมด้วย ส่วนรายที่ดื้อยาใช้ rituximab

name: Immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS)
formal: Paradoxical worsening of an infection or onset of inflammation after antiretroviral recovery of the immune system in HIV, such as with cryptococcal meningitis, TB or PML.
simple: A worsening of infection symptoms when the immune system recovers after starting HIV treatment.
aN: iris | immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome

name: Immune-mediated encephalitis
formal: Brain inflammation due to autoimmune or paraneoplastic mechanisms, such as anti-NMDA receptor or LGI1 antibodies, with seizures, memory loss, psychiatric change and movement disorders.
simple: The immune system attacking the brain, causing confusion, seizures and memory or behaviour changes.

name: Immune-mediated neurological diseases
formal: Neurological disorders from immune attack on the nervous system, such as multiple sclerosis, myasthenia gravis, Guillain-Barre syndrome, autoimmune encephalitis and CIDP.
simple: Conditions in which the body's own immune system damages the brain, nerves or muscles.

name: Immunoglobulin G4-related disease (IgG4-RD)
formal: Fibro-inflammatory disease with IgG4-positive plasma cells, causing hypertrophic pachymeningitis, hypophysitis, orbital pseudotumour and cranial neuropathies; responds to steroids and rituximab.
simple: An immune condition causing swollen, scarred tissues that can affect the brain coverings, pituitary, eye sockets and nerves.
nN: immunoglobulin g4 related disease igg4 rd
aN: igg4 rd | immunoglobulin g4 related disease

name: Impulsive behavior disorders
formal: Impulse control disorders such as pathological gambling, compulsive shopping, hypersexuality and binge eating, frequently dopamine agonist related in Parkinson disease.
simple: Strong urges to do things like gamble, shop or overeat that are hard to resist, often triggered by Parkinson treatment.
more: Screen at each visit and lower or stop the dopamine agonist; cognitive behavioural therapy can help. Symptoms usually improve after the drug is adjusted.

name: Inclusion body myositis (IBM)
formal: Late-onset inflammatory myopathy with asymmetric weakness of finger flexors and quadriceps, rimmed vacuoles, endomysial inflammation, and poor response to immunotherapy.
simple: A slowly progressing muscle disease in older people, causing weak grip and thigh muscles and falls.
more: Diagnose from biopsy with rimmed vacuoles, p62 or TDP-43 aggregates, and positive anti-cN1A antibodies; CK is mildly raised and EMG shows mixed myopathic and neurogenic changes. Dysphagia is frequent; supportive care and exercise are the main management.
th: กล้ามเนื้ออักเสบเรื้อรังในผู้สูงอายุ — นิ้วมือกำไม่แน่นและต้นขาอ่อนแรง ไม่ตอบสนองต่อสเตียรอยด์
feat: Over 50, slowly progressive, often asymmetric
Weak deep finger flexors and quadriceps (falls, knees giving way)
Dysphagia common
Poor response to immunosuppression
inv: CK normal to mildly raised
Anti-cN1A antibody
Biopsy: endomysial inflammation, rimmed vacuoles, protein aggregates
Muscle MRI: forearm flexor and quadriceps involvement

case.story: Three years of falls on stairs and difficulty gripping a golf club.
case.exam: Wasted forearms with weak finger flexors, quadriceps 3/5, knee jerks reduced, sensation normal.
case.tests: CK 600 U/L; biopsy: rimmed vacuoles with endomysial CD8 T cells.
case.q: Which two muscle groups give the diagnosis away at the bedside?
case.a: Deep finger flexors and quadriceps.

read.where: บทที่ 6 IIM หน้า 104–136 (แนวทางวินิจฉัย แผนภูมิ 6.1 หน้า 106; MSA ตารางที่ 6.1 หน้า 107; พยาธิวิทยา ตารางที่ 6.2–6.3 หน้า 108–109)

ddx.pt: Symmetric proximal, much higher CK, responds to steroids
UMN signs and fasciculations; neurogenic EMG
Myotonia, ptosis, cataracts, family history

aN: ibm | inclusion body myositis | sibm | sporadic inclusion body myositis

det.patho: A slowly progressive myopathy of older adults combining cytotoxic CD8 T-cell inflammation with degenerative features — rimmed vacuoles, protein aggregates (TDP-43, p62) and mitochondrial abnormalities. Antibodies against cytosolic 5′-nucleotidase 1A (cN1A) are found in a proportion of patients. It is the most common acquired myopathy after 50, more frequent in men, and does not respond to standard immunotherapy, suggesting the degenerative process is not simply driven by inflammation.
det.clinical: Weakness develops over years, typically asymmetric, with selective involvement of deep finger flexors (weak grip, difficulty turning keys) and quadriceps (knees buckling, falls on stairs). Ankle dorsiflexors and facial muscles may be involved, and dysphagia affects over half. Wasting of the medial forearm and thigh is a visual clue. Sensation is normal, but a mild neuropathy can coexist, causing confusion with motor neuron disease.
det.diagnosis: CK is normal or moderately raised (usually under 15 times the upper limit). EMG shows myopathic and often neurogenic-looking units with fibrillations. Muscle MRI or ultrasound highlights selective flexor digitorum profundus and quadriceps involvement with relative rectus femoris sparing. Biopsy shows endomysial inflammation invading non-necrotic fibres, rimmed vacuoles, protein aggregates and mitochondrial changes; anti-cN1A is supportive but not specific (also seen in Sjögren and SLE). The ENMC 2011 criteria are commonly used.
det.treatment: No drug has proven effective; corticosteroids and conventional immunosuppressants do not halt progression. Management centres on physiotherapy and safe exercise, falls prevention with knee-ankle orthoses and walking aids, occupational therapy for grip, and swallowing assessment with dilatation or cricopharyngeal myotomy for severe dysphagia. IVIG may help dysphagia in some reports. Patients should be offered clinical trials where available.
det.prognosis: Slow progression over years; many need a walking aid within 10–15 years, but life expectancy is near normal unless dysphagia causes aspiration.
pearls: Older man, weak finger flexors and quadriceps, poor steroid response = IBM.
Steroid-refractory polymyositis should prompt reconsideration of IBM.
det.thd: IBM เป็นโรคกล้ามเนื้ออักเสบเรื้อรังในผู้ที่อายุเกิน 50 ปี มีทั้งการอักเสบจาก CD8 T cell และการเสื่อมที่พบ rimmed vacuoles ในชิ้นเนื้อ อาการค่อย ๆ อ่อนแรงหลายปีแบบไม่เท่ากันสองข้าง เด่นที่กล้ามเนื้องอนิ้วมือ (กำไม่แน่น) และ quadriceps (เข่าทรุด หกล้ม) และกลืนลำบาก CK สูงเล็กน้อย ตรวจแอนติบอดี anti-cN1A, MRI กล้ามเนื้อ และตัดชิ้นเนื้อช่วยยืนยัน โรคนี้ไม่ตอบสนองต่อสเตียรอยด์และยากดภูมิ การรักษาเน้นกายภาพบำบัด อุปกรณ์ช่วยเดิน และดูแลการกลืน

name: Index brainstem reticular myoclonus
formal: Cortical-subcortical myoclonus arising from the brainstem reticular formation, producing generalised jerks with startle-like characteristics, often after hypoxic brain injury or in hyperekplexia.
simple: Sudden muscle jerks involving the whole body that originate in the brainstem, often after brain injury.

name: Index classical essential tremor
formal: Common postural and kinetic tremor, mostly of the hands, slowly progressive, often familial, improved by alcohol and responsive to propranolol or primidone.
simple: A very common tremor of the hands that appears with action, often runs in families and improves with alcohol.

name: Index globoid cell leucodystrophy (Krabbe’s disease)
formal: Autosomal recessive lysosomal disease from galactocerebrosidase deficiency, causing demyelination with irritability, spasticity, seizures and optic atrophy, usually in infancy.
simple: An inherited disease where nerves lose their insulating coating, leading to stiffness, seizures and developmental loss, most often in babies.
nN: index globoid cell leucodystrophy krabbe disease
aN: krabbe disease | index globoid cell leucodystrophy

name: Index heavy metal poisoning
formal: Neurotoxicity from lead, mercury, arsenic, manganese or thallium, producing encephalopathy, peripheral neuropathy, tremor or parkinsonism depending on the agent and exposure.
simple: Nerve and brain damage caused by poisoning with metals such as lead, mercury or arsenic.

name: Index hemidystonia
formal: Dystonia affecting one half of the body, usually symptomatic of contralateral basal ganglia or thalamic lesions, such as stroke, trauma or perinatal injury.
simple: Twisting muscle spasms on one side of the body, usually from damage to the opposite side of the brain.

name: Index palatal myoclonus/tremor
formal: Rhythmic palatal movements at 1 to 3 Hz from hypertrophic olivary degeneration after Guillain-Mollaret triangle lesions, either symptomatic with ear click or essential.
simple: A rhythmic jerking of the soft palate, often with a clicking sound in the ear, usually after damage in the brainstem.

name: Index pantothenate kinase-associated neurodegeneration
formal: Autosomal recessive NBIA from PANK2 mutation, with childhood dystonia, rigidity, retinopathy and the eye-of-the-tiger sign in the globus pallidus on MRI.
simple: An inherited childhood disease with iron build-up in the brain, causing stiffness and twisting movements.

name: Index progressive myoclonus epilepsy and progressive myoclonic ataxia
formal: Syndrome of myoclonus, seizures and progressive neurological decline, including Unverricht-Lundborg, Lafora, MERRF and neuronal ceroid lipofuscinoses, or myoclonic ataxia (Ramsay Hunt).
simple: A group of inherited disorders with muscle jerks, seizures and worsening coordination and thinking.
nN: index progressive myoclonus epilepsy and progressive myoclonic ataxia

name: Index restless legs syndrome (RLS)
formal: Sensorimotor disorder with urge to move the legs at rest, worse at night and relieved by movement, associated with iron deficiency and dopaminergic dysfunction; treated with gabapentinoids or iron.
simple: An irresistible urge to move the legs, especially in the evening or at rest, relieved by movement.
aN: rls | index restless legs syndrome

name: Index subcortical dementia
formal: Dementia from basal ganglia, thalamus and white matter disease, with slowed thinking, apathy, executive dysfunction and movement abnormalities, as in Parkinson, Huntington disease and HIV.
simple: Memory and thinking problems with slowed thinking and mood change, caused by damage to deep brain structures.

name: Index systemic lupus erythematosus and antiphospholipid antibody
formal: Systemic autoimmune disease with antiphospholipid antibodies, causing stroke, seizures, chorea, myelitis, cognitive dysfunction and cerebral venous thrombosis through vasculopathy and thrombosis.
simple: An immune disease that can lead to strokes, seizures and thinking problems, in part through blood clots in brain vessels.
nN: index systemic lupus erythematosus and antiphospholipid antibody

name: Indian childhood cirrhosis
formal: Infantile copper-associated liver disease of rural India with progressive cirrhosis and marked hepatic copper deposits, linked to copper-contaminated milk in brass vessels with a genetic susceptibility.
simple: A fatal childhood liver disease from too much copper in the diet seen in rural India, historically.
more: Liver biopsy shows copper and Mallory bodies. Early chelation (penicillamine) and stopping copper exposure help; it is now rare after public health changes.

name: Infantile neuroaxonal dystrophy
formal: Autosomal recessive PLA2G6-related disorder with onset in infancy of psychomotor regression, hypotonia, optic atrophy and cerebellar atrophy, with axonal spheroids on biopsy.
simple: An inherited disease starting in infancy in which a child loses skills and develops weak muscles, vision problems and later stiffness.
more: Diagnosed by PLA2G6 testing; MRI shows cerebellar atrophy with iron accumulation in the globus pallidus and a characteristic clock-hand sign in the thin cord. Biopsy of skin or conjunctiva shows spheroids; prognosis is poor and care is supportive.

name: Infantile neuroaxonal dystrophy (INAD
formal: Infantile neuroaxonal dystrophy, PLA2G6-associated, with early psychomotor regression, hypotonia, tetraparesis, visual failure and cerebellar atrophy; iron accumulation in globus pallidus later.
simple: An inherited disease starting in infancy in which a child loses skills and develops weak muscles, vision problems and later stiffness.

name: Infantile neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis (Haltia-Santavuori disease)
formal: Santavuori-Haltia disease, a CLN1 PPT1-related lysosomal storage disorder with onset before 2 years of microcephaly, myoclonus, visual failure and flat EEG, with granular osmiophilic deposits.
simple: An inherited childhood disease causing loss of skills, seizures, blindness and early death, from build-up of waste material in brain cells.
nN: infantile neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis haltia santavuori disease
aN: haltia santavuori disease | infantile neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis

name: Infantile onset spinocerebellar ataxia (IOSCA)
formal: Finnish autosomal recessive disorder from C10orf2 (Twinkle) variants with infantile ataxia, athetosis, ophthalmoplegia, sensory neuropathy, deafness and epilepsy.
simple: An inherited childhood disease causing worsening balance, abnormal movements, deafness and nerve damage beginning in infancy.
more: Confirmed by genetic testing and MRI showing cerebellar atrophy. Treatment is supportive, and affected individuals often lose mobility in adolescence.
aN: iosca | infantile onset spinocerebellar ataxia

name: Infantile Pompe disease
formal: Severe lysosomal glycogen storage disease from GAA deficiency, with hypotonia, cardiomegaly and hepatomegaly in the first months of life; treated with enzyme replacement.
simple: An inherited disorder in babies where sugar stores build up in muscles and the heart, causing floppiness and heart enlargement.

name: Infantile spasms
formal: Epileptic spasms in infancy, typically with hypsarrhythmia on EEG and developmental regression (West syndrome); causes include tuberous sclerosis and hypoxic injury; treated with ACTH or vigabatrin.
simple: A serious type of seizure in babies, with sudden clusters of jerks and developmental delay, which needs prompt treatment.

name: Infectious intracranial aneurysms (IIAs)
formal: Mycotic aneurysms of cerebral arteries, usually distal, from septic emboli in infective endocarditis, which may cause subarachnoid or intracerebral haemorrhage.
simple: Weak bulges in brain arteries caused by infection that can burst and bleed into the brain.
aN: iias | infectious intracranial aneurysms

name: Infective endocarditis
formal: Infection of heart valves producing septic emboli to the brain, with ischaemic stroke, mycotic aneurysm, abscess, meningitis and haemorrhage as neurological complications.
simple: An infection of the heart valves that can send clots or germs to the brain and cause strokes or abscesses.

tempoNote: Embolic events are sudden, on a background of fever and malaise over days to weeks; most occur before or in the first 2 weeks of antibiotics
feat: Fever, new murmur, anaemia and raised CRP in a patient with stroke or encephalopathy
Multiple small infarcts in several territories, cortical microbleeds or convexity SAH
Mycotic (infectious) aneurysms on distal MCA branches that may bleed
Brain abscess, meningitis or toxic encephalopathy
Risk groups: injecting drug use, prosthetic valve, rheumatic heart disease, haemodialysis, recent dental or line infection
inv: Three sets of blood cultures before antibiotics
Transthoracic then transoesophageal echocardiography (TOE more sensitive for small vegetations and abscess)
MRI with SWI: scattered infarcts and microbleeds; CTA or catheter angiography for mycotic aneurysm
Modified Duke (2023 Duke-ISCVID) criteria

case.who: 41-year-old man with rheumatic mitral disease, rice farmer, Surin
case.story: Two weeks of evening fevers and weight loss, then sudden inability to speak this morning.
case.exam: Temp 38.6°C, pansystolic murmur, splinter haemorrhages; global aphasia with right facial weakness.
case.tests: CT: left frontal hypodensity; MRI: further tiny infarcts in both hemispheres; blood cultures grow viridans streptococci; TOE: 12 mm mitral vegetation.
case.q: Should he receive IV thrombolysis, and what should happen next?
case.a: No — thrombolysis is contraindicated in IE because of bleeding risk; start IV antibiotics, screen for mycotic aneurysm and refer early to cardiac surgery given a large vegetation with embolism.

det.patho: Bacteria (most often Staphylococcus aureus, streptococci or enterococci) colonise damaged or prosthetic valves and form friable vegetations of fibrin, platelets and organisms. Pieces break off and reach the brain in roughly 20–40% of cases, causing infarcts that may turn haemorrhagic, abscesses and meningitis. Septic emboli lodging in distal arteries infect the vessel wall and create mycotic aneurysms. Rheumatic heart disease remains an important substrate in Thailand.
det.clinical: Neurological complications are often the presenting feature and include ischaemic stroke, encephalopathy, intracranial haemorrhage, abscess and meningitis; many more patients have silent lesions on MRI. Embolic risk is highest with S. aureus, mitral vegetations and vegetations larger than 10 mm, and drops sharply after the first week of effective antibiotics. Haemorrhage can arise from haemorrhagic transformation, rupture of a mycotic aneurysm or septic arteritis.
det.diagnosis: Any stroke with fever, a murmur or a raised inflammatory picture deserves blood cultures before antibiotics and echocardiography. Brain MRI with susceptibility imaging reveals clinically silent emboli and microbleeds, which count as a vascular phenomenon. Angiography is indicated for haemorrhage or when mycotic aneurysms are suspected. Culture-negative cases need serology (Bartonella, Coxiella) and consideration of NBTE.
det.treatment: Prolonged pathogen-directed intravenous antibiotics are the basis of care. IV thrombolysis is contraindicated; mechanical thrombectomy can be considered for large-vessel occlusion in experienced centres. Anticoagulation and antiplatelet therapy are generally not started for the embolism itself; interrupt existing anticoagulation if bleeding occurs. Early valve surgery is advised for heart failure, uncontrolled infection or persistent large vegetations, and can usually proceed after ischaemic stroke without major haemorrhage. Mycotic aneurysms that bleed or enlarge are treated endovascularly or surgically.
det.prognosis: Neurological complications roughly double in-hospital mortality; outcome depends on organism, haemorrhage and timely surgery.
pearls: Stroke + fever = blood cultures and echo before giving any thrombolytic.
Embolic risk falls rapidly once appropriate antibiotics start.
Distal branch aneurysm in a febrile patient is mycotic until proved otherwise.

ddx.pt: Sterile vegetations with negative cultures, usually in cancer or lupus
Ring-enhancing lesion; may itself complicate IE
Meningism dominates; IE is suspected when a murmur and multiple emboli coexist

aN: ie | bacterial endocarditis | septic embolism | mycotic aneurysm | infectious intracranial aneurysm | endocarditis stroke | sbe

name: Infective vasculitis
formal: Inflammation of cerebral blood vessels caused by infection such as VZV, syphilis, tuberculosis or fungi, leading to ischaemic stroke or aneurysm and cranial neuropathy.
simple: Brain blood vessel inflammation caused by an infection, which can lead to stroke.

name: Infiltrative optic neuropathy
formal: Visual loss from optic nerve infiltration by lymphoma, leukaemia, carcinoma, sarcoidosis or granuloma, with optic disc swelling or pallor, often with a sluggish course.
simple: Loss of vision caused by cancer cells or inflammatory tissue growing into the optic nerve.

name: Inflammatory bowel disease
formal: Chronic inflammatory gut disease, Crohn disease or ulcerative colitis, with extra-intestinal neurological associations such as peripheral neuropathy, stroke, venous thrombosis and demyelination.
simple: Long-term gut inflammation, such as Crohn disease, that can also be linked to nerve problems and blood clots.
more: Neurological syndromes include natalizumab progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy and demyelination during anti-TNF therapy. Evaluate for B12 and copper deficiency or vasculitis; treat the gut disease and associated thromboembolism risk.

name: Inflammatory disease of orbit
formal: Idiopathic orbital inflammation, or orbital pseudotumour, causing painful proptosis, diplopia and ophthalmoplegia, responsive to corticosteroids; differential includes IgG4 disease and thyroid orbitopathy.
simple: Painful swelling inside the eye socket that causes a bulging eye and double vision, usually improving with steroids.

name: Inflammatory myopathies
formal: Group of immune-mediated muscle diseases such as polymyositis, dermatomyositis and inclusion body myositis causing proximal weakness, elevated CK and inflammatory infiltrates.
simple: A group of muscle conditions caused by inflammation, leading to weakness, usually in the shoulders and hips.
more: Check myositis-specific antibodies (anti-Jo-1, Mi-2, TIF1-gamma, SRP, NT5c1A), EMG with irritable myopathy, MRI and biopsy. Treat PM and DM with steroids plus methotrexate or azathioprine and IVIG; IBM is resistant and screen for malignancy in DM.

name: Inflammatory myopathy
formal: Acquired muscle disease with inflammatory infiltrates, such as dermatomyositis, polymyositis or inclusion body myositis, giving progressive proximal weakness with raised CK.
simple: A muscle disease with inflammation that causes weakness, usually of the shoulders and hips.

name: Inflammatory neuropathies
formal: Immune-mediated nerve diseases such as Guillain-Barre syndrome and CIDP, with demyelination causing weakness, areflexia and sensory loss, treatable with IVIG, plasma exchange or steroids.
simple: Conditions in which the immune system attacks nerves, causing weakness and numbness.

name: Infratentorial haemorrhage
formal: Bleeding in the posterior fossa, such as cerebellar or brainstem haemorrhage, causing vomiting, ataxia, coma and risk of hydrocephalus and herniation; may need surgical decompression.
simple: Bleeding in the lower part of the brain, around the cerebellum or brainstem, which can quickly become life-threatening.

name: Inherited ataxia syndromes
formal: Group of genetic cerebellar disorders, including spinocerebellar ataxias, Friedreich ataxia and episodic ataxias, with progressive gait and limb incoordination and dysarthria.
simple: A group of inherited conditions causing poor balance and coordination that worsen over time.

name: Inherited Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease (iCJD)
formal: Genetic prion disease caused by PRNP mutations, with CJD-like rapid dementia, myoclonus and ataxia, with autosomal dominant inheritance.
simple: A rare inherited form of Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease that runs in families and causes fast-progressing dementia.
aN: icjd | inherited creutzfeldt jakob disease

name: Inherited leukodystrophies, adult-onset
formal: Genetic white matter disorders presenting in adulthood, including ALSP, adrenomyeloneuropathy, Alexander disease and CADASIL-like disorders, with spastic gait, ataxia and cognitive decline.
simple: Inherited diseases of the brain's white matter that begin in adulthood and cause stiffness, imbalance and memory problems.
aN: inherited leukodystrophies | adult onset

name: Inherited muscle disorders
formal: Genetic myopathies, including muscular dystrophies, congenital and metabolic myopathies and channelopathies, with progressive weakness and often elevated creatine kinase.
simple: Inherited conditions that weaken and waste muscles over time.

name: Inherited neuromyotonia and paroxysmal ataxia
formal: Episodic ataxia type 1, from KCNA1 mutation, with brief ataxia attacks lasting seconds to minutes, interictal myokymia and neuromyotonia, triggered by startle or exercise.
simple: An inherited condition with short attacks of unsteadiness and muscle twitching, set off by sudden movement or fright.

name: Inherited neuropathies
formal: Genetic peripheral nerve diseases, such as Charcot-Marie-Tooth, hereditary neuropathy with pressure palsies and hereditary sensory neuropathies, causing slowly progressive weakness and sensory loss.
simple: Inherited conditions that damage the nerves in the arms and legs, causing weakness and numbness.

name: Inherited neuropathy
formal: Genetic peripheral neuropathy, such as Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease, with slowly progressive distal weakness, foot deformities, and reduced reflexes.
simple: An inherited condition affecting nerves to the feet and hands, causing weakness, numbness and high-arched feet.

name: Inherited peripheral nerve diseases
formal: Genetic disorders of peripheral nerves such as CMT, HNPP and familial amyloid neuropathy, causing slowly progressive weakness and sensory loss, often with foot deformities.
simple: Inherited conditions that damage nerves in the arms and legs, causing weakness and numbness.

name: Inherited prion diseases
formal: Genetic prion disorders from PRNP mutation, including familial CJD, Gerstmann-Straussler-Scheinker disease and fatal familial insomnia, with rapidly progressive dementia and ataxia.
simple: Rare inherited brain diseases from faulty prion protein that cause dementia, imbalance and sleep problems.

name: Initiation tremor
formal: Tremor that appears at the start of voluntary movement, as in Holmes tremor or primary orthostatic tremor variants, due to cerebellar outflow disturbance or other basal ganglia lesions.
simple: A tremor that shows up at the start of a movement and often settles once the movement is under way.

name: Insomnia
formal: Chronic difficulty initiating or maintaining sleep with daytime impairment; may be primary or secondary to psychiatric, medical or neurological disease, medicines or sleep disorders.
simple: Ongoing trouble falling or staying asleep that affects how a person feels and functions in the daytime.

name: Insulin neuritis
formal: Acute painful small fibre neuropathy with autonomic features after rapid glycaemic correction in poorly controlled diabetes, such as treatment-induced neuropathy of diabetes.
simple: Severe nerve pain and autonomic symptoms that can follow a sudden fall in blood sugar after starting diabetes treatment.

name: Intention tremor
formal: Tremor on goal-directed movement that increases toward the target, characteristic of cerebellar outflow lesions in the dentate-rubro-thalamic pathway, seen in multiple sclerosis, stroke and toxins.
simple: A tremor that gets worse as the hand approaches a target, such as touching the nose, usually from cerebellar damage.

name: Intermittent ataxias
formal: Episodic ataxia syndromes with attacks of incoordination between normal intervals, due to channelopathies or metabolic disorders; episodic ataxia types 1 and 2 are common.
simple: Conditions in which attacks of poor balance and coordination come and go.

name: Intermittent metabolic ataxias
formal: Episodic ataxia from inborn errors of metabolism, such as maple syrup urine disease, pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency, urea cycle defects and Hartnup disease, triggered by illness or protein load.
simple: Attacks of unsteady walking caused by inherited metabolic disorders, often brought on by infection or a high-protein meal.

name: Internal carotid artery (ICA) disease
formal: Stenosis or occlusion of the ICA, usually atherosclerotic at the bifurcation, causing amaurosis fugax, TIA or hemispheric stroke; also dissection, treated with endarterectomy or stenting.
simple: Narrowing or blockage of the main neck artery to the brain, which can cause temporary vision loss or stroke.
aN: ica | internal carotid artery disease

name: Internal carotid artery disease
formal: Stenosis, occlusion or dissection of the internal carotid artery causing amaurosis fugax, TIA or stroke through emboli or haemodynamic failure.
simple: Narrowing or blockage of the main neck artery to the brain, which can cause temporary vision loss or stroke.

name: Internuclear ophthalmoplegia (INO)
formal: Impaired adduction of the ipsilateral eye on lateral gaze, with nystagmus of the abducting eye, from MLF lesions; commonly multiple sclerosis in young adults and brainstem stroke in older patients.
simple: Poor inward movement of one eye when looking sideways, caused by damage in a brainstem pathway.
aN: ino | internuclear ophthalmoplegia

name: Internuclear ophthalmoplegia of abduction
formal: Posterior or Lutz INO with weakness of abduction, rather than adduction, due to dysfunction of the contralateral side or lesions of paramedian pontine fibres, a variant of internuclear ophthalmoplegia.
simple: A rare eye movement problem in which the eye cannot move outward properly, due to damage to a brainstem pathway.

name: Interstitial lung disease (ILD)
formal: Diffuse parenchymal lung disease commonly associated with antisynthetase syndrome and other inflammatory myopathies, causing dyspnoea and restrictive physiology.
simple: Scarring or inflammation of the lungs, often seen alongside autoimmune muscle disease, causing breathlessness.
more: Diagnosed with HRCT and lung function tests; treated with steroids and immunosuppressants such as mycophenolate; strongly affects prognosis in myositis.
aN: ild | interstitial lung disease

name: Intracerebral haematoma
formal: Focal collection of blood within the brain parenchyma, typically from hypertensive vasculopathy, amyloid angiopathy, trauma or vascular malformation, with sudden deficit and mass effect.
simple: A pocket of blood inside the brain tissue that causes sudden weakness or other deficits.

name: Intracerebral haemorrhage (ICH)
formal: Haemorrhagic stroke from rupture of a vessel in the parenchyma, most often hypertensive deep bleed or amyloid lobar bleed, with sudden headache, deficit and reduced consciousness.
simple: A stroke caused by bleeding inside the brain, often linked to high blood pressure.

case.story: Sudden left arm and leg weakness and headache while lifting a box; vomited twice; drowsier over 2 hours.
case.exam: BP 220/120, GCS 13, dense left hemiplegia and hemisensory loss, eyes deviated to the right.
case.tests: CT: 30 mL right putaminal haematoma with intraventricular extension.
case.q: Name the likely mechanism and two immediate management priorities.
case.a: Hypertensive deep ICH. Lower systolic BP promptly and safely, correct any coagulopathy, and monitor for hydrocephalus/expansion (neurosurgical review).

aN: ich | intracerebral hemorrhage | hemorrhagic stroke | brain bleed

det.patho: Rupture of a small penetrating artery bleeds into brain parenchyma; chronic hypertension damages deep perforators (lipohyalinosis, arteriolosclerosis), whereas amyloid angiopathy weakens cortical and leptomeningeal vessels in older people. Other causes include anticoagulants, vascular malformations, cavernomas, tumours, venous thrombosis, sympathomimetic drugs such as amphetamine or cocaine, and haemorrhagic transformation of infarcts. ICH makes up a larger share of strokes in Asian populations than in Western ones. Injury comes in two waves: mass effect and haematoma growth in the first hours (about a third expand, mostly within 6 hours), then perihaematomal oedema and inflammation from blood breakdown products over days.
det.clinical: Onset is sudden with a focal deficit, often accompanied by headache, vomiting, very high BP and progressive drowsiness, though small bleeds are clinically indistinguishable from infarction. Site predicts the syndrome: putamen (hemiplegia, gaze toward lesion), thalamus (sensory loss, downward gaze deviation, small unreactive pupils), lobar (seizures, cortical signs), pons (coma, pinpoint pupils, quadriplegia), cerebellum (vertigo, ataxia, inability to stand, gaze palsy). Cerebellar haematomas can rapidly compress the brainstem or block the fourth ventricle. Deterioration in the first day usually reflects expansion, intraventricular extension or hydrocephalus, so frequent GCS checks are essential.
det.diagnosis: Non-contrast CT confirms the bleed; estimate volume with ABC/2 and look for ventricular blood and hydrocephalus. A spot sign on CTA, or swirl and blend signs on plain CT, marks risk of expansion. Check coagulation, platelets, renal function and timing of the last anticoagulant dose. In young or normotensive patients and in lobar or unusually placed bleeds, look for an underlying lesion with CTA, MRI with SWI (microbleed pattern, siderosis, cavernoma, tumour) and catheter angiography when doubt remains; the DIAGRAM score helps decide who needs angiography. The ICH score helps communicate severity but should not by itself justify early withdrawal of care, and do-not-resuscitate decisions are best deferred for at least a day.
det.treatment: Start a bundle within the first hour: lower systolic BP early and smoothly toward about 140 mmHg (target range 130–150, avoiding big swings), correct glucose and fever, and reverse anticoagulation at once; this combined approach improved functional outcome in a large trial. Reversal: vitamin K plus four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate for warfarin, idarucizumab for dabigatran, and andexanet alfa or PCC for factor Xa inhibitors (andexanet limits expansion better but carries a thrombotic signal). Platelet transfusion is not helpful for antiplatelet-associated ICH unless surgery is planned, and tranexamic acid is not established. Cerebellar haematomas over about 3 cm or with brainstem compression or hydrocephalus need evacuation; external ventricular drainage treats obstructive hydrocephalus, and minimally invasive evacuation of moderate lobar haematomas within 24 hours improved outcome in a recent trial. Treat seizures if they occur (no routine prophylaxis), use intermittent pneumatic compression early, and later restarting an antiplatelet is reasonably safe, whereas resuming anticoagulation for AF is an individual decision weighing ischaemic benefit against rebleeding (higher with CAA), with appendage occlusion as an alternative.
det.prognosis: Thirty-day mortality is around 40%; volume, GCS, age, intraventricular blood and infratentorial site predict poor outcome, but early pessimism can become self-fulfilling.
pearls: Deep bleed + hypertension = arteriolopathy; lobar bleed in the elderly = think CAA.
Cerebellar haemorrhage is a neurosurgical emergency even if the patient looks well.
Do not give platelets routinely for antiplatelet-related ICH.
Haematoma growth is the main modifiable target: early BP lowering plus rapid reversal, ideally in the first hour.

name: Intracranial epidural abscess
formal: Collection of pus between dura and skull, from sinusitis, otitis, trauma or surgery, causing fever, headache and subtle focal signs; needs drainage and antibiotics.
simple: A pocket of pus between the skull and the brain's outer covering, usually after a sinus or ear infection or surgery.

name: Intracranial haemorrhage
formal: Bleeding within the cranium, including epidural, subdural, subarachnoid, intracerebral and intraventricular, from trauma, vascular rupture or coagulopathy, with raised pressure and focal deficits.
simple: Bleeding inside the skull, which can press on the brain and cause headache, weakness or loss of consciousness.

name: Intradural extramedullary (ID-EM) tumours
formal: Spinal tumours inside the dura but outside the cord, such as meningioma and schwannoma, causing slowly progressive radicular pain and myelopathy; usually resectable.
simple: Slow-growing tumours near the spinal cord that press on nerves or the cord, usually removable by surgery.
aN: id em | intradural extramedullary tumours

name: Intradural spinal tumours
formal: Tumours within the dural sac of the spine, either extramedullary such as meningioma and schwannoma, or intramedullary such as ependymoma and astrocytoma, causing pain and myelopathy.
simple: Growths inside the spinal canal that can press on the spinal cord and nerve roots.

name: Intramedullary abscess
formal: Rare pyogenic infection within the spinal cord, often from haematogenous spread or dermal sinus, with fever, pain and rapid myelopathy; needs MRI and drainage.
simple: A rare pus-filled infection inside the spinal cord that causes fever, back pain and rapid weakness.

name: Intramedullary spinal tumours
formal: Tumours arising within the cord, most often ependymoma or astrocytoma, and haemangioblastoma, causing pain, dissociated sensory loss and myelopathy; treated by microsurgical resection.
simple: Tumours that grow inside the spinal cord, causing pain, numbness and weakness.

name: Intravascular cerebral B cell lymphoma
formal: Intravascular large B cell lymphoma with neoplastic cells within small vessels, causing multifocal infarcts, dementia and encephalopathy; diagnosis often needs biopsy.
simple: A rare lymphoma growing inside tiny brain vessels, causing multiple small strokes and confusion.

name: Intraventricular haemorrhage
formal: Blood within the cerebral ventricles from germinal matrix bleeding in premature infants or extension of intracerebral or subarachnoid haemorrhage, risking hydrocephalus.
simple: Bleeding into the brain's fluid-filled chambers, which can block fluid flow and cause hydrocephalus.

name: Intrinsic cord tumours
formal: Tumours originating within the spinal cord, especially ependymoma, astrocytoma and haemangioblastoma, causing pain, segmental sensory loss and myelopathy.
simple: Tumours growing inside the spinal cord itself, causing back pain, numbness and weakness.

name: Ipsiversive seizures
formal: Focal seizures with head and eye version toward the side of the epileptic focus, an uncommon pattern in semiology compared with contraversive turning; lateralising value is debated.
simple: Seizures in which the head and eyes turn toward the same side as the seizure's starting point.

name: Iris hamartomas
formal: Lisch nodules, benign pigmented iris hamartomas that are a diagnostic criterion for neurofibromatosis type 1 and appear in childhood.
simple: Small harmless bumps on the coloured part of the eye that are a sign of neurofibromatosis type 1.

name: Iron akathisia
formal: Akathisia related to iron deficiency, overlapping with restless legs syndrome and responding to iron replacement; low ferritin is linked to reduced dopamine function.
simple: Inner restlessness and the need to move, linked to low iron stores and improved by iron treatment.

name: Iron deficiency
formal: Reduced body iron stores, linked to restless legs syndrome, akathisia, breath-holding spells, pica and cognitive effects in children; ferritin below 50 is relevant in RLS.
simple: Not having enough iron in the body, which can cause tiredness and is linked to restless legs.

name: Isaacs’ syndrome
formal: Acquired peripheral nerve hyperexcitability with muscle stiffness, fasciculation, myokymia and cramps, from VGKC complex antibodies (CASPR2), sometimes with thymoma; responds to immunotherapy.
simple: A condition in which overactive nerves cause constant muscle twitching, stiffness and cramps.
more: Diagnose with EMG showing neuromyotonic, myokymic or doublet discharges that persist during sleep and nerve block, with anti-CASPR2 or LGI1 antibodies. Treat with carbamazepine, phenytoin, plasma exchange or IVIG.
th: เส้นประสาทส่วนปลายทำงานเกิน — กล้ามเนื้อกระตุกเป็นคลื่น แข็ง ตะคริว เหงื่อออกมาก สัมพันธ์แอนติบอดี CASPR2 และ thymoma

Excess sweating; may have insomnia, confusion or seizures (Morvan overlap)
Associated with thymoma and other tumours
inv: EMG: myokymic and neuromyotonic discharges that persist during sleep and after nerve block
CASPR2 (and LGI1) antibodies; CT chest for thymoma

case.story: Months of muscle stiffness, painful cramps and constant twitching under the skin of the calves; he sweats heavily and sleeps poorly.
case.exam: Visible undulating myokymia in both calves, slow hand opening after a firm grip, normal strength and reflexes.
case.tests: EMG: doublet and multiplet neuromyotonic discharges persisting in sleep; CASPR2 antibodies positive; CT chest: anterior mediastinal mass.
case.q: What is the likely mediastinal mass and why look for it?
case.a: Thymoma — CASPR2-associated neuromyotonia can be paraneoplastic, and treating the tumour helps.

Fasciculations with progressive weakness and UMN signs
