aN: acquired neuromyotonia | isaacs syndrome | caspr2 neuromyotonia | peripheral nerve hyperexcitability | continuous muscle fibre activity

det.patho: Acquired neuromyotonia arises from hyperexcitability of motor axons, usually distal. Antibodies against proteins of the voltage-gated potassium channel complex — chiefly CASPR2 at the juxtaparanode — reduce potassium currents, so axons fire repetitively and spontaneously. A paraneoplastic origin, especially thymoma, is found in a substantial minority. Combined central involvement (Morvan syndrome) indicates a broader autoimmune process.
det.clinical: Patients describe continuous twitching, rippling, stiffness, cramps and slow relaxation after a grip; symptoms persist during sleep. Hyperhidrosis and other autonomic features are common, and neuropathic pain or paraesthesia may occur. Insomnia, agitation, hallucinations, dysautonomia and weight loss suggest Morvan syndrome. A coexisting myasthenia gravis raises suspicion of thymoma.
det.diagnosis: EMG shows myokymic and neuromyotonic discharges (high-frequency bursts with decrementing amplitude), and after-discharges following nerve stimulation. Test for CASPR2 and LGI1 antibodies with cell-based assays; many patients remain seronegative. Image the chest for thymoma and screen for other tumours, such as lung cancer. Distinguish from cramp-fasciculation syndrome, stiff-person syndrome and hereditary forms (e.g. KCNA1).
det.treatment: Symptomatic control uses sodium-channel blocking drugs such as carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, phenytoin or lamotrigine. Plasma exchange, IVIG, corticosteroids and rituximab are used for antibody-positive or disabling disease. Remove a thymoma if present. Morvan syndrome often needs more aggressive immunotherapy.
det.prognosis: Non-paraneoplastic disease often improves with treatment and may remit; outcome in paraneoplastic cases depends on the tumour.
pearls: Twitching that continues during sleep and after nerve block points to peripheral nerve hyperexcitability.
Thymoma links Isaacs, Morvan and myasthenia gravis — image the chest.
det.thd: Isaacs’ syndrome คือภาวะเส้นประสาทส่วนปลายถูกกระตุ้นง่ายเกินไป มักเกิดจากแอนติบอดีต่อ CASPR2 ทำให้กล้ามเนื้อกระตุกเป็นคลื่นตลอดเวลา แข็ง เป็นตะคริว และเหงื่อออกมาก แม้ขณะหลับ EMG พบ myokymic และ neuromyotonic discharges ต้องตรวจหาเนื้องอก thymoma เสมอ รักษาอาการด้วยยากลุ่ม sodium-channel blocker เช่น carbamazepine และใช้ภูมิคุ้มกันบำบัดเช่น plasma exchange หรือ IVIG ในรายที่รุนแรง

name: Ischaemic ocular syndromes
formal: Disorders of reduced ocular blood flow from carotid disease, with amaurosis fugax, central retinal artery occlusion, ischaemic optic neuropathy and ocular ischaemic syndrome with painful eye.
simple: Eye problems caused by poor blood flow to the eye, from temporary vision loss to permanent damage.

name: Ischaemic stroke
formal: Focal brain infarction from arterial occlusion due to large vessel atherosclerosis, cardioembolism or small vessel disease, with sudden focal deficit; treated with thrombolysis or thrombectomy.
simple: A stroke caused by a blocked blood vessel in the brain, causing sudden weakness, speech or vision problems.

name: Isolated cerebral angiitis
formal: Primary angiitis of the central nervous system, an inflammatory vasculitis confined to cerebral vessels, with headache, strokes and cognitive change; diagnosed by angiography or biopsy.
simple: Inflammation limited to the blood vessels of the brain, causing headaches, strokes and confusion.

name: Isolated sleep paralysis
formal: Brief inability to move or speak on falling asleep or waking, with full awareness, from REM atonia intruding into wakefulness; not accompanied by narcolepsy.
simple: Being unable to move or speak for a short time when falling asleep or waking up, while fully aware.

name: Isolated thalamic degeneration (pure thalamic atrophy)
formal: Rare degenerative disease with neuronal loss limited to thalamic nuclei, causing cognitive decline, ataxia and sleep disturbance, sometimes with familial or prion-like mechanisms such as fatal insomnia.
simple: A rare brain condition in which only the thalamus shrinks, causing memory problems and balance and sleep trouble.
more: Diagnosis is by imaging or pathology. No treatment, and prion testing should be considered when sleep failure and dysautonomia are present.
nN: isolated thalamic degeneration pure thalamic atrophy
aN: pure thalamic atrophy | isolated thalamic degeneration

name: Isolated vertigo
formal: Vertigo as the only symptom without other neurological signs; causes include BPPV, vestibular neuritis, Meniere disease, and rarely posterior circulation stroke.
simple: A spinning sensation that is the only symptom, often from a problem in the inner ear.

name: Isolated ‘primary’ angiitis of CNS
formal: Primary angiitis of the CNS, a rare vasculitis restricted to brain and spinal cord vessels, causing headaches, stroke and cognitive change, confirmed by biopsy.
simple: Rare inflammation of blood vessels in the brain and spinal cord without disease elsewhere in the body.

name: Isometric tremor
formal: Tremor from voluntary muscle contraction against a rigid object, such as in primary orthostatic tremor or functional tremor, without movement.
simple: A shaking that occurs when muscles tighten against something without moving, such as gripping a bar.

name: Isovaleric acidaemia (IVA)
formal: Autosomal recessive organic aciduria from isovaleryl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency, with sweaty-feet odour, vomiting, lethargy and coma, triggered by illness or protein load.
simple: An inherited condition in which the body cannot break down part of protein, causing vomiting and drowsiness and a sweaty-feet smell.
aN: iva | isovaleric acidemia

name: Issacs’ syndrome
formal: Acquired peripheral nerve hyperexcitability syndrome with continuous muscle fibre activity, myokymia, cramps and delayed relaxation, often autoimmune (CASPR2 or LGI1 antibodies).
simple: A condition where nerves fire too much, causing constant twitching, stiffness and cramps.
more: Neuromyotonic discharges on EMG; test for CASPR2 antibodies and thymoma. Treat with carbamazepine or phenytoin, and immunotherapy for autoimmune cases.

name: Jacksonian motor partial seizures
formal: Focal motor seizures with march of clonic jerking from a distal body part up the limb, caused by a lesion in the contralateral primary motor cortex; may be followed by Todd paralysis.
simple: Seizures starting with jerking in one hand or foot that spreads up the limb as the seizure moves across the brain.

name: Jansky-Bieschowsky disease (late infantile neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis)
formal: Late infantile neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis CLN2 with seizures, ataxia and regression between ages 2 and 4, caused by TPP1 deficiency; treated with cerliponase alfa enzyme replacement.
simple: An inherited childhood disease causing seizures, loss of skills and vision, from a faulty enzyme in brain cells.
nN: jansky bieschowsky disease late infantile neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis
aN: late infantile neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis | jansky bieschowsky disease

name: Japanese B encephalitis
formal: Mosquito-borne flavivirus encephalitis in Asia, with fever, seizures, parkinsonism and flaccid paralysis; vaccine preventable and often leaves persistent deficits.
simple: A brain infection spread by mosquitoes in Asia that causes fever, seizures and confusion.

name: Japanese encephalitis
formal: Mosquito-borne flavivirus encephalitis in Asia, with fever, headache, seizures, parkinsonian features, and thalamic lesions on MRI; vaccine preventable and often leaves sequelae.
simple: A brain infection spread by mosquitoes in Asia that causes fever, seizures and confusion.

name: Jaw tremor
formal: Rhythmic tremor of the jaw, from Parkinson disease, essential tremor, drug-induced causes such as antipsychotics (rabbit syndrome), dystonic tremor or functional movement disorder.
simple: A shaking of the jaw, which can occur with Parkinson disease or as a drug side effect.

name: JC virus granule cell neuronopathy (JCV-GCN)
formal: JC virus infection of cerebellar granule neurons in immunosuppressed patients, with progressive ataxia and cerebellar atrophy, a variant of PML.
simple: A cerebellar infection by a common virus in people with weak immune systems, causing worsening balance problems.
nN: jc virus granule cell neuronopathy jcv gcn
aN: jcv gcn | jc virus granule cell neuronopathy

name: Jerking stiff man syndrome
formal: Stiff-person-like syndrome with painful spasms and prominent startle-induced jerks, often with brainstem involvement and glycine receptor antibodies, as in PERM.
simple: A rare condition with muscle stiffness, painful spasms and sudden jerks, often set off by noise or touch.

name: Joubert syndrome
formal: Autosomal recessive ciliopathy with hypoplasia of the cerebellar vermis and the molar tooth sign on MRI, with hypotonia, abnormal breathing and developmental delay.
simple: An inherited condition of the brain in which a part of the cerebellum is underdeveloped, causing poor muscle tone and delayed development.

name: Jugular foramen syndrome
formal: Combined lesion of cranial nerves IX, X and XI at the jugular foramen, causing dysphagia, hoarseness and shoulder weakness; typically from glomus tumours or skull base disease.
simple: Damage to three cranial nerves leaving the skull, causing trouble swallowing, hoarse voice and weak shoulder.

name: Juvenile Huntington’s disease
formal: Huntington disease starting in childhood or adolescence, with rigidity, dystonia, seizures and cognitive decline rather than chorea, associated with large CAG repeat expansions inherited paternally.
simple: Huntington disease that starts in childhood or the teens, causing stiffness, seizures and learning decline.

name: Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy
formal: Genetic generalised epilepsy starting in adolescence with morning myoclonic jerks, generalised tonic-clonic seizures and sometimes absences, with polyspike-wave on EEG; responds to valproate and levetiracetam.
simple: An epilepsy of teenagers with sudden arm jerks, mostly in the morning, often triggered by sleep loss.

Generalised tonic-clonic seizures, often after sleep deprivation or alcohol
Absence seizures in some
Photosensitivity; worsened by carbamazepine/phenytoin
inv: EEG: generalised 4–6 Hz polyspike-and-wave, photoparoxysmal response
MRI normal

case.story: First convulsion after an all-night party; admits she has jerked and spilled her coffee most mornings for a year.
case.exam: Normal.
case.tests: EEG: generalised polyspike-wave discharges with photic stimulation.
case.q: Which common antiseizure drug class may worsen her seizures?
case.a: Sodium-channel blockers such as carbamazepine/phenytoin; valproate (if not of childbearing concern), levetiracetam or lamotrigine are preferred.

files.chapter: 18 - Myoclonus: Phenomenology, etiology, physiology, and treatment

ddx.pt: Aura, lateralised features, focal EEG/MRI abnormality
Eyes closed, side-to-side movements, long duration, normal EEG during event

aN: jme | janz syndrome | impulsive petit mal

det.patho: JME is a common idiopathic generalised epilepsy with complex polygenic inheritance; first-degree relatives often have generalised epilepsies. Imaging and network studies suggest altered thalamo-frontal connectivity, though routine MRI is normal. Onset is usually between 12 and 18 years, and it accounts for roughly 5–10% of all epilepsies.
det.clinical: The hallmark is brief bilateral myoclonic jerks of the arms, mostly within an hour or two of waking, with preserved awareness; patients often regard them as clumsiness. Most patients also have generalised tonic-clonic seizures, often provoked by lack of sleep, alcohol or stress, and some have absence seizures. Photosensitivity is common. Because the jerks go unreported, the diagnosis is frequently missed until the first convulsion — direct questioning about morning jerks is essential.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical, supported by EEG showing generalised 4–6 Hz polyspike-and-wave discharges on a normal background, often triggered by photic stimulation or sleep deprivation. A sleep-deprived EEG improves yield. MRI is normal and is not required in a typical case. Focal-looking EEG asymmetries are common and should not redirect the diagnosis to focal epilepsy if the clinical picture fits.
det.treatment: Broad-spectrum antiseizure medication is used: valproate is the most effective but should be avoided in women and girls who could become pregnant because of teratogenic and neurodevelopmental risks; levetiracetam and lamotrigine (which can sometimes worsen myoclonus) are common alternatives, with topiramate or perampanel as further options. Carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, phenytoin, gabapentin and pregabalin may aggravate myoclonic and absence seizures. Counsel about regular sleep, alcohol limits and driving regulations.
det.prognosis: Seizures are usually well controlled with treatment, but the condition is typically lifelong, with high relapse rates after drug withdrawal.
pearls: Always ask a teenager with a first convulsion whether they drop things or jerk in the morning.
Sodium-channel blockers can make JME worse.
Plan contraception and pregnancy counselling before choosing a drug for a young woman.

name: Juvenile neuroaxonal dystrophy
formal: Childhood or adolescent onset neuroaxonal dystrophy with progressive dystonia, parkinsonism, cognitive decline and iron accumulation, as in PLA2G6-associated neurodegeneration.
simple: A rare inherited disease starting in childhood or teens that causes stiffness, movement problems and loss of skills.

name: Juvenile neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis (Spielmeyer-Vogt-Sjögren disease)
formal: Batten disease, CLN3, a lysosomal storage disorder starting at age 4 to 7 with visual loss, then seizures, dementia and parkinsonism, with vacuolated lymphocytes.
simple: An inherited childhood disease that first causes loss of vision, followed by seizures and loss of skills.
nN: juvenile neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis spielmeyer vogt sjogren disease
aN: spielmeyer vogt sjogren disease | juvenile neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis

name: Juvenile neuronopathic Gaucher’s disease
formal: Neuronopathic Gaucher disease with onset in childhood, causing supranuclear gaze palsy, myoclonic seizures and ataxia, plus organomegaly, from glucocerebrosidase deficiency.
simple: An inherited enzyme disorder in children that affects the brain, causing abnormal eye movements, seizures and balance problems.

name: Juvenile parkinsonism
formal: Early onset parkinsonism before age 21, often from PARK genes such as parkin or PINK1, with dystonia and good levodopa response, and also in Wilson disease or Huntington disease.
simple: Parkinson-like stiffness, slowness and tremor beginning in childhood or the teens.

name: Juvenile segmental SMA
formal: Focal lower motor neuron disease affecting one limb with asymmetric wasting, usually self-limited, as in monomelic amyotrophy (Hirayama or Sobue).
simple: A rare condition where muscles of one arm or leg waste away in young people and then the disease stops on its own.
more: EMG shows anterior horn cell loss in a segment; MRI may show cord flexion changes. A neck collar may help; typically plateaus within 1-5 years.

name: Juvenile-onset Huntington’s disease
formal: Huntington disease with onset before age 20, with rigidity, bradykinesia, seizures and cognitive decline rather than chorea, associated with CAG repeats over 60.
simple: Huntington disease that starts in childhood or teens, causing stiffness, seizures and learning decline.

name: Kallmann syndrome
formal: Genetic disorder with hypogonadotropic hypogonadism and anosmia from failed migration of GnRH neurons; may include mirror movements, renal agenesis and hearing loss.
simple: An inherited condition causing absent sense of smell and delayed puberty.

name: Kanner’s disease
formal: Early infantile autism as originally described by Kanner, a neurodevelopmental disorder with impaired social interaction, language delay and repetitive behaviours.
simple: The original name for classic autism, a developmental condition affecting communication, social interaction and behaviour.

name: Karak syndrome
formal: Rare autosomal recessive neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation from PLA2G6 or related variants, with childhood onset dystonia, spasticity, cognitive loss and cerebellar atrophy first reported in Pakistan.
simple: A rare inherited disease where iron collects in the brain, causing stiffness, dystonia and mental decline in children.
more: MRI shows iron in the globus pallidus and cerebellar atrophy. Care is supportive, and the disease is progressive.

name: Katayama syndrome
formal: Acute schistosomiasis with fever, urticaria and eosinophilia occurring several weeks after exposure, sometimes with encephalopathy or cord involvement from egg migration.
simple: A feverish illness caused by schistosome worms in people newly infected, which can rarely affect the brain or spinal cord.

name: Kearns–Sayre syndrome
formal: Mitochondrial disorder from large mtDNA deletion with onset before age 20: progressive external ophthalmoplegia, pigmentary retinopathy and cardiac conduction block, often with ataxia and raised CSF protein.
simple: A mitochondrial disease with drooping eyelids, restricted eye movement, retinal changes and heart rhythm problems.
more: Diagnose from the clinical triad, muscle biopsy with ragged red fibres, and a large single mtDNA deletion in muscle. Monitor ECG and pacemaker as needed, and screen for diabetes, hypoparathyroidism and short stature; prognosis is poor.

feat: Progressive ptosis and ophthalmoplegia beginning before age 20
Salt-and-pepper pigmentary retinopathy, usually with only mild visual loss
Cardiac conduction block that can progress suddenly to complete heart block
Cerebellar ataxia, raised CSF protein, short stature, hearing loss
Endocrine problems: diabetes, hypoparathyroidism, delayed puberty

Fundoscopy; CSF protein (often >1 g/L); serum lactate
Muscle mtDNA analysis for a large single deletion; biopsy shows ragged-red fibres
MRI brain: symmetric T2 change in subcortical white matter, basal ganglia and brainstem

case.story: Droopy eyelids since age 12, now clumsy when walking; fainted twice at school this month.
case.exam: Short stature, bilateral ptosis and near-complete ophthalmoplegia, pigmentary retinopathy, mild limb ataxia.
case.tests: ECG: bifascicular block; Holter shows intermittent complete heart block. CSF protein 1.4 g/L. Muscle shows a 5 kb mtDNA deletion.
case.q: What is the most urgent management step?
case.a: Prophylactic permanent pacemaker (or ICD as advised by cardiology) — sudden death from heart block is the main preventable risk.

det.patho: KSS is caused by a large single mtDNA deletion (classically about 5 kb) that is almost always sporadic, arising during early embryonic development. The deleted mtDNA is spread widely through tissues, which explains the multisystem nature. Pearson syndrome (marrow and pancreas failure in infancy) can evolve into KSS in survivors.
det.clinical: The defining triad is onset before 20, PEO and pigmentary retinopathy, with at least one of heart block, cerebellar ataxia or CSF protein above 1 g/L. Many also have deafness, short stature, diabetes, hypoparathyroidism, renal tubular disease and cognitive decline. Syncope in a young person with ptosis is a red flag for advancing conduction disease.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis rests on the clinical criteria plus detection of a large mtDNA deletion, best in muscle (blood may also show it in KSS more often than in CPEO). Serial ECG and Holter are mandatory. Low CSF folate is common and is worth measuring because it is treatable.
det.treatment: Early pacemaker or ICD prevents sudden death and should be considered even for lesser blocks. Replace calcium, vitamin D and hormones as needed; manage diabetes and hearing. Folinic acid is given when CSF folate is low. Coenzyme Q10 is often used but evidence is weak.
det.prognosis: Progressive, with death often in early to mid adulthood from cardiac or multisystem failure; pacing has improved survival.
pearls: Triad: under 20, PEO, pigmentary retinopathy; plus heart block, ataxia or CSF protein >1 g/L.
Sporadic deletion: recurrence risk for siblings is low.
Check CSF folate — cerebral folate deficiency responds to folinic acid.

name: Kennedy’s disease
formal: X-linked spinal and bulbar muscular atrophy from an androgen receptor CAG expansion, with proximal weakness, fasciculations, bulbar signs, gynaecomastia and sensory neuropathy in men.
simple: An inherited disease in men that causes slowly worsening muscle weakness, twitching and swallowing problems.
more: Diagnosed by AR gene CAG repeat testing (more than 38 repeats); CK is raised and EMG shows chronic denervation with reduced sensory action potentials. Management is supportive; the disease is slowly progressive and lifespan is near normal.

Perioral and chin fasciculations on pursing the lips; cramps; postural tremor
Gynaecomastia, reduced fertility, diabetes (androgen insensitivity)
Mild sensory neuropathy (reduced sensory potentials) — unusual for a motor neuron disease

CK often moderately raised; EMG neurogenic; sensory potentials reduced

case.story: Ten years of thigh cramps and slow decline climbing stairs; recently nasal speech; breast enlargement for years.
case.exam: Proximal weakness, twitching of the chin when whistling, tongue wasting, reduced reflexes, mild distal vibration loss, gynaecomastia.
case.tests: CK 1,100 U/L; sural SNAP absent; AR CAG repeat 47.
case.q: Which two findings argue strongly against ALS?
case.a: Sensory nerve involvement and signs of androgen insensitivity (gynaecomastia), together with an X-linked family pattern and very slow course.

No sensory or endocrine features; SMN1 deletion
Fatigable bulbar weakness without wasting or fasciculation

aN: sbma | spinal and bulbar muscular atrophy | x linked bulbospinal neuronopathy | kennedy disease

det.patho: Spinal and bulbar muscular atrophy is X-linked and caused by an expanded CAG repeat (generally 38 or more) in the androgen receptor gene. The mutant receptor, when bound by testosterone, enters the nucleus, misfolds and aggregates, damaging lower motor neurons, dorsal root ganglion cells and muscle. Partial loss of receptor function produces signs of androgen insensitivity. Female carriers are usually asymptomatic because of lower androgen levels.
det.clinical: Men develop symptoms in their 30s to 50s, often preceded by years of cramps, tremor or gynaecomastia. Proximal limb weakness, facial and tongue weakness with chin fasciculations on lip pursing, dysarthria and dysphagia progress slowly. Laryngospasm episodes may occur. Reduced sensation and absent sensory responses, gynaecomastia, testicular atrophy, reduced fertility, and metabolic abnormalities (diabetes, fatty liver, dyslipidaemia) complete the picture.
det.diagnosis: Genetic testing for the AR CAG repeat is diagnostic. Supportive findings are a raised CK (often moderately high), neurogenic EMG with fasciculations, and reduced or absent sensory nerve action potentials. It is frequently misdiagnosed as ALS; the absence of UMN signs, sensory involvement, endocrine signs and X-linked family history should prompt testing.
det.treatment: There is no proven disease-modifying therapy in most countries; androgen-reduction strategies have been studied with limited benefit. Management is supportive with speech and swallowing therapy, physiotherapy, respiratory monitoring, treatment of diabetes and dyslipidaemia, and genetic counselling. Testosterone supplementation should be avoided.
det.prognosis: it advances slowly and survival is close to normal, though late aspiration pneumonia can occur.
pearls: Gynaecomastia plus bulbar and limb LMN signs in a man = test the androgen receptor gene.
Absent sensory potentials in a 'motor neuron disease' argue against ALS.
Daughters of an affected man are obligate carriers; his sons are unaffected.
det.thd: Kennedy's disease เป็นโรคพันธุกรรมแบบ X-linked จากการขยายตัวของ CAG repeat ในยีน androgen receptor พบในผู้ชายวัยกลางคน มีอาการอ่อนแรงต้นแขนต้นขาและกล้ามเนื้อพูดกลืน คางและริมฝีปากเต้น ร่วมกับเต้านมโตและมีบุตรยาก ตรวจพบการรับความรู้สึกเสียและ SNAP ลดลง ซึ่งช่วยแยกจาก ALS การวินิจฉัยใช้การตรวจยีน ยังไม่มียารักษาเฉพาะ การดูแลเป็นแบบประคับประคอง และโรคดำเนินไปช้า

name: Kinetic tremor
formal: Tremor during voluntary movement, including intention and action components, from cerebellar disease, drug effects or essential tremor.
simple: A tremor that occurs while moving a body part, such as reaching or writing.

name: Kjer’s optic neuropathy
formal: Autosomal dominant optic atrophy from OPA1 mutation, with childhood onset of slowly progressive bilateral central visual loss and temporal disc pallor, with blue-yellow colour defect.
simple: An inherited eye nerve disease causing slow, symmetric vision loss that starts in childhood.

name: Kleine–Levin syndrome
formal: Rare disorder of recurrent episodes of hypersomnia lasting days to weeks with cognitive change, hyperphagia and hypersexuality in adolescent boys; thought to involve hypothalamic dysfunction.
simple: A rare condition in which teenagers have repeated bouts of extreme sleepiness, strange behaviour and overeating.

name: Klinefelter’s disease
formal: Sex chromosome disorder, 47,XXY, with hypogonadism, tall stature and learning difficulties; associated with tremor, epilepsy and an increased risk of cerebral venous disease.
simple: A genetic condition in males with an extra X chromosome, causing small testes, tall height and learning problems.

name: Klippel–Feil syndrome
formal: Congenital fusion of cervical vertebrae causing a short neck, low hairline and limited motion, with risk of cord compression, Chiari malformation and mirror movements.
simple: A condition from birth in which neck bones are fused, giving a short neck and limited motion.

name: Klüver–Bucy syndrome
formal: Bilateral anterior temporal lobe lesion syndrome with visual agnosia, hyperorality, hypersexuality, placidity and memory loss; seen after herpes encephalitis, trauma or frontotemporal dementia.
simple: Behaviour changes with a compulsion to put objects in the mouth and loss of fear, caused by damage to both temporal lobes.

name: Korsakoff syndrome
formal: Amnestic syndrome from thiamine deficiency with severe anterograde amnesia, retrograde loss and confabulation, with damage to the mammillary bodies and thalamus; follows Wernicke encephalopathy.
simple: Severe memory loss, often with made-up stories to fill gaps, caused by a lack of vitamin B1, usually in heavy drinkers.

name: Kosaka–Shibayama disease
formal: Diffuse Lewy body disease variant described by Kosaka, with widespread cortical Lewy bodies, dementia and parkinsonism; an earlier term for dementia with Lewy bodies.
simple: An older name for a type of dementia with widespread Lewy bodies, causing memory trouble and Parkinson-like symptoms.

name: Krabbe disease
formal: Autosomal recessive lysosomal disorder from galactocerebrosidase deficiency, causing demyelination, irritability, spasticity, seizures and blindness; globoid cells on pathology.
simple: An inherited disease in which the brain's nerve coating breaks down, causing irritability, stiffness and seizures.
more: Diagnosed by low galactocerebrosidase activity in leucocytes and GALC mutations; MRI shows symmetric periventricular white matter and optic nerve change, with slowed nerve conduction. Early stem cell transplant helps if given before symptoms.

name: Krabbe’s disease (globoid cell leucodystrophy)
formal: Galactosylceramide lipidosis with globoid cell leucodystrophy: infant irritability, stiffness, seizures and optic atrophy, from GALC enzyme deficiency; later-onset forms exist.
simple: An inherited disease in which the brain's nerve coating breaks down, causing irritability, stiffness and seizures.
aN: globoid cell leucodystrophy | krabbe disease

name: Kufor-Rakeb disease
formal: Autosomal recessive ATP13A2-related juvenile parkinsonism with pyramidal signs, supranuclear gaze palsy and dementia, a PARK9 disorder.
simple: An inherited form of Parkinson disease that starts in teens or twenties, with dementia and eye movement trouble.
more: Diagnosis by ATP13A2 mutation testing; MRI shows generalised or pallidal-pyramidal atrophy and iron accumulation in some. Usually levodopa-responsive at first with early motor complications; patients may show visual hallucinations.

name: Kufs’ disease (adult neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis)
formal: Adult-onset neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis (CLN4 or CLN6) with dementia, ataxia, seizures and movement disorders, without visual loss.
simple: A rare inherited adult disease causing seizures, memory loss and movement problems from waste build-up in brain cells.
nN: kufs disease adult neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis
aN: adult neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis | kufs disease

name: Kugelberg–Welander disease
formal: Juvenile-onset spinal muscular atrophy (SMA type III) from SMN1 deficiency, with proximal weakness, a waddling gait and loss of ambulation in some patients.
simple: An inherited condition causing slowly progressive weakness of hip and shoulder muscles in children and young adults.
more: Diagnose with SMN1 deletion, with copy number of SMN2 predicting severity; EMG shows chronic denervation and CK may be mildly raised. Treat with nusinersen, risdiplam or onasemnogene gene therapy, with scoliosis and respiratory care.

name: L-dopa responsive parkinsonism
formal: Parkinsonism with a clear improvement in bradykinesia and rigidity on levodopa, typical of Parkinson disease and some genetic and dopa-responsive forms.
simple: Parkinson-type slowness and stiffness that improve well when levodopa is taken.
more: A good levodopa response supports Parkinson disease; if lost early, consider atypical causes. Treat with levodopa titration and adjuncts.

name: L-dopa-induced myoclonus
formal: Myoclonus induced by levodopa in parkinsonism, often from drug peak dose or neuroplasticity, usually mild and reversible with dose reduction.
simple: Muscle jerks caused by levodopa medicine in people with Parkinson disease.

name: L-dopa-responsive dystonia
formal: Childhood-onset dystonia, often with diurnal fluctuation and sometimes parkinsonism, due to dopamine synthesis defects such as GCH1, TH or SPR variants, dramatically responsive to low-dose levodopa.
simple: An inherited form of dystonia in children that improves dramatically with small doses of levodopa.
more: Diagnosed by CSF pterins and genetic tests, or a levodopa trial. Long-term low-dose levodopa works lifelong without causing dyskinesia.

name: Labyrinthitis
formal: Inflammation of the membranous labyrinth, usually viral or bacterial, with vertigo, hearing loss, nausea and tinnitus; differs from vestibular neuritis by cochlear involvement.
simple: Inner ear inflammation causing spinning dizziness, nausea and hearing loss.

name: Lacunar infarct
formal: Small deep infarct from occlusion of a penetrating artery in the basal ganglia, thalamus, internal capsule or pons, usually due to hypertensive small vessel disease.
simple: A tiny stroke deep in the brain caused by blockage of a small artery, often from high blood pressure.

case.who: 63-year-old male rice farmer from Suphan Buri with long-standing untreated hypertension
case.story: Woke at 5 a.m. unable to lift his left arm and dragging his left leg; no headache, speech is understood normally. Weakness worsened again around midday then partially improved.
case.exam: BP 196/104. Left face, arm and leg equally weak (MRC 3/5), extensor left plantar. Sensation, visual fields, language and attention are normal.
case.tests: CT brain normal; MRI DWI 12 mm bright spot in the right internal capsule (posterior limb); carotids and ECG unremarkable; HbA1c 6.9%.
case.q: Which classic syndrome is this, and why did it fluctuate?
case.a: Pure motor hemiparesis from a lacunar infarct; occlusion of a lenticulostriate perforator often causes fluctuating (capsular warning) symptoms before the deficit settles.

Chapter 4 Which arterial territory is involved?

det.patho: Most lacunes arise from disease of single deep perforating arterioles 40–800 µm wide — lenticulostriate, thalamoperforating and paramedian pontine branches. Chronic hypertension drives lipohyalinosis and fibrinoid change in the smallest vessels, while larger perforators are blocked by microatheroma at their origin or by parent-artery plaque (branch atheromatous disease, which tends to give larger, elongated infarcts and more progression). Lacunar stroke accounts for about a quarter of ischaemic strokes and is especially common in Asian populations. Embolism is an uncommon cause but must be considered when no small vessel risk factors exist.
det.clinical: C. Miller Fisher described the core syndromes. Pure motor hemiparesis is the commonest; the weakness involves face, arm and leg proportionately because fibres are tightly packed in the capsule or pons. Pure sensory stroke from VPL/VPM thalamic infarcts gives hemibody numbness or paraesthesia, sometimes followed months later by central post-stroke pain. Sensorimotor stroke combines both from thalamocapsular lesions. Ataxic hemiparesis pairs pyramidal weakness, usually leg-predominant, with same-sided limb incoordination that clearly exceeds the weakness. Dysarthria–clumsy hand shows marked slurring, facial weakness and a fine-motor clumsy hand with little power loss. Other recognised lacunar presentations include hemichorea-hemiballism from subthalamic or striatal infarcts and isolated dysarthria. Early fluctuation and worsening in the first days is common and does not change the diagnosis.
det.diagnosis: Clinical syndromes are only about 70–80% predictive: a small cortical infarct or an embolic deep infarct can produce an identical picture, so imaging is essential. DWI-MRI confirms a single small deep lesion and shows co-existing markers of small vessel disease (white matter hyperintensities, old lacunes, microbleeds). Deep infarcts larger than 15–20 mm, especially striatocapsular comma-shaped ones, suggest MCA stem occlusion or embolism rather than a true lacune. Still perform vascular and cardiac work-up, because carotid stenosis or AF changes management even when the infarct looks lacunar.
det.treatment: Acute: eligible patients receive IV thrombolysis (alteplase or tenecteplase) within 4.5 h; lacunar syndromes benefit as much as other subtypes. Minor stroke (NIHSS ≤ 3–5) or fluctuating syndromes: short dual antiplatelet therapy (aspirin plus clopidogrel for about 21 days) then single antiplatelet; cilostazol is a reasonable long-term option in Asian patients. Secondary prevention centres on blood pressure (target generally < 130/80 mmHg), statin, diabetes control, stopping smoking and exercise. Avoid long-term dual antiplatelets, which raised bleeding without reducing recurrence in small vessel stroke.
det.prognosis: Early mortality is low and functional recovery is often good, but recurrence (~2–4%/year) and cumulative cognitive decline make it a marker of progressive small vessel disease.
pearls: Pure motor hemiparesis = face, arm, leg equal, with nothing cortical; it is the most frequent lacunar syndrome.
Ataxic hemiparesis: ataxia far worse than the weakness, on the same side.
A fluctuating hemiparesis over hours (capsular warning syndrome) predicts a capsular infarct — treat early and aggressively.
Lacunar syndrome does not equal lacunar mechanism: always image and screen for embolic and large artery sources.
det.thd: Lacunar infarct คือสมองส่วนลึกขาดเลือดขนาดเล็กจากหลอดเลือดแดงแขนงเล็ก (perforator) อุดตัน มักสัมพันธ์กับความดันโลหิตสูงและเบาหวาน อาการคลาสสิกได้แก่ pure motor hemiparesis, pure sensory stroke, sensorimotor stroke, ataxic hemiparesis และ dysarthria–clumsy hand โดยไม่มีอาการเปลือกสมอง เช่น aphasia หรือ neglect ยืนยันด้วย MRI DWI รักษาเหมือน ischaemic stroke ทั่วไป (thrombolysis ได้), ให้ DAPT ระยะสั้นในรายอาการน้อย และคุมความดันอย่างเข้มงวด

name: Lacunar syndrome
formal: Clinical syndromes from small deep infarcts: pure motor, pure sensory, sensorimotor, ataxic hemiparesis and dysarthria-clumsy hand, with no cortical signs.
simple: A set of stroke patterns from small deep blockages that affect weakness or sensation without affecting thinking or speech.

name: Lafora body disease (EPM2B)
formal: Autosomal recessive progressive myoclonic epilepsy with onset in adolescence and Lafora bodies, from mutations in EPM2A (laforin) or EPM2B (NHLRC1), with myoclonus, dementia and visual hallucinations.
simple: A severe inherited disease in teenagers causing seizures, muscle jerks and rapid loss of mental abilities.

name: Lafora disease
formal: Autosomal recessive progressive myoclonic epilepsy with adolescent onset, seizures, visual hallucinations, myoclonus and dementia, with polyglucosan Lafora bodies on biopsy.
simple: A severe inherited disease in teenagers causing seizures, muscle jerks and rapid loss of mental abilities.

name: Laing distal myopathy
formal: Autosomal dominant distal myopathy from MYH7 variants, beginning with weakness of toe and ankle dorsiflexors and later finger extensors, with slender legs.
simple: An inherited condition where weakness begins in the feet and lower legs and later reaches the hands.
more: Diagnosed by MYH7 genetic testing and MRI; progress is slow, treatment is supportive with orthoses.

name: Lambert–Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS)
formal: Presynaptic neuromuscular junction disorder with antibodies to voltage-gated calcium channels causing proximal weakness, areflexia and autonomic features; often paraneoplastic in small cell lung cancer.
simple: An immune disease causing muscle weakness and dry mouth, often linked to lung cancer.
more: Diagnosis uses electrodiagnosis with incremental response (greater than 100 percent) after exercise or high-rate stimulation, and P/Q-type VGCC antibodies. Search for small cell lung cancer; treat with 3,4-diaminopyridine, pyridostigmine and immunotherapy.

det.patho: Autoantibodies to the presynaptic P/Q calcium channel (VGCC) reduce calcium entry into motor and autonomic nerve terminals, so fewer acetylcholine quanta are released. Repeated activation lets calcium accumulate, temporarily boosting release — the basis of facilitation. About half of cases are paraneoplastic, nearly always small-cell lung cancer; the rest are autoimmune, often in younger patients with HLA-B8-DR3.
det.clinical: Proximal leg weakness with difficulty rising and climbing stairs is the presenting complaint in most; ocular and bulbar symptoms are milder than in MG. Autonomic features — dry mouth, constipation, erectile dysfunction, orthostatic symptoms — are characteristic. Reflexes are reduced or absent but may return briefly after sustained contraction. Paraneoplastic cases may also have cerebellar ataxia, and symptoms may precede detection of the tumour by months or years.
det.diagnosis: VGCC antibodies are positive in most cases. Electrodiagnosis shows low resting CMAP amplitudes, decrement at low-rate stimulation and an increment of more than 100% after 10 seconds of maximal exercise or 50 Hz stimulation (60% is often used as a sensitive cut-off). The DELTA-P score estimates the likelihood of underlying SCLC. Screen with CT chest and FDG-PET, repeating periodically for at least two years if negative.
det.treatment: Treating the tumour often improves LEMS. Amifampridine (3,4-diaminopyridine) is the first-line symptomatic drug, blocking potassium channels to prolong depolarisation; pyridostigmine adds little. Immunotherapy with prednisolone and azathioprine is used for persistent weakness, and IVIG or plasma exchange for severe disability. Avoid neuromuscular-blocking drugs and agents that impair transmission, and anticipate prolonged paralysis after anaesthesia.
det.prognosis: Prognosis is determined by the cancer in paraneoplastic cases; non-tumour LEMS is chronic but usually controllable.
pearls: Proximal leg weakness + dry mouth + low reflexes that improve after exercise = LEMS.
Look for small-cell lung cancer repeatedly, not just once.
Increment after brief exercise is the electrophysiological signature.

name: Lance–Adams syndrome
formal: Chronic post-hypoxic action myoclonus, often with intention myoclonus and ataxia, after cardiac arrest or asphyxia, usually with preserved intellect.
simple: Muscle jerks on movement and unsteadiness that persist after brain injury from lack of oxygen.

name: Large vessel vasculitis
formal: Vasculitis of large arteries such as giant cell arteritis and Takayasu arteritis, with headache, jaw claudication, visual loss and stroke from stenosis or occlusion.
simple: Inflammation of the body's largest arteries that can cause headache, vision loss and stroke.

name: Large-fibre neuropathies
formal: Peripheral neuropathies affecting large myelinated fibres, with loss of vibration and proprioception, sensory ataxia and areflexia, as in CIDP, B12 deficiency and ganglionopathies.
simple: Nerve damage affecting touch and position sense, leading to unsteadiness, especially in the dark.

name: Laryngo-pharyngeal dystonia
formal: Focal dystonia of the laryngeal and pharyngeal muscles, causing spasmodic dysphonia or dysphagia, often task-specific, or drug-induced.
simple: Involuntary muscle spasms in the voice box or throat, affecting speech or swallowing.

name: Late infantile neuroaxonal dystrophy
formal: Neuroaxonal dystrophy beginning at 2 to 3 years with psychomotor regression, ataxia, optic atrophy and seizures, with axonal spheroids on biopsy, often PLA2G6-related.
simple: A rare inherited childhood disease with loss of skills, unsteadiness and vision problems.

name: Late onset Huntington’s disease
formal: Huntington disease beginning after age 50 with milder chorea and slower decline, often with smaller CAG expansions and no family history.
simple: Huntington disease that starts late in life and tends to progress more slowly.

name: Late-onset cerebellar degenerations
formal: Sporadic or hereditary cerebellar atrophy starting after age 40, such as MSA-C, alcohol-related, autoimmune or SAOA, causing progressive ataxia.
simple: Gradual loss of balance and coordination in older age due to degeneration of the cerebellum.

name: Late-onset nemaline myopathy
formal: Adult-onset myopathy with nemaline rods, sometimes associated with monoclonal gammopathy or HIV, causing rapidly progressive proximal and axial weakness.
simple: A form of muscle disease starting in adulthood, with rod-like structures in muscle, causing weakness that can progress quickly.
more: Screen for monoclonal gammopathy; treat the underlying clone, for example with chemotherapy and stem cell transplantation.

det.patho: Nemaline rods are aggregates of Z-disc material, mainly α-actinin, within muscle fibres. In the sporadic late-onset form the cause is probably acquired and immune-related, as about half of patients carry a monoclonal protein and response to clone-directed therapy suggests a pathogenic role. HIV and other inflammatory states are also associated. When a paraprotein is present, SLONM fits the modern idea of a monoclonal gammopathy of clinical significance: the clone is small and not malignant, yet its product damages an organ, which is the rationale for treating the clone. This acquired disorder should be kept separate from congenital nemaline myopathy, in which variants in thin-filament genes (NEB most often, also ACTA1, TPM2, TPM3, TNNT1 and others) produce rods from infancy.
det.clinical: Patients over 40 develop subacute weakness of proximal limbs, neck and trunk; head drop and camptocormia are typical. Bulbar, facial and respiratory muscles can be involved, sometimes leading to ventilatory failure as the first presentation, so orthopnoea or morning headache deserve direct questions. Course without treatment is relentless, and patients with a paraprotein tend to progress faster. Unlike the congenital forms, there is no lifelong slender build, long face, high-arched palate or delayed motor milestones, and the family history is negative. Myalgia and skin or lung involvement are absent, which helps separate it from inflammatory myopathies.
det.diagnosis: SLONM should be considered in any adult with new progressive axial and proximal myopathy, especially with head drop or respiratory weakness. Serum and urine immunofixation and free light chains are mandatory, and an HIV test should be done. Biopsy shows rods in a variable proportion of fibres with little inflammation; EMG is myopathic, often irritable, and muscle MRI often highlights paraspinal and posterior thigh involvement. Myositis-specific antibodies are negative, and a 'polymyositis' that fails to respond to glucocorticoids should prompt re-review of the biopsy with trichrome staining or electron microscopy. Because MGUS is common in older adults, the biopsy rather than the paraprotein makes the diagnosis; HIV-associated rod myopathy may have a high CK and necrotic fibres. Exclude congenital nemaline myopathy, myositis, MG, Pompe disease and ALS.
det.treatment: Patients with a monoclonal protein have the best responses to high-dose chemotherapy with autologous stem-cell transplantation or modern anti-plasma-cell therapy (for example daratumumab-based regimens), and deeper suppression of the paraprotein tends to bring better muscle recovery, so haematology should be involved from the start. IVIG can stabilise or improve some patients and is often used as a bridge. Patients without a paraprotein may respond to immunotherapy but evidence is limited; corticosteroids alone rarely help. Respiratory monitoring (FVC, nocturnal oximetry or blood gases) and non-invasive ventilation are essential, together with swallowing assessment and physiotherapy.
det.prognosis: Untreated, many die from respiratory failure within a few years; with clone-directed treatment a substantial proportion improve or stabilise.
pearls: Dropped head plus a paraprotein in a middle-aged adult: think SLONM and biopsy.
A treatable myopathy hiding behind 'MGUS' — always check immunofixation in unexplained adult myopathy.
Rods can be missed on routine H&E; ask for trichrome staining or EM.
Seronegative 'polymyositis' with axial weakness that ignores steroids: re-examine the biopsy for rods and check immunofixation.

aN: slonm | sporadic late onset nemaline myopathy | adult onset nemaline myopathy | mgus associated nemaline myopathy

name: Lateral orbitofrontal syndrome
formal: Frontal lobe syndrome from lateral orbitofrontal damage with disinhibition, impulsivity, irritability and loss of social judgement, as in frontotemporal dementia or traumatic brain injury.
simple: Impulsive, rude and socially inappropriate behaviour caused by damage to the lower part of the frontal lobes.

name: LCAD deficiency
formal: Rare long-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase defect of fatty acid oxidation causing hypoglycaemia, cardiomyopathy, and myopathy with rhabdomyolysis.
simple: A very rare inherited defect in breaking down fats for energy, leading to low blood sugar and muscle breakdown.
more: Acylcarnitine analysis and enzyme or gene tests; avoid fasting, use a low-fat diet with medium-chain triglycerides.

name: Lead poisoning
formal: Toxic exposure producing encephalopathy in children and motor neuropathy (wrist drop) in adults, anaemia with basophilic stippling, and abdominal pain; treated with chelation.
simple: Harm to nerves and brain from lead exposure, causing weakness, abdominal pain, learning problems and anaemia.
th: พิษตะกั่ว — ผู้ใหญ่มีข้อมือตก ปวดท้อง ซีด; เด็กมีสมองบวมและพัฒนาการล่าช้า
tempoNote: Usually weeks to months of ongoing exposure
feat: Adults: motor-predominant neuropathy, classically bilateral wrist and finger drop (radial territory) with little sensory loss
Abdominal colic, constipation, fatigue, arthralgia; blue-grey gum line
Microcytic anaemia with basophilic stippling of red cells
Children: irritability, cognitive and behavioural problems, encephalopathy with raised ICP at high levels
Hypertension, gout and renal impairment with chronic exposure
inv: Venous blood lead level (key test)
CBC with blood film (basophilic stippling), zinc protoporphyrin
NCS/EMG: motor axonal neuropathy, radial-predominant
Renal function, uric acid; abdominal X-ray for ingested lead in children

case.who: 34-year-old man working at a car-battery recycling shop
case.story: Three months of cramping abdominal pain and constipation; for two weeks he cannot lift his wrists to ride his motorbike.
case.exam: Bilateral wrist and finger extensor weakness, brachioradialis spared on one side, normal sensation; grey line along gingival margin; pale.
case.tests: Hb 9.8 g/dL, microcytic with basophilic stippling; blood lead 92 µg/dL; NCS: low radial CMAPs, normal sensory responses.
case.q: What is the treatment?
case.a: Remove from exposure, report as occupational disease, and chelate (succimer orally, or CaNa2EDTA ± dimercaprol for very high levels or encephalopathy) with toxicology input.

det.patho: Lead substitutes for calcium and zinc, inhibits haem synthesis enzymes (ALA dehydratase, ferrochelatase) and damages mitochondria and endothelium. Peripheral nerves develop motor axonal (with some demyelinating) damage, while in children the immature blood–brain barrier allows cerebral oedema and lasting cognitive harm. Common sources are batteries, paint, smelting, traditional medicines, ceramic glazes and contaminated cosmetics.
det.clinical: Adults present with fatigue, abdominal colic, joint pains and a motor neuropathy favouring the most-used muscles, most famously radial wrist drop. Sensation is usually spared. Children show developmental delay, behavioural change and, at high levels, encephalopathy with seizures and coma. Anaemia, hypertension and renal impairment add to the picture.
det.diagnosis: Blood lead level confirms exposure; there is no safe threshold in children. Supporting findings are microcytic anaemia with basophilic stippling and raised zinc protoporphyrin. Electrodiagnosis shows motor axonal involvement. Search for the source and test co-workers or family.
det.treatment: Remove the source first. Chelation is guided by blood level and symptoms: oral succimer (DMSA) for moderate levels, and parenteral CaNa2EDTA (preceded by dimercaprol in encephalopathy) for severe toxicity. Correct iron deficiency, which increases lead absorption. Use splints and physiotherapy for wrist drop.
det.prognosis: Adult neuropathy generally improves after exposure ends; childhood cognitive effects are often permanent.
pearls: Bilateral wrist drop with colic and anaemia = lead until proved otherwise.
Ask about occupation, hobbies and traditional remedies.
Porphyria shares colic plus motor neuropathy — check both lead and urine PBG.
det.thd: พิษตะกั่วในผู้ใหญ่ทำให้เกิด motor neuropathy โดยเฉพาะข้อมือตกทั้งสองข้าง ร่วมกับปวดท้อง ท้องผูก โลหิตจางที่มี basophilic stippling และเส้นสีเทาที่เหงือก ในเด็กทำให้พัฒนาการและสติปัญญาเสียได้ถาวร วินิจฉัยด้วยระดับตะกั่วในเลือด รักษาโดยหยุดการสัมผัสและให้ยาขับโลหะ เช่น succimer หรือ EDTA

17. THE TOXIC NEUROPATHIES: INDUSTRIAL, OCCUPATIONAL, AND ENVIRONMENTAL AGENTS

ddx.pt: Conduction block, anti-GM1 antibodies, no anaemia or colic
Also colic plus motor neuropathy, but raised urine PBG; lead level normal
Painful sensory-predominant neuropathy with skin and nail changes

name: Lead toxicity
formal: Lead-induced toxicity causing encephalopathy, motor neuropathy with wrist drop, anaemia, abdominal colic and cognitive impairment, treated with chelation.
simple: Harm to nerves and brain from lead exposure, causing weakness, abdominal pain and learning problems.

name: Leber’s hereditary optic atrophy (LHON)
formal: Mitochondrial inherited optic atrophy from mtDNA mutations (11778, 3460, 14484), causing painless subacute central vision loss in young men, with telangiectatic microangiopathy.
simple: An inherited condition causing sudden painless loss of central vision, usually in young men.
aN: lhon | leber hereditary optic atrophy

name: Leber’s hereditary optic neuropathy (LHON)
formal: Maternally inherited mitochondrial optic neuropathy from mtDNA point mutations, causing subacute painless bilateral central vision loss mainly in young men, with disc hyperaemia.
simple: An inherited eye nerve disease that causes sudden, painless loss of central vision, mostly in young men.
more: Diagnosis by MT-ND4 (11778), MT-ND1 (3460) or MT-ND6 (14484) mutation testing; OCT shows retinal nerve fibre swelling and later atrophy. Idebenone is used and gene therapy is under development; spontaneous recovery occurs in some (14484).
aN: lhon | leber hereditary optic neuropathy

name: Leg tremor
formal: Rhythmic shaking of the leg, from orthostatic tremor, Parkinson disease, essential tremor, cerebellar lesions or functional disorders; orthostatic tremor appears on standing.
simple: Shaking of the leg or legs, often on standing, with various possible causes.

name: Leigh syndrome
formal: Subacute necrotising encephalomyelopathy of mitochondrial or nuclear gene origin, with infant regression, hypotonia, dystonia, brainstem signs and basal ganglia lesions with lactic acidosis.
simple: A severe inherited mitochondrial disease of children causing loss of skills, weak muscles, movement problems and breathing trouble.
more: Diagnose by MRI showing symmetric basal ganglia and brainstem lesions, raised lactate, and genetic testing (SURF1, MT-ATP6, PDHA1 and others). Care is supportive; biotin, thiamine or ketogenic diet help selected defects; prognosis is poor.

name: Leigh’s disease
formal: Subacute necrotising encephalomyelopathy from mitochondrial or nuclear gene defects, with infantile regression, dystonia, brainstem dysfunction and symmetrical basal ganglia lesions.
simple: A severe inherited mitochondrial disease of children causing loss of skills, weak muscles, movement problems and breathing trouble.

name: Length-dependent polyneuropathy
formal: Polyneuropathy with distal onset and progressive proximal spread, most often axonal from diabetes, alcohol or toxins, causing stocking glove sensory loss and ankle areflexia.
simple: Nerve damage that begins in the toes and feet and moves upward, causing numbness, tingling and weakness.
more: Look for diabetes, B12, thyroid, alcohol, paraprotein or inherited causes; treat the cause and manage pain with duloxetine or gabapentinoids.

name: Lennox–Gastaut syndrome
formal: Severe childhood epileptic encephalopathy with multiple seizure types including tonic seizures, slow spike-wave on EEG, intellectual disability and poor response to treatment.
simple: A severe childhood epilepsy with several seizure types, learning problems and difficult control.
more: EEG shows slow spike-wave with generalised paroxysmal fast activity during sleep; MRI and genetic panel investigate cause (tuberous sclerosis, prior West syndrome). Valproate, lamotrigine, rufinamide, clobazam and cannabidiol.
ab: childhood epileptic encephalopathy with slow spike-wave
th: เด็กมีชักหลายแบบ โดยเฉพาะชักเกร็งตอนหลับและล้มลงทันที ร่วมกับปัญญาอ่อน EEG เป็น slow spike-wave <2.5 Hz — ดื้อยามาก
tempoNote: Onset usually 18 months to 8 years; daily multiple seizure types persisting into adulthood
feat: Several seizure types at once: tonic (especially in sleep), atypical absences, atonic drops, myoclonic and tonic-clonic
Sudden falls causing facial and dental injuries; many children wear helmets
Intellectual disability and behaviour problems that worsen over time
Frequent non-convulsive status with fluctuating responsiveness
Often follows infantile spasms or has a structural or genetic cause
inv: Sleep EEG: slow spike-and-wave below 2.5 Hz while awake and bursts of generalised paroxysmal fast activity (about 10 Hz) during sleep
Video-EEG to document tonic seizures and separate them from behavioural events
MRI brain and genetic testing (panel or exome) to find a cause

case.story: Had spasms as an infant. Now drops suddenly several times a day, has split his lip twice, stares with slow fading responsiveness, and stiffens briefly many times at night.
case.exam: Moderate intellectual disability, healed facial scars, wears a soft helmet; no focal deficit.
case.tests: EEG: 2 Hz generalised slow spike-wave awake; runs of 10 Hz fast activity during sleep with axial stiffening.
case.q: Which drug should be avoided because it may worsen atypical absences and drops, and what surgical option helps drop attacks?
case.a: Carbamazepine (and other sodium-channel drugs can aggravate some seizures); corpus callosotomy is effective for drop attacks, VNS is an alternative.

det.patho: LGS is a developmental and epileptic encephalopathy in which diffuse cortical–subcortical network dysfunction produces generalised discharges regardless of the initial cause. Causes include hypoxic–ischaemic injury, malformations, tuberous sclerosis, prior infantile spasms and many single-gene or chromosomal disorders; in a minority none is found. It accounts for a small percentage of childhood epilepsy but a large share of refractory cases.
det.clinical: Diagnosis rests on a triad: multiple drug-resistant seizure types including tonic seizures, a characteristic EEG, and cognitive impairment, which may not be present at first. Tonic seizures in sleep can be missed unless specifically sought. Atonic and tonic drops cause injury, and episodes of non-convulsive status may look like lethargy or worsened behaviour. In adulthood tonic seizures remain while slow spike-wave may become less obvious.
det.diagnosis: Sleep and wake EEG, ideally with video, should show slow spike-wave and generalised paroxysmal fast activity; documenting tonic seizures is central. Early in the course features may be incomplete, so repeat EEG over time. Cause should be pursued with MRI and genetic testing since some causes have specific therapy.
det.treatment: Valproate is a usual first drug, with lamotrigine, clobazam, rufinamide, topiramate and felbamate as add-ons; fenfluramine and cannabidiol have trial evidence for drop seizures. Carbamazepine and other sodium-channel agents can worsen atypical absences or myoclonus, and benzodiazepines given IV may provoke tonic status. Non-drug options include ketogenic diet, vagus nerve stimulation, corpus callosotomy for drops and resective surgery for a clear focal lesion. Goals are to reduce injurious seizures and sedation rather than achieve complete freedom.
det.prognosis: Seizure freedom is uncommon, most patients have lifelong intellectual disability and need support, and premature mortality including SUDEP is increased.
pearls: Tonic seizures in sleep plus slow spike-wave = LGS; record sleep.
Helmets and callosotomy target the injurious drop attacks.
IV benzodiazepines can paradoxically trigger tonic status in LGS.
det.thd: LGS เป็น developmental and epileptic encephalopathy ในเด็กอายุราว 1.5–8 ปี มีชักหลายแบบโดยเฉพาะชักเกร็งตอนหลับ ล้มฟุบ และเหม่อแบบ atypical absence ร่วมกับปัญญาอ่อน EEG เป็น slow spike-wave <2.5 Hz และ fast activity ตอนหลับ สาเหตุหลากหลายและมักต่อมาจาก West syndrome รักษายากด้วย valproate, lamotrigine, clobazam, rufinamide, cannabidiol หรือ fenfluramine อาจใช้อาหารคีโต VNS หรือผ่าตัด corpus callosotomy

Infant onset of clustered spasms with hypsarrhythmia; may later evolve into LGS
