name: Leprosy
formal: Chronic mycobacterial infection (Mycobacterium leprae) causing a granulomatous mononeuropathy multiplex with thickened nerves, hypoaesthetic skin patches and neuropathic ulcers.
simple: A long-term bacterial infection that damages skin and nerves, causing numb patches and weakness.
more: Diagnose by skin smear for acid-fast bacilli, slit-skin test or nerve biopsy, with thickened greater auricular, ulnar and peroneal nerves. Treat with multidrug therapy (dapsone, rifampicin, clofazimine) and prednisolone for reactions.
th: โรคเรื้อนต่อระบบประสาท — ผื่นชา เส้นประสาทโตคลำได้ เส้นประสาทเสียหลายเส้น แผลไม่หาย
tempoNote: Indolent; acute worsening during lepra reactions
feat: Hypopigmented or erythematous skin patches with loss of temperature and pain sensation
Palpably thickened nerves: ulnar at elbow, greater auricular, common peroneal, superficial radial
Mononeuritis multiplex with claw hand, foot drop, lagophthalmos; painless ulcers
Pure neuritic form has no skin lesions
inv: Slit-skin smear and skin biopsy (acid-fast bacilli)
Nerve ultrasound or MRI: thickened nerves; nerve biopsy in pure neuritic cases
NCS: multifocal sensory > motor axonal loss

case.story: A pale numb patch on his forearm for a year; now his little and ring fingers curl and he burned his hand without noticing.
case.exam: Anaesthetic hypopigmented patch, thickened tender ulnar nerve at the elbow, ulnar claw hand, thickened great auricular nerve.
case.tests: Skin biopsy: granulomas with acid-fast bacilli.
case.q: Which treatment is added if the nerve becomes acutely painful and weak during therapy?
case.a: Corticosteroids for the lepra (reversal) reaction, alongside multidrug therapy (rifampicin, dapsone, clofazimine).

files.chapter: Chapter 12 Infection in the Nervous System

ddx.pt: Systemic inflammation, no anaesthetic skin patches or thickened nerves
Single compressive lesion without skin changes
Recurrent painless palsies with family history

aN: hansen disease | leprous neuropathy | pure neuritic leprosy | lepra reaction

det.patho: Mycobacterium leprae has a tropism for Schwann cells and multiplies best in cooler tissues, explaining involvement of superficial nerves and skin. The host immune response shapes the disease spectrum: strong cell-mediated immunity gives tuberculoid (paucibacillary) disease with few lesions and granulomatous nerve damage, while weak immunity gives lepromatous (multibacillary) disease with many bacilli and diffuse involvement. Immune reactions (type 1 reversal, type 2 erythema nodosum leprosum) cause acute nerve inflammation and much of the permanent disability. Transmission is via respiratory droplets after prolonged contact.
det.clinical: Hypopigmented or reddish skin patches with reduced temperature, pain and touch sensation are typical, often with loss of sweating and hair. Peripheral nerves become thickened and sometimes tender, especially the ulnar, median, common peroneal, posterior tibial, great auricular and superficial radial nerves. The neuropathy is a mononeuritis multiplex that can coalesce into a symmetric distal pattern, preferentially in cool body regions. Complications include claw hand, foot drop, facial weakness with lagophthalmos, painless ulcers, burns and bone resorption. Pure neuritic leprosy, common in India, lacks skin lesions.
det.diagnosis: WHO cardinal signs are loss of sensation in a skin patch, thickened peripheral nerve with sensory or motor loss, and acid-fast bacilli on slit-skin smear or biopsy. Skin biopsy shows granulomas around nerves; smears are often negative in paucibacillary disease. NCS show multifocal, sensory-predominant axonal changes, and ultrasound demonstrates focal nerve enlargement. Nerve biopsy or PCR is helpful in pure neuritic cases. Exclude other causes of thickened nerves such as CIDP, CMT and amyloidosis.
det.treatment: WHO multidrug therapy combines rifampicin, dapsone and clofazimine, now recommended for both paucibacillary (6 months) and multibacillary (12 months) disease. Type 1 reactions and acute neuritis need prompt oral corticosteroids for several months; ENL may require steroids, thalidomide (with strict precautions) or clofazimine. Disability prevention includes self-care education, protective footwear, eye care and reconstructive surgery. Contacts should be screened and may receive single-dose rifampicin prophylaxis.
det.prognosis: Infection is curable with MDT, but nerve damage present at diagnosis often persists. Early recognition and steroid treatment of reactions prevent much of the disability.
pearls: Palpate the great auricular and ulnar nerves in any unexplained mononeuritis multiplex in an endemic area.
Acute painful nerve during therapy = reaction, treat with steroids, continue MDT.
Pure neuritic leprosy has no skin lesions — nerve biopsy may be needed.
det.thd: โรคเรื้อนเกิดจากเชื้อ M. leprae ซึ่งชอบ Schwann cell และบริเวณที่อุณหภูมิต่ำ ทำให้มีผื่นสีจางที่ชา เส้นประสาทโตคลำได้ (ulnar, great auricular, peroneal) และเส้นประสาทเสียหลายเส้น เช่น มือกรงเล็บ เท้าตก หลับตาไม่สนิท วินิจฉัยจาก cardinal signs ของ WHO, slit-skin smear และ skin/nerve biopsy รักษาด้วย MDT (rifampicin, dapsone, clofazimine) และให้ steroid เมื่อมี lepra reaction เพื่อป้องกันความพิการถาวร

name: Lesch–Nyhan syndrome
formal: X-linked recessive HPRT deficiency, with hyperuricaemia, choreoathetosis and dystonia, intellectual disability and compulsive self-injury, usually boys.
simple: An inherited disorder in boys causing movement problems, learning difficulty and self-injury, due to an enzyme deficiency.
more: Diagnosis by low HPRT enzyme activity and HPRT1 gene analysis, with urinary uric acid raised. Allopurinol controls hyperuricaemia but not neurological features; manage self-injury with protective devices, dental extraction, and behavioural therapy.

name: Lethal catatonia (LC)
formal: Severe catatonia with high fever, autonomic instability, agitation or stupor and delirium, with high mortality unless treated early by benzodiazepines or ECT.
simple: A life-threatening form of catatonia with fever, rigid or agitated behaviour and unstable vital signs.
aN: lc | lethal catatonia

name: Leucodystrophies
formal: Group of inherited diseases of myelin, such as metachromatic leucodystrophy, Krabbe disease, adrenoleukodystrophy and Alexander disease, with progressive motor and cognitive regression.
simple: Inherited diseases that damage the protective coating of nerves in the brain, causing progressive loss of abilities.

name: Leucoencephalopathy
formal: Disease of cerebral white matter from toxic, ischaemic, inflammatory, infectious, metabolic or genetic causes, such as PML, PRES, chemotherapy toxicity and CADASIL.
simple: Damage to the brain's white matter, which can be caused by many things and affects thinking and movement.

name: Leucoencephalopathy with vanishing white matter
formal: Autosomal recessive leucodystrophy from EIF2B mutations, with cerebellar ataxia, spasticity and episodic worsening after fever or head trauma, with vanishing white matter on MRI.
simple: An inherited brain disease in which minor illness or injury can cause sudden worsening of balance and stiffness.

name: Leukodystrophy
formal: Heritable disorder primarily affecting brain white matter with progressive spasticity, ataxia, cognitive decline and symmetrical MRI myelin changes; examples include MLD, Krabbe, ALD and Alexander.
simple: A genetic disease in which the brain's white matter breaks down, causing progressive weakness, stiffness and loss of skills.
more: Diagnosed by MRI pattern, enzyme tests and gene panels. Transplantation or gene therapy may help in selected types; most care is supportive.

name: Leukodystrophy and tubulopathy
formal: Mitochondrial disease combining white matter degeneration with renal tubular dysfunction, as in some respiratory chain defects such as BCS1L and FARS2-related disorders.
simple: An inherited disease that damages the brain's white matter and also the kidney tubules.
more: Lactate, MRI and kidney function testing with genetic confirmation. Treatment is supportive and prognosis is variable.

name: Leukoencephalopathy (CARASAL)
formal: Cathepsin A-related arteriopathy with strokes and leukoencephalopathy, an autosomal recessive small vessel disease with stroke, migraine and white matter lesions.
simple: A rare inherited disease of small brain vessels causing strokes and white matter damage.
more: Caused by CTSA mutation, with MRI showing white matter lesions, microbleeds and strokes; diagnosis by genetic testing and skin biopsy shows nonspecific changes. Cathepsin A deficiency is distinct from galactosialidosis.
aN: carasal | leukencephalopathy

name: Levine-Critchley syndrome
formal: Eponym for neuroacanthocytosis (chorea-acanthocytosis), with progressive orofacial dyskinesia, tongue biting, chorea, seizures, neuropathy and acanthocytosis on blood film.
simple: An older name for a rare inherited disease with uncontrolled movements, biting the tongue, and spiky red blood cells.
more: VPS13A mutations underlie it and CK is raised. Treatment is symptomatic with antiseizure drugs and movement therapies; no cure.

name: Levodopa-induced chorea
formal: Chorea occurring at peak dose of levodopa in Parkinson disease from pulsatile stimulation of denervated striatal dopamine receptors.
simple: Dancing, flowing involuntary movements that appear when a Parkinson drug is at its strongest effect.
more: Treat by reducing the single dose, splitting doses, adding amantadine or advanced therapies such as deep brain stimulation.

name: Levodopa-induced dyskinesias
formal: Involuntary choreic or dystonic movements complicating long-term levodopa therapy in Parkinson disease, usually at peak dose, but also biphasic or off-period dystonia.
simple: Involuntary writhing or jerking movements that develop after years of Parkinson treatment with levodopa.
more: Managed by dose fractionation, amantadine, avoiding dopamine peaks, continuous infusions or deep brain stimulation.

name: Levodopa-induced myoclonus
formal: Myoclonus following levodopa therapy in Parkinson disease, usually at peak dose or at night, benign and responsive to dose reduction.
simple: Muscle jerks triggered by levodopa medicine in people with Parkinson disease.

name: Levodopa-responsive parkinsonism
formal: Parkinsonian syndrome in which levodopa gives sustained improvement of motor signs, supporting a nigrostriatal dopamine deficit as in Parkinson disease.
simple: Parkinson-like symptoms that improve clearly with levodopa treatment.
more: Response supports a diagnosis of Parkinson disease; evaluate also for genetic forms in young patients. Long-term use can cause motor fluctuations and dyskinesia.

name: Lewy body dementia
formal: Dementia with Lewy bodies, with fluctuating cognition, recurrent visual hallucinations, parkinsonism and REM sleep behaviour disorder, from alpha-synuclein pathology.
simple: A dementia with visual hallucinations, alertness changes and Parkinson-like movement problems.

name: Lewy body disease
formal: Spectrum of alpha-synuclein disorders including dementia with Lewy bodies, Parkinson disease and Parkinson disease dementia, with cortical and brainstem Lewy bodies.
simple: A group of brain diseases caused by protein clumps called Lewy bodies, including Parkinson disease.

name: LHON and dystonia
formal: Leber hereditary optic neuropathy plus dystonia, from mitochondrial DNA variants (for example m.14459G>A), with subacute visual loss and childhood dystonia with basal ganglia lesions.
simple: An inherited mitochondrial disease combining sudden vision loss with dystonia.
more: Genetic testing of mtDNA confirms; maternal inheritance. Idebenone may help vision; dystonia is treated symptomatically.

name: Limb girdle muscular dystrophies (LGMD)
formal: Group of inherited muscular dystrophies with progressive weakness of shoulder and pelvic girdle muscles, due to defects in sarcoglycans, calpain, dysferlin and other proteins.
simple: Inherited muscle diseases that cause gradual weakness of the hip and shoulder muscles.
more: Diagnosis uses CK, muscle MRI, immunohistochemistry or Western blot and gene panel; LGMD R2 (dysferlin) and R1 (calpain 3) are common types. Management is supportive with cardiac screening and respiratory surveillance; there is no cure.
th: กล้ามเนื้อเสื่อมกลุ่มต้นแขนต้นขาทางพันธุกรรม — หลายยีน ทั้งชายหญิง อ่อนแรงสะโพกไหล่ ค่อยเป็นค่อยไป
feat: Progressive symmetric hip and shoulder girdle weakness; face usually spared

Subtype clues: scapular winging with calf contractures (calpain-3), calf weakness and very high CK in young adults (dysferlin), Duchenne-like childhood picture (sarcoglycans), cardiomyopathy (FKRP, lamin)
Autosomal recessive or dominant
inv: CK (very high in dysferlin/sarcoglycan, moderate in calpain)
Muscle MRI pattern; biopsy immunostaining; multigene panel
Cardiac and respiratory surveillance

case.story: Could not stand on tiptoe since 20; now difficulty climbing stairs. Parents are cousins.
case.exam: Calf wasting with weak plantar flexion, mild hip weakness, normal face.
case.tests: CK 9,000 U/L; MRI: posterior calf fatty change; DYSF biallelic variants.
case.q: Why is this often misdiagnosed as polymyositis?
case.a: Dysferlinopathy can show inflammatory cells on biopsy and very high CK, but it does not respond to steroids.

ddx.pt: Subacute, steroid responsive
Male, X-linked, abnormal dystrophin
Early respiratory weakness and axial involvement; low GAA activity

aN: lgmd | limb girdle muscular dystrophies | limb girdle dystrophy | calpainopathy | dysferlinopathy | sarcoglycanopathy | lgmdr1 | lgmdr2

det.patho: LGMDs are genetic myopathies caused by mutations in proteins of the sarcolemma (sarcoglycans, dysferlin), sarcomere (titin), enzymes (calpain-3), and glycosylation of alpha-dystroglycan (FKRP and others). The 2018 classification names them LGMD R (recessive) or D (dominant) with a number and the protein, and requires description in at least two unrelated families with independent walking achieved. Recessive forms are far more common, especially in populations with consanguinity. Prevalence of individual subtypes varies by region.
det.clinical: Weakness of hip and shoulder girdle muscles develops in childhood to adulthood and progresses slowly, with facial muscles usually spared. Subtype clues include scapular winging and early Achilles contractures (calpainopathy), calf or anterior tibial onset with very high CK (dysferlinopathy), a Duchenne-like course (sarcoglycanopathies), and cardiomyopathy or respiratory failure (FKRP, sarcoglycans). Cognitive development is normal.
det.diagnosis: CK level, muscle MRI pattern and EMG help narrow the differential. Genetic testing with multigene panels or exome sequencing is now the first-line test; biopsy with immunostaining and western blotting is used when genetics is inconclusive. Exclude dystrophinopathy, Pompe disease (enzyme assay), myositis, FSHD and myotonic dystrophy. Baseline and periodic cardiac and respiratory assessment are required.
det.treatment: There is no approved disease-modifying therapy, though gene therapy trials are ongoing for some sarcoglycanopathies and other subtypes. Care is supportive: physiotherapy, contracture management, mobility aids, cardiac and respiratory monitoring with timely ventilation, and genetic counselling. Corticosteroids are not helpful in dysferlinopathy.
det.prognosis: Highly variable by subtype, from near-normal life expectancy with mild disability to early loss of ambulation and cardiorespiratory failure.
pearls: Dysferlinopathy with inflammation on biopsy is often mistaken for polymyositis.
Always exclude Pompe disease — it is treatable.
FKRP-related LGMD needs cardiac and respiratory screening even when limbs are mildly affected.
det.thd: LGMD เป็นกลุ่มโรคกล้ามเนื้อเสื่อมทางพันธุกรรมหลายยีน ทำให้กล้ามเนื้อรอบสะโพกและไหล่อ่อนแรงช้าๆ ทั้งในชายและหญิง ส่วนใหญ่ถ่ายทอดแบบยีนด้อย แต่ละชนิดมีลักษณะเฉพาะ เช่น calpainopathy มีสะบักยื่นและข้อเท้าติด ส่วน dysferlinopathy มีน่องอ่อนแรงและ CK สูงมาก การวินิจฉัยใช้ MRI กล้ามเนื้อและตรวจยีนแบบ panel ต้องตัดโรค Pompe ซึ่งรักษาได้ออกก่อน ปัจจุบันยังไม่มียาเฉพาะ จึงเน้นกายภาพบำบัด และเฝ้าระวังหัวใจกับการหายใจ

name: Limb kinetic ataxia (LKA)
formal: Loss of fine, skilled movement of a limb, especially the hand, without weakness, sensory loss or true cerebellar signs, from lesions of premotor or frontal circuits, seen in corticobasal syndrome.
simple: Clumsiness of fine hand movements despite normal strength, due to brain damage.
more: It is a feature of frontal or corticobasal disease. Occupational therapy is helpful; treat the underlying disorder.
aN: lka | limb kinetic ataxia

name: Limb-kinetic apraxia
formal: Apraxia with loss of fine, precise finger and hand movements in the limb contralateral to a premotor or parietal lesion, without weakness, sensory loss or ataxia.
simple: Clumsiness of fine hand and finger movements despite normal strength, from brain damage.

name: Limbic encephalitis
formal: Inflammation of limbic structures, autoimmune or paraneoplastic (LGI1, GABA-B, anti-Hu), with amnesia, seizures, psychiatric change and mesial temporal MRI hyperintensity.
simple: Brain inflammation in memory areas, causing confusion, memory loss and seizures.

name: Lip tremor
formal: Rhythmic perioral tremor, as in rabbit syndrome from antipsychotics or Parkinson disease, with 3 to 7 Hz oscillation of the lip.
simple: A shaking of the lips, often as a side effect of certain medicines or in Parkinson disease.

name: Lipid metabolism disorders
formal: Inherited or acquired defects of fat transport or oxidation, such as carnitine or CPT II deficiency and ETF defects, producing myopathy, rhabdomyolysis and hypoglycaemia.
simple: Problems with how the body uses fat for energy, which can cause weakness, muscle breakdown and low blood sugar.
more: Diagnose by acylcarnitines, enzyme and genetic testing; treat with avoiding fasting, carnitine, riboflavin or diet changes as appropriate.

name: Lipid storage disorders
formal: Inherited metabolic disorders with accumulation of lipids in lysosomes, including Gaucher, Niemann-Pick, Tay-Sachs and Fabry diseases, with neurological regression and organomegaly.
simple: Inherited conditions where fatty substances build up in the body's cells and damage the brain and organs.

name: Lipid storage myopathies
formal: Myopathies with excessive lipid droplets in muscle fibres, e.g. primary carnitine deficiency, neutral lipid storage disease or multiple acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency.
simple: Muscle diseases where fat builds up inside muscle fibres, causing weakness.
more: Muscle biopsy shows lipid vacuoles; carnitine and riboflavin treatment may help in some types.

name: Lithium catatonia
formal: Catatonia or toxicity associated with lithium treatment, with stupor, rigidity, tremor and confusion, particularly at high serum levels or with neuroleptics; requires lithium withdrawal.
simple: Stupor, stiffness or confusion occurring during lithium treatment, usually linked to toxic drug levels.

name: Liver disease/failure chorea
formal: Acquired hepatocerebral degeneration, chorea with ataxia, parkinsonism and dementia in chronic liver disease, with manganese deposition in pallidum on MRI.
simple: Involuntary movements and thinking problems caused by chronic liver failure.

name: Locked-in syndrome
formal: Quadriplegia with preserved consciousness and vertical eye movement, from bilateral ventral pontine lesions such as basilar artery occlusion, central pontine myelinolysis or ALS.
simple: A state in which a person is awake and aware but cannot move or speak, apart from the eyes.

name: Logopenic aphasia (LPA)
formal: Primary progressive aphasia variant with word-finding pauses and impaired sentence repetition, usually from Alzheimer pathology involving the left temporoparietal junction.
simple: A form of language decline with trouble finding words and repeating sentences, often due to Alzheimer disease.
aN: lpa | logopenic aphasia

name: Long-chain HAD deficiency
formal: Defect in mitochondrial trifunctional protein (HADHA/HADHB), causing hypoketotic hypoglycaemia, cardiomyopathy, rhabdomyolysis, and peripheral neuropathy with retinopathy.
simple: An inherited problem burning fat for energy, causing weak muscles, nerve damage, and low blood sugar.
more: Raised hydroxyacylcarnitines; treat with avoidance of fasting, a low-long-chain-fat diet, and medium-chain triglycerides; triheptanoin has been used.

name: Long-QT syndrome
formal: Inherited or acquired cardiac channelopathy with delayed repolarisation, leading to torsades de pointes, syncope and seizure-like events; commonly misdiagnosed as epilepsy.
simple: A heart rhythm condition that can cause fainting or seizure-like episodes and sudden cardiac arrest.

name: Lou Gehrig disease
formal: Alternative name for amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, a progressive degenerative disorder of upper and lower motor neurons causing weakness, wasting and bulbar failure.
simple: Another name for ALS, a disease where nerve cells controlling muscles die, causing worsening weakness.
more: Diagnosed clinically with EMG; riluzole and edaravone modestly prolong survival, tofersen for SOD1; median survival 3-5 years, usually from respiratory failure.

name: Louis-Bar syndrome
formal: Alternative name for ataxia-telangiectasia, an autosomal recessive ATM disorder with cerebellar ataxia, oculocutaneous telangiectasia, immunodeficiency and malignancy risk.
simple: An inherited disease with worsening balance, widened eye blood vessels, weak immunity and cancer risk.

name: Low pressure headaches
formal: Headaches from reduced CSF volume, such as spontaneous intracranial hypotension or post-lumbar puncture, worse on standing and eased by lying flat, with meningeal enhancement on MRI.
simple: Headaches that worsen on standing and ease on lying down, from low spinal fluid pressure.

name: Low-grade gliomas
formal: Slow-growing gliomas (WHO grade 1 or 2) such as pilocytic astrocytoma and diffuse astrocytoma, often presenting with seizures, with variable behaviour.
simple: Slow-growing brain tumours that often cause seizures and may progress over years.

name: Low-grade glioneuronal tumours
formal: Group of low-grade neuroepithelial tumours, such as DNET and ganglioglioma, typically in children and young adults with temporal lobe epilepsy and indolent course.
simple: Slow-growing brain tumours made of mixed cell types, often causing seizures in young people.

name: Lower extremity neuropathy
formal: Peripheral nerve disorder affecting the lower limb, such as sciatic, peroneal, tibial, femoral or lateral femoral cutaneous lesions, causing focal weakness, sensory loss and often pain.
simple: Damage to a nerve in the leg that causes weakness, numbness or pain, for example foot drop.
more: Localised by examination and electrodiagnostic studies, with imaging for compressive or mass causes. Treatment targets the cause, such as decompression, bracing or physiotherapy.

name: Lower half parkinsonism
formal: Vascular parkinsonism with gait freezing, short shuffling steps and postural instability but relatively preserved arm function, usually from subcortical small-vessel ischaemia.
simple: Parkinson-like walking trouble affecting mainly the legs, with small shuffling steps while arms work fairly normally.
more: MRI shows widespread white matter lesions or lacunes. Response to levodopa is poor; manage vascular risk factors and use physiotherapy.

name: Lower motor neuron lesions
formal: Damage to anterior horn cells or peripheral axons, with weakness, atrophy, fasciculations and hypotonia, areflexia; causes include ALS, polyneuropathy and radiculopathy.
simple: Damage to the nerves that connect the spinal cord to muscles, causing weak, thin muscles and twitching.

name: Lower-half/lower-body parkinsonism
formal: Gait disorder with parkinsonism mainly in the legs and relatively preserved arms, usually from vascular disease or normal pressure hydrocephalus, with poor levodopa response.
simple: Shuffling, short-stepped walking with stiff legs but a relatively normal upper body, often from small vessel disease.

name: Lowe’s syndrome
formal: X-linked oculocerebrorenal syndrome from OCRL mutation, with congenital cataracts, hypotonia, intellectual disability and renal tubular dysfunction.
simple: An inherited disorder in boys causing cataracts, weak muscles, learning problems and kidney trouble.

name: Lubag (X-linked dystonia-parkinsonism)
formal: X-linked dystonia-parkinsonism (DYT3), from Filipino Panay island ancestry, with adult-onset focal dystonia progressing to parkinsonism; associated with a TAF1 mutation.
simple: An inherited disease in men from the Philippines causing twisting muscle spasms that later become Parkinson-like.
aN: x linked dystonia parkinsonism | lubag

name: Lubag dystonia–parkinsonism (XDP
formal: X-linked dystonia-parkinsonism (Lubag) is a Filipino X-linked disorder from a SVA retrotransposon insertion in TAF1, with adult onset focal dystonia becoming generalised, followed by parkinsonism.
simple: An inherited condition in men of Filipino descent causing dystonia that later turns into parkinsonism.
more: Diagnosis by genetic testing of the TAF1 haplotype; no cure. Treat with anticholinergics, benzodiazepines, botulinum toxin and deep brain stimulation.

name: Lumbar arachnoiditis
formal: Inflammation or scarring of the lumbar arachnoid membrane, after surgery, infection or contrast, causing chronic pain, radiculopathy and cauda equina symptoms with clumped nerve roots on MRI.
simple: Scarring around the nerves of the lower spine that causes chronic back and leg pain and weakness.

name: Lumbar disc disease
formal: Degenerative lumbar disc herniation or degeneration with radiculopathy or cauda equina syndrome, causing back pain, sciatica, weakness and sphincter disturbance.
simple: Wear or bulging of discs in the lower back that can press on nerves and cause back and leg pain.

name: Lumbar spine degenerative disease
formal: Age-related degeneration of lumbar discs, facets and ligaments causing spinal stenosis, radiculopathy and neurogenic claudication, with back pain and leg symptoms on walking.
simple: Wear and tear in the lower spine that can narrow the canal and cause pain, numbness or weakness in the legs.

name: Lumbosacral monoradiculopathies
formal: Single lumbosacral nerve root lesions, usually from disc herniation, producing radicular leg pain with dermatomal sensory and myotomal motor loss, for example L5 foot drop or S1 absent ankle reflex.
simple: A pinched nerve in the lower back causing leg pain, numbness, and weakness.
more: MRI and EMG confirm. Most improve with conservative care; surgery for severe or progressive deficits or cauda equina.

name: Lumbosacral plexopathies
formal: Lesions of the lumbosacral plexus due to diabetes, tumour, haematoma, radiation, or trauma causing multi-root leg weakness, pain, and sensory loss.
simple: Damage to the nerve network in the pelvis that supplies the legs.
more: MRI of the pelvis and EMG localise it. Treat the cause; immunotherapy for inflammatory forms; recovery varies.

name: Lumbosacral plexopathy
formal: Disorder of the lumbosacral plexus from diabetes, tumour, haematoma, radiation, trauma or inflammation, with leg pain and multi-root weakness and sensory loss.
simple: Damage to the network of nerves in the lower back and pelvis, causing leg pain, weakness and numbness.
more: MRI or CT of pelvis and EMG localise the lesion; treatment is directed to the cause, such as immunotherapy for diabetic amyotrophy.

name: Lumbosacral polyradiculopathies
formal: Multiple nerve root involvement, for example from cauda equina syndrome, stenosis, carcinomatous or infectious meningitis, and diabetic or inflammatory causes.
simple: Several nerve roots in the lower back are damaged at once, affecting both legs.
more: MRI with contrast and CSF analysis are key; management depends on cause, with urgent decompression for cauda equina.

name: Lumbosacral polyradiculopathy
formal: Disease of multiple lumbosacral nerve roots causing leg weakness, sensory loss and areflexia; causes include stenosis, infection, inflammation, infiltration or compressive cauda equina disease.
simple: Several nerves at the base of the spine are damaged, causing weakness, numbness or pain in the legs.

name: Lumbosacral radiculoplexopathy
formal: Lesion involving lumbosacral roots and plexus with asymmetric leg pain, weakness and wasting; seen in diabetic amyotrophy, malignant infiltration, radiation, or retroperitoneal haematoma.
simple: Damage to the nerve roots and nerve network in the lower back and pelvis, causing painful leg weakness and wasting, often in diabetes or cancer.

name: Lung carcinoma
formal: Primary pulmonary malignancy with neurological relevance through brain and spinal metastases, paraneoplastic syndromes (Lambert-Eaton, limbic encephalitis), Pancoast brachial plexopathy and Horner syndrome.
simple: Cancer that starts in the lungs and can spread to the brain or cause nerve problems elsewhere in the body.

name: LVO syndromes
formal: Acute ischaemic stroke from large vessel occlusion (ICA, M1 MCA, basilar) with severe deficits such as hemiplegia, aphasia or neglect; candidates for urgent endovascular thrombectomy.
simple: Strokes caused by a blockage in a major brain artery, producing severe sudden weakness or speech problems and needing urgent clot removal.

name: Lyme disease
formal: Tick-borne infection by Borrelia burgdorferi causing erythema migrans, then lymphocytic meningitis, cranial neuritis (especially facial palsy) and radiculoneuritis; later arthritis and encephalopathy.
simple: An infection from tick bites that can cause a rash, facial weakness, meningitis and nerve pain if untreated.
more: Confirm with serum and CSF Lyme antibodies by two-tier ELISA and immunoblot, with CSF showing lymphocytosis and intrathecal antibody. Treat neuroborreliosis with IV ceftriaxone or oral doxycycline, with usually good recovery but facial palsy may persist.
th: โรคติดเชื้อ Borrelia จากเห็บ — อาจทำให้ใบหน้าเบี้ยว ปวดร้าวตามรากประสาท และเยื่อหุ้มสมองอักเสบ พบในผู้ที่เดินทางจากพื้นที่ระบาด
tempoNote: Early neurological disease weeks to months after the tick bite; late forms over months to years
feat: Expanding red rash (erythema migrans) at the bite site in many, though often missed
Facial nerve palsy, sometimes bilateral
Painful radiculitis with severe, often nocturnal, dermatomal pain (Bannwarth syndrome)
Lymphocytic meningitis with headache and mild neck stiffness
Others: carditis with AV block, arthritis; rare encephalomyelitis
inv: Serology: two-tier ELISA then immunoblot (or two EIAs)
CSF: lymphocytic pleocytosis, raised protein; CSF/serum Borrelia antibody index
ECG for heart block; MRI if myelitis or encephalitis suspected

case.who: 29-year-old Thai woman returning from hiking in central Europe
case.story: Three weeks after the trip, a ring-shaped rash on her thigh faded; now severe burning pain wraps around her left chest at night, and her right face droops.
case.exam: Right lower motor neuron facial palsy, band of hyperaesthesia over left T6–T7, mild meningism.
case.tests: CSF: 140 lymphocytes, protein 1.1 g/L, positive intrathecal Borrelia antibody index; serum immunoblot positive.
case.q: What is the treatment?
case.a: Oral doxycycline for 14–21 days (or IV ceftriaxone); oral therapy is as effective as IV for neuroborreliosis without parenchymal involvement.

det.patho: Borrelia burgdorferi sensu lato is transmitted by Ixodes ticks and spreads from the skin through blood to meninges, roots and cranial nerves. Neurological disease reflects both direct infection and the immune response. Species differ by region: European strains (B. garinii) favour painful meningoradiculitis, while North American strains more often cause meningitis and facial palsy.
det.clinical: Early disseminated neuroborreliosis brings lymphocytic meningitis, cranial neuropathies (especially facial) and painful radiculoneuritis, sometimes with limb weakness. Late manifestations include chronic encephalomyelitis and a distal sensory neuropathy linked to acrodermatitis. Lyme is not endemic in Thailand, so travel history to North America or Europe is essential.
det.diagnosis: In a compatible case, serology plus CSF showing lymphocytic pleocytosis and intrathecal antibody production confirms neuroborreliosis. Serology can be negative early and stays positive long after cure, so it must be read with the clinical picture. PCR of CSF has low sensitivity. Think of HIV, syphilis, sarcoidosis and VZV in the differential.
det.treatment: Doxycycline orally for 14–21 days or ceftriaxone IV for 14–21 days are effective; parenchymal CNS disease is often treated IV. Steroids for facial palsy remain debated. Persisting fatigue or pain afterwards ('post-treatment Lyme disease syndrome') does not respond to prolonged antibiotics.
det.prognosis: Most recover well after treatment; facial palsy usually resolves, and late complications are prevented by timely therapy.
pearls: Facial palsy plus CSF lymphocytes in a traveller: test for Lyme.
Bannwarth: severe night-time radicular pain + facial palsy + lymphocytic CSF.
Antibodies persist after cure — do not treat a positive test without disease.
det.thd: Lyme disease เกิดจากเชื้อ Borrelia ที่เห็บ Ixodes นำมา ไม่พบเป็นโรคประจำถิ่นในไทย จึงต้องถามประวัติเดินทางไปยุโรปหรืออเมริกาเหนือ อาการทางประสาท ได้แก่ หน้าเบี้ยว ปวดแสบตามรากประสาทมากตอนกลางคืน และเยื่อหุ้มสมองอักเสบชนิด lymphocytic วินิจฉัยด้วย serology และตรวจน้ำไขสันหลัง รักษาด้วย doxycycline หรือ ceftriaxone 2–3 สัปดาห์ ส่วนใหญ่หายดี

Bilateral facial palsy with hilar nodes, uveitis and raised ACE; no tick exposure
Ear vesicles and pain with facial palsy; VZV PCR positive

aN: lyme neuroborreliosis | neuroborreliosis | borrelia burgdorferi infection | bannwarth syndrome

name: Lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus
formal: Rodent-borne arenavirus causing aseptic meningitis or meningoencephalitis, and congenital infection with chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus and microcephaly; transmitted via mouse excreta.
simple: A virus carried by mice that can cause meningitis, and can harm the brain and eyes of an unborn baby.

name: Lymphocytic hypophysitis
formal: Autoimmune lymphocytic infiltration of the pituitary, often peripartum, causing headache, hypopituitarism and a mass-like enlargement mimicking adenoma; also associated with checkpoint inhibitors.
simple: Inflammation of the pituitary gland, often around pregnancy, causing headaches and low hormone levels.

name: Lymphoma
formal: Lymphoid malignancy affecting the CNS as primary CNS lymphoma (enhancing periventricular lesions, steroid-responsive) or secondary leptomeningeal or nerve involvement.
simple: A cancer of lymphocytes that can involve the brain, spinal cord or nerves, causing headaches, confusion or weakness.

name: Lysosomal disorders
formal: Inherited enzyme or transporter defects of lysosomes causing accumulation of undegraded substrate, producing neurodegeneration, organomegaly, dysmorphism and developmental regression.
simple: Genetic conditions in which the cell's waste-recycling units fail, so material builds up and damages the brain and other organs.
more: Diagnose by enzyme assays in leukocytes or fibroblasts, urinary oligosaccharides or glycosaminoglycans, and genetic testing. Enzyme replacement, haematopoietic stem cell transplantation, substrate reduction and chaperones are available for selected disorders.

name: Lysosomal storage disorders
formal: Inherited deficiencies of lysosomal hydrolases or related proteins, with substrate accumulation, including Gaucher, Niemann-Pick, Tay-Sachs and Fabry, producing neurodegeneration and systemic disease.
simple: Genetic diseases where cells cannot break down certain substances, which build up and cause developmental and nerve problems.

name: Machado–Joseph disease
formal: Spinocerebellar ataxia type 3 from CAG expansion in ATXN3, with ataxia, ophthalmoplegia, spasticity, dystonia, bulging eyes and parkinsonism; autosomal dominant, notably in Azorean and Portuguese families.
simple: An inherited disease causing progressive loss of balance and coordination, stiffness and eye movement problems.

name: Macrophagic myofasciitis
formal: Condition with myalgia and fatigue with deltoid biopsy showing macrophage infiltrates containing aluminium crystals at prior vaccine injection sites; causal significance remains debated.
simple: A muscle condition with pain and tiredness where biopsy shows immune cells containing aluminium at old vaccine sites.

name: Macular degeneration
formal: Degeneration of the central retina in older people, dry or neovascular, causing painless central visual loss with metamorphopsia and scotoma but preserved peripheral vision.
simple: An eye disease in older people that damages the central part of the retina, blurring or distorting the middle of vision.

name: MAD deficiency
formal: Multiple acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency (glutaric aciduria type II), disorder of electron transfer flavoprotein pathway causing lipid storage myopathy and metabolic decompensation.
simple: An inherited disorder that stops the body using fats and proteins for energy, causing weakness and episodes of illness.
more: Abnormal acylcarnitines and urine organic acids; riboflavin, carnitine, and CoQ10, plus a low-fat diet, help in late-onset disease.

name: Magnesium deficiency
formal: Hypomagnesaemia causing neuromuscular hyperexcitability: tremor, tetany, hyperreflexia, myoclonus, seizures and arrhythmias; often with hypocalcaemia and hypokalaemia, due to alcohol, diuretics or PPIs.
simple: Low magnesium in the blood, causing muscle cramps, twitching, tremor and sometimes seizures.

name: Magnesium disorders
formal: Altered serum magnesium: hypomagnesaemia causes tetany, tremor, cramps and seizures while hypermagnesaemia causes areflexia and weakness.
simple: Too little or too much magnesium in the blood, causing cramps, tremor or weakness.
more: Check renal function, drugs and calcium and potassium; replace magnesium or treat toxicity with calcium and dialysis.

name: Malformations of cortical development (MCDs)
formal: Group of developmental disorders of neuronal proliferation, migration or organisation, including lissencephaly, heterotopia, polymicrogyria and focal cortical dysplasia; cause of drug-resistant epilepsy and developmental delay.
simple: Conditions in which the brain surface forms abnormally before birth, often causing seizures and developmental delay.
aN: mcds | malformations of cortical development

name: Malignant brachial plexopathies
formal: Brachial plexus infiltration by tumour (breast, lung, lymphoma) producing painful, progressive lower-trunk predominant weakness and sensory loss, often with Horner syndrome.
simple: Cancer invading the nerve network in the shoulder, causing pain, weakness and numbness in the arm and hand.

name: Malignant brachial plexopathy
formal: Brachial plexus infiltration by tumour (breast, lung, lymphoma) producing painful, progressive lower-trunk predominant weakness and sensory loss, often with Horner syndrome.
simple: Cancer invading the nerve network in the shoulder, causing pain, weakness and numbness in the arm and hand.

name: Malignant hyperthermia
formal: Pharmacogenetic hypermetabolic crisis of skeletal muscle, mostly from RYR1 variants, triggered by volatile anaesthetics or succinylcholine, causing hyperthermia, rigidity and rhabdomyolysis.
simple: A dangerous reaction to certain anaesthetic drugs where muscles overheat and stiffen, caused by an inherited tendency.
more: Treat with immediate dantrolene, cooling and stopping triggers; test with caffeine-halothane contracture or genetics. Autosomal dominant; relatives need counselling.

name: Malignant MCA infarction
formal: Massive middle cerebral artery territory infarct with severe cerebral oedema, midline shift and herniation within days; young patients benefit from early decompressive hemicraniectomy.
simple: A very large stroke with dangerous brain swelling that can be life threatening and may need surgery to relieve pressure.

name: Malignant melanoma
formal: Melanocytic cancer with a high propensity for brain and leptomeningeal metastasis, often haemorrhagic; rare primary CNS and neurocutaneous melanosis variants exist.
simple: A serious skin cancer that often spreads to the brain, where it can bleed and cause headaches, seizures or weakness.

name: Manganese poisoning
formal: Chronic exposure to manganese (mining, welding, parenteral nutrition) causing basal ganglia deposition with T1 pallidal hyperintensity and a levodopa-poor parkinsonism with dystonia and psychiatric features.
simple: Poisoning from too much manganese, for example in welders, causing movement problems like Parkinson disease and mood changes.

name: Manganese toxicity
formal: Excess manganese exposure causing basal ganglia deposition with T1 pallidal hyperintensity and a levodopa-poor parkinsonism with dystonia and psychiatric features.
simple: Harm to the brain from too much manganese, leading to slow movement, stiffness, tremor and mood changes.

name: Manic-depressive disorder
formal: Older term for bipolar disorder, characterised by episodes of mania or hypomania and depression; relevant neurologically to secondary mania and mood-stabiliser effects.
simple: An older name for bipolar disorder, in which mood swings between very high and very low states.

name: Maple syrup urine disease (MSUD)
formal: Autosomal recessive branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase deficiency causing leucine, isoleucine and valine accumulation, with neonatal encephalopathy, maple syrup odour, ketoacidosis and later dystonia.
simple: An inherited disorder in which the body cannot process certain amino acids, causing sweet-smelling urine, poor feeding and brain damage if untreated.
aN: msud | maple syrup urine disease

name: Marantic endocarditis
formal: Non-bacterial thrombotic endocarditis with sterile fibrin vegetations on valves in cancer or hypercoagulable states, causing embolic multifocal infarcts.
simple: Sterile clots on the heart valves in people with cancer that can break off and cause strokes.

name: Marchiafava–Bignami syndrome
formal: Demyelination and necrosis of the corpus callosum, classically in chronic alcoholism, presenting with confusion, dementia, seizures, apraxia or disconnection signs; MRI shows callosal lesions.
simple: A rare brain disease, mostly in heavy drinkers, damaging the bundle of fibres joining the two hemispheres and causing confusion and dementia.
more: Diagnosis by MRI showing T2 or DWI hyperintensity with swelling of corpus callosum; treat with high-dose thiamine, B-complex vitamins and nutrition support, plus steroids sometimes. Prognosis varies from death to recovery.

name: Marin–Amat syndrome
formal: Inverse jaw-winking phenomenon, where mouth opening causes ipsilateral eyelid closure, usually after facial nerve palsy from aberrant regeneration.
simple: After facial weakness, the eye closes when the person opens their mouth because nerves have regrown in the wrong pattern.

name: Maternal phenylketonuria syndrome
formal: Fetal damage from uncontrolled maternal hyperphenylalaninaemia in pregnancy, causing microcephaly, intellectual disability, congenital heart disease and growth restriction.
simple: Harm to a baby when a mother with phenylketonuria does not keep her diet controlled in pregnancy, causing a small head and learning problems.

name: May White syndrome
formal: Rare syndrome of progressive myoclonic epilepsy with ataxia and sensorineural hearing loss, often with lipomas, associated with mitochondrial tRNA mutations.
simple: A rare inherited condition causing jerky muscle movements, seizures, poor balance, deafness and fatty lumps under the skin.

name: MCA infarction
formal: Ischaemic stroke in the middle cerebral artery territory causing contralateral face and arm predominant weakness, sensory loss, aphasia (dominant) or neglect (non-dominant) and gaze deviation.
simple: A stroke from a blocked main brain artery, causing weakness on one side of the body, with speech or attention problems.

name: MCAD deficiency
formal: Autosomal recessive medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency (ACADM), a fatty-acid oxidation disorder causing fasting-induced hypoketotic hypoglycaemia and encephalopathy.
simple: An inherited problem burning fats for energy, so going without food can cause low blood sugar and illness, mainly in children.
more: Newborn screening finds elevated octanoylcarnitine; treated by avoiding fasting and giving sugars in illness. With prevention outlook is excellent.

name: McArdle disease
formal: Glycogen storage disease type V from myophosphorylase deficiency causing exercise intolerance, cramps, contractures, second-wind phenomenon and myoglobinuria with flat lactate response.
simple: An inherited muscle disease where muscles cannot use stored sugar, causing cramps and fatigue with exercise.
more: Diagnose by non-ischaemic forearm exercise test with no lactate rise and ammonia rise, then PYGM gene testing; avoid vigorous exercise and consider sucrose before exertion. Autosomal recessive; rhabdomyolysis can cause renal failure.
th: โรคขาดเอนไซม์สลายไกลโคเจนในกล้ามเนื้อ — ปวดเกร็งเมื่อออกแรงหนัก พักแล้วออกต่อได้ดีขึ้น (second wind) ปัสสาวะสีเข้ม
feat: Exercise intolerance from childhood with pain and contracture in the first minutes of intense effort
Second-wind phenomenon after brief rest
Episodes of myoglobinuria and rhabdomyolysis; fixed weakness may develop later
inv: CK raised at rest
Forearm exercise test: ammonia rises but lactate does not
PYGM genetic testing (common R50X variant)

case.story: Always had cramps sprinting; after weightlifting today his arms locked and his urine turned dark brown. If he slows down when jogging, he can carry on.
case.exam: Tender, swollen biceps; otherwise normal.
case.tests: CK 45,000 U/L; urine myoglobin positive; forearm test flat lactate with normal ammonia rise; PYGM variant.
case.q: What practical advice reduces attacks?
case.a: Regular moderate aerobic exercise with a gentle warm-up, avoid intense isometric effort, and take sugar before planned exercise; hydrate and seek care for dark urine.

ddx.pt: Symptoms after prolonged exercise or fasting, normal CK between attacks, no second wind
Calf hypertrophy and DMD in-frame deletion
Progressive limb-girdle and respiratory weakness, not exercise-induced cramps

aN: mcardle | glycogen storage disease type v | gsd v | myophosphorylase deficiency | pygm

det.patho: Autosomal recessive loss of muscle glycogen phosphorylase (PYGM) blocks the breakdown of muscle glycogen, so fibres cannot use their own carbohydrate stores during the first minutes of intense or isometric effort. Energy failure leads to painful contracture and fibre necrosis. As blood-borne glucose and free fatty acids reach muscle after several minutes, exercise capacity improves — the second wind. It is the commonest muscle glycogenosis; p.R50X (R49X) is frequent in Europeans, while other variants dominate in Asian populations.
det.clinical: Symptoms usually date from childhood but diagnosis is often delayed into adulthood after labels of laziness or poor fitness. Patients describe early fatigue, tachycardia, cramps and muscle locking with sprinting, lifting or carrying, and pigmenturia after heavy exertion. Slowing down briefly and then resuming allows them to continue at a better level. About a quarter develop fixed proximal weakness with age. Severe rhabdomyolysis can cause acute kidney injury, and compartment syndrome is a rare complication.
det.diagnosis: Baseline CK is raised in nearly all patients even between episodes. A non-ischaemic forearm exercise test shows a flat lactate curve with an exaggerated ammonia rise. A 12-minute cycle test demonstrates the second wind as a fall in heart rate at constant workload. PYGM sequencing is the confirmatory test and has largely replaced biopsy, which shows subsarcolemmal glycogen and absent phosphorylase staining. Exclude other glycolytic defects (e.g. PFK deficiency, with haemolysis and no second wind).
det.treatment: There is no disease-modifying therapy. Regular supervised moderate aerobic training improves capacity and reduces attacks, while avoiding sudden maximal or static effort. A small sucrose drink a few minutes before planned exercise boosts tolerance, but chronic high sugar intake promotes weight gain and is not advised. Treat rhabdomyolysis with fluids and renal monitoring; warn patients about dark urine. Statins may aggravate symptoms, and anaesthetists should be informed although the malignant hyperthermia link is uncertain.
det.prognosis: Life expectancy is normal; quality of life depends largely on staying active and avoiding severe rhabdomyolysis. Some fixed weakness may appear in later life.
pearls: Second wind is virtually specific for McArdle among metabolic myopathies.
Raised resting CK plus exercise-triggered pigmenturia in a young adult: think McArdle.
Forearm test: flat lactate, brisk ammonia.

name: McArdle’s disease
formal: Glycogen storage disease type V from myophosphorylase deficiency causing exercise intolerance, cramps, contractures, second-wind phenomenon and myoglobinuria with flat lactate response.
simple: An inherited muscle disease where muscles cannot use stored sugar, causing cramps and fatigue with exercise.

name: McLeod syndrome
formal: X-linked neuroacanthocytosis from XK gene mutation with Kell antigen weakness, causing chorea, tics, myopathy, cardiomyopathy, raised CK and acanthocytes, in adulthood.
simple: A rare X-linked disorder causing involuntary movements, muscle and heart problems and unusual blood cells, starting in adulthood.
more: Diagnosis by absent Kx antigen with weak Kell antigens on blood typing, XK gene sequencing; blood transfusion carries risk of anti-Kx antibodies, so avoid unmatched transfusion. Treat symptomatically; cardiac surveillance for arrhythmia and cardiomyopathy.

name: Measles encephalitis
formal: Neurological complications of measles: acute postinfectious demyelinating encephalitis, immunosuppressed inclusion body encephalitis, and subacute sclerosing panencephalitis years later.
simple: Brain inflammation caused by measles infection, which can occur during illness, soon after, or many years later.

name: Median neuropathy
formal: Focal neuropathy of the median nerve, most commonly carpal tunnel syndrome, causing thenar weakness and sensory loss in the lateral three and a half fingers.
simple: Damage to the median nerve, such as carpal tunnel syndrome, causing hand numbness and weakness.
more: Nerve conduction confirms it; treat with splints, steroid injection or carpal tunnel release.

name: Mediterranean myoclonus
formal: Historical term for Unverricht-Lundborg disease, an autosomal recessive progressive myoclonic epilepsy from CSTB mutations with stimulus-sensitive myoclonus, seizures and mild decline.
simple: An older name for an inherited condition with jerking muscle movements and seizures, common around the Mediterranean.

name: Medium vessel vasculitis
formal: Inflammation of medium-sized arteries, such as polyarteritis nodosa and Kawasaki disease, causing mononeuritis multiplex, stroke, and visceral and skin ischaemia.
simple: Inflammation of medium-sized blood vessels that can damage nerves, skin and organs, causing pain, numbness or strokes.

name: Medulloblastoma
formal: Malignant embryonal posterior fossa tumour of childhood, arising in cerebellar vermis, with hydrocephalus, ataxia and vomiting; molecular groups include WNT, SHH, group 3 and 4, with CSF seeding.
simple: A fast-growing brain cancer in children arising in the back of the brain, causing poor balance, headaches and vomiting.

name: Meige’s syndrome (Breughel’s syndrome)
formal: Cranial dystonia combining blepharospasm with oromandibular dystonia, usually in older adults, with sensory tricks and response to botulinum toxin.
simple: A movement disorder causing involuntary eye squeezing together with jaw and mouth spasms.
more: Usually an idiopathic disorder, sometimes secondary to dopamine blockers; treat with botulinum toxin injections to orbicularis oculi, with oral trihexyphenidyl, clonazepam or tetrabenazine as alternatives. Rarely DBS is used for refractory cases.
aN: breughel syndrome | meige syndrome

name: MELAS syndrome
formal: Mitochondrial disease (commonly m.3243A>G) with encephalopathy, lactic acidosis and stroke-like episodes that do not follow vascular territories, plus seizures, migraine, deafness and diabetes.
simple: An inherited mitochondrial energy disorder causing stroke-like episodes, seizures, migraines and muscle weakness.

name: Melkersson–Rosenthal syndrome
formal: Rare granulomatous disorder with recurrent orofacial swelling, relapsing facial palsy and fissured tongue.
simple: A rare condition with repeated swelling of the lips and face, facial weakness and a furrowed tongue.

name: Membranous lipodystrophy
formal: Nasu-Hakola disease, a recessive disorder from TYROBP or TREM2 mutations with polycystic bone lesions, fractures, and presenile frontal dementia with white matter change.
simple: A rare inherited disease causing bone cysts and fractures in adulthood followed by early dementia.
more: Diagnosis with imaging and genetic testing; no specific treatment is available. Course is progressive and care is supportive.

name: Meniere’s disease
formal: Inner ear disorder with recurrent vertigo lasting minutes to hours, fluctuating low-frequency hearing loss, tinnitus and aural fullness attributed to endolymphatic hydrops.
simple: An inner ear problem causing attacks of spinning dizziness, ringing in the ear and hearing loss that comes and goes.

name: Meningiomas
formal: Common extra-axial, usually benign, dural-based tumours from arachnoid cap cells, with dural tail enhancement; present with seizures, focal deficits or cranial nerve compression; associated with NF2 and radiation.
simple: Usually slow-growing, non-cancerous tumours of the brain or spinal cord coverings that press on the brain and cause headaches, seizures or weakness.

name: Meningitis
formal: Inflammation of the leptomeninges due to bacteria, viruses, fungi or non-infectious causes, with fever, headache, neck stiffness and photophobia; diagnosed by CSF analysis.
simple: Infection or inflammation of the membranes around the brain and spinal cord, causing fever, bad headache and a stiff neck.

name: Meningococcal meningitis
formal: Acute bacterial meningitis due to Neisseria meningitidis with fever, neck stiffness, petechial or purpuric rash and meningococcaemia; risk of shock, deafness and epidemic spread.
simple: A dangerous bacterial infection of the brain coverings causing fever, stiff neck and a purple rash, needing urgent antibiotics.

name: Meningoencephalitis
formal: Infection or inflammation of both meninges and brain parenchyma, with headache, fever, altered consciousness, seizures, and focal deficits.
simple: Inflammation of both the brain and its covering layers, usually from infection.
more: CSF analysis, MRI, and PCR for pathogens; treat with antimicrobials such as aciclovir and supportive care; early treatment improves outcome.

name: Meningovascular syphilis
formal: Form of neurosyphilis from endarteritis of small and medium arteries months to years after infection, causing strokes in young adults with prodromal headache and cranial neuropathies.
simple: Syphilis infection affecting the brain coverings and blood vessels, which can cause strokes in younger people.

name: Menkes kinky-hair disease
formal: X-linked ATP7A defect of copper transport causing infantile seizures, hypotonia, developmental regression, kinky hair, connective tissue problems and early death.
simple: An inherited disease in infant boys with brittle, kinky hair, seizures and developmental loss due to poor copper handling.
more: Low serum copper and ceruloplasmin; early copper-histidinate injections can help in some. Prognosis is poor and most affected children die in early childhood.

name: Menkes’ disease
formal: X-linked copper transport defect (ATP7A) causing infantile seizures, hypotonia, kinky hair, neurodegeneration, connective tissue abnormalities and low serum copper and ceruloplasmin.
simple: An inherited problem of copper handling in baby boys causing seizures, brittle kinky hair and severe developmental problems.

name: Mercury neurotoxicity
formal: Toxicity from inorganic or organic mercury causing tremor, erethism, ataxia, paraesthesias, visual field constriction and, in infants, acrodynia or developmental harm (Minamata disease).
simple: Nerve damage from mercury poisoning, causing tremor, mood changes, numbness and poor coordination.

name: Metabolic encephalopathies
formal: Diffuse brain dysfunction from systemic metabolic derangement such as hepatic, uraemic, hypoglycaemic or electrolyte disturbance, causing fluctuating consciousness, asterixis and myoclonus.
simple: Brain dysfunction caused by body chemistry problems such as liver or kidney failure, leading to confusion and drowsiness.

name: Metabolic encephalopathy
formal: Diffuse brain dysfunction from systemic metabolic derangement such as hepatic, uraemic, hypoglycaemic or electrolyte disturbance, causing fluctuating consciousness, asterixis and myoclonus.
simple: Brain dysfunction caused by a body chemistry problem such as liver or kidney failure, leading to confusion and drowsiness.

name: Metabolic muscle diseases
formal: Inherited disorders of glycogen, lipid or purine metabolism affecting muscle energy supply, with exercise intolerance, cramps, recurrent myoglobinuria or fixed weakness.
simple: Inherited problems in how muscles make energy, causing tiring, cramps and sometimes muscle breakdown with exercise.
more: Investigate with forearm exercise test, CK, acylcarnitine profile, lactate, muscle biopsy and gene panels; avoid fasting and strenuous exercise. Treatment depends on the defect: carbohydrate loading, carnitine, or enzyme replacement where available.

name: Metabolic myoclonus
formal: Myoclonus resulting from systemic metabolic disturbance such as uraemia, hepatic failure, hypoxia or hyponatraemia, often multifocal with asterixis.
simple: Sudden muscle jerks caused by body chemistry problems such as kidney or liver failure.

name: Metabolic neuropathies
formal: Peripheral neuropathies caused by metabolic disease such as diabetes, uraemia, hypothyroidism or porphyria, usually length-dependent axonal sensorimotor.
simple: Nerve damage in the hands and feet caused by body chemistry problems such as diabetes or kidney failure.
more: Nerve conduction shows axonal sensorimotor neuropathy, and treatment relies on addressing the underlying disorder, including glycaemic control and dialysis. Check B12, thyroid and monoclonal protein; pain is managed symptomatically.

name: Metabolic syndrome
formal: Cluster of central obesity, hypertension, dyslipidaemia and impaired glucose tolerance that increases risk of stroke, diabetes and cardiovascular disease; also linked to neuropathy and cognitive decline.
simple: A group of conditions, including belly fat, high blood pressure and raised sugar and cholesterol, that raise the risk of heart disease and stroke.
more: Diagnosis from waist, blood pressure, lipids and glucose measurements. Treat with lifestyle change, weight loss and drugs for each component.

name: Metachromatic leucodystrophy
formal: Autosomal recessive arylsulfatase A deficiency causing sulfatide accumulation, with progressive demyelination, motor regression, ataxia, neuropathy and dementia; late-infantile, juvenile and adult forms.
simple: An inherited lysosomal disease that gradually destroys myelin in the brain and nerves, causing loss of movement and thinking skills.

name: Metachromatic leukodystrophy
formal: Autosomal recessive arylsulfatase A deficiency causing sulfatide accumulation, with progressive demyelination, motor regression, ataxia, neuropathy and dementia; late-infantile, juvenile and adult forms.
simple: An inherited lysosomal disease that gradually destroys myelin in the brain and nerves, causing loss of movement and thinking skills.
more: Diagnosed by low leucocyte arylsulfatase A activity and ARSA mutations, with raised urinary sulfatides; MRI shows confluent periventricular T2 hyperintensity with a tigroid pattern. Stem cell transplant in early disease; gene therapy for late-infantile.

name: Metastatic spinal cord tumours
formal: Epidural or intradural spread of cancer (lung, breast, prostate) causing back pain, myelopathy and cord compression; an oncological emergency needing steroids, radiotherapy or surgery.
simple: Cancer that has spread to the spine and presses on the spinal cord, causing back pain, leg weakness and numbness.

name: Methyl bromide-induced myoclonus
formal: Toxic action myoclonus and ataxia after inhalational exposure to the fumigant methyl bromide, with seizures and encephalopathy; resembles Lance-Adams syndrome.
simple: Jerking muscle movements and poor balance caused by breathing in a pesticide gas called methyl bromide.

name: Methylmalonic acidaemia (MMA)
formal: Inherited disorder of methylmalonyl-CoA mutase or cobalamin metabolism, causing recurrent ketoacidosis, hyperammonaemia, encephalopathy, basal ganglia infarction and developmental delay.
simple: An inherited condition where the body cannot break down some proteins, leading to acid build-up, vomiting, lethargy and brain damage.
aN: mma | methylmalonic acidemia

name: Methylphenidate akathisia
formal: Drug-induced motor restlessness and inability to stay still related to stimulant methylphenidate, a form of medication-induced movement disorder.
simple: Inner restlessness and an urge to keep moving caused by the medicine methylphenidate.

name: MGUS neuropathy
formal: Peripheral neuropathy associated with monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance, often IgM with anti-MAG antibodies causing distal demyelinating sensory ataxic neuropathy and tremor.
simple: Nerve damage associated with an abnormal protein in the blood that is not cancer, causing numbness and unsteadiness.
more: Serum immunofixation, anti-MAG antibodies, and nerve conduction studies; rituximab for IgM; IVIG or steroids in IgG or IgA forms.
ab: monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance neuropathy

case.story: Three years of slowly spreading numbness in both feet; walks normally and has no other symptoms.
case.exam: Stocking loss of pinprick to mid-shin, reduced ankle jerks, normal strength.
case.tests: IgG-kappa band 6 g/L, normal free light chain ratio, normal blood count, calcium and creatinine; marrow plasma cells 4%; NCS: length-dependent axonal neuropathy.
case.q: Does the paraprotein need treatment for the neuropathy?
case.a: Usually not — a slowly progressive axonal IgG MGUS neuropathy is monitored (M-protein every 6–12 months); treatment is reserved for CIDP-like or disabling forms.

det.patho: MGUS is a premalignant clonal plasma-cell or B-cell disorder present in about 3% of people over 50 and more in older age. When neuropathy and MGUS coexist the link may be causal (IgM with anti-MAG or anti-ganglioside activity) or coincidental. IgM MGUS can evolve, at a low yearly rate, into Waldenström macroglobulinaemia or lymphoma, and non-IgM MGUS to myeloma or AL amyloidosis, at roughly 1% per year overall.
det.clinical: IgM MGUS usually produces a distal demyelinating, sensory-predominant neuropathy with ataxia. IgG or IgA MGUS is associated with either a CIDP-like syndrome with proximal weakness or a slowly progressive axonal neuropathy indistinguishable from idiopathic neuropathy of the elderly. New pain, autonomic symptoms or systemic features should prompt a search for amyloid or malignancy.
det.diagnosis: MGUS requires an M-protein below 30 g/L, fewer than 10% clonal marrow plasma cells and no end-organ damage (no hypercalcaemia, renal failure, anaemia or bone lesions) or lymphoma features. Characterise the neuropathy carefully with NCS, test anti-MAG when IgM, and exclude other causes such as diabetes, B12 deficiency and alcohol. Haematological follow-up with periodic M-protein levels and blood counts is advised.
det.treatment: CIDP-like IgG/IgA MGUS neuropathy is treated like CIDP with IVIG, steroids or plasma exchange. IgM anti-MAG disease is managed as anti-MAG neuropathy. Mild axonal neuropathy needs symptomatic treatment (neuropathic pain agents, foot care) rather than immunotherapy.
det.prognosis: Most patients have slowly progressive disability; the main long-term risk is haematological transformation, which needs lifelong surveillance.
pearls: MGUS is common in older adults — finding it does not prove it caused the neuropathy.
Check the M-protein isotype: IgM points to anti-MAG; IgG/IgA with demyelination points to a CIDP-like disorder.

name: Microangiopathy
formal: Small-vessel endothelial injury with thrombosis, hemolysis and ischaemia, as in thrombotic microangiopathy, CNS cerebral small vessel disease or diabetic microangiopathy.
simple: Damage to the smallest blood vessels, leading to clots and poor blood supply to organs.
more: Management depends on type, such as plasma exchange for TTP and complement inhibitors for atypical HUS; control of diabetes and hypertension for chronic forms.

name: Micronutrient deficiency
formal: Deficiency of vitamins or trace elements such as B12, thiamine, copper, vitamin E or folate, causing neuropathy, myelopathy, ataxia or encephalopathy.
simple: Lack of small amounts of vitamins or minerals the body needs, which can damage nerves and the brain.

name: Microscopic polyangiitis
formal: ANCA-associated small-vessel vasculitis (usually MPO-ANCA) with necrotising glomerulonephritis, pulmonary haemorrhage and mononeuritis multiplex or, less often, CNS involvement.
simple: An inflammatory disease of small blood vessels that can damage kidneys, lungs and nerves.
more: Diagnose with MPO-ANCA, urine sediment, and biopsy of kidney or nerve; treat with high-dose steroids plus cyclophosphamide or rituximab, and plasma exchange in severe cases. Relapse is common; maintenance with azathioprine or rituximab.

name: Midbrain tremor
formal: Holmes tremor: slow, large-amplitude rest, postural and intention tremor from lesions of the cerebellothalamic and nigrostriatal pathways, often after stroke or trauma.
simple: A slow, large shaking of the arm present at rest and on movement, usually after damage to the midbrain.

name: Migraine
formal: Primary headache disorder of recurrent unilateral pulsating attacks with nausea, photophobia and phonophobia, with or without aura, from trigeminovascular activation and cortical spreading depression.
simple: A common condition causing repeated severe throbbing headaches, often with nausea and sensitivity to light and sound.

case.exam: Normal, including fundi.

det.patho: Migraine is a genetically influenced brain disorder of sensory processing. Activation of the trigeminovascular system releases CGRP and other neuropeptides, sensitising meningeal nociceptors and central pain pathways; aura corresponds to cortical spreading depolarisation. The hypothalamus and brainstem probably drive the premonitory phase. It affects roughly 15% of people, with a threefold female predominance during reproductive years.
det.clinical: Attacks can include a premonitory phase (yawning, food cravings, neck stiffness), aura in about a third, the headache phase and a postdrome of fatigue. Aura is typically visual (scintillating zigzags or scotoma), sometimes sensory or speech-related, developing gradually and lasting 5–60 minutes. Chronic migraine means headache on half or more of the days in a month (15+) with migraine features on at least eight; medication overuse often drives this. Red flags (SNOOP4) include systemic symptoms, neurological deficit, sudden onset, onset after 50, positional or Valsalva-triggered pain, and a change in pattern. Vestibular migraine, hemiplegic migraine and migraine with brainstem aura are recognised variants.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis follows ICHD-3 clinical criteria: at least five attacks of 4–72 hours with two of unilateral, pulsating, moderate-severe or activity-worsened pain, plus nausea or photophobia and phonophobia. A headache diary clarifies frequency and medication use. Neuroimaging is not needed with a typical history and normal examination; image when red flags are present or the aura is atypical (motor weakness, prolonged, or always on the same side). First-ever aura after 50 should be evaluated as possible TIA.
det.treatment: For acute attacks, give an NSAID or paracetamol early, with an antiemetic, and use a triptan for moderate-severe attacks; gepants and lasmiditan are alternatives when triptans are contraindicated. Limit acute treatment to fewer than 10–15 days a month to avoid medication-overuse headache. Prevention is offered for frequent or disabling attacks: propranolol, amitriptyline, topiramate, candesartan, flunarizine or valproate (not in people who could become pregnant), and for refractory cases CGRP monoclonal antibodies, gepants or onabotulinumtoxinA for chronic migraine. Regular sleep, meals, exercise and treatment of comorbid anxiety, depression or sleep disorders support any drug plan.
det.prognosis: Migraine often eases after menopause and with age, but it remains a leading cause of disability in young adults; migraine with aura carries a small increase in ischaemic stroke risk, enhanced by smoking and oestrogen-containing contraception.
pearls: Aura spreads over minutes (march); TIA symptoms appear all at once.
Ask about painkiller days per month in every patient with frequent headache.
Combined oestrogen contraception should be avoided in migraine with aura.

simple: A mild head injury, often called concussion, causing headache, dizziness and trouble concentrating.

name: Miller Fisher syndrome
formal: Variant of Guillain-Barré syndrome with ophthalmoplegia, ataxia and areflexia, associated with anti-GQ1b antibodies after infection.
simple: A variant of Guillain-Barré syndrome causing weak eye movements, poor balance and absent reflexes.
more: Anti-GQ1b IgG is positive in most cases; CSF shows albuminocytologic dissociation. Prognosis is excellent with spontaneous recovery over weeks to months, and IVIG is used in severe cases; Bickerstaff encephalitis is the central overlap variant.
