det.patho: After an infection (often respiratory, sometimes Campylobacter or Haemophilus influenzae), cross-reactive IgG is produced against GQ1b and GT1a. GQ1b is concentrated in the paranodal regions of the nerves to the extraocular muscles and in muscle spindle afferents and dorsal root ganglion neurons, explaining ophthalmoplegia, ataxia and areflexia. Antibody binding at nerve terminals may also contribute. It accounts for a larger share of GBS spectrum disorders in East Asia.
det.clinical: Diplopia is usually the first symptom, followed within days by unsteady gait. Ptosis, facial or bulbar weakness and pupillary abnormalities may accompany it. Overlap with limb-weakness GBS or with Bickerstaff brainstem encephalitis (drowsiness, hyperreflexia) occurs and these form one anti-GQ1b spectrum. Incomplete forms include acute ophthalmoparesis without ataxia or acute ataxic neuropathy. Respiratory failure is uncommon unless it overlaps with GBS.
det.diagnosis: The diagnosis is clinical, supported by anti-GQ1b IgG in most cases. CSF protein may be normal in the first week. Nerve conduction may show reduced sensory amplitudes or be normal. MRI brain is important to exclude brainstem stroke, Wernicke encephalopathy or tumour. Also consider botulism, myasthenia and diphtheria.
det.treatment: Pure MFS usually recovers well without immunotherapy; IVIG has not been proven to change outcome, though many clinicians treat severe or overlapping cases. Monitor for evolving limb or respiratory weakness, which would prompt standard GBS treatment. Supportive care includes prism or patch for diplopia, fall prevention and physiotherapy.
det.prognosis: Most patients recover fully over 3–6 months; recurrence is uncommon.
pearls: Ophthalmoplegia + ataxia + areflexia after infection: send anti-GQ1b and get an MRI brain.
Drowsiness or extensor plantars suggests Bickerstaff encephalitis on the same spectrum.
det.thd: Miller Fisher syndrome เป็น GBS ชนิดหนึ่ง เกิดหลังการติดเชื้อ ร่างกายสร้างแอนติบอดีต่อ GQ1b ซึ่งพบมากที่เส้นประสาทกลอกตา จึงมีอาการเห็นภาพซ้อน กลอกตาไม่ได้ เดินเซ และรีเฟล็กซ์หาย การวินิจฉัยอาศัยอาการและตรวจ anti-GQ1b ควรทำ MRI สมองเพื่อแยกโรคก้านสมอง ส่วนใหญ่หายเองได้ดีภายในไม่กี่เดือน แต่ต้องเฝ้าระวังกรณีที่มีแขนขาอ่อนแรงหรือหายใจลำบากร่วมด้วย

name: Minamata disease
formal: Methylmercury poisoning from contaminated fish, causing cerebellar ataxia, constriction of visual fields, sensory disturbance, dysarthria and hearing loss, with fetal exposure producing congenital disease.
simple: A mercury poisoning from eating contaminated fish that causes clumsiness, numbness, tunnel vision and hearing loss.
more: Diagnosed from exposure history and blood or hair mercury levels. Chelation is of limited use; prevention by avoiding exposure is key and damage is mostly permanent.

name: Minipolymyoclonus
formal: Small, irregular, multifocal finger and hand twitching seen in anterior horn cell disease and some neuropathies, as visible tremulous movements without joint displacement.
simple: Tiny irregular twitches of the fingers or hands, seen in some nerve and spinal cord diseases.

name: Mitochodrial encephalomyopathy
formal: Mitochondrial disorder affecting brain and muscle with seizures, stroke-like episodes, myopathy, exercise intolerance and lactic acidosis; syndromes include MELAS, MERRF and Kearns-Sayre.
simple: A group of inherited energy-production diseases affecting the brain and muscles, causing weakness, seizures and developmental problems.

name: Mitochondrial ataxia syndromes
formal: Ataxia syndromes arising from mitochondrial DNA or nuclear POLG-related defects, often with neuropathy, epilepsy, ophthalmoplegia and, sometimes, NARP or SANDO phenotypes.
simple: Inherited energy-production problems that cause poor balance and clumsiness along with other nerve problems.

name: Mitochondrial cytopathy
formal: General term for disease from impaired oxidative phosphorylation, affecting high-energy tissues such as brain, muscle, heart and eye, with variable multisystem presentations.
simple: An illness where the cell's energy factories do not work properly, affecting organs such as brain and muscle.

name: Mitochondrial disease
formal: Heterogeneous disorders of mitochondrial or nuclear DNA affecting oxidative phosphorylation, with multisystem presentations including myopathy, encephalopathy, neuropathy, ophthalmoplegia and diabetes.
simple: Inherited conditions in which the cell's energy-making parts fail, causing problems in muscles, brain and other organs.
more: Investigate lactate and pyruvate, muscle biopsy (ragged-red fibres), MRI, and mtDNA or nuclear gene panel; heteroplasmy affects phenotype and maternal inheritance for mtDNA. Management is supportive: avoid valproate and aminoglycosides, give CoQ10.

name: Mitochondrial disorders
formal: Heterogeneous disorders of mitochondrial or nuclear DNA affecting oxidative phosphorylation, with multisystem presentations including myopathy, encephalopathy, neuropathy, ophthalmoplegia and diabetes.
simple: Inherited conditions in which the cell's energy-making parts fail, causing problems in muscles, brain and other organs.

name: Mitochondrial encephalomyopathy
formal: Mitochondrial disorder affecting brain and muscle with seizures, stroke-like episodes, myopathy, exercise intolerance and lactic acidosis; syndromes include MELAS, MERRF and Kearns-Sayre.
simple: A group of inherited energy-production diseases affecting the brain and muscles, causing weakness, seizures and developmental problems.

name: Mitochondrial encephalopathy
formal: Brain dysfunction from impaired oxidative phosphorylation, with seizures, developmental regression, stroke-like episodes, movement disorders and raised lactate; examples include Leigh disease and MELAS.
simple: Brain disease caused by faulty cell energy production, leading to seizures, developmental setbacks and movement problems.

name: Mitochondrial myopathies
formal: Primary muscle diseases from mitochondrial dysfunction, with exercise intolerance, proximal weakness, ptosis, ophthalmoplegia, lactic acidosis and ragged-red fibres on biopsy.
simple: Muscle diseases caused by faulty cell energy production, causing weakness and tiredness with exercise.
more: Diagnosed with serum lactate, CK, biopsy showing ragged-red and COX-deficient fibres, and mitochondrial DNA or nuclear gene sequencing. Treatment is supportive; exercise training may help, and aminoglycosides and valproate should be avoided in some syndromes.

name: Mitochondrial myopathy
formal: Primary muscle disease from mitochondrial dysfunction, with exercise intolerance, proximal weakness, ptosis, ophthalmoplegia, lactic acidosis and ragged-red fibres on biopsy.
simple: A muscle disease caused by faulty cell energy production, causing weakness and tiredness with exercise.

name: Mitochondrial myopathy lactic acidosis and strokes (MELAS)
formal: Maternally inherited mitochondrial disorder, mainly from m.3243A>G in MT-TL1, with stroke-like episodes, lactic acidosis, seizures, myopathy and deafness.
simple: An inherited energy-production disease causing stroke-like episodes, seizures, muscle weakness and hearing loss.
more: Diagnosed by genetic testing, lactate and MRI; treatment is supportive, with L-arginine for acute episodes and avoidance of valproate.
ab: Mitochondrial myopathy lactic acidosis and strokes
mitochondrial encephalomyopathy with lactic acidosis and stroke-like episodes
th: โรคไมโทคอนเดรียที่มี stroke-like episode ซ้ำ ๆ ในคนอายุน้อย ร่วมกับชัก ปวดศีรษะ และ lactate สูง
tempoNote: Attacks evolve over hours to days on a background of slowly accumulating deficits; onset usually before 40
feat: Stroke-like episodes in a young person: hemianopia, aphasia or cortical blindness, often with headache, vomiting and seizures
Lesions favour the occipital and parietal cortex and do not obey arterial territories
Short stature, sensorineural hearing loss and diabetes in the patient or maternal relatives
Exercise intolerance or mild proximal weakness; cardiomyopathy may coexist
Stepwise cognitive decline after repeated episodes
inv: MRI: cortical/subcortical T2 and DWI change crossing vascular borders, with mixed diffusion signal that can migrate over weeks; MR spectroscopy lactate peak
Serum and CSF lactate (raised), glucose, ECG and echo, audiogram
mtDNA testing for m.3243A>G (urine sediment or muscle preferred over blood because blood heteroplasmy falls with age)
Muscle biopsy if genetics negative: ragged-red fibres, COX-positive strongly SDH-reactive vessels

case.story: Severe headache and vomiting, then a focal seizure; next morning he cannot see on the right. His mother is deaf and has diabetes.
case.exam: Short, thin build; right homonymous hemianopia, bilateral hearing aids, mild proximal weakness.
case.tests: MRI: swollen left occipital cortex with DWI change spilling beyond the PCA territory; MRA normal. Lactate 4.8 mmol/L.
case.q: What genetic test fits best, and which sample should be sent?
case.a: MELAS — test for m.3243A>G, ideally on urine epithelial cells or muscle, as blood can give a false-negative result.

det.patho: Most cases stem from the m.3243A>G point change in the mitochondrial tRNA-Leu gene, inherited through the mother with variable heteroplasmy. Faulty oxidative phosphorylation causes an energy crisis in neurons and in the smooth muscle and endothelium of small vessels, and nitric oxide depletion may impair vasodilatation. Stroke-like lesions are thought to be metabolic and partly vascular rather than embolic or atherothrombotic.
det.clinical: Typical onset is in childhood or early adult life, although first episodes after 40 are recognised. Attacks begin with headache, vomiting or seizures and leave a cortical deficit that may improve over weeks; recurrent attacks cause cumulative cognitive and visual loss. The same mutation can produce only diabetes and deafness (MIDD) in relatives, so family history must be taken across the maternal line. Look for cardiomyopathy, WPW, renal tubular problems, gut dysmotility and short stature.
det.diagnosis: Suspect it when a young person has a stroke with cortical, non-territorial lesions and normal vessels. MRI and MRS (lactate doublet) support it; serum lactate is raised in most but not all. Genetic confirmation is key, and urine sediment gives higher yield than blood. Exclude encephalitis, venous thrombosis, vasculitis, PRES and status-related cortical change.
det.treatment: During an attack, give IV L-arginine where available and treat seizures aggressively, since status worsens the energy failure. Avoid valproate, which can precipitate liver failure and worsen mitochondrial function; take care with metformin and prolonged propofol. Long-term care includes L-arginine or citrulline prophylaxis (evidence moderate), cardiac and diabetes surveillance, hearing aids or cochlear implants, and genetic counselling for maternal relatives.
det.prognosis: Course is progressive with accumulating disability; many patients develop dementia, and median survival after first stroke-like event is limited to roughly a decade or two.
pearls: Cortical lesion not respecting arterial borders plus normal MRA in a young patient: think MELAS.
Blood can miss the mutation; send urine or muscle.
Do not use valproate for MELAS seizures.
det.thd: MELAS เป็นโรคไมโทคอนเดรียถ่ายทอดทางแม่ ส่วนใหญ่จาก m.3243A>G ทำให้สมองขาดพลังงานเป็นพัก ๆ ผู้ป่วยมีอาการคล้ายอัมพาตเฉียบพลันร่วมกับปวดศีรษะ อาเจียน และชัก รอยโรคใน MRI ไม่ตรงกับเขตหลอดเลือด และมี lactate สูง ยืนยันด้วยการตรวจยีนจากปัสสาวะหรือกล้ามเนื้อ รักษาด้วย L-arginine คุมชัก และหลีกเลี่ยง valproate

files.chapter: Section 3 Hereditary and Genetic Conditions and Malformations

ddx.pt: Fever, CSF pleocytosis and temporal-lobe predominance; HSV PCR positive
Venous sinus filling defect on MRV; lesions follow venous drainage, often haemorrhagic
Fully reversible aura under an hour with normal MRI; no lactate rise or permanent deficit

nN: mitochondrial myopathy lactic acidosis and strokes melas
aN: melas | mitochondrial myopathy lactic acidosis and strokes | mitochondrial encephalomyopathy with lactic acidosis and stroke like episodes | m 3243a g disease

name: Mitochondrial neurogastrointestinal encephalopathy (MNGIE)
formal: Autosomal recessive TYMP deficiency causing thymidine accumulation, with gut dysmotility, cachexia, ptosis, ophthalmoplegia, peripheral neuropathy and leukoencephalopathy.
simple: An inherited disease causing severe gut movement problems, weight loss, nerve damage and eye muscle weakness.
more: Diagnosed by raised plasma thymidine and deoxyuridine and low leucocyte thymidine phosphorylase activity; MRI shows diffuse leukoencephalopathy. Allogeneic stem cell or liver transplant corrects the enzyme defect but is risky; nutritional support.
aN: mngie | mitochondrial neurogastrointestinal encephalopathy

name: Mitochondrial neuropathies
formal: Peripheral neuropathies due to mitochondrial dysfunction, as in POLG disorders, MNGIE or NARP, usually axonal sensorimotor and combined with other multisystem features.
simple: Nerve damage in the limbs caused by faulty cell energy production, often seen with other mitochondrial problems.

name: Mitochondrial trifunctional protein deficiency
formal: Autosomal recessive fatty-acid beta-oxidation defect (HADHA or HADHB) causing neonatal cardiomyopathy, hypoglycaemia, recurrent rhabdomyolysis and peripheral neuropathy.
simple: An inherited disorder in burning long-chain fats, leading to heart, muscle and nerve problems.
more: Elevated hydroxyacylcarnitines on screening; management with avoiding fasting, MCT oil and triheptanoin; prognosis variable.

name: Mixed connective tissue disease
formal: Autoimmune overlap syndrome with high-titre anti-U1 RNP, combining features of lupus, scleroderma and myositis, and sometimes trigeminal neuropathy.
simple: An autoimmune disease with features of several others like lupus and scleroderma, including joint pain, rashes and muscle weakness.
more: Diagnosis by anti-U1 RNP antibody; treat with steroids, hydroxychloroquine or immunosuppressants.

name: Miyoshi distal myopathy
formal: Autosomal recessive dysferlinopathy (DYSF) with early distal posterior calf weakness, markedly raised CK and inflammatory features on biopsy.
simple: An inherited muscle disease that begins with weak calf muscles in young adults.
more: Genetic testing of DYSF or dysferlin protein studies; no specific therapy, so physiotherapy and avoiding eccentric exercise.

name: Mobile spasms (myorhythmia)
formal: Slow, rhythmic 1 to 4 Hz repetitive movements of face, limbs or palate, often from brainstem lesions; seen in Whipple disease with oculomasticatory myorhythmia.
simple: Slow repeating rhythmic movements, often of the jaw or limbs, usually from a brainstem problem.
aN: myorhythmia | mobile spasms

name: Moebius syndrome
formal: Congenital facial diplegia with abducens palsy from brainstem cranial nerve nuclei hypoplasia, causing expressionless face, inability to abduct eyes and sometimes limb anomalies.
simple: A rare condition from birth where facial muscles and eye movements to the side are weak, giving a face with little expression.

name: MOG-associated optic neuritis (MOG-ON)
formal: Optic neuritis in MOG antibody-associated disease, often bilateral with marked disc swelling, long optic nerve involvement, steroid-responsive but relapsing.
simple: Inflammation of the optic nerve linked to an antibody against MOG, causing vision loss and eye pain.
nN: mog associated optic neuritis mog on
aN: mog on | mog associated optic neuritis

name: Mohr-Tranebjaerg syndrome
formal: X-linked deafness-dystonia-optic neuronopathy syndrome from TIMM8A mutations, with childhood sensorineural deafness, then dystonia, visual loss and cognitive decline.
simple: A rare X-linked condition causing early deafness, followed by movement problems, vision loss and dementia.
more: Diagnosis by TIMM8A sequencing; MRI is often normal early, and females are mildly affected carriers. Some have contiguous gene deletion with BTK deficiency; therapy is supportive, with hearing aids or cochlear implants and symptomatic dystonia treatment.

name: Mollaret’s meningitis
formal: Recurrent benign aseptic lymphocytic meningitis with large Mollaret cells in CSF, often caused by herpes simplex virus type 2 reactivation, with self-limited attacks.
simple: Repeated attacks of viral meningitis that go away by themselves, often caused by a herpes virus.

name: Monge’s disease
formal: Chronic mountain sickness: excessive erythrocytosis with hypoxaemia and pulmonary hypertension at high altitude, causing headache, dizziness and cognitive slowing.
simple: A long-term illness in people living at high altitude where too many red blood cells cause headache, tiredness and dizziness.

name: Monoamine disorders
formal: Inherited disorders of dopamine, noradrenaline and serotonin synthesis or metabolism, such as tyrosine hydroxylase or AADC deficiency, with hypotonia, oculogyric crises, dystonia and autonomic features.
simple: Inherited disorders of brain chemicals such as dopamine and serotonin, causing floppiness, abnormal movements and developmental delay in infants.
more: Diagnosed by CSF neurotransmitter metabolites and genetics. Treatment with levodopa, dopamine agonists or gene therapy depends on type.

name: Monoballism
formal: Violent flinging movements of a single limb caused by a basal ganglia lesion, typically contralateral subthalamic nucleus stroke; a restricted form of hemiballism.
simple: Wild flinging movements of just one limb, usually from a small stroke in a deep brain area.

name: Monoclonal gammopathy
formal: Presence of a clonal plasma cell paraprotein, such as MGUS, associated with demyelinating neuropathy (anti-MAG IgM), POEMS, amyloidosis and other neuropathies.
simple: A blood condition where abnormal immune cells make one abnormal protein, which can sometimes cause nerve damage.

name: Monomelic polyneuropathies
formal: Asymmetric sensorimotor neuropathy confined to one limb, such as monomelic amyotrophy or focal neuropathy of a limb, usually with a slow or self-limiting course.
simple: Nerve disease affecting only one arm or leg.
more: Workup includes EMG and MRI; treatment depends on cause, with immunotherapy for immune cases.

name: Mononeuropathies
formal: Focal disorders of a single peripheral nerve from entrapment, compression, trauma, or ischaemia, such as median at the wrist or peroneal at the fibular head.
simple: Damage to a single nerve, causing weakness or numbness in the area it supplies.
more: Nerve conduction studies and ultrasound locate the lesion; splinting, avoiding compression, steroid injection, or surgical decompression depending on cause.

name: Mononeuropathy
formal: Focal injury of a single peripheral nerve by compression, entrapment, trauma, ischaemia or infiltration, with deficits in its distribution.
simple: Damage to a single nerve, causing numbness, weakness or pain in the area it supplies.
more: Electrodiagnosis localises the lesion; entrapments are managed with splinting, injection or surgery.

name: Monoradiculopathies
formal: Disorder of a single spinal nerve root, usually from disc herniation or foraminal stenosis, producing dermatomal pain or sensory loss, myotomal weakness and reduced reflex.
simple: Pinching or irritation of one nerve root near the spine, causing pain, numbness or weakness in the area that nerve supplies.
more: Confirmed by MRI and EMG; most cases improve with conservative care, while persistent deficits or cord compromise may need steroid injection or surgical decompression.

name: Mood disorders
formal: Psychiatric conditions including major depression and bipolar disorder, with persistent disturbance of affect; common comorbidities of epilepsy, stroke, Parkinson disease and dementia.
simple: Conditions such as depression and bipolar disorder where mood is persistently very low or very high.

name: Morvan syndrome
formal: Autoimmune syndrome with peripheral nerve hyperexcitability, autonomic dysfunction, insomnia and encephalopathy, linked to CASPR2 antibodies and sometimes thymoma.
simple: An autoimmune condition causing muscle twitching and cramps, severe insomnia, sweating and confusion.
th: โรคจากแอนติบอดีต่อ CASPR2 — กล้ามเนื้อกระตุกเป็นคลื่น ปวดแสบร้อน นอนไม่หลับรุนแรง สับสน และระบบอัตโนมัติแปรปรวน มักสัมพันธ์กับ thymoma
tempoNote: Builds over weeks to months; CASPR2 disease overall can be slowly progressive or fluctuating
feat: Peripheral nerve hyperexcitability: myokymia, cramps, fasciculation and stiffness
Severe insomnia with agitated dream enactment (agrypnia excitata), confusion and hallucinations
Dysautonomia: drenching sweats, tachycardia, blood pressure swings, weight loss
Neuropathic pain, burning or itching in the limbs
Mostly men over 50; thymoma (often malignant) in a sizeable minority
inv: CASPR2 IgG by cell-based assay (serum more sensitive than CSF); LGI1 may coexist in Morvan syndrome
EMG: myokymic and neuromyotonic discharges, after-discharges following nerve stimulation
CT or MRI chest for thymoma; polysomnography shows loss of normal sleep architecture
Sodium (can fall), MRI brain usually normal, CSF often bland

case.story: Three months of worm-like twitching in both calves, burning feet and nightly sweats soaking the bed. His wife says he has barely slept for weeks and talks and gestures as if working on the boat at night.
case.exam: Continuous rippling of calf and thigh muscles, slow relaxation after grip, resting heart rate 118, fluctuating attention, no weakness.
case.tests: EMG: myokymic doublets and neuromyotonic discharges. Serum CASPR2 strongly positive. CT chest: 6 cm anterior mediastinal mass.
case.q: What is the syndrome, and which treatment step is essential besides immunotherapy?
case.a: Morvan syndrome from CASPR2 autoimmunity; resection of the thymoma is central, combined with steroids, IVIG or PLEX and symptomatic relief of hyperexcitability.

det.patho: CASPR2 (contactin-associated protein-like 2) clusters Kv1 potassium channels at juxtaparanodes of myelinated axons and is also expressed in brain. Mostly IgG4 antibodies disturb its interaction with contactin-2, lowering potassium channel function and causing spontaneous repetitive firing of peripheral nerves. Morvan syndrome is the most severe phenotype and is strongly tied to thymoma, where faulty T-cell selection may explain combined antibodies.
det.clinical: CASPR2 antibodies produce a spectrum: isolated neuromyotonia, painful neuropathy, limbic encephalitis, cerebellar ataxia, episodic ataxia-like attacks, or the full Morvan picture. Morvan syndrome combines nerve hyperexcitability, insomnia with dream-like behaviour, hallucinations, autonomic storms and weight loss. Severe cases risk arrhythmia and sudden death. Ask about myasthenia, as thymoma-related autoimmunity can overlap.
det.diagnosis: Confirm CASPR2 IgG by cell-based assay, interpreting low-titre serum-only positives cautiously because false positives occur. EMG documents peripheral hyperexcitability, and sleep studies show disorganised sleep without normal cycling. Image the chest for thymoma in every patient. Exclude prion disease, delirium tremens, thyrotoxicosis and drug toxicity.
det.treatment: Treat the tumour where present, then give corticosteroids with IVIG or plasma exchange; rituximab is used for refractory or relapsing disease. Sodium-channel blockers such as carbamazepine or phenytoin reduce cramps and myokymia, and neuropathic pain agents help discomfort. Monitor cardiac rhythm and autonomic parameters in severe cases.
det.prognosis: Many patients improve substantially with tumour removal and immunotherapy, but relapse may herald tumour recurrence; untreated Morvan syndrome can be fatal.
pearls: Twitching muscles plus profound insomnia and sweating: test CASPR2 and image the mediastinum.
LGI1 = mostly CNS; CASPR2 = peripheral nerve plus variable CNS.
Thymoma recurrence can present as a neurological relapse.
det.thd: Morvan syndrome เกิดจากแอนติบอดีต่อ CASPR2 ซึ่งทำให้เส้นประสาทส่วนปลายทำงานเกิน จึงมีกล้ามเนื้อกระตุกเป็นคลื่น ตะคริว ปวดแสบร้อน ร่วมกับนอนไม่หลับรุนแรง ละเมอทำงาน สับสน และเหงื่อออกมาก ใจสั่น พบ thymoma ได้บ่อย ต้องตรวจ CT ทรวงอกทุกราย รักษาด้วยการผ่าตัดเนื้องอก steroid IVIG หรือ PLEX และยาลดการกระตุกของเส้นประสาท

3. EVALUATION AND MANAGEMENT OF THE PATIENT WITH PERIPHERAL NEUROPATHY

ddx.pt: Peripheral hyperexcitability alone, without insomnia, encephalopathy or marked dysautonomia
Genetic prion disease (PRNP D178N) with progressive insomnia and no myokymia; does not respond to immunotherapy
Rapid dementia with myoclonus and DWI cortical/striatal signal; no nerve hyperexcitability on EMG

aN: morvan fibrillary chorea | anti caspr2 encephalitis | caspr2 antibody associated disease | caspr2 autoimmunity | la choree fibrillaire

name: Motor neuron degeneration (MND)
formal: Progressive degeneration of upper and lower motor neurons causing weakness, wasting, fasciculations and spasticity, as in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.
simple: Gradual loss of the nerve cells controlling muscles, leading to weakness, wasting and stiffness.
aN: mnd | motor neuron degeneration

name: Motor neuron disease
formal: Progressive neurodegeneration of upper and lower motor neurons, most commonly ALS, causing weakness, wasting, fasciculations, bulbar dysfunction and respiratory failure without sensory loss.
simple: A disease where the nerves controlling muscles slowly die, causing progressive weakness, muscle wasting and trouble speaking, swallowing and breathing.
more: Diagnose by El Escorial criteria, EMG showing widespread acute and chronic denervation, and exclusion of mimics with MRI and labs. Riluzole and edaravone modestly prolong survival; non-invasive ventilation and gastrostomy help; median survival 3 to 5 years.

name: Motor neuropathies
formal: Peripheral neuropathies predominantly affecting motor axons, such as multifocal motor neuropathy, distal hereditary motor neuropathy, or lead and dapsone toxicity.
simple: Nerve disorders that mainly cause muscle weakness with little numbness.

name: Motor neuropathy
formal: Peripheral neuropathy predominantly affecting motor axons, such as multifocal motor neuropathy, distal hereditary motor neuropathy, or lead and dapsone toxicity.
simple: A nerve disorder that mainly causes muscle weakness with little numbness.

name: Motor tics
formal: Sudden, brief, repetitive stereotyped movements, such as blinking or head jerks, preceded by premonitory urge and temporarily suppressible; core feature of Tourette syndrome.
simple: Quick, repeated, involuntary movements such as eye blinking or head jerking that a person can sometimes hold back briefly.

name: Moyamoya disease
formal: Progressive steno-occlusive disease of distal ICA and proximal circle of Willis vessels, with fragile collaterals giving the puff of smoke angiographic appearance; causes ischaemic or haemorrhagic strokes.
simple: A disease where brain arteries narrow and tiny fragile vessels form to compensate, causing strokes in children and adults.
more: Diagnosis by MRA or catheter angiography; RNF213 variants are a susceptibility locus in East Asians. Treat with revascularisation (STA-MCA bypass or indirect synangiosis); children present with TIAs on crying or hyperventilation, so avoid hypocapnia.
ab: spontaneous occlusion of the circle of Willis
th: หลอดเลือดแดง ICA ส่วนปลายและแขนงต้นของ ACA/MCA ตีบตันแบบค่อยเป็นค่อยไปทั้งสองข้าง เกิดเส้นเลือดฝอยข้างเคียงคล้าย 'กลุ่มควัน' พบมากในเอเชียตะวันออก (RNF213) เด็กมาด้วย TIA/stroke ผู้ใหญ่มักมาด้วยเลือดออก
tempoNote: Progressive arteriopathy over years; children have repeated TIAs triggered by crying or hyperventilation, adults may present suddenly with haemorrhage
feat: Bimodal onset: children around 5 years and adults in their 30s–40s; female predominance
Children: recurrent TIAs or strokes provoked by crying, blowing, hot food or exercise (hyperventilation), alternating sides
Adults: intraventricular, deep or subarachnoid haemorrhage from fragile collaterals, as well as ischaemia
Headache, seizures, involuntary movements (chorea) and cognitive decline
Moyamoya syndrome: same angiogram secondary to sickle cell, Down syndrome, NF1, radiation, thyroid disease
inv: MRI/MRA: stenosis of terminal ICA, ACA and MCA; flow voids in basal ganglia; FLAIR 'ivy sign'
Catheter angiography: Suzuki staging and external carotid collaterals (pre-surgical planning)
Perfusion imaging (SPECT, CT/MR perfusion with acetazolamide challenge) for haemodynamic reserve
Screen for associated conditions (thyroid, sickle cell, NF1); RNF213 variant testing in familial cases

case.story: While blowing up balloons at a birthday party and again while crying, her right arm went limp for ten minutes; last month a similar episode affected the left leg.
case.exam: Normal between attacks except a mild left pronator drift.
case.tests: MRI: small cortical infarct in the right frontal lobe and FLAIR hyperintense sulci (ivy sign); MRA: bilateral severe stenosis of distal ICAs with basal collateral networks.
case.q: Why do attacks follow blowing or crying, and what treatment is offered?
case.a: Hyperventilation lowers CO2 and constricts vessels, dropping flow beyond the stenoses; aspirin and surgical revascularisation (indirect bypass such as EDAS in children) are recommended.

read.where: Chapter 14 Stroke in children and young adults
Chapter 33 A case of moya moya

det.patho: A non-inflammatory, non-atherosclerotic occlusive vasculopathy affecting the terminal ICAs and proximal circle of Willis, with intimal fibrocellular thickening and thin media. Reduced flow drives growth of fragile lenticulostriate and thalamoperforating collaterals (the angiographic 'puff of smoke'), plus transdural collaterals. The RNF213 p.R4810K founder variant is strongly linked in Japanese, Korean and Chinese patients and also occurs in Thailand. Microaneurysms on stressed collaterals explain adult haemorrhage.
det.clinical: Paediatric disease usually presents with ischaemia — TIAs, strokes, cognitive impairment and headaches — and attacks are classically triggered by hyperventilation. Adults present either with ischaemic events or with haemorrhage (intraventricular or basal ganglia), which carries higher mortality. Unilateral involvement can progress to bilateral disease, especially in children. Pregnancy and dehydration may destabilise patients.
det.diagnosis: Angiography or high-quality MRA showing stenosis/occlusion of the terminal ICA and proximal ACA/MCA with abnormal collateral networks establishes the diagnosis; Suzuki stages I–VI describe progression. 'Moyamoya disease' implies no associated cause; when an underlying condition is present the term moyamoya syndrome is used. Vessel wall MRI helps distinguish it from atherosclerosis (concentric, non-enhancing narrowing with small outer diameter) and vasculitis. Perfusion studies with vasodilatory challenge identify those at risk who need revascularisation.
det.treatment: Revascularisation is the mainstay for symptomatic ischaemic disease: direct bypass (superficial temporal to MCA anastomosis) in adults, indirect procedures (EDAS, EDAMS, pial synangiosis, multiple burr holes) particularly in children, or combined approaches. In haemorrhagic adult moyamoya, direct bypass reduces rebleeding. Aspirin is commonly given for ischaemic presentations. Avoid hyperventilation, dehydration and hypotension, especially during anaesthesia. Thrombolysis is used with caution because of fragile collaterals.
det.prognosis: Untreated paediatric disease frequently progresses with accumulating deficits and cognitive decline; successful revascularisation substantially lowers future stroke risk.
pearls: Child with TIAs when crying, blowing or eating hot noodles: think moyamoya.
Adult moyamoya often presents with intraventricular haemorrhage.
Avoid hypocapnia and hypotension during anaesthesia in moyamoya patients.
det.thd: Moyamoya disease คือหลอดเลือด ICA ส่วนปลายและต้น ACA/MCA ตีบตันทั้งสองข้างอย่างช้า ๆ ทำให้เกิดหลอดเลือดข้างเคียงเล็ก ๆ คล้ายกลุ่มควัน พบบ่อยในเอเชียตะวันออกและสัมพันธ์กับยีน RNF213 เด็กมักมี TIA หรือ stroke เวลาร้องไห้หรือเป่าลูกโป่ง ผู้ใหญ่อาจมาด้วยเลือดออกในสมอง วินิจฉัยด้วย MRA/angiography รักษาด้วยการผ่าตัด revascularisation (direct/indirect bypass) และหลีกเลี่ยงภาวะหายใจเร็วหรือความดันต่ำ

formal: Immune-mediated pure motor neuropathy with asymmetric distal arm weakness, motor conduction block, and often anti-GM1 IgM antibodies, without sensory loss.
simple: An immune-related nerve condition causing slowly progressive weakness of the hands and arms, with no numbness.
more: Nerve conduction shows multifocal conduction block; IVIG is first-line treatment; steroids are ineffective or may worsen it.

files.chapter: 13. Chronic Inflammatory Demyelinating Polyradiculoneuropathy, Multifocal Motor Neuropathy, and Related Disorders

ddx.pt: UMN signs, no conduction block, relentless spread
Symmetric, sensory involvement, raised CSF protein; Lewis–Sumner variant is asymmetric but sensory

aN: mmn | multifocal motor neuropathy | mmncb | multifocal motor neuropathy with conduction block | anti gm1 neuropathy

det.patho: MMN is an immune neuropathy of motor axons in which IgM antibodies, often against GM1, bind at or near the nodes and activate complement, causing focal conduction block. Why motor fibres are selectively targeted is uncertain; motor and sensory axons differ in ganglioside composition and ion-channel properties. Ongoing block leads to secondary axonal loss over years. It affects men more often, usually with onset between 20 and 50.
det.clinical: Weakness begins in one hand or forearm, following the territory of an individual nerve (often radial, ulnar or median), and spreads slowly to other nerves over years. Strength may be lost well before obvious wasting. Cramps, fasciculations and cold-worsened weakness are common, reflexes are variable, and sensation stays normal. There are no bulbar or upper motor neuron signs, and legs are affected less than arms.
det.diagnosis: The core finding is motor conduction block at sites away from common entrapment points, with normal sensory conduction through the same segment; the 2021 EAN/PNS guideline defines definite and probable block. IgM anti-GM1 is present in roughly half. Nerve ultrasound or MRI of the brachial plexus may show focal enlargement. CSF protein is normal or only mildly raised. The main mimic is lower motor neuron-predominant ALS; also exclude Lewis–Sumner syndrome and HNPP.
det.treatment: IVIG is first-line: a loading course of 2 g/kg followed by individualised maintenance infusions (intravenous or subcutaneous) at the lowest effective dose and interval. Corticosteroids and plasma exchange are generally ineffective and may worsen weakness. Cyclophosphamide is rarely used because of toxicity. Complement-targeted agents are under clinical study. Track grip strength and functional scores to adjust dosing.
det.prognosis: Most patients improve with IVIG, but many need long-term infusions and slow axonal loss can still accumulate. Life expectancy is normal.
pearls: Asymmetric hand weakness with no sensory loss and no UMN signs: look for conduction block before diagnosing ALS.
Steroids can make MMN worse — unlike CIDP.
A negative anti-GM1 test does not exclude MMN.
det.thd: MMN เป็นโรคเส้นประสาทสั่งการอักเสบจากภูมิคุ้มกัน มักพบในชายวัยทำงาน อ่อนแรงมือหรือแขนตามเส้นประสาทแต่ละเส้นแบบไม่สมมาตร มีตะคริวและกล้ามเนื้อเต้นได้ แต่ไม่มีอาการชาและไม่มี UMN signs การตรวจไฟฟ้าพบ conduction block ในเส้นประสาทสั่งการ ส่วน sensory ปกติ และประมาณครึ่งหนึ่งพบ IgM anti-GM1 รักษาด้วย IVIG ซึ่งได้ผลดีแต่มักต้องให้ต่อเนื่อง ไม่ควรใช้สเตียรอยด์เพราะอาจทำให้อาการแย่ลง

name: Multifocal motor neuropathy with conduction block (MMNCB)

simple: An immune disease attacking motor nerves in the arms and legs, causing uneven weakness and cramps without numbness.

name: Multifocal myoclonus
formal: Myoclonic jerks involving multiple body regions, often from metabolic, hypoxic or neurodegenerative encephalopathies.
simple: Sudden muscle jerks occurring in several parts of the body.

name: Multifocal neuropathy
formal: Neuropathy with multiple nerve involvement, as in multifocal motor neuropathy, MADSAM, vasculitis or hereditary pressure palsies, giving asymmetric deficits.
simple: A condition affecting several separate nerves, causing patchy weakness and numbness.
more: Investigate with nerve conduction and biopsy; therapy depends on the cause, such as IVIG for immune neuropathies.

name: Multiple acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency
formal: Glutaric aciduria type II, a disorder of electron transfer flavoprotein or ETF-QO affecting fatty acid and amino acid oxidation, with hypoglycaemia, myopathy and encephalopathy; riboflavin-responsive in late forms.
simple: An inherited disorder of fat and protein breakdown causing low blood sugar, muscle weakness and sometimes brain problems, which can improve with riboflavin.

name: Multiple cervical radiculopathies
formal: Compression or irritation of more than one cervical nerve root, commonly from cervical spondylosis, with neck and arm pain, weakness and possible myelopathy.
simple: Pinched nerves at several levels in the neck, causing arm pain, numbness and weakness.
more: MRI and EMG confirm it; managed with physiotherapy, medications and decompression surgery if progressive.

name: Multiple cranial neuropathies (MCNs)
formal: Involvement of two or more cranial nerves from skull base disease, carcinomatous or infectious meningitis, cavernous sinus lesions, sarcoidosis, Lyme or Tolosa-Hunt syndrome.
simple: Damage to several nerves of the head and face at once, causing problems such as double vision, facial weakness or hearing loss.

name: Multiple sclerosis (MS)
formal: Chronic immune-mediated demyelinating and neurodegenerative CNS disease with relapsing-remitting or progressive course, optic neuritis, myelitis and brainstem syndromes with periventricular lesions.
simple: A long-term disease where the immune system attacks the covering of nerves in the brain and spinal cord, causing vision, strength and balance problems.
more: Diagnose with MRI brain and spine (McDonald criteria), CSF oligoclonal bands and evoked potentials. Use high-dose steroids for relapses and disease-modifying therapy such as interferon, ocrelizumab, natalizumab or fingolimod to reduce relapses.

aN: ms | multiple sclerosis | disseminated sclerosis | rrms | relapsing remitting ms

det.patho: An immune-mediated disease in which autoreactive T and B cells cross the blood–brain barrier and cause focal inflammatory demyelination with axonal injury, alongside a slower compartmentalised process (smouldering lesions, microglial activation) that drives progression. Risk is shaped by genetics (HLA-DRB1*15:01), Epstein–Barr virus infection, low vitamin D, smoking and obesity in youth. It is commoner in women and at higher latitudes, and less common in Thailand than in Western countries.
det.clinical: Most patients start with relapsing-remitting disease: optic neuritis with painful eye movement, partial myelitis, brainstem syndromes such as INO, or cerebellar symptoms, evolving over days and recovering over weeks. Fatigue, heat sensitivity, Lhermitte sign, bladder urgency, depression and cognitive slowing are common. Many later enter secondary progressive MS; about one in ten has primary progressive disease from onset, often as a spastic paraparesis. Red flags for another diagnosis include fever, encephalopathy, peripheral neuropathy and very extensive cord lesions.
det.diagnosis: The McDonald criteria (2017, with later revisions recognising optic nerve lesions and central vein sign) require dissemination in space and time with no better explanation. MRI shows ovoid periventricular, juxtacortical/cortical, infratentorial and spinal cord lesions; new enhancing lesions or CSF-specific oligoclonal bands satisfy dissemination in time. In Asian patients, test for AQP4-IgG and MOG-IgG before diagnosing MS. Exclude B12 deficiency, sarcoidosis, vasculitis, infection and small vessel disease.
det.treatment: Relapses that impair function are treated with high-dose methylprednisolone (typically 1 g IV per day over 3–5 days), with plasma exchange for severe steroid-unresponsive attacks. Disease-modifying therapies range from moderate efficacy (interferons, glatiramer, teriflunomide, dimethyl fumarate) to high efficacy (S1P modulators, natalizumab, anti-CD20 antibodies such as ocrelizumab, alemtuzumab, cladribine); early high-efficacy treatment is increasingly favoured. Ocrelizumab is approved for primary progressive MS. Monitor for PML, infections and lymphopenia, and address spasticity, bladder, fatigue, mood and rehabilitation.
det.prognosis: Disease course is highly variable; early effective therapy has substantially reduced long-term disability, and life expectancy is only modestly reduced.
pearls: Bilateral INO in a young adult is MS until proven otherwise.
Always test AQP4-IgG and MOG-IgG in suspected MS — some MS drugs worsen NMOSD.
Oligoclonal bands can substitute for dissemination in time under McDonald 2017.
det.thd: MS เป็นโรคภูมิคุ้มกันทำลายปลอกประสาทในสมอง ไขสันหลัง และเส้นประสาทตา เกิดเป็นครั้ง ๆ ต่างตำแหน่งต่างเวลา พบในหญิงวัยหนุ่มสาวมากกว่า อาการเช่น optic neuritis, myelitis บางส่วน, INO, ชา และอ่อนเพลีย วินิจฉัยตาม McDonald criteria ด้วย MRI และ oligoclonal bands ในน้ำไขสันหลัง และในคนเอเชียต้องตรวจ AQP4-IgG และ MOG-IgG แยกก่อนเสมอ รักษาอาการกำเริบด้วย methylprednisolone ขนาดสูง และป้องกันระยะยาวด้วยยาปรับภูมิคุ้มกัน (DMT) โดยปัจจุบันนิยมเริ่มยาประสิทธิภาพสูงเร็ว

files.chapter: 9 - Atypical parkinsonism, parkinsonism-­plus syndromes and secondary parkinsonian disorders

ddx.pt: Autonomic failure milder and later, good levodopa response

aN: msa | multiple system atrophy | msa p | msa c | shy drager syndrome | olivopontocerebellar atrophy | striatonigral degeneration

det.patho: MSA is an alpha-synucleinopathy in which the protein accumulates mainly inside oligodendrocytes as glial cytoplasmic inclusions, leading to neuronal loss in the striatonigral system, the olivopontocerebellar circuits and central autonomic nuclei. Degeneration of brainstem and spinal autonomic neurons causes preganglionic autonomic failure. Onset is usually in the sixth decade and the disease is sporadic.
det.clinical: Patients present with parkinsonism (MSA-P, commoner in Western series) or cerebellar ataxia (MSA-C, relatively commoner in East Asia), together with prominent autonomic failure. Urinary urgency, incomplete emptying and erectile dysfunction often precede motor symptoms by years; symptomatic orthostatic hypotension can cause syncope. Other clues are night-time inspiratory stridor, sleep apnoea, disproportionate antecollis, Pisa syndrome, jerky postural tremor, cold violaceous hands and emotional incontinence. Levodopa responsiveness is poor or transient and may provoke facial dystonia. Progression is noticeably faster than in PD, with walking aids needed within a few years.
det.diagnosis: The 2022 MDS criteria define clinically established and clinically probable MSA based on autonomic dysfunction plus parkinsonism and/or cerebellar syndrome, supported by MRI markers and red flags. Document orthostatic hypotension (a fall of at least 20/10 mmHg, ideally with a blunted heart-rate rise) and measure post-void residual volume. MRI may show putaminal atrophy with a hypointense rim and hyperintense lateral margin, pontine cruciform hyperintensity, and middle cerebellar peduncle or pontine atrophy. Cardiac MIBG uptake is usually preserved, unlike PD and DLB. Exclude fragile X tremor-ataxia syndrome, SCAs and other secondary ataxias in MSA-C.
det.treatment: Treatment is supportive. For orthostatic hypotension use non-drug measures first (fluids, salt, head-up tilt at night, compression garments) then midodrine, fludrocortisone or droxidopa. Bladder symptoms need urodynamic assessment; clean intermittent catheterisation is often required because of high residual volumes. A levodopa trial is worth doing, and CPAP or tracheostomy may be needed for stridor. Botulinum toxin, physiotherapy, speech and swallowing therapy and palliative care input are central.
det.prognosis: Median survival is about 7–10 years from symptom onset; sudden death at night, aspiration and infections are major causes of mortality.
pearls: Early urogenital and orthostatic failure in a patient with parkinsonism or ataxia: think MSA.
Nocturnal stridor is a red flag for sudden death — refer for airway assessment.
A normal cardiac MIBG scan favours MSA over PD/DLB because MSA is a preganglionic failure.
det.thd: MSA เป็นโรคเสื่อมจาก alpha-synuclein ที่สะสมในเซลล์ oligodendrocyte ทำให้มีอาการพาร์กินสัน (MSA-P) หรือเดินเซ (MSA-C) ร่วมกับระบบประสาทอัตโนมัติล้มเหลวตั้งแต่ต้น เช่น ความดันตกเมื่อลุกยืน ปัสสาวะค้าง หย่อนสมรรถภาพทางเพศ เสียงหายใจดังตอนนอน MRI อาจเห็น hot cross bun sign ตอบสนองต่อ levodopa ไม่ดี การรักษาเป็นแบบประคับประคอง เช่น แก้ความดันตก สวนปัสสาวะเป็นระยะ และดูแลทางเดินหายใจ

name: Multiplex mononeuropathy
formal: Mononeuritis multiplex, with asymmetric involvement of separate nerves, often due to vasculitis, diabetes, leprosy, or infections.
simple: Several different nerves are damaged one after another, causing patchy weakness and numbness.
more: Nerve and muscle biopsy, and vasculitis work-up; treat with immunosuppression for vasculitis.

name: Multisystem atrophy
formal: Alternative term for multiple system atrophy, an alpha-synucleinopathy with parkinsonism, cerebellar ataxia and autonomic failure.
simple: Another name for multiple system atrophy, a progressive brain disease with stiffness, balance problems and blood pressure problems.

name: Multisystem mitochondrial disorders
formal: Mitochondrial diseases affecting several organs, such as brain, muscle, heart, eye, ear and endocrine glands, from mtDNA or nuclear DNA mutations.
simple: Energy-production diseases of the cell that affect many organs of the body at once.

name: Multivitamin malabsorption syndromes
formal: Conditions such as coeliac disease, short bowel or bariatric surgery causing multiple vitamin deficiencies (B12, E, thiamine, copper), leading to neuropathy, myelopathy and ataxia.
simple: Gut problems that stop the body absorbing vitamins, leading to nerve and balance problems.

name: Munchausen syndrome
formal: Factitious disorder in which a person deliberately feigns or induces illness to assume the sick role without external gain; can present with neurological symptoms such as seizures or weakness.
simple: A mental health condition in which someone makes up or causes illness so as to receive medical care.
more: Diagnosis requires excluding real disease and finding inconsistent history. Management is supportive psychiatric care; confrontation is often unhelpful.

name: Muscle-specific kinase myasthenia gravis (MuSK MG)
formal: Autoimmune myasthenia with anti-MuSK antibodies, prominent bulbar, facial, neck and respiratory weakness, muscle atrophy and poor response to cholinesterase inhibitors.
simple: A type of myasthenia gravis causing weakness of the face, throat and neck, often responding poorly to usual medicines.
nN: muscle specific kinase myasthenia gravis musk mg
aN: musk mg | muscle specific kinase myasthenia gravis

name: Muscle–eye–brain disease (MEB)
formal: Congenital muscular dystrophy with cobblestone lissencephaly, eye malformations and severe developmental delay, from defective alpha-dystroglycan glycosylation (POMGNT1).
simple: A severe inherited condition from birth that affects muscle, eyes and brain.
more: Autosomal recessive; MRI shows brain malformation and CK is high; care is supportive, with limited survival in severe cases.
aN: meb | muscle eye brain disease

name: Muscular dystrophies
formal: Inherited progressive myopathies with muscle fibre degeneration, elevated CK and dystrophic biopsy, including Duchenne, Becker, limb-girdle and facioscapulohumeral types.
simple: Inherited conditions in which muscles gradually become weaker and waste away.
more: Diagnosed by CK, EMG, muscle imaging, biopsy with dystrophin, sarcoglycan or merosin immunostaining, and genetic testing. Corticosteroids help Duchenne; management is supportive with cardiac and respiratory surveillance and physiotherapy.

name: Muscular dystrophy
formal: Group of inherited primary muscle diseases with progressive degeneration and weakness, raised CK and dystrophic biopsy changes; caused by mutations in genes for muscle structural or membrane proteins.
simple: Inherited conditions in which muscles gradually break down and become weaker over time.
more: Diagnosis by CK, biopsy and genetic testing; patterns include Duchenne, limb-girdle, myotonic and facioscapulohumeral. Care is supportive with steroids, respiratory and cardiac care; some have gene-targeted therapy.

name: Muscular dystrophy (MDC) 1C
formal: Congenital muscular dystrophy from FKRP mutations causing alpha-dystroglycan hypoglycosylation, with proximal weakness, calf hypertrophy and respiratory or cardiac involvement.
simple: An inherited muscle disease from early life causing weakness, large calves and breathing trouble.
more: Autosomal recessive; very high CK; monitor respiration and heart; management supportive.
aN: mdc | muscular dystrophy 1c

name: Musicians occupational cramps
formal: Task-specific focal dystonia in musicians affecting hands or embouchure, with loss of motor control during playing but normal other activities.
simple: Involuntary cramping or curling of the hand or lips that only occurs when playing a musical instrument.

name: Myasthenia
formal: Autoimmune neuromuscular junction disorder with fatigable weakness caused by antibodies to AChR, MuSK or LRP4, often with ocular and bulbar symptoms.
simple: A condition where the immune system blocks nerve signals to muscles, causing weakness that worsens with activity.
more: Diagnosis with antibodies, repetitive stimulation or single-fibre EMG; treat with pyridostigmine, immunosuppression, thymectomy, IVIG and complement or FcRn inhibitors.

name: Myasthenia gravis (MG)
formal: Autoimmune neuromuscular junction disease with antibodies to acetylcholine receptors, MuSK or LRP4, causing fatigable ptosis, diplopia, bulbar and limb weakness; associated with thymoma.
simple: An autoimmune disease causing muscle weakness that worsens with activity, often affecting the eyelids, eyes, face and swallowing.
more: Diagnose with repetitive nerve stimulation showing decrement, single-fibre EMG with increased jitter, and antibody testing; CT chest for thymoma. Treat with pyridostigmine, immunosuppression, thymectomy and rescue IVIG or plasma exchange in crisis.

feat: Fatigable ptosis and diplopia; pupils always spared
Bulbar weakness (nasal speech, chewing fatigue) and proximal limb weakness
Reflexes and sensation normal
Myasthenic crisis: respiratory failure, often triggered by infection or drugs

case.story: Droopy eyelids and double vision that are worse in the evening; her voice becomes nasal by the end of a long conversation.
case.exam: Right ptosis increases after 60 s of upgaze, variable diplopia, normal pupils, neck flexion 4/5, normal reflexes.
case.tests: AChR antibody positive; RNS 3 Hz: 20% decrement; CT chest: anterior mediastinal mass.
case.q: What does the mass likely represent and how does it change management?
case.a: Thymoma — thymectomy is indicated regardless of MG severity.
