8 The Localization of Lesions Affecting the Ocular Motor System

ddx.pt: Proximal leg weakness, autonomic symptoms, reduced reflexes that improve after exercise; incremental response
Slowly progressive, non-fatigable ptosis and dysphagia, late onset, family history
Symmetric, non-fluctuating ophthalmoplegia; diplopia rare
Descending paralysis with dilated unreactive pupils
Proptosis and restrictive myopathy; ptosis absent (lid retraction instead)

aN: mg | myasthenia gravis | myasthenia | achr myasthenia | generalised myasthenia | ocular myasthenia gravis

det.patho: Autoantibodies against postsynaptic proteins at the neuromuscular junction — the acetylcholine receptor in about 85% of generalised cases, MuSK or LRP4 in a minority — reduce the safety factor of transmission. AChR antibodies are complement-fixing IgG1/3, whereas MuSK antibodies are IgG4 and do not activate complement. The thymus is central: thymic hyperplasia in early-onset disease and thymoma in about 10–15%. Incidence peaks in young women and in older men.
det.clinical: Fatigable weakness is the core feature: ptosis and diplopia that worsen through the day, then bulbar weakness (nasal speech, chewing fatigue, dysphagia), neck flexor and proximal limb weakness. About half start with ocular symptoms and most of those generalise within two years. MuSK-MG favours bulbar, neck and respiratory muscles with tongue atrophy. Myasthenic crisis — respiratory or severe bulbar failure — is often precipitated by infection, surgery, pregnancy or drugs such as aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, magnesium and beta-blockers.
det.diagnosis: Antibody testing comes first (AChR, then MuSK and LRP4 if negative); about half of purely ocular cases are seronegative. Repetitive nerve stimulation at 3 Hz shows a decrement above 10%, and single-fibre EMG jitter is the most sensitive test but not specific. The ice pack test supports ocular MG at the bedside. Image the chest for thymoma and check thyroid function. Exclude LEMS, botulism, mitochondrial myopathy, thyroid eye disease and brainstem lesions.
det.treatment: Pyridostigmine relieves symptoms. Most generalised patients need immunotherapy: prednisolone (start low and increase slowly to avoid early worsening) plus azathioprine or mycophenolate to spare steroids. Thymectomy benefits AChR-positive generalised patients aged roughly 18–65 and is mandatory for thymoma. Refractory disease options include rituximab (especially MuSK-MG), complement inhibitors (eculizumab, ravulizumab, zilucoplan) and FcRn blockers (efgartigimod, rozanolixizumab). Crisis is treated with ventilatory support and IVIG or plasma exchange, with temporary withdrawal of pyridostigmine if intubated.
det.prognosis: With modern therapy most patients achieve minimal manifestations and near-normal life expectancy; crisis mortality is now low.
pearls: Pupils are never involved in MG; if they are, think of a third nerve lesion or botulism.
High-dose steroids can transiently worsen MG — start low or admit.
Know the drugs to avoid: aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, macrolides, IV magnesium, some beta-blockers.
det.thd: MG เป็นโรคภูมิคุ้มกันสร้างแอนติบอดีต่อ acetylcholine receptor (หรือ MuSK, LRP4) ที่รอยต่อเส้นประสาทกับกล้ามเนื้อ อาการเด่นคืออ่อนแรงที่แย่ลงเมื่อใช้งานหรือช่วงเย็น เช่น หนังตาตก เห็นภาพซ้อน เสียงขึ้นจมูก กลืนลำบาก แต่รูม่านตาและความรู้สึกปกติ วินิจฉัยด้วยการตรวจแอนติบอดี RNS ที่พบ decrement และ CT ทรวงอกหา thymoma รักษาด้วย pyridostigmine สเตียรอยด์ ยากดภูมิ ผ่าตัด thymectomy และยาใหม่ เช่น complement inhibitor หรือ FcRn blocker ส่วน crisis ให้ IVIG หรือ plasma exchange

name: Myasthenia gravis-like syndrome
formal: Neuromuscular junction disorders mimicking myasthenia, including Lambert-Eaton syndrome, drug-induced myasthenia, botulism and congenital myasthenic syndromes, with fatigable weakness.
simple: A group of conditions that cause muscle weakness that worsens with activity, similar to myasthenia gravis.
more: Repetitive nerve stimulation, antibodies (VGCC, AChR) and drug history differentiate them. Treat the cause with 3,4-diaminopyridine, immunotherapy or withdrawal of the drug.

name: Myasthenic crisis
formal: Life-threatening exacerbation of myasthenia gravis with respiratory or bulbar failure needing ventilation, often precipitated by infection or drugs; treated with IVIG or plasma exchange.
simple: A dangerous worsening of myasthenia gravis in which breathing or swallowing muscles become too weak.

name: Myelitis
formal: Inflammation of the spinal cord causing motor, sensory and sphincter dysfunction; causes include MS, NMOSD, MOG disease, infections and post-infectious or paraneoplastic disease.
simple: Inflammation of the spinal cord that can cause weakness, numbness and bladder problems.

name: Myeloneuropathy
formal: Combined spinal cord and peripheral nerve disorder with spastic gait and neuropathy, seen in B12 or copper deficiency, HIV, HTLV-1 and nitrous oxide toxicity.
simple: A condition where both the spinal cord and the nerves in the limbs are damaged, causing stiff, weak and numb legs.

name: Myelopathy
formal: Disorder of the spinal cord with upper motor neuron signs, sensory level and sphincter disturbance, caused by compression (spondylosis), inflammation, vascular, infective or metabolic disease.
simple: Damage to the spinal cord causing weakness, numbness and bladder or bowel problems.
more: Investigate with MRI of the spine, CSF analysis (oligoclonal bands, AQP4 and MOG antibodies), B12, copper, HIV and syphilis serology, and urgent decompression for compressive lesions. Prognosis depends on the cause and the severity at presentation.

name: Myoadenylate deaminase (MAD) deficiency
formal: Common metabolic myopathy from AMPD1 variants with exercise intolerance and cramps, though often asymptomatic, and absent histochemical activity.
simple: An enzyme shortage in muscle that can cause tiredness or cramps with exercise, though many people have no symptoms.
more: Diagnosed by absent AMPD1 staining or genetic testing; the ischaemic forearm test shows low ammonia rise; reassurance and graded exercise.
aN: mad | myoadenylate deaminase deficiency

name: Myocardial infarction (MI)
formal: Acute heart muscle necrosis from coronary occlusion; neurologically relevant as a cause of cardioembolic stroke, hypoxic brain injury and syncope.
simple: A heart attack, when blood flow to part of the heart is blocked; it can lead to stroke or brain injury.
aN: mi | myocardial infarction

name: Myocarditis
formal: Inflammation of heart muscle, relevant to neurology as a source of cardioembolic stroke and association with myopathies, Duchenne and some autoimmune diseases.
simple: Inflammation of the heart muscle, which can cause strokes if clots form.

name: Myoclonic dystonia
formal: Early-onset disorder with alcohol-responsive myoclonic jerks and dystonia of neck and arms, often from SGCE mutation (DYT11), sometimes with anxiety or alcohol use.
simple: An inherited condition with sudden jerks and twisting postures of the neck and arms, often improving with alcohol.

name: Myoclonic encephalopathy
formal: Disorder with myoclonus and encephalopathy from metabolic, toxic, post-hypoxic or neurodegenerative causes, or opsoclonus-myoclonus in childhood.
simple: A brain condition with muscle jerks and reduced alertness caused by various illnesses or poisons.

name: Myoclonic encephalopathy of infancy
formal: Opsoclonus-myoclonus syndrome in infants with chaotic eye movements, myoclonus, ataxia and irritability, often paraneoplastic from neuroblastoma or post-infectious.
simple: A rare childhood illness with jerking limbs, rapid chaotic eye movements and poor balance, sometimes linked to a tumour.

name: Myoclonic epilepsy
formal: Epilepsy syndromes dominated by myoclonic seizures, including juvenile myoclonic epilepsy and progressive myoclonic epilepsies, with generalised spike-wave discharges.
simple: A kind of epilepsy in which the main seizures are sudden muscle jerks.

name: Myoclonic epilepsy with ragged red fibres (MERRF)
formal: Mitochondrial disease (m.8344A>G) with myoclonus, generalised epilepsy, ataxia and myopathy showing ragged-red fibres; lipomas and deafness may occur.
simple: An inherited energy-production disease causing muscle jerks, seizures, poor coordination and muscle weakness.
more: Diagnose by MT-TK m.8344A>G testing in blood or muscle, raised lactate, and EEG with generalised spike-wave and photosensitivity; MRI may show cerebellar atrophy. Treat seizures with levetiracetam, avoiding valproate.
ab: Myoclonic epilepsy with ragged red fibres
nN: myoclonic epilepsy with ragged red fibres merrf
aN: merrf | myoclonic epilepsy with ragged red fibres

name: Myoclonic seizures
formal: Brief, shock-like involuntary jerks from cortical epileptic discharge, often generalised, as in juvenile myoclonic epilepsy.
simple: Sudden, very brief muscle jerks caused by abnormal electrical activity in the brain.

name: Myoclonic-astatic epilepsy (Doose syndrome)
formal: Childhood generalised epilepsy with myoclonic, atonic and myoclonic-atonic seizures causing sudden falls, with generalised spike-wave EEG, variable cognitive outcome and links to SLC2A1 or SCN1A variants.
simple: A childhood epilepsy with sudden jerks and drop attacks causing falls, that may affect learning.
aN: doose syndrome | myoclonic astatic epilepsy

name: Myoclonus (PERM)
formal: Progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity and myoclonus: brainstem and spinal inflammatory disease with stiffness, spasms, myoclonus and hyperekplexia, linked to glycine receptor antibodies.
simple: A rare autoimmune disease causing muscle stiffness, spasms and jerks from inflammation in the brainstem and spinal cord.
more: Check glycine receptor antibodies, and CSF pleocytosis; MRI often normal. Treat with high-dose steroids, IVIG or plasmapheresis, and symptomatic benzodiazepines or baclofen; screen for tumours, and outcome is variable, with some fatal.
aN: perm | myoclonus

name: Myoclonus dystonia
formal: Early-onset inherited disorder with alcohol-responsive myoclonic jerks and dystonia of neck and arms, often from SGCE mutation (DYT11).
simple: An inherited condition with sudden jerks and twisting postures of the neck and arms, often improving with alcohol.
more: Diagnosis by SGCE gene testing, which is maternally imprinted so inherited paternally; EEG normal and EMG with brief myoclonic bursts. Treat with benzodiazepines, valproate, zonisamide or botulinum toxin; DBS to GPi is highly effective in severe cases.

name: Myoclonus epilepsy
formal: Progressive myoclonic epilepsy with action myoclonus, tonic-clonic seizures and ataxia, from conditions such as Unverricht-Lundborg, Lafora disease, MERRF and sialidosis.
simple: A group of rare seizure disorders with sudden muscle jerks, seizures and gradual loss of coordination.
more: Genetic testing confirms the type (CSTB, EPM2A, mitochondrial). Treat with valproate, levetiracetam, piracetam and avoid phenytoin; prognosis varies.

name: Myoclonus epilepsy and ragged-red fibre syndrome (MERRF)
formal: Mitochondrial disease (m.8344A>G) with myoclonus, generalised epilepsy, ataxia and myopathy showing ragged-red fibres; lipomas and deafness may occur.
simple: An inherited energy-production disease causing muscle jerks, seizures, poor coordination and muscle weakness.
ab: Myoclonus epilepsy and ragged-red fibre syndrome
nN: myoclonus epilepsy and ragged red fibre syndrome merrf
aN: merrf | myoclonus epilepsy and ragged red fibre syndrome

name: Myofacial pain syndrome (MPS)
formal: Regional musculoskeletal pain disorder with trigger points and taut bands, causing local and referred pain and restricted motion.
simple: A common muscle pain problem with tender knots that can send pain to other areas.
more: Diagnosis is clinical; treated with physiotherapy, stretching, trigger point injection and analgesics.
aN: mps | myofacial pain syndrome

name: Myofibrillar myopathies
formal: Genetically heterogeneous muscle diseases (desmin, myotilin, BAG3) with myofibrillar disorganisation and protein aggregates on biopsy, causing distal or proximal weakness, cardiomyopathy and neuropathy.
simple: Inherited muscle diseases where the internal structure of muscle fibres breaks down, causing weakness and sometimes heart problems.

name: Myofibrillar myopathy (MFM)
formal: Group of genetic myopathies caused by mutations in DES, MYOT, CRYAB, FLNC, and others, with myofibrillar disorganisation, Z-disc dissolution, desmin accumulation, and cardiomyopathy.
simple: An inherited muscle disease where the internal muscle fibres break down, causing slowly progressive weakness and often heart problems.
more: Biopsy shows desmin-positive aggregates; gene panel; monitor cardiac and respiratory function; no specific therapy.
aN: mfm | myofibrillar myopathy

name: Myopathies
formal: Heterogeneous group of primary muscle disorders causing weakness, including inherited, inflammatory, metabolic, toxic and endocrine causes.
simple: A broad group of diseases that directly affect muscles and cause weakness.
more: Evaluate with CK, EMG, MRI, biopsy and genetics; treatment depends on the cause.

name: Myopathies associated with malignancy
formal: Muscle diseases accompanying cancer, such as paraneoplastic dermatomyositis, necrotising myopathy or steroid and cachectic myopathy, with proximal weakness.
simple: Muscle weakness linked to cancer, either from the cancer itself or its treatment.

name: Myopathy
formal: Primary disease of skeletal muscle causing proximal weakness with raised CK and myopathic EMG; causes include inherited, inflammatory, endocrine, toxic and metabolic.
simple: A disease of the muscles themselves that leads to weakness, usually of the hips and shoulders.
more: Evaluation with CK, EMG, MRI, biopsy and genetics. Treatment depends on cause: steroids for inflammatory, stop statins or correct hormones for acquired forms.

name: Myorhythmia (mobile spasms)
formal: Slow, rhythmic 1 to 4 Hz repetitive movements of face, limbs or palate, often from brainstem lesions; seen in Whipple disease with oculomasticatory myorhythmia.
simple: Slow repeating rhythmic movements, often of the jaw or limbs, usually from a brainstem problem.
aN: mobile spasms | myorhythmia

name: Myosin storage disorders
formal: Myosin storage myopathy (hyaline body myopathy) from MYH7 variants, with subsarcolemmal hyaline bodies in type 1 fibres and scapuloperoneal or proximal weakness.
simple: An inherited muscle disease where a protein clumps inside muscle fibres, causing weakness.
more: Biopsy and MYH7 sequencing confirm it; supportive care and monitoring of cardiac and respiratory function.

name: Myositis
formal: Inflammatory myopathies such as polymyositis, dermatomyositis and inclusion body myositis, with proximal weakness, raised CK and inflammatory infiltrates on biopsy.
simple: Inflammation of muscles causing weakness, pain and tiredness.

name: Myotonia
formal: Delayed muscle relaxation after voluntary contraction or percussion due to channel dysfunction, as in myotonic dystrophy and myotonia congenita; improves with repeated activity (warm-up).
simple: A muscle that is slow to relax after being used, such as difficulty letting go of a handshake.
more: EMG shows repetitive discharges with waxing-waning frequency, and clinical myotonia can be provoked by percussion; the aetiology is determined by genetic testing. Treat symptoms with mexiletine, lamotrigine or carbamazepine and avoid beta-blockers.

name: Myotonia congenita
formal: Inherited chloride channel (CLCN1) disorder with myotonia and muscle hypertrophy, Thomsen (dominant) and Becker (recessive) types, with warm-up phenomenon.
simple: An inherited muscle condition with stiffness after rest that eases with repeated movement.
more: Electromyography shows myotonic discharges, and genetics identifies CLCN1 mutations; short exercise testing shows decrement with cooling. Mexiletine is first line; avoid depolarising agents such as suxamethonium.
th: กล้ามเนื้อคลายตัวช้าแต่กำเนิด (ช่องคลอไรด์) — กำมือแล้วปล่อยยาก ดีขึ้นเมื่อทำซ้ำ (warm-up) กล้ามเนื้อโต
feat: Stiffness after rest that eases with repeated movement (warm-up)
Athletic-looking muscle hypertrophy
Recessive (Becker) form: transient weakness at the start of movement; dominant (Thomsen) milder
No cataract, cardiac or endocrine features
inv: EMG: abundant myotonic discharges; short exercise test pattern
CLCN1 genetic testing

case.story: Stiff legs when he first runs off the start line; after a few strides he is fine. Shaking hands lingers.
case.exam: Muscular build, grip and percussion myotonia that improve after repeated grips, normal strength.
case.tests: EMG: myotonic discharges in all muscles; CLCN1 biallelic variants.
case.q: Which treatment reduces the stiffness?
case.a: Sodium-channel blockers such as mexiletine; avoid suxamethonium during anaesthesia.

ddx.pt: Stiffness worse with repetition and cold; face and hands
Distal weakness, ptosis, cataract, cardiac block
Proximal pain and weakness in older adults

aN: myotonia congenita | thomsen disease | becker myotonia | clcn1 | chloride channel myotonia

det.patho: Loss-of-function variants in CLCN1 reduce the resting chloride conductance of the muscle membrane. Without this electrical buffer, potassium accumulating in the T-tubules after activity depolarises the fibre and triggers repetitive self-sustaining discharges, so relaxation is delayed. Dominant (Thomsen) and recessive (Becker) forms exist; the recessive form is more common and more severe.
det.clinical: Stiffness is most noticeable at the start of movement after rest — rising from a chair, starting to run, releasing a grip — and lessens with repeated contractions (warm-up). Muscles are often hypertrophied, giving an athletic build. Becker patients may have brief transient weakness when first moving and mild fixed distal weakness later. Cold, pregnancy and emotional startle can worsen stiffness. There are no systemic features, which separates it from myotonic dystrophy.
det.diagnosis: Grip and percussion myotonia on examination with warm-up favour the diagnosis. Needle EMG shows abundant myotonic discharges in many muscles. The short exercise test, ideally with cooling, displays a characteristic CMAP pattern that helps separate chloride from sodium channel myotonia. CLCN1 sequencing confirms the diagnosis; CK is normal or slightly raised. Check ECG and eyes only if myotonic dystrophy is still in question.
det.treatment: Many patients need no drugs and learn to warm up. When stiffness limits function, mexiletine is the best-supported option (with baseline ECG); alternatives include lamotrigine, carbamazepine or other sodium-channel blockers. Depolarising muscle relaxants such as suxamethonium can cause severe masseter spasm and must be avoided; some drugs like beta-agonists may aggravate myotonia.
det.prognosis: Life expectancy is normal and the disorder is usually stable. Recessive forms may develop mild distal weakness over time.
pearls: Warm-up = chloride channel (CLCN1); worsening with repetition = sodium channel (paramyotonia).
Hypertrophied muscles without cataract or cardiac block distinguish it from DM1.
Flag suxamethonium risk on the anaesthetic record.
det.thd: Myotonia congenita เกิดจากยีน CLCN1 ทำให้ช่องคลอไรด์ของกล้ามเนื้อทำงานลดลง กล้ามเนื้อจึงคลายตัวช้า โดยเฉพาะหลังพักนาน ๆ แต่เมื่อทำซ้ำจะดีขึ้น (warm-up) กล้ามเนื้อมักโตคล้ายนักกีฬาและไม่มีอาการนอกกล้ามเนื้อ วินิจฉัยด้วย EMG ที่พบ myotonic discharge และตรวจยีน CLCN1 ถ้าอาการรบกวนใช้ mexiletine และต้องหลีกเลี่ยง suxamethonium เมื่อดมยาสลบ

name: Myotonia congenital (MC)
formal: Skeletal muscle chloride channelopathy (CLCN1) with myotonia and warm-up phenomenon, as dominant Thomsen or recessive Becker disease.
simple: An inherited muscle condition where muscles stay stiff after contraction, improving with repetition.
more: EMG shows myotonic discharges; Becker form also has transient weakness; mexiletine helps.
aN: mc | myotonia congenital

name: Myotonia fluctuans
formal: Nondystrophic myotonia from SCN4A mutations with fluctuating myotonia, triggered by potassium or exercise, but with no weakness or pain.
simple: A rare inherited muscle stiffness that comes and goes, often after exercise or potassium-rich food.
more: Sodium channel gene testing and EMG; mexiletine is the first-line treatment, with trigger avoidance.

name: Myotonia permanens
formal: Severe sodium channel myotonia (SCN4A) with continuous myotonia and muscle hypertrophy, with potential for respiratory difficulty.
simple: A severe inherited form where muscles stay stiff constantly, with bulky muscles, and sometimes breathing difficulty.
more: EMG shows continuous myotonic discharges; mexiletine is effective; avoid triggers such as potassium.

name: Myotonic dystrophies (DM)
formal: Autosomal dominant multisystem disorders (DM1 CTG expansion in DMPK; DM2 CCTG in CNBP) with myotonia, weakness, cataracts, cardiac conduction defects and endocrine disorders.
simple: Inherited conditions causing muscle weakness and stiffness along with problems in the eyes, heart and hormones.
aN: dm | myotonic dystrophies

name: Myotonic dystrophy
formal: Autosomal dominant multisystem disorder (DM1 CTG expansion in DMPK) with myotonia, distal weakness, cataracts, cardiac conduction defects, frontal balding and endocrine problems.
simple: An inherited condition causing muscle weakness and stiffness along with problems in the eyes, heart and hormones.
more: Diagnosis rests on DMPK CTG repeat testing; CK is mildly raised and EMG shows myotonic discharges with a dive-bomber sound. Annual ECG and respiratory review are required, as arrhythmia and aspiration are leading causes of death; mexiletine for myotonia.

name: Myotonic dystrophy type 1 (DM1)
formal: Autosomal dominant multisystem disorder from CTG expansion in DMPK, with myotonia, distal weakness, cataracts, cardiac conduction defects and anticipation.
simple: An inherited disease causing muscle stiffness and wasting, cataracts, and heart and other problems.
more: Diagnosed by DMPK repeat testing; manage with cardiac surveillance, mexiletine, cataract surgery and ventilation care; congenital form is severe.
th: กล้ามเนื้อเสื่อมพันธุกรรมที่มีอาการกำมือแล้วคลายช้า หนังตาตก หน้ายาว ต้อกระจก และหัวใจเต้นผิดจังหวะ
feat: Grip and percussion myotonia
Distal-predominant weakness, ptosis, temporal and masseter wasting, frontal balding
Multisystem: cataract, cardiac conduction block, diabetes, hypersomnia
Anticipation with expanding CTG repeats
inv: Genetic testing: DMPK CTG expansion
EMG myotonic discharges
ECG/Holter, slit-lamp eye exam, glucose

case.story: Hard to let go of door handles in the cold; he has had cataract surgery already.
case.exam: Bilateral ptosis, hatchet face, slow grip release, weak finger and ankle dorsiflexors.
case.tests: ECG: PR 240 ms; DMPK CTG expansion 600 repeats.
case.q: Why does the ECG matter more than the weakness for survival?
case.a: Conduction disease can cause sudden death; he may need a pacemaker or ICD.

ddx.pt: Proximal weakness, muscle pain, milder; CCTG in CNBP
Myotonia with muscle hypertrophy, no dystrophy or systemic features
No myotonia; scapular winging

aN: dm1 | myotonic dystrophy type 1 | steinert disease | dystrophia myotonica | myotonic dystrophy

det.patho: An autosomal dominant disorder caused by CTG repeat expansion within the non-coding 3′ end of the DMPK gene (chromosome 19). The mutant RNA forms nuclear foci that sequester MBNL splicing regulators, causing mis-splicing of many transcripts, such as the muscle chloride channel (myotonia) and insulin receptor (insulin resistance). Repeat size tends to grow across generations (anticipation), especially via maternal transmission, and larger expansions cause earlier, more severe disease, including congenital DM1.
det.clinical: Adult-onset DM1 causes distal limb weakness (finger flexors, ankle dorsiflexors), facial, jaw and neck flexor weakness with ptosis, temporal wasting and frontal balding producing a 'hatchet face', and grip or percussion myotonia. Multisystem features include early cataracts, cardiac conduction disease and arrhythmias, insulin resistance, hypogonadism, excessive daytime sleepiness, apathy, gastrointestinal dysmotility and respiratory muscle weakness. Congenital DM1 presents with neonatal hypotonia, respiratory failure and intellectual disability.
det.diagnosis: Genetic testing for the DMPK CTG expansion is definitive (normal under about 35 repeats; disease usually above 50). EMG shows myotonic discharges with myopathic units, which may be used if genetics is delayed. CK is normal or mildly raised. Baseline assessment includes ECG and Holter, echocardiography, slit-lamp examination, glucose and HbA1c, thyroid and gonadal function, pulmonary function tests and a sleep evaluation.
det.treatment: Management is multidisciplinary and largely supportive. Annual ECG screening, with electrophysiology study and pacemaker or ICD when conduction disease or arrhythmia is found, is the main life-saving intervention. Mexiletine can relieve troublesome myotonia (with cardiac screening), modafinil helps sleepiness, and NIV treats respiratory failure. Provide cataract surgery, orthoses, diabetes care and genetic counselling. Anaesthesia carries risk because of sensitivity to sedatives and respiratory weakness.
det.prognosis: Life expectancy is reduced, mainly from respiratory failure and sudden cardiac death; severity correlates loosely with repeat length.
pearls: Distal weakness + myotonia + ptosis + early cataracts = DM1.
The heart, not the muscles, often determines survival — screen ECG yearly.
Anaesthesia is hazardous: sensitivity to opioids and sedatives.
det.thd: DM1 เป็นโรคกล้ามเนื้อเสื่อมทางพันธุกรรมแบบ autosomal dominant จาก CTG repeat ที่ยาวผิดปกติในยีน DMPK และยาวขึ้นในรุ่นต่อไป (anticipation) อาการคือกล้ามเนื้อคลายช้าหลังกำมือ (myotonia) อ่อนแรงส่วนปลาย หนังตาตก หน้ายาวขมับตอบ ศีรษะล้านด้านหน้า ร่วมกับต้อกระจกเร็ว หัวใจนำไฟฟ้าผิดปกติ เบาหวาน และง่วงนอนมาก วินิจฉัยด้วยการตรวจยีน การรักษาเป็นแบบประคับประคอง ที่สำคัญคือตรวจ ECG ทุกปีและใส่ pacemaker หรือ ICD เมื่อจำเป็น และระวังการดมยาสลบ

name: Myotonic dystrophy type 2 (DM2) or proximal myotonic myopathy (PROMM)
formal: Autosomal dominant multisystem myopathy from CCTG expansion in CNBP, with proximal weakness, myalgia, myotonia, cataracts and cardiac involvement.
simple: An inherited disease mainly with thigh and hip weakness, muscle pain and cataracts, milder than type 1.
more: Genetic testing; clinical care is symptomatic with cardiac and eye monitoring.
ab: Myotonic dystrophy type 2  or proximal myotonic myopathy
th: myotonic dystrophy ชนิดที่ 2 — อ่อนแรงต้นขา ปวดกล้ามเนื้อ myotonia เล็กน้อย เริ่มวัยผู้ใหญ่ อาการเบากว่า DM1
tempoNote: Onset usually in the 30s–60s; slow progression; no congenital form
feat: Proximal leg weakness (hip flexors, thigh) and neck flexor weakness; face and distal muscles less affected
Muscle pain and stiffness, often the main complaint; myotonia mild or intermittent
Early cataract, insulin resistance, hypogonadism, cardiac conduction defects
Mildly raised CK and GGT; often misdiagnosed as fibromyalgia or polymyositis
inv: EMG: myotonic discharges (may be patchy, need many muscles) with myopathic units
CNBP (ZNF9) CCTG repeat expansion test
ECG/Holter, slit-lamp eye exam, HbA1c

case.story: Several years of aching thighs, trouble rising from low chairs and squatting at the market; had cataract surgery at 45. Her brother has similar thigh weakness.
case.exam: Mild hip-flexor and neck-flexor weakness, subtle grip myotonia after repeated effort, normal face.
case.tests: CK 350 U/L; EMG: waning myotonic discharges in proximal muscles; CCTG expansion in CNBP; ECG first-degree AV block.
case.q: Name two key differences from DM1.
case.a: DM2 is proximal rather than distal/facial weakness, has no congenital form or clear anticipation, and is generally milder with pain as a prominent symptom.

det.patho: DM2 is caused by an expanded CCTG tetranucleotide repeat in intron 1 of CNBP. Like DM1, expanded RNA accumulates in nuclear foci and sequesters splicing regulators (MBNL), so muscle-chloride-channel and insulin-receptor transcripts are mis-spliced, producing myotonia and insulin resistance. Repeat size correlates poorly with severity and anticipation is minimal.
det.clinical: Presentation is in adulthood with proximal weakness, myalgia, stiffness and fatigue. Myotonia may be subtle and missed on bedside testing. Multisystem features—cataract, diabetes, testicular failure, hyperhidrosis and cardiac conduction disease—are common but less severe than in DM1; cognitive involvement is mild. Many patients spend years with diagnoses such as fibromyalgia or seronegative myositis.
det.diagnosis: Suspect DM2 with proximal weakness plus pain, early cataract, or myotonic discharges on EMG. Genetic testing for the CNBP expansion is diagnostic; standard PCR may miss it, so repeat-primed or Southern methods are used. Muscle biopsy is nonspecific but may show type 2 fibre atrophy and nuclear clumps. Screen heart, eyes, glucose and endocrine function at diagnosis.
det.treatment: Management is supportive: exercise and physiotherapy, pain control (NSAIDs, gabapentinoids), and mexiletine for disabling myotonia after cardiac assessment. Annual ECG with Holter or electrophysiology for conduction disease, cataract surgery when needed, and diabetes management. Statins may worsen muscle symptoms. Inform anaesthetists given sensitivity to sedatives and possible arrhythmia.
det.prognosis: Most patients remain ambulant into old age; lifespan is near normal unless significant cardiac disease occurs.
pearls: Proximal weakness with muscle pain and early cataract in a middle-aged adult: test for DM2.
Myotonia may only be found on EMG — sample many muscles.
DM2 has no congenital form, unlike DM1.
det.thd: DM2 เกิดจาก CCTG repeat expansion ในยีน CNBP เริ่มอาการในวัยผู้ใหญ่ด้วยกล้ามเนื้อต้นขาและคออ่อนแรง ปวดตึงกล้ามเนื้อ myotonia เล็กน้อย ร่วมกับต้อกระจกเร็ว เบาหวาน และ conduction block ของหัวใจ อาการเบากว่า DM1 และไม่มีรูปแบบแต่กำเนิด มักถูกวินิจฉัยผิดเป็น fibromyalgia ยืนยันด้วยการตรวจยีน และต้องตรวจหัวใจ ตา และน้ำตาลเป็นระยะ

ddx.pt: Distal and facial weakness, ptosis, temporal wasting, prominent grip myotonia, congenital form
Quadriceps and finger flexor weakness, no myotonia, age > 50
Prominent myotonia with warm-up and muscle hypertrophy; no cataract, little weakness

nN: myotonic dystrophy type 2 dm2 or proximal myotonic myopathy promm
aN: dm2 | promm | myotonic dystrophy type 2 or proximal myotonic myopathy | proximal myotonic myopathy | cnbp myotonic dystrophy | znf9 myotonic dystrophy

name: Myotonic syndromes
formal: Group of muscle channelopathies and dystrophies featuring myotonia, including myotonia congenita, paramyotonia congenita, and DM1 and DM2.
simple: A group of conditions where muscles are slow to relax after contraction.

name: Mystonic dystrophy type 1 (DM1)
formal: Autosomal dominant CTG repeat expansion in DMPK causing multisystem disease with myotonia, distal weakness, cataracts, cardiac conduction defects, insulin resistance, and cognitive involvement.
simple: An inherited condition causing muscle weakness and stiffness, cataracts, and heart rhythm and thinking problems that can worsen across generations.
more: Confirm with repeat-expansion testing; EMG shows myotonia. Monitor with ECG, treat myotonia with mexiletine, and provide respiratory and cardiac surveillance.
aN: dm1 | mystonic dystrophy type 1

name: Ménière’s disease
formal: Inner ear disorder with recurrent vertigo lasting minutes to hours, fluctuating low-frequency hearing loss, tinnitus and aural fullness attributed to endolymphatic hydrops.
simple: An inner ear problem causing attacks of spinning dizziness, ringing in the ear and hearing loss that comes and goes.

name: Möbius syndrome
formal: Congenital facial diplegia with abducens palsy from brainstem cranial nerve nuclei hypoplasia, causing expressionless face, inability to abduct eyes and sometimes limb anomalies.
simple: A rare condition from birth where facial muscles and eye movements to the side are weak, giving a face with little expression.

name: Narcolepsy
formal: Chronic hypersomnia disorder with excessive daytime sleepiness, cataplexy (type 1) from hypocretin loss, hypnagogic hallucinations, sleep paralysis and short REM latency; associated with HLA-DQB1*06:02.
simple: A sleep disorder with overwhelming daytime sleepiness and sometimes sudden muscle weakness triggered by emotion.

name: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma
formal: Epithelial tumour of the nasopharynx associated with EBV, spreading through the skull base to cause multiple cranial neuropathies, headache and cervical nodes.
simple: A cancer at the back of the nose that can invade the skull base and damage nerves of the face and eyes.

name: Nasu-Hakola disease
formal: Polycystic lipomembranous osteodysplasia with sclerosing leukoencephalopathy from TREM2 or TYROBP mutations, causing bone cysts and presenile frontal dementia.
simple: A rare inherited disease causing bone cysts and an early dementia with personality change.

name: Neck flexion dystonia
formal: Anterocollis, a cervical dystonia pattern with forward neck flexion, seen in idiopathic dystonia, multiple system atrophy, Parkinson disease and myopathy, such as the dropped head syndrome.
simple: Abnormal forward bending of the neck so the chin drops toward the chest.
more: Distinguish from neck extensor myopathy and parkinsonian syndromes. Botulinum toxin to the longus colli and sternocleidomastoid has mixed results; collars and physiotherapy help.

name: Necrotising autoimmune myopathy (NAM)
formal: Immune-mediated myopathy with subacute proximal weakness, very high CK and necrotic fibres without much inflammation; anti-SRP or anti-HMGCR antibodies, may follow statins.
simple: An autoimmune muscle disease causing rapidly progressing weakness, sometimes after using cholesterol drugs.
aN: nam | necrotising autoimmune myopathy

name: Necrotising myelopathy
formal: Acute or subacute spinal cord necrosis, as in paraneoplastic, infective, post-radiation or vascular causes, with severe and often irreversible paraplegia.
simple: Severe damage and death of tissue in the spinal cord, causing sudden leg weakness and loss of feeling.

name: Necrotizing myopathy
formal: Myopathy with prominent muscle fibre necrosis and little inflammation, including immune-mediated forms with anti-SRP or anti-HMGCR antibodies and statin or paraneoplastic forms.
simple: A muscle disease where muscle fibres die, causing marked weakness, often linked to statin drugs or immune antibodies.
more: CK is very high; check anti-SRP and anti-HMGCR antibodies; immunotherapy with steroids, IVIG, and others is required.

name: Necrotizing vasculitis/vasculopathy
formal: Inflammatory destruction of vessel walls causing ischaemic neuropathy or myopathy, as in polyarteritis nodosa or ANCA vasculitis.
simple: Inflammation of blood vessels cutting off blood supply to nerves and muscles, leading to pain and weakness.
more: Diagnosed by biopsy and serology; treated with steroids and cyclophosphamide or rituximab.

name: Negative myoclonus
formal: Brief lapses of muscle tone causing sudden postural loss without prior contraction, such as asterixis, from epileptic or non-epileptic cortical mechanisms.
simple: Sudden brief loss of muscle strength causing a limb to drop or the body to sag.

name: Nelson’s syndrome
formal: Enlargement of an ACTH-secreting pituitary adenoma after bilateral adrenalectomy for Cushing disease, causing hyperpigmentation, headaches and visual field defects.
simple: Growth of a pituitary tumour after removal of the adrenal glands, causing darker skin, headaches and vision problems.

name: Nemaline myopathy
formal: Congenital myopathy with rod-shaped nemaline bodies on biopsy, hypotonia, facial and proximal weakness and respiratory involvement; NEB, ACTA1 and TPM mutations.
simple: An inherited muscle disease present from birth, with floppiness and weakness, including the face and breathing muscles.
more: Muscle biopsy with Gomori trichrome stain shows rods on a background of normal fibres; CK is usually normal. Genetics clarifies the subtype; management is supportive with respiratory and nutritional care, and severity is mostly determined by the age of onset.

name: Neonatal myoclonic epilepsy
formal: Early myoclonic encephalopathy or similar neonatal syndrome with erratic myoclonus, burst-suppression EEG and metabolic or structural causes with poor prognosis.
simple: A serious seizure disorder in newborns with muscle jerks and developmental problems.

name: Neonatal pyridoxine deficiency
formal: Pyridoxine-dependent epilepsy (ALDH7A1) causing intractable neonatal seizures that respond to pyridoxine, with developmental risk if untreated.
simple: A rare condition where newborns have seizures that only stop with vitamin B6.

name: Neoplastic parkinsonism
formal: Parkinsonism secondary to tumours, particularly frontal, basal ganglia or midbrain lesions, or paraneoplastic processes.
simple: Stiffness, slowness and tremor caused by a tumour in the brain.

name: Neuro-Behçet syndrome (NBS)
formal: Neurological involvement of Behcet disease, parenchymal brainstem and diencephalic inflammation or cerebral venous thrombosis, with oral ulcers, uveitis and genital ulcers.
simple: Behcet disease affecting the brain or nerves, causing headaches, weakness or balance problems alongside mouth ulcers.
aN: nbs | neuro behcet syndrome

name: Neuroacanthocytosis
formal: Group of disorders with chorea, orofacial dyskinesia and acanthocytes, notably chorea-acanthocytosis (VPS13A) and McLeod syndrome, with self-mutilation, seizures and neuropathy.
simple: Rare inherited disorders causing involuntary movements, lip and tongue biting and unusual spiky red blood cells.
more: Blood smear for acanthocytes, CK and Kell phenotype in McLeod; chorea-acanthocytosis is autosomal recessive VPS13A with caudate atrophy on MRI. No disease-modifying therapy; manage with dopamine-depleting drugs, antiepileptics and bite protection.

name: Neuroaxonal dystrophy
formal: Infantile or late-onset neurodegeneration with axonal spheroids, PLA2G6 mutation, developmental regression, hypotonia, optic atrophy and iron accumulation.
simple: A rare inherited disease where nerves in the brain gradually deteriorate, causing loss of skills and weakness in children.
more: Nerve or skin biopsy shows axonal spheroids; MRI shows cerebellar atrophy with T2 hypointensity in the globus pallidus and cerebellar cortex hyperintensity. Autosomal recessive, with no cure; treatment is supportive with seizure and spasticity control.

name: Neuroaxonal leucodystrophy
formal: Rare adult-onset disorder with axonal spheroids and leukoencephalopathy, including hereditary diffuse leukoencephalopathy with spheroids from CSF1R mutations.
simple: A rare adult brain disease in which white matter degenerates, causing thinking and movement problems.

name: Neuroblastoma
formal: Paediatric tumour of sympathetic neural crest, with opsoclonus-myoclonus syndrome, spinal cord compression from dumbbell tumour and Horner syndrome.
simple: A childhood cancer from nerve tissue, usually in the abdomen, that can cause jerking eye movements or spine compression.

name: Neurocognitive disorders, HIV-associated
formal: HIV-associated neurocognitive disorder spectrum from asymptomatic impairment to HIV dementia, with subcortical slowing, apathy and motor features.
simple: Thinking, memory and movement problems in people with HIV infection.
aN: neurocognitive disorders | hiv associated

name: Neurocutaneous syndromes
formal: Phakomatoses such as neurofibromatosis, tuberous sclerosis, Sturge-Weber and von Hippel-Lindau with combined skin lesions and nervous system tumours or malformations.
simple: Genetic conditions with skin marks together with tumours or abnormalities of the brain and nerves.

name: Neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation (NBIA)
formal: Group of genetic disorders (PKAN, PLA2G6, BPAN) with basal ganglia iron deposition on MRI, causing dystonia, parkinsonism, spasticity and cognitive decline.
simple: Inherited diseases where iron builds up in the brain, causing stiffness, abnormal postures and decline in movement and thinking.
more: MRI (eye-of-the-tiger sign in PKAN; cerebellar atrophy in PLA2G6) with T2* sequences showing iron; genetic testing. Treatment is symptomatic; deferiprone has been trialled in PKAN, and BPAN is X-linked dominant (WDR45) with early epilepsy.
nN: neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation nbia
aN: nbia | neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation

name: Neuroepithelial tumours
formal: Group of primary CNS tumours from neuroepithelial cells, including gliomas, ependymomas, embryonal and choroid plexus tumours.
simple: Brain tumours arising from the brain's own supporting and nerve cells.

name: Neuroferritinopathy
formal: Autosomal dominant FTL mutation causing basal ganglia iron and ferritin deposition with adult-onset chorea, dystonia or parkinsonism and low serum ferritin.
simple: An inherited iron-storage brain disease causing involuntary movements and stiffness in adulthood.
more: Diagnosis by FTL gene sequencing, with MRI showing iron deposition and cystic changes in basal ganglia; normal or low ferritin raises suspicion. No iron chelation benefit has been proven; treatment is symptomatic with poor response to levodopa.

name: Neurofibromas
formal: Benign peripheral nerve sheath tumours of Schwann cells and fibroblasts, solitary or multiple in NF1, with plexiform types having malignant potential.
simple: Non-cancerous tumours of nerve tissue, often forming lumps under the skin.

name: Neurofibromas, spinal
formal: Spinal nerve root neurofibromas, solitary or multiple in NF1, causing radiculopathy or cord compression with dumbbell extension through foramina.
simple: Non-cancerous nerve growths near the spine that can press on the spinal cord or nerve roots.
aN: neurofibromas | spinal

name: Neurofibromatosis
formal: Group of autosomal dominant tumour predisposition syndromes (NF1, NF2, schwannomatosis) with neurofibromas, schwannomas, skin lesions and CNS tumours.
simple: Inherited conditions causing growths on nerves and skin changes.

name: Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1)
formal: Autosomal dominant NF1 gene disorder with cafe-au-lait spots, neurofibromas, axillary freckling, Lisch nodules, optic glioma, sphenoid dysplasia and learning difficulties.
simple: An inherited condition with brown skin spots and many soft nerve lumps, sometimes with learning difficulties.
aN: nf1 | neurofibromatosis type 1

name: Neurofibromatosis type 2 (NF2)
formal: Autosomal dominant NF2 (merlin) disorder with bilateral vestibular schwannomas, meningiomas and ependymomas, causing deafness, tinnitus and imbalance.
simple: An inherited condition with tumours on the hearing nerves on both sides, causing hearing loss and balance problems.
aN: nf2 | neurofibromatosis type 2

name: Neurogenic atrophy
formal: Muscle atrophy resulting from denervation due to lower motor neuron or nerve disease, with angulated fibres and fibre type grouping on biopsy.
simple: Muscle wasting because the nerve supplying it is damaged.
more: EMG shows chronic denervation; treat underlying neuropathy or motor neuron disease.

name: Neurogenic thoracic outlet syndrome
formal: Compression of the lower trunk of the brachial plexus by a cervical rib or band, causing hand wasting, mainly of thenar muscles, with ulnar sensory loss.
simple: Pressure on nerves near the collarbone that causes wasting and weakness of the hand.
more: Diagnosed by EMG showing low median motor and ulnar sensory amplitudes and imaging; treat with surgical resection of the band or rib.

name: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS)
formal: Life-threatening reaction to dopamine antagonists with fever, lead-pipe rigidity, autonomic instability, altered consciousness and raised CK; treatment is stopping drug and supportive care.
simple: A dangerous reaction to certain psychiatric or anti-nausea medicines, causing high fever, severe stiffness and confusion.
more: Diagnose from clinical features; CK often over 1000, with leucocytosis and low iron. Stop dopamine antagonists, give IV fluids, cooling, benzodiazepines, dantrolene or bromocriptine; rhabdomyolysis and renal failure are the main complications.

tempoNote: Develops over 1–3 days, usually within the first 2 weeks of starting or increasing a dopamine blocker
feat: Lead-pipe rigidity of the whole body, often with tremor
High fever (often over 38.5 °C) not explained by infection
Altered consciousness: confusion, mutism, stupor
Autonomic instability: tachycardia, labile blood pressure, sweating, incontinence
Rigidity typically precedes fever; hyperreflexia and clonus are not typical
inv: CK (often several thousand or higher), creatinine, potassium, urine myoglobin
Leucocytosis, low serum iron, liver enzymes, coagulation
Septic work-up, lumbar puncture if CNS infection is possible
CT/MRI and EEG if diagnosis unclear (encephalitis, NCSE)

case.who: 28-year-old man admitted to a psychiatric ward in Khon Kaen
case.story: Given IM haloperidol repeatedly over 2 days for agitation; now stiff, sweating and barely responding.
case.exam: Temp 40.1 °C, HR 132, BP 170/100 then 95/60; generalised lead-pipe rigidity, mute, reflexes normal, no clonus, pupils normal.
case.tests: CK 28,000 U/L, WBC 16,000, creatinine rising; blood cultures and CSF normal.
case.q: What are the immediate management steps?
case.a: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome: stop all dopamine blockers, ICU care with cooling, IV fluids for rhabdomyolysis, benzodiazepines; add bromocriptine and/or dantrolene if severe; consider ECT if refractory.

det.patho: Abrupt central D2 blockade in hypothalamus and striatum disturbs thermoregulation and causes rigidity, while sympathetic overactivity drives autonomic instability; muscle breakdown adds heat and CK. Risk factors are high-potency or depot drugs, rapid escalation, parenteral route, dehydration, agitation, restraint and previous NMS. Withdrawal of levodopa in Parkinson disease produces a similar picture.
det.clinical: Onset is usually within days of a new drug or dose increase but can occur at any time. Mental change and rigidity often come first, followed by fever and autonomic swings. Complications include rhabdomyolysis with renal failure, DIC, aspiration pneumonia, venous thrombosis and cardiac arrhythmia. Atypical NMS with second-generation drugs may have less rigidity or lower fever.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical, supported by high CK and leucocytosis; international expert consensus criteria list exposure, hyperthermia, rigidity, mental change, CK rise and autonomic features. Exclude sepsis, meningitis/encephalitis, serotonin syndrome, malignant hyperthermia, anticholinergic toxicity, heat stroke, thyroid storm and non-convulsive status.
det.treatment: Stop the culprit drug (or restart dopaminergic therapy in PD), move to monitored care, cool actively, hydrate and correct electrolytes, and prevent thrombosis. Benzodiazepines (lorazepam) are useful early. In moderate-severe cases add bromocriptine or amantadine and dantrolene for extreme hyperthermia. ECT is effective for refractory cases or overlapping catatonia. Wait at least two weeks after recovery before cautious rechallenge with a low-potency agent.
det.prognosis: Mortality is now around 5–10% with early recognition; most recover over 1–2 weeks (longer after depot drugs).
pearls: Rigidity + fever + confusion after a dopamine blocker = NMS until proven otherwise.
Clonus and hyperreflexia point to serotonin syndrome instead.
Abrupt stop of levodopa in PD can cause the same syndrome.
det.thd: NMS เป็นภาวะฉุกเฉินที่เกิดจากยาต้านโดปามีน หรือหยุดยาพาร์กินสันกะทันหัน ผู้ป่วยมีไข้สูง กล้ามเนื้อแข็งแบบ lead-pipe ซึม และความดัน ชีพจรแปรปรวน CK สูงมาก เสี่ยงไตวาย ต้องหยุดยาทันที ดูแลใน ICU ลดไข้ ให้สารน้ำ ให้ benzodiazepine และพิจารณา bromocriptine หรือ dantrolene ในรายรุนแรง

name: Neuroleptics akathisia
formal: Drug-induced motor restlessness from antipsychotics, with inability to sit still, pacing and subjective inner tension.
simple: Strong inner restlessness and need to move caused by antipsychotic medicines.

name: Neuromascular transmission (NMT) disorders
formal: Disorders of signal transmission at the neuromuscular junction, including myasthenia gravis, Lambert-Eaton syndrome, congenital myasthenia and botulism.
simple: Conditions where nerve signals fail to pass properly to muscle, producing fatigable weakness.
more: Evaluate with repetitive stimulation and antibodies; treatment depends on mechanism.

name: Neuromuscular diseases
formal: Broad group of disorders of the motor unit, including motor neuron, nerve, junction and muscle diseases.
simple: Diseases affecting the nerves and muscles that control movement.
more: Work-up includes examination, EMG, CK, imaging and genetics, guiding specific therapy.

name: Neuromuscular junction (NMJ) disorders
formal: Disorders of synaptic transmission between nerve and muscle, such as myasthenia gravis, Lambert-Eaton syndrome, botulism and congenital myasthenic syndromes, with fatigable weakness.
simple: Conditions where messages from nerves to muscles are blocked, causing weakness that worsens with use.

name: Neuromuscular transmission disorders
formal: Disorders of signal transmission at the neuromuscular junction, including myasthenia gravis, Lambert-Eaton syndrome, congenital myasthenia and botulism.
simple: Conditions where nerve signals fail to pass properly to muscle, producing fatigable weakness.
more: Evaluate with repetitive stimulation and antibodies; treatment depends on mechanism.

name: Neuromyelitis optica
formal: Autoimmune astrocytopathy with optic neuritis and longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis, associated with AQP4-IgG, area postrema syndrome and relapses.
simple: An autoimmune disease causing inflammation of the eye nerves and spinal cord, leading to vision loss and weakness.

name: Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (NMOSD)
formal: Autoimmune AQP4 antibody-mediated disorder with optic neuritis, longitudinally extensive myelitis, area postrema syndrome and brainstem or diencephalic syndromes with relapses.
simple: An autoimmune disease causing inflammation of the eye nerves and spinal cord, leading to vision loss and weakness.
th: โรคภูมิต้านทานทำลายเส้นประสาทตาและไขสันหลังรุนแรง ตรวจพบแอนติบอดี AQP4 พบมากในหญิงเอเชีย
feat: Severe, often bilateral or sequential optic neuritis with poor recovery
Longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis (≥3 vertebral segments)
Area postrema syndrome: intractable hiccups, nausea and vomiting
Relapses accumulate disability; MS drugs may worsen it
inv: Serum AQP4-IgG (cell-based assay)
MRI spine: central longitudinally extensive lesion; MRI orbit: long optic nerve/chiasm lesion
CSF may show neutrophils; oligoclonal bands usually absent

case.story: Two weeks of hiccups and vomiting, then over 3 days weakness of both legs and urinary retention.
case.exam: Paraparesis, T4 sensory level, extensor plantars; visual acuity normal.
case.tests: MRI: central cord lesion C7–T8; serum AQP4-IgG positive.
case.q: What did the hiccups and vomiting represent?
case.a: Area postrema syndrome — the dorsal medulla is rich in AQP4 and is a typical NMOSD target.
