det.patho: An antibody-mediated astrocytopathy: IgG against aquaporin-4 water channels on astrocyte end-feet activates complement, destroys astrocytes and causes secondary demyelination and necrosis. Lesions cluster in AQP4-rich regions — optic nerves, central spinal cord, area postrema and periependymal areas. It is much more common in women and has a relatively higher share of demyelinating disease in East and Southeast Asian populations; it frequently coexists with other autoimmune conditions, notably Sjögren syndrome and lupus.
det.clinical: Core syndromes are severe optic neuritis (often bilateral or involving the chiasm), longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis, area postrema syndrome with intractable hiccups or vomiting, acute brainstem syndromes, diencephalic syndromes with hypersomnolence, and symptomatic cerebral lesions. Attacks are typically more severe and recover less than in MS, so disability accumulates with each relapse. Painful tonic spasms after myelitis are characteristic. A progressive course independent of relapses is unusual.
det.diagnosis: The 2015 IPND criteria require one core clinical characteristic with positive AQP4-IgG (cell-based assay preferred), or stricter clinical and MRI requirements when seronegative. MRI typically shows a central cord lesion spanning three or more vertebral segments, and long posterior optic nerve or chiasmal lesions. CSF may show neutrophils or eosinophils with pleocytosis; oligoclonal bands are usually absent. Test MOG-IgG in seronegative cases, and avoid labelling as MS.
det.treatment: Acute attacks need high-dose IV methylprednisolone, with early plasma exchange for severe or steroid-unresponsive attacks. Long-term relapse prevention is essential after the first attack: rituximab, azathioprine and mycophenolate are widely used, and approved targeted agents include eculizumab and ravulizumab (complement), inebilizumab (anti-CD19) and satralizumab (IL-6 receptor). Several MS drugs, including interferon-beta, natalizumab and fingolimod, can worsen NMOSD and should be avoided.
det.prognosis: Untreated disease leads to blindness or paraplegia in many patients; effective preventive therapy has greatly reduced relapses and mortality.
pearls: Intractable hiccups and vomiting with myelitis or optic neuritis = area postrema syndrome.
Long central cord lesion (≥3 segments) argues for NMOSD over MS.
Interferon-beta and natalizumab can harm patients with NMOSD.
det.thd: NMOSD เกิดจากแอนติบอดีต่อ aquaporin-4 บนเซลล์ astrocyte ทำให้เซลล์ถูกทำลายผ่าน complement พบมากในหญิงเอเชีย ตำแหน่งที่เป็นคือเส้นประสาทตา ไขสันหลังยาว ≥3 ปล้อง และ area postrema (สะอึกและอาเจียนไม่หยุด) การกำเริบแต่ละครั้งมักรุนแรงและหายไม่สมบูรณ์ วินิจฉัยด้วย AQP4-IgG แบบ cell-based assay และ MRI รักษาครั้งกำเริบด้วย methylprednisolone และ plasma exchange ป้องกันระยะยาวด้วย rituximab, azathioprine หรือยาใหม่ เช่น eculizumab, inebilizumab, satralizumab และห้ามใช้ยา MS บางตัว เช่น interferon-beta

name: Neuromyotonia
formal: Peripheral nerve hyperexcitability (Isaacs syndrome) with continuous muscle fibre activity, stiffness, myokymia, cramps and delayed relaxation, from VGKC complex (CASPR2) antibodies.
simple: Constant twitching and stiffness of muscles from overactive nerves, often autoimmune.
more: Detect with EMG showing myokymic and neuromyotonic discharges, with CASPR2 and LGI1 antibodies, and search for thymoma or other tumour. Treat with carbamazepine or phenytoin, with plasma exchange or IVIG for severe cases; Morvan syndrome combines CNS features.

name: Neuromyotonic syndromes
formal: Peripheral nerve hyperexcitability syndromes including Isaacs syndrome and Morvan syndrome, with myokymia, cramps, stiffness and autoimmune CASPR2 or LGI1 antibodies.
simple: Conditions where nerves fire too much, causing constant muscle twitching, stiffness and cramps.

name: Neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis
formal: Group of lysosomal storage disorders (Batten disease) with progressive visual loss, seizures, myoclonus and dementia, with lipopigment accumulation; CLN genes.
simple: Inherited childhood diseases that cause seizures, vision loss and loss of skills (Batten disease).

name: Neuronal intranuclear inclusion body disease
formal: Neurodegenerative disease (NOTCH2NLC GGC repeat expansions) with eosinophilic intranuclear inclusions, dementia, parkinsonism, neuropathy and DWI corticomedullary junction hyperintensity.
simple: A rare brain disease with abnormal clumps inside nerve cell nuclei, causing dementia, tremor and nerve problems.

name: Neuropathic pain
formal: Pain arising from lesion or disease of the somatosensory nervous system, with burning, shooting character, allodynia and hyperalgesia, as in diabetic neuropathy and post-herpetic neuralgia.
simple: Burning or shooting pain caused by damaged nerves.

name: Neuropathic scoliosis
formal: Spinal curvature resulting from neuromuscular disease such as cerebral palsy, spina bifida or Duchenne dystrophy, with progressive long C-shaped curves and pelvic obliquity.
simple: Curving of the spine caused by weak or imbalanced muscles from a nerve or muscle disease.

name: Neuropathic tremor syndrome
formal: Postural and action tremor associated with demyelinating neuropathy, as in CIDP, anti-MAG neuropathy and Charcot-Marie-Tooth (Roussy-Levy), thought to arise from sensory afferent loss.
simple: A shaking of the hands that occurs in people with certain nerve diseases.

name: Neuropathies anterior interosseus syndrome
formal: Posterior interosseous or anterior interosseous nerve syndrome causing isolated weakness of flexor pollicis longus and index flexor digitorum profundus (pinch deficit), often from neuralgic amyotrophy.
simple: A condition affecting a branch of the median nerve that causes weak pinching between thumb and index finger.
more: Diagnosed with EMG and MRI; often improves with observation, with surgery if no recovery.

name: Neuropathy (MADSAM)
formal: Multifocal acquired demyelinating sensory and motor neuropathy (Lewis-Sumner syndrome) with asymmetric multifocal weakness and sensory loss, a CIDP variant treated with IVIG.
simple: An immune nerve disease causing uneven patchy weakness and numbness in arms and legs.
more: Nerve conduction shows persistent motor conduction block outside typical entrapment sites; anti-GM1 is sometimes present. Steroids often fail and may worsen disease; IVIG is first line, and the course is slowly progressive without maintenance.
ab: multifocal acquired demyelinating sensory and motor neuropathy
th: CIDP แบบหลายตำแหน่งไม่สมมาตร — ทั้งอ่อนแรงและชาตามเส้นประสาท แขนเป็นก่อน ตอบสนองการรักษาแบบ CIDP
feat: Asymmetric painless weakness and numbness in individual nerve territories, arms first
Slow progression over months to years
Distinguished from MMN by sensory involvement
inv: NCS: multifocal demyelination with persistent conduction block in motor and sensory fibres
CSF protein raised; MRI/ultrasound: focal nerve or plexus enlargement

case.story: A year of numbness and weakness in the left median territory, then the right ulnar hand.
case.exam: Weak left thumb abduction with median sensory loss; right ulnar weakness and numbness; reflexes reduced in affected limbs.
case.tests: Conduction block in left median forearm and right ulnar forearm, abnormal sensory conduction across same segments; CSF protein 0.9 g/L.
case.q: How does sensory involvement change treatment compared with MMN?
case.a: Like CIDP, MADSAM may respond to steroids as well as IVIG, whereas MMN responds to IVIG and may worsen with steroids.

ddx.pt: Pure motor, sensory studies normal, anti-GM1
Painful, axonal, systemic inflammation
Episodes at compression sites; diffuse background slowing; PMP22 deletion

aN: madsam | neuropathy | lewis sumner syndrome | multifocal cidp | multifocal acquired demyelinating sensory and motor neuropathy

det.patho: MADSAM is an immune-mediated demyelinating neuropathy classified as a multifocal variant of CIDP in the 2021 EAN/PNS guideline. Inflammation targets discrete nerve segments, causing persistent conduction block in both motor and sensory fibres rather than diffuse length-dependent involvement. Specific antibodies are usually absent, and the trigger is unknown.
det.clinical: Patients develop asymmetric weakness and sensory loss in the territories of individual nerves, most often starting in the arm (median or ulnar) and spreading over months or years to other limbs. Pain is usually mild, and reflexes are reduced in affected limbs. Cranial neuropathies occasionally occur. The pattern can mimic multiple entrapments, but deficits appear at non-compression sites.
det.diagnosis: Electrodiagnosis shows multifocal demyelinating features — conduction block, temporal dispersion and focal slowing — in motor nerves, with abnormal sensory conduction in the same segments, meeting CIDP criteria for a multifocal pattern. CSF protein is often raised. MRI or ultrasound may show focal nerve or plexus thickening and enhancement. Exclude MMN (normal sensory studies), vasculitis (axonal, painful), HNPP, paraproteinaemia and lymphoma infiltration.
det.treatment: First-line options are IVIG (a 2 g/kg loading course, followed by maintenance infusions) or corticosteroids, and plasma exchange in selected patients. Unlike MMN, steroids are generally effective. Response should be judged with objective strength and disability measures, and the maintenance dose tapered to the lowest effective level. Refractory cases may receive rituximab or other immunosuppressants.
det.prognosis: Most patients respond to immunotherapy, though fewer reach complete remission than in typical CIDP. Long-standing conduction block with axonal loss leaves residual deficits.
pearls: Asymmetric sensory plus motor multifocal demyelination = MADSAM; pure motor = MMN.
Steroids help MADSAM but may worsen MMN.
Conduction block at non-entrapment sites suggests immune neuropathy.
det.thd: MADSAM (Lewis–Sumner) เป็น CIDP ชนิดหลายตำแหน่งไม่สมมาตร เกิดจากภูมิคุ้มกันทำลายเยื่อหุ้มเส้นประสาทเป็นช่วง ๆ ทำให้ทั้งอ่อนแรงและชาตามเส้นประสาทแต่ละเส้น มักเริ่มที่แขน NCS พบ conduction block ทั้งใยประสาทสั่งการและรับความรู้สึก CSF protein สูง ต่างจาก MMN ที่เป็นแค่อ่อนแรง รักษาด้วย IVIG หรือ steroid ได้

name: Neuropathy related to acrylamide
formal: Toxic axonal sensorimotor neuropathy and ataxia from acrylamide exposure in industrial or grouting work, with sweating and skin peeling.
simple: Nerve damage with numbness and unsteady walking after exposure to a chemical used in grouts and plastics.
more: Remove from exposure; recovery is gradual over months, and may be incomplete.

name: Neuropathy related to arsenic
formal: Subacute axonal sensorimotor neuropathy mimicking Guillain-Barre, with painful paraesthesia, Mees lines, skin changes, and gastrointestinal symptoms.
simple: Nerve damage causing painful numbness and weakness after arsenic poisoning.
more: Measure urine arsenic, and give chelation therapy; slow partial recovery is typical.
th: ปลายประสาทเสื่อมจากพิษสารหนู — ชาปวดแสบปลายเท้า อ่อนแรง อาจคล้าย GBS ร่วมกับผิวหนังและเล็บผิดปกติ
tempoNote: Acute poisoning: GI illness then neuropathy 1–3 weeks later; chronic exposure: slow over months
feat: After acute ingestion: vomiting, diarrhoea and hypotension, followed weeks later by a rapidly ascending painful sensorimotor neuropathy
Painful burning feet, distal sensory loss, distal weakness and areflexia
Skin: hyperpigmentation (raindrop pattern), palmar-plantar hyperkeratosis
Transverse white nail bands (Mees lines) appearing weeks after exposure
Anaemia, liver dysfunction, encephalopathy in heavy exposure
inv: 24-hour urine arsenic (avoid seafood for 48–72 h before; speciate organic vs inorganic)
Hair and nail arsenic for chronic or past exposure
NCS: axonal sensorimotor neuropathy; early studies can show demyelinating-like features
CBC, LFT, renal function, ECG (QT prolongation)

case.who: 38-year-old man from Ron Phibun district, Nakhon Si Thammarat
case.story: Uses shallow well water near an old tin-mining area. Over 6 months feet burn and tingle; he trips on stairs.
case.exam: Dark spotted pigmentation of trunk, thickened soles, white transverse nail bands; stocking sensory loss, weak toe extension, absent ankle jerks.
case.tests: Urine inorganic arsenic markedly high; NCS: axonal sensorimotor neuropathy; mild anaemia.
case.q: What are the first steps?
case.a: Remove the source (stop well water, notify public health), and consider chelation (DMSA or DMPS) with toxicology advice, especially after recent or high exposure.

read.where: Case series and discussion: chronic arsenic poisoning from drinking water
Chapter 7 Occupational, Biologic, and Environmental Toxic Neuropathies (Arsenic)

det.patho: Inorganic trivalent arsenic binds sulfhydryl groups and disrupts pyruvate dehydrogenase and other enzymes, impairing energy production in long axons. The result is a dying-back axonopathy with secondary changes. Exposure sources include contaminated ground water, mining, pesticides, some traditional remedies and deliberate poisoning. Large-diameter sensory and motor fibres bear the brunt, and the metalloid also injures gut, skin, marrow, liver and kidney, so the neuropathy is one part of a multisystem illness. Worldwide on the order of a hundred million people drink groundwater with unsafe arsenic levels, with the heaviest burden in South and Southeast Asia, and contaminated herbal, Ayurvedic or homeopathic preparations remain a recurring source.
det.clinical: Acute poisoning starts with GI upset and cardiovascular instability; the neuropathy follows after roughly one to four weeks and keeps advancing for weeks even without further exposure, sometimes to bifacial and respiratory weakness, closely mimicking GBS. Chronic low-level exposure causes a slowly developing painful sensorimotor neuropathy in a glove-and-stocking pattern with characteristic skin changes, and increases risk of skin, lung and bladder cancer. Systemic clues include gingival and skin melanosis, palmar–plantar hyperkeratosis, transient leucopenia or pancytopenia with anaemia, raised transaminases, coarse tremor and QT prolongation. Neuropathy appearing at the same time in several members of one household or village, who share water or a remedy, is a powerful pointer to a toxin. Thailand's Ron Phibun district is a historically known endemic area.
det.diagnosis: Measure urine arsenic in a 24-hour collection, with speciation because seafood contains non-toxic organic arsenic; a high value proves exposure, but toxicity needs the matching clinical picture. Blood arsenic is cleared within hours, so a normal blood level does not exclude chronic poisoning; hair and nails reflect exposure over months. Studies done soon after acute exposure can meet demyelinating criteria (slowing, conduction block, dispersion, absent F waves), but early loss of the sural response — the opposite of the sural sparing typical of AIDP — is a clue, and repeat studies evolve into a severe dying-back axonal pattern. CSF protein may be raised without cells, so albuminocytological dissociation does not settle the question. Mees lines, basophilic stippling and skin changes are strong supporting clues, and testing the household water or remedy identifies the source.
det.treatment: Stop exposure and give supportive care, including cardiac monitoring for QT prolongation and torsades, hydration to keep urine output high, and respiratory monitoring in acute cases. Chelation with DMSA or DMPS (or intramuscular dimercaprol in severe acute cases) is most effective soon after exposure and has limited, debated benefit for established neuropathy; DMSA is generally preferred when chronic poisoning is treated, and dimercaprol can cause haemolysis in G6PD deficiency. Plasma exchange and IVIG do not alter the course. Treat pain and provide rehabilitation; notify public-health authorities, test family members sharing the same water, and arrange an arsenic-safe supply.
det.prognosis: Recovery is slow and often incomplete over months to years, depending on severity and duration of exposure; younger patients with milder deficits may recover fully within about a year once the source is removed.
pearls: GBS-like illness preceded by vomiting and diarrhoea: think heavy metals and check urine arsenic.
Mees lines appear weeks after exposure, so their position on the nail dates the poisoning.
Tell the patient to avoid seafood for 2–3 days before urine testing.
'GBS' with an absent sural response, cytopenia and raised liver enzymes — or a second 'GBS' in the same home — means arsenic until proven otherwise.
det.thd: พิษสารหนูทำให้เกิด axonal neuropathy ปวดแสบปลายมือปลายเท้าและอ่อนแรง ในพิษเฉียบพลันจะมีอาเจียนท้องเสียก่อน แล้วอาการปลายประสาทตามมาใน 1–4 สัปดาห์ คล้าย GBS และ NCS ระยะแรกอาจดูเหมือน demyelinating แต่ sural มักหายไปตั้งแต่ต้น ส่วนพิษเรื้อรังมีผิวหนังและเหงือกดำ ฝ่ามือฝ่าเท้าหนา เส้นขาวขวางเล็บ (Mees lines) เม็ดเลือดขาวต่ำ และตับอักเสบ ถ้าคนในบ้านเดียวกันเป็นพร้อมกันให้นึกถึงน้ำดื่มปนเปื้อน วินิจฉัยด้วยการวัดสารหนูในปัสสาวะ 24 ชั่วโมง (ระดับในเลือดมักปกติ) รักษาด้วยการหยุดแหล่งสัมผัส ติดตาม QTc และพิจารณายาขับโลหะ เช่น DMSA พร้อมแจ้งหน่วยงานสาธารณสุข

files.chapter: 7. Occupational, Biologic, and Environmental Toxic Neuropathies
17. THE TOXIC NEUROPATHIES: INDUSTRIAL, OCCUPATIONAL, AND ENVIRONMENTAL AGENTS

ddx.pt: No GI prodrome from toxin, no skin/nail changes; urine arsenic normal
Prominent hair loss two to three weeks after exposure
Motor-predominant (wrist drop), abdominal colic, basophilic stippling

aN: arsenic neuropathy | arsenical polyneuropathy | arsenic poisoning neuropathy

name: Neuropathy related to gold
formal: Neuropathy with myokymia, from chrysotherapy in rheumatoid arthritis, sometimes resembling Guillain-Barre syndrome.
simple: Nerve damage that can occur in people treated with gold salts for arthritis.
more: Stop the gold treatment; recovery usually follows, and corticosteroids may help.

name: Neuropathy related to hydrocarbons
formal: Sensorimotor axonal neuropathy from n-hexane and methyl butyl ketone inhalation, for example in glue sniffing and industrial exposure, with giant axonal swellings.
simple: Nerve damage from breathing in solvents such as glue fumes, causing numbness and weakness.
more: Stop exposure; urinary 2,5-hexanedione can confirm exposure; improvement occurs over months.

name: Neuropathy related to isoniazid
formal: Pyridoxine-deficiency axonal sensory neuropathy from isoniazid, most common in slow acetylators, malnourished patients, or those with alcohol use or diabetes.
simple: Numb, tingling feet caused by the tuberculosis drug isoniazid, which depletes vitamin B6.
more: Prevent with pyridoxine supplementation; treat by continuing B6 and reducing the dose if possible.

name: Neuropathy related to lead
formal: Predominantly motor neuropathy with wrist drop and basophilic stippling, and abdominal colic, in adults with chronic lead exposure.
simple: Weakness, especially wrist drop, caused by long-term lead poisoning.
more: Blood lead level and free erythrocyte protoporphyrin; treat with removal from exposure and chelation.

name: Neuropathy related to mercury
formal: Sensory neuropathy with ataxia, tremor, and erethism following inorganic or organic mercury exposure, with acrodynia in children.
simple: Nerve damage with numbness, tremor, and mood change after mercury exposure.
more: Blood and urine mercury; remove the source and use chelation; recovery may be incomplete.

name: Neuropathy related to nitrofurantoin
formal: Dose-related axonal sensorimotor neuropathy from nitrofurantoin, often severe in renal failure, and sometimes mimicking Guillain-Barre syndrome.
simple: Nerve damage with numbness and weakness in people taking the antibiotic nitrofurantoin, especially with poor kidney function.
more: Stopping the drug early is crucial; recovery is variable and may be incomplete.

name: Neuropathy related to organophosphates
formal: Acute cholinergic syndrome followed by intermediate syndrome and delayed axonal polyneuropathy (OPIDN) after exposure to certain organophosphates.
simple: Nerve damage that appears a couple of weeks after pesticide poisoning, causing weakness of legs.
more: Axonal pattern on nerve studies; supportive treatment; recovery slow and may be incomplete.

name: Neuropathy related to thalidomide
formal: Dose-related length-dependent sensory axonal neuropathy from thalidomide, with painful paraesthesias and numbness that may persist after stopping.
simple: Numbness or pain in the hands and feet caused by the drug thalidomide.
more: Risk rises with cumulative dose; monitor with symptoms and nerve conduction. Dose reduction or stopping helps, but recovery may be incomplete.

name: Neuropathy related to thallium
formal: Painful ascending axonal neuropathy with alopecia appearing about 2 weeks after exposure, accompanied by gastrointestinal symptoms.
simple: Nerve damage with severe foot pain followed by hair loss after thallium poisoning.
more: Urine thallium confirms it; give Prussian blue and haemodialysis; prognosis depends on the dose.

name: Neuropathy, ataxia, and retinitis pigmentosa (NARP)
formal: Maternally inherited mitochondrial disorder (m.8993T>G in MT-ATP6) with sensory neuropathy, ataxia, retinitis pigmentosa, seizures and developmental delay.
simple: An inherited energy-production disease causing nerve damage, poor balance and gradual vision loss.
nN: neuropathy ataxia and retinitis pigmentosa narp
aN: narp | neuropathy ataxia and retinitis pigmentosa

name: Neuropsychiatric systemic lupus erythematosus (NPSLE)
formal: Neuropsychiatric manifestations of lupus, including seizures, psychosis, stroke, myelitis, neuropathy and cognitive disorder, related to vasculopathy, antiphospholipid antibodies and autoantibodies.
simple: Lupus affecting the brain or nerves, causing seizures, mood or thinking changes, or strokes.
aN: npsle | neuropsychiatric systemic lupus erythematosus

name: Neuropsychiatry catatonia
formal: Psychomotor syndrome with stupor, mutism, posturing, negativism and waxy flexibility, from psychiatric, autoimmune or medical causes, responsive to benzodiazepines or ECT.
simple: A condition where a person is unresponsive, still or mute, or shows odd repeated movements, which can improve with treatment.

name: Neuroretinitis
formal: Optic disc swelling with macular star exudates from optic nerve and retinal inflammation, often due to Bartonella henselae infection.
simple: Swelling of the optic nerve with a star-shaped pattern in the retina causing blurred vision, often from infection such as cat-scratch disease.

name: New daily persistent headache (NDPH)
formal: Primary headache beginning abruptly with daily and unremitting course from onset, usually within 3 days, with migraine or tension-type features; secondary causes must be excluded.
simple: A headache that starts suddenly and then continues every day without letting up.
aN: ndph | new daily persistent headache

name: New-onset refractory status epilepticus (NORSE)
formal: Refractory status epilepticus without prior epilepsy and no clear structural or toxic cause; often autoimmune or cryptogenic, with FIRES as a childhood subtype after febrile illness.
simple: A serious state of continuous seizures in a previously healthy person that does not respond to usual medicines and has no obvious cause.
nN: new onset refractory status epilepticus norse
aN: norse | new onset refractory status epilepticus

name: Niacin (vitamin B3) deficiency
formal: Pellagra with dermatitis, diarrhoea and dementia, along with neuropathy, ataxia and encephalopathy, seen in alcoholism, malnutrition and carcinoid.
simple: Lack of vitamin B3 causing skin rash, diarrhoea and confusion or memory problems.
aN: vitamin b3 | niacin deficiency

name: Niemann Pick C disease (NPC)
formal: Autosomal recessive lysosomal lipid storage disorder from NPC1 or NPC2 variants with vertical supranuclear gaze palsy, ataxia, dystonia, dementia, splenomegaly and neonatal cholestasis.
simple: An inherited disease in which fats build up in cells, causing balance problems, eye movement problems and decline in thinking.
more: Diagnosed by plasma oxysterols and genetic testing; filipin staining. Miglustat slows neurological progression, and the course is progressive.
aN: npc | niemann pick c disease

name: Niemann–Pick disease type C
formal: Autosomal recessive NPC1 or NPC2 cholesterol trafficking defect with vertical supranuclear gaze palsy, cerebellar ataxia, dystonia, cataplexy, splenomegaly and psychiatric features.
simple: An inherited disease where cholesterol builds up in cells, causing balance problems, eye movement problems and dementia.
more: Diagnosis by filipin staining of fibroblasts, oxysterol or lyso-sphingomyelin levels, and NPC1 or NPC2 sequencing; the gaze palsy is vertical saccades. Miglustat slows neurological progression, and arimoclomol and levacetylleucine are newer options.
th: โรคสะสมไขมันในไลโซโซมจากยีน NPC1/NPC2 — กลอกตาลงล่างไม่ได้ (vertical supranuclear gaze palsy) ร่วมกับ ataxia, dystonia, cataplexy, ม้ามโต และโรคจิตหรือสมองเสื่อม
tempoNote: Any age from infancy to adulthood; neurological course runs over years, faster with earlier onset
feat: Slow or absent vertical saccades, downward first, with preserved vestibulo-ocular reflex
Progressive cerebellar ataxia, dysarthria and dysphagia
Dystonia and gelastic cataplexy (collapse with laughter)
Psychosis, behavioural change or early cognitive decline in teens and adults
Splenomegaly (may be mild) or a history of prolonged neonatal jaundice
inv: Plasma oxysterols (cholestane-triol), lysosphingomyelin-509 or bile acid markers as screening
NPC1 and NPC2 gene sequencing (confirmatory)
Abdominal ultrasound for spleen size; video-oculography for saccade velocity
Filipin staining of cultured fibroblasts when genetics is inconclusive

case.story: Grades fell over two years, then auditory hallucinations; psychiatric drugs made her stiffer. Her legs give way when she laughs.
case.exam: Clumsy gait, mild limb dystonia, very slow downward saccades with full movement on doll's-head manoeuvre; spleen tip palpable.
case.tests: Ultrasound spleen 14 cm; plasma oxysterols raised; NPC1 biallelic pathogenic variants.
case.q: Which eye sign links her psychiatric illness to a neurometabolic disease?
case.a: Vertical supranuclear gaze palsy — with ataxia, cataplexy and splenomegaly it indicates Niemann–Pick type C.

read.where: Review: Autosomal recessive cerebellar ataxias for which treatment is available; Table 3

det.patho: NPC1 (about 95%) or NPC2 variants impair export of unesterified cholesterol from late endosomes and lysosomes. Cholesterol and glycosphingolipids accumulate, damaging Purkinje cells, cortical neurons and the reticuloendothelial system. It is panethnic, with an estimated birth incidence of around 1 in 100,000, though adult cases are underdiagnosed.
det.clinical: Presentation depends on age: neonatal cholestasis or hepatosplenomegaly, childhood clumsiness and learning decline, or adolescent/adult psychiatric illness with ataxia, dystonia and dementia. Vertical supranuclear gaze palsy is the hallmark and is often present long before the patient notices it. Cataplexy, seizures, dysphagia and dysarthria accrue over time. Splenomegaly can be subtle or absent in adults.
det.diagnosis: Use a suspicion index: combinations of vertical gaze palsy, ataxia, cataplexy, psychosis and splenomegaly or prior neonatal jaundice. Screen with plasma oxysterols, lyso-SM-509 or bile acid metabolites, then confirm by NPC1/NPC2 genetics; filipin testing is now a second-line tool. MRI may be normal or show cerebellar and frontal atrophy.
det.treatment: Miglustat (substrate reduction) is approved in many countries and may slow neurological progression. In 2024 the FDA approved arimoclomol (used with miglustat) and levacetylleucine. Symptomatic care covers cataplexy, seizures, dystonia, dysphagia and psychosis; antipsychotics should be used cautiously because of parkinsonism. Swallowing assessment and gastrostomy planning are important.
det.prognosis: Earlier neurological onset predicts faster decline; adult-onset patients may live for decades after diagnosis.
pearls: Teen or adult psychosis + vertical saccade slowing + ataxia: think NPC.
Check vertical saccade speed, not just range, at the bedside.
Laughter-induced falls (gelastic cataplexy) are a classic clue.
det.thd: Niemann–Pick type C เกิดจากยีน NPC1 หรือ NPC2 ทำให้ cholesterol ค้างในไลโซโซม อาการเด่นคือกลอกตาขึ้นลงช้าหรือไม่ได้แต่ doll's eye ปกติ ร่วมกับเดินเซ dystonia ล้มเมื่อหัวเราะ (cataplexy) ม้ามโต และในวัยรุ่นหรือผู้ใหญ่มักเริ่มด้วยโรคจิตหรือความจำถดถอย ตรวจ oxysterol และยืนยันด้วยยีน รักษาด้วย miglustat และยาใหม่เช่น arimoclomol หรือ levacetylleucine

name: Niemann–Pick type A disease
formal: Infantile acid sphingomyelinase deficiency with hepatosplenomegaly, severe neurodegeneration, cherry-red macula and early death.
simple: A severe infant form of Niemann-Pick disease causing a swollen liver, loss of skills and early death.

name: Niemann–Pick type B disease
formal: Visceral acid sphingomyelinase deficiency with hepatosplenomegaly and lung disease, with little or no neurological involvement.
simple: A milder form of Niemann-Pick disease affecting mainly liver, spleen and lungs rather than the brain.

name: Niemann–Pick type C disease
formal: Autosomal recessive NPC1 or NPC2 cholesterol trafficking defect with vertical supranuclear gaze palsy, cerebellar ataxia, dystonia, cataplexy, splenomegaly and psychiatric features.
simple: An inherited disease where cholesterol builds up in cells, causing balance problems, eye movement problems and dementia.

name: Niemann–Pick type D disease
formal: Nova Scotia variant of Niemann-Pick type C, due to NPC1 mutation, with similar neurovisceral cholesterol storage disease.
simple: A form of Niemann-Pick type C found in a Nova Scotia population, with the same brain and eye movement problems.

name: Niemann–Pick type E disease
formal: Historical, rarely used category of adult non-neuronopathic Niemann-Pick disease with sphingomyelin storage; no longer a distinct entity.
simple: An old name for a mild adult form of Niemann-Pick disease, no longer used as a separate type.

name: Nijmegen Breakage syndrome
formal: Autosomal recessive NBN mutation disorder with microcephaly, growth failure, immunodeficiency, radiosensitivity and lymphoid malignancy.
simple: An inherited condition with a small head, weak immunity, and high risk of cancers, sensitive to radiation.

name: Nitrous oxide, neurotoxicity
formal: Recreational or occupational nitrous oxide inactivates vitamin B12, causing subacute combined degeneration with myeloneuropathy, paraesthesias, sensory ataxia and megaloblastosis.
simple: Nerve and spinal cord damage from repeated laughing gas use because it blocks vitamin B12.
aN: nitrous oxide | neurotoxicity

name: Njimegen breakage syndrome
formal: Autosomal recessive NBN mutation disorder (misspelled Nijmegen) with microcephaly, growth failure, immunodeficiency, radiosensitivity and lymphoid malignancy.
simple: An inherited condition with a small head, weak immunity, and high risk of cancers, sensitive to radiation.

name: NMJ disorder
formal: Disorder of synaptic transmission between nerve and muscle, such as myasthenia gravis, Lambert-Eaton syndrome, botulism and congenital myasthenic syndromes, with fatigable weakness.
simple: A condition where messages from nerves to muscles are blocked, causing weakness that worsens with use.

name: Nociplastic pain
formal: Chronic pain from altered nociceptive processing without clear tissue or nerve damage, as in fibromyalgia, with widespread pain, fatigue, sleep and mood disturbance.
simple: Long-lasting pain from a nervous system that is overly sensitive, without clear injury, as in fibromyalgia.

name: Nocturnal epileptic seizures
formal: Seizures arising during sleep, often frontal lobe in origin, with brief stereotyped hypermotor, tonic or dystonic events clustering in NREM sleep, as in autosomal dominant nocturnal frontal lobe epilepsy.
simple: Seizures that happen only or mostly during sleep, causing sudden movements or stiffening at night.
more: Video-EEG polysomnography helps diagnosis; carbamazepine is effective and genetic testing may show CHRNA4 variants.

name: Nocturnal myoclonus
formal: Periodic limb movements in sleep: repetitive stereotyped leg flexion movements at intervals of 20 to 40 seconds, often with restless legs syndrome.
simple: Repeated leg jerks during sleep that can disturb sleep.

name: Nocturnal paroxysmal dystonia
formal: Brief stereotyped dystonic or hyperkinetic attacks from NREM sleep, now generally recognised as a form of nocturnal frontal lobe epilepsy.
simple: Short episodes of twisting or thrashing movements during sleep, usually from seizures in the frontal lobe.
more: Diagnosed with video-EEG; carbamazepine often abolishes attacks. Prognosis is generally benign.

name: Non-24-hour sleep–wake rhythm disorder
formal: Circadian rhythm disorder where the sleep-wake cycle drifts later each day, due to lack of light entrainment, typical in blind people, with insomnia and daytime sleepiness.
simple: A body clock problem where sleep time shifts later and later each day, common in people who are blind.
nN: non 24 hour sleep wake rhythm disorder

name: Non-arteritic anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy (AION)
formal: Acute painless optic nerve head infarction, usually with crowded small cup-to-disc ratio, causing altitudinal visual loss with disc swelling; vascular risk factors.
simple: Sudden painless loss of part of vision in one eye from reduced blood flow to the optic nerve.
nN: non arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy aion
aN: aion | non arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy

formal: Sterile fibrin and platelet vegetations on heart valves in cancer or hypercoagulable states, causing embolic multifocal infarcts.
simple: Sterile clots on the heart valves in people with cancer that can break off and cause strokes.

case.exam: Afebrile, no murmur; right hand ataxia, left homonymous hemianopia, inattentive.

det.patho: Sterile vegetations of platelets and fibrin settle on valves — most often the aortic, then the mitral, sometimes both — usually on leaflets that were structurally normal, where endothelial injury from circulating cytokines meets a hypercoagulable blood. In cancer, mucin from adenocarcinomas (pancreas, lung, ovary, stomach, colon, breast, prostate) binds selectins on platelets and endothelium, and tumour cells release tissue factor and cancer procoagulant, so NBTE is often regarded as a valvular expression of chronic, low-grade DIC; together NBTE and DIC account for much of the ischaemic stroke seen in cancer, with DIC dominating in leukaemia, lymphoma and breast cancer and NBTE in mucin-secreting tumours. In lupus and antiphospholipid syndrome, immune-complex and antibody-mediated endothelial damage produce the same lesion (Libman–Sacks endocarditis), and sepsis, burns and wasting illnesses are rarer substrates. The vegetations are small, friable and free of inflammatory cells, so fragments break off easily and shower many vascular beds.
det.clinical: Embolic stroke is the commonest presentation and may be the first sign of an occult cancer; systemic emboli occur in about half of patients and reach kidneys, spleen, limbs, bowel and coronary arteries. Brain infarcts are typically multiple, widely scattered and of varying size across both hemispheres and the anterior and posterior circulations, and the clinical picture is often a fluctuating or progressive encephalopathy with or without focal signs rather than a single clean stroke syndrome; TIAs sometimes come first. Patients are usually afebrile, murmurs are often absent and valvular dysfunction is unusual, which is why the diagnosis is missed. Clues include migratory superficial or deep vein thrombosis (Trousseau syndrome), weight loss, abnormal coagulation tests and, in lupus, other features of SLE or APS. Without anticoagulation, recurrent embolism within days to weeks is common.
det.diagnosis: Suspect NBTE when DWI shows acute infarcts in three or more territories at once, particularly with known or suspected cancer, lupus or a very high D-dimer (raised BNP and fibrinogen are also associated). Transoesophageal echocardiography is the key test because vegetations are usually under 1 cm and are often missed on transthoracic study; a normal TOE does not exclude micro-vegetations, and autopsy series still find lesions that imaging missed. Take at least three sets of blood cultures before antibiotics and consider serology for culture-negative organisms (Bartonella, Coxiella) to exclude infective endocarditis. When no cancer is known, look for one with CT of chest, abdomen and pelvis (and mammography or tumour markers as indicated), and check platelets, fibrinogen, PT/aPTT, a blood film for DIC, and antiphospholipid antibodies and ANA. Serial D-dimer can help track coagulopathy and response to anticoagulation, although cancer and its treatment raise it independently.
det.treatment: Acute reperfusion follows usual rules: thrombectomy is reasonable for a large vessel occlusion, whereas IV thrombolysis needs individual judgement because of cancer-related bleeding risk, thrombocytopenia or DIC. For secondary prevention, therapeutic anticoagulation with LMWH (or unfractionated heparin when bleeding risk is high or procedures are planned) is the preferred approach in cancer-associated NBTE, continued while the cancer is active or until bleeding or intolerance intervenes; recurrence has been reported after switching to warfarin, and trial data on DOACs in cancer-related stroke are small and inconclusive. Libman–Sacks endocarditis with antiphospholipid syndrome is generally managed with warfarin rather than a DOAC, alongside treatment of the lupus. Antiplatelet therapy alone is not adequate, and atrial fibrillation or conventional risk factors should still be sought and treated. Treating the underlying cancer is essential, and valve surgery is reserved for rare cases with large vegetations, recurrent emboli despite anticoagulation, or valve dysfunction in patients with a good outlook.
det.prognosis: Prognosis is mostly set by the underlying malignancy, which is often advanced, and many patients die within months; recurrent embolism is frequent if anticoagulation is stopped, while lupus-related disease carries a better outlook.
pearls: Multi-territory acute infarcts + cancer (or weight loss) + high D-dimer = ask for TOE and think NBTE.
Choose heparin (usually LMWH), not warfarin or a DOAC, in cancer-associated NBTE.
Stroke may unmask a hidden mucin-producing adenocarcinoma: screen for cancer when no cause is found.
A patchy, fluctuating encephalopathy in a cancer patient may be showers of emboli — check DWI before blaming metabolism or drugs.
det.thd: NBTE คือก้อน fibrin และเกล็ดเลือดบนลิ้นหัวใจ (มักเป็นลิ้น aortic หรือ mitral) ที่ไม่มีเชื้อโรค เกิดจากภาวะเลือดแข็งตัวง่ายในมะเร็ง โดยเฉพาะ adenocarcinoma ที่สร้าง mucin เช่น ตับอ่อน ปอด รังไข่ กระเพาะ หรือใน SLE/APS ก้อนเปราะหลุดง่าย ทำให้สมองขาดเลือดหลายจุดหลายเขตหลอดเลือดทั้งสองซีกพร้อมกัน บางรายมาด้วยสับสนเป็น ๆ หาย ๆ มากกว่าอ่อนแรงชัดเจน และมี emboli ไปไต ม้าม แขนขาได้ ผู้ป่วยมักไม่มีไข้ D-dimer สูงมาก ต้องตรวจ TOE เพราะก้อนเล็ก เพาะเชื้อในเลือดให้ผลลบ และค้นหามะเร็งที่ซ่อนอยู่ รักษาด้วย heparin (มักเป็น LMWH) ระยะยาวตราบที่มะเร็งยัง active ร่วมกับรักษามะเร็ง ส่วน Libman–Sacks ใน APS ใช้ warfarin การพยากรณ์โรคขึ้นกับมะเร็งเป็นหลัก

name: Non-convulsive status
formal: Prolonged seizure activity without prominent motor signs, causing confusion or altered consciousness and diagnosed by EEG.
simple: A long-lasting seizure state with no obvious shaking, causing confusion or drowsiness.

name: Non-convulsive status epilepticus (NCSE)
formal: Prolonged electrographic seizure activity without prominent convulsions, presenting with confusion, behavioural change or reduced consciousness, diagnosed by EEG.
simple: A long-lasting seizure state with no obvious shaking, causing confusion or drowsiness.

formal: Paroxysmal events resembling seizures without epileptiform EEG activity, either psychogenic (functional) or physiological such as syncope.
simple: Episodes that look like seizures but are not caused by abnormal electrical activity, often related to stress.

name: Non-germinomatous germ cell tumours (NGGCT)
formal: Malignant intracranial germ cell tumours (yolk sac, embryonal carcinoma, choriocarcinoma) in pineal or suprasellar regions with raised AFP or beta-HCG and hydrocephalus; Parinaud syndrome.
simple: Aggressive brain tumours from germ cells, usually near the pineal gland or pituitary, in young people.

formal: Erdheim-Chester disease: non-Langerhans histiocytosis with bone sclerosis, diabetes insipidus, retroperitoneal fibrosis and CNS lesions, with BRAF V600E mutation in many.
simple: A rare disease with abnormal immune cells in bones, brain and other organs.

aN: chester erdheim disease | non langerhans histiocytosis

name: Non-progressive myoclonic encephalopathies
formal: Disorders with static encephalopathy and myoclonus, often following hypoxia or from neonatal causes, without neurodegeneration.
simple: Non-worsening brain conditions with muscle jerks, often after oxygen deprivation or in childhood.

name: Non-progressive myoclonic encephalopathy
formal: Disorder with static encephalopathy and myoclonus, often following hypoxia or from neonatal causes, without neurodegeneration.
simple: A non-worsening brain condition with muscle jerks, often after oxygen deprivation or in childhood.

name: Non-systemic vasculitis
formal: Vasculitis restricted to the peripheral nerves (non-systemic vasculitic neuropathy), causing painful mononeuritis multiplex without other organ involvement.
simple: Inflammation of blood vessels supplying nerves only, causing painful patchy nerve damage.

name: Nonaka distal myopathy
formal: Autosomal recessive GNE myopathy (distal myopathy with rimmed vacuoles) with tibialis anterior weakness in early adulthood and sparing of the quadriceps.
simple: An inherited muscle disease starting in young adults with foot drop that spreads slowly.
more: Biopsy shows rimmed vacuoles; GNE genetics; no approved therapy, supportive care.

name: Nondystrophic myotonias and hereditary periodic paralysis
formal: Group of skeletal muscle ion channelopathies including myotonia congenita, paramyotonia and periodic paralyses, from CLCN1, SCN4A and CACNA1S mutations.
simple: Inherited muscle conditions causing stiffness or attacks of weakness due to faulty ion channels.
more: Genetics and EMG exercise tests; treat with mexiletine, acetazolamide or dichlorphenamide.
nN: nondystrophic myotonias and hereditary periodic paralysis

name: Normal pressure hydrocephalus (NPH)
formal: Communicating hydrocephalus with ventriculomegaly and normal opening pressure, producing gait apraxia, cognitive decline and urinary incontinence; may improve after shunting.
simple: A condition with extra fluid in the brain causing walking difficulty, memory problems and bladder control problems, sometimes treatable with a shunt.

Urinary urgency/incontinence
Subcortical cognitive slowing
Arm swing and upper limbs relatively preserved (unlike Parkinson’s disease)

case.exam: Wide-based shuffling gait with start hesitation, arms swing normally, no rest tremor.
case.tests: MRI: Evans index 0.36 with tight convexity sulci; 30% faster 10-m walk after a 40 mL tap.

case.a: Likely improvement with ventriculoperitoneal shunting.

det.patho: Communicating hydrocephalus in older adults in which CSF dynamics are disturbed while lumbar opening pressure remains normal or mildly raised. Idiopathic NPH probably reflects impaired CSF absorption and reduced intracranial compliance, often with coexisting small vessel disease; secondary NPH follows SAH, meningitis or head injury. Ventricular enlargement stretches periventricular fibres serving leg control, bladder and frontal circuits.
det.clinical: Gait disturbance comes first and dominates: broad-based, short, shuffling, 'magnetic' steps with poor turning and start hesitation, but arm swing and upper-limb movement are relatively preserved. Cognitive slowing, apathy and inattention follow, and urinary urgency progresses to incontinence. The full triad is present in only some patients. Comorbid Parkinson disease, vascular disease and Alzheimer pathology often coexist and limit shunt response.
det.diagnosis: Imaging shows ventriculomegaly (Evans index >0.3) with a disproportionately enlarged subarachnoid space pattern: tight high-convexity sulci with widened Sylvian fissures (DESH), and a narrow callosal angle. Confirm likely shunt-responsiveness with a high-volume tap test (30–50 mL) or extended lumbar drainage, measuring gait speed and cognition before and after. A negative tap test does not exclude benefit. Exclude obstructive hydrocephalus and other causes of gait apraxia.
det.treatment: Ventriculoperitoneal (or lumboperitoneal) shunting with an adjustable valve is the definitive treatment. Gait improves most reliably; cognition and continence less so. Complications include over-drainage with subdural collections, infection and shunt blockage, so follow-up is needed. Physiotherapy and management of comorbidities support recovery.
det.prognosis: Most carefully selected patients improve after shunting, especially those with a short history and gait-led presentation; benefit may wane over years.
pearls: Gait first, then cognition, then bladder — reversed order argues against NPH.
Normal arm swing and no rest tremor separate NPH from Parkinson disease.
DESH on MRI predicts a good shunt response.

name: Norrie’s disease
formal: X-linked NDP mutation disorder with congenital blindness from retinal dysplasia, progressive deafness and intellectual disability.
simple: A rare inherited condition in boys causing blindness from birth, later hearing loss and learning problems.

name: Northern epilepsy
formal: Progressive epilepsy with mental retardation (EPMR) from CLN8 mutation in Finland, with seizures starting in childhood and cognitive decline.
simple: An inherited childhood epilepsy from Finland with seizures and gradual decline in thinking skills.

name: Nosocomial meningitis
formal: Hospital-acquired meningitis, usually after neurosurgery, shunts or drains; caused by Gram-negative bacilli or staphylococci, with atypical presentation and need for broad empirical cover.
simple: A brain-lining infection caught during a hospital stay, often after brain surgery or a drain, and caused by hospital-type germs.

name: NREM arousal disorders
formal: Parasomnias from slow wave sleep including sleepwalking, sleep terrors and confusional arousals, with partial arousal and amnesia, common in childhood.
simple: Sleep problems such as sleepwalking and night terrors in which a person partly wakes up and does not remember.
more: Diagnosed clinically and polysomnography if atypical. Treat triggers such as poor sleep and sleep apnoea; safety measures and sometimes clonazepam.

name: Nucleoside neuropathies
formal: Painful distal axonal sensory neuropathy from nucleoside analogue antiretroviral and antiviral drugs (ddI, ddC, d4T), via mitochondrial toxicity.
simple: Nerve damage with burning and numbness in the feet, caused by some HIV drugs.
more: Withdraw the drug; symptom control with neuropathic pain medications; improvement may take months.

name: Numb chin syndrome
formal: Mental neuropathy with numbness of the chin and lip from inferior alveolar or mental nerve involvement; an ominous sign of metastatic or haematological malignancy, or dental or mandibular disease.
simple: Numbness of the chin and lower lip from damage to a facial nerve, which can be an early warning of cancer spread.

name: Nummular headache
formal: Primary headache with chronic focal pain in a small coin-shaped scalp area of 1-6 cm, with stable location and often paroxysmal exacerbations; benign, may respond to gabapentin or indomethacin.
simple: A long-lasting headache felt in one small round patch of the scalp, about the size of a coin.

name: Nutritional and toxic optic neuropathies
formal: Bilateral symmetric painless visual loss with centrocaecal scotomas from vitamin B12 or folate deficiency, or toxins such as methanol, ethambutol and tobacco; mitochondrial vulnerability of papillomacular fibres.
simple: Slowly worsening vision in both eyes caused by poor diet or poisons that damage the nerves carrying signals from the eyes.

name: Obsessive–compulsive disorder (OCD)
formal: Psychiatric disorder of intrusive obsessions and repetitive compulsions linked to cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical circuit dysfunction; associated with tics, Tourette syndrome and basal ganglia disease.
simple: A condition with unwanted repeated thoughts and rituals that a person feels driven to carry out, even though they know they are excessive.
more: Treat with high-dose SSRIs and exposure and response prevention; augment with antipsychotics, and consider DBS for refractory disease. Neuroimaging is usually normal; rule out secondary causes such as PANDAS and structural lesions.
aN: ocd | obsessive compulsive disorder

name: Obsessive–compulsive personality disorders (OCPD)
formal: Personality disorder marked by perfectionism, rigidity, orderliness and control, without true obsessions or compulsions, and ego-syntonic unlike OCD.
simple: A lasting personality style with extreme perfectionism and a need for order and control that interferes with relationships and flexibility.
aN: ocpd | obsessive compulsive personality disorders

name: Obstetrically related plexopathies
formal: Brachial or lumbosacral plexus injuries related to childbirth, such as Erb palsy from shoulder dystocia or maternal lumbosacral trunk compression.
simple: Nerve injury connected with childbirth, either in the baby (arm weakness) or in the mother (leg weakness).
more: Most recover spontaneously; severe infant cases may need microsurgical repair.

name: Obstructive hydrocephalus
formal: Ventricular dilatation from blockage of CSF flow within the ventricular system, for example aqueduct stenosis or a posterior fossa mass, causing raised intracranial pressure.
simple: A build-up of fluid in the brain because a blockage stops it draining, causing headache, vomiting and drowsiness.

name: Obstructive sleep apnoea/hypopnoea syndrome (OSAHS)
formal: Recurrent upper airway collapse in sleep causing hypoxaemia, fragmented sleep and daytime somnolence; risk factor for stroke, hypertension and arrhythmia; treated with CPAP.
simple: Breathing repeatedly stops or becomes shallow during sleep because the throat closes, leading to loud snoring and daytime tiredness.
nN: obstructive sleep apnea hypopnea syndrome osahs
aN: osahs | obstructive sleep apnea hypopnea syndrome

name: Obturator neuropathy
formal: Injury to the obturator nerve (L2-4) from pelvic surgery, hernia, labour or tumour, causing weak hip adduction and sensory loss over the medial thigh.
simple: Damage to a nerve in the pelvis causing weakness pulling the leg inward and numbness on the inner thigh.

name: Occupational cramp
formal: Task-specific focal dystonia such as writer's cramp or musician's dystonia, with abnormal posturing triggered by a repetitive skilled movement; linked to impaired sensorimotor plasticity.
simple: Cramping or twisting of the hand or arm that occurs only during a repeated skilled task such as writing or playing an instrument.

name: Ocular apraxia
formal: Impaired voluntary initiation of horizontal saccades with preserved reflex movements, compensated by head thrusts; congenital (Cogan) or acquired from bilateral frontoparietal lesions.
simple: Difficulty deliberately moving the eyes to look sideways, so the person turns the head to shift gaze.

name: Ocular ischaemic syndrome
formal: Chronic hypoperfusion of the eye from severe ipsilateral carotid stenosis or occlusion, causing visual loss, orbital pain, venous stasis retinopathy and neovascularisation.
simple: Reduced blood flow to the eye from a badly narrowed neck artery, causing vision loss and eye pain.

name: Ocular motor apraxia
formal: Deficit of voluntary horizontal saccade initiation with intact reflexive eye movements, congenital or associated with ataxia-telangiectasia and bilateral cerebral lesions; head thrusts are typical.
simple: Trouble starting eye movements on command, so the person jerks the head to look to the side.

name: Ocular myasthenia
formal: Myasthenia gravis limited to ptosis and diplopia, often AChR antibody positive, with possible generalization within two years.
simple: A form of myasthenia affecting only eye muscles, causing droopy eyelids and double vision.
more: Diagnosed by ice-pack test, antibodies and single-fibre EMG; treat with pyridostigmine or low-dose prednisolone.

name: Oculomotor (IIIrd) nerve palsy
formal: Ptosis, ophthalmoplegia with eye down and out, and mydriasis from lesion of the third nerve; pupil-involving cases suggest compressive causes such as posterior communicating aneurysm, pupil-sparing suggests diabetic ischaemia.
simple: Damage to the third eye nerve causing a drooping eyelid, an eye turned down and outward, and often a large pupil.
aN: iiird | oculomotor nerve palsy

name: Oculomotor apraxia
formal: Impaired voluntary initiation of horizontal saccades with preserved reflex eye movements, compensated by head thrusts; congenital or associated with ataxia-telangiectasia and bilateral cortical lesions.
simple: Difficulty starting voluntary sideways eye movements, so the person turns the head to look at things.

name: Oculopalatal tremor
formal: Pendular vertical ocular oscillations with synchronous palatal tremor following brainstem or cerebellar lesion, with hypertrophic olivary degeneration within the Guillain-Mollaret triangle.
simple: Rhythmic eye wobbling together with a rhythmic movement of the soft palate, usually after a stroke in the brainstem.

name: Oculopharyngeal dystrophy
formal: Late-onset autosomal dominant muscular dystrophy with ptosis, dysphagia and limb weakness caused by GCG repeat expansion in PABPN1, with intranuclear inclusions.
simple: An inherited muscle disease starting in middle age with drooping eyelids and trouble swallowing.

name: Oculopharyngeal muscular dystrophy
formal: Late-onset autosomal dominant muscular dystrophy with ptosis, dysphagia and proximal limb weakness due to GCG repeat expansion in PABPN1; common in French Canadian families.
simple: An inherited muscle disease causing drooping eyelids and swallowing difficulty from midlife.
more: Diagnosed with GCG trinucleotide expansion (more than 10 repeats) in PABPN1; biopsy shows intranuclear filamentous inclusions and rimmed vacuoles. Treatment is cricopharyngeal myotomy for dysphagia and ptosis surgery; disease progresses slowly.

CK normal or mildly raised; swallow assessment

case.story: Eyelids have drooped over 10 years; now chokes on solid food. His mother had the same.
case.exam: Bilateral ptosis with frontalis overactivity, mild upgaze limitation, mild hip weakness.
case.tests: PABPN1 expansion; no fatigability on sustained upgaze.
case.q: What helps the dysphagia?
case.a: Cricopharyngeal myotomy or dilatation after swallow assessment; ptosis surgery for the eyelids.

ddx.pt: Fatigable and fluctuating, antibody positive
Marked ophthalmoplegia, mitochondrial DNA changes, ragged-red fibres
Myotonia, distal weakness, cataracts, cardiac conduction

aN: opmd | oculopharyngeal dystrophy | pabpn1

det.patho: OPMD is usually autosomal dominant and caused by a short expansion of the GCN trinucleotide repeat in PABPN1, lengthening a polyalanine tract. The mutant protein forms intranuclear filamentous inclusions in muscle fibres and impairs RNA processing. Founder populations include French-Canadians and Bukhara Jews, but it occurs worldwide.
det.clinical: Bilateral ptosis and dysphagia begin after age 40–50 and progress slowly over years. Patients compensate by tilting the head back and contracting the frontalis. Mild ophthalmoparesis, tongue weakness, dysphonia and proximal limb weakness appear later; diplopia is uncommon. Aspiration pneumonia, weight loss and social isolation are the major complications.
det.diagnosis: Genetic testing for the PABPN1 repeat expansion confirms the diagnosis. CK is normal or mildly elevated, and muscle biopsy (rarely needed) shows rimmed vacuoles and intranuclear inclusions. Videofluoroscopy assesses swallowing safety. Distinguish from myasthenia gravis (fluctuation, antibodies), mitochondrial CPEO (marked ophthalmoplegia) and myotonic dystrophy.
det.treatment: Ptosis is managed with levator resection or frontalis sling surgery when vision is obscured. Dysphagia may improve with cricopharyngeal myotomy, dilatation or botulinum toxin, along with diet modification and speech therapy; gastrostomy is used in advanced disease. Physiotherapy addresses limb weakness. Genetic counselling is offered to families.
det.prognosis: Life expectancy is usually close to normal, but severe dysphagia and aspiration can shorten survival if not managed.
pearls: Late-onset ptosis + dysphagia + family history = OPMD; check the PABPN1 repeat.
Lack of fatigability helps separate OPMD from ocular-bulbar myasthenia.
det.thd: OPMD เป็นโรคกล้ามเนื้อเสื่อมทางพันธุกรรมแบบยีนเด่น จากการขยายตัวของ repeat ในยีน PABPN1 มักเริ่มหลังอายุ 40–50 ปี ด้วยหนังตาตกสองข้างและกลืนลำบากที่ค่อยๆ เป็นมากขึ้น ผู้ป่วยมักเงยหน้าเพื่อมอง ต่อมาอาจมีต้นแขนต้นขาอ่อนแรง การวินิจฉัยใช้การตรวจยีน และต้องแยกจาก myasthenia gravis ที่อาการเปลี่ยนแปลงตามความล้า การรักษาคือผ่าตัดแก้หนังตาตก และผ่าตัดหรือขยายหูรูดหลอดอาหารเพื่อช่วยการกลืน

name: Off period dyskinesias
formal: Dystonic or choreic movements during the low levodopa state in Parkinson disease, often painful foot dystonia in early morning; related to fluctuating dopaminergic stimulation.
simple: Twisting or painful muscle spasms that occur in Parkinson disease when the medicine has worn off.

name: Off-dystonia
formal: Painful dystonic posturing, typically of the foot, during wearing-off of levodopa in Parkinson disease or early morning; responds to improved dopaminergic coverage.
simple: Painful cramping or twisting of a foot or leg in Parkinson disease when the medicine wears off, often in the morning.

name: Olanzapine akathisia
formal: Drug-induced restlessness with inner urge to move after olanzapine, due to dopamine receptor blockade; managed by dose reduction, beta-blockers, benzodiazepines or anticholinergics.
simple: Feeling unable to sit still, caused as a side effect of the antipsychotic medicine olanzapine.

name: Olfactory groove meningioma
formal: Slow-growing anterior skull base tumour causing anosmia, frontal lobe behaviour change and Foster Kennedy syndrome; often large at diagnosis.
simple: A slow-growing tumour under the front of the brain that can cause loss of smell and personality change.

name: Oligodendroglial α-synucleinopathy
formal: Multiple system atrophy, characterised by glial cytoplasmic inclusions of alpha-synuclein in oligodendrocytes, producing parkinsonism, cerebellar ataxia and autonomic failure.
simple: A progressive brain disease caused by an abnormal protein in support cells, causing stiffness, imbalance and blood pressure and bladder problems.
more: Diagnosed by clinical criteria and MRI; no disease-modifying therapy. Treat orthostatic hypotension and urinary symptoms; survival is about 6 to 10 years.

name: Oligodendrogliomas
formal: Diffuse glioma with IDH mutation and 1p/19q codeletion, typically frontal, calcified and presenting with seizures; better chemosensitivity and prognosis than astrocytoma.
simple: A type of brain tumour, often in the frontal lobe, that commonly causes seizures and tends to grow slowly.

name: Olivoponto-cerebellar atrophy
formal: Neurodegenerative cerebellar syndrome with loss of inferior olive, pontine nuclei and Purkinje cells, a pattern of multiple system atrophy or hereditary ataxias.
simple: Shrinking of parts of the brainstem and cerebellum causing progressive unsteadiness and poor coordination.
more: Neuropathological diagnosis of loss of olivary, pontine and cerebellar neurons; MRI shows the hot cross bun sign in MSA-C. Genetic testing for SCA mutations and autonomic tests help differentiate; treatment is supportive.

name: Olivopontocerebellar atrophy (OPCA)
formal: Neurodegeneration of inferior olives, pons and cerebellum causing progressive ataxia; sporadic form is multiple system atrophy with cerebellar predominance, also familial SCAs.
simple: Progressive shrinking of brainstem and cerebellum causing worsening balance and clumsiness.
more: MRI shows the hot cross bun sign and atrophy of cerebellum, middle cerebellar peduncles and pons; autonomic testing is needed. Sporadic cases have the MSA-C phenotype; consider SCA genetic testing for familial cases, and treatment is symptomatic.
aN: opca | olivopontocerebellar atrophy

name: One and a half syndrome
formal: Pontine lesion involving the PPRF or abducens nucleus and ipsilateral MLF, causing ipsilateral gaze palsy and internuclear ophthalmoplegia so only abduction of the contralateral eye remains.
simple: A brainstem problem leaving one eye unable to move sideways and the other able to move only outward.

name: Ophthalmoplegia (CPEO)
formal: Chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia with ptosis and slowly worsening eye movement paralysis, usually mitochondrial DNA deletion or POLG-related disease; part of Kearns-Sayre syndrome.
simple: Slowly worsening weakness of the eye muscles causing drooping lids and limited eye movement, usually due to a mitochondrial problem.
aN: cpeo | ophthalmoplegia

name: Opioid toxicity
formal: Overdose causing coma, miosis and respiratory depression via mu receptor agonism; reversed by naloxone; chronic use may cause leukoencephalopathy and myoclonus.
simple: Too much opioid medicine or drug, causing deep drowsiness, tiny pupils and slow breathing that can be fatal.

name: OPMD (oculopharyngeal muscular dystrophy)
formal: Late-onset autosomal dominant muscular dystrophy due to GCN expansions in PABPN1, with ptosis, dysphagia and proximal limb weakness, and intranuclear inclusions.
simple: An inherited muscle disease in later life that causes droopy eyelids, trouble swallowing and weak legs.
more: Diagnosed by PABPN1 repeat testing. Treatment is eyelid surgery, cricopharyngeal myotomy for swallowing and supportive care; more common in French-Canadian and Bukhara Jewish populations.
aN: oculopharyngeal muscular dystrophy | opmd

name: Opportunistic infections
formal: CNS infections in immunocompromised hosts such as HIV, with toxoplasmosis, cryptococcus, PML, CMV and TB; present with subacute focal deficits, headache or encephalopathy.
simple: Infections of the nervous system that mainly occur when the immune system is weak, such as in advanced HIV.

name: Opsoclonus myoclonus syndrome (OMS)
formal: Chaotic multidirectional saccades with myoclonus, ataxia and irritability; paraneoplastic (neuroblastoma in children, breast or lung cancer in adults) or parainfectious and immune-mediated.
simple: A condition with rapid, random jerking eye movements and muscle jerks, often linked to an immune reaction to cancer.
th: ตากระตุกไวทุกทิศทางอย่างไม่เป็นจังหวะ ร่วมกับกล้ามเนื้อกระตุกและเดินเซ — ในเด็กเล็กต้องหา neuroblastoma ในผู้ใหญ่เกิดหลังติดเชื้อหรือร่วมกับมะเร็ง
tempoNote: Develops over days to a few weeks; in children may relapse with infections or steroid tapering
feat: Opsoclonus: rapid, chaotic, multidirectional conjugate saccades without intersaccadic pause, persisting in sleep or eye closure
Action and resting myoclonus of trunk, limbs and head; truncal ataxia with refusal to walk
Irritability, sleep disturbance and behavioural regression in toddlers
Children aged 1–3 years: neuroblastoma in about half
Adults: post-infectious, or paraneoplastic with SCLC or breast/gynaecological cancer (anti-Ri, others)
inv: Children: MRI or CT chest/abdomen/pelvis, urine catecholamine metabolites (HVA, VMA), MIBG scan
Adults: paraneoplastic antibody panel (Ri, Hu, others), CT chest/abdomen/pelvis, mammography or PET
CSF: oligoclonal bands, B-cell expansion in children; infectious studies
MRI brain usually normal; exclude brainstem or cerebellar structural lesions

case.story: Two weeks after a cold he became irritable, stopped walking and could not hold his cup. His mother says his eyes 'shake in all directions'.
case.exam: Bursts of chaotic conjugate saccades in every direction, multifocal myoclonus of arms and head, unable to sit unsupported, crying constantly.
case.tests: MRI brain normal. Urine HVA and VMA mildly raised. CT abdomen: 2 cm right adrenal mass; MIBG avid.
case.q: What is the syndrome and what does treatment involve beyond tumour removal?
case.a: Neuroblastoma-associated opsoclonus-myoclonus syndrome; resection treats the tumour, but the neurological syndrome needs sustained immunotherapy (ACTH or steroids with IVIG, often rituximab) to protect long-term development.

det.patho: OMS is thought to arise from immune disinhibition of brainstem omnipause neurons and their cerebellar control (fastigial nucleus), releasing saccadic burst neurons into chaotic firing. B-cell activation is prominent in paediatric cases, while in adults onconeural antibodies such as anti-Ri mark the immune response but no single target explains most cases. Tumours, especially neuroblastoma, and infections act as triggers.
det.clinical: In toddlers, irritability and loss of walking often come first, and opsoclonus may be intermittent and missed. Adults present with opsoclonus or ocular flutter, myoclonus, ataxia and sometimes encephalopathy; younger adults often have a post-infectious, benign course, while older patients more often harbour a cancer. Long-term behavioural, learning and sleep problems are frequent in children.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical; in children at least three of four features (opsoclonus, myoclonus/ataxia, behavioural or sleep disturbance, neuroblastoma) are used. Search for neuroblastoma thoroughly and repeat if the first screen is negative. In adults, perform a full paraneoplastic workup and tumour search. Ocular flutter (horizontal only) belongs to the same spectrum.
det.treatment: Children need early, adequately long immunotherapy: ACTH or high-dose corticosteroids with IVIG, plus rituximab for moderate to severe or relapsing cases, alongside tumour resection. Adults with post-infectious OMS often respond to steroids or IVIG, while paraneoplastic adults require tumour therapy and immunotherapy. Clonazepam or levetiracetam can reduce myoclonus symptomatically.
det.prognosis: Children frequently have residual cognitive and behavioural problems, worse with delayed or insufficient treatment; adults with idiopathic or post-infectious OMS usually recover well, whereas paraneoplastic adult cases fare worse.
pearls: Toddler who stops walking and is irritable with dancing eyes: search for neuroblastoma.
Opsoclonus continues with eyes closed and during sleep.
The tumour is usually low grade; the neurological outcome depends on immunotherapy.
det.thd: Opsoclonus-myoclonus syndrome คือตากระตุกเร็วอย่างไม่เป็นระเบียบทุกทิศทาง ร่วมกับกล้ามเนื้อกระตุกและเดินเซ ในเด็กเล็กประมาณครึ่งหนึ่งพบ neuroblastoma จึงต้องตรวจภาพช่องท้องทรวงอกและ urine HVA/VMA ส่วนผู้ใหญ่มักเกิดหลังติดเชื้อหรือร่วมกับมะเร็ง ต้องตรวจแอนติบอดีและหามะเร็ง รักษาด้วยการผ่าตัดเนื้องอกร่วมกับ ACTH หรือ steroid, IVIG และ rituximab
