ddx.pt: Ataxia after varicella or other infection without opsoclonus or myoclonus; self-limiting
Ophthalmoplegia with drowsiness and ataxia; anti-GQ1b antibodies; no opsoclonus
Adult rapidly progressive dementia with myoclonus; DWI and RT-QuIC abnormalities

aN: oms | opsoclonus myoclonus syndrome | opsoclonus myoclonus ataxia syndrome | omas | dancing eyes dancing feet | kinsbourne syndrome | myoclonic encephalopathy of infancy

name: Opsoclonus-myoclonus (myoclonic encephalopathy of infancy)
formal: Childhood opsoclonus-myoclonus-ataxia syndrome, often paraneoplastic with neuroblastoma, with irritability and sleep disturbance; treated with immunotherapy and tumour removal.
simple: A rare childhood illness with dancing eye movements, jerks and unsteadiness, often triggered by a hidden tumour.
nN: opsoclonus myoclonus myoclonic encephalopathy of infancy
aN: myoclonic encephalopathy of infancy | opsoclonus myoclonus

name: Opsoclonus–myoclonus syndrome
formal: Chaotic multidirectional saccades with myoclonus and ataxia, paraneoplastic (neuroblastoma, small cell lung or breast cancer) or post-infectious; probable cerebellar disinhibition.
simple: Constant random eye jerking with muscle jerks and poor balance, often caused by an immune reaction to a cancer.

name: Optic and optochiasmal gliomas
formal: Pilocytic low-grade astrocytomas of optic nerve or chiasm, frequent in neurofibromatosis type 1, causing visual loss, proptosis and endocrine dysfunction.
simple: Slow-growing tumours of the vision pathway that can cause vision loss and are common in neurofibromatosis.

name: Optic atrophy plus syndrome
formal: Inherited optic atrophy with additional neurological features such as deafness, ataxia or neuropathy, as in OPA1 or mitochondrial disease.
simple: Inherited loss of the optic nerve that comes with other problems like deafness or poor coordination.

name: Optic gliomas
formal: Low-grade pilocytic astrocytomas of the optic pathway, linked to NF1, in children causing progressive visual loss, proptosis and optic atrophy.
simple: Slow-growing tumours of the optic nerve, mostly in children, that can reduce vision.

name: Optic neuritis
formal: Acute inflammatory optic neuropathy with painful subacute monocular visual loss, dyschromatopsia and RAPD; commonly first presentation of multiple sclerosis, also NMO and MOG disease.
simple: Inflammation of the eye nerve causing pain on eye movement and blurred, dull vision, often linked to multiple sclerosis.

name: Optic neuritis associated with neuromyelitis optica (NMO-ON)
formal: Severe, often bilateral or longitudinally extensive optic neuritis with AQP4 antibodies, poor recovery and risk of blindness; needs early steroids or plasma exchange.
simple: A severe form of optic nerve inflammation linked to neuromyelitis optica, which can cause lasting vision loss.
ab: Optic neuritis associated with neuromyelitis optica
nN: optic neuritis associated with neuromyelitis optica nmo on
aN: nmo on | optic neuritis associated with neuromyelitis optica

name: Optic neuropathy
formal: Damage to the optic nerve from inflammation, ischaemia, compression, toxins or inheritance, causing visual loss, colour desaturation, RAPD and a visual field defect.
simple: Damage to the nerve connecting the eye to the brain, causing reduced vision and dull colours.

name: Optic pathway glioma (OPG)
formal: Pilocytic astrocytoma of the optic nerve, chiasm or tract, usually in childhood and associated with NF1, causing visual loss, proptosis, precocious puberty or hypothalamic signs.
simple: A usually slow-growing tumour along the vision pathway in children that can affect sight and hormones.
aN: opg | optic pathway glioma

name: Optic perineuritis
formal: Inflammation of optic nerve sheath with eye pain, visual loss and ring enhancement around the nerve on MRI; responds well to corticosteroids, may follow infection or autoimmune disease.
simple: Swelling of the covering around the eye nerve causing pain and blurred vision, which usually improves with steroids.

name: Orbicularis oculi cranial dystonias
formal: Benign essential blepharospasm, focal cranial dystonia with involuntary bilateral eyelid closure; may combine with oromandibular dystonia (Meige syndrome); treated with botulinum toxin.
simple: Involuntary squeezing shut of the eyelids caused by overactive eye muscles.

name: Orbital inflammatory syndromes
formal: Idiopathic or IgG4-related inflammation of orbital tissues causing pain, proptosis, diplopia and ophthalmoplegia; diagnosis of exclusion, responsive to steroids.
simple: Swelling and inflammation behind the eye that can cause pain, bulging of the eye and double vision.

name: Orbital pseudotumour
formal: Idiopathic non-infectious orbital inflammation with painful proptosis, ophthalmoplegia and chemosis, rapidly responsive to corticosteroids; excludes thyroid eye disease, lymphoma and infection.
simple: A non-cancerous swelling behind the eye causing pain, bulging and double vision, which usually responds to steroids.

name: Organic acidaemias
formal: Inherited disorders of amino acid or fatty acid catabolism, such as methylmalonic or propionic acidaemia, causing metabolic acidosis, encephalopathy and basal ganglia injury.
simple: Inherited conditions where the body cannot break down certain proteins, causing acid build-up and brain problems.

name: Organic acidurias
formal: Group of inherited metabolic diseases such as propionic, methylmalonic and glutaric aciduria with accumulation of organic acids, causing metabolic acidosis, encephalopathy, and basal ganglia injury.
simple: Inherited disorders in which the body cannot break down certain protein parts, causing acid build-up and brain injury.
more: Urine organic acid analysis and newborn screening diagnose them. Treat with protein restriction, carnitine and emergency fluids; early treatment improves outcome.

name: Organic solvents, neurological toxicity
formal: Chronic or acute exposure to toluene, n-hexane or related solvents causing encephalopathy, cerebellar ataxia, leukoencephalopathy and peripheral neuropathy.
simple: Nerve and brain damage caused by breathing or touching industrial solvents such as glue or paint thinner.
aN: organic solvents | neurological toxicity

name: Organophosphate poisoning
formal: Cholinesterase inhibition producing cholinergic crisis with muscarinic, nicotinic and CNS features and intermediate syndrome with proximal weakness.
simple: Poisoning by pesticides that overstimulates nerves, causing sweating, small pupils, weakness and breathing failure.
more: Treat with atropine, pralidoxime, decontamination and ventilatory support; delayed neuropathy can follow.
th: พิษยาฆ่าแมลงกลุ่ม organophosphate — มีอาการ cholinergic เฉียบพลัน, intermediate syndrome และ neuropathy ภายหลัง
tempoNote: Cholinergic crisis in minutes–hours; intermediate syndrome day 1–4; delayed neuropathy 2–3 weeks later
feat: Muscarinic excess: pinpoint pupils, sweating, salivation, bronchorrhoea, bradycardia, vomiting, diarrhoea
Nicotinic effects: fasciculations, then weakness; CNS: confusion, seizures, coma
Intermediate syndrome: neck flexor, proximal and respiratory muscle weakness 1–4 days later
OP-induced delayed neuropathy: distal motor-predominant axonal neuropathy with later spasticity
Garlic or solvent smell; history of farm work or self-poisoning
inv: Red-cell acetylcholinesterase (or plasma butyrylcholinesterase) activity — supportive, do not delay treatment
Serial neck-flexion strength, single-breath count / vital capacity for intermediate syndrome
NCS/EMG weeks later if distal weakness develops

case.story: Drank an insecticide after a family argument; brought in drooling, vomiting and short of breath.
case.exam: Pupils 1 mm, wet crackles, HR 48, diffuse fasciculations; responsive to voice.
case.tests: Plasma cholinesterase markedly reduced; SpO2 88% on room air.
case.q: On day 3, after atropine is tapered, he cannot lift his head and breathing becomes shallow. What is this?
case.a: Intermediate syndrome — postsynaptic NMJ failure needing ventilatory support; atropine does not reverse it. Watch neck flexion and vital capacity daily.

read.where: Chapter 26 Toxic, Metabolic and Physical Insults to the Nervous System (organophosphates and carbamates)
Chapter 17 The toxic neuropathies: industrial, occupational and environmental agents (organophosphates)

det.patho: Organophosphorus insecticides (and the related military nerve agents) phosphorylate the active site of acetylcholinesterase, so acetylcholine builds up at muscarinic endings, autonomic ganglia, the neuromuscular junction and central synapses. Over minutes to days, depending on the compound, the enzyme–poison complex 'ages' into a permanent bond that oximes can no longer reverse; carbamates bind reversibly and do not age, which is why their toxicity is shorter. Intermediate syndrome reflects sustained postsynaptic nicotinic failure at the motor end-plate, whereas the delayed polyneuropathy (OPIDN) follows inhibition and ageing of neuropathy target esterase by certain compounds, triggering a central–peripheral distal axonopathy of the longest motor fibres and corticospinal tracts. Many products also contain solvents that add aspiration and CNS toxicity.
det.clinical: The acute cholinergic crisis appears within minutes to hours: miosis, salivation, lacrimation, sweating, bronchorrhoea and bronchospasm, vomiting, diarrhoea and urination, with bradycardia (though tachycardia and hypertension from nicotinic or hypoxic drive are common), then fasciculations, weakness, agitation, seizures and coma; most deaths are from respiratory failure. About 1–4 days later, often as muscarinic signs seem controlled, intermediate syndrome brings weakness of neck flexors, proximal limbs, cranial muscles and the diaphragm with sudden respiratory failure, but no sensory loss. Some 1–3 weeks after exposure to particular compounds, OPIDN starts with cramping calf pain and distal paraesthesia, then foot and hand weakness and foot drop; as peripheral nerves recover, spasticity, hyperreflexia and a spastic gait may be unmasked. In Thailand most severe cases follow deliberate ingestion or agricultural exposure, and some patients also have late neuropsychiatric problems.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis rests on the toxidrome plus exposure history (product container, farm work, smell of garlic or solvent); never delay atropine for laboratory confirmation. Red-cell acetylcholinesterase mirrors synaptic inhibition more closely than plasma butyrylcholinesterase, although the plasma assay is more widely available; both support the diagnosis and help track recovery but correlate imperfectly with severity. Watch for intermediate syndrome with serial neck-flexion strength, single-breath count, vital capacity and blood gases; repetitive nerve stimulation may show a decrement or repetitive CMAPs after single shocks. OPIDN is confirmed by NCS showing low motor amplitudes with denervation on EMG, and later corticospinal signs. Differentials include carbamate, paraquat or mixed pesticide poisoning, myasthenic crisis, GBS and botulism.
det.treatment: Resuscitate: secure the airway early (avoid succinylcholine, whose action is greatly prolonged), give oxygen, remove contaminated clothes and wash the skin, with staff wearing gloves. Give IV atropine 1–3 mg and double the dose every 5 minutes until the chest is clear on auscultation, heart rate exceeds about 80, systolic pressure exceeds about 80 mmHg, and the skin and axillae are dry, then maintain with an infusion of roughly 10–20% of the loading total per hour, titrating to avoid atropine toxicity (confusion, hyperthermia, absent bowel sounds). Pralidoxime may be added early, particularly for diethyl compounds, but trials have not shown a clear survival benefit; benzodiazepines treat seizures and agitation. Monitor in a high-dependency bed for at least several days for intermediate syndrome and ventilate promptly; OPIDN has no specific treatment, so rehabilitation, orthoses and spasticity care are the mainstays.
det.prognosis: Mortality depends on the compound, dose and speed of atropinisation and ventilation; highly toxic or fast-ageing compounds and large deliberate ingestions carry the highest risk. Intermediate syndrome resolves within about 1–3 weeks with ventilatory support; OPIDN recovers slowly and incompletely, and residual spasticity is common when the corticospinal tracts are involved.
pearls: Atropine endpoints are a dry chest, heart rate above 80 and adequate BP — not pupil size.
Neck flexion weakness after the crisis settles is the warning sign of intermediate syndrome.
Fasciculations plus pinpoint pupils plus wet lungs in a farm worker: treat for organophosphate poisoning immediately.
Do not use succinylcholine for intubation — paralysis may last hours.
det.thd: Organophosphate ยับยั้ง acetylcholinesterase ทำให้ acetylcholine คั่งที่ปลายประสาท muscarinic, nicotinic และในสมอง ระยะแรกภายในไม่กี่ชั่วโมงมีน้ำลายและเสมหะมาก รูม่านตาเล็ก เหงื่อออก อาเจียน ถ่ายเหลว หัวใจเต้นช้า กล้ามเนื้อเต้นระริก แล้วซึมหรือชัก ต้องดูแลทางเดินหายใจ ล้างตัว และให้ atropine 1–3 mg เพิ่มเป็นสองเท่าทุก 5 นาทีจนปอดแห้ง ชีพจรมากกว่า 80 และความดันดี แล้วต่อด้วยยาหยด อาจให้ pralidoxime ร่วม ห้ามใช้ succinylcholine ช่วงวันที่ 1–4 อาจเกิด intermediate syndrome คือคออ่อน แขนขาส่วนต้นอ่อน และหายใจล้มเหลวทันที ต้องเฝ้าดูกำลังกล้ามเนื้อคอและการหายใจ อีก 1–3 สัปดาห์ต่อมาบางรายเกิด OPIDN คือปลายประสาทสั่งการเสีย เท้าตก และอาจเกร็งภายหลัง

Known MG, no muscarinic secretions or miosis, normal cholinesterase
Ascending weakness with areflexia and albuminocytologic dissociation; no cholinergic signs

name: Orgasmic sex headache
formal: Primary headache of explosive onset at orgasm, lasting minutes to hours; must exclude subarachnoid haemorrhage and reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome; usually benign.
simple: A sudden severe headache at the moment of sexual climax, usually harmless but needing a check for serious causes.

name: Orofacial apraxia
formal: Inability to perform voluntary mouth and face movements on command with preserved automatic movements, from left frontal or opercular lesions, often with Broca aphasia.
simple: Difficulty making face and mouth movements on request, such as blowing or sticking out the tongue, although they happen automatically.

name: Orofacial chorea
formal: Involuntary irregular movements of lips, tongue and jaw, as in Huntington disease or tardive dyskinesia, or after levodopa or neuroleptics.
simple: Irregular uncontrolled movements of the mouth, lips and tongue.

name: Orofacial dyskinesia
formal: Involuntary repetitive lip smacking, tongue protrusion and chewing, as in tardive dyskinesia from dopamine blockers, edentulous states or levodopa.
simple: Uncontrolled chewing, lip-smacking or tongue movements, often a side effect of some medicines.
more: Review drug history and dental status; stop or reduce the neuroleptic and consider switching to clozapine or quetiapine. VMAT2 inhibitors (valbenazine, deutetrabenazine) are effective in tardive forms; spontaneous orofacial dyskinesia occurs in older people.

name: Orofacial tremor
formal: Rhythmic movement of lips, jaw or tongue, for example rabbit syndrome from antipsychotics, or tremor in Parkinson disease.
simple: Rhythmic shaking of the lips, jaw or tongue.

name: Orolingual dyskinesia
formal: Repetitive involuntary movements of tongue, lips and jaw, such as chewing, lip smacking and tongue protrusion, typical of tardive dyskinesia from dopamine blockers or edentulous states.
simple: Repeated involuntary tongue, lip and jaw movements such as chewing or smacking.
more: Treat by withdrawing the offending drug if feasible, with VMAT2 inhibitors (valbenazine, deutetrabenazine) as first-line; may persist for years.

name: Orolingual tremors
formal: Rhythmic tremor of tongue and perioral muscles, seen in parkinsonism, essential tremor, drug-induced syndromes or other basal ganglia disease.
simple: Rhythmic shaking of the tongue and mouth.

name: Oromandibular dystonia
formal: Focal cranial dystonia with involuntary jaw, lip and tongue contractions causing jaw opening, closing or deviation; worsened by speaking or eating, relieved by sensory tricks; treated with botulinum toxin.
simple: Involuntary muscle spasms of the jaw, lips and tongue that make speaking and eating difficult.

name: Orthostatic hypotension (OH)
formal: Sustained fall in blood pressure of at least 20/10 mmHg within three minutes of standing, from autonomic failure, hypovolaemia or drugs; seen in Parkinson disease, MSA and neuropathy.
simple: A drop in blood pressure on standing up that causes dizziness or fainting.
aN: oh | orthostatic hypotension

name: Orthostatic myoclonus
formal: Brief jerks of the legs and trunk on standing that improve on walking or sitting, causing unsteadiness; often cortical and seen in neurodegenerative disease.
simple: Sudden jerks in the legs when standing that make a person unsteady, easing when they sit.

name: Orthostatic tremor
formal: Very fast (13–18 Hz) tremor of the legs and trunk that appears only when standing still and eases on walking or sitting; felt as unsteadiness rather than visible shaking.
simple: A fast shaking of the legs when standing still that makes a person feel unsteady but stops when they walk or sit.
th: ขาสั่นความถี่สูงมากและรู้สึกไม่มั่นคงเฉพาะตอนยืนนิ่ง ดีขึ้นทันทีเมื่อเดินหรือนั่ง วินิจฉัยด้วย EMG พบ 13–18 Hz
tempoNote: Onset usually after 50; slowly progressive over years
feat: Feeling of unsteadiness or impending fall when standing still, relieved by walking, sitting or leaning
Tremor often not visible; can be felt with a hand on the thigh or heard with a stethoscope as a 'helicopter' sound
Patients avoid queues, standing in the shower or cooking
Neurological examination otherwise near normal; falls are uncommon
inv: Surface EMG of leg muscles while standing: synchronous 13–18 Hz bursts (diagnostic)
MRI and DAT-SPECT if other signs suggest parkinsonism or cerebellar disease (orthostatic tremor 'plus')
Stethoscope over the calf or thigh at the bedside

case.story: For 5 years she cannot stand in line at the market; her legs feel shaky and she must walk or hold the trolley. Walking is fine.
case.exam: Fine rippling of quadriceps on standing, heard as a rapid thumping with the stethoscope on the thigh; settles at once when she walks; rest of exam normal.
case.tests: Surface EMG during standing: 16 Hz coherent bursts in both legs.
case.q: Which drug is commonly tried first?
case.a: Primary orthostatic tremor: clonazepam is commonly tried first; gabapentin or primidone are alternatives.

read.where: Chapter 16 Essential Tremor and Other Tremors

det.patho: Primary orthostatic tremor is thought to arise from a central oscillator in the brainstem or cerebello-thalamo-cortical circuit, as the 13–18 Hz rhythm is coherent across all leg, trunk and even arm muscles bearing weight. It is rare, sporadic and slightly more common in women.
det.clinical: The main complaint is unsteadiness rather than tremor, which worsens the longer the patient stands and resolves with walking or sitting. The upper limbs can show the same tremor when weight-bearing (e.g. pushing on a table). Some develop additional parkinsonism, cerebellar signs or cognitive change (OT plus), and slower 'pseudo-orthostatic' tremor occurs in other disorders.
det.diagnosis: Surface EMG showing high-frequency (13–18 Hz) synchronous bursts on standing confirms it. Bedside clues are palpable or audible thigh/calf tremor. Exclude orthostatic myoclonus, slower orthostatic tremor in parkinsonism, orthostatic hypotension, cerebellar disorders and functional gait disturbance.
det.treatment: Clonazepam is the most commonly used drug; gabapentin, primidone and perampanel are alternatives, and levodopa may help a subset. Responses are often partial. Walking aids, a seat stick and avoiding prolonged standing help daily life. Thalamic or spinal cord stimulation has been tried in refractory cases.
det.prognosis: Slowly progressive and seldom disabling for walking, but quality of life is affected; a minority develop other neurological features.
pearls: Unsteady standing still, fine when walking: think orthostatic tremor.
Put a stethoscope on the thigh — a helicopter-like rumble is a clue.
Confirm with leg surface EMG: 13–18 Hz.
det.thd: Primary orthostatic tremor คืออาการขาสั่นความถี่สูง 13–18 Hz เฉพาะเวลายืนนิ่ง ผู้ป่วยรู้สึกจะล้มแต่เมื่อเดินหรือนั่งก็หายทันที มองด้วยตามักไม่เห็นการสั่น แต่คลำหรือใช้หูฟังที่ต้นขาได้ยินเสียงสั่นเร็ว ยืนยันด้วย surface EMG ยาที่ใช้บ่อยคือ clonazepam หรือ gabapentin และใช้อุปกรณ์ช่วยเลี่ยงการยืนนาน

ddx.pt: Irregular, non-rhythmic EMG bursts on standing; often older people with neurodegeneration
Visible arm action tremor at 4–12 Hz; leg involvement less prominent and not standing-specific
Light-headedness on standing with blood pressure fall; no high-frequency EMG bursts

aN: primary orthostatic tremor | pot | ot | shaky legs syndrome | 13 18 hz leg tremor

name: Oscillatory myoclonus
formal: Repetitive rhythmic myoclonic jerks, as in some cortical or spinal forms, or stimulus-triggered; considered between myoclonus and tremor.
simple: Repeated rhythmic muscle jerks.

name: Osler-Rendu-Weber disease
formal: Hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia, an autosomal dominant vascular disorder (ENG, ACVRL1) with mucocutaneous telangiectasias, recurrent epistaxis and visceral arteriovenous malformations, causing stroke and brain abscess.
simple: An inherited disease with fragile abnormal blood vessels, causing nosebleeds and sometimes strokes or brain abscess.
more: Curacao criteria and genetic testing; screen for pulmonary and cerebral AVMs. Treat with embolisation, bevacizumab and iron replacement.

name: Osmotic demyelination
formal: Pontine and extrapontine demyelination after rapid correction of chronic hyponatraemia, causing quadriparesis, dysarthria, locked-in state and parkinsonism.
simple: Brain damage after sodium levels in the blood are corrected too quickly, causing weakness and speech problems.

name: Osteoid osteoma
formal: Benign bone tumour with a nidus, causing nocturnal pain relieved by NSAIDs; in the spine may cause painful scoliosis and radiculopathy.
simple: A small non-cancerous bone growth causing night pain that aspirin-like drugs relieve, sometimes in the spine.

name: Osteosarcoma, spinal
formal: Rare primary malignant bone tumour of the spine, causing pain and cord or root compression, often after radiation or in Paget disease.
simple: A rare cancer of the spine bone that may press on the nerves.
aN: osteosarcoma | spinal

name: Otosclerosis
formal: Bone remodelling of the otic capsule that fixes the stapes and causes progressive conductive hearing loss, tinnitus and paracusis; Schwartz sign on otoscopy.
simple: Abnormal bone growth in the middle ear that stops sound passing and gradually causes hearing loss.

name: Otosyphilis
formal: Syphilitic involvement of cochlea and labyrinth causing sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus and vertigo; part of neurosyphilis, treated with penicillin and steroids.
simple: Syphilis infection of the inner ear that causes hearing loss, ringing and dizziness.

name: Overlap myositis
formal: Inflammatory myopathy occurring with another connective tissue disease such as scleroderma or lupus; often anti-synthetase, PM-Scl or Ku antibodies.
simple: Muscle inflammation occurring together with another autoimmune disease.

name: Pachymeningitis
formal: Thickening and inflammation of the dura causing headache and cranial neuropathies, from IgG4-related disease, sarcoidosis, granulomatosis with polyangiitis, TB or infection.
simple: Inflammation of the thick outer covering of the brain causing headache and nerve problems.

name: Paediatric-onset multiple sclerosis
formal: MS beginning before age 18, with a higher relapse rate than adult-onset but slower progression; needs distinction from ADEM and MOG disease.
simple: Multiple sclerosis that starts in childhood or teenage years.

name: Paget’s disease
formal: Disordered bone remodelling with bone enlargement causing deafness, spinal stenosis, cranial neuropathies and platybasia; raised alkaline phosphatase; treated with bisphosphonates.
simple: A bone disease in which bones grow too large and weak, which can squeeze nerves and cause deafness.

name: Painful legs and moving toes syndrome
formal: Persistent leg pain with involuntary writhing toe movements, due to nerve root, nerve or spinal lesion; treated symptomatically with gabapentin or nerve blocks.
simple: Pain in the legs with toes that move on their own in a writhing way.
nN: painful legs and moving tes syndrome

name: Painful neuropathies
formal: Peripheral nerve disorders in which neuropathic pain dominates, typically burning or shooting, from small-fibre involvement; causes include diabetes, toxins, amyloid, HIV and inherited channelopathies.
simple: Nerve damage that causes burning, stabbing or electric-shock-like pain, often in the feet and hands.
more: Work up includes glucose, B12, skin biopsy and nerve conduction studies. Treatment targets the cause and uses duloxetine, gabapentinoids or tricyclics; topical agents help some people.

name: Painful ophthalmoplegia
formal: Orbital or cavernous sinus pain with ocular motor palsies, as in Tolosa-Hunt syndrome, aneurysm, diabetes, tumour or infection; steroids respond in idiopathic cases.
simple: Eye pain together with weak eye movements, often caused by inflammation or pressure behind the eye.

name: Painful sensory neuropathies
formal: Predominantly small-fibre sensory neuropathies with burning pain, allodynia and autonomic features, often with normal conduction studies; causes include diabetes, impaired glucose tolerance, Fabry disease and SCN9A variants.
simple: Damage to the small sensory nerves that makes the feet and hands burn, tingle or hurt, sometimes from light touch.
more: Skin biopsy for intra-epidermal nerve fibre density is useful. Manage underlying disease and use neuropathic pain drugs; the course is usually chronic but not disabling for movement.

name: Painful sensory neuropathy
formal: Neuropathy dominated by burning, stabbing pain from small-fibre dysfunction, from diabetes, toxins, or idiopathic causes.
simple: Nerve damage causing burning or stabbing pain, mostly in the feet.
more: Skin biopsy for fibre density; treat with duloxetine, pregabalin, gabapentin, or tricyclics, and address the cause.

name: Palatal myoclonus
formal: Rhythmic soft palate contractions, 1-3 Hz, persistent during sleep; symptomatic form follows brainstem lesion with olivary hypertrophy, essential form causes ear click.
simple: Rhythmic jerks of the soft palate at the back of the mouth, sometimes heard as a clicking in the ear.

name: Palatal myoclonus/tremor
formal: Rhythmic soft palate movements, either symptomatic with olivary hypertrophy after brainstem lesion or essential with ear click; classified as palatal tremor.
simple: Rhythmic jerking of the soft palate, either after a brainstem injury or without a clear cause.

name: Palatal tremor
formal: Rhythmic soft palate movement of 1-3 Hz; symptomatic after brainstem or cerebellar lesion with hypertrophic olivary degeneration, or essential with ear click.
simple: Regular rhythmic jerking of the soft palate that may cause a clicking noise in the ear.

name: Pallidoluysian atrophy (PLA)
formal: Degeneration of the globus pallidus and subthalamic nucleus, as in DRPLA, producing chorea, ataxia, myoclonus, epilepsy and dementia.
simple: Loss of cells in deep brain areas that control movement, causing jerks, imbalance and dementia.
more: Genetic testing for atrophin-1 CAG repeats in DRPLA is typical. Treatment is symptomatic and the disease is progressive.
aN: pla | pallidoluysian atrophy

name: Pallidoluysian dentate atrophy (PLDA)
formal: Dentatorubral-pallidoluysian atrophy, a CAG repeat disorder of ATN1 with progressive ataxia, choreoathetosis, myoclonic epilepsy and dementia, more frequent in Japan.
simple: A rare inherited brain disease with clumsiness, jerking movements, seizures and dementia, seen mostly in Japan.
more: Autosomal dominant with anticipation; confirm by ATN1 repeat testing. MRI shows brainstem and cerebellar atrophy; treat symptomatically.
aN: plda | pallidoluysian dentate atrophy

name: Pallidonigral atrophy (PNA)
formal: Rare degeneration of the globus pallidus and substantia nigra producing parkinsonism with poor levodopa response, sometimes with pyramidal signs, described pathologically.
simple: A rare brain degeneration affecting two movement centres, causing stiffness and slowness.
more: Diagnosis made at autopsy; treatments have limited effect and care is supportive.
aN: pna | pallidonigral atrophy

name: Pallidonigroluysian atrophy (PNLA)
formal: Rare neurodegeneration of the pallidum, substantia nigra and subthalamic nucleus with parkinsonism, dystonia or chorea, possibly with pyramidal signs and dementia.
simple: A rare brain disease with cell loss in three deep movement-control areas, causing stiffness and slow movement.
more: Definitive diagnosis is pathological; some cases overlap with PSP. Treatment is symptomatic.
aN: pnla | pallidonigroluysian atrophy

name: Pallidopyramidal disease or pallidonigrospinal degeneration (PPD/S)
formal: Rare juvenile parkinsonism with pyramidal signs, dystonia and early onset, often from PLA2G6 or ATP13A2 variants, with levodopa responsiveness at first.
simple: A rare early-onset condition combining parkinsonism and stiff, brisk limb reflexes from spinal cord pathway involvement.
more: Genetic testing identifies causes (e.g. PARK9 Kufor-Rakeb). Levodopa helps initially but dyskinesia and decline occur.
nN: pallidopyramidal disease or pallidonigrospinal degeneration ppd s
aN: ppd | s | pallidopyramidal disease or pallidonigrospinal degeneration

name: Pantothenate kinase-associated neurodegeneration
formal: Autosomal recessive PANK2 disorder with iron accumulation in globus pallidus (eye-of-the-tiger sign), causing dystonia, parkinsonism, retinopathy and acanthocytes.
simple: An inherited brain disease with iron build-up causing stiffness, twisting movements and sometimes vision problems.
ab: neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation type 1
th: โรคพันธุกรรม PANK2 ที่มีเหล็กสะสมใน globus pallidus เด็กมี dystonia รุนแรงโดยเฉพาะปากและขากรรไกร MRI เห็น eye-of-the-tiger
tempoNote: Classic form begins before age 6 and progresses rapidly; atypical form begins in the teens with slower progression
feat: Gait difficulty and falls in early childhood, then generalized dystonia
Prominent oromandibular dystonia: jaw opening, tongue biting, dysarthria and dysphagia
Pigmentary retinopathy in many classic cases
Spasticity, extensor plantars; atypical form shows speech problems, psychiatric features and parkinsonism
Risk of status dystonicus
inv: MRI: T2/SWI hypointense globus pallidus with central hyperintensity — 'eye-of-the-tiger' sign
PANK2 genetic testing (autosomal recessive)
Ophthalmology with ERG for retinopathy; peripheral blood smear for acanthocytes

case.story: Clumsy and falling since age 3; over a year his jaw keeps pulling open, he bites his tongue and his speech is slurred. Parents are first cousins.
case.exam: Generalized dystonia with prominent jaw-opening dystonia, brisk reflexes, toe-walking; fundi show pigmentary retinal changes.
case.tests: MRI: bilateral pallidal T2 hypointensity with central bright spot; biallelic PANK2 variants.
case.q: Name the MRI sign and the disease group.
case.a: Eye-of-the-tiger sign of PKAN, the most common form of neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation (NBIA).

read.where: Chapter 15 Inherited Metabolic Disorders Associated with Extrapyramidal Symptoms

det.patho: Biallelic PANK2 mutations impair mitochondrial pantothenate kinase 2, the key enzyme for coenzyme A synthesis. CoA deficiency disrupts lipid metabolism and mitochondrial function, and iron accumulates in the globus pallidus with axonal spheroids. It accounts for roughly half of NBIA cases.
det.clinical: Classic PKAN starts in early childhood with gait problems and progresses rapidly to severe generalized dystonia, with characteristic oromandibular involvement, dysarthria and loss of ambulation within years. Retinopathy is common in classic disease. Atypical PKAN presents in adolescence with speech difficulty, neuropsychiatric change and parkinsonism, progressing more slowly. Status dystonicus is a dangerous complication.
det.diagnosis: MRI with T2/SWI showing the eye-of-the-tiger sign strongly suggests PKAN and is confirmed by PANK2 testing. Other NBIA disorders (PLAN, MPAN, BPAN, neuroferritinopathy, aceruloplasminemia) have different MRI patterns. Exclude Wilson disease in every child or young adult with dystonia.
det.treatment: Treatment is symptomatic: trihexyphenidyl, baclofen (oral or intrathecal), botulinum toxin for focal dystonia, and GPi DBS for severe generalized or status dystonicus. Iron chelation with deferiprone lowers pallidal iron but has not clearly changed progression. Feeding support (gastrostomy), physiotherapy, vision care and palliative care planning are important.
det.prognosis: Classic disease often leads to loss of walking within 10–15 years and shortened life; atypical disease is milder and slower.
pearls: Eye-of-the-tiger: dark pallidum with a bright centre on T2 — PKAN.
Severe jaw-opening dystonia with tongue biting in a child suggests PKAN.
Always check copper studies before labelling NBIA.
det.thd: PKAN เกิดจากยีน PANK2 แบบ autosomal recessive ทำให้มีเหล็กสะสมใน globus pallidus เด็กมีปัญหาการเดินแล้วตามด้วย dystonia ทั่วตัว เด่นที่ปากและขากรรไกร พูดไม่ชัด กัดลิ้น และอาจมีจอประสาทตาเสื่อม MRI พบ eye-of-the-tiger sign รักษาตามอาการด้วยยา botulinum toxin และ DBS ร่วมกับดูแลการกลืน ต้องตรวจแยก Wilson disease เสมอ

ddx.pt: Low ceruloplasmin, raised urinary copper, KF rings and liver disease; treatable with chelation
Adult onset, dominant inheritance, low serum ferritin, cystic basal ganglia change
Rigidity, seizures and cognitive decline with paternal HD history; HTT CAG expansion

aN: pkan | pank2 | nbia1 | hallervorden spatz syndrome | hallervorden spatz disease | neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation type 1 | eye of the tiger

name: Pantothenate kinase-associated parkinsonism
formal: Atypical late-onset PANK2 disease with parkinsonism, gait freezing, speech disorder and psychiatric features; pallidal iron accumulation on MRI.
simple: A later-onset form of an inherited iron-storage brain disease causing stiffness, slowness and speech problems.

name: Paraballism
formal: Bilateral ballistic flinging movements of both legs, usually from bilateral basal ganglia or subthalamic lesions, or less commonly spinal causes.
simple: Wild flinging movements of both legs, usually after damage to deep brain areas.

name: Paralysis agitans
formal: Historical term for Parkinson disease, meaning shaking palsy, referring to rest tremor with rigidity and bradykinesia.
simple: An old name for Parkinson disease.

name: Paralysis, sleep
formal: Temporary inability to move or speak while falling asleep or waking, with preserved awareness from REM atonia intrusion; common in narcolepsy and sleep deprivation.
simple: Waking up unable to move or speak for a short time, which can feel frightening but is harmless.
aN: paralysis | sleep

name: Paramnesias
formal: Distortions of memory with false recognition or recall such as déjà vu, confabulation or reduplicative paramnesia; seen in temporal lobe epilepsy and frontal or right hemispheric lesions.
simple: Memory distortions in which a person believes a false memory or feels wrongly familiar with something.

name: Paramyotonia
formal: Sodium channel myotonia (SCN4A) with cold-induced myotonia that worsens with exercise and may cause episodes of weakness.
simple: An inherited condition where muscles become stiff in the cold and stiffness worsens with repeated use.
more: Cooling EMG test and genetic testing; mexiletine is effective.

name: Paramyotonia congenita
formal: Autosomal dominant SCN4A sodium channelopathy with cold-induced myotonia worsening with exercise, and episodic weakness; mexiletine helpful.
simple: An inherited muscle disease where muscles stiffen in the cold and with repeated use.
more: Cold provocation with EMG shows a drop in compound muscle amplitude; the common mutation is T1313M or R1448C in SCN4A. Avoid cold and potassium loading; mexiletine or acetazolamide reduces attacks.
th: กล้ามเนื้อคลายช้าแบบที่แย่ลงเมื่อทำซ้ำและเมื่อเย็น — ใบหน้า มือ เปลือกตา (SCN4A)
feat: Paradoxical myotonia: stiffness increases with repeated action
Cold provokes stiffness and then weakness of face, eyelids and hands
Eyelid myotonia (slow opening after forced closure); may overlap with hyperkalaemic periodic paralysis
inv: EMG myotonia; cooling worsens findings
SCN4A genetic testing

case.story: In cold weather her face stiffens and she cannot open her eyes quickly after squeezing them shut; in winter her hands become weak.
case.exam: Eyelid myotonia increasing with repeated closures, mild grip myotonia that worsens with repetition.
case.tests: EMG myotonic discharges; SCN4A variant.
case.q: Which bedside feature separates this from myotonia congenita?
case.a: Worsening (not improving) with repetition, and cold sensitivity.

files.chapter: Chapter 1: Neuromuscular Disorders: A Clinical Approach

ddx.pt: Warm-up phenomenon, muscle hypertrophy
Episodes of flaccid weakness with high K; may overlap

aN: paramyotonia | eulenburg disease | scn4a myotonia | paradoxical myotonia

det.patho: Autosomal dominant gain-of-function variants in SCN4A stop the muscle Nav1.4 channel from inactivating quickly, particularly at low temperatures. Persistent inward sodium current produces repetitive firing (myotonia) and, with more sustained depolarisation, inexcitability and weakness. Some variants overlap with hyperkalaemic periodic paralysis.
det.clinical: Symptoms begin in infancy or childhood and mainly affect the face, eyelids, tongue and hands. Stiffness becomes worse rather than better with repeated movement (paradoxical myotonia) and is provoked by cold, leading to weakness that can last hours after rewarming. Eyelid myotonia after forced closure is a typical bedside sign. Some patients also have episodic flaccid weakness, particularly after potassium intake or rest following exercise.
det.diagnosis: Clinical history of cold sensitivity and paradoxical myotonia is very suggestive. EMG shows myotonic discharges; on short exercise testing with cooling, CMAP amplitude falls progressively, unlike chloride channel myotonia. SCN4A testing confirms the diagnosis. CK may be mildly elevated.
det.treatment: Keep the body and hands warm and avoid triggers such as cold water swimming. Mexiletine is effective for cold-induced stiffness; acetazolamide or thiazide-type diuretics may reduce weakness episodes in overlap patients. As with other myotonias, avoid depolarising muscle relaxants and monitor temperature during anaesthesia.
det.prognosis: The course is non-progressive and life expectancy is normal; quality of life is mainly affected in cold climates or occupations.
pearls: Paradoxical myotonia (worse with repetition) plus cold sensitivity = SCN4A.
Test eyelid opening after repeated forced closures.
Ask about episodic weakness: overlap with hyperPP is common.
det.thd: Paramyotonia congenita เกิดจากยีน SCN4A ทำให้ช่องโซเดียมของกล้ามเนื้อปิดไม่สนิทโดยเฉพาะเมื่อเย็น อาการเด่นคือใบหน้า เปลือกตา และมือแข็งเกร็งมากขึ้นเมื่อทำซ้ำหรือโดนอากาศเย็น ตามด้วยอ่อนแรงได้ ต่างจาก myotonia congenita ที่ดีขึ้นเมื่อทำซ้ำ ตรวจ EMG ร่วมกับทำให้กล้ามเนื้อเย็น และตรวจยีน SCN4A รักษาด้วยการรักษาความอบอุ่นและ mexiletine

name: Paraneoplastic autonomic neuropathy
formal: Autonomic neuropathy related to cancer, commonly anti-Hu or ganglionic AChR antibodies, causing gastroparesis, orthostatic hypotension and pseudo-obstruction.
simple: Nerve damage affecting automatic body functions caused by the immune response to a cancer.
more: Search for tumour, e.g. small cell lung cancer; treat tumour and immunotherapy; prognosis often poor.

name: Paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration (PCD)
formal: Subacute pancerebellar syndrome with Purkinje cell loss due to onconeural antibodies such as anti-Yo, Hu or Tr, associated with ovarian, breast, lung cancer or Hodgkin lymphoma.
simple: Rapidly worsening balance and coordination caused by the immune system attacking the cerebellum in response to a cancer.
th: สมองน้อยเสื่อมจากภูมิต้านทานที่สัมพันธ์กับมะเร็ง โดยเฉพาะ anti-Yo ในผู้หญิงที่มีมะเร็งรังไข่หรือเต้านม — เซรุนแรงภายในไม่กี่สัปดาห์
tempoNote: Ataxia evolves rapidly over days to weeks and plateaus within about 3 months, often before the cancer is known
feat: Rapidly progressive pancerebellar syndrome: gait and limb ataxia, dysarthria
Downbeat nystagmus, oscillopsia and vertigo with nausea at onset
Patient often bedbound or chairbound within weeks
Anti-Yo (PCA-1): almost always women with ovarian, uterine, fallopian tube or breast cancer
Other antibodies: Tr/DNER (Hodgkin lymphoma), Hu, CV2, Ri, KLHL11, VGCC (small-cell lung cancer)
inv: Paraneoplastic panel: Yo (CDR2/CDR2L) by immunoblot confirmed with tissue immunohistochemistry
MRI brain: normal early, cerebellar atrophy later; exclude metastasis and stroke
CSF: early mild pleocytosis, raised protein, oligoclonal bands
Tumour search: mammography/breast MRI, pelvic ultrasound or CT, CA-125, then FDG-PET if negative

case.who: 57-year-old woman, rubber plantation owner in Surat Thani
case.story: Five weeks of dizziness and vomiting, then rapidly worsening imbalance; now she cannot sit without support and speech is slurred.
case.exam: Downbeat nystagmus, scanning dysarthria, severe limb and truncal ataxia, normal strength and sensation.
case.tests: MRI brain normal. CSF: 12 lymphocytes, protein 62 mg/dL, OCB positive. Anti-Yo strongly positive. Pelvic CT: complex left adnexal mass; CA-125 410 U/mL.
case.q: Why is urgent tumour treatment important even though the ataxia rarely improves?
case.a: Anti-Yo PCD reflects an occult gynaecological cancer, often small at diagnosis; early oncological treatment improves survival and may stabilise the neurological deficit, which results from rapid Purkinje cell loss.

det.patho: Tumours express onconeural proteins such as CDR2/CDR2L, provoking an immune response that also attacks cerebellar Purkinje cells, which normally express these antigens. Because the targets are intracellular, cytotoxic T cells are the main effectors and Purkinje cell loss occurs quickly and irreversibly. The antibody serves as a diagnostic marker rather than the main cause of damage.
det.clinical: Onset is often heralded by dizziness, nausea and visual blurring, followed within weeks by severe pancerebellar ataxia. Neurological symptoms precede the cancer diagnosis in most patients. Mild extracerebellar signs (hyperreflexia, neuropathy) can occur, especially with other antibodies. Tr/DNER cases occur in younger patients with Hodgkin lymphoma and may have a better prognosis.
det.diagnosis: Updated PNS-Care criteria (2021) treat subacute cerebellar syndrome as a high-risk phenotype; a high-risk antibody plus cancer gives definite diagnosis. Confirm commercial line-blot Yo results with tissue-based assays because isolated weak blots can be false. Early MRI is normal, which helps distinguish from structural lesions. If the initial screen is negative, repeat tumour screening at intervals up to about 2 years.
det.treatment: Treat the tumour as the priority. Immunotherapy (steroids, IVIG, plasma exchange, cyclophosphamide or rituximab) is given early, but responses in anti-Yo PCD are modest because neurons are lost quickly. Rehabilitation, safety aids and symptomatic therapy for vertigo and nystagmus are important.
det.prognosis: Most anti-Yo patients remain severely disabled; survival depends mainly on the cancer, while Tr/DNER-associated cases can improve with lymphoma therapy.
pearls: Subacute severe ataxia in a middle-aged woman with normal MRI: think anti-Yo and look for ovarian or breast cancer.
Downbeat nystagmus is common in PCD.
Hodgkin lymphoma plus subacute ataxia points to Tr/DNER antibodies.

name: Paraneoplastic encephalitis
formal: Immune-mediated limbic or diffuse encephalitis with memory loss, seizures and psychiatric features associated with tumour and antibodies such as anti-Hu, Ma2 or NMDA receptor.
simple: Brain inflammation caused by the immune system reacting to a hidden cancer, causing memory loss, seizures and confusion.

name: Paraneoplastic neurological disorders (PND)
formal: Immune-mediated nervous system syndromes remote from cancer, with onconeural antibodies; includes encephalomyelitis, cerebellar degeneration, neuropathy and Lambert-Eaton syndrome.
simple: Nerve and brain problems caused by the body's immune response to a cancer elsewhere in the body.
aN: pnd | paraneoplastic neurological disorders

name: Paraneoplastic opsoclonus–myoclonus (POM)
formal: Opsoclonus-myoclonus with ataxia associated with neuroblastoma in children and breast, lung or other tumours in adults, with anti-Ri antibodies in some.
simple: Wild eye movements and muscle jerks caused by the immune system reacting to a cancer.
aN: pom | paraneoplastic opsoclonus myoclonus

name: Paraneoplastic sensorimotor polyneuropathy
formal: Subacute or chronic sensorimotor neuropathy associated with underlying cancer, often lung, lymphoma, or myeloma, via immune or paraproteinaemic mechanisms.
simple: Nerve damage causing numbness and weakness as a remote effect of a hidden cancer.
more: Investigate with antibodies and cancer screening; treat the tumour and use immunotherapy.

name: Paraneoplastic sensory neuropathy/ganglionopathy
formal: Anti-Hu (ANNA-1) related dorsal root ganglionopathy with asymmetric sensory loss, ataxia, and pain, typically with small-cell lung cancer.
simple: Immune damage to sensory nerve cells in a ganglion, causing numbness and balance loss, often with a lung cancer.
more: Check anti-Hu antibodies and search for tumour; treat the tumour; immunotherapy is rarely beneficial.

name: Paraneoplastic stiff man syndrome
formal: Stiff-person variant with progressive rigidity and spasms associated with anti-amphiphysin antibodies and breast or lung cancer.
simple: A rare condition of muscle stiffness and spasms triggered by the body's immune response to cancer.

name: Paraneoplastic syndrome
formal: Remote effects of malignancy on the nervous system or other organs from immune mechanisms or secreted factors, with antibodies such as Hu, Yo, Ri and CV2.
simple: Symptoms caused not by a tumour itself but by the body's immune response to it.
more: Test for onconeural antibodies (anti-Hu, Yo, Ri, CV2/CRMP5, amphiphysin, Ma2) and screen for tumour with CT, PET and mammography. Treat the tumour and give immunotherapy, but prognosis is poor; neurological syndromes often precede detection of the cancer.

name: Paraplegia
formal: Paralysis of both legs from thoracic or lumbar cord, cauda equina or cerebral lesion, with sensory level and sphincter disturbance; causes include trauma, myelitis and tumour.
simple: Weakness or paralysis of both legs, usually caused by spinal cord injury or disease.

name: Paraproteinaemic neuropathy
formal: Neuropathy occurring with a monoclonal immunoglobulin (M-protein) produced by a clonal plasma-cell or B-cell population — most often MGUS, sometimes myeloma, Waldenström macroglobulinaemia, lymphoma, AL amyloidosis, cryoglobulinaemia or POEMS; mechanisms include antibody binding to nerve antigens and deposition of immunoglobulin or amyloid.
simple: Nerve damage that comes with an abnormal single type of antibody protein in the blood, made by an overgrown family of blood cells; sometimes that family is a cancer, so it must be looked for.
th: เส้นประสาทเสื่อมที่พบร่วมกับโปรตีนโมโนโคลนอลในเลือด — ต้องตรวจหาโรคเม็ดเลือดชนิด plasma cell/B cell ที่ซ่อนอยู่

Three clinical patterns: distal demyelinating (often IgM/anti-MAG), CIDP-like (often IgG/IgA), or length-dependent axonal
The neuropathy may appear years before the blood disorder declares itself
Red flags for malignancy: weight loss, bone pain, organomegaly, anaemia, renal failure, autonomic failure
inv: Serum protein electrophoresis with immunofixation (more sensitive than electrophoresis alone) and serum free light chains
Urine protein electrophoresis/immunofixation
NCS to define demyelinating vs axonal pattern
Haematology referral: bone marrow, skeletal survey; anti-MAG if IgM; VEGF if POEMS suspected; fat pad biopsy for amyloid

case.exam: Stocking sensory loss, reduced vibration at the knees, absent ankle jerks, mild toe extensor weakness.
case.tests: Serum immunofixation: IgG-lambda band; free light chain ratio abnormal; skeletal survey: lytic lesions.

det.patho: A clone of plasma cells or B cells secretes a single immunoglobulin (M-protein). Nerve injury can arise because the M-protein acts as an autoantibody (anti-MAG, anti-ganglioside), because light chains form amyloid deposits, because cryoglobulins cause vasculitis, through cytokines such as VEGF in POEMS, or through direct infiltration. In many older patients with an IgG or IgA band the M-protein is incidental, since MGUS is common in the elderly. IgM gammopathies are proportionally more often truly linked to neuropathy.
det.clinical: Most patients have a slowly worsening distal sensory or sensorimotor neuropathy. Three main patterns guide work-up: distal acquired demyelinating (typical of IgM/anti-MAG), CIDP-like with proximal weakness, and length-dependent axonal. Red flags for a serious underlying disorder include weight loss, bone pain, organomegaly, autonomic failure, painful small-fibre neuropathy, rapid progression, renal impairment and skin changes.
det.diagnosis: Screen any unexplained neuropathy with serum electrophoresis plus immunofixation and serum free light chains; electrophoresis alone misses small bands. Characterise the neuropathy with NCS. Then tailor tests: anti-MAG for IgM, VEGF and bone imaging for lambda bands with demyelination, fat pad or nerve biopsy for amyloid, cryoglobulins and hepatitis C for vasculitic pictures. Refer to haematology for marrow examination and staging.
det.treatment: Treatment depends on the mechanism. CIDP-like IgG/IgA cases are treated as CIDP. Anti-MAG disease is treated with rituximab when disabling. Malignant causes (myeloma, Waldenström, AL amyloid, POEMS) require haematological therapy directed at the clone. Slow axonal neuropathy with an incidental MGUS usually needs only symptomatic care and monitoring.
det.prognosis: Outlook depends on the underlying disorder, ranging from a benign course with MGUS to serious systemic disease with amyloidosis or POEMS.
pearls: Immunofixation and free light chains are more sensitive than SPEP — order them together.
A lambda paraprotein with a demyelinating neuropathy is POEMS until proven otherwise.
An IgG MGUS in an elderly patient may be a bystander; do not over-attribute.
det.thd: Paraproteinaemic neuropathy คือเส้นประสาทเสื่อมที่พบร่วมกับโปรตีนโมโนโคลนอลในเลือด ซึ่งสร้างจากกลุ่มเซลล์พลาสมาหรือ B cell ที่เจริญผิดปกติ กลไกมีหลายแบบ เช่น โปรตีนทำหน้าที่เป็นแอนติบอดีต่อเส้นประสาท หรือสะสมเป็นอะไมลอยด์ ควรตรวจ immunofixation และ free light chain ในผู้ป่วยเส้นประสาทเสื่อมที่ไม่ทราบสาเหตุ และส่งปรึกษาโลหิตวิทยาเพื่อหาโรคมะเร็ง การรักษาขึ้นกับสาเหตุ เช่น แบบคล้าย CIDP รักษาเหมือน CIDP ส่วนแบบที่เป็นมะเร็งต้องรักษาตัวโรคเลือด

name: Parasagittal meningioma
formal: Meningioma along the superior sagittal sinus causing focal seizures and contralateral leg weakness from parasagittal motor cortex involvement.
simple: A slow-growing brain-lining tumour near the midline that can cause seizures and leg weakness.

name: Parasitic neurological infections
formal: CNS infection by helminths or protozoa such as neurocysticercosis, toxoplasmosis, malaria and schistosomiasis, producing seizures, mass lesions and meningitis.
simple: Nervous system infections caused by parasites, such as tapeworm cysts in the brain.

name: Parasomnias
formal: Abnormal sleep behaviours, either NREM (sleepwalking, night terrors) or REM (REM sleep behaviour disorder, nightmares), reflecting incomplete state dissociation.
simple: Unusual behaviours during sleep such as sleepwalking, talking or acting out dreams.

name: Parathyroid disorders
formal: Hyper- or hypoparathyroidism causing calcium disturbance, with neuromuscular irritability, tetany, seizures, basal ganglia calcification and proximal myopathy.
simple: Problems with the glands controlling calcium, which can cause muscle cramps, weakness and seizures.
more: Check serum calcium, phosphate, PTH and vitamin D, with CT or MRI showing basal ganglia calcification. Neuromuscular signs improve with correction of calcium: calcium and calcitriol for hypoparathyroidism, parathyroidectomy for primary hyperparathyroidism.

name: Parathyroid-induced myopathy
formal: Proximal muscle weakness and wasting from primary hyperparathyroidism or vitamin D deficiency osteomalacia, with normal CK, reversible after treatment.
simple: Muscle weakness in the thighs and hips caused by an overactive parathyroid gland or low vitamin D.

name: Parenchymal CNS tuberculosis
formal: Tuberculoma or abscess of brain or spinal cord from Mycobacterium tuberculosis, causing focal deficits and seizures with ring-enhancing lesions.
simple: Tuberculosis forming lumps within the brain or spinal cord, causing weakness or seizures.

name: Parinaud syndrome
formal: Dorsal midbrain syndrome with impaired upgaze, convergence-retraction nystagmus, light-near dissociation and lid retraction, from pineal tumour, hydrocephalus or midbrain stroke.
simple: A problem with looking upward and abnormal pupils, caused by damage to the top of the brainstem.

name: Parinaud’s syndrome
formal: Dorsal midbrain syndrome with vertical gaze palsy, convergence-retraction nystagmus, light-near dissociation and Collier sign, typically from pineal region tumour or hydrocephalus.
simple: Trouble looking upward with abnormal pupils, caused by pressure on the back of the midbrain.

name: Parkin disease
formal: Autosomal recessive early-onset Parkinson disease from PRKN mutations, with dystonia, slow progression, good levodopa response and usually no Lewy bodies.
simple: An inherited form of Parkinson disease starting in young adults, caused by a change in the parkin gene.

name: Parkinsonian rigidity
formal: Lead-pipe or cogwheel increased resistance to passive movement of limbs, a cardinal sign of parkinsonism from nigrostriatal dopamine loss.
simple: Stiffness of the arms and legs when someone moves them, a typical sign of Parkinson disease.

name: Parkinsonian-dementia syndromes
formal: Disorders combining parkinsonism and cognitive decline, including Parkinson disease dementia, dementia with Lewy bodies, PSP and corticobasal degeneration.
simple: Illnesses that cause both movement slowness or stiffness and memory or thinking problems.

name: Parkinsonism
formal: Clinical syndrome of bradykinesia with rest tremor, rigidity or postural instability; due to Parkinson disease, atypical parkinsonism, vascular disease or drugs.
simple: A set of symptoms including slowness, stiffness and shaking, from Parkinson disease or other causes.
more: Evaluate with levodopa trial, MRI, DAT-SPECT, and drug history; atypical features include early falls, poor levodopa response, and autonomic failure. Treatment depends on cause, and drug-induced parkinsonism often resolves in weeks to months after withdrawal.

name: Parkinsonism-plus syndromes
formal: Atypical parkinsonian disorders such as MSA, PSP and corticobasal degeneration, with poor levodopa response, early falls, autonomic failure or gaze palsy.
simple: Parkinson-like illnesses with extra problems such as early falls or blood pressure trouble, which respond poorly to treatment.

name: Parkinsonism–dementia complex of Guam (PDC)
formal: Western Pacific tauopathy with parkinsonism and dementia, linked to ALS-parkinsonism-dementia complex, with neurofibrillary tangles; possible environmental cycad toxin link.
simple: A rare illness on the island of Guam causing Parkinson-like symptoms and dementia.
nN: parkinsonism dementia complex of guam pdc
aN: pdc | parkinsonism dementia complex of guam

name: Parkinson’s disease (PD)
formal: Neurodegenerative synucleinopathy with nigrostriatal dopamine loss causing bradykinesia, rest tremor and rigidity, with non-motor symptoms; levodopa-responsive.
simple: A brain disease causing slowness, stiffness and tremor because cells that make dopamine are lost.
more: Diagnosis is clinical, supported by DAT-SPECT showing reduced striatal uptake; MRI excludes secondary causes. Treat with levodopa, dopamine agonists, MAO-B inhibitors, COMT inhibitors and amantadine; DBS for motor fluctuations; LRRK2.
th: โรคพาร์กินสัน — เคลื่อนไหวช้า สั่นขณะพัก แข็งเกร็ง เริ่มข้างเดียว ตอบสนองดีต่อยาเลโวโดปา
feat: Bradykinesia with decrement plus rest tremor and/or rigidity
Asymmetric onset that stays asymmetric
Prodrome: hyposmia, constipation, REM sleep behaviour disorder, depression
Clear, sustained levodopa response; later motor fluctuations and dyskinesia
inv: Clinical diagnosis (MDS criteria)
Dopamine transporter SPECT if uncertain (vs essential or drug-induced tremor)
MRI to look for atypical features if red flags

case.exam: Right pill-rolling rest tremor, decrementing finger taps on the right, cogwheel rigidity at the right wrist, reduced arm swing.
case.tests: None required; marked improvement on levodopa.
case.q: Which sleep symptom is a prodromal clue?
case.a: REM sleep behaviour disorder (dream enactment) — a synucleinopathy marker.

aN: pd | parkinson disease | idiopathic parkinson disease | paralysis agitans | ipd

det.patho: Misfolded alpha-synuclein aggregates into Lewy bodies and Lewy neurites, and pigmented dopaminergic cells of the substantia nigra pars compacta die off, starving the dorsal putamen of dopamine. Pathology probably begins years earlier in the olfactory bulb and lower brainstem (and possibly the gut), which explains the non-motor prodrome. Most cases are sporadic; monogenic forms (LRRK2, SNCA, PRKN, PINK1) and GBA variants as a risk factor account for a minority. Age is the dominant risk factor, with a modest male excess.
det.clinical: Motor onset is typically one-sided, with slowness and fatiguing of repetitive movements, a 4–6 Hz resting tremor and lead-pipe or cogwheel rigidity. Patients describe small handwriting, a quiet voice, reduced facial expression and a shuffling gait with less arm swing. Non-motor problems — smell loss, constipation, dream enactment, mood change, pain, urinary urgency and later orthostasis and cognitive decline — often matter more for quality of life. After some years on levodopa, wearing-off, peak-dose dyskinesia and freezing of gait appear. Red flags pointing elsewhere include early falls, early dementia, early severe autonomic failure, rapid progression, symmetric onset and a poor drug response.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical, built on the 2015 MDS criteria: establish parkinsonism (bradykinesia plus rest tremor or rigidity), then weigh supportive features against absolute exclusions and red flags. A convincing, sustained response to dopaminergic therapy strongly supports the diagnosis. DAT SPECT shows presynaptic dopaminergic loss but cannot separate PD from MSA or PSP; it is mainly useful against essential tremor, dystonic tremor and drug-induced parkinsonism. Routine MRI is normal; order it if atypical signs are present. Skin biopsy or CSF seed amplification assays for alpha-synuclein are emerging biomarkers, mostly in research or specialist use.
det.treatment: Start symptomatic treatment when symptoms impair function; levodopa with a decarboxylase inhibitor is the most effective drug, while dopamine agonists and MAO-B inhibitors are alternatives in younger or milder patients. Warn every patient on agonists about impulse control disorders and sudden sleep attacks. Fluctuations are managed by fractionating levodopa, adding COMT or MAO-B inhibitors, amantadine for dyskinesia, and rescue apomorphine or inhaled levodopa. Advanced options include deep brain stimulation (STN or GPi) and continuous levodopa or apomorphine infusion. Exercise, physiotherapy, speech therapy and treatment of non-motor symptoms are integral; avoid typical antipsychotics and metoclopramide, and never stop levodopa abruptly.
det.prognosis: Progression is slow over 10–20 years, with life expectancy only modestly reduced; falls, dementia and dysphagia drive late disability and death.
pearls: Tremor that is absent when the hands are held out but returns after a few seconds (re-emergent tremor) is still a Parkinsonian rest tremor.
Abrupt levodopa withdrawal can cause a hyperpyrexic crisis resembling neuroleptic malignant syndrome.
Strictly symmetric onset, early falls or no levodopa benefit should make you rethink the diagnosis.
det.thd: โรคพาร์กินสันเกิดจากเซลล์สร้างโดปามีนใน substantia nigra ตายลงพร้อมการสะสมของโปรตีน alpha-synuclein อาการหลักคือเคลื่อนไหวช้าที่เริ่มข้างเดียว ร่วมกับสั่นขณะพักหรือเกร็ง และมีอาการนำ เช่น จมูกไม่ได้กลิ่น ท้องผูก ละเมอตามความฝัน การวินิจฉัยใช้อาการทางคลินิกตามเกณฑ์ MDS ส่วน DAT scan ช่วยเมื่อแยกจาก essential tremor หรือยาที่ทำให้เกิดอาการ ยาหลักคือ levodopa และเมื่อโรคก้าวหน้าอาจใช้ DBS หรือยาแบบให้ต่อเนื่อง

name: Parkinson’s disease dementia (PDD)
formal: Dementia developing after at least a year of established Parkinson disease, with attention and executive deficits, hallucinations and Lewy body pathology.
simple: Memory and thinking decline that develops in someone who has had Parkinson disease for some time.
aN: pdd | parkinson disease dementia

name: Parkinson’s disease with mild cognitive impairment (PD-MCI)
formal: Cognitive decline in Parkinson disease not interfering with daily function, with executive or visuospatial deficits; risk factor for later dementia.
simple: Mild thinking and memory problems in a person with Parkinson disease that do not yet affect daily life.
ab: Parkinson’s disease with mild cognitive impairment
nN: parkinson disease with mild cognitive impairment pd mci
aN: pd mci | parkinson disease with mild cognitive impairment

name: Paroxysmal (nonepileptic) movement disorders
formal: Episodic attacks of dyskinesia without loss of consciousness or EEG epileptiform activity, including kinesigenic, nonkinesigenic and exertional dyskinesias, episodic ataxias and hypnogenic forms.
simple: Sudden short episodes of abnormal movements such as twisting or jerking that are not seizures.
more: Classified by trigger and duration; genes include PRRT2, MR-1 and SLC2A1. Treatment is trigger avoidance and drugs such as carbamazepine or acetazolamide depending on subtype.
aN: nonepileptic | paroxysmal movement disorders

name: Paroxysmal choreoathetosis
formal: Episodic attacks of chorea, athetosis or dystonia, either kinesigenic, non-kinesigenic or exercise-induced, often genetic channelopathies or PRRT2 mutations.
simple: Short attacks of twisting or writhing movements that come and go.

name: Paroxysmal dyskinesia
formal: Episodic involuntary movements, dystonia or chorea with normal examination between attacks, classified as kinesigenic, non-kinesigenic or exercise-induced.
simple: Sudden short episodes of abnormal movements with normal movement in between.
more: PKD (PRRT2 mutations) responds to carbamazepine or phenytoin; PNKD (MR-1) responds poorly to medication and is triggered by alcohol, caffeine. Video recording is helpful; interictal exam and EEG are normal.

name: Paroxysmal dystonia
formal: Episodic dystonic attacks, genetic or secondary, with preserved consciousness; includes kinesigenic, nonkinesigenic and exercise-induced forms.
simple: Short episodes of muscle twisting or cramping that come and go.

name: Paroxysmal exercise-induced dyskinesia
formal: Dystonic attacks triggered by prolonged exercise lasting 5-30 minutes, often from SLC2A1 (GLUT1) mutations; may respond to ketogenic diet.
simple: Attacks of muscle twisting in the legs set off by long exercise.
more: Examine for GLUT1 deficiency with CSF glucose, lactate and SLC2A1 testing; PED can also result from PRRT2, ATP1A3 or dopa-responsive dystonia genes. Ketogenic diet or modified Atkins is effective, and avoidance of triggers helps.

name: Paroxysmal exertional dyskinesia
formal: Episodic dystonia or choreoathetosis after prolonged exercise lasting 5 to 30 minutes, often from SLC2A1 (GLUT1) variants, with epilepsy or hemolytic anaemia in some.
simple: Attacks of twisting or jerky movements of the legs triggered by prolonged exercise such as walking or running.
more: Lumbar puncture may show low CSF glucose; ketogenic diet is effective in GLUT1 deficiency and acetazolamide sometimes helps.

name: Paroxysmal hypnic dyskinesia
formal: Nocturnal episodes of dystonic or choreic movements arising from NREM sleep, likely frontal lobe epilepsy mimic and responsive to carbamazepine.
simple: Short attacks of abnormal movements that wake a person from sleep, probably a form of sleep seizure.

name: Paroxysmal hypnic dystonia
formal: Nocturnal dystonic attacks from NREM sleep, now regarded as nocturnal frontal lobe epilepsy responsive to carbamazepine.
simple: Brief episodes of twisting movements out of sleep, now thought to be a type of seizure.

name: Paroxysmal kinesigenic dyskinesia
formal: Brief attacks of dystonia or chorea triggered by sudden movement, due to PRRT2 mutations, with excellent response to low-dose carbamazepine.
simple: Brief attacks of abnormal movements set off by suddenly starting to move, which respond well to a seizure medicine.
th: อาการบิดเกร็งหรือกระตุกชั่วครู่ไม่กี่วินาที เกิดทันทีเมื่อเริ่มขยับตัวแบบกะทันหัน ไม่หมดสติ ตอบสนองดีมากต่อ carbamazepine ขนาดต่ำ
tempoNote: Brief attacks (<1 minute), often many per day; onset in childhood or adolescence, tends to lessen after age 20–30
feat: Attacks triggered by sudden movement after rest (standing up, starting to run, startle)
Dystonic, choreic or ballistic movements of one or both sides lasting seconds
Awareness preserved; often a brief sensory aura in the limb
Normal examination between attacks
Personal or family history of benign infantile seizures or migraine (PRRT2 spectrum)
inv: Video of attacks (phone recording is very helpful)
EEG normal interictally and usually during attacks
MRI normal; check calcium/PTH, glucose and thyroid to exclude secondary PKD
PRRT2 genetic testing (most familial cases)

case.who: 15-year-old boy, high-school student in Hat Yai
case.story: When the bell rings and he jumps up from his chair, his right arm and leg twist for about 10 seconds; he stays fully aware. It happens several times daily. As a baby he had brief seizures that stopped by age 2.
case.exam: Normal neurological examination; an attack is reproduced by asking him to stand quickly.
case.tests: EEG and MRI normal; calcium normal; PRRT2 c.649dupC detected.
case.q: Which drug and dose range typically controls these attacks?
case.a: Paroxysmal kinesigenic dyskinesia (PRRT2): low-dose carbamazepine (e.g. 50–200 mg/day) or oxcarbazepine usually abolishes attacks.

det.patho: Most familial and many sporadic cases carry heterozygous loss-of-function PRRT2 variants; PRRT2 interacts with SNARE proteins and regulates neurotransmitter release and sodium-channel availability. The same gene causes self-limited infantile epilepsy and infantile convulsions with choreoathetosis (ICCA), and is linked to hemiplegic migraine and episodic ataxia. Secondary PKD occurs with MS, hypoparathyroidism, hyperglycaemia, head injury or basal ganglia lesions.
det.clinical: Onset is usually between 6 and 16 years, with male predominance in sporadic cases. Attacks are very brief, can occur up to dozens of times a day and may be preceded by tingling or tightness. Some patients learn to slow their movements to avoid them. Frequency often decreases in adulthood, and some remit.
det.diagnosis: Clinical criteria include identified kinesigenic trigger, short duration (<1 min), no loss of consciousness, normal examination, exclusion of other causes, onset age 1–20 years and response to phenytoin or carbamazepine. Home video and genetic testing support the diagnosis. Look for secondary causes, especially hypoparathyroidism and MS in adults.
det.treatment: Low-dose sodium-channel blockers — carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine or phenytoin, and lacosamide as an option — are highly effective, often at doses well below those used for epilepsy. Avoidance of sudden movements and of sleep deprivation also helps. Offer genetic counselling given autosomal dominant inheritance.
det.prognosis: Excellent — attacks are usually fully controlled with treatment and often wane with age.
pearls: Seconds-long dystonia on sudden standing, with full awareness: think PKD.
Dramatic response to a small dose of carbamazepine is almost diagnostic.
Ask about infantile seizures in the patient or family (PRRT2).
det.thd: PKD เป็นโรคที่มีอาการบิดเกร็งหรือกระตุกของแขนขาเพียงไม่กี่วินาที เกิดเมื่อเริ่มเคลื่อนไหวกะทันหัน เช่น ลุกจากเก้าอี้ ผู้ป่วยรู้สึกตัวตลอด ส่วนใหญ่เกิดจากยีน PRRT2 อาจมีประวัติชักในวัยทารก การตรวจระหว่างอาการปกติ EEG และ MRI ปกติ รักษาด้วย carbamazepine หรือ oxcarbazepine ขนาดต่ำซึ่งได้ผลดีมาก

Not consistently provoked by sudden movement, may impair awareness; EEG change
Variable triggers and duration, distractibility, onset often in adulthood

aN: pkd | paroxysmal kinesigenic choreoathetosis | pkc | prrt2 dyskinesia | episodic kinesigenic dyskinesia | prrt2 related disorder

name: Paroxysmal kinesiogenic dyskinesia (PKD)
formal: Brief attacks of dystonia or chorea lasting seconds, triggered by sudden movement, linked to PRRT2 variants, starting in childhood or adolescence, with a usually benign course.
simple: Short episodes of involuntary movements triggered by suddenly starting to move, such as getting up quickly.
more: Dramatic response to low-dose carbamazepine or phenytoin; many remit in adulthood. Genetics reveal PRRT2 in most families.
aN: pkd | paroxysmal kinesiogenic dyskinesia

name: Paroxysmal non-kinesigenic dyskinesia
formal: Attacks of dystonia and chorea lasting minutes to hours, triggered by alcohol, caffeine, stress or fatigue, caused by MR-1 (PNKD) mutations.
simple: Longer attacks of abnormal movements triggered by alcohol, coffee or stress.

name: Paroxysmal nonkinesiogenic dyskinesia (PNKD)
formal: Attacks of dystonia or chorea lasting minutes to hours, triggered by alcohol, caffeine, fatigue or stress and not movement, from MR-1 variants, autosomal dominant.
simple: Longer episodes of abnormal movements triggered by alcohol, coffee or stress rather than movement.
more: Avoid triggers; clonazepam or benzodiazepines work better than carbamazepine. Prognosis is good and may improve with age.
aN: pnkd | paroxysmal nonkinesiogenic dyskinesia

name: Paroxysmal sympathetic hyperactivity
formal: Episodes of tachycardia, hypertension, hyperthermia, sweating and dystonia after severe brain injury, from disconnection of autonomic control; treated with beta-blockers, gabapentin, bromocriptine.
simple: Episodes of racing heart, high blood pressure, sweating and fever after serious brain injury.

name: Parry–Romberg syndrome
formal: Progressive hemifacial atrophy affecting skin, fat, muscle and bone, with trigeminal neuralgia, migraine or epilepsy; related to linear scleroderma.
simple: A rare condition where one side of the face slowly shrinks, sometimes with headaches or seizures.

name: Partial spinal cord syndrome
formal: Incomplete cord lesion patterns such as Brown-Séquard, anterior or central cord syndromes, with characteristic motor and sensory distributions below the lesion.
simple: Spinal cord damage that affects only part of the cord, so some movement or feeling is lost and some is kept.

name: Paucibacillary leprosy
formal: Tuberculoid or indeterminate leprosy with few skin patches and nerve thickening, causing sensory loss and mononeuropathy; strong cell-mediated response.
simple: A milder form of leprosy with few skin patches and numb areas.

name: PCOM artery aneurysm
formal: Posterior communicating artery aneurysm, often causing painful third nerve palsy with pupil involvement, or subarachnoid haemorrhage when ruptured.
simple: A bulge in a brain artery that can press on a nerve to the eye or bleed.

name: Peak-dose dyskinesias
formal: Choreiform or dystonic movements during peak plasma levodopa levels in treated Parkinson disease, related to pulsatile dopaminergic stimulation; amantadine may help.
simple: Involuntary wriggling movements when medicine levels are highest in Parkinson disease.

name: Pelizaeus–Merzbacher disease (PMD)
formal: X-linked hypomyelinating leukodystrophy from PLP1 mutations, with nystagmus, hypotonia, spasticity and developmental delay in infancy.
simple: An inherited condition in boys where nerve insulation fails to form properly, causing abnormal eye movements and delayed development.
more: PLP1 duplication is the most common cause (also point mutations and null); MRI shows diffuse hypomyelination; sequencing or MLPA. Treatment is supportive with antispasticity and seizure management; milder spastic paraplegia SPG2 allelic.
aN: pmd | pelizeus merzbacher disease

name: Pelizaeus–Merzbacher-like disease (PMLD)
formal: Hypomyelinating leukodystrophy clinically like PMD but without PLP1 mutation, often due to GJC2 (connexin 47) mutations, with nystagmus and developmental delay.
simple: A rare inherited disorder similar to Pelizaeus-Merzbacher disease with poorly formed nerve insulation.
aN: pmld | pelizeus merzbacher like disease

name: Penicillamine dermatopathy
formal: Skin complications of penicillamine such as elastosis perforans serpiginosa, pemphigus and cutis laxa-like change, occurring during treatment of Wilson disease and other conditions.
simple: Skin damage, including wrinkling, blistering and fragile skin, caused by penicillamine treatment.
more: Diagnosed from drug history and skin biopsy. Switch to trientine or reduce dose; some lesions heal slowly or leave scars.

name: Penicillin cortical myoclonus
formal: Myoclonus and encephalopathy from high-dose penicillin, especially in renal failure, due to GABA-A antagonism by beta-lactams.
simple: Muscle jerks and confusion caused by very high levels of penicillin antibiotic.

name: Periarteritis nodosa
formal: Necrotising medium-vessel vasculitis causing mononeuritis multiplex, stroke and renal involvement; associated with hepatitis B.
simple: Inflammation of medium-sized blood vessels that can damage nerves and organs.

name: Periodic paralysis
formal: Channelopathy causing episodic flaccid weakness, hypo- or hyperkalaemic, triggered by rest after exercise or carbohydrate meals, from CACNA1S or SCN4A mutations.
simple: Attacks of temporary muscle weakness, usually inherited and linked to potassium levels.

name: Perioperative plexopathies
formal: Brachial or lumbosacral plexus injury from surgical positioning, traction, tourniquets or retractors during an operation.
simple: Nerve network injury occurring during or after surgery, from stretch or pressure.
more: Most are neurapraxic and recover over weeks to months; EMG and imaging guide prognosis.

name: Peripheral myoclonus
formal: Myoclonic jerks arising from peripheral nerve, plexus or root lesions, such as hemifacial spasm or spinal root disease.
simple: Muscle jerks that start from a damaged nerve outside the brain and spinal cord.

name: Peripheral neuropathies
formal: Disorders of peripheral nerves producing sensory loss, weakness and autonomic features; axonal or demyelinating, with causes such as diabetes, toxins, immune and inherited disease.
simple: Damage to nerves outside the brain and spinal cord, causing numbness, tingling and weakness.

name: Peripheral neuropathy
formal: Dysfunction of peripheral nerves causing distal sensory loss, weakness and areflexia, from diabetes, alcohol, drugs, vitamin deficiency, immune or hereditary causes.
simple: Damage to nerves in the hands and feet, causing numbness, tingling, pain or weakness.

name: Peripheral vertigo
formal: Vestibular spinning sensation from labyrinth or vestibular nerve disease such as BPPV, neuritis or Menière disease, with horizontal-torsional nystagmus suppressed by fixation.
simple: Spinning dizziness caused by a problem in the inner ear or its nerve.

name: Peritonitis
formal: Inflammation of the peritoneum, usually bacterial infection; neurologically relevant as shunt infection and abdominal complication of ventriculoperitoneal shunts.
simple: Infection or inflammation of the lining of the abdomen, causing severe belly pain and fever.
more: Diagnose from abdominal tenderness, fever and leucocytosis; ascitic neutrophils over 250 per mm3 define spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, and coagulase-negative staphylococci typify shunt infection. Treat with antibiotics and shunt externalisation.

name: Peroneal neuropathies
formal: Common peroneal nerve injury at the fibular neck, causing foot drop and sensory loss over the dorsum of foot, from compression, trauma or weight loss.
simple: Damage to a nerve near the knee causing a dropped foot and numbness on the top of the foot.
th: เส้นประสาท peroneal ถูกกดที่หัวกระดูกน่อง — เท้าตก ชาหลังเท้า แต่การบิดเท้าเข้า (inversion) ยังดี
feat: Foot drop with weak dorsiflexion and eversion; inversion and plantar flexion preserved
Numbness of lateral shin and dorsum of foot
Triggers: crossing legs, weight loss, prolonged squatting, casts, bed rest, knee surgery
inv: NCS/EMG: conduction block or axon loss at the fibular head; short head of biceps femoris normal
Ultrasound/MRI if no compression history (ganglion cyst)

case.story: After losing 15 kg and sitting cross-legged for hours at a meditation retreat, her right foot slaps when she walks.
case.exam: Weak ankle dorsiflexion and eversion, normal inversion, numb dorsum of foot, normal ankle jerk.
case.tests: Peroneal motor conduction block across the fibular head; normal L5 paraspinals.
case.q: Which muscle test separates this from an L5 radiculopathy?
case.a: Ankle inversion (tibialis posterior, tibial nerve, L5) — preserved in peroneal neuropathy, weak in L5 radiculopathy.
