det.patho: PMEs form an uncommon family of largely recessively inherited conditions in which neuronal degeneration produces cortical myoclonus, epilepsy and decline. Unverricht–Lundborg disease (EPM1) usually results from an expanded dodecamer repeat in the promoter of CSTB, reducing cystatin B, a protease inhibitor. Lafora disease results from EPM2A (laforin) or NHLRC1 (malin) variants, which lead to poorly branched glycogen accumulating as Lafora bodies in neurons, liver, muscle and sweat glands. Other causes include neuronal ceroid lipofuscinoses, MERRF, sialidosis, action myoclonus–renal failure and some dentatorubral–pallidoluysian cases.
det.clinical: Unverricht–Lundborg begins at about 6–15 years with stimulus-sensitive myoclonus and morning convulsions; myoclonus becomes disabling over years, but intellect is relatively spared and survival often extends into later adulthood. Lafora disease begins in adolescence with visual occipital seizures, myoclonus and convulsions, then rapid cognitive and behavioural decline, leading to a vegetative state within about ten years. The early stage can look exactly like juvenile myoclonic epilepsy, so decline, ataxia or poor drug response are the clues.
det.diagnosis: Suspect PME when generalised epilepsy with myoclonus is accompanied by progressive neurological signs, a slowing EEG background or failure of standard drugs. Genetic testing is the main tool; note that the common CSTB repeat expansion is missed by standard exome sequencing and needs a specific assay. Skin biopsy for Lafora bodies, muscle biopsy for MERRF, fundoscopy for cherry-red spot or retinopathy, and enzyme or neuropathology studies help with other causes.
det.treatment: Treatment is symptomatic: valproate, levetiracetam, clonazepam, piracetam, brivaracetam, perampanel, topiramate and zonisamide may reduce myoclonus and seizures. Phenytoin worsens Unverricht–Lundborg disease and should be avoided, as should carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, gabapentin and pregabalin in myoclonic states. Supportive care includes physiotherapy, mobility aids, nutrition and genetic counselling; disease-modifying therapies for Lafora (e.g. glycogen-targeting approaches) are in research.
det.prognosis: Unverricht–Lundborg disease is slowly progressive with variable disability but often normal or near-normal lifespan; Lafora disease is relentlessly fatal, usually within about a decade.
pearls: JME that keeps worsening, with decline or ataxia, is a PME until proven otherwise.
Avoid phenytoin in Unverricht–Lundborg — it accelerates deterioration.
Exome can miss the CSTB repeat; order a specific test.
Visual seizures plus myoclonus and dementia in a teen: think Lafora and do an axillary skin biopsy.

simple: A rare form of multiple sclerosis where one main area of damage causes slowly worsening problems.

simple: A brain disease causing early falls, stiffness and trouble moving the eyes up and down.

case.exam: Slow vertical saccades with limited downgaze that overcomes on doll's-eye manoeuvre, axial rigidity, applause sign.

files.chapter: 9 - Atypical parkinsonism, parkinsonism-­plus syndromes and secondary parkinsonian disorders
14 Progressive Supranuclear Palsy and Corticobasal Degeneration

ddx.pt: Asymmetric rest tremor, good levodopa response, falls late
Autonomic failure and cerebellar signs; hot cross bun sign
Asymmetric limb apraxia, alien limb, cortical sensory loss

aN: psp | steele richardson olszewski syndrome | richardson syndrome

det.patho: PSP is a four-repeat tauopathy in which tau aggregates as tufted astrocytes, neurofibrillary tangles and coiled bodies in the subthalamic nucleus, globus pallidus, midbrain and dentate nucleus. Loss of midbrain gaze centres (riMLF) explains the vertical saccade failure. It is mostly sporadic, with MAPT H1 haplotype as a risk factor, and onset is usually after 60.
det.clinical: The classic Richardson phenotype brings backward falls within the first year, slowed then restricted vertical saccades, axial rigidity with an extended neck, a staring wide-eyed face and frontal dysexecutive change with apathy. Speech becomes slurred and spastic, swallowing worsens and patients may rush to stand impulsively (rocket sign). Other phenotypes present predominantly with parkinsonism (PSP-P, can respond partly to levodopa early), progressive gait freezing, speech/language disorder or a corticobasal syndrome. Examiners like to ask about the applause sign, preserved doll's-eye responses and the square-wave jerks seen on fixation.
det.diagnosis: The 2017 MDS criteria combine four domains — ocular motor, postural instability, akinesia and cognitive dysfunction — at levels of certainty from suggestive to probable. Look carefully at the speed of vertical saccades before range becomes limited; slow downward saccades are an early and specific clue. MRI showing midbrain atrophy with relative pontine preservation (hummingbird or morning-glory appearance, low midbrain-to-pons ratio, raised MR parkinsonism index) supports the diagnosis. DAT SPECT is abnormal and does not separate PSP from PD. Exclude mimics such as Niemann–Pick type C, Whipple disease, vascular parkinsonism and normal pressure hydrocephalus.
det.treatment: No disease-modifying treatment exists; anti-tau antibodies have failed in trials. A levodopa trial (up to around 1 g/day) is reasonable, though benefit is small and brief. Management is multidisciplinary: physiotherapy and walking aids for falls, speech and swallow assessment with diet modification, prism glasses or reading aids, botulinum toxin for blepharospasm or apraxia of lid opening, and early advance care planning around feeding and aspiration.
det.prognosis: Median survival is roughly 6–8 years from onset, with aspiration pneumonia and fall-related injury the usual causes of death.
pearls: Ask 'Does he fall backwards?' — early backward falls in a new parkinsonian patient point to PSP, not PD.
Vertical saccades slow down before their range shrinks — test speed, not only range.
Preserved oculocephalic movements prove the gaze palsy is supranuclear.

name: Progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP)
formal: 4R tauopathy with early postural instability and falls, vertical supranuclear gaze palsy, axial rigidity and frontal cognitive change; midbrain atrophy gives the hummingbird sign.
simple: A brain disease causing early falls, stiffness and trouble moving the eyes up and down.
more: MRI shows midbrain atrophy with a reduced midbrain-to-pons ratio and the morning glory sign; MDS clinical criteria apply. Poor levodopa response; botulinum toxin for blepharospasm; survival about 6 to 8 years, with aspiration a common cause of death.
aN: psp | progressive supranuclear palsy

name: Progressive writer’s cramp
formal: Task-specific focal hand dystonia with gradually spreading cramping and posturing during writing, which may progress to involve other tasks or the other hand.
simple: Hand cramping and twisting when writing that slowly gets worse and may start to affect other tasks.

name: Prolactinoma
formal: Prolactin-secreting pituitary adenoma causing amenorrhoea, galactorrhoea, hypogonadism, and with macroadenomas headache and bitemporal hemianopia; treated first with dopamine agonists.
simple: A noncancerous pituitary gland tumour that makes too much prolactin hormone, causing hormone problems and sometimes headaches and vision loss.

name: Prolonged disorder of consciousness (PDOC)
formal: Disorder of consciousness persisting beyond 28 days after brain injury, including vegetative state (unresponsive wakefulness) and minimally conscious state, assessed with serial behavioural scales and functional imaging.
simple: A long-lasting state after severe brain injury in which a person is awake or partly aware but cannot reliably communicate.
aN: pdoc | prolonged disorder of consciousness

name: Propionic acidaemia
formal: Autosomal recessive organic aciduria from propionyl-CoA carboxylase deficiency causing neonatal metabolic acidosis, hyperammonaemia, encephalopathy, basal ganglia injury and later dystonia or chorea.
simple: An inherited metabolic disease where the body cannot process certain proteins, causing acid and ammonia build-up that harms the brain.

name: Propranolol akathisia
formal: Drug-induced akathisia, an inner restlessness with inability to sit still, reported as a rare adverse effect of beta-blockers such as propranolol.
simple: A feeling of inner restlessness and urge to move that can be caused by the blood pressure drug propranolol.

name: Propriospinal myoclonus
formal: Axial jerks arising from a spinal generator and spreading slowly up and down the cord via propriospinal pathways; often occurs on lying down and is frequently functional.
simple: Sudden jerks of the trunk and limbs, often when lying down trying to sleep, thought to start in the spinal cord.

name: Prosopagnosia
formal: Selective inability to recognize familiar faces despite intact vision, from lesions of the right fusiform or occipitotemporal cortex, or developmental.
simple: Not being able to recognize people by their faces, even close family, though vision is normal.

name: Protozoan neurological infections
formal: Central nervous system infections by protozoa such as Toxoplasma, Plasmodium falciparum, trypanosomes, Naegleria and Acanthamoeba, causing encephalitis, abscesses or meningoencephalitis.
simple: Infections of the brain or nerves caused by single-celled parasites such as those causing malaria or toxoplasmosis.

name: Proximal hereditary motor neuropathy
formal: Hereditary motor neuropathy with predominantly proximal weakness and wasting, as in HMN-P due to TFG or related variants.
simple: An inherited nerve disease that weakens the muscles near the hips and shoulders.
more: Genetic testing and EMG exclude SMA; supportive management.

name: Pseudo-orthostatic tremor
formal: Lower limb tremor resembling orthostatic tremor on standing but at lower frequency (below 13 Hz), with other tremor or parkinsonian features, unlike primary orthostatic tremor.
simple: A leg shaking while standing that looks like orthostatic tremor but has a slower rhythm and a different cause.

name: Pseudo-parkinsonism
formal: Parkinsonian features such as rigidity, bradykinesia and tremor not caused by nigrostriatal degeneration, e.g. drug-induced, vascular or functional.
simple: Symptoms that look like Parkinson's disease but have another cause, such as medication.

name: Pseudoakathisia
formal: Restless-looking movement or pacing from sensory disturbance, e.g. leg pain or paraesthesia, lacking the inner restlessness of true akathisia.
simple: Restless movement that looks like akathisia but comes from discomfort in the legs rather than inner restlessness.

name: Pseudobulbar palsy
formal: Bilateral corticobulbar lesions causing dysarthria, dysphagia, brisk jaw jerk, spastic tongue and emotional lability; seen in motor neuron disease, PSP and bilateral strokes.
simple: A condition from damage to nerve pathways to the brainstem, causing slurred speech, trouble swallowing and sudden laughing or crying.

name: Pseudodementia
formal: Cognitive impairment caused by depression that mimics dementia, with variable effort, prominent complaints and good response to antidepressants.
simple: Memory and thinking problems caused by depression rather than true dementia, which often improve with treatment.

name: Pseudosclerosis
formal: Historical term for Westphal-Strumpell disease; a syndrome of tremor and rigidity resembling multiple sclerosis, now recognised as Wilson disease.
simple: An old name for a condition with tremor and stiffness that looks like multiple sclerosis, now known to be Wilson disease.

name: Pseudoseizure
formal: Older term for psychogenic non-epileptic or functional seizures, paroxysmal events resembling epileptic seizures without epileptiform EEG correlates, linked to psychological stress.
simple: Seizure-like attacks that are not caused by abnormal electrical brain activity but by psychological stress.

name: PSP-corticobasal syndrome (PSPCBS)
formal: Clinical presentation of corticobasal syndrome with underlying progressive supranuclear palsy pathology, showing asymmetric rigidity, apraxia and alien limb with eventual gaze palsy and falls.
simple: A condition that looks like corticobasal syndrome but is due to progressive supranuclear palsy, causing arm clumsiness and later eye movement problems.
more: MRI shows midbrain atrophy; diagnosis confirmed at autopsy. Symptomatic therapy only and survival is similar to PSP.
aN: pspcbs | psp corticobasal syndrome

name: Psychogenic dystonia
formal: Functional dystonia with fixed postures, abrupt onset, inconsistency and distractibility, often following injury, commonly affecting a limb with pain and complex regional pain features.
simple: Twisted or fixed postures of a limb caused by a functional nervous system problem rather than structural damage.
more: Consider the Fahn-Williams criteria, with clinical clues of fixed dystonia, pain and no response to botulinum toxin. Treat with physiotherapy, CBT and explanation of the diagnosis; early recognition improves outcome.

name: Psychogenic myoclonus
formal: Functional jerks with variable features, long latency, distractibility and absent EEG correlate, often with Bereitschaftspotential preceding the jerk.
simple: Sudden muscle jerks caused by a functional problem in how the brain controls movement.
more: Diagnosis supported by EEG with back-averaging for Bereitschaftspotential, and EMG showing long-latency jerks; the jerks may be provoked by suggestion. Treatment is explanation, physiotherapy and psychological therapy.

name: Psychogenic parkinsonism
formal: Functional parkinsonism with inconsistent, distractible slowness and tremor, sudden onset, lack of fatigue, entrainable tremor and normal dopamine imaging.
simple: Parkinson-like symptoms that arise from a functional brain problem rather than neurodegeneration, with signs that vary or improve when distracted.
more: Normal DaT scan helps. Explanation, physiotherapy and psychotherapy are the main treatments, and many improve.

name: Psychogenic tremor
formal: Functional tremor with abrupt onset, variability, entrainment to external rhythm and distractibility, with coactivation sign and suggestibility.
simple: A shake that comes from a functional problem rather than disease damage, and often changes when attention is distracted.
more: Use accelerometry or surface EMG for entrainment and coherence; tremor frequency changes when tapping with the opposite hand. Treatment includes explanation, physiotherapy and CBT; prognosis is variable, with improvement in many.

name: Pulmonary artery aneurysms (PAA)
formal: Focal pulmonary artery dilatation seen with Behcet disease, Hughes-Stovin syndrome and infection; may rupture causing haemoptysis and is relevant to neurology via cerebral venous thrombosis.
simple: A bulge in a lung artery that can burst, linked to inflammatory conditions such as Behcet disease.
aN: paa | pulmonary artery aneurysms

name: Pyogenic intracranial epidural abscess
formal: Collection of pus between dura and skull usually from sinusitis, otitis or neurosurgery, causing fever, headache and focal signs; needs drainage and antibiotics.
simple: A pocket of pus between the skull and the brain's outer covering, usually after a sinus or ear infection or surgery.

name: Pyomyositis
formal: Bacterial muscle abscess, usually Staphylococcus aureus, in tropical or immunocompromised patients, with fever, pain, swelling and raised CK.
simple: A pus-forming bacterial infection inside a muscle, causing fever and pain.
more: MRI or ultrasound is diagnostic; treat with drainage and antibiotics.

name: Pyridoxine (vitamin B6) deficiency
formal: Deficiency causing peripheral neuropathy, seizures in infants, dermatitis and anaemia; seen with isoniazid, alcohol or malnutrition, whereas excess also produces a sensory neuronopathy.
simple: Too little vitamin B6, which can cause nerve damage, seizures in babies and skin problems.
more: Check erythrocyte transaminase activity or plasma pyridoxal phosphate; infantile seizures respond to IV pyridoxine, and pyridoxine-dependent epilepsy involves ALDH7A1. Give prophylactic B6 with isoniazid; avoid chronic high-dose supplements.
aN: vitamin b6 | pyridoxine deficiency

name: Pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) deficiency
formal: X-linked (PDHA1) or recessive disorder of pyruvate metabolism with lactic acidosis, hypotonia, ataxia, seizures, developmental delay and brain malformations such as Leigh-like lesions.
simple: An inherited energy metabolism disease causing weakness, seizures, and developmental delay due to lactic acid build-up.
more: Raised lactate and pyruvate; enzyme assay and genetics. A ketogenic diet and thiamine may help, but prognosis is guarded.
aN: pdh | pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency

name: Quetiapine akathisia
formal: Antipsychotic-induced akathisia presenting with subjective restlessness and motor urge, reported with quetiapine despite its low dopamine D2 affinity.
simple: Inner restlessness and an urge to keep moving caused by the medicine quetiapine.

name: Rabbit syndrome
formal: Late antipsychotic-related perioral tremor producing rapid rhythmic lip movements about 5 Hz, distinct from tardive dyskinesia and responsive to anticholinergics.
simple: Fast regular lip movements, like a rabbit chewing, that can be a side effect of antipsychotic medicines.

name: Radiation-induced leucoencephalopathy
formal: Delayed diffuse white matter injury after cranial irradiation, often with methotrexate, causing cognitive decline, gait disorder and incontinence with periventricular T2 hyperintensity.
simple: White matter damage in the brain that appears months to years after radiation, causing memory, walking and bladder problems.

name: Radiation-induced neurological disease
formal: Spectrum of acute, early delayed and late injury to brain, spinal cord and nerves after radiotherapy, including necrosis, myelopathy, cognitive decline and neuropathies.
simple: Damage to the brain, spinal cord or nerves caused by radiation treatment, which can appear soon or many years later.

name: Radiation-induced optic neuropathy
formal: Delayed painless visual loss 3 to 24 months after irradiation of the anterior visual pathway, with optic nerve or chiasm enhancement on MRI and poor recovery.
simple: Painless loss of vision months after radiation treatment near the eye or brain damages the optic nerve.

name: Radiation-induced plexopathy
formal: Progressive brachial or lumbosacral plexus injury after radiotherapy, with painless weakness, sensory loss and myokymia on EMG; differentiated from tumour recurrence by pain absence.
simple: Nerve damage in the shoulder or pelvis area after radiation, causing slowly progressive weakness and numbness in the arm or leg.

name: Radiation-induced tumours
formal: Secondary neoplasms such as meningiomas, gliomas and sarcomas arising years after radiotherapy in the irradiated field.
simple: Tumours that develop many years after radiation treatment, within the area that was treated.

name: Radiculoneuropathy
formal: Combined disease of nerve roots and peripheral nerves, seen in diabetes, CIDP, Lyme, sarcoidosis and lymphomatous infiltration.
simple: Damage to both the nerve roots at the spine and the nerves beyond them, causing weakness, numbness and pain.

name: Radiculopathies
formal: Dysfunction of spinal nerve roots, most often compressive from disc or spondylosis, causing radicular pain, dermatomal sensory loss and myotomal weakness.
simple: Irritation or pinching of nerve roots at the spine, causing pain, numbness or weakness.
more: MRI and EMG; mostly improve with conservative management; surgery for severe deficits.

name: Radiculopathy
formal: Dysfunction of a spinal nerve root, commonly from disc herniation or spondylosis, causing dermatomal pain, sensory loss, myotomal weakness and reduced reflexes.
simple: A pinched or irritated nerve at the spine causing pain, numbness or weakness that travels down an arm or leg.

name: Radiculoplexus neuropathy
formal: Immune-mediated, microvasculitic painful neuropathy affecting lumbosacral or cervical plexus with weight loss and monophasic course, sometimes diabetic.
simple: A painful condition from inflammation of nerve roots and plexus, usually leading to weakness in one limb.
more: Biopsy may show vasculitis; treatment with immunotherapy and pain management; gradual partial recovery.

name: Radiological contrast toxicity
formal: Neurotoxicity from iodinated or gadolinium contrast, causing encephalopathy, seizures, cortical blindness or transient deficits, especially with blood-brain barrier disruption or renal failure.
simple: Brain side effects such as confusion, seizures or temporary blindness after receiving imaging contrast dye.

name: Raeder (paratrigeminal) syndrome
formal: Unilateral oculosympathetic palsy (miosis, ptosis, usually without anhidrosis) with trigeminal pain, from middle cranial fossa or carotid pathology.
simple: A drooping eyelid and small pupil with facial pain on one side, due to a problem near the base of the skull.
aN: paratrigeminal | reder syndrome

name: Ramsay Hunt syndrome
formal: Varicella zoster reactivation in the geniculate ganglion causing facial palsy, ear pain and vesicles in the ear canal, sometimes with hearing loss and vertigo.
simple: Shingles near the ear that causes facial weakness, ear pain and blisters.

name: Ramsey–Hunt syndrome
formal: Varicella zoster reactivation in the geniculate ganglion causing facial palsy, ear pain and vesicles in the ear canal, sometimes with hearing loss and vertigo.
simple: Shingles near the ear that causes facial weakness, ear pain and blisters.

name: Rapid eye movement behaviour disorder (RBD)
formal: Parasomnia with loss of REM atonia leading to dream enactment; strongly predicts alpha-synucleinopathy (Parkinson, Lewy body dementia, MSA) and is treated with clonazepam or melatonin.
simple: Acting out dreams, with shouting or punching in sleep, because muscles are not paralysed in dream sleep; it can be an early sign of Parkinson's disease.
more: Diagnosis by video-polysomnography showing REM sleep without atonia; MRI is usually normal, and the majority convert to alpha-synucleinopathy within 10 to 15 years. Make the bedroom safe, avoid SSRIs and beta-blockers as precipitants.
nN: rapid eye movement behaviour disorder rbd
aN: rbd | rapid eye movement behaviour disorder

name: Rapid progressive hemidystonia
formal: Hemidystonia developing over days to weeks, raising concerns about structural, vascular, inflammatory or neoplastic lesions of the contralateral basal ganglia, as well as drugs and metabolic causes.
simple: Twisting of one side of the body that gets worse quickly, which is a warning sign of an underlying brain problem.
more: Urgent MRI and blood tests, including glucose and autoimmune screen. Treatment is directed to the cause plus symptomatic therapy.

name: Rapid-onset dystonia
formal: Autosomal dominant ATP1A3-related disorder with abrupt onset of dystonia and parkinsonism over hours to days, bulbar predominant, triggered by stress or fever (DYT12).
simple: An inherited condition in which twisting muscle spasms and slowness appear suddenly over hours to days.

name: Rapid-onset dystonia parkinsonism
formal: ATP1A3-related disorder with abrupt dystonia and bradykinesia with bulbar involvement and rostrocaudal gradient, triggered by physical or emotional stress, with poor levodopa response.
simple: An inherited condition where stiffness, slowness and twisting spasms appear suddenly, often after stress.
more: ATP1A3 mutations cause autosomal dominant disease with variable penetrance; MRI is normal and DAT-SPECT may be normal. No effective treatment; alternating hemiplegia of childhood and CAPOS syndrome are allelic disorders, so avoid stress triggers.

name: Rapsyn deficiency
formal: Congenital myasthenic syndrome from RAPSN mutations (N88K common), with neonatal hypotonia, arthrogryposis and episodic crises.
simple: An inherited myasthenia where a protein that holds receptors in place at the muscle junction is faulty.
more: Autosomal recessive; responds to pyridostigmine and 3,4-diaminopyridine; crises triggered by infection.

name: Rasmussen syndrome
formal: Rasmussen encephalitis is a unilateral chronic inflammatory brain disease of children with refractory focal seizures, epilepsia partialis continua, progressive hemiparesis and cognitive decline.
simple: A rare childhood brain inflammation affecting one half of the brain, causing hard-to-control seizures and weakness.
more: MRI shows progressive hemispheric atrophy; immunotherapy slows it, but hemispherectomy is the definitive treatment for seizures.

name: Rasmussen’s encephalitis
formal: Unilateral chronic inflammatory encephalitis in children with focal seizures, epilepsia partialis continua, progressive hemiparesis and hemisphere atrophy; T-cell mediated, treated with immunotherapy or hemispherectomy.
simple: A rare childhood brain inflammation on one side that causes difficult seizures, weakness and loss of brain tissue.

name: Rathke’s pouch tumours
formal: Developmental sellar and suprasellar lesions, including Rathke cleft cysts and craniopharyngiomas, arising from pouch remnants, causing visual loss, headache and pituitary dysfunction.
simple: Growths near the pituitary gland that come from leftover tissue from early development and can affect vision and hormones.

name: Recessive intermediate CMT disease
formal: Charcot-Marie-Tooth neuropathy with autosomal recessive inheritance and intermediate nerve conduction velocities (25 to 45 m/s), e.g. GDAP1 or KARS mutations.
simple: An inherited nerve disease causing weakness and numbness in the feet and hands, passed on when both parents carry the gene.

name: Recurrent meningitis
formal: Repeated episodes of meningeal inflammation due to CSF leaks, immune defects, parameningeal foci, Mollaret syndrome (HSV-2) or autoinflammatory disorders.
simple: Meningitis that keeps coming back, often because of a leak of spinal fluid, weak immunity or a hidden infection.

name: Recurrent vertigo
formal: Repeated episodes of vertigo arising from vestibular migraine, Meniere disease, BPPV or posterior circulation ischaemia.
simple: Repeated attacks of spinning dizziness, which can be from inner ear problems, migraine or reduced blood flow to the brain.

name: Red nucleus tremor (Bindearmchorea)
formal: Coarse low-frequency proximal rest, postural and intention tremor from midbrain lesions affecting the dentato-rubro-thalamic pathway and nigrostriatal fibres (Holmes tremor).
simple: A large, slow shaking of the arm at rest and with movement, caused by damage in the midbrain.
aN: bindearmchorea | red nucleus tremor

name: Reducing body myopathy
formal: Rare myopathy from FHL1 mutations with reducing bodies, which stain with menadione NBT, and variable weakness from infancy to adulthood.
simple: A rare inherited muscle disease where unusual clumps form inside muscle fibres.
more: X-linked; biopsy and FHL1 genetics; supportive care with cardiac and respiratory monitoring.

name: Reflex sympathetic dystrophy (RSD)
formal: Older term for complex regional pain syndrome type 1, with disproportionate pain, allodynia, swelling, colour and temperature changes and trophic change after injury without nerve lesion.
simple: A long-lasting pain condition after an injury, with swelling, skin changes and extreme sensitivity in a limb.
more: Diagnosis by Budapest criteria; bone scintigraphy shows periarticular uptake, with type 2 CRPS following nerve injury. Treat with physiotherapy, desensitisation, bisphosphonates, steroids early, and neuropathic pain drugs.
aN: rsd | reflex sympathetic dystrophy

name: Refractory status epilepticus
formal: Status epilepticus persisting despite first and second line anticonvulsants, requiring anaesthetic agents and intensive care, with high morbidity.
simple: Seizures that continue even after the usual medicines have been tried, needing intensive care treatment.

name: Refsum disease
formal: Peroxisomal disorder from phytanoyl-CoA hydroxylase deficiency causing retinitis pigmentosa, polyneuropathy, ataxia, ichthyosis and deafness; treated with dietary phytanic acid restriction.
simple: An inherited disorder where a fat from food builds up, causing vision loss, nerve damage, unsteadiness and dry skin.
more: Diagnose by raised plasma phytanic acid and PHYH or PEX7 testing; nerve conduction shows demyelinating neuropathy with raised CSF protein. Plasmapheresis or lipid apheresis lowers levels in acute attacks; avoid fasting; arrhythmia can occur.

tempoNote: Onset late childhood to early adulthood with slow progression; acute worsenings follow fasting, weight loss, illness or surgery

case.story: Cannot see at dusk for years; now numb feet and unsteady. He mentions he cannot smell fish sauce. Recent crash diet made him much weaker.
case.exam: Constricted visual fields, pigment in both retinae, palpable thick peroneal nerves, distal weakness, areflexia, ataxia, dry scaly shins; fourth toes short.
case.tests: NCS demyelinating range slowing; CSF protein 1.8 g/L; plasma phytanic acid 900 µmol/L (normal < 10).
case.q: Why did the diet make him worse, and what is the long-term treatment?
case.a: Weight loss mobilises phytanic acid from fat stores; treat with a phytanic-acid-restricted diet while avoiding fasting, and use plasmapheresis or lipid apheresis for acute crises.

det.patho: Phytanic acid, a branched-chain fatty acid that comes only from diet (ruminant meat and dairy fat, some fish), needs peroxisomal alpha-oxidation. Variants in PHYH (phytanoyl-CoA hydroxylase) or less often PEX7 block this step, so phytanic acid accumulates in nerve myelin, retina, skin and heart. Toxicity is roughly related to plasma levels, which explains rapid deterioration when fat stores are mobilised.
det.clinical: Retinitis pigmentosa and anosmia are the most constant features and often precede everything else. A demyelinating, sometimes relapsing neuropathy, ataxia, deafness and ichthyosis follow. Skeletal shortening of metatarsals is a helpful clue. Arrhythmia may cause sudden death, particularly during metabolic crises.
det.diagnosis: Measure plasma phytanic acid in any patient with retinopathy plus neuropathy or ataxia; it is grossly elevated. Confirm genetically. Infantile Refsum and other peroxisomal biogenesis disorders differ in age and have raised very-long-chain fatty acids and pristanic acid.
det.treatment: Restrict dietary phytanic acid (limit beef, lamb, dairy fat and certain fish) with dietitian support, maintaining adequate calories to prevent lipolysis. During acute deterioration, plasmapheresis or lipid apheresis rapidly lowers levels. Cardiac monitoring is essential; avoid prolonged fasting around surgery. Neuropathy, ataxia and ichthyosis improve with control; retinopathy, anosmia and deafness rarely recover.
det.prognosis: Long survival is possible with strict dietary control; untreated or poorly controlled patients risk sudden cardiac death.
pearls: Retinitis pigmentosa + anosmia + demyelinating neuropathy: send phytanic acid.
Never put a Refsum patient on a fasting or crash diet.
One of the few hereditary neuropathies with a dietary treatment.

Similar nerve conduction slowing but no retinal, smell or skin findings

name: Refsum’s disease
formal: Peroxisomal disorder from phytanoyl-CoA hydroxylase deficiency causing retinitis pigmentosa, polyneuropathy, ataxia, ichthyosis and deafness; treated with dietary phytanic acid restriction.
simple: An inherited disorder where a fat from food builds up, causing vision loss, nerve damage, unsteadiness and dry skin.

name: Relapsed glioblastoma
formal: Recurrent grade 4 IDH-wildtype glioma after standard temozolomide chemoradiotherapy, with dismal prognosis; options include re-resection, re-irradiation, lomustine or bevacizumab.
simple: An aggressive brain tumour that has come back after treatment.

name: Relapsing remitting multiple sclerosis
formal: Most common course of multiple sclerosis with episodes of neurological deficit followed by recovery, driven by inflammatory demyelination; treated with disease-modifying drugs.
simple: A form of multiple sclerosis with flare-ups of symptoms followed by periods of recovery.

name: REM sleep behavior disorder
formal: Parasomnia with loss of REM atonia leading to dream enactment, violent or injurious movements and vocalisation; is a strong prodromal marker of alpha-synucleinopathies.
simple: A sleep problem where a person acts out their dreams by shouting, punching or kicking in sleep.
more: Polysomnography confirms REM sleep without atonia. Treat with bedroom safety, melatonin or clonazepam; many later develop Parkinson disease or Lewy body dementia.

name: REM sleep behaviour disorder (RBD)
formal: Parasomnia with loss of REM atonia leading to dream enactment; strongly predicts alpha-synucleinopathy (Parkinson, Lewy body dementia, MSA) and is treated with clonazepam or melatonin.
simple: Acting out dreams, with shouting or punching in sleep, because muscles are not paralysed in dream sleep; it can be an early sign of Parkinson's disease.
aN: rbd | rem sleep behaviour disorder

name: Renal failure
formal: Kidney failure with neurological complications including uraemic encephalopathy, asterixis, neuropathy, restless legs, seizures and dialysis disequilibrium.
simple: Kidney failure, which can poison the brain and nerves, leading to confusion, shaking hands, numbness and seizures.

name: Repeat expansion diseases
formal: Inherited disorders from unstable nucleotide repeat expansions (e.g. Huntington, fragile X, SCAs, myotonic dystrophy) showing anticipation and variable penetrance.
simple: Inherited illnesses caused by a gene stretch repeated too many times, often getting worse or starting earlier in later generations.

name: Respiratory chain diseases
formal: Mitochondrial disorders from defects of oxidative phosphorylation complexes, causing multisystem disease with encephalopathy, myopathy, stroke-like episodes and lactic acidosis.
simple: Inherited problems with the cell's energy factories, affecting the brain, muscles and other organs.

name: Rest tremor
formal: Tremor appearing in a fully supported, relaxed limb, typically 4 to 6 Hz pill-rolling in Parkinson disease, and reducing with action.
simple: A shake that appears when a limb is relaxed and supported, typical of Parkinson's disease.

name: Restless arm syndrome
formal: Variant of restless legs syndrome with urge to move the arms and unpleasant sensations worse at rest in the evening, relieved by movement.
simple: An uncomfortable urge to move the arms, worse when resting in the evening and relieved by moving.

name: Restless legs syndrome (RLS)
formal: Sensorimotor disorder with urge to move the legs, worse at rest and evening, relieved by movement; linked to iron deficiency, renal failure and dopaminergic dysfunction.
simple: An urge to move the legs with uncomfortable feelings, mainly at night, relieved by moving.

Starts or worsens at rest and in the evening or night
Relieved, at least partly, by walking or stretching
Periodic limb movements of sleep in most patients; insomnia and daytime fatigue
Triggers: iron deficiency, pregnancy, CKD/dialysis, antidepressants, antihistamines, antipsychotics

case.story: For a year she cannot sit through a TV drama at night because her legs feel like ants crawling inside; she must get up and walk. Sleep is broken; her husband says she kicks in sleep.
case.exam: Normal neurological examination; pale conjunctivae.
case.tests: Hb 10.2 g/dL, ferritin 18 µg/L, TSAT 9%.
case.q: What is the first treatment step?
case.a: Restless legs syndrome with iron deficiency: replace iron (oral or IV) aiming for ferritin above 75 µg/L, look for the cause of iron loss, and review aggravating drugs before considering other agents.

det.patho: RLS reflects brain iron deficiency in the substantia nigra and related circuits combined with altered dopaminergic and glutamatergic signalling, with strong genetic contribution (MEIS1, BTBD9 and others). Prevalence is several percent of adults, higher in women, pregnancy and kidney failure. Secondary forms arise with iron deficiency, uraemia and some drugs.
det.clinical: Patients describe an irresistible need to move with sensations that are hard to describe (crawling, pulling, electric) deep in the legs, sometimes the arms. Symptoms follow a circadian pattern and are triggered by immobility such as flights or meetings. Insomnia, mood disturbance and reduced quality of life are common. Augmentation — earlier, stronger, more widespread symptoms — can develop on dopamine agonists.
det.diagnosis: IRLSSG criteria need all five: urge to move, rest-induced, relieved by movement, evening/night predominance and not explained by another condition. Check iron status in all patients. Exclude mimics: leg cramps, positional discomfort, neuropathy, akathisia, venous disease and arthritis.
det.treatment: Correct iron (oral if ferritin ≤75 µg/L, IV ferric carboxymaltose if oral fails or TSAT very low) and remove aggravating drugs, alcohol and caffeine. Current guidance (AASM 2024) prefers alpha-2-delta ligands (gabapentin, gabapentin enacarbil, pregabalin) first-line and discourages routine dopamine agonists because of augmentation. Low-dose opioids help refractory or augmented cases. In pregnancy rely on iron and non-drug measures.
det.prognosis: Chronic but manageable; secondary forms often improve once iron is replaced or after pregnancy or kidney transplant.
pearls: Ferritin target in RLS (≥75 µg/L) is higher than the usual 'normal' cut-off.
Augmentation on dopamine agonists is the major long-term problem.
Ask about antihistamines, SSRIs/SNRIs, mirtazapine and antipsychotics.

name: Restrictive ophthalmopathy
formal: Limited eye movement from mechanical tethering of orbital muscles, as in thyroid eye disease, orbital myositis or entrapment, confirmed by positive forced duction test.
simple: Difficulty moving the eyes because the muscles around the eye are stiff or trapped, as in thyroid eye disease.

name: Reticular myoclonus
formal: Brainstem-generated generalized jerks, with muscle activation ascending from the caudal medulla and rostral spread; triggered by action or stimuli, as in hypoxic brain injury.
simple: Sudden whole-body muscle jerks that start in the brainstem, often after oxygen loss to the brain.

name: Retinal degeneration
formal: Progressive loss of photoreceptors or retinal pigment epithelium, genetic or acquired, causing nyctalopia, field loss and eventual blindness.
simple: A gradual loss of the light-sensing cells in the eye that leads to vision loss.

name: Retinal hamartomas
formal: Benign glial retinal tumours seen in tuberous sclerosis and neurofibromatosis, usually asymptomatic.
simple: Small non-cancerous growths in the retina often seen in tuberous sclerosis.

name: Retinitis
formal: Inflammation of the retina from infection (CMV, toxoplasma, syphilis) or immune disease, with floaters, reduced vision and retinal whitening.
simple: Inflammation of the light-sensitive layer at the back of the eye, causing blurred vision and floaters.

name: Retinitis pigmentosa
formal: Inherited rod-cone dystrophy with night blindness, concentric field constriction and bone-spicule pigmentation; may occur in syndromes such as Refsum and Usher.
simple: An inherited eye disease with night blindness and gradually shrinking side vision.

name: Retinitis, CMV
formal: Necrotising retinitis from cytomegalovirus in severely immunocompromised patients, especially AIDS, causing painless visual loss with haemorrhagic retinal lesions.
simple: A serious eye infection from cytomegalovirus in people with very weak immunity, causing vision loss.

name: Retinoblastoma (Rb)
formal: Childhood retinal malignancy from RB1 mutation presenting with leukocoria and strabismus; heritable form increases risk of pineoblastoma and second tumours.
simple: A cancer of the eye in young children caused by a gene change, often first noticed as a white pupil.

name: Retinopathy
formal: Disease of the retina from diabetes, hypertension or other vascular or toxic causes, with microaneurysms, haemorrhages and exudates and visual loss.
simple: Damage to the back of the eye, often from diabetes or high blood pressure, that can reduce vision.

name: Rett syndrome
formal: X-linked MECP2 disorder in girls with normal early development then regression, loss of hand skills, stereotypic hand wringing, seizures and breathing irregularity.
simple: A genetic condition mainly in girls where early development is normal then speech and hand use are lost, with hand wringing and seizures.

name: Rett’s syndrome

simple: Sudden severe headaches caused by temporary narrowing of brain arteries, which can occasionally cause stroke.

case.who: 33-year-old woman, 9 days after caesarean section, Khon Kaen
case.story: Three sudden 'worst ever' headaches in four days, each peaking within a minute; the latest came while bending to lift her baby. She was given pseudoephedrine for a cold last week.
case.exam: BP 150/95; alert, no neck stiffness, no focal signs.
case.tests: CT: thin blood in one right frontal sulcus; CTA: no aneurysm but beaded narrowing of both MCAs and the basilar artery.
case.q: What is the likely diagnosis and which drug class should be avoided?
case.a: Postpartum RCVS triggered by a vasoactive decongestant; stop the trigger, control BP, avoid glucocorticoids (linked to worse outcome) and triptans; calcium-channel blockers such as nimodipine are often used for pain.

det.patho: A transient disorder of cerebral arterial tone in which sympathetic overdrive, endothelial dysfunction and oxidative stress cause segmental constriction and dilatation of medium and large intracranial arteries. Exposure to vasoactive substances or the postpartum state is found in roughly two-thirds. It mainly affects women aged 20–50 and overlaps biologically with PRES, cervical artery dissection and eclampsia.
det.clinical: The defining picture is a run of thunderclap headaches, sometimes with nausea, photophobia and agitation, separated by milder background pain. Complications follow a time pattern: convexity SAH and lobar bleeds tend to appear in the first week, while ischaemia in border zones typically comes later, as constriction spreads proximally. Seizures, cortical blindness and transient focal deficits occur. A severe fulminant course with diffuse infarction and oedema is rare but recognised, especially postpartum.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis rests on acute severe headache plus documented multifocal segmental narrowing that normalises within about 12 weeks, with no aneurysmal SAH and normal or near-normal CSF. Early angiography may be falsely normal because spasm starts distally, so repeat imaging is reasonable. Transcranial Doppler can follow velocities. Treat a fixed, non-reversing narrowing with abnormal CSF or vessel-wall enhancement as possible vasculitis instead. Look for and remove triggers with a careful drug and recreational history.
det.treatment: Management is supportive: stop vasoactive and serotonergic drugs, rest, analgesia, laxatives, and avoid straining. Oral nimodipine or verapamil is widely used to ease headache, although it has not been proved to prevent strokes. Keep blood pressure moderate (avoid hypotension that may worsen ischaemia). Glucocorticoids are associated with worse outcome and should be avoided; intra-arterial vasodilators are reserved for rapid deterioration.
det.prognosis: Most recover fully within weeks to months; a few are left with deficits from infarction or haemorrhage, and recurrence is uncommon (about 5%).
pearls: Repeated thunderclaps over days, normal first CT/CTA: do not stop at one negative scan.
Cortical SAH over the convexity in someone under 60 points to RCVS; over 60, think of CAA.
Steroids help vasculitis but harm RCVS; get the diagnosis right before giving them.

name: Rhabdomyolysis
formal: Breakdown of skeletal muscle releasing myoglobin and CK, from trauma, exertion, drugs, toxins or metabolic myopathy, causing myalgia, dark urine and AKI.
simple: Rapid muscle damage releasing contents into the blood, causing pain and dark urine and risk of kidney injury.
more: CK above 5 times the upper limit; treat with aggressive fluids and manage electrolytes; look for the cause.
th: กล้ามเนื้อสลายเฉียบพลัน — ปวด อ่อนแรง ปัสสาวะสีเข้ม CK สูงมาก เสี่ยงไตวาย
tempoNote: Hours to days after trigger; recurrent episodes suggest a metabolic myopathy
feat: Muscle pain, swelling and weakness, often in the exercised or compressed limbs
Tea- or cola-coloured urine; dipstick blood positive without red cells
Triggers: extreme exertion, heat, crush or prolonged immobilisation, alcohol, drugs, infection, seizures, hypokalaemia
Complications: acute kidney injury, hyperkalaemia, compartment syndrome, DIC
inv: CK (usually >5× upper limit, often far higher), serial until falling
Creatinine, potassium, calcium, phosphate, urinalysis
If recurrent or unexplained: metabolic work-up (acylcarnitines, forearm exercise test), genetic myopathy panel, biopsy after recovery

case.story: After a 10-km march in April heat followed by hundreds of squats, his thighs swelled and his urine turned dark brown.
case.exam: Tender, tense thighs, mild proximal weakness, normal reflexes, temperature 37.8 °C.
case.tests: CK 98,000 U/L, K 5.9 mmol/L, creatinine 2.1 mg/dL, urine dipstick 3+ blood with no RBC on microscopy.
case.q: What is the immediate management, and when would you look for an underlying myopathy?
case.a: Aggressive IV isotonic fluid to maintain high urine output, treat hyperkalaemia, monitor compartments. Investigate for a metabolic myopathy if episodes recur, follow mild exertion, or occur with fasting or fever.

det.patho: Injury to the sarcolemma lets calcium flood the muscle cell, activating proteases and depleting ATP, so fibres necrose and release myoglobin, potassium, phosphate, urate and CK. Myoglobin causes kidney injury through tubular obstruction, direct haem toxicity and renal vasoconstriction, worsened by dehydration and acidic urine. Causes are physical (exertion, crush, heat), toxic (alcohol, cocaine, statins), infectious, electrolyte-related, or genetic disorders of muscle energy metabolism and membrane.
det.clinical: Presentation ranges from asymptomatic CK elevation to severe pain, swelling, weakness and dark urine. Muscle findings may be subtle in obtunded patients after a fall or overdose. Compartment syndrome should be suspected with a tense, very painful limb. In athletes and military trainees, unaccustomed eccentric exercise in heat is a common setting; an individual with several episodes or episodes after modest triggers likely has an underlying myopathy.
det.diagnosis: CK at least five times the upper limit with a compatible picture establishes the diagnosis; peak CK occurs at 1–3 days. Haem-positive dipstick without red cells supports myoglobinuria. Monitor potassium, calcium, phosphate, creatinine and coagulation. After recovery, recurrent or unexplained cases warrant metabolic testing (acylcarnitine profile, lactate/ammonia exercise testing), genetic panels (CPT2, PYGM, RYR1, LPIN1 and others) and sometimes biopsy, done weeks after the episode.
det.treatment: Give early, generous isotonic crystalloid to maintain urine output around 200–300 mL/h in adults, adjusting for cardiac function. Correct hyperkalaemia; avoid treating early hypocalcaemia unless symptomatic. Bicarbonate and mannitol lack clear benefit. Dialysis is used for refractory hyperkalaemia, acidosis or fluid overload; fasciotomy for compartment syndrome. Remove triggers and counsel on graded return to exercise.
det.prognosis: Most patients recover fully; acute kidney injury usually reverses with prompt treatment. Mortality is mainly from hyperkalaemia, multiorgan failure or the underlying cause.
pearls: Dark urine with blood on dipstick but no red cells on microscopy suggests myoglobin.
Recurrent episodes or episodes after modest triggers = look for a metabolic or genetic myopathy.
Defer metabolic testing and biopsy until weeks after the attack.
det.thd: Rhabdomyolysis คือกล้ามเนื้อสลายเฉียบพลันจากการออกกำลังหนัก ความร้อน การถูกกดทับ ยา แอลกอฮอล์ หรือการติดเชื้อ ปล่อย myoglobin และโพแทสเซียมออกมา ผู้ป่วยปวดกล้ามเนื้อ ปัสสาวะสีโค้ก CK สูงมาก เสี่ยงไตวายและโพแทสเซียมสูง รักษาด้วยการให้สารน้ำทางหลอดเลือดจำนวนมากและแก้เกลือแร่ หากเป็นซ้ำหรือเกิดจากเหตุกระตุ้นเล็กน้อยควรตรวจหาโรคกล้ามเนื้อทางเมตาบอลิก

Cramps within minutes of intense exercise, second-wind phenomenon, raised baseline CK

name: Rheumatic fever chorea gravidarum
formal: Sydenham chorea recurring in pregnancy (chorea gravidarum) after streptococcal rheumatic fever, with antibasal ganglia antibodies.
simple: Involuntary writhing movements in pregnancy in women who earlier had rheumatic fever.

name: Rheumatoid arthritis
formal: Chronic autoimmune synovitis with neurological complications including atlantoaxial subluxation, compressive neuropathies, vasculitic neuropathy and rare pachymeningitis.
simple: An autoimmune joint disease that can also squeeze or damage nerves and the spinal cord.
more: Seropositive disease with anti-CCP and rheumatoid factor; cervical MRI assesses atlantoaxial instability and myelopathy. Treat with DMARDs and surgical stabilisation if cord compression; vasculitic neuropathy needs steroids and cyclophosphamide.

name: Rhythmic movement disorder
formal: Sleep-related repetitive stereotyped movements such as head banging or body rocking, common in infants and usually benign, occurring at sleep onset.
simple: Repeated rocking or head banging around sleep time, common in young children and usually outgrown.
more: Differentiate from epilepsy or restless legs syndrome by video-polysomnography when needed; no investigation is required for typical childhood cases. Usually resolves by age 5; protect the head with padding, and consider clonazepam in persistent cases.

name: Rhythmic myoclonus
formal: Regular repetitive myoclonic jerks at 1 to 3 Hz, as in palatal myoclonus or spinal myoclonus, from brainstem or cord lesions.
simple: Regular repeated jerks of a body part, often from damage in the brainstem or spinal cord.

name: Riboflavin deficiency
formal: Vitamin B2 deficiency causing angular stomatitis, glossitis, anaemia and rarely neuropathy; relevant to riboflavin-responsive Brown-Vialetto-Van Laere syndrome.
simple: Too little vitamin B2, causing mouth sores, anaemia and sometimes nerve problems.

name: Richardson syndrome (RS)
formal: Classic progressive supranuclear palsy phenotype with early postural instability and falls, vertical supranuclear gaze palsy, axial rigidity, frontal cognitive change and tau pathology.
simple: The typical form of progressive supranuclear palsy with early falls, trouble looking up and down and thinking changes.
more: MRI shows a hummingbird sign of midbrain atrophy. Levodopa response is poor; care is supportive with a survival of 6 to 8 years.
aN: rs | richardson syndrome

name: Rickettsial disease
formal: Vector-borne infections (Rocky Mountain spotted fever, scrub typhus) causing fever, rash, headache and meningoencephalitis via vasculitis, treated with doxycycline.
simple: Infections spread by ticks, mites or lice that cause fever, rash and sometimes brain inflammation.

name: Riddoch syndrome
formal: Perception of motion in a blind visual field after occipital lesions, with preserved awareness of moving but not stationary stimuli (statokinetic dissociation).
simple: After brain damage a person cannot see still objects in a blind area but can notice things that move.

name: Rigid Huntington’s disease (Westphal
formal: Juvenile or Westphal variant of Huntington disease with parkinsonian rigidity, bradykinesia, dystonia, seizures and large CAG repeats rather than chorea.
simple: A form of Huntington's disease, often in young people, with stiffness and slowness instead of jerky movements.

name: Rigid spine syndrome
formal: Congenital muscular dystrophy or myopathy with early spinal stiffness, scoliosis, and respiratory insufficiency, most often from SEPN1 mutation.
simple: A condition where the spine becomes stiff early in life, with weak trunk muscles and breathing problems.
more: Genetic testing; monitor respiratory function with early nocturnal ventilation; surgery for scoliosis where needed.

name: Riley–Day syndrome
formal: Familial dysautonomia, autosomal recessive HSAN III from IKBKAP mutation in Ashkenazi Jews, with absent tears, hypotension, labile blood pressure and insensitivity to pain.
simple: An inherited nerve disease causing poor pain sensation, no tears and unstable blood pressure.

name: Rire spasmodique
formal: Forced grinning facial spasm from sustained contraction of risorius, seen in tetanus (risus sardonicus) and some basal ganglia or brainstem disorders.
simple: A fixed, forced smile caused by muscle spasm, classically seen in tetanus.

name: Rosai–Dorfman disease (RDD)
formal: Non-Langerhans histiocytosis with S100-positive emperipolesis, causing lymphadenopathy and rarely dural-based CNS masses that mimic meningioma.
simple: A rare disease in which immune cells build up in lymph nodes and sometimes form growths in the brain coverings.
aN: rdd | rosai dorfman disease

name: Ross syndrome
formal: Triad of tonic pupil, segmental anhidrosis and hyporeflexia from dysautonomic involvement of postganglionic sudomotor and dorsal root ganglion neurons.
simple: A rare condition with a large slow-reacting pupil, patchy lack of sweating and reduced reflexes.

name: Roussy–Levy syndrome
formal: CMT type 1 phenotype with postural tremor and areflexia due to PMP22 duplication or MPZ mutations, with slowed nerve conduction.
simple: An inherited nerve disease with weak feet, absent reflexes and a hand tremor.

name: Rubella encephalitis, chronic
formal: Progressive rubella panencephalitis, rare late complication of congenital or childhood rubella causing dementia, ataxia and seizures, with high CSF antibodies.
simple: A very rare slowly worsening brain infection that appears years after rubella infection.
aN: rubella encephalitis | chronic

name: Rucksack palsy
formal: Brachial plexus injury from compression by heavy backpack straps, affecting upper trunk with shoulder and arm weakness, usually a neurapraxia.
simple: Temporary arm nerve injury from carrying a heavy backpack.
more: EMG confirms; resolves with rest and avoiding load over weeks to months.

name: Ruptured intracranial aneurysm
formal: Cause of aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage with thunderclap headache, meningism and raised intracranial pressure, treated with coiling or clipping.
simple: A weak bulge on a brain artery that bursts, causing a sudden severe headache and bleeding around the brain.

name: Sandhoff’s disease
formal: GM2 gangliosidosis from hexosaminidase A and B deficiency with infantile regression, startle, macular cherry-red spot and macrocephaly.
simple: An inherited fat storage disease in babies causing loss of skills, exaggerated startle and seizures.

name: Sandifer’s syndrome
formal: Gastro-oesophageal reflux in infants causing paroxysmal head and neck dystonic posturing mimicking seizures or torticollis.
simple: Infants with acid reflux who arch or twist the neck in a way that can look like seizures.

name: Sanfilippo disease
formal: Mucopolysaccharidosis type III from heparan sulfate degradation defects with early behavioural change, hyperactivity, sleep disruption and rapid dementia.
simple: An inherited metabolic disease in children causing behaviour problems and loss of learned skills.

name: Sarcoglycanopathies
formal: Autosomal recessive limb-girdle muscular dystrophies (LGMD R3-R6) from SGCA, SGCB, SGCG, and SGCD mutations, with early proximal weakness and often cardiomyopathy.
simple: A group of inherited muscle diseases, mainly weakening the hips and shoulders from childhood.
more: CK is very high; biopsy shows sarcoglycan deficiency; genetic confirmation; supportive care; cardiac screening.

name: Sarcoid encephalopathy
formal: Neurosarcoidosis involving cerebral parenchyma or leptomeninges, causing cognitive decline, seizures and hypothalamic dysfunction; steroid responsive.
simple: Brain involvement of sarcoidosis causing confusion, seizures or hormone problems.

name: Sarcoid myopathy
formal: Granulomatous muscle involvement in sarcoidosis causing nodular, acute, or chronic myopathy with proximal weakness.
simple: Muscle inflammation caused by sarcoidosis, leading to weakness and sometimes lumps.
more: Biopsy shows non-caseating granulomas; corticosteroids are the main treatment.

name: Sarcoid-related optic neuropathy
formal: Optic nerve inflammation from sarcoidosis causing subacute visual loss, disc swelling and enhancement, responsive to steroids.
simple: Swelling of the vision nerve caused by sarcoidosis, causing blurred or lost vision.

name: Sarcoidosis
formal: Multisystem noncaseating granulomatous disease; neurological involvement includes facial palsy, optic neuropathy, meningitis, hypothalamic and neuropathic disease.
simple: A condition where clumps of inflamed cells form in organs, which can affect the nerves and brain.
more: Raised serum ACE and soluble IL-2 receptor support diagnosis; MRI shows leptomeningeal enhancement and CSF lymphocytosis; confirm with biopsy of accessible tissue. First-line is corticosteroids, then methotrexate, azathioprine or infliximab.

name: Sarcotubular myopathy
formal: Rare autosomal recessive myopathy with dilated sarcotubular elements and TRAPPC11 variants or similar, with exertional weakness.
simple: A rare inherited muscle disease with changes in internal muscle membranes.
more: Biopsy shows vacuoles; genetics; supportive.

name: Satoyashi syndrome
formal: Rare syndrome of progressive painful muscle spasms with alopecia, diarrhoea and endocrine disturbance, often with autoimmune features, in young females.
simple: A rare illness with painful muscle spasms, hair loss and diarrhoea.
more: Reported responses to corticosteroids and immunotherapy; carbamazepine or dantrolene may reduce spasms; mostly reported from Japan.

name: Satoyoshi’s syndrome
formal: Rare progressive disorder of painful muscle spasms, alopecia and diarrhoea with skeletal abnormalities, probably autoimmune.
simple: A rare illness with severe muscle cramps, hair loss and diarrhoea.

name: SCAD deficiency
formal: Short-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency (ACADS) with raised ethylmalonic acid, often clinically benign but sometimes causing myopathy and developmental delay.
simple: A fat-processing enzyme deficiency that is often harmless, but can cause weakness or delay in some people.
more: Diagnosed by urine organic acids and gene testing; usually requires no treatment other than avoiding fasting.

name: Scapuloperoneal muscular dystrophy
formal: Muscular dystrophy with weakness in shoulder girdle and peroneal muscles, from FHL1, LMNA or other mutations; includes dominant and X-linked forms.
simple: An inherited muscle disease affecting the shoulders and lower legs.
more: Genetic testing; evaluate for cardiomyopathy, as cardiac disease is common.

name: Scapuloperoneal neuropathy
formal: Neurogenic scapuloperoneal syndrome with shoulder girdle and peroneal weakness from SMA or nerve disease (Davidenkow syndrome).
simple: Nerve disease causing weakness in the shoulder muscles and front of the lower legs.
more: Dominant; EMG shows neurogenic changes; supportive.

name: Schwannomas
formal: Benign nerve sheath tumours, including vestibular schwannoma, strongly associated with neurofibromatosis type 2 and schwannomatosis.
simple: Non-cancerous growths from nerve covering cells that can press on nerves.

name: Schwartz–Jampel syndrome
formal: Autosomal recessive perlecan disorder causing myotonia, blepharophimosis, short stature and skeletal changes with continuous muscle fibre activity.
simple: An inherited condition with muscle stiffness, small eye openings and short stature.
more: HSPG2 mutations; EMG shows complex repetitive discharges and neuromyotonia-like activity, and CK may be mildly raised. Carbamazepine, phenytoin or mexiletine reduce stiffness; intellect is normal and life expectancy is generally preserved.

name: Sciatic neuropathy
formal: Injury to the sciatic nerve, from hip surgery, injection or compression, causing foot drop, posterior leg weakness and sensory loss with peroneal division predominance.
simple: Damage to the large nerve at the back of the leg, causing weakness and numbness in the leg and foot.

name: Scombroid poisoning
formal: Histamine fish poisoning from spoiled fish, with flushing, headache, palpitations and abdominal pain.
simple: Food poisoning from spoiled fish causing flushing, headache and stomach upset.

name: Secondary headache
formal: Headache attributed to underlying disease such as haemorrhage, tumour, infection or raised pressure, identified by red flag features.
simple: A headache caused by another medical problem rather than a primary headache disorder like migraine.

name: Secondary paroxysmal dyskinesia
formal: Paroxysmal movement attacks due to underlying lesions such as multiple sclerosis, stroke or trauma.
simple: Short attacks of involuntary movements caused by another brain disease.

name: Secondary progressive multiple sclerosis
formal: Phase of multiple sclerosis after relapsing disease with gradual worsening independent of relapses from neurodegeneration and chronic inflammation.
simple: A later stage of multiple sclerosis when disability slowly worsens even without clear relapses.

name: Secondary tumours
formal: Metastatic cancers of brain, spine or nerves arising from lung, breast, melanoma or other primaries; commonly multiple with surrounding oedema.
simple: Cancers that spread to the brain or spine from elsewhere in the body.

name: Secondary vasculitis
formal: Vessel wall inflammation due to infection, drugs, malignancy or connective tissue disease, causing stroke, neuropathy or encephalopathy.
simple: Blood vessel inflammation caused by another illness or drug, which can damage the brain or nerves.

name: Segawa syndrome
formal: Dopa-responsive dystonia from GCH1 deficiency with childhood leg dystonia, diurnal fluctuation and dramatic response to low-dose levodopa.
simple: An inherited condition in children with leg stiffness worse later in the day that improves with small doses of levodopa.

name: Segawa’s disease
formal: Dopa-responsive dystonia from GCH1 deficiency with childhood leg dystonia, diurnal fluctuation and dramatic response to low-dose levodopa.
simple: An inherited condition in children with leg stiffness worse later in the day that improves with small doses of levodopa.

name: Segmental myoclonus
formal: Rhythmic jerks restricted to muscles of adjacent spinal or brainstem segments, from focal lesions such as palatal tremor or cord damage.
simple: Repeated jerks in a small group of neighbouring muscles caused by a local nerve problem.

name: Seitelberger’s disease (infantile neuroaxonal dystrophy)
formal: Infantile neuroaxonal dystrophy from PLA2G6 mutation with psychomotor regression, hypotonia, optic atrophy and cerebellar atrophy with iron deposition.
simple: An inherited disease in infants causing loss of skills, floppiness and vision loss.
aN: infantile neuroaxonal dystrophy | seitelberger disease

name: Seitelberger’s disease)
formal: Infantile neuroaxonal dystrophy from PLA2G6 mutation with psychomotor regression, hypotonia, optic atrophy and cerebellar atrophy with iron deposition.
simple: An inherited disease in infants causing loss of skills, floppiness and vision loss.

name: Seizure
formal: Transient episode of abnormal excessive or synchronous neuronal activity producing altered awareness, motor, sensory or autonomic phenomena.
simple: A short burst of abnormal electrical activity in the brain causing shaking, staring or loss of awareness.

name: Selenium deficiency
formal: Trace element deficiency linked to cardiomyopathy and myopathy, seen in total parenteral nutrition and malabsorption.
simple: Too little selenium in the body, which can weaken muscles and the heart.

name: Semantic dementia
formal: Frontotemporal dementia variant with fluent speech and progressive loss of word meaning, from anterior temporal atrophy, usually TDP-43 pathology.
simple: A kind of dementia where people gradually lose the meaning of words and objects but speak fluently.

name: Senile chorea
formal: Late-onset chorea without family history or identifiable cause, often vascular, with benign course.
simple: Jerky involuntary movements starting late in life with no clear cause or family history.

name: Senile dementia of Lewy body type (SDLT)
formal: Dementia with Lewy bodies, with fluctuating cognition, visual hallucinations, parkinsonism and REM sleep behaviour disorder due to alpha-synuclein pathology.
simple: A dementia with changing alertness, vivid hallucinations and movement problems.
ab: Senile dementia of Lewy body type
nN: senile dementia of lewy body type sdlt
aN: sdlt | senile dementia of lewy body type

name: Sensorimotor neuropathy
formal: Peripheral nerve disorder affecting both motor and sensory fibres, from diabetes, Charcot-Marie-Tooth, toxins or inflammation.
simple: Nerve damage that causes both weakness and numbness.

name: Sensorimotor polyneuropathy
formal: Generalised length-dependent mixed nerve disease causing distal weakness and sensory loss, from metabolic, toxic, hereditary or inflammatory causes.
simple: Widespread nerve damage causing weakness and numbness, usually starting in the feet.
more: Nerve conduction shows reduced sensory and motor amplitudes with mild slowing in axonal types; the sural response is lost first. Look for treatable causes: glucose, B12, thyroid function, SPEP and medication review, and treat the cause.

name: Sensory ganglionopathy
formal: Selective dorsal root ganglion neuron disease causing nonlength-dependent asymmetric sensory loss and sensory ataxia; associated with Sjogren, cisplatin and paraneoplastic anti-Hu.
simple: A condition damaging sensory nerve cell bodies, causing numbness and balance problems.

name: Sensory neuronopathy
formal: Selective destruction of dorsal root ganglion sensory neurons causing sensory ataxia, pseudoathetosis and areflexia, with paraneoplastic, autoimmune or toxic causes.
simple: Loss of the nerve cells that carry feeling, causing numbness and poor balance.

name: Sensory neuropathies
formal: Group of peripheral nerve disorders predominantly affecting sensation, such as small fibre neuropathy, ganglionopathy and hereditary sensory neuropathies.
simple: Nerve diseases mainly causing numbness, tingling or pain.

name: Septic encephalopathy
formal: Diffuse brain dysfunction accompanying systemic infection without direct CNS infection, via inflammation and impaired perfusion, causing delirium and EEG slowing.
simple: Confusion or drowsiness caused by severe body-wide infection.

name: Seronegative spondyloarthropathies
formal: Inflammatory axial arthropathies with HLA-B27 association (ankylosing spondylitis, psoriatic arthritis); neurological complications include myelopathy, cauda equina syndrome and atlantoaxial instability.
simple: Joint and spine inflammation diseases, such as ankylosing spondylitis, that can lead to spinal cord or nerve problems.

name: Serotonin syndrome
formal: Drug-induced hyperserotonergic toxicity with hyperthermia, clonus, hyperreflexia, tremor and agitation, typically after combining serotonergic drugs.
simple: A dangerous reaction to excess serotonin from medicines, causing fever, agitation, tremor and muscle jerks.

name: Sex headache
formal: Primary headache related to sexual activity, either preorgasmic dull ache or explosive orgasmic headache; thunderclap onset requires exclusion of subarachnoid haemorrhage.
simple: A headache that comes on during sex, sometimes suddenly and severe.

name: Sheehan syndrome
formal: Postpartum pituitary necrosis after haemorrhage with hypopituitarism, causing failure of lactation, amenorrhoea and fatigue.
simple: Pituitary gland damage after heavy bleeding in childbirth, causing hormone shortages.

name: Shellfish poisoning
formal: Marine toxin intoxications including paralytic (saxitoxin), neurotoxic and amnesic (domoic acid) syndromes with paraesthesia, weakness, respiratory failure or memory loss.
simple: Poisoning from eating contaminated shellfish, causing tingling, weakness or memory loss.

name: Short-lasting unilateral neuralgiform headache
formal: Trigeminal autonomic cephalalgia with brief severe stabbing orbital pain and prominent lacrimation and conjunctival injection (SUNCT/SUNA).
simple: Very short, severe attacks of pain around one eye with tearing and redness.

name: Shy-Drage syndrome (SDS)
formal: Multiple system atrophy with prominent autonomic failure including orthostatic hypotension, urinary dysfunction and parkinsonian or cerebellar signs; an older term, now MSA.
simple: An older name for multiple system atrophy with strong blood pressure and bladder problems along with stiffness or imbalance.
more: Autonomic testing and MRI help diagnosis. Treat orthostatic hypotension with fludrocortisone, midodrine and droxidopa; no cure.
aN: sds | shy drage syndrome

name: Shy–Drager syndrome
formal: Historical name for multiple system atrophy with prominent autonomic failure, parkinsonism and cerebellar signs, caused by alpha-synuclein glial inclusions.
simple: An older name for multiple system atrophy, with fainting on standing, stiffness and balance problems.

name: Sickle cell disease
formal: Haemoglobinopathy causing ischaemic stroke, silent infarcts, moyamoya-like vasculopathy and transcranial Doppler velocity elevation in children.
simple: An inherited blood disease where abnormal red blood cells can block brain arteries and cause stroke.
th: โรคเม็ดเลือดแดงรูปเคียว (HbSS) — เด็กเสี่ยง stroke สูง จากหลอดเลือดใหญ่ตีบ (ICA ปลาย/MCA) และ silent infarct คัดกรองด้วย TCD และป้องกันด้วยการให้เลือดสม่ำเสมอ
tempoNote: Strokes are acute events on a lifelong background; silent infarcts accumulate silently through childhood
feat: Ischaemic stroke peaks in children 2–9 years old with HbSS; haemorrhagic stroke more often in young adults
Steno-occlusive disease of the distal ICA and proximal MCA/ACA, sometimes with moyamoya collaterals
Silent cerebral infarcts in deep white matter causing learning and attention problems
Triggers: acute chest syndrome, severe anaemia, dehydration, infection, recent transfusion
Other neurological issues: headache, seizures, cerebral venous thrombosis, aneurysms
inv: Transcranial Doppler yearly from age 2 to 16: time-averaged mean maximum velocity ≥200 cm/s in ICA/MCA = high stroke risk
Acute stroke: MRI/MRA, full blood count, reticulocytes and HbS percentage
Haemoglobin electrophoresis/HPLC if genotype unknown

case.who: 7-year-old boy with HbSS, attending a regional hospital in Ubon Ratchathani
case.story: Woke up unable to lift his right arm and with slurred words after two days of fever and cough.
case.exam: Right hemiparesis with facial weakness, expressive aphasia; SpO2 92%, crackles at the left base.
case.tests: Hb 6.4 g/dL, HbS 88%; MRI: left MCA territory infarct; MRA: narrowing of the left terminal ICA.
case.q: What is the urgent treatment and how is recurrence prevented?
case.a: Exchange transfusion to bring HbS below 30% (with total Hb about 10 g/dL); then long-term transfusion programme (and hydroxyurea, or haematopoietic stem cell transplant where feasible).

read.where: Chapter 14 Stroke in children and young adults
Chapter 7 Unusual causes of ischemic stroke and transient ischemic attack

det.patho: A single substitution in the beta-globin gene produces HbS, which polymerises when deoxygenated, making red cells rigid and sickle-shaped. Chronic haemolysis depletes nitric oxide, and adhesive cells injure endothelium, leading to intimal hyperplasia of large intracranial arteries and small-vessel ischaemia. Anaemia raises cerebral blood flow and lowers reserve, so border-zone regions are vulnerable. The disease is most frequent in people of African, Middle Eastern and Indian ancestry; in Thailand haemoglobin E and thalassaemia are far more common.
det.clinical: Without screening, about one in ten children with HbSS has an overt stroke by age 20, and over a third accumulate silent infarcts. Strokes present with hemiparesis, aphasia or seizures, sometimes triggered by acute chest syndrome or aplastic crisis. Adults have more haemorrhagic strokes from moyamoya collaterals or aneurysms. Cognitive impairment, headache and posterior reversible encephalopathy after transfusion or steroids are also seen.
det.diagnosis: Confirm the genotype with haemoglobin HPLC or electrophoresis. Children need annual TCD screening; abnormal or conditional velocities guide transfusion. Acute focal deficits require urgent MRI with diffusion and MRA, and a blood count with HbS percentage. Consider screening MRI for silent infarcts at least once in school-age children.
det.treatment: Acute ischaemic stroke: urgent exchange transfusion (simple transfusion if exchange is delayed), oxygen, hydration and treatment of infection; adults may follow standard reperfusion pathways alongside transfusion. Secondary prevention is chronic transfusion keeping HbS below about 30% with iron chelation; hydroxyurea can replace transfusion in selected children with abnormal TCD after vessel normalisation. Stem cell transplantation, and newer gene-based therapies, offer cure in suitable patients. Revascularisation surgery may be considered for progressive moyamoya.
det.prognosis: Without transfusion, recurrence after a first childhood stroke is very high (over half); TCD screening with transfusion has cut first-stroke rates by about 90%.
pearls: TCD velocity ≥200 cm/s = start regular transfusion (STOP trial logic).
Exchange transfusion, not thrombolysis alone, is the cornerstone in a child with SCD stroke.
Over-transfusing to high haematocrit raises viscosity and can itself cause stroke.

det.patho: SVD is a collection of disorders of small penetrating arteries, arterioles, capillaries and venules. The commonest form, age- and hypertension-related arteriolosclerosis, thickens and stiffens vessel walls, impairs autoregulation and breaks down the blood–brain barrier; the result is chronic hypoperfusion of white matter, focal occlusions (lacunes) and rupture (deep haemorrhage). Cerebral amyloid angiopathy is the second sporadic form; genetic forms include CADASIL, CARASIL, COL4A1/2 disease and Fabry disease. SVD causes about a quarter of ischaemic strokes, most deep haemorrhages, and is the leading vascular contributor to dementia.
det.clinical: Presentations include acute lacunar syndromes, insidious cognitive decline marked by slowed processing and executive dysfunction, gait apraxia-like disturbance with falls, mood disorder, apathy and urinary symptoms. Many people are asymptomatic despite striking imaging. Progression is usually gradual with stepwise elements; WMH burden predicts stroke, dementia and death.
det.diagnosis: Imaging is defined by consensus STRIVE criteria (updated 2023): recent small subcortical infarct, lacunes of presumed vascular origin, WMH, perivascular spaces, cerebral microbleeds, cortical superficial siderosis and brain atrophy. A 'total SVD score' summarises burden. Microbleed distribution separates hypertensive arteriolopathy (deep) from CAA (lobar). In patients under about 55 or with family history, think of monogenic causes; confluent WMH reaching the temporal poles suggests CADASIL. Exclude demyelination, leukodystrophy and NPH when the pattern is atypical.
det.treatment: There is no specific disease-modifying drug. Control blood pressure (intensive lowering slows WMH progression), treat diabetes and dyslipidaemia, stop smoking and encourage physical and cognitive activity. After a lacunar stroke, use a single antiplatelet (cilostazol is attractive in Asia because of lower bleeding); avoid antiplatelets in purely incidental disease without stroke. Manage cognitive and mood symptoms, gait training and continence. Cholinesterase inhibitors have only modest effect.
det.prognosis: Variable: many remain stable for years, but heavy WMH load roughly doubles to triples risk of stroke and dementia.
pearls: Executive slowing + small-step gait + urinary urgency + WMH = classic SVD triad of symptoms.
Deep microbleeds suggest hypertensive SVD; strictly lobar microbleeds and siderosis suggest CAA.
BP control is the single most evidence-based intervention for slowing SVD.

det.patho: SFN damages thinly myelinated Aδ and unmyelinated C fibres that carry pain, temperature and autonomic signals. Common causes are diabetes and prediabetes, Sjögren and other immune disorders, alcohol, chemotherapy, celiac disease, infections, paraproteins, amyloidosis and genetic sodium-channel variants (SCN9A, SCN10A, SCN11A). In roughly half, no cause is found despite full testing.
det.clinical: Patients describe burning, tingling, cold or stabbing pain that starts in the feet and may rise to the knees and then hands. Examination is often near normal apart from reduced pin and temperature sense or allodynia; preserved reflexes and vibration are typical. Autonomic involvement can cause sweating changes, orthostatic intolerance, gastrointestinal or sexual dysfunction. Patchy, face- or trunk-predominant pain points towards a ganglionopathy-type immune or metabolic process.
det.diagnosis: A normal NCS combined with typical symptoms and small-fibre signs supports the diagnosis; confirmation comes from reduced intraepidermal nerve fibre density on distal-leg punch biopsy or abnormal sudomotor/autonomic testing. Corneal confocal microscopy and quantitative sensory testing are adjuncts. A structured search for treatable causes is the main work, including a 2-hour glucose tolerance test, since fasting glucose and HbA1c can miss prediabetes.
det.treatment: Treat the cause: glycaemic control and weight loss, stopping alcohol or neurotoxic drugs, managing Sjögren or celiac disease. Neuropathic pain is treated with gabapentinoids, duloxetine, or tricyclics, with topical lidocaine or high-concentration capsaicin for focal pain. Immunotherapy is considered only in well-characterised immune-mediated cases, ideally in trials. Foot care and sleep support matter.
det.prognosis: Most patients do not progress to large-fibre neuropathy; pain often persists but can be controlled. Outcomes are better when a treatable cause is identified.
pearls: Normal NCS does not exclude neuropathy — it excludes large-fibre neuropathy.
Order an oral glucose tolerance test; prediabetes is a common hidden cause.
Pain beginning in face or trunk suggests a non-length-dependent, often immune process.

case.story: For 8 months her head keeps turning to the right with an aching neck; it settles if she rests a finger on her chin. She has never taken antipsychotics or metoclopramide.
