det.patho: Cervical dystonia is a network disorder involving basal ganglia, cerebellum and sensorimotor cortex, with loss of surround inhibition and abnormal sensorimotor integration. Most adult cases are idiopathic, though a few genes (e.g. GNAL, ANO3, THAP1) and trauma or drugs can cause it. It is more common in women and peaks in mid-life.
det.clinical: Posture is described by its components: rotation (torticollis), tilt (laterocollis), flexion (anterocollis), extension (retrocollis) and lateral or sagittal shift. Pain is common and often drives disability more than the posture. Up to a third have head tremor, and some later develop dystonia in the arm, jaw or eyelids. Spontaneous remission occurs in a minority, often relapsing later.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis rests on recognising patterned, directional muscle overactivity, a sensory trick and the null point. Imaging is needed if onset is in childhood, if there is fixed posture, pain from bone or other neurological signs. Exclude drugs, Wilson disease in younger patients, atlantoaxial subluxation, posterior fossa or cervical lesions and ocular torticollis from trochlear palsy.
det.treatment: Botulinum toxin injections every three months are first-line and help most patients; doses and muscles depend on the posture pattern, and EMG or ultrasound guidance improves targeting of deep muscles. Oral anticholinergics, clonazepam or baclofen give modest help. Physiotherapy supports injections. Pallidal (GPi) deep brain stimulation is an option for refractory cases.
det.prognosis: It is a long-term condition, but most patients achieve worthwhile relief with repeated toxin injections; a small proportion remit spontaneously.
pearls: A sensory trick strongly supports dystonia over other causes of abnormal neck posture.
Rotation to one side is driven by the opposite SCM and the same-side splenius.
Always ask about metoclopramide, antipsychotics and antiemetics.

case.who: 58-year-old taxi driver from Bangkok with hypertension and diabetes
case.story: While lifting a suitcase he felt a sudden stabbing pain between his shoulder blades; within 30 minutes both legs gave way and he could not pass urine.
case.exam: Flaccid paraplegia, areflexia, loss of pinprick and temperature below T6, but vibration and joint position normal at the toes; distended bladder.
case.tests: MRI at 8 h: longitudinal T2 hyperintensity of the anterior thoracic cord with restricted diffusion; CTA aorta: no dissection; CSF 2 cells, protein normal.
case.q: Which arterial syndrome explains this sensory pattern?

det.patho: The cord is supplied by one anterior spinal artery (anterior two-thirds) and paired posterior spinal arteries (dorsal columns), reinforced by segmental radicular arteries, most importantly the artery of Adamkiewicz (usually T9–L2 on the left). The upper thoracic cord is a relative watershed. Causes include aortic disease and surgery (open or endovascular repair), systemic hypotension, atherosclerosis or dissection of segmental arteries, fibrocartilaginous embolism of disc material, vasculitis and hypercoagulable states; a substantial proportion remain cryptogenic. Spinal cord infarction makes up about 1% of all strokes.
det.clinical: The anterior spinal artery syndrome — bilateral weakness, spinothalamic sensory loss and sphincter failure with preserved posterior column sensation — is the commonest form. Posterior spinal artery infarcts produce loss of proprioception and vibration with milder weakness. Sulcal artery infarcts give a hemicord (Brown-Séquard-like) picture, and central watershed infarcts after hypotension can cause pure motor loss. Pain at onset is common; peak deficit is usually reached within hours, which helps separate it from inflammatory myelitis.
det.diagnosis: Use clinical tempo plus MRI. Early MRI may be normal; repeat within 24–72 h with axial T2 and DWI. Supportive features include paired bright dots in both anterior horns on axial T2 ('owl-eye' sign), adjacent vertebral body infarction, and absence of enhancement initially. CSF is typically non-inflammatory. Image the aorta and look for embolic or haematological causes. Published diagnostic criteria (2019) rely on hyperacute onset, typical MRI and exclusion of alternatives.
det.treatment: There is no proven acute reperfusion therapy, though thrombolysis has been used in selected cases. Raise mean arterial pressure, avoid hypotension, and after aortic surgery use lumbar CSF drainage to improve cord perfusion pressure. Treat the cause (aortic repair, antiplatelet and statin for atherosclerotic disease). Supportive care includes bladder catheterisation, bowel regimen, pressure-area care, VTE prophylaxis and early rehabilitation.
det.prognosis: Outcome is variable: severe initial deficit and absent early improvement predict poor recovery, but many patients regain some walking ability; mortality is related to the underlying aortic or systemic disease.
pearls: Sudden back pain + paraplegia + spared vibration/position sense = anterior spinal artery infarct.
Peak deficit within hours favours infarction; days favours myelitis.
A normal MRI at 3 hours does not exclude it — repeat with DWI.
det.thd: Spinal cord infarction คือไขสันหลังขาดเลือดเฉียบพลัน มักเป็นเขต anterior spinal artery ผู้ป่วยมีปวดหลังเฉียบพลันแล้วขาอ่อนแรงภายในไม่กี่ชั่วโมง สูญเสียความรู้สึกเจ็บและร้อนเย็นใต้ระดับรอยโรค ปัสสาวะไม่ออก แต่การรับรู้ตำแหน่งข้อและการสั่นยังปกติ สาเหตุที่สำคัญคือโรคเอออร์ตา การผ่าตัดเอออร์ตา และความดันต่ำ วินิจฉัยด้วย MRI รวม DWI ซึ่งอาจต้องทำซ้ำ รักษาโดยเพิ่มความดัน ระบาย CSF ในรายหลังผ่าตัดเอออร์ตา แก้สาเหตุ และฟื้นฟู

name: Spinal cord intramedullary abscess
formal: Rare pus collection within the cord from haematogenous spread or contiguous infection, causing fever, myelopathy and requiring surgery and antibiotics.
simple: A rare pocket of infection inside the spinal cord causing weakness and fever.

name: Spinal cord tumours
formal: Intradural or intramedullary neoplasms such as ependymoma and astrocytoma causing progressive myelopathy.
simple: Growths in or around the spinal cord that cause weakness, numbness and bladder problems.

name: Spinal epidural abscess
formal: Infection in the epidural space (Staphylococcus aureus) causing back pain, fever and rapidly progressive neurological deficit, an emergency.
simple: A pocket of infection near the spinal cord causing back pain, fever and weakness.

name: Spinal epidural haematoma
formal: Collection of blood in the epidural space, spontaneous or anticoagulant related, with sudden back pain and cord compression.
simple: Bleeding around the spinal cord that causes sudden severe back pain and weakness.

name: Spinal muscular atrophy (SMA)
formal: Autosomal recessive SMN1-related motor neuron disease causing hypotonia, proximal weakness and areflexia; treated with nusinersen and gene therapy.
simple: An inherited disease where nerve cells to muscles are lost, causing weakness, mainly in children.
more: Diagnosis by SMN1 homozygous deletion testing; SMN2 copy number predicts severity. Risdiplam is an oral splice modifier; early presymptomatic treatment from newborn screening greatly improves outcome.
th: โรคพันธุกรรมเซลล์ประสาทสั่งการไขสันหลังเสื่อม (SMN1) — อ่อนแรงต้นแขนต้นขาสมมาตร ตั้งแต่ทารกถึงผู้ใหญ่ มียารักษา
feat: Symmetric proximal weakness, legs more than arms; hypotonia and areflexia
Severity by type: type 1 never sits, type 2 sits but never walks, type 3 walks, type 4 adult onset
Tongue fasciculation and fine hand tremor (minipolymyoclonus); face relatively spared
Respiratory weakness with relatively spared diaphragm (bell-shaped chest in infants)
inv: SMN1 exon 7 homozygous deletion; SMN2 copy number predicts severity
CK normal or mildly raised; EMG neurogenic

case.story: Could sit unsupported at 8 months but has never pulled to stand; parents notice his tongue 'quivers'.
case.exam: Symmetric proximal leg weakness, absent knee jerks, tongue fasciculation, normal eye movements and alert face.
case.tests: SMN1 exon 7 homozygous deletion; 3 copies of SMN2.
case.q: Which treatments target the underlying defect?
case.a: SMN-enhancing therapies — nusinersen (antisense), risdiplam (oral splicing modifier) or onasemnogene (gene replacement); earlier treatment gives better outcomes.

files.chapter: 15: Approach to the Differential Diagnosis of Hypotonia in Infancy
Chapter 15 Disorders of the Motor Cells: The Motor Neuron Diseases

ddx.pt: Calf pseudohypertrophy, very high CK, myopathic EMG
Facial weakness, ptosis, myopathic EMG; normal SMN1
Adult male, X-linked, bulbar and sensory features

aN: sma | spinal muscular atrophy | 5q sma | werdnig hoffmann | kugelberg welander | smn1

det.patho: 5q SMA is autosomal recessive and caused by loss of the SMN1 gene, usually by homozygous exon 7 deletion. The nearby SMN2 gene produces mostly truncated protein because of exon 7 skipping, so the number of SMN2 copies determines how much functional SMN protein remains and therefore the severity. Low SMN levels cause degeneration of anterior horn cells and lower brainstem motor nuclei. Before modern therapy it was a leading genetic cause of death in infancy.
det.clinical: Weakness is symmetric, proximal and greater in the legs than the arms, with hypotonia, areflexia, tongue fasciculations and preserved alertness. Type 0 presents before birth; type 1 infants never sit and have paradoxical breathing; type 2 sit but never walk; type 3 walk but may later lose ambulation; type 4 begins in adulthood. Intercostal weakness with a relatively spared diaphragm causes a bell-shaped chest. Scoliosis, contractures and feeding difficulty are major complications.
det.diagnosis: SMN1 deletion testing (MLPA or qPCR) confirms most cases, and SMN2 copy number is reported for prognosis and treatment planning. About 5% are compound heterozygous for a deletion and a point mutation, requiring sequencing. Newborn screening allows treatment before symptoms. CK is normal or mildly raised and EMG is neurogenic; biopsy is no longer needed.
det.treatment: Disease-modifying options include intrathecal nusinersen (antisense oligonucleotide increasing full-length SMN2 transcript), oral daily risdiplam (SMN2 splicing modifier) and onasemnogene abeparvovec (one-time AAV9 SMN1 gene therapy). Earliest possible treatment, ideally presymptomatic, gives the best results. Standard care covers respiratory support, nutrition, scoliosis management and physiotherapy.
det.prognosis: Treatment has transformed the outlook: many presymptomatically treated infants reach motor milestones close to normal, while untreated type 1 is usually fatal within two years.
pearls: Alert, floppy infant with tongue fasciculations and absent reflexes: test SMN1.
SMN2 copy number is the main modifier of severity.
Time is motor neurons — treat as early as possible.
det.thd: SMA เป็นโรคพันธุกรรมแบบยีนด้อย เกิดจากการขาดยีน SMN1 ทำให้เซลล์ประสาทสั่งการในไขสันหลังเสื่อม ความรุนแรงขึ้นกับจำนวนสำเนาของยีน SMN2 อาการคืออ่อนแรงต้นแขนต้นขาสมมาตร กล้ามเนื้อปวกเปียก รีเฟล็กซ์หาย ลิ้นเต้น แต่เด็กยังตื่นตัวดี การวินิจฉัยใช้การตรวจยีน SMN1 ปัจจุบันมียารักษา ได้แก่ nusinersen, risdiplam และ onasemnogene ซึ่งได้ผลดีที่สุดเมื่อเริ่มก่อนมีอาการ

name: Spinal myoclonus
formal: Jerks from spinal cord lesions or irritation, rhythmic or arrhythmic and persisting during sleep, caused by tumour, myelitis or trauma.
simple: Muscle jerks that begin in the spinal cord.

name: Spinal neuronitis
formal: Inflammatory disorder of anterior horn or dorsal root ganglia, often post-infectious, with segmental weakness or sensory loss.
simple: Inflammation of nerve cells in the spinal cord causing weakness or numbness.

name: Spinal osteomyelitis
formal: Vertebral bone infection, usually bacterial or tuberculous, with back pain, fever and risk of epidural abscess.
simple: An infection of the spine bones causing back pain and fever.

name: Spinal segmental myoclonus
formal: Rhythmic jerks of muscles supplied by one or a few cord segments, from focal spinal lesions.
simple: Repeated jerks in muscles linked to one area of the spinal cord.

name: Spinal stroke
formal: Acute cord ischaemia, e.g. anterior spinal artery syndrome after aortic surgery or dissection.
simple: A sudden loss of blood flow to the spinal cord causing weakness or numbness.

name: Spinal subdural abscess
formal: Rare infection between dura and arachnoid, with back pain, fever and cord compression, requiring surgery and antibiotics.
simple: A rare spinal infection that can press on the spinal cord.

name: Spinal tuberculosis
formal: Pott disease with vertebral destruction, kyphosis, paraspinal abscess and myelopathy.
simple: Tuberculosis of the spine causing back pain, spinal curvature and sometimes weakness.

name: Spinal tumours
formal: Primary or metastatic lesions of vertebrae, meninges or cord causing pain, radiculopathy and myelopathy.
simple: Growths in the spine or around the spinal cord that cause pain and weakness.

name: Spinocerebellar ataxias (SCAs)
formal: Dominantly inherited cerebellar degenerations, many from CAG repeat expansions, with progressive gait ataxia, dysarthria and oculomotor signs.
simple: Inherited conditions that slowly cause poor balance and clumsy movement.
more: Test for common expansions (SCA1, 2, 3, 6, 7, 17) and use MRI to look for cerebellar and brainstem atrophy; SCA3 is most common worldwide. There is no disease-modifying treatment; riluzole or varenicline may give symptomatic benefit, and rehabilitation is key.
th: กลุ่มโรคเดินเซทางพันธุกรรมแบบเด่น — SCA3 พบบ่อยในเอเชีย มักมีอาการเริ่มอายุ 30–50 ปี
tempoNote: Insidious adult onset with slow progression over 10–20+ years; anticipation in repeat-expansion types
feat: Progressive gait ataxia, dysarthria and limb incoordination with a parent similarly affected
Type-specific extras: slow saccades (SCA2), bulging eyes, dystonia and amyotrophy (SCA3), pure late ataxia with downbeat nystagmus (SCA6), retinal degeneration (SCA7)
Pyramidal signs, neuropathy, parkinsonism or cognitive change in several subtypes
Earlier and more severe onset in successive generations (anticipation) for CAG expansions
inv: MRI brain: cerebellar ± pontine atrophy
Gene panel for common repeat expansions (the common polyglutamine SCAs and DRPLA) then wider panels/genome testing
Exclude acquired causes: alcohol, drugs, thyroid, vitamin E/B12, anti-GAD and paraneoplastic antibodies

case.story: Five years of unsteady walking and slurred speech; her father had a similar problem and used a wheelchair by 55.
case.exam: Gait ataxia, dysarthria, gaze-evoked nystagmus, staring look with eyelid retraction, brisk knee jerks, faint fasciculation of the tongue.
case.tests: MRI: atrophy of cerebellum and pons; CAG expansion in ATXN3.
case.q: Which SCA is this, and what counselling is needed for her children?
case.a: SCA3 (Machado–Joseph disease). Each child has a 50% risk; predictive testing is offered only with genetic counselling.

det.patho: SCAs are dominantly inherited degenerations of the cerebellum and its connections. The most frequent types are caused by expanded CAG repeats encoding polyglutamine tracts in different proteins (ataxins, CACNA1A, TBP), which misfold and disrupt neuronal function; others arise from non-coding repeats or conventional mutations in ion channels and signalling genes. Longer repeats produce earlier onset, explaining anticipation, particularly with paternal transmission in some types. SCA3 is the commonest type worldwide and in many Asian populations.
det.clinical: The core is a slowly worsening cerebellar syndrome of gait ataxia, dysarthria, limb incoordination and abnormal eye movements. Accompanying features depend on subtype and help guide testing: very slow saccades in SCA2, a mix of dystonia, spasticity, parkinsonism and neuropathy in SCA3, a fairly pure late-onset ataxia in SCA6, visual loss in SCA7, and psychiatric or chorea features in SCA17 and DRPLA. Dysphagia and falls drive late disability.
det.diagnosis: A detailed family history across generations is the most useful starting point, though a parent may have died early or been misdiagnosed. MRI shows cerebellar atrophy with pontine involvement in several types. Targeted repeat-expansion testing of common SCAs is first line; repeat-primed PCR or long-read sequencing is needed for some, and exome/genome panels cover the conventional variants. Treatable acquired ataxias should be excluded even when a family history exists.
det.treatment: No therapy alters progression yet; antisense oligonucleotide trials are under way for SCA3 and others. Intensive physiotherapy and coordination training improve function. Symptomatic options include riluzole (modest evidence), levodopa for parkinsonism, botulinum toxin for dystonia, and 4-aminopyridine for episodic or downbeat features. Speech and swallowing therapy, fall prevention and genetic counselling are integral.
det.prognosis: Most types progress over 10–30 years to wheelchair dependence; SCA6 is slower and has near-normal lifespan. Aspiration pneumonia is a common terminal event.
pearls: Slow saccades point to SCA2; bulging eyes with fasciculation and dystonia point to SCA3.
A 'sporadic' late ataxia can still be an SCA — ask about parents who died young.
Predictive testing in at-risk relatives requires pre- and post-test counselling.
Harding's bedside grouping still helps: ADCA I = ataxia plus other neurological signs, ADCA II = ataxia with retinal degeneration (SCA7), ADCA III = near-pure cerebellar ataxia.
Attacks of ataxia beginning before age 20 and lasting hours to days call for testing of episodic-ataxia genes (KCNA1, CACNA1A); some carriers later progress to a fixed ataxia.
When repeat testing is negative, exome or genome sequencing finds a cause in roughly one third, far more than small targeted panels.
det.thd: SCA เป็นกลุ่มโรคเดินเซที่ถ่ายทอดแบบเด่น ส่วนใหญ่เกิดจาก CAG repeat expansion ทำให้สมองน้อยและก้านสมองฝ่อช้า ๆ อาการเริ่มวัยผู้ใหญ่ ได้แก่ เดินเซ พูดไม่ชัด ตากระตุก และมีอาการเฉพาะชนิด เช่น SCA2 saccade ช้า SCA3 ตาโปน dystonia กล้ามเนื้อลีบ ซึ่ง SCA3 พบบ่อยในเอเชีย วินิจฉัยด้วยประวัติครอบครัว MRI และตรวจยีน การรักษาเน้นกายภาพบำบัดและให้คำปรึกษาทางพันธุกรรม

name: Spinocerebellar degenerations
formal: Group of hereditary or sporadic degenerations of cerebellum and spinal tracts with progressive ataxia.
simple: Diseases where parts of the brain and spinal cord gradually degenerate, leading to unsteadiness.

name: Spirochete infection
formal: Neurological infection by spirochetes such as Treponema pallidum or Borrelia burgdorferi, causing meningitis, cranial neuropathy and neurosyphilis or neuroborreliosis.
simple: Infection with spiral-shaped bacteria such as those causing syphilis or Lyme disease, which can harm the nervous system.

name: Split hand syndrome
formal: Selective wasting of abductor pollicis brevis and first dorsal interosseous with preserved hypothenar muscles, typical for ALS.
simple: Wasting of the thumb-side hand muscles but not the little-finger side, typical in motor neuron disease.

name: Spondylodiscitis
formal: Infection of intervertebral disc and adjacent vertebrae with back pain and fever, risk of epidural abscess.
simple: Infection of the spine disc and bone causing back pain.

name: Spontaneous oro-facial chorea
formal: Chorea of mouth and face in the elderly without drug exposure, similar to edentulous dyskinesia.
simple: Involuntary mouth and face movements in older people without a clear cause.

name: Sporadic Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease (sCJD)
formal: Rapidly progressive prion disease with dementia, myoclonus, ataxia, cortical ribboning on DWI, periodic sharp waves and positive RT-QuIC.
simple: A rapidly progressing brain disease from abnormal proteins, causing quick loss of memory and movement control.

name: Sporadic hyperekplexia
formal: Exaggerated startle with stiffness and falls without GLRA1 mutation, may be symptomatic of brainstem lesions.
simple: An excessive startle reaction with stiffness and falls but no known gene cause.

name: Sporadic myopathy
formal: Muscle disease occurring without family history, such as sporadic inclusion body myositis or acquired inflammatory, toxic or endocrine myopathies, with proximal or distal weakness.
simple: Muscle weakness that appears without a family history and has an acquired cause.
more: Evaluate with CK, EMG, MRI and muscle biopsy. Treat the underlying cause; inclusion body myositis responds poorly to immunotherapy.

name: Sporadic prion disease
formal: Prion protein misfolding disease arising without mutation or exposure, mainly sporadic CJD.
simple: A brain disease from abnormal proteins that arises spontaneously, causing rapid dementia.

name: Sports concussion
formal: Mild traumatic brain injury in sport causing transient headache, confusion, amnesia and imbalance; repeated injury linked to chronic traumatic encephalopathy.
simple: A brain injury from a knock during sport that causes headache, confusion and memory problems.

name: Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC)
formal: Malignancy of squamous epithelium whose head and neck forms spread perineurally to cranial nerves or metastasise to brain.
simple: A skin or mouth cancer that can spread along nerves to the brain.
aN: scc | squamous cell carcinoma

name: St Louis encephalitis
formal: Mosquito-borne flavivirus in the Americas causing fever, headache, confusion and SIADH, especially in the elderly.
simple: A mosquito-spread viral brain infection, most serious in older people.

name: Stabbing headache
formal: Primary stabbing headache with brief ice-pick pain in the head, lasting seconds, often in migraineurs.
simple: Very brief, sharp jabs of head pain like an ice pick.

name: Stargardt disease
formal: Autosomal recessive ABCA4 macular dystrophy with central visual loss in youth and yellow flecks.
simple: An inherited eye disease that causes loss of central vision in young people.

name: Startle epilepsy
formal: Epilepsy with seizures precipitated by sudden unexpected stimuli, typically in children with hemiplegia or brain damage.
simple: Seizures set off by a sudden noise or touch.

name: Statin myopathy
formal: Muscle toxicity from statins ranging from myalgia to necrotising immune-mediated myopathy with HMGCR antibodies and raised CK.
simple: Muscle pain or weakness caused by cholesterol-lowering statin medicines.
th: ปวดหรืออ่อนแรงกล้ามเนื้อจากยาลดไขมันกลุ่ม statin — ส่วนใหญ่ดีขึ้นเมื่อหยุดยา ถ้าไม่ดีขึ้นให้นึกถึง anti-HMGCR myopathy
tempoNote: Weeks to months after starting or raising the dose; toxic form settles within weeks of stopping
feat: Aching, cramps or heaviness in thighs and calves, often symmetric
Spectrum: myalgia with normal CK → mild CK rise → true weakness → rarely rhabdomyolysis
Risk rises with high-intensity statin, CYP3A4 inhibitors (macrolides, azoles), fibrates, hypothyroidism, renal impairment, older age
Toxic form improves after withdrawal; persisting or worsening weakness with very high CK suggests immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy
inv: CK at baseline and when symptomatic; TSH, renal and liver function
Anti-HMGCR antibody if weakness or high CK persists beyond 6–12 weeks off the drug
EMG/MRI thigh and muscle biopsy for persistent or atypical cases

case.who: 66-year-old man with diabetes and coronary stents
case.story: Atorvastatin was raised to 80 mg; a month later clarithromycin was added for pneumonia. He now has aching thighs and struggles to climb onto a songthaew.
case.exam: Mild symmetric hip flexor weakness, tender thighs, normal reflexes and sensation.
case.tests: CK 4,800 U/L, TSH normal, creatinine slightly raised; urine dipstick heme negative.
case.q: What is the next step, and when would you test for anti-HMGCR?
case.a: Stop the statin and the interacting antibiotic, hydrate and follow CK. If weakness or CK fails to settle after about 2–3 months off the statin, check anti-HMGCR for immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy.

det.patho: Statins block HMG-CoA reductase, lowering not only cholesterol but also downstream products such as ubiquinone and prenylated proteins that muscle needs for energy and membrane repair. Toxicity is dose-related and amplified by high blood levels from drug interactions or a SLCO1B1 transporter variant. A separate, much rarer entity is an autoimmune necrotizing myopathy in which antibodies target HMG-CoA reductase itself and the disease continues after the drug is gone.
det.clinical: Most patients describe muscle aches without weakness and with normal or near-normal CK; true myopathy with proximal weakness is less common, and rhabdomyolysis is rare. Symptoms usually begin within the first months or after a dose increase or new interacting drug. Nocebo effects are frequent, so symptoms that vanish on rechallenge with placebo are well documented. Red flags are objective weakness, dark urine, CK above ten times normal, and progression after stopping.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis rests on timing, CK and response to withdrawal. Check thyroid, renal and liver function, vitamin D and interacting drugs. If symptoms and CK resolve within weeks, the toxic form is likely. Persisting proximal weakness with high CK after withdrawal calls for anti-HMGCR serology, EMG (irritable myopathic pattern), MRI for oedema and a biopsy showing scattered necrotic fibres with little inflammation.
det.treatment: Stop or reduce the statin and correct contributing factors. After recovery, options include a lower dose, a hydrophilic statin such as rosuvastatin or pravastatin, alternate-day dosing, or non-statin agents (ezetimibe, PCSK9 inhibitors, bempedoic acid). Coenzyme Q10 has weak evidence. Anti-HMGCR myopathy needs immunotherapy—typically IVIG with steroids and a steroid-sparing agent—and permanent statin avoidance.
det.prognosis: Toxic myopathy recovers fully in nearly all patients within weeks to a few months. Anti-HMGCR myopathy is chronic and often needs long-term immunotherapy.
pearls: Normal CK with aches is usually not dangerous myopathy; weakness plus high CK is.
Getting worse after the statin is stopped is the clue to anti-HMGCR necrotizing myopathy.
Look for the interacting drug: macrolides, azole antifungals, gemfibrozil, ciclosporin, amiodarone.
det.thd: Statin ทำให้กล้ามเนื้อปวดหรืออ่อนแรงได้ โดยเฉพาะขนาดสูงหรือใช้ร่วมกับยาที่ยับยั้ง CYP3A4 ส่วนใหญ่ CK ปกติหรือสูงเล็กน้อยและหายภายในไม่กี่สัปดาห์หลังหยุดยา หากอ่อนแรงต่อเนื่องและ CK สูงมากแม้หยุดยาแล้ว ต้องตรวจ anti-HMGCR เพราะอาจเป็น immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy ซึ่งต้องรักษาด้วยยากดภูมิ

name: Status dysmyelinisatus

name: Status epilepticus

simple: A seizure that will not stop, or repeated seizures without waking, needing emergency treatment.
th: ชักต่อเนื่องเกิน 5 นาทีหรือชักซ้ำโดยไม่ฟื้น — ภาวะฉุกเฉิน ต้องให้ยาตามลำดับเวลา

Continuous EEG if not waking up

ddx.pt: Prolonged events with eyes closed, pelvic thrusting, normal lactate/EEG
Posturing in coma from brainstem compromise, no EEG seizure activity

aN: se | convulsive status | status epilepticus | gcse

det.patho: Status occurs when seizure-terminating mechanisms fail or seizure-sustaining mechanisms take over: GABA-A receptors are internalised while NMDA and AMPA receptors move to the synapse, so benzodiazepines lose potency the longer the seizure lasts. Prolonged seizures lead to excitotoxic neuronal injury, systemic hyperthermia, acidosis, rhabdomyolysis and cardiorespiratory compromise. Time point t1 (5 minutes) marks when to treat and t2 (around 30 minutes) when lasting damage becomes likely.
det.clinical: Convulsive status is obvious, but subtle motor signs (eyelid or facial twitching) may be all that remain later. Non-convulsive status presents as confusion, behavioural change, aphasia or coma and is common in ICU and elderly patients. Common triggers include low antiseizure drug levels, alcohol withdrawal, stroke, CNS infection, metabolic derangement, toxins and autoimmune encephalitis. Refractory status persists despite benzodiazepine and a second-line drug; super-refractory status continues 24 hours after anaesthesia. NORSE describes new-onset refractory status in a previously healthy person.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis of convulsive status is clinical; check capillary glucose at once. Send electrolytes, calcium, magnesium, renal and liver function, CK, blood gas, drug levels, toxicology and pregnancy test where relevant. Arrange urgent CT and, as indicated, MRI and lumbar puncture. Start continuous EEG if the patient does not wake within the expected time after convulsions stop, to detect non-convulsive status. Dissociative seizures, rigors and posturing in coma are key mimics.
det.treatment: Secure airway, breathing and circulation, give oxygen, and correct hypoglycaemia; give IV thiamine before glucose if alcohol misuse or malnutrition is possible. At 5 minutes give a benzodiazepine (IV lorazepam or diazepam, or IM midazolam/buccal midazolam pre-hospital), repeating once if needed. If seizures continue, load a second-line IV drug — levetiracetam, valproate or fosphenytoin/phenytoin are similarly effective. Refractory status requires intubation and anaesthetic infusion (midazolam, propofol or thiopental) titrated to EEG; treat the underlying cause in parallel, including immunotherapy for suspected autoimmune aetiology.
det.prognosis: Mortality is around 10–20% overall and higher in older patients, with acute symptomatic causes and refractory status; drug withdrawal-related status in known epilepsy has a better outlook.
pearls: Under-dosing benzodiazepines is the commonest treatment error — give a full dose early.
A patient who is not waking after convulsions stop may still be seizing: get an EEG.
Check glucose first and give thiamine where malnutrition or alcohol is possible.
det.thd: Status epilepticus คือชักต่อเนื่องเกิน 5 นาที หรือชักซ้ำโดยไม่ฟื้นระหว่างครั้ง ยิ่งชักนานยิ่งดื้อต่อยา benzodiazepine และสมองเสียหาย การรักษาเริ่มด้วย ABC ตรวจน้ำตาลทันที ให้ thiamine ถ้ามีความเสี่ยง แล้วให้ benzodiazepine ขนาดเต็มภายใน 5 นาที ถ้ายังชักให้ยาลำดับสอง เช่น levetiracetam, valproate หรือ phenytoin ถ้าไม่หยุดต้องใส่ท่อช่วยหายใจและให้ยาสลบต่อเนื่องร่วมกับ EEG ระหว่างนี้ต้องค้นหาและรักษาสาเหตุ

name: Status marmoratus
formal: Perinatal hypoxic-ischaemic basal ganglia injury with marbled gliosis, leading to dyskinetic cerebral palsy.
simple: Brain injury around birth causing marbled scarring in deep brain areas and later movement problems.

name: Steal syndromes
formal: Haemodynamic diversion of blood from a vascular bed, e.g. subclavian steal causing vertebrobasilar insufficiency.
simple: Conditions where blood is diverted away from the brain or arm because of a narrowed artery.

name: Steele–Richardson–Olszewski disease
formal: Progressive supranuclear palsy, a tauopathy with vertical gaze palsy, early falls and axial rigidity.
simple: A brain disease causing falls, stiffness and trouble moving the eyes up and down.
more: Pathology shows neurofibrillary tangles and tufted astrocytes in the midbrain and basal ganglia; levodopa response is poor. Treatment is supportive, with botulinum toxin for dystonia and swallowing assessment.

name: Steele–Richardson–Olszewski syndrome
formal: Progressive supranuclear palsy, a tauopathy with vertical gaze palsy, early falls and axial rigidity.
simple: A brain disease causing falls, stiffness and trouble moving the eyes up and down.

name: Stereotypy
formal: Repetitive purposeless coordinated movements that are patterned, seen in autism, tardive syndromes and neurodegeneration.
simple: Repeated, patterned movements such as rocking or hand flapping.

name: Steroid myopathy
formal: Proximal weakness from chronic glucocorticoid excess with normal CK and type 2 fibre atrophy.
simple: Muscle weakness in the thighs and shoulders caused by long-term steroid use.
more: CK is normal and EMG is usually normal, with biopsy showing type 2 fibre atrophy without inflammation; MRI is unremarkable. Treat by reducing or switching steroids, using a fluorinated-steroid-free regimen and exercise, with improvement over weeks to months.
th: กล้ามเนื้อต้นแขนต้นขาอ่อนแรงจากการใช้ steroid นาน ๆ — CK ปกติ
tempoNote: Chronic form develops over weeks to months of treatment; an acute form occurs with high-dose IV steroids in ICU
feat: Painless proximal weakness, legs before arms: trouble rising from chairs and climbing stairs
Cushingoid features: moon face, central obesity, skin thinning
Normal CK, normal sensation and reflexes
Higher risk with fluorinated steroids (dexamethasone) and doses above about 30 mg/day prednisolone
Acute ICU form (critical illness myopathy) with high-dose steroids ± neuromuscular blockers
inv: CK (normal) — helps separate from active myositis
EMG often normal or mildly myopathic without spontaneous activity
Muscle biopsy (rarely needed): type 2b fibre atrophy
Check potassium, thyroid, and vitamin D

case.story: CK fell from 6,000 to normal on prednisolone 60 mg daily for 3 months, but she now struggles more to stand from a squat.
case.exam: Cushingoid face, symmetric hip flexor weakness, no muscle tenderness, normal reflexes.
case.tests: CK 90 U/L; EMG without fibrillations; MRI thigh shows no oedema, only fatty atrophy.
case.q: Is her myositis relapsing, or is this steroid myopathy, and what should be done?
case.a: Normal CK, no fibrillations and no MRI oedema favour steroid myopathy; taper prednisolone while adding a steroid-sparing agent, and encourage resistance exercise.

det.patho: Glucocorticoids increase muscle protein breakdown through the ubiquitin–proteasome pathway and reduce protein synthesis by inhibiting IGF-1 and mTOR signalling. Fast-twitch type 2 fibres are most affected, so atrophy rather than necrosis is the result. Fluorinated compounds carry the highest risk.
det.clinical: The chronic form develops gradually with proximal leg weakness, often accompanied by other steroid side effects. It is easy to confuse with a relapse of the condition being treated, especially myositis or myasthenia. The acute form arises within days of very high doses, often in ICU with sepsis, and can include rhabdomyolysis.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical, supported by normal CK and a quiet EMG. In treated myositis, the absence of fibrillations and of MRI muscle oedema helps distinguish steroid myopathy from active inflammation; a trial of dose reduction is often decisive. Exclude hypokalaemia, thyroid dysfunction and vitamin D deficiency.
det.treatment: Reduce the steroid dose to the lowest effective level, switch to non-fluorinated agents, or use alternate-day dosing and steroid-sparing drugs. Resistance and aerobic exercise counteract atrophy. Ensure adequate protein intake and treat coexisting metabolic issues.
det.prognosis: Strength usually recovers over weeks to months after dose reduction.
pearls: Treated myositis getting weaker with normal CK: think steroids before escalating immunotherapy.
Dexamethasone is more myotoxic than equivalent prednisolone.
Exercise prevents and treats steroid myopathy.
det.thd: Steroid myopathy เกิดจากการใช้ corticosteroid ขนาดสูงหรือนาน ทำให้กล้ามเนื้อต้นขาต้นแขนอ่อนแรงโดยไม่ปวด CK ปกติ EMG มักปกติ ต้องแยกจากโรคเดิมกำเริบ เช่น myositis ซึ่งมี CK สูงและ EMG พบ fibrillation การรักษาคือลดขนาด steroid ใช้ยาลด steroid และออกกำลังกาย ส่วนใหญ่ดีขึ้นในหลายสัปดาห์ถึงเดือน

name: Steroid responsive encephalopathy
formal: Hashimoto encephalopathy or SREAT with confusion, seizures and anti-thyroid antibodies, dramatically responding to steroids.
simple: A brain inflammation linked to thyroid antibodies causing confusion and seizures that improves with steroids.

name: Stiff baby syndrome
formal: Hyperekplexia in infants with generalised hypertonia, exaggerated startle and apnoea, often GLRA1-related, relieved by clonazepam.
simple: A condition in newborns with very stiff muscles and an exaggerated startle.
more: Treat with clonazepam, and the Vigevano manoeuvre can abort attacks; consider shared pathogenic variants in GLRA1 and genetic testing. Attacks of apnoea can be fatal, and symptoms usually improve with age, although startle persists.

name: Stiff leg/stiff limb syndrome
formal: Autoimmune disorder with progressive limb or trunk stiffness and painful spasms, often asymmetric and confined to one limb; linked to anti-GAD or glycine receptor antibodies and spinal interneuron dysfunction.
simple: A condition where one leg or arm becomes stiff and goes into painful spasms because the immune system disturbs nerve signals in the spinal cord.

name: Stiff man syndrome
formal: Older name for stiff-person syndrome: progressive axial and proximal limb rigidity with superimposed spasms, startle-provoked, associated with anti-GAD65 antibodies and other autoimmune disease.
simple: A rare immune condition causing muscles in the trunk and legs to become stiff and to cramp painfully, often set off by sudden noise or touch.

name: Stiff-person spectrum disorders (SPSD)
formal: Umbrella term covering classic stiff-person syndrome, stiff-limb variants, progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity and myoclonus, and paraneoplastic forms, united by autoantibodies and CNS hyperexcitability.
simple: A group of related rare immune conditions in which the nervous system causes muscle stiffness and spasms.
aN: spsd | stiff person spectrum disorders

name: Stiff-person syndrome (SPS)
formal: Autoimmune CNS hyperexcitability disorder with fluctuating axial and limb rigidity, stimulus-sensitive spasms and lumbar hyperlordosis; anti-GAD65 antibodies are typical and it responds to benzodiazepines and baclofen.
simple: A rare immune disease making the back and leg muscles stiff and prone to painful spasms triggered by noise, touch or stress.
more: EMG shows continuous motor unit firing that stops with sleep or diazepam; also check anti-amphiphysin and anti-glycine antibodies, and screen for breast cancer or thymoma. Add IVIG, plasmapheresis or rituximab.
ab: progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity and myoclonus

feat: Fluctuating stiffness of trunk and proximal legs, exaggerated lumbar lordosis
Painful spasms triggered by noise, touch, emotion or sudden movement
Task-specific phobia (fear of open spaces or falling); often misdiagnosed as functional
Associations: type 1 diabetes, thyroid disease, vitiligo; amphiphysin antibodies suggest breast cancer
inv: Anti-GAD65 at high titre (also glycine receptor, amphiphysin)
EMG: ongoing firing of normal motor units, with simultaneous contraction of opposing muscles, abolished by sleep or diazepam

case.story: Two years of a 'board-like' back and legs; a slammed door makes her fall rigidly. Labelled anxiety.
case.exam: Rigid paraspinal and abdominal muscles, hyperlordosis, stiff-legged gait, normal strength and sensation.
case.tests: Anti-GAD65 >2,000 IU/mL; EMG: co-contraction that melts with IV diazepam.
case.q: What symptomatic treatment usually helps first?
case.a: GABA-enhancing drugs — diazepam (often high doses) and baclofen; IVIG for disabling disease.

files.chapter: Chapter 14 - Autoimmunity Against the Inhibitory Synapsis

ddx.pt: No continuous motor unit activity; antibodies negative
Peripheral myokymia and cramps, neuromyotonic EMG; CASPR2

aN: sps | stiff person syndrome | stiff man syndrome | anti gad syndrome | perm | progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity and myoclonus

det.patho: SPS is an autoimmune disorder of central inhibitory circuits: antibodies against GAD65 (the enzyme producing GABA), amphiphysin or the glycine receptor are associated with reduced GABAergic and glycinergic inhibition of spinal and brainstem motor neurons. The result is continuous simultaneous firing of opposing muscle groups plus heightened startle-triggered spasms. It is rare, more common in women, and frequently coexists with other autoimmune conditions.
det.clinical: Onset is insidious in mid-adult life with aching stiffness of the lower back and abdomen, a fixed lumbar hyperlordosis and a slow, wide-based, stiff gait. Superimposed painful spasms are triggered by sudden noise, touch, cold or emotion and can cause falls 'like a statue'. Anxiety and fear of open spaces are common and secondary, often leading to a functional label. Variants include stiff-limb syndrome, and PERM with brainstem signs, myoclonus and encephalopathy. GAD antibodies may also accompany cerebellar ataxia, epilepsy or limbic encephalitis.
det.diagnosis: Very high serum anti-GAD65 titres (far above those seen in type 1 diabetes) support the diagnosis; CSF GAD antibodies with intrathecal synthesis add weight. Surface EMG shows continuous normal motor unit firing in paraspinal and abdominal muscles with simultaneous agonist–antagonist activity that disappears in sleep or after IV diazepam. Amphiphysin antibodies demand a search for breast or small-cell lung cancer. Exclude tetanus, myelopathy, dystonia and neuromyotonia.
det.treatment: Symptomatic treatment centres on GABA-enhancing drugs: benzodiazepines (diazepam often in high divided doses) and baclofen, with gabapentin, pregabalin or levetiracetam as add-ons; intrathecal baclofen is used in refractory cases. Immunotherapy with IVIG has the best evidence; rituximab, plasma exchange and steroids are alternatives. Paraneoplastic cases need tumour treatment. Avoid abrupt benzodiazepine withdrawal, which can precipitate dangerous spasms.
det.prognosis: Course is variable and often progressive, with falls and disability; many patients improve partly with treatment. Paraneoplastic and PERM forms carry a worse outlook.
pearls: Board-like abdomen and hyperlordosis that melt under anaesthesia or sleep: think SPS.
Low-titre GAD is common in diabetes; SPS titres are usually very high.
Amphiphysin antibodies point to breast cancer.
det.thd: Stiff-person syndrome เป็นโรคภูมิคุ้มกันต่อระบบยับยั้งในไขสันหลังและก้านสมอง (anti-GAD65, amphiphysin, glycine receptor) ทำให้กล้ามเนื้อหลังและท้องแข็งตลอด หลังแอ่น และกระตุกปวดเมื่อตกใจหรือถูกสัมผัส มักถูกวินิจฉัยผิดเป็นโรควิตกกังวล วินิจฉัยด้วย anti-GAD ระดับสูงมาก และ EMG ที่เห็นกล้ามเนื้อหดตัวพร้อมกันต่อเนื่องซึ่งหายเมื่อหลับหรือให้ diazepam รักษาด้วย diazepam, baclofen และ IVIG

name: Strachan syndrome
formal: Syndrome of painful sensory neuropathy, optic neuropathy and sometimes spastic paraparesis, described in nutritionally deprived populations, probably related to deficiency of B vitamins and other nutrients.
simple: A condition from poor nutrition causing burning pain and numb feet, vision loss and sometimes stiff legs.

name: Striatocapsular infarction
formal: Infarct of the striatum and anterior internal capsule from occlusion of lenticulostriate branches or the MCA stem, causing contralateral hemiparesis with or without aphasia or neglect.
simple: A stroke in deep brain structures that causes weakness on one side of the body and sometimes trouble with speech.

name: Striatonigral degeneration (SND)
formal: Parkinsonian variant of multiple system atrophy with neuronal loss and gliosis in putamen and substantia nigra, causing akinetic-rigid syndrome with poor levodopa response and autonomic failure.
simple: A brain degeneration causing slowness and stiffness like Parkinson disease, but responding poorly to Parkinson medicines.
more: MRI shows reduced putaminal volume with T2 hypointensity of the posterolateral putamen and rim of hyperintensity; autonomic testing is helpful. Treat with levodopa trial (may produce orofacial dystonia), droxidopa, and supportive care.
aN: snd | striatonigral degeneration

name: Striatopallido-dentate calcification
formal: Bilateral calcification of basal ganglia, dentate nuclei and other regions, producing parkinsonism, chorea, ataxia, dementia or psychiatric signs; idiopathic (Fahr) or secondary to hypoparathyroidism and genetic causes.
simple: Calcium deposits in deep brain areas that can cause movement problems, memory loss and mood changes.

name: Stroke
formal: Acute focal neurological deficit from cerebral ischaemia or haemorrhage; ischaemic subtypes include large-artery, cardioembolic, small-vessel and cryptogenic, managed by reperfusion and secondary prevention.
simple: Sudden loss of brain function when blood flow to part of the brain is blocked or a vessel bleeds, causing weakness, speech or vision problems.

name: Stroke-like migraine attacks
formal: Migraine with aura presenting with prolonged or severe focal deficits that mimic cerebral infarction, or occurring in conditions such as MELAS or SMART syndrome, requiring exclusion of true ischaemia.
simple: Migraine episodes whose symptoms, like weakness or speech trouble, look like a stroke but are caused by the migraine process.

name: Strychnine poisoning
formal: Convulsant poisoning from glycine receptor antagonism in the spinal cord, causing generalised muscle spasms, opisthotonos and risus sardonicus while consciousness is preserved; treated with benzodiazepines and supportive care.
simple: A poisoning that blocks calming signals in the spinal cord, causing violent painful muscle spasms while the person stays awake.

name: Sturge–Weber syndrome
formal: Neurocutaneous disorder from somatic GNAQ mutation with facial port-wine stain, leptomeningeal angioma, seizures, glaucoma, hemiparesis and cognitive impairment; tram-track calcification on imaging.
simple: A birth condition with a facial birthmark and blood-vessel malformation on the brain surface, often causing seizures and eye pressure problems.

name: Stuve–Wiedemann syndrome
formal: Rare autosomal recessive disorder (LIFR mutation) with neonatal bowel, respiratory and feeding difficulties, bone dysplasia with bowing, autonomic dysfunction and sweating or temperature instability.
simple: A rare inherited condition in babies with bent bones, feeding and breathing trouble and unstable body temperature control.

name: Subacute combined degeneration
formal: Vitamin B12 deficiency myelopathy affecting dorsal columns and corticospinal tracts, with paraesthesias, sensory ataxia, spasticity and often neuropathy and megaloblastic anaemia.
simple: Spinal cord damage from low vitamin B12 causing tingling, poor balance and weak stiff legs.

Spastic weakness with extensor plantars yet absent ankle jerks (cord + nerve)
Cognitive change, macrocytic anaemia
Nitrous oxide abuse can precipitate it
inv: Serum B12, methylmalonic acid, homocysteine; full blood count
MRI spine: dorsal column T2 'inverted V'
Intrinsic factor/parietal cell antibodies

case.tests: B12 borderline, MMA high; MRI: dorsal column hyperintensity C2–C6.

aN: scd | b12 deficiency myelopathy | subacute combined degeneration of the cord | cobalamin deficiency

det.patho: Vitamin B12 is needed for methionine synthase and methylmalonyl-CoA mutase; deficiency disrupts myelin synthesis, particularly in the large myelinated fibres of the dorsal columns and lateral corticospinal tracts, beginning in the cervical and upper thoracic cord. Peripheral nerves, optic nerves and the brain may also be affected. Common causes are pernicious anaemia, gastric surgery, malabsorption, strict vegan diet, metformin or proton pump inhibitor use, and nitrous oxide, which inactivates B12.
det.clinical: Symmetric tingling in the feet (sometimes the hands first) is followed by impaired vibration and proprioception, sensory ataxia and Romberg positivity. Corticospinal involvement gives spastic leg weakness and extensor plantars, while a coexisting neuropathy may abolish ankle jerks. Cognitive change, depression, visual loss from optic neuropathy, and Lhermitte phenomenon can occur. Neurological damage may develop without anaemia or macrocytosis, especially if folate intake is high.
det.diagnosis: Measure serum B12 together with methylmalonic acid and homocysteine, because B12 levels in the low-normal range may hide true deficiency; both metabolites rise in B12 deficiency, only homocysteine in folate deficiency. Look for the cause: intrinsic factor and parietal cell antibodies, gastrin, coeliac serology, diet and drug history, and nitrous oxide use. MRI may show T2 hyperintensity of the dorsal columns (inverted V on axial images). Check copper, which can produce an identical myelopathy, and consider nerve conduction studies.
det.treatment: Start parenteral hydroxocobalamin or cyanocobalamin promptly, with frequent intramuscular injections in the first weeks for neurological involvement, then lifelong maintenance if the cause persists; high-dose oral B12 can be used for maintenance in many patients. Do not give folate alone, which can worsen the neurological picture. In nitrous oxide users, stop exposure and treat even if the B12 level looks normal. Physiotherapy helps recovery of gait.
det.prognosis: Improvement occurs over 6–12 months; the extent of recovery depends on severity and duration before treatment, and long-standing deficits may be permanent.
pearls: Normal haemoglobin does not exclude neurological B12 deficiency.
Recreational nitrous oxide is now a leading cause in young adults — ask directly.
Extensor plantars with absent ankle jerks: B12, copper, Friedreich ataxia, or combined cord and nerve disease.
det.thd: Subacute combined degeneration เกิดจากขาดวิตามินบี 12 ทำให้ปลอกประสาทของไขสันหลังส่วน dorsal column และ corticospinal tract เสื่อม ร่วมกับปลายประสาทอักเสบ อาการคือชาปลายเท้า สูญเสียการรับรู้การสั่นและตำแหน่งข้อ ยืนหลับตาแล้วล้ม ขาเกร็ง Babinski บวก แต่ ankle jerk หาย สาเหตุพบบ่อยคือ pernicious anaemia ผ่าตัดกระเพาะ ยา metformin และการสูดก๊าซไนตรัสออกไซด์ ตรวจ B12 ร่วมกับ MMA และ homocysteine รักษาด้วยการฉีด B12 โดยเร็ว ห้ามให้ folate อย่างเดียว

name: Subacute myelo-optic neuropathy
formal: Toxic myelopathy and optic neuropathy with abdominal symptoms and green tongue, caused by clioquinol; epidemic in Japan in the 1960s, causing sensory neuropathy, visual loss and paraparesis.
simple: A poisoning from an old anti-diarrhoea drug that caused stomach pain, numb legs and loss of vision.

name: Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE)
formal: Fatal progressive encephalitis from persistent defective measles virus after early childhood infection, with myoclonic jerks, cognitive decline, periodic EEG complexes and raised CSF measles antibodies.
simple: A rare, fatal brain infection years after measles, causing jerks, memory decline and loss of function.

name: Subarachnoid haemorrhage
formal: Bleeding into the subarachnoid space, usually from ruptured saccular aneurysm, causing thunderclap headache, meningism and often reduced consciousness; complications include rebleeding, vasospasm and hydrocephalus.
simple: Bleeding around the brain surface, usually from a burst aneurysm, causing a sudden severe headache and neck stiffness.

files.chapter: Chapter 15: Specific treatment of aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage
Section 6 Systemic Disorders That Also Involve the Cerebrovascular System

ddx.pt: Recurrent thunderclap headaches over days; beaded vessels that normalise; small convexity SAH
Builds over minutes to hours with prior similar attacks
Fever and gradual onset; CSF neutrophils rather than xanthochromia
Sudden headache with visual loss/ophthalmoplegia and a sellar mass

aN: sah | aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage | thunderclap headache | subarachnoid hemorrhage

det.patho: About 85% of non-traumatic SAH comes from rupture of a saccular aneurysm at the circle of Willis, typically at the anterior communicating, posterior communicating or MCA bifurcation; about 10% is perimesencephalic non-aneurysmal SAH, a benign venous variant, and the rest stems from dissection, AVM, RCVS or other rare causes. Risk factors are smoking, hypertension, heavy alcohol use, family history and inherited conditions such as polycystic kidney disease; aneurysm size, site and irregular shape raise rupture risk. Blood in the subarachnoid space causes a sudden pressure surge with global ischaemia, meningeal irritation and impaired CSF absorption. Delayed cerebral ischaemia is now understood as multifactorial — large-artery vasospasm plus microvascular dysfunction, microthrombosis and spreading depolarisations.
det.clinical: The hallmark is a headache that peaks within a minute, often with vomiting, neck stiffness, photophobia, brief loss of consciousness or seizure; a minor warning (sentinel) bleed may precede it by days. Neck stiffness may take hours to appear and is absent in deep coma. Focal signs suggest the aneurysm site or a haematoma: painful pupil-involving third nerve palsy with PComm aneurysm, bilateral leg weakness or abulia with AComm, and subhyaloid (Terson) haemorrhages imply a large rise in pressure. Complications follow a timeline: rebleeding (highest in the first 6–24 hours), acute hydrocephalus, delayed cerebral ischaemia (days 3–14), hyponatraemia, neurogenic pulmonary oedema and stress cardiomyopathy. Severity is graded with the WFNS or Hunt–Hess scales and blood load with the modified Fisher scale, which predicts vasospasm.
det.diagnosis: In an alert patient with thunderclap headache, non-contrast CT within 6 hours of onset on a modern scanner read by an expert is close to fully sensitive; sensitivity falls with time. If CT is negative and more than 6 hours have passed, perform LP at least 12 hours after onset to look for xanthochromia (spectrophotometry where available). The Ottawa SAH rule helps decide who needs the work-up in neurologically intact patients. CTA identifies most aneurysms; DSA with 3D rotation remains the reference standard, and a negative first DSA with a diffuse bleed should be repeated. Consider RCVS, CVT, pituitary apoplexy, arterial dissection, intracranial hypotension and meningitis as alternative explanations.
det.treatment: Secure the aneurysm early, ideally within 24 hours, by endovascular coiling (preferred when both options suit) or surgical clipping. Until then control systolic BP (commonly below about 160), give analgesia and antiemetics, reverse anticoagulation and treat acute hydrocephalus with ventricular drainage; routine antifibrinolytics did not improve outcome. Give oral nimodipine 60 mg every 4 hours for 21 days, reducing the dose or splitting it if it causes hypotension. Maintain euvolaemia (prophylactic hypervolaemia and triple-H are abandoned), avoid hypotension and hyponatraemia, and monitor for DCI with frequent examination, transcranial Doppler or CT perfusion; lumbar drainage of blood-laden CSF reduced DCI-related infarction in a recent trial. Symptomatic DCI is treated with induced hypertension and, if refractory, intra-arterial vasodilators or angioplasty; statins and magnesium add nothing, and seizure prophylaxis, if used, should be brief.
det.prognosis: Overall case fatality approaches one third, with many survivors left with cognitive, mood or fatigue problems; grade on admission is the strongest predictor.
pearls: Thunderclap headache = SAH until proven otherwise; CT then LP if needed.
Nimodipine improves outcome but does not reliably prevent angiographic spasm.
Hyponatraemia after SAH is often cerebral salt wasting — do not fluid-restrict.
New deficit or drowsiness between days 3 and 14 = DCI until excluded; check sodium, hydrocephalus and perfusion.

name: Subchoreic Huntington’s disease (status subchoreacticus)
formal: Late phase of Huntington disease with reduced chorea turning to rigidity, bradykinesia and dystonia in advanced or juvenile-onset cases; the title wording is nonstandard for an akinetic-rigid stage.
simple: A late stage of Huntington disease in which the jerky movements fade and the body becomes stiff and slow.

name: Subclavian steal syndrome
formal: Haemodynamic syndrome from proximal subclavian stenosis or occlusion causing retrograde vertebral flow, with arm claudication, blood pressure difference and posterior circulation symptoms on arm exercise.
simple: A blocked artery to the arm that steals blood from the brain's back circulation, causing dizziness or fainting when the arm is used.
th: หลอดเลือด subclavian (มักข้างซ้าย) ตีบก่อนแยก vertebral artery ทำให้เลือดไหลย้อนลง vertebral ไปเลี้ยงแขน ส่วนใหญ่ไม่มีอาการ อาจมีเวียนศีรษะเมื่อใช้แขนข้างนั้น ความดันแขนสองข้างต่างกันชัด
tempoNote: Usually a silent haemodynamic finding; symptomatic patients have brief attacks provoked by arm exercise
feat: Systolic BP difference of ≥ 15–20 mmHg between the arms, weak or delayed radial pulse on the affected side
Arm claudication: aching, fatigue or coolness of the arm with use
Rarely, brief dizziness, vertigo, diplopia or syncope triggered by exercising the affected arm
Supraclavicular bruit
Angina in patients with an internal mammary coronary graft (coronary-subclavian steal)

Duplex: reversed or alternating flow in the ipsilateral vertebral artery, accentuated by arm exercise or cuff hyperaemia test
CTA/MRA of aortic arch and great vessels to grade the stenosis

case.story: When hammering overhead with his left arm for several minutes he becomes light-headed and his left arm aches and tingles; symptoms settle within a minute of resting.
case.exam: BP right arm 158/84, left arm 118/70; diminished left radial pulse; left supraclavicular bruit; neurological exam normal.
case.tests: Duplex: retrograde flow in the left vertebral artery; CTA: 85% stenosis of the proximal left subclavian artery.
case.q: Explain the mechanism and the treatment options.
case.a: Proximal subclavian stenosis lowers pressure in the distal subclavian, so blood is drawn down the vertebral artery from the basilar system during arm exercise; symptomatic disease is treated with angioplasty/stenting, plus antiplatelet and statin.

det.patho: Stenosis or occlusion of the subclavian artery proximal to the vertebral origin (left side in about three-quarters, because of its origin from the arch) reduces pressure beyond the lesion. The vertebral artery then fills retrogradely from the basilar junction to supply the arm. The brain is usually protected by the circle of Willis, which is why most patients have no neurological symptoms. Atherosclerosis is the main cause; Takayasu arteritis, radiation, thoracic outlet compression and congenital arch anomalies are others.
det.clinical: The steal phenomenon (reversed vertebral flow on ultrasound) is common and benign; the syndrome (symptoms) is rare. When present, posterior-circulation symptoms are brief and exercise-related; persistent stroke from steal alone is unusual, and a stroke should prompt a search for another mechanism. Arm claudication and finger ischaemia from emboli may occur. Coronary steal causes angina in patients whose bypass uses the left internal mammary artery.
det.diagnosis: The arm BP gradient is the bedside clue. Duplex documents vertebral flow direction (partial, alternating or complete reversal). CTA or MRA shows the culprit lesion and other arch disease. Coexisting carotid or vertebrobasilar stenosis increases symptom likelihood and should be sought.
det.treatment: Asymptomatic steal needs only vascular risk management (antiplatelet, statin, BP control using the higher arm reading, smoking cessation). Symptomatic patients, or those needing a patent left internal mammary graft, are treated by endovascular angioplasty and stenting or by surgical carotid-subclavian bypass/transposition. Takayasu disease requires immunosuppression before revascularisation.
det.prognosis: Benign neurologically in most cases; overall prognosis is governed by the associated coronary and cerebrovascular atherosclerosis.
pearls: Always measure BP in both arms; use the higher one for management decisions.
Steal on Doppler is common, but steal symptoms are rare — look for another cause of a stroke.
Vertigo or dizziness provoked by arm exercise is the classic history.
det.thd: Subclavian steal syndrome เกิดจาก subclavian artery (มักข้างซ้าย) ตีบก่อนแยกแขนง vertebral ทำให้เลือดไหลย้อนจาก vertebral ลงไปเลี้ยงแขน ส่วนใหญ่ไม่มีอาการ ตรวจพบความดันแขนสองข้างต่างกันมากกว่า 15–20 mmHg และชีพจรข้างนั้นเบา บางรายเวียนศีรษะหรือเห็นภาพซ้อนเมื่อใช้แขนข้างนั้น วินิจฉัยด้วย duplex เห็น vertebral flow ย้อนกลับ รักษาด้วยยาและคุมปัจจัยเสี่ยง ส่วนรายมีอาการทำ angioplasty/stenting หรือ bypass

name: Subcortical infarcts and leukoencephalopathy (CARASIL)
formal: Autosomal recessive HTRA1-related small vessel disease with early leukoencephalopathy, alopecia, spondylosis and recurrent lacunar strokes leading to dementia in young adults.
simple: An inherited condition of small brain vessels causing early strokes, memory loss, hair loss and back problems.
ab: cerebral autosomal recessive arteriopathy with subcortical infarcts and leukoencephalopathy
th: small vessel disease ยีนด้อยจาก HTRA1 — สมองเสื่อมและ stroke ในวัย 20–40 ร่วมกับผมร่วงศีรษะล้านตั้งแต่วัยรุ่น และปวดหลังจากหมอนรองกระดูกเสื่อม (แบบ heterozygous ทำให้ CSVD ผู้ใหญ่ได้)
tempoNote: Hair loss in the teens, back pain in the 20s, gait disorder and strokes in the 20s–30s, then stepwise decline over about a decade
feat: Premature scalp hair loss (alopecia) starting in adolescence
Early lumbar spondylosis and disc herniation causing back pain
Lacunar strokes, spastic gait and pseudobulbar palsy in young adults without hypertension
Progressive subcortical dementia with apathy and mood change
Parental consanguinity; reported mainly from Japan and China, also elsewhere in Asia

case.who: 32-year-old man, parents first cousins, Nakhon Si Thammarat
case.story: Nearly bald since age 17, recurrent low back pain since 24; over two years he has become slow and indifferent and walks stiffly. Two brief episodes of left leg weakness.
case.exam: Spastic gait, brisk reflexes, bilateral Babinski, emotional lability, MoCA 20/30; BP 118/76.
case.tests: MRI brain: confluent white matter disease with lacunes and pontine arc-shaped hyperintensity; MRI L-spine: multilevel disc herniations; NOTCH3 negative; HTRA1 homozygous pathogenic variant.
case.q: Which two non-neurological features point to this diagnosis rather than CADASIL?
case.a: Early alopecia and premature spondylosis (with recessive inheritance and normotension) indicate HTRA1-related CARASIL.

det.patho: Loss-of-function of HTRA1, a serine protease that modulates TGF-beta signalling, causes degeneration of arterial smooth muscle, intimal thickening and splitting of the elastic lamina within small penetrating arteries, without the granular osmiophilic material seen in CADASIL. Altered TGF-beta signalling in other tissues probably explains hair loss and disc degeneration. Biallelic variants cause CARASIL; some heterozygous variants cause a later-onset dominant small vessel disease that is now recognised as more common than the recessive form.
det.clinical: Onset is typically in the teens to 30s with alopecia and back pain preceding neurological disease. Lacunar strokes or a progressive gait disorder appear in young adulthood, followed by cognitive decline with apathy, irritability and pseudobulbar signs. Patients are usually normotensive. Heterozygous carriers present later (40s–60s) with stroke and leukoencephalopathy, often without alopecia.
det.diagnosis: Suspect it in a young normotensive patient with diffuse leukoencephalopathy and lacunes, particularly with consanguinity, early baldness or premature spondylosis. MRI resembles CADASIL, including temporal pole involvement, and a pontine arc lesion is suggestive. Confirm by HTRA1 sequencing after excluding NOTCH3, COL4A1/2, Fabry disease and acquired causes.
det.treatment: No disease-modifying treatment exists. Manage with antiplatelet therapy after ischaemic events (weighing bleeding risk), physiotherapy for spasticity and gait, treatment of mood disorders, orthopaedic care for spinal disease and support for cognitive decline. Offer genetic counselling to the family, including carriers, given the dominant risk of some heterozygous variants.
det.prognosis: The disease advances to severe dementia and dependence over roughly 10 years from neurological onset.
pearls: Young bald man + back pain + leukoencephalopathy = check HTRA1.
Unlike CADASIL, migraine with aura is not a typical feature.
Heterozygous HTRA1 variants are a cause of adult-onset familial small vessel disease.
det.thd: CARASIL เป็นโรคหลอดเลือดสมองขนาดเล็กทางพันธุกรรมแบบยีนด้อยจากยีน HTRA1 ผู้ป่วยผมร่วงจนศีรษะล้านตั้งแต่วัยรุ่น ปวดหลังจากหมอนรองกระดูกเสื่อมเร็ว และเกิด lacunar stroke เดินเกร็ง ความคิดถดถอยตั้งแต่อายุ 20–40 ปีโดยไม่มีความดันสูง MRI พบ white matter disease แพร่กระจายคล้าย CADASIL ยืนยันด้วยการตรวจยีน ยังไม่มียารักษาเฉพาะ ใช้การรักษาประคับประคอง

name: Subcortical ischaemic stroke
formal: Ischaemic stroke in deep white matter, basal ganglia or internal capsule due to small-vessel disease, typically presenting as lacunar syndromes such as pure motor or sensory stroke.
simple: A stroke deep in the brain from blockage of a tiny vessel, often causing weakness or numbness on one side.

name: Subcortical-cortical myoclonus
formal: Myoclonus generated by cortical hyperexcitability and relayed through subcortical pathways, producing multifocal jerks with cortical EEG correlates on back-averaging, in metabolic or degenerative disease.
simple: Sudden muscle jerks arising from overactive brain circuits involving the cortex and deeper brain areas.

name: Subcortical–nonsegmental myoclonus
formal: Myoclonus with subcortical generator and nonsegmental distribution, such as reticular reflex myoclonus or startle syndromes, lacking a consistent cortical EEG correlate.
simple: Sudden muscle jerks arising from deep brain regions, affecting widespread muscles rather than one body segment.

name: Subcortico-cortical myoclonus
formal: Myoclonus in which cortical discharges drive subcortical structures, giving jerks with cortical spike precedence on EEG back-averaging; seen in post-hypoxic and progressive myoclonic conditions.
simple: Sudden muscle jerks that begin with abnormal electrical activity in the brain's outer layer and spread to deeper brain areas.

name: Subcutaneous neurofibromas
formal: Benign nerve sheath tumours under the skin in neurofibromatosis type 1, appearing as soft, fleshy nodules along peripheral nerves, often multiple and sometimes painful.
simple: Soft lumps under the skin along nerves, typical of a genetic condition called neurofibromatosis.

name: Subdural and extradural haematoma
formal: Intracranial collections of blood in the subdural or epidural space, usually traumatic, causing raised pressure and focal signs; epidural lesions are arterial and lens shaped, subdural venous and crescentic.
simple: Blood collecting between the skull and the brain's coverings after head injury, which can press on the brain.

name: Subdural haematoma
formal: Collection of blood between dura and arachnoid from torn bridging veins, acute or chronic, particularly in elderly or anticoagulated patients, presenting with headache, confusion or hemiparesis.
simple: A slow or sudden bleed under the brain's outer covering, often after a minor head knock in older people.

name: Subhyaloid haemorrhage
formal: Retinal bleeding between the internal limiting membrane or hyaloid face and retina, often with subarachnoid haemorrhage (Terson syndrome) or raised pressure, causing sudden visual loss.
simple: A pool of blood in front of the retina that can suddenly blur vision, sometimes after a brain bleed.

name: Sudden adult cardiac death syndrome (SADS)
formal: Sudden death in adults with no structural cause on autopsy, often attributed to inherited arrhythmia such as channelopathy, sometimes with overlap with epilepsy-related deaths.
simple: An unexpected death in a young or healthy adult with no clear cause found, often due to a heart rhythm disorder.
nN: sudden adult cardiac death syndrome sads
aN: sads | sudden adult cardiac death syndrome

name: Sudden unexpected death in epilepsy (SUDEP)
formal: Unexpected, non-traumatic death in a person with epilepsy, with or without a witnessed seizure, excluding status epilepticus; risk rises with frequent generalised tonic-clonic seizures, especially nocturnal.
simple: A sudden unexplained death in someone with epilepsy, mostly linked to poorly controlled seizures.
nN: sudden unexpected death in epilepsy sudep
aN: sudep | sudden unexpected death in epilepsy

name: Sudeck’s atrophy
formal: Complex regional pain syndrome with patchy bone demineralisation after trauma or immobilisation, causing pain, swelling, temperature and skin changes and stiffness in the affected limb.
simple: A painful condition after injury where a limb swells, changes colour and becomes stiff and weak.

name: Sulphite oxidase deficiency
formal: Autosomal recessive inborn error of sulphite metabolism with neonatal intractable seizures, lens dislocation and severe encephalopathy; sulphite accumulates, with raised urinary S-sulphocysteine.
simple: A rare inherited disorder where a toxic substance builds up and causes severe seizures and brain damage in babies.

name: Super-refractory status epilepticus
formal: Status epilepticus persisting or recurring for 24 hours or more despite anaesthetic therapy, requiring continuous intravenous anaesthetics; causes include autoimmune encephalitis and cryptogenic FIRES.
simple: A seizure emergency that continues despite strong anaesthetic drugs for a day or more.

name: Superior orbital fissure syndrome
formal: Lesion at the superior orbital fissure involving cranial nerves III, IV, V1 and VI, causing ophthalmoplegia, ptosis, proptosis and forehead numbness, from tumour, trauma, inflammation or infection.
simple: Damage at the gap behind the eye that causes eye movement paralysis, drooping eyelid and forehead numbness.

name: Supranuclear gaze palsy (SGP)
formal: Gaze paralysis from lesions above the oculomotor nuclei, as in progressive supranuclear palsy, with preserved reflex movements on oculocephalic testing and impaired voluntary vertical gaze.
simple: Difficulty voluntarily moving the eyes, especially looking up or down, caused by problems in the brain rather than the eye muscles.
aN: sgp | supranuclear gaze palsy

name: Supranuclear ophthalmoplegia
formal: Loss of voluntary eye movements with preserved reflex movements due to supranuclear lesions, typical of progressive supranuclear palsy and midbrain disease, often affecting vertical gaze first.
simple: Inability to move the eyes on command, though they still move reflexively, due to a brain rather than eye problem.

name: Supratentorial gliomas
formal: Primary brain tumours of the cerebral hemispheres, including astrocytoma, oligodendroglioma and glioblastoma in adults, presenting with seizures, headache or focal deficits.
simple: Tumours that grow from supporting brain cells in the upper brain, often causing seizures, headaches or weakness.

name: Surgical brachial plexopathies
formal: Iatrogenic injury to the brachial plexus from positioning, traction, retraction, sternotomy or regional anaesthesia, producing a patchy arm weakness and sensory deficit in the perioperative period.
simple: Damage to the nerve bundle supplying the arm that happens during or after an operation, causing arm weakness or numbness.
more: EMG and MRI or ultrasound localise the lesion. Most are neurapraxic and recover within weeks to months with physiotherapy; severe lesions may need nerve repair or transfer.

name: Susac’s syndrome
formal: Immune-mediated microangiopathy of brain, retina and cochlea causing encephalopathy, branch retinal artery occlusions and low-frequency hearing loss; callosal snowball lesions on MRI.
simple: A rare immune disease harming tiny vessels in the brain, eyes and ears, causing confusion, vision loss and deafness.
th: endotheliopathy จากภูมิคุ้มกันของหลอดเลือดเล็ก ทำให้ triad สมอง (encephalopathy, รอยโรคกลาง corpus callosum แบบ snowball) + branch retinal artery occlusion + หูดับความถี่ต่ำ พบในหญิงอายุ 20–40
tempoNote: Encephalopathy evolves over weeks; may run a monocyclic, polycyclic or chronic-continuous course over 1–5 years
feat: Headache, confusion, memory loss and behavioural change; sometimes ataxia or dysarthria
Branch retinal artery occlusions causing scotomas, often unnoticed by the patient
Low-to-mid frequency sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus and vertigo
The full triad is present at onset in only a minority
inv: MRI: central corpus callosum 'snowball' lesions and later 'holes', plus internal capsule 'string of pearls' and leptomeningeal enhancement
Fluorescein angiography: branch occlusions and arterial wall hyperfluorescence (Gass plaques)
Pure-tone audiometry: low-frequency loss
CSF: high protein, few cells; oligoclonal bands usually absent

case.story: Four weeks of severe headache and increasing forgetfulness; she now repeats questions and her colleagues report strange behaviour. She mentions ringing in the left ear and a grey patch in her vision.
case.exam: Disoriented, mild gait ataxia; fundoscopy shows a whitish arteriolar segment in the right eye.
case.tests: MRI: multiple round lesions in the middle of the corpus callosum; audiogram: left low-frequency hearing loss; CSF protein 140 mg/dL, 3 cells, no OCB.
case.q: Name the syndrome and the eye test that best supports it.
case.a: Susac’s syndrome; fluorescein angiography showing branch retinal artery occlusion and segmental wall leakage.

det.patho: An immune-mediated (likely CD8 T-cell driven) injury to the endothelium of precapillary arterioles in the brain, retina and cochlea causes microinfarcts. Anti-endothelial antibodies are found in some patients but are not specific. Women aged 20–40 are mainly affected.
det.clinical: Brain involvement produces a subacute encephalopathy with headache, cognitive and psychiatric change, and sometimes long-tract or cerebellar signs. Retinal occlusions cause patchy field defects and may be silent; hearing loss is often bilateral and permanent. Because the triad seldom appears together at first, many patients are initially labelled as MS, ADEM or a primary psychiatric illness.
det.diagnosis: The 2016 diagnostic criteria require evidence of involvement of brain (typical MRI), retina (BRAO or arterial wall hyperfluorescence on fluorescein angiography) and inner ear (audiometry); incomplete forms are labelled probable or possible. Central callosal lesions and spokes are highly characteristic. Every patient with suspected Susac’s needs fluorescein angiography and audiometry even without symptoms. CSF often shows raised protein without oligoclonal bands.
det.treatment: Early and sustained immunosuppression prevents irreversible deficits: intravenous methylprednisolone followed by oral steroids, combined with IVIG, and add mycophenolate, rituximab or cyclophosphamide in severe or relapsing disease. Treatment usually continues for at least 2 years with slow tapering guided by MRI, fluorescein angiography and audiometry. Aspirin is often added. MS disease-modifying drugs are ineffective.
det.prognosis: The disease is often self-limiting after a few years, but hearing loss, visual field defects and cognitive deficits can persist if treatment is delayed.
pearls: Corpus callosum lesions in the middle (not the underside) + hearing loss = look at the retina.
Order fluorescein angiography even when vision seems normal.
Interferons and natalizumab are not for Susac’s.
det.thd: Susac’s syndrome เป็นโรคภูมิคุ้มกันทำลายผนังหลอดเลือดแดงขนาดเล็กในสมอง จอตา และหูชั้นใน พบในหญิงวัยหนุ่มสาว ผู้ป่วยมีอาการสับสน ความจำเสีย ปวดศีรษะ ตามัวเป็นบางส่วนจาก branch retinal artery occlusion และหูดับความถี่ต่ำ MRI พบรอยโรคกลม ๆ ตรงกลาง corpus callosum วินิจฉัยด้วย MRI, fluorescein angiography และ audiogram รักษาด้วย steroid ร่วมกับ IVIG และยากดภูมิ

name: Sydenham’s chorea
formal: Post-streptococcal autoimmune chorea in childhood, with rapid irregular movements, hypotonia, emotional lability and association with rheumatic fever; usually self-limiting over months.
simple: Jerky involuntary movements in children after a strep throat infection, linked to rheumatic fever.
th: chorea ในเด็กหลังติดเชื้อ streptococcus กลุ่ม A เป็นส่วนหนึ่งของไข้รูมาติก มักมีอารมณ์แปรปรวน ต้องให้ penicillin ป้องกันระยะยาว
tempoNote: Begins weeks to months after a streptococcal throat infection, builds over days to weeks, usually remits within 6 months but can recur
feat: Chorea in a child aged 5–15, often worse on one side (hemichorea in some)
Motor impersistence: milkmaid grip and darting tongue
Hypotonia; clumsiness and dysarthria; occasionally severe weakness (chorea paralytica)
Emotional lability, obsessive-compulsive symptoms, anxiety or attention problems

case.story: Two months after a sore throat she drops things, cannot sit still and her handwriting is untidy; she cries easily. Mother thought she was being naughty.
case.exam: Continuous flowing movements of the face and limbs, worse on the right; milkmaid grip, darting tongue, mild hypotonia; soft apical pansystolic murmur.
case.tests: ASO 640 IU/mL, anti-DNase B high; echo: mild mitral regurgitation; ANA negative.
case.q: Besides treating the chorea, what long-term step is mandatory?
case.a: Sydenham chorea with rheumatic carditis — secondary prophylaxis with benzathine penicillin every 3–4 weeks for many years (into adulthood given carditis).

det.patho: Antibodies raised against group A streptococcal antigens cross-react with basal ganglia neurons (molecular mimicry), altering dopaminergic signalling. It is a major criterion of acute rheumatic fever and remains common in low- and middle-income settings. Girls are affected more than boys, especially after puberty.
det.clinical: Chorea appears after a latent period of 1–6 months, often when other rheumatic signs have faded. Neuropsychiatric symptoms (emotional lability, OCD features, ADHD-like behaviour) can precede or outlast the movements. Most episodes last weeks to months; recurrences occur in a sizeable minority, sometimes triggered by pregnancy (chorea gravidarum) or oral contraceptives.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical within the Jones criteria; chorea alone is enough for rheumatic fever once other causes are excluded, and streptococcal serology is not mandatory because of the long latency. Always perform echocardiography because subclinical carditis is common. Exclude SLE, antiphospholipid syndrome, hyperthyroidism, drugs, Wilson disease and Huntington disease in atypical cases.
det.treatment: Give a course of penicillin to eradicate streptococci and start long-term secondary prophylaxis with benzathine penicillin. Mild chorea may need no symptomatic drugs; for disabling chorea use valproate, carbamazepine or a low-dose dopamine blocker (risperidone or haloperidol). Steroids (prednisolone) or IVIG are used for severe or refractory chorea. Address school and psychological needs.
det.prognosis: Usually resolves within 6–12 months, but recurrence and persistent neuropsychiatric symptoms are common; prognosis is mostly determined by heart involvement.
pearls: Chorea in a child: look for the heart — always order an echocardiogram.
Milkmaid grip and darting tongue show motor impersistence.
Secondary penicillin prophylaxis is as important as treating the movements.
