det.patho: Atheroma forms at the carotid bifurcation and proximal ICA where flow separation and low shear stress occur. Strokes usually result from artery-to-artery embolism of thrombus or plaque debris from an unstable, ulcerated or haemorrhagic plaque, and less often from low flow beyond a tight stenosis with poor collaterals. Risk factors are age, male sex, smoking, hypertension, diabetes and dyslipidaemia; extracranial carotid disease is less frequent in East and South-East Asians than intracranial atherosclerosis, but still important.
det.clinical: A stenosis is called symptomatic when ipsilateral retinal or hemispheric TIA or non-disabling stroke occurred within the preceding 6 months. Clinical features include amaurosis fugax, cortical hand weakness, aphasia or neglect. Limb-shaking TIAs — brief jerky movements of a contralateral limb on standing — signal haemodynamic compromise. Recurrence risk is highest in the first 48 h to 2 weeks (perhaps 10–20% without treatment), so these patients need fast-track assessment.
det.diagnosis: Duplex ultrasound is the usual first test; a second modality (CTA or contrast-enhanced MRA) should confirm the degree before intervention. Measure stenosis by NASCET (narrowest lumen compared with normal distal ICA). Near-occlusion with distal collapse behaves differently and gains little from surgery. Plaque features such as intraplaque haemorrhage on MRI or microembolic signals on transcranial Doppler identify higher risk. Always look for alternative sources (AF, small vessel disease) because a coexisting stenosis may be incidental.
det.treatment: For 70–99% symptomatic stenosis, carotid endarterectomy markedly reduces stroke risk and should be performed within 2 weeks of the event if the surgical complication rate is low; for 50–69% the benefit is smaller and greatest in men, older patients and hemispheric events. Below 50%, intervention is harmful. Carotid stenting is an alternative, with outcomes closer to surgery in patients under about 70, those with hostile necks (radiation, restenosis) or high surgical risk. All patients need antiplatelet therapy (short dual therapy around the event), high-intensity statin with LDL target < 70 mg/dL (or lower), BP control and smoking cessation.
det.prognosis: With timely revascularisation and medical therapy, the subsequent annual stroke risk falls to roughly that of asymptomatic disease; delay forfeits much of the benefit.
pearls: The benefit of endarterectomy decays fast — aim for surgery within 14 days of the index event.
Use NASCET measurement; 70–99% gains most, near-occlusion and < 50% do not benefit.
Limb-shaking TIA is a haemodynamic warning of a critical carotid stenosis, not a seizure.

name: Symptomatic choreic syndromes
formal: Chorea due to an underlying cause such as drugs, stroke, autoimmune disease or metabolic disorders rather than a primary hereditary chorea.
simple: Jerky involuntary movements caused by another illness, drug or brain injury rather than inherited disease.

name: Symptomatic generalized myoclonus
formal: Myoclonus affecting the body widely, resulting from diffuse brain disorder such as metabolic, toxic, post-hypoxic or neurodegenerative encephalopathy.
simple: Widespread sudden muscle jerks caused by a brain problem such as poisoning, low oxygen or metabolic disease.

name: Symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage (sICH)
formal: Haemorrhagic transformation of ischaemic infarct or thrombolysis-related bleed with neurological worsening, defined by haematoma and clinical deterioration within about 24-36 hours of treatment.
simple: A bleed in the brain after a stroke or clot-busting treatment that makes symptoms worse.
aN: sich | symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage

name: Symptomatic myoclonus
formal: Myoclonus caused by an identifiable underlying disorder such as metabolic, post-anoxic, toxic or structural disease rather than essential or epileptic.
simple: Sudden muscle jerks caused by another illness such as organ failure, brain injury or medication.

name: Symptomatic palatal tremor
formal: Rhythmic palatal movements due to a lesion in the Guillain-Mollaret triangle, often with inferior olive hypertrophy after brainstem stroke, with ear clicking and sometimes ocular oscillation.
simple: Rhythmic movements of the soft palate at the back of the mouth after brainstem damage, sometimes causing ear clicking.

name: Symptomatic startle syndromes
formal: Exaggerated startle responses secondary to brainstem or diffuse brain lesions or metabolic disease, distinct from hereditary hyperekplexia.
simple: Excessive jumping or stiffening when startled, caused by brain injury or illness.

name: Symptomatic tremors
formal: Tremors resulting from identifiable disease such as stroke, multiple sclerosis, drugs or metabolic causes, as opposed to essential tremor.
simple: Shaking caused by another disease, injury or drug rather than inherited or essential tremor.

name: Synaptic CMS
formal: Group of congenital myasthenic syndromes due to defects in synaptic proteins such as acetylcholinesterase, rapsyn or agrin pathway, causing fatigable weakness from infancy.
simple: Inherited conditions of the nerve-muscle junction causing weakness that worsens with activity, starting in early life.

name: Synaptic disorders related to CMS
formal: Congenital myasthenic syndromes from presynaptic, synaptic basal lamina or postsynaptic defects, with fatigable weakness from infancy.
simple: Inherited disorders where signal passing at the nerve-muscle junction is faulty.
more: Genetic panel; treatments tailored, e.g. pyridostigmine, 3,4-DAP, salbutamol; avoid cholinesterase inhibitors in COLQ and DOK7.

name: Syndrome (CANVAS)
formal: Cerebellar ataxia with neuropathy and vestibular areflexia syndrome from biallelic RFC1 expansion, presenting with imbalance, sensory neuronopathy and bilateral vestibular loss, with chronic cough often.
simple: A late-onset inherited balance disorder with unsteady walking, numb feet and failing inner-ear function.
more: Diagnose by RFC1 biallelic AAGGG repeat expansion on repeat-primed PCR or Southern blot, with cerebellar vermis atrophy on MRI and absent sensory potentials on NCS. Late-onset, autosomal recessive; no disease-modifying therapy, so give rehabilitation.

name: Syndrome (ICANS)
formal: Immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome after CAR-T or bispecific antibody therapy, with confusion, aphasia, seizures or cerebral oedema, linked to cytokine release.
simple: Confusion, speech trouble or seizures that can follow certain immune cell cancer treatments.

formal: Infection by Treponema pallidum that can invade the nervous system, causing meningitis, meningovascular disease, tabes dorsalis and general paresis; diagnosed by serology and treated with penicillin.

name: Systemic vasculitis
formal: Inflammation of blood vessels of various sizes, which may involve CNS and peripheral nerves causing stroke, mononeuritis multiplex or encephalopathy.
simple: Inflammation of blood vessel walls throughout the body, which can damage the brain and nerves.

name: Takayasu’s arteritis (pulseless disease)
formal: Large-vessel granulomatous arteritis of the aorta and branches in young women, causing absent pulses, arm claudication, dizziness and stroke from stenosis.
simple: Inflammation of the body's main arteries in young women that narrows them, causing weak pulses, dizziness and strokes.

name: Takayasu’s disease
formal: Large-vessel granulomatous arteritis affecting the aorta and its branches, producing stenosis, aneurysm and reduced pulses with ischaemic cerebral or ocular symptoms.

name: Tangier disease
formal: Autosomal recessive ABCA1 disorder with near-absent HDL, orange tonsils and recurrent or relapsing multifocal sensorimotor neuropathy.
simple: An inherited disease with very low HDL cholesterol, enlarged orange tonsils and nerve problems.
more: ABCA1 genetics and lipid profile; neuropathy is often multifocal or syringomyelia-like; supportive therapy.

name: Tardive akathisia
formal: Persistent inner restlessness with an urge to move after long-term dopamine blocker exposure, often with dyskinesia; difficult to treat.
simple: A distressing feeling of needing to keep moving that develops after prolonged use of certain psychiatric medicines.

name: Tardive dyskinesia (TD)
formal: Late-onset involuntary orofacial and limb movements after prolonged dopamine receptor blocker exposure, treated with VMAT2 inhibitors or drug withdrawal.
simple: Involuntary mouth and body movements that develop after long use of certain antipsychotic drugs.
more: Diagnosis by exposure history; risk factors include age, female sex and duration; switch to clozapine or quetiapine when needed. Valbenazine and deutetrabenazine are FDA-approved; prevent with the lowest dose of antipsychotic, and monitor with AIMS.

Patterned, stereotyped movements; patients are often unaware of them
Trunk rocking, pelvic thrusting, finger piano-playing or respiratory dyskinesia
Often unmasked or worsened when the causative drug is reduced or stopped

case.who: 58-year-old woman from Nakhon Si Thammarat with schizophrenia
case.story: On haloperidol for 6 years; her daughter notices she keeps chewing and pushing out her tongue, worse since the dose was reduced last month.
case.exam: Continuous orobuccolingual movements, finger piano-playing, mild bradykinesia; she can stop the tongue movements briefly when asked.
case.tests: Glucose, TSH normal; AIMS score 18.

det.patho: Chronic D2-receptor blockade is thought to cause postsynaptic dopamine receptor supersensitivity, maladaptive striatal plasticity and possibly oxidative injury. Risk rises with older age, female sex, diabetes, mood disorders, cumulative dose and first-generation agents, though second-generation antipsychotics also cause it. Metoclopramide is an important non-psychiatric culprit.
det.clinical: Classic TD is a rhythmic, stereotyped orobuccolingual dyskinesia, but the tardive spectrum also includes dystonia (often retrocollis), akathisia, myoclonus, tics and tremor. Symptoms commonly emerge on dose reduction (withdrawal-emergent) and may be masked by increasing the dose. Severe cases impair eating, speech, breathing and social life.
det.diagnosis: Requires at least a few months of dopamine-blocker exposure (shorter in the elderly) with onset during or within weeks of stopping. Use AIMS at baseline and regularly. Exclude Huntington disease, Wilson disease, chorea from systemic causes and edentulous dyskinesia. Tardive dystonia and akathisia should be recognised because their treatment differs.
det.treatment: Prevent by using the lowest effective dose, avoiding long metoclopramide courses and monitoring. Once present, reassess the need for the drug; switching to clozapine or quetiapine may help. VMAT2 inhibitors (valbenazine, deutetrabenazine, tetrabenazine) have the best evidence. Clonazepam and ginkgo biloba have weaker support; anticholinergics may worsen TD. Botulinum toxin for focal tardive dystonia, and GPi DBS for severe refractory cases.
det.prognosis: Many cases persist for years even after the drug is stopped; remission is more likely in young patients and when detected early.
pearls: Ask about metoclopramide and flunarizine — not only antipsychotics.
Anticholinergics help acute dystonia and parkinsonism but can worsen TD.
VMAT2 inhibitors are the specific evidence-based treatment.

name: Tardive dystonia
formal: Sustained abnormal postures and twisting after chronic dopamine antagonist exposure, often involving neck, trunk or face, and persistent after withdrawal.

name: Tardive myoclonus
formal: Brief, shock-like involuntary jerks arising after prolonged exposure to dopamine blockers, forming part of tardive syndromes.
simple: Sudden muscle jerks that appear after long use of certain antipsychotic medicines.

name: Tardive parkinsonism
formal: Parkinsonism persisting or emerging late after prolonged neuroleptic exposure, sometimes persisting after withdrawal and needing differentiation from Parkinson disease.
simple: Slowness and stiffness like Parkinson disease that persist after long-term use of certain psychiatric drugs.

name: Tardive stereotypies
formal: Repetitive, purposeless, stereotyped movements such as rocking or lip smacking emerging after chronic dopamine blocker exposure.
simple: Repetitive purposeless movements, such as lip smacking or rocking, after long-term use of some psychiatric drugs.

name: Tardive syndromes
formal: Group of delayed-onset movement disorders from dopamine receptor blockers, including dyskinesia, dystonia, akathisia, tremor, myoclonus and stereotypies.
simple: A set of movement problems that appear after long-term use of certain psychiatric or stomach medicines.

name: Tardive tremor
formal: Postural or action tremor appearing late after prolonged dopamine receptor antagonist therapy.
simple: Shaking that develops after long use of certain psychiatric drugs.
more: Distinguish from Parkinson tremor by history of neuroleptic exposure and by DAT-SPECT being normal. Management is to reduce or stop the offending drug and consider propranolol or VMAT2 inhibitors.

name: Tarui disease
formal: Glycogen storage disease type VII, phosphofructokinase deficiency (PFKM), with exercise intolerance, cramps, myoglobinuria and compensated haemolysis; avoidance of high-carbohydrate load before exercise.
simple: An inherited muscle energy disorder causing cramps, weakness and dark urine after intense exercise.
more: Diagnosis by muscle biopsy enzyme studies and genetic testing. Avoid strenuous exercise and high carbohydrate meals before activity; a ketogenic diet may help.

name: Task-specific tremor
formal: Tremor appearing only during a specific skilled task such as writing, a form of action tremor often with dystonic features.
simple: Shaking of the hand that only occurs when doing a particular task such as writing.

name: Tauopathies
formal: Neurodegenerative disorders characterised by tau protein accumulation, including Alzheimer disease, progressive supranuclear palsy, corticobasal degeneration and frontotemporal dementias.
simple: Brain diseases in which an abnormal protein called tau builds up, causing memory, movement or behaviour problems.
more: Diagnosis uses MRI patterns, FDG-PET, CSF tau and amyloid, and tau-PET research; pathology confirms tau isoforms (3R, 4R, or both). Currently no disease-modifying therapy exists, though anti-tau trials are in progress; the genes MAPT and GRN are relevant.

name: Tay–Sachs disease
formal: Autosomal recessive HEXA deficiency causing GM2 ganglioside storage; the infantile form brings regression, startle and a cherry-red spot, whereas late-onset (juvenile or adult) disease presents with cerebellar ataxia, lower motor neuron weakness and psychiatric illness.
simple: An inherited fat-storage disease that in babies causes loss of skills, but in teenagers or adults causes unsteadiness, leg weakness and mental health problems.

Cerebellar ataxia and halting, stuttering dysarthria
Psychosis, mood disorder or cognitive decline in a third or more
Tremor or dystonia; reflexes may be brisk or reduced
Infantile form: exaggerated startle, macular cherry-red spot, macrocephaly and regression

case.story: Since his late teens he struggles to climb stairs; for two years his speech has become hesitant and he walks unsteadily. Treated for depression last year.
case.exam: Bilateral quadriceps wasting with fasciculations, mild finger–nose ataxia, broad gait, stammering dysarthria, preserved sensation.
case.tests: CK mildly raised; EMG chronic denervation; MRI striking cerebellar atrophy; leucocyte hexosaminidase A 4% of normal.
case.q: Which lysosomal disorder unites the motor neuron, cerebellar and psychiatric features?
case.a: Late-onset GM2 gangliosidosis (adult Tay–Sachs, HEXA).

det.patho: Hexosaminidase A, made of an alpha subunit (HEXA) and a beta subunit (HEXB), degrades GM2 ganglioside within lysosomes. Null variants cause the infantile disease; variants leaving a few percent of activity cause juvenile or adult forms in which cerebellar Purkinje cells and spinal motor neurons are most affected. Founder variants occur in Ashkenazi Jewish and other groups, but cases are seen worldwide.
det.clinical: Late-onset Tay–Sachs usually begins in the teens or twenties with proximal leg weakness and wasting that mimics a motor neuron disease, then cerebellar ataxia and a characteristic hesitant, stuttering speech. Psychiatric presentations (psychosis, bipolar disorder, depression) are common and may come first. Infantile disease, by contrast, causes loss of milestones from about 6 months, startle to sound, seizures, blindness and death in early childhood.
det.diagnosis: Measure hexosaminidase A (and total hexosaminidase to detect Sandhoff disease) in any young adult with LMN weakness plus cerebellar atrophy or psychiatric illness. Confirm with gene testing. EMG shows chronic denervation, and MRI shows disproportionate cerebellar atrophy.
det.treatment: Treatment is supportive; substrate reduction with miglustat has not shown clear benefit, and gene therapy is in trials. Some antipsychotics (notably haloperidol and other phenothiazine-type drugs) and tricyclics have been reported to worsen neurology; mood stabilisers such as lithium are often preferred. Provide physiotherapy, speech therapy and genetic counselling, including carrier testing.
det.prognosis: Late-onset disease is slowly progressive with many decades of survival; infantile disease is usually fatal by 3–5 years.
pearls: Young adult with quadriceps wasting, stuttering speech and cerebellar atrophy: check hexosaminidase A.
Psychosis may precede motor signs; choose psychiatric drugs carefully.
Sandhoff disease (HEXB) gives a similar adult picture with low total hexosaminidase.

name: Temporal arteritis
formal: Giant cell arteritis: granulomatous vasculitis of cranial arteries in people over 50, with headache, jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, visual loss risk and raised ESR; treated with steroids.
simple: Inflammation of arteries at the temples in older people, causing headache and jaw pain and risking sudden blindness.

name: Temporal lobe epilepsy
formal: Focal epilepsy from mesial or lateral temporal onset, commonly hippocampal sclerosis, with epigastric aura, déjà vu, automatisms and impaired awareness; may need surgery.
simple: Seizures starting in the temple area of the brain, often with odd feelings, staring and repetitive movements.
th: ลมชักจากสมองกลีบขมับ — มีลางบอกเหตุแบบรู้สึกคุ้นเคยหรือจุกท้อง แล้วเหม่อ ทำปากขมุบขมิบ
feat: Aura: rising epigastric sensation, déjà vu, fear, olfactory hallucination
Behavioural arrest, oral and manual automatisms, dystonic contralateral hand
Post-ictal confusion; dysphasia if dominant hemisphere
Hippocampal sclerosis often after childhood febrile seizures
inv: MRI epilepsy protocol (hippocampal sclerosis)
EEG/video-EEG; surgical work-up if drug resistant

case.story: Episodes beginning with a rising feeling in his stomach and intense familiarity, then he stares and smacks his lips for a minute and cannot recall it.
case.exam: Normal.
case.tests: MRI: right hippocampal atrophy with T2 hyperintensity.
case.q: If two appropriate drugs fail, what should be offered?
case.a: Referral for epilepsy surgery evaluation — drug-resistant mesial TLE has good surgical outcomes.

ddx.pt: Postural prodrome, brief, quick recovery without confusion
Single prolonged amnesic episode with retained awareness of self

aN: tle | mesial temporal lobe epilepsy | mtle | complex partial seizures | focal impaired awareness seizures

det.patho: Mesial temporal lobe epilepsy most often stems from hippocampal sclerosis — neuronal loss and gliosis in CA1 and CA3 — frequently following prolonged febrile seizures or other early insults. Other causes include low-grade tumours, cavernomas, focal cortical dysplasia, post-encephalitic damage and autoimmune encephalitis. It is the commonest drug-resistant focal epilepsy in adults.
det.clinical: Seizures often start with an aura that is in fact a focal aware seizure: rising epigastric sensation, déjà vu or jamais vu, fear, or an unpleasant smell or taste. These may evolve into impaired awareness with motionless staring, lip-smacking, chewing and fumbling hand automatisms, and contralateral dystonic arm posturing that helps lateralise. Seizures last 1–2 minutes and are followed by confusion; dominant-side onset may leave temporary language difficulty. Some seizures spread to bilateral tonic-clonic attacks. Memory complaints and mood disorders are common comorbidities.
det.diagnosis: A detailed witness account is central. MRI with an epilepsy protocol (thin coronal T2/FLAIR perpendicular to the hippocampus) detects hippocampal sclerosis and other lesions. Routine EEG may show anterior temporal spikes, but a normal EEG between seizures never rules it out; video-EEG telemetry captures typical events. In drug-resistant cases, pre-surgical evaluation adds neuropsychology, PET, functional MRI and sometimes intracranial EEG. New-onset adult TLE warrants consideration of autoimmune (e.g. LGI1) or neoplastic causes.
det.treatment: Focal-onset seizures respond to drugs such as lamotrigine, levetiracetam, carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, lacosamide or zonisamide; choice depends on age, sex, comorbidity and interactions. Drug resistance is defined as failure of two tolerated, appropriately chosen drugs; at that point refer for surgical evaluation. Anterior temporal lobectomy or selective amygdalohippocampectomy offers seizure freedom to about two-thirds of suitable patients; laser ablation, vagus nerve stimulation, responsive neurostimulation or deep brain stimulation are alternatives.
det.prognosis: About a third of patients remain drug-resistant; surgery in well-selected hippocampal sclerosis yields high seizure freedom and better quality of life.
pearls: Dystonic posturing of one hand usually points to seizure onset in the opposite temporal lobe.
Two failed drugs means refer for surgery — do not keep adding a third and fourth for years.
Late-onset TLE with memory loss and hyponatraemia: check LGI1 antibodies.

name: Tension-type headache (TTH)
formal: Most common primary headache with bilateral pressing, non-pulsatile mild to moderate pain lasting hours, without nausea or aura, and not worsened by activity.
simple: A common headache feeling like a tight band around the head, usually mild and without nausea.
aN: tth | tension type headache

name: Terminal tremor
formal: Tremor that increases in amplitude as the limb approaches a target, typical of cerebellar outflow lesions.
simple: Shaking that gets worse as the hand reaches for a target, caused by cerebellar damage.

name: Terson’s syndrome
formal: Vitreous haemorrhage associated with subarachnoid haemorrhage or raised intracranial pressure, causing visual loss.
simple: Bleeding in the eye jelly that occurs with brain bleeds, causing blurred vision.

name: Thalamocortical seizures
formal: Generalised epileptic seizures arising from abnormal thalamocortical oscillation, as in absence epilepsy with spike-wave discharges.
simple: Seizures caused by abnormal electrical loops between the thalamus and cortex, such as brief staring spells.

name: Thallium poisoning
formal: Heavy metal poisoning with painful ascending neuropathy, alopecia, gastrointestinal upset and encephalopathy.
simple: A poisoning causing painful nerve damage, hair loss and stomach upset.

name: Thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency
formal: Thiamine deficiency causing Wernicke encephalopathy, Korsakoff syndrome and beriberi, typically in alcohol misuse or malnutrition.
simple: Low vitamin B1 that can cause confusion, eye movement problems, poor balance and nerve damage.
more: Treat suspected Wernicke encephalopathy immediately with IV thiamine before glucose; diagnosis is clinical with ophthalmoplegia, ataxia and confusion; MRI shows mammillary body and periaqueductal change. Measure red cell transketolase or whole-blood thiamine.
aN: vitamin b1 | thiamine deficiency

name: Thioridazine akathisia
formal: Akathisia caused by the antipsychotic thioridazine, with inner restlessness and inability to stay still.
simple: A feeling of restlessness and need to move caused by a particular antipsychotic medicine.

name: Thomsen’s disease
formal: Autosomal dominant myotonia congenita from CLCN1 mutations with muscle stiffness after rest that eases with exercise, with muscle hypertrophy.
simple: An inherited condition where muscles stay stiff after rest but loosen with repeated movement.

name: Thoracic arteriovenous malformations (AVMs)
formal: Spinal vascular malformations in the thoracic region causing progressive myelopathy, venous congestion or haemorrhage.
simple: Abnormal tangles of blood vessels in the mid spine that can cause leg weakness and numbness.
aN: avms | thoracic arteriovenous malformations

name: Thoracic radiculopathies
formal: Dysfunction of thoracic nerve roots, causing band-like trunk pain and sensory loss in a dermatomal pattern; causes include disc or spondylotic compression, herpes zoster, diabetes and tumour.
simple: A pinched or irritated nerve at chest level that causes belt-like pain or numbness around the ribs or abdomen.
more: MRI of the thoracic spine and sometimes EMG guide diagnosis. Treat the cause (decompression, antivirals, glycaemic control) plus neuropathic pain drugs; diabetic forms often improve over months.

name: Thoracic spine degenerative disease
formal: Wear-related degeneration of thoracic discs and joints, rarely causing myelopathy or radiculopathy with band-like pain.
simple: Age-related wear in the mid back that can sometimes press on the spinal cord or nerves.

name: Thoracic spine disease
formal: Disorders of the thoracic spine such as degenerative disease, tumour or infection causing myelopathy and radicular pain.
simple: Problems in the middle of the spine that can compress the spinal cord or nerve roots.

name: Thought disorder
formal: Disorganised thinking evident as derailed, tangential or incoherent speech, a core feature of schizophrenia and some organic brain states.
simple: Muddled, jumbled thinking that makes speech hard to follow.

name: Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura
formal: Thrombotic microangiopathy from ADAMTS13 deficiency causing haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia, fever, renal dysfunction and fluctuating neurological deficits.
simple: A blood clotting disorder causing low platelets and tiny clots that can cause confusion, stroke-like symptoms and kidney problems.

name: Thunderclap headache
formal: Abrupt severe headache reaching maximum intensity within a minute, requiring exclusion of subarachnoid haemorrhage, RCVS, dissection and venous thrombosis.
simple: A sudden extremely severe headache that peaks within a minute and needs urgent investigation.

name: Thymoma
formal: Tumour of the thymus often associated with myasthenia gravis, requiring surgical removal; also linked to red cell aplasia and hypogammaglobulinaemia.
simple: A growth in the thymus gland in the chest, often linked with a muscle weakness disease.

name: Thymoma, myasthenia gravis
formal: Thymoma associated with myasthenia gravis, producing fatigable weakness due to acetylcholine receptor antibodies; thymectomy is recommended.
simple: A thymus gland tumour that frequently occurs with myasthenia gravis, a condition causing tiring muscle weakness.
aN: thymoma | myasthenia gravis

name: Thyroid disorders
formal: Over- or underactive thyroid states that affect nerve and muscle: thyrotoxic myopathy and periodic paralysis, hypothyroid myopathy with slow reflexes, neuropathy, carpal tunnel and ataxia.
simple: Problems with the thyroid gland that can cause muscle weakness, cramps, numbness or slowed reflexes.
more: Diagnosed with thyroid function tests and raised CK in hypothyroid myopathy. Correcting the hormone level usually reverses the neuromuscular problems, though recovery can take months.

name: Thyrotoxic myopathy
formal: Proximal muscle weakness and wasting in hyperthyroidism, often with normal CK, and thyrotoxic periodic paralysis in some patients.
simple: Muscle weakness and wasting caused by an overactive thyroid.
more: Treat hyperthyroidism, and give propranolol; strength usually recovers in weeks.

name: Thyrotoxic periodic paralysis
formal: Hypokalaemic periodic paralysis triggered by hyperthyroidism, with episodic proximal weakness, mainly in Asian men.
simple: Episodes of sudden muscle weakness in people with an overactive thyroid, due to low potassium shifts.
more: Check low potassium during attacks with low urinary potassium excretion; thyroid function is abnormal and CACNA1S is usually normal. Treat attacks with cautious oral potassium, avoid rebound hyperkalaemia, give propranolol, and cure the hyperthyroidism.

name: Thyrotoxicosis chorea
formal: Chorea resulting from hyperthyroidism, typically resolving when thyroid function is normalised.
simple: Jerky involuntary movements caused by an overactive thyroid.

name: Tic convulsif
formal: Hemifacial spasm sometimes combined with trigeminal neuralgia, producing painful facial spasms.
simple: Painful twitching of one side of the face combined with facial nerve pain.

name: Tic disorders
formal: Group of neurodevelopmental conditions with sudden repetitive movements or vocalisations, including Tourette syndrome and persistent motor or vocal tic disorders.
simple: Conditions causing sudden repeated movements or sounds that are hard to control.
more: Diagnosis is clinical (DSM-5): onset before 18 years, with motor and vocal tics for more than a year in Tourette. Treat with behavioural therapy (CBIT), alpha-2 agonists or antipsychotics, and botulinum toxin; many improve in adolescence.

name: Tic douloureux
formal: Paroxysmal severe stabbing pain in the trigeminal distribution, usually vascular compression of the nerve root, treated with carbamazepine.
simple: Older name for trigeminal neuralgia: sudden electric-shock facial pain.

name: Tick paralysis
formal: Acute ascending flaccid paralysis caused by a neurotoxin from feeding engorged ticks, producing areflexia and ataxia through blocked neuromuscular or axonal conduction.
simple: Weakness spreading up the body from a tick bite, which usually goes away once the tick is found and removed.
more: Diagnosis is clinical, by finding the tick, often on the scalp. Nerve studies may show low motor amplitudes. Prompt tick removal leads to recovery within hours to days; untreated cases can cause respiratory failure.

name: Tickborne disease
formal: Infections transmitted by ticks with neurological involvement, such as Lyme neuroborreliosis, tick-borne encephalitis and Rocky Mountain spotted fever.
simple: Infections spread by tick bites that can sometimes affect the brain and nerves.

name: Tics
formal: Brief, stereotyped, suppressible movements or vocalisations preceded by premonitory urge, characteristic of Tourette syndrome.
simple: Sudden repeated movements or sounds that a person feels a build-up urge to make.

name: Tilted optic disc
formal: Congenital anomaly where the optic disc appears oblique, causing a bitemporal visual field defect that mimics chiasmal disease.
simple: A harmless birth variation in the shape of the optic nerve head that can mimic a visual field loss.

name: Tin neurotoxicity
formal: Neurotoxicity of organotin compounds causing headache, cerebral oedema, seizures and cognitive changes.
simple: Brain damage from poisoning with tin-containing chemicals.

name: Tocopherol (vitamin E) deficiency
formal: Vitamin E deficiency causing spinocerebellar ataxia, neuropathy and retinopathy, from malabsorption or ataxia with vitamin E deficiency (TTPA gene).
simple: Low vitamin E causing poor balance, nerve damage and sometimes vision problems.
aN: vitamin e | tocopherol deficiency

name: Todd’s paralysis
formal: Transient focal weakness after a seizure, lasting minutes to hours, and resolving spontaneously.
simple: Temporary weakness of a limb after a seizure that usually clears within hours.

name: Tolosa–Hunt syndrome
formal: Painful ophthalmoplegia from idiopathic granulomatous inflammation of the cavernous sinus or orbital apex, responsive to steroids.
simple: Painful inflammation behind the eye causing eye movement problems that responds quickly to steroids.

name: Tongue protrusion dystonia
formal: Focal oromandibular dystonia where the tongue pushes involuntarily out of the mouth, often task-specific or tardive.
simple: Involuntary pushing of the tongue out of the mouth.

name: Tongue tremor
formal: Rhythmic tongue movement from essential tremor, parkinsonism or palatal tremor.
simple: Shaking of the tongue.

name: Tonic limb and axial seizures
formal: Seizures with simultaneous tonic stiffening of axial and limb muscles, as in Lennox-Gastaut syndrome.
simple: Seizures where the trunk and limbs stiffen suddenly.

name: Tonic seizures
formal: Seizures with sustained muscle contraction and stiffening, often in children with diffuse brain disease.
simple: Seizures in which muscles stiffen and the body becomes rigid.

name: Tonic spasms
formal: Brief painful contractions of muscle, as in multiple sclerosis (paroxysmal tonic spasms) or stiff-person syndrome.
simple: Short, painful muscle tightening episodes, often seen in multiple sclerosis.

name: Tonic–clonic seizure
formal: Generalised seizure with tonic stiffening followed by rhythmic clonic jerking and postictal state.
simple: A seizure with stiffening followed by shaking and then drowsiness.

name: Tonic–clonic status
formal: Prolonged or repeated generalised tonic-clonic seizures without recovery between them, a medical emergency requiring benzodiazepines and antiseizure drugs.
simple: A seizure emergency with prolonged convulsions that requires urgent drug treatment.

name: Torsion dystonia
formal: Generalised dystonia, typically early onset (DYT1), with sustained twisting postures and torsion of the limbs and trunk.
simple: Twisting, sustained abnormal body postures from muscle contractions, often starting in childhood.

name: Touch epilepsy
formal: Reflex epilepsy in which seizures are provoked by tactile stimuli.
simple: Seizures triggered by being touched.

name: Tourette’s syndrome
formal: Chronic tic disorder with multiple motor and one or more vocal tics for over a year, onset in childhood, often with ADHD or OCD.
simple: A condition with repeated movement and sound tics, starting in childhood.
th: tic ทั้งการเคลื่อนไหวและเสียงหลายแบบ เริ่มก่อนอายุ 18 ปี เป็นนานกว่า 1 ปี มักมี ADHD หรือ OCD ร่วม และดีขึ้นเมื่อโตเป็นผู้ใหญ่
tempoNote: Onset around 5–7 years, peak severity about 10–12, waxing and waning; often lessens by adulthood
feat: Multiple motor tics (blinking, grimacing, shoulder shrug) and at least one vocal tic (sniffing, throat clearing, words)
Premonitory urge relieved by the tic; tics can be briefly suppressed with rebound later
Waxing and waning course with changing tic repertoire; worse with stress, excitement or fatigue
Frequent comorbid ADHD, OCD, anxiety and learning or behaviour difficulties
Coprolalia is uncommon (minority of patients)

Screen for ADHD, OCD, anxiety, depression and school problems
EEG only if episodes could be seizures; MRI or labs only if atypical (late onset, regression, other neurological signs)

case.story: Two years of eye blinking, then head jerks and repeated throat clearing; he says he feels an itch in the throat that he has to release. Teachers note poor attention.
case.exam: Several brief eye-blinking and neck-jerk tics during the visit, suppressible when asked; neurological examination otherwise normal.
case.tests: None needed; Conners rating scale suggests ADHD.
case.q: What is the first-line approach for tics that bother him at school?
case.a: Tourette syndrome: education plus behavioural therapy (CBIT/habit reversal); if medication is needed, an alpha-2 agonist such as clonidine or guanfacine also helps the ADHD.

det.patho: Tourette syndrome is a polygenic neurodevelopmental disorder with strong heritability, involving cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical circuits and dopaminergic hyperactivity. Interneuron loss in the striatum has been described. It is about three to four times more common in boys and affects up to roughly 1% of school-aged children.
det.clinical: Simple motor tics in the face usually appear first, followed by vocal tics a year or two later. Complex tics include touching, echolalia and copropraxia. Comorbidities such as ADHD and OCD frequently cause more impairment than the tics themselves. Severity peaks in early adolescence and declines in most by adulthood, though a minority have persistent or severe tics, including self-injurious ones.
det.diagnosis: DSM-5 requires multiple motor tics and at least one vocal tic (not necessarily concurrently) for over a year, onset before 18, and no other cause. Distinguish tics from chorea, myoclonus, dystonia, stereotypies and functional tics. Investigations are reserved for atypical features such as onset in adulthood, rapid change or neurological deficit.
det.treatment: Education and reassurance suffice for many. Comprehensive Behavioural Intervention for Tics is first-line when treatment is needed. Medications include alpha-2 agonists, then aripiprazole or other dopamine blockers and VMAT2 inhibitors for severe tics; topiramate is an option. Botulinum toxin helps focal troublesome tics and DBS is reserved for severe refractory adults. Treat ADHD and OCD in their own right.
det.prognosis: Most children improve markedly by early adulthood; the comorbidities often determine long-term outcome.
pearls: Premonitory urge plus brief suppressibility identifies a tic.
Coprolalia is not required; most patients never have it.
Ask about ADHD and OCD — they often drive the disability.

name: Toxic and metabolic encephalopathy
formal: Diffuse brain dysfunction from systemic metabolic derangement or toxins, causing confusion, asterixis, tremor, myoclonus and seizures.
simple: Confusion and brain dysfunction caused by poisons or body chemistry problems.

name: Toxic and nutritional neuropathies
formal: Neuropathies caused by toxins such as alcohol, solvents, metals or drugs and nutritional deficits such as B vitamins, causing distal sensory-motor loss.
simple: Nerve damage from poisons or poor nutrition.

name: Toxic and nutritional optic neuropathies
formal: Optic nerve damage caused by toxins, such as methanol or ethambutol, and deficiencies, leading to central visual loss and colour impairment.
simple: Vision loss from poisoning or poor nutrition that damages the optic nerves.

name: Toxic cooking oil-induced myoclonus
formal: Myoclonus from contaminated cooking oil poisoning, historically reported in outbreaks.
simple: Muscle jerks caused by eating poisoned cooking oil.

name: Toxic encephalopathies
formal: Diffuse brain dysfunction from exogenous toxins, with delirium, seizures and coma.
simple: Brain dysfunction caused by poisons.

name: Toxic encephalopathy
formal: Acute or subacute brain dysfunction due to poisoning, causing confusion and reduced consciousness; often reversible when the toxin is removed.
simple: Confusion or drowsiness caused by a poison affecting the brain.

name: Toxic leukoencephalopathy
formal: White matter injury from toxins such as toluene, heroin vapour or chemotherapy, causing subacute dementia, ataxia and spasticity.
simple: Damage to the brain's wiring from poisons or certain drugs.

name: Toxic myoclonus
formal: Myoclonus secondary to toxins or drugs such as bismuth, lithium or antibiotics.
simple: Muscle jerks caused by drugs or poisons.

name: Toxic neuropathies
formal: Nerve disease due to toxin exposure including heavy metals, solvents, drugs and alcohol, usually with distal sensory-motor deficits.
simple: Nerve damage caused by chemical poisons or certain drugs.
more: Diagnose from exposure history plus NCS showing axonal, length-dependent neuropathy; check blood and urine levels (lead, arsenic, thallium). Removal of the agent is key, and recovery is slow and often incomplete, especially with arsenic or thallium.

name: Toxic oil syndrome
formal: Epidemic multisystem illness in Spain in 1981 linked to ingestion of adulterated rapeseed oil, with eosinophilic pneumonitis then scleroderma-like change, myalgia and sensorimotor neuropathy.
simple: A mass poisoning from contaminated cooking oil that caused lung illness, muscle pain, skin hardening and nerve damage.
more: Contaminant anilides in denatured oil were implicated; eosinophilia was a marker. Treatment is supportive with steroids and immunosuppressants; many survivors had chronic neuropathy and pain.

name: Toxic serotonin syndrome
formal: Excess serotonergic activity causing hyperthermia, clonus, hyperreflexia, tremor and agitation, usually after serotonergic drug combinations.
simple: A dangerous reaction to excess serotonin from medicines, causing fever, muscle jerks and agitation.

name: Transient global amnesia (TGA)
formal: Sudden temporary anterograde amnesia lasting hours, with preserved alertness and personal identity, typically in middle-aged or older people and without lasting deficits.
simple: Sudden temporary memory loss lasting some hours, after which memory returns.
aN: tga | transient global amnesia

name: Transmissible encephalopathies
formal: Prion diseases transmitted between individuals, including kuru, iatrogenic Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease and variant CJD.
simple: Brain diseases caused by abnormal proteins that can be passed from one person to another.

name: Transverse myelitis
formal: Inflammation of a spinal cord segment, causing weakness, sensory level and sphincter dysfunction, from MS, NMOSD, MOGAD, infection or post-infectious causes.
simple: Inflammation across the spinal cord causing leg weakness, numbness and bladder trouble.

Band-like pain at the level

det.patho: Transverse myelitis is immune-mediated inflammation across one or more spinal cord segments, damaging ascending and descending tracts and the grey matter. It may follow infection or vaccination, or be the first event of MS, NMOSD or MOGAD; systemic diseases (SLE, Sjögren syndrome, sarcoidosis) and direct infections (HSV, VZV, HIV, syphilis, TB, schistosomiasis) are other causes. When no cause is found it is labelled idiopathic.
det.clinical: Symptoms develop over hours to days and peak within 4 hours to 3 weeks: bilateral but often asymmetric weakness, a sensory level, band-like truncal pain and early bladder and bowel dysfunction. Reflexes may be reduced during spinal shock before becoming brisk. A partial myelitis with asymmetric sensory symptoms and a short lesion is typical of MS, whereas a complete, severe myelitis with a longitudinally extensive lesion (three or more segments) points to NMOSD or MOGAD. Hyperacute onset within minutes suggests infarction rather than inflammation.
det.diagnosis: Image the whole spine urgently to exclude compression, then confirm intrinsic cord inflammation (T2 lesion, often enhancing). CSF usually shows pleocytosis and/or raised IgG index; check oligoclonal bands. Test serum AQP4-IgG and MOG-IgG with cell-based assays, and screen for systemic autoimmunity, infections, B12, copper and HIV/syphilis. Brain MRI estimates future MS risk. Mimics include cord infarction, dural arteriovenous fistula (venous congestion), compressive myelopathy, radiation myelopathy and nutritional myelopathy.
det.treatment: First-line treatment is high-dose IV methylprednisolone (commonly 1 g per day, given for 3–5 days); plasma exchange is added for severe or steroid-unresponsive cases, especially when motor function is poor. Antimicrobials are given if an infectious cause is suspected. Supportive care covers bladder catheterisation, bowel care, DVT prophylaxis, pressure care, pain and spasticity management and early rehabilitation. Long-term immunotherapy depends on the cause — MS disease-modifying therapy or NMOSD relapse prevention.
det.prognosis: Roughly a third of patients recover well, a third have moderate and a third severe residual disability; rapid onset, complete paraplegia and spinal shock predict poorer recovery.
pearls: Every acute myelopathy is compressive until the MRI says otherwise.
Longitudinally extensive myelitis: check AQP4 and MOG antibodies.
Onset in minutes with back pain and a spared dorsal column suggests cord infarction.

name: Trauma cervical dystonia
formal: Cervical dystonia that follows neck or head injury.
simple: Neck twisting or abnormal head postures that begin after an injury.

name: Traumatic axonal injury (TAI)
formal: Diffuse shearing injury to white matter axons after rotational head trauma, producing coma or persistent disability with microbleeds on MRI.
simple: Widespread stretching damage to brain wiring from a severe head injury.
aN: tai | traumatic axonal injury

name: Traumatic brachial plexus lesions
formal: Injury to the brachial plexus from trauma, such as traction or avulsion, causing arm weakness and sensory loss, depending on roots involved.
simple: Nerve damage at the shoulder from injury, causing arm weakness and numbness.

name: Traumatic brain injury (TBI)
formal: Brain injury from external mechanical force, causing a spectrum from concussion to coma, with focal contusions, haematomas and diffuse axonal injury.
simple: Brain damage caused by a blow or violent movement of the head.
aN: tbi | traumatic brain injury

name: Traumatic optic neuropathy
formal: Optic nerve injury following head trauma, causing sudden visual loss, relative afferent pupillary defect, and variable optic atrophy.
simple: Vision loss from damage to the optic nerve after an injury.

name: Traumatic SAH
formal: Subarachnoid haemorrhage resulting from head injury, commonly overlying cortex, associated with contusion.
simple: Bleeding around the brain surface after a head injury.

name: Traumatic subarachnoid haemorrhage
formal: Bleeding into the subarachnoid space following head trauma, often over convexities.
simple: Bleeding around the brain after a head injury.

name: Tremor
formal: Involuntary rhythmic oscillation of a body part, classified into rest, postural, kinetic and intention tremors; includes essential tremor and parkinsonian tremor.
simple: Involuntary rhythmic shaking of a body part.

name: Tremor akinetic–rigid syndromes

simple: Conditions with shaking along with slowness and stiffness.

name: Tricyclic antidepressants akathisia

simple: Restlessness and need to keep moving caused by a type of antidepressant.

name: Trigeminal neuralgia
formal: Episodic severe unilateral lancinating facial pain in trigeminal territory, usually from vascular root compression; treated with carbamazepine or surgery.

aN: tn | tic douloureux | trigeminal neuralgia

det.patho: Classical TN results from a blood vessel, most often the superior cerebellar artery, pressing on the trigeminal root at or near its entry into the pons and distorting it; focal demyelination lowers the firing threshold so that light touch sets off bursts of ectopic discharge that spread between neighbouring fibres (ephaptic transmission). Secondary TN is due to an identifiable disease — a multiple sclerosis plaque in the pontine root entry zone or a cerebellopontine angle tumour such as an epidermoid cyst, meningioma or schwannoma — and idiopathic TN shows neither on MRI. Annual incidence is roughly 4–13 per 100,000, rising with age, with a modest excess in women. People with MS have a much higher lifetime risk, and their TN is more often bilateral.
det.clinical: Pain arrives as abrupt electric-shock or stabbing paroxysms lasting from a fraction of a second up to two minutes, confined to one or more trigeminal divisions — V2 and V3 most often, V1 alone rarely. Harmless stimuli over trigger zones around the nose, lips or gums — touch, talking, chewing, brushing teeth, shaving or a cold breeze — set off attacks, and a short refractory period may follow a volley; patients often freeze their face mid-attack. Some have a concomitant continuous ache between paroxysms, which responds less well to drugs and to surgery. Remissions of weeks to years are typical early on, but bouts tend to lengthen over time and patients may stop eating or drinking for fear of triggering pain. Red flags for a secondary cause are onset before 40, bilateral pain, objective sensory loss or a reduced corneal reflex, hearing loss, other cranial nerve signs or poor response to carbamazepine.
det.diagnosis: ICHD-3 defines TN by recurrent one-sided facial paroxysms in a trigeminal distribution, lasting up to two minutes, of severe electric, shooting or stabbing quality and provoked by innocuous stimuli. Every patient should have MRI including high-resolution 3D T2 (CISS/FIESTA) and MR angiography sequences through the cerebellopontine angle, to show neurovascular contact with root displacement or atrophy (supporting classical TN) and to exclude MS plaques or tumours; simple contact without deformity is common in healthy people and is not diagnostic on its own. The examination should check trigeminal sensation and corneal reflex symmetry specifically. Trigeminal reflex studies can help where MRI is not possible. Main mimics are dental pain, temporomandibular disorder, post-herpetic neuralgia, painful post-traumatic trigeminal neuropathy, giant cell arteritis in older patients and SUNCT/SUNA (autonomic signs, longer bursts).
det.treatment: Carbamazepine (started low, e.g. 100–200 mg twice daily, and titrated to effect) or oxcarbazepine is first-line and helps most patients; monitor sodium, blood count and liver tests, and test for HLA-B*15:02 before carbamazepine in Thai, Han Chinese and other Southeast Asian patients because of the Stevens–Johnson/TEN risk, which extends to oxcarbazepine. Lamotrigine, baclofen, gabapentin, pregabalin or botulinum toxin injections can be added or substituted when control is incomplete. Severe exacerbations that stop the patient eating or drinking may need admission for IV fluids and IV fosphenytoin or lidocaine, or a local anaesthetic nerve block as a bridge. Refer early for surgery when drugs fail or are poorly tolerated: microvascular decompression is the most durable option for classical TN in fit patients, while percutaneous balloon compression, glycerol rhizolysis, radiofrequency thermocoagulation or stereotactic radiosurgery suit older or frail patients and MS-related TN, at the price of some facial numbness. Concomitant continuous pain may need added amitriptyline or a gabapentinoid.
det.prognosis: Most patients respond to drugs at first, but benefit often fades or side effects accumulate; after microvascular decompression roughly 70–80% are pain-free at ten years, whereas ablative procedures and radiosurgery give shorter relief with more sensory loss.
pearls: Ask Thai and other Southeast Asian patients' HLA-B*15:02 status before starting carbamazepine.
Facial numbness between attacks is not classical TN — image for a lesion.
Patients may avoid eating and lose weight; check nutrition and hydration.
Constant burning pain lasting hours is not classical TN — rethink dental, TMJ or neuropathic causes.

simple: Non-cancerous tumours of the facial sensation nerve, causing numbness or pain in the face.

name: Trigeminal sensory neuropathy
formal: Disease of the trigeminal nerve causing facial numbness, often with connective tissue disease or idiopathic, sparing motor function.
simple: Numbness of part of the face due to disease of the trigeminal nerve.

name: Trilaminar myopathy
formal: Rare congenital myopathy with trilaminar fibres on oxidative staining, with variable weakness.
simple: A very rare muscle disease named from the three-layered appearance of fibres on biopsy.

name: Triosephosphate isomerase deficiency
formal: Autosomal recessive glycolytic enzyme defect causing haemolytic anaemia, progressive neuromuscular disease and early death.

simple: Weakness of an eye muscle causing double vision, often with the head tilted.

name: Tropical ataxic myeloneuropathy
formal: Myeloneuropathy in tropical regions linked to cassava cyanide toxicity and nutritional deficiency, with ataxia, spastic paraparesis and optic atrophy.
simple: A disease in tropical areas causing leg weakness, unsteady walking and nerve damage, linked to diet.

name: Tropical spastic paraparesis (TSP)
formal: Chronic myelopathy associated with HTLV-1 infection, causing progressive spastic paraparesis and bladder dysfunction.
simple: A slowly progressive stiffness and weakness of the legs caused by a virus (HTLV-1).

name: True primary myoclonic epilepsies
formal: Generalised epilepsies with myoclonic seizures as the main feature, including juvenile myoclonic epilepsy.

name: Trunk tremor
formal: Tremor of the trunk, as in essential tremor or orthostatic tremor.
simple: Shaking of the body trunk.

name: TTR-related amyloidosis
formal: Hereditary or wild-type transthyretin amyloidosis with progressive sensorimotor and autonomic neuropathy, carpal tunnel syndrome, and cardiomyopathy.

more: Diagnosed by TTR gene testing and biopsy; treat with patisiran, vutrisiran, inotersen, eplontersen, tafamidis, or liver transplantation.

name: Tuberculosis
formal: Infection by Mycobacterium tuberculosis that can involve the CNS as meningitis, tuberculoma or spinal disease.
simple: A bacterial infection that mostly affects the lungs but can spread to brain and spine.

name: Tuberculous abscess
formal: Pus-filled collection within brain parenchyma caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
simple: A pocket of pus in the brain caused by tuberculosis.

name: Tuberculous granuloma
formal: Focal intracerebral mass of inflammatory tissue due to tuberculosis, presenting with seizures or focal deficits and with ring enhancement.
simple: A lump of inflamed tissue in the brain from tuberculosis.

name: Tuberculous meningitis (TBM)
formal: Subacute basal meningitis from Mycobacterium tuberculosis with cranial nerve palsies, hydrocephalus, stroke and low CSF glucose.
simple: A serious infection of the brain coverings from tuberculosis, causing headache, fever and confusion.

aN: tbm | tuberculous meningitis | tb meningitis

det.patho: During the bacteraemia of primary or reactivated infection, Mycobacterium tuberculosis lodges in small caseous foci beneath the pia or ependyma (Rich foci); when one discharges into the subarachnoid space meningitis follows, whereas a focus that enlarges instead becomes a tuberculoma. A thick, sticky exudate settles in the basal cisterns, where it traps cranial nerves, blocks CSF flow at the aqueduct, fourth-ventricle outlets and arachnoid villi, and inflames the walls of the supraclinoid carotid, proximal MCA and their perforators. The result is the typical triad of hydrocephalus, basal ganglia–capsular infarcts and cranial neuropathies. HIV is the strongest risk factor; diabetes, alcohol, malnutrition, corticosteroids and TNF blockers also raise risk, and Thailand remains a high-burden country.
det.clinical: A prodrome of malaise, poor appetite, low-grade fever and headache usually lasts one to several weeks before vomiting, meningism (only about half have a stiff neck), confusion and falling consciousness appear. Cranial nerve palsies are common—VI most often, then III, IV and VII—and hearing loss or bulbar palsy can follow; vision may fail from papilloedema, optochiasmatic arachnoiditis, a compressive tuberculoma or later ethambutol toxicity. Hemiparesis from perforator infarcts, seizures, movement disorders (tremor, chorea, myoclonus, dystonia), choroidal tubercles and hyponatraemia are other clues, and spinal arachnoiditis can add radicular pain, paraparesis and bladder failure. Severity is graded by the modified British MRC scale (I: GCS 15 without focal signs; II: GCS 11–14 or focal signs; III: GCS 10 or less), which strongly predicts outcome.
det.diagnosis: CSF is usually clear with raised pressure, a few to several hundred cells (lymphocytic, though neutrophils can predominate early or in HIV), protein typically 1–5 g/L (higher with spinal block) and glucose below half the blood level. No single test is sensitive: smear for acid-fast bacilli is positive in only 10–50% and needs a large volume (ideally 6–10 mL) read carefully; culture remains the reference and gives susceptibilities but takes up to six weeks; Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra detects roughly half to three-quarters of cases and reports rifampicin resistance, so a negative result never excludes TBM. Contrast MRI may show basal enhancement, hydrocephalus, infarcts in the caudate–capsule–thalamus region and tuberculomas. Search for disease elsewhere (chest X-ray abnormal in about half, sputum Xpert, abdominal ultrasound, node or marrow biopsy) and test for HIV; TST and IGRA cannot separate latent from active infection. Start treatment on clinical grounds when suspicion is reasonable — waiting for confirmation costs lives.
det.treatment: Begin isoniazid, rifampicin and pyrazinamide plus a fourth drug for 2 months, then isoniazid and rifampicin to complete 9–12 months, always with pyridoxine; because ethambutol enters the CSF poorly, many experts choose moxifloxacin or levofloxacin as the fourth agent. Dexamethasone (starting near 0.4 mg/kg per day in severe disease, tapered off over 6–8 weeks) reduces death in HIV-negative adults, but a 2023 trial in adults with HIV found no survival benefit, so practice there varies. In HIV, start ART after a delay of several weeks rather than immediately to limit severe immune reconstitution. Obstructive or symptomatic hydrocephalus needs external drainage, VP shunt or endoscopic third ventriculostomy; check sodium, liver tests and vision regularly, and seek expert input when drug resistance is suspected. Intensified regimens (higher-dose rifampicin, linezolid) and adjunctive aspirin are still being evaluated in trials.
det.prognosis: Mortality remains above 20% (much higher with HIV, MRC grade III or drug resistance) and around a third of survivors have serious sequelae; treatment started before consciousness falls gives the best chance of a good recovery.
pearls: Subacute meningitis with a sixth nerve palsy and low sodium in Thailand: start anti-TB treatment early rather than waiting for cultures.
Lymphocytic CSF with low glucose: TB, cryptococcus, partially treated or Listeria meningitis, malignant meningitis — and GFAP astrocytopathy as a mimic.
New tuberculomas or worsening after starting treatment is usually a paradoxical reaction, not drug failure — but check adherence and resistance.
Send big CSF volumes repeatedly; one negative smear or Xpert means little.

name: Tuberculous spondylitis
formal: Pott disease: tuberculous infection of vertebrae, causing back pain, kyphosis, paraplegia and paravertebral abscess.
simple: Tuberculosis infection of the spine causing pain, deformity and possible leg weakness.

name: Tuberous sclerosis
formal: Neurocutaneous disorder from TSC1 or TSC2 mutation with cortical tubers, subependymal nodules, seizures, angiofibromas and cognitive impairment.
simple: An inherited disorder causing benign growths in the brain, skin and organs, with seizures and learning problems.

name: Tubular aggregate myopathy
formal: Myopathy with proximal weakness, myalgia or cramps where biopsy shows tubular aggregates of sarcoplasmic reticulum; caused by STIM1 or ORAI1 calcium-handling gene variants or sporadic forms.
simple: A muscle disease causing weakness and cramps in which muscle samples show abnormal tube-like clumps.
more: CK may be mildly raised; diagnosis by biopsy and genetics, often dominant inheritance. Treatment is supportive; progression is usually slow.

name: Tumour-related epilepsy
formal: Seizures caused by brain tumour, particularly low-grade glioma.
simple: Seizures caused by a growth in the brain.

name: Type II glycogenosis
formal: Pompe disease from GAA deficiency causing lysosomal glycogen accumulation, with infantile cardiomyopathy or adult-onset proximal and respiratory weakness.
simple: An inherited disease where muscle cells cannot break down glycogen, causing weakness and breathing problems.
more: Reduced acid alpha-glucosidase activity and gene testing; enzyme replacement with alglucosidase or avalglucosidase alfa.

name: Type III glycogenosis
formal: Cori-Forbes disease from AGL debranching enzyme deficiency causing hypoglycaemia, hepatomegaly, myopathy, and cardiomyopathy.
simple: An inherited problem storing sugar in liver and muscle, causing low blood sugar and weakness.
more: Diagnosed by AGL testing and enzyme assays; frequent high-protein feeds and cornstarch.

name: Type IV glycogenosis
formal: Andersen disease from GBE1 mutation producing abnormal polyglucosan, with liver cirrhosis, myopathy, or adult polyglucosan body disease.
simple: An inherited glycogen-storage condition forming abnormal sugar chains, damaging liver, muscle, or nerves.
more: Biopsy shows polyglucosan bodies; GBE1 testing; liver transplantation is considered in progressive liver disease.

name: Type IX glycogenosis
formal: Phosphorylase kinase deficiency with X-linked or autosomal recessive forms (PHKA1, PHKA2, PHKB, PHKG2), causing hepatomegaly, hypoglycaemia, or exercise intolerance.
simple: An inherited glycogen-processing problem causing an enlarged liver or muscle cramps.
more: Diagnosed by gene testing; dietary management with cornstarch and protein.

name: Type V glycogenosis
formal: McArdle disease, myophosphorylase deficiency (PYGM), with exercise intolerance, cramps, second-wind phenomenon, and myoglobinuria.
simple: An inherited condition where muscles run out of energy during exercise, causing cramps and dark urine.
more: Forearm exercise test, CK, and PYGM sequencing; pre-exercise sucrose and graded aerobic exercise help.

name: Type VII glycogenosis
formal: Tarui disease, phosphofructokinase deficiency (PFKM), with exertional cramps, myoglobinuria, and haemolysis, and carbohydrate-triggered worsening.
simple: An inherited condition where muscle cannot use sugar properly, causing cramps on exercise and sometimes anaemia.
more: Diagnosed by enzyme assay and gene testing; avoid strenuous exercise and high-carbohydrate meals before activity.

name: Type VIII glycogenosis
formal: Older designation for phosphorylase b kinase deficiency, now classed with type IX, with exercise intolerance or hepatic glycogenosis.
simple: An old name for a rare inherited sugar-storage disease affecting muscle or liver.
more: Diagnosed by genetic testing of PHKA/PHKB genes; treatment is supportive with dietary management.

name: Type X glycogenosis
formal: Phosphoglycerate mutase deficiency (PGAM2) with exercise-induced cramps and myoglobinuria.
simple: A rare inherited condition where muscles lack an enzyme needed for energy, causing cramps and dark urine after exercise.
more: Enzyme assay and gene testing; avoid strenuous exertion; no specific therapy.

name: Type XI glycogenosis
formal: Lactate dehydrogenase A deficiency (LDHA) with exertional myalgia, rhabdomyolysis, and skin lesions.
simple: A rare condition with muscle breakdown and pain after exercise from lacking a muscle enzyme.
more: Low lactate production on forearm test; gene testing; avoid heavy exercise.

name: Type XII glycogenosis
formal: Aldolase A deficiency (ALDOA), with exercise intolerance, rhabdomyolysis, and haemolytic anaemia.
simple: A rare inherited enzyme deficiency causing muscle pain and breakdown with exercise, and anaemia.
more: Enzyme assay and gene testing; supportive care and exercise avoidance.

name: Type XIII glycogenosis
formal: Beta-enolase deficiency (ENO3) causing exercise intolerance and myalgia with raised CK.
simple: A very rare inherited muscle enzyme deficiency causing exercise-related pain and fatigue.
more: Gene testing; supportive management.

name: Type XIV glycogenosis
formal: Phosphoglucomutase 1 deficiency (PGM1), a congenital disorder of glycosylation with hepatopathy, myopathy, cleft palate, and hypoglycaemia.
simple: A rare inherited condition affecting sugar processing, with muscle, liver, and other problems.
more: Galactose supplementation is effective; diagnosis by transferrin glycosylation and gene testing.

name: Typical absence seizure
formal: Brief generalised nonconvulsive seizure with abrupt impaired awareness and 3 Hz spike-wave on EEG, typical of childhood absence epilepsy.
simple: A brief staring spell with sudden loss of awareness, mainly in children.

name: UDD distal myopathy
formal: Late-onset autosomal dominant distal myopathy (tibial muscular dystrophy) from titin gene variants, causing anterior compartment weakness with foot drop after age 35 to 45.
simple: An inherited muscle disease starting in middle age, causing weakness in the front of the lower legs and difficulty lifting the foot.
more: MRI shows tibialis anterior involvement; confirmed by TTN testing, with severe disease in homozygotes (limb-girdle phenotype). Progression is slow and most remain walking; orthoses help.

name: Ulcerative colitis
formal: Chronic inflammatory bowel disease associated with neurological complications such as venous thrombosis, neuropathy and myelopathy.
simple: A bowel inflammation disease that can sometimes affect nerves and brain vessels.

name: Ullrich congenital muscular dystrophy (UCMD)
formal: Collagen VI-related congenital muscular dystrophy with proximal weakness, distal joint hyperlaxity, proximal contractures, follicular hyperkeratosis and respiratory failure, from COL6A1-3 variants.
simple: An inherited muscle disease present from birth with weakness, very loose finger joints, tight hips and knees, and breathing problems.
more: Diagnosis by collagen VI immunostaining and gene testing; inheritance may be recessive or de novo dominant. Management is respiratory support, orthopaedic care and nocturnal ventilation.
aN: ucmd | ullrich congenital muscular dystrophy

name: Ulnar neuropathies
formal: Compression of the ulnar nerve at the elbow (cubital tunnel) or wrist, causing numbness of little finger and hand weakness.
simple: Pressure on the nerve at the elbow or wrist causing tingling in the ring and little fingers.

2. Entrapment Neuropathies of the Upper Extremity

ddx.pt: C8 root: neck pain, medial forearm sensory loss, thenar (median) muscles also weak
Thenar wasting with medial forearm numbness; cervical rib
Split hand with no sensory loss and UMN signs

aN: ulnar neuropathy | ulnar neuropathy at the elbow | une | cubital tunnel syndrome | guyon canal

det.patho: The ulnar nerve is vulnerable where it runs superficially behind the medial epicondyle and through the cubital tunnel under the aponeurosis of flexor carpi ulnaris. Elbow flexion narrows the tunnel and stretches the nerve, while external pressure from leaning adds compression. Less common sites are Guyon's canal at the wrist (ganglion, cycling, fracture) and the axilla. Leprosy, diabetes and HNPP increase susceptibility.
det.clinical: Elbow lesions cause numbness of the little finger, the ulnar half of the ring finger and the ulnar border of the hand both dorsally and on the palm. Motor involvement causes weak pinch and finger spreading, wasting of the first web space, and clawing of the fourth and fifth digits in advanced cases. Froment's sign reflects adductor pollicis weakness, and Wartenberg's sign is a persistently abducted little finger. Symptoms are worse at night or when the elbow is held flexed. Wrist lesions vary by branch involved and may be purely motor.
det.diagnosis: Nerve conduction studies localise the lesion by showing focal slowing or conduction block across the elbow; short-segment inching improves precision. EMG documents axon loss and, by sparing flexor carpi ulnaris or not, can help. Check the dorsal ulnar cutaneous sensory response to separate elbow from wrist lesions. Ultrasound shows nerve swelling and can reveal subluxation or a mass. Exclude C8/T1 radiculopathy, lower trunk plexopathy and motor neuron disease, which affect median-innervated hand muscles too.
det.treatment: Mild cases are managed conservatively: avoid leaning on the elbow and prolonged flexion, use a padded elbow or a night splint holding the elbow in extension, and review after several months. Persistent sensory symptoms, progressive weakness or axon loss justify surgical decompression (in situ release or transposition), which have broadly similar outcomes. Space-occupying lesions at Guyon's canal need excision.
det.prognosis: Sensory symptoms usually improve; established wasting recovers incompletely, particularly in older patients with long-standing denervation.
pearls: Dorsal ulnar hand numbness places the lesion proximal to the wrist.
Medial forearm numbness suggests C8/T1 root or lower trunk, not ulnar nerve.
Thenar weakness with ulnar signs: look beyond the ulnar nerve.

aN: vci | vad | vascular dementia | subcortical ischemic vascular dementia | multi infarct dementia | post stroke dementia

det.patho: Cerebrovascular disease damages cognition through several routes: multiple cortical infarcts, single strategic infarcts (thalamus, angular gyrus, caudate, genu of the internal capsule), haemorrhages, and — most commonly — small vessel disease with white matter rarefaction, lacunes and microinfarcts that disconnect frontal–subcortical circuits. Hypertension, diabetes, smoking and ageing drive arteriolosclerosis, with chronic hypoperfusion, blood–brain barrier leakage and impaired perivascular clearance contributing; CAA and genetic arteriopathies such as CADASIL (NOTCH3) are other causes. Mixed vascular and Alzheimer pathology is the norm in older people, and each lowers the threshold at which the other produces dementia. VCI is the second commonest cause of dementia and is especially prevalent in Asian populations with high hypertension and stroke rates.
det.clinical: The cognitive profile is dominated by slowed thinking, poor attention, executive dysfunction, apathy and depression, with memory retrieval worse than storage, so cueing helps recall. Course may be stepwise after strokes or gradually progressive with small vessel disease, and the two often combine. Associated features include short-stepped gait with falls, urinary urgency, pseudobulbar affect, parkinsonism of the lower body and focal signs. Post-stroke cognitive impairment affects a large proportion of survivors in the first year; dementia after a first stroke is around one in ten and much higher after recurrent or severe strokes. Examiners often ask how to separate it from Alzheimer disease and NPH.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis requires cognitive impairment plus imaging evidence of cerebrovascular disease judged sufficient to explain it, using frameworks such as VICCCS or VasCog that grade severity (mild VCI vs major VCD) and subtype (post-stroke, subcortical ischaemic, multi-infarct, mixed). MRI shows white matter hyperintensities (graded by Fazekas), lacunes, microbleeds, enlarged perivascular spaces and infarcts, described with STRIVE terminology. Neuropsychological testing should include processing speed and executive tasks; MoCA (with Thai versions) is more sensitive than MMSE. Screen for depression, B12 deficiency, thyroid disease, syphilis and NPH, and consider amyloid or tau biomarkers when mixed disease is suspected. Young onset, family history, migraine with aura or anterior temporal and external capsule lesions prompt NOTCH3 testing.
det.treatment: Aggressive vascular risk control is the core: BP lowering (intensive targets reduced incident MCI in trial data), diabetes and lipid control, stopping smoking, physical activity and treating hearing loss and sleep apnoea. Secondary stroke prevention follows usual rules, but antiplatelets are given for prior stroke, not for white matter disease alone; cilostazol is being studied for small vessel disease. Cholinesterase inhibitors and memantine give modest cognitive benefit and are mainly used in mixed or post-stroke dementia. Treat depression, address apathy, and support function with rehabilitation, occupational therapy, caregiver education and planning for capacity and safety. Avoid anticholinergic and sedative drugs that worsen cognition and gait.
det.prognosis: Progression is variable and often steeper than in Alzheimer disease, with higher rates of further stroke, falls and death.
pearls: Slowness and dysexecutive features outweigh amnesia in subcortical VCI.
Most late-life dementia is mixed — vascular plus Alzheimer pathology.
Young onset with migraine aura and anterior temporal white matter lesions = test for CADASIL (NOTCH3).
Good BP control in midlife is the best-evidenced way to protect the brain from VCI.

det.patho: Cerebral small vessel disease disrupts the frontal–basal ganglia–thalamic loops and long periventricular fibres that control gait initiation and posture, rather than destroying nigral dopaminergic neurons. Less often a single lacune in the putamen, globus pallidus or substantia nigra produces acute contralateral parkinsonism. Hypertension and diabetes are the main risk factors; it accounts for a few percent of all parkinsonism.
det.clinical: The typical patient is elderly with a gait disorder dominated by short steps, start hesitation and freezing, a broad base and poor balance, while hand movements and facial expression are relatively normal. Falls come early. Cognitive slowing, pseudobulbar affect, urinary urgency and pyramidal signs reflect the underlying white matter disease. Progression is steady or stepwise rather than fluctuating.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical, supported by neuroimaging showing substantial small vessel disease or strategically placed infarcts, and by a temporal link to strokes when present. White matter changes are common in the elderly, so imaging alone does not prove the diagnosis; a normal DaT scan helps exclude coexisting Parkinson’s disease. Consider NPH, PSP and drug-induced parkinsonism, and recognise that mixed pathology is frequent.
det.treatment: Give an adequate levodopa trial because a minority, especially those with nigrostriatal lacunes, benefit. Physiotherapy focusing on gait, balance, cueing strategies and fall prevention is the mainstay. Control vascular risk factors (blood pressure, diabetes, lipids, smoking) and treat depression and urinary symptoms. Deep brain stimulation is not effective.
det.prognosis: Disability progresses over years, with falls and cognitive decline driving loss of independence; survival is shorter than in Parkinson’s disease.
pearls: 'Lower-body parkinsonism': legs stuck, arms normal.
Brisk reflexes and Babinski in a shuffling elderly patient argue against idiopathic PD.
Always try levodopa before calling it non-responsive.
det.thd: Vascular parkinsonism เกิดจากโรคหลอดเลือดสมองขนาดเล็กทำลายวงจรควบคุมการเดินในเนื้อขาวและ basal ganglia ผู้ป่วยสูงอายุเดินก้าวสั้น ซอยเท้า ฐานกว้าง เท้าติดพื้น หกล้มง่าย แต่แขนแกว่งปกติและมักไม่สั่น อาจมี reflex ไวและความคิดช้าลง MRI พบ white matter disease หรือ lacune ตอบสนองต่อ levodopa ไม่ดี การรักษาหลักคือกายภาพบำบัดและควบคุมปัจจัยเสี่ยงหลอดเลือด

det.patho: Inflammation and necrosis of the walls of epineurial arteries cause ischaemic infarction of nerve fascicles. Because nerve blood supply is patchy, infarcts produce discrete axonal lesions in individual nerves, often in watershed regions of the mid-arm and mid-thigh. Systemic causes include ANCA-associated vasculitis (especially EGPA and MPA), polyarteritis nodosa, rheumatoid arthritis, Sjögren syndrome, cryoglobulinaemia from hepatitis C, and drugs or infections. Nonsystemic vasculitic neuropathy is confined to the peripheral nerves.
det.clinical: Classic presentation is acute or subacute painful mononeuritis multiplex, with new deficits appearing in different nerves over days to weeks, often peroneal, tibial, ulnar or median. As lesions accumulate, the picture may resemble an asymmetric or even symmetric distal polyneuropathy, so the history of stepwise onset is key. Burning or deep aching pain is prominent. Systemic vasculitis adds constitutional symptoms, skin lesions, arthritis, renal or pulmonary involvement, and eosinophilia with asthma in EGPA.
det.diagnosis: NCS show asymmetric axonal loss, sometimes with pseudo-conduction block in the first days after infarction. Investigations include inflammatory markers, ANCA, ANA, ENA, rheumatoid factor, cryoglobulins, complement, hepatitis B and C, HIV, eosinophil count, urinalysis and renal function. A combined nerve and muscle biopsy (e.g. superficial peroneal nerve with peroneus brevis, or sural nerve), chosen from an affected but not absent nerve, gives the highest yield. Definite diagnosis requires vessel wall inflammation with damage; supportive features are probable. Diabetic and infectious mimics must be considered.
det.treatment: Treat promptly to prevent further nerve infarcts. Induction uses high-dose corticosteroids, combined with cyclophosphamide or rituximab for systemic vasculitis or severe/progressive nonsystemic disease; maintenance uses azathioprine, methotrexate or rituximab. Hepatitis-related vasculitis also needs antiviral treatment. Neuropathic pain, physiotherapy and orthoses are essential, and steroid-related bone and infection prophylaxis should be considered.
det.prognosis: Most patients stabilise with treatment and many improve slowly over months to years, though residual pain and weakness are common. Systemic vasculitis outcome depends on organ involvement; relapses occur.
pearls: Painful stepwise mononeuropathies in different limbs: rule out vasculitis.
Biopsy a nerve that is affected but still conducting.
Nonsystemic vasculitic neuropathy has normal markers — biopsy is the only route to diagnosis.
