det.patho: Vestibular neuritis (acute unilateral vestibulopathy) is believed to be an inflammatory, probably viral, neuropathy of the vestibular nerve; reactivation of latent herpes simplex virus type 1 in the vestibular (Scarpa) ganglion is the favoured explanation, though direct proof is lacking. The superior division, which serves the horizontal and anterior canals and the utricle, is affected far more often than the inferior division, possibly because its bony channel is longer and tighter. Abrupt loss of resting input from one labyrinth unbalances the two vestibular nuclei, producing spontaneous nystagmus, vertigo and postural imbalance until the brain recalibrates through central compensation. It is among the commonest causes of acute peripheral vertigo, usually in adults aged 30–60; when hearing is also lost the term labyrinthitis is used.
det.clinical: Severe rotatory vertigo builds over minutes to hours and persists for days, with nausea, vomiting and unsteadiness; patients prefer to lie still with the affected ear up, and any head movement makes it worse. Spontaneous horizontal-torsional nystagmus beats toward the healthy side, increases when looking in that direction, and is dampened by visual fixation; the patient leans or falls toward the affected side but can usually stand. A viral upper respiratory illness sometimes precedes it, hearing is preserved and there are no other neurological symptoms. The rarer inferior-division form spares the horizontal canal, so the bedside head impulse may look normal and the picture can be confused with a central lesion. Symptoms settle over days to weeks, though dizziness with quick head turns can linger, and some patients go on to persistent postural-perceptual dizziness (PPPD) or secondary BPPV.
det.diagnosis: This is a diagnosis of the acute vestibular syndrome made at the bedside. The HINTS examination in a patient with ongoing vertigo and nystagmus favours a peripheral cause when the head impulse is abnormal toward the affected side, nystagmus is unidirectional (beating away, increased with gaze in that direction and suppressed by fixation) and there is no skew deviation. Any central sign — a normal head impulse, direction-changing nystagmus, skew, severe truncal ataxia (unable to stand unaided) or new hearing loss — requires MRI with DWI, remembering that DWI in the first 48 hours can miss small posterior circulation strokes and should be repeated if suspicion persists. HINTS-plus adds a bedside hearing check, because sudden one-sided hearing loss with vertigo may signal AICA territory ischaemia. Video head impulse testing (reduced gain, typically below about 0.7, with corrective saccades) and caloric testing (canal paresis above about 25%) confirm the deficit, and vestibular evoked myogenic potentials help show which nerve division is involved.
det.treatment: Antiemetics and vestibular suppressants (such as dimenhydrinate, ondansetron or a brief benzodiazepine) are for the first three days at most, because sedation slows compensation. Corticosteroids begun within about 72 hours of onset, given as a tapering course over roughly 2–3 weeks, improve recovery of measured vestibular function, although the long-term gain in symptoms is less certain; antivirals add nothing. Early mobilisation and a structured vestibular rehabilitation programme of gaze-stabilisation, balance and habituation exercises are the cornerstone and should start within days. At follow-up, check for secondary BPPV and for PPPD, which is managed with rehabilitation, explanation and sometimes an SSRI.
det.prognosis: Most patients return to normal activity within weeks; caloric or head-impulse function recovers fully in about half, but central compensation makes any residual deficit unnoticeable except during rapid head movements. Recurrence is rare, while a minority later develop BPPV in the same ear or PPPD.
pearls: HINTS is only valid in a patient with continuous vertigo and spontaneous nystagmus at the time of examination.
A normal head impulse in acute vertigo is a dangerous finding — it suggests stroke.
Get patients moving early; bed rest and prolonged vestibular sedatives slow recovery.
Always test hearing: new one-sided deafness with acute vertigo can be an AICA stroke, not labyrinthitis.
det.thd: Vestibular neuritis คือการอักเสบของเส้นประสาทการทรงตัว (มักเป็น superior division) น่าจะเกิดจากไวรัสเริมที่แฝงอยู่ใน vestibular ganglion ทำให้บ้านหมุนรุนแรงต่อเนื่องหลายวัน คลื่นไส้อาเจียน เดินเซไปด้านที่เป็น แต่การได้ยินปกติ และเห็น nystagmus ทิศทางเดียวตีไปด้านปกติ การตรวจ HINTS ที่บ่งว่าเป็นส่วนปลาย คือ head impulse ผิดปกติ nystagmus ทิศทางเดียว และไม่มี skew ถ้ามีลักษณะของ central หรือการได้ยินลดลงเฉียบพลันต้องทำ MRI เพื่อหาสโตรก (DWI ช่วงแรกอาจปกติ) ยืนยันได้ด้วย video head impulse test หรือ caloric test รักษาด้วยยาแก้เวียนและแก้อาเจียนไม่เกิน 3 วัน ให้ steroid ภายใน 72 ชั่วโมงแรกเพื่อช่วยการฟื้นตัวของเส้นประสาท และสำคัญที่สุดคือรีบลุกเดินและทำกายภาพฟื้นฟูการทรงตัว

name: Vestibular schwannoma
formal: Benign tumour of the vestibulocochlear nerve sheath, causing unilateral hearing loss, tinnitus and imbalance; bilateral in NF2.
simple: A non-cancerous growth on the hearing and balance nerve causing hearing loss and unsteadiness.

name: Vestibulocochlear (VIIIth) nerve disorders
formal: Disorders of the eighth cranial nerve causing hearing loss, tinnitus and vertigo.
simple: Conditions affecting the nerve for hearing and balance.
aN: viiith | vestibulocochlear nerve disorders

name: Viral agents producing poliomyelitis
formal: Neurotropic enteroviruses, chiefly poliovirus and also enterovirus 71 and D68, that infect anterior horn cells and cause acute asymmetric flaccid paralysis with preserved sensation.
simple: Viruses that attack the nerve cells controlling muscles and cause sudden floppy weakness of the limbs.
more: Diagnosed by stool or CSF viral studies and CSF pleocytosis. No antiviral cure exists; vaccination prevents polio, and post-polio syndrome can develop decades later.

name: Viral and post-infectious myoclonus
formal: Myoclonus following viral infection or post-infectious inflammation, such as opsoclonus-myoclonus.
simple: Muscle jerks that develop after a viral illness.

name: Viral encephalopathies
formal: Brain dysfunction due to viral infection or post-infectious processes causing confusion, seizures and altered consciousness.
simple: Brain illness caused by a virus, causing confusion or seizures.

name: Viral meningitis
formal: Aseptic meningitis, usually enteroviral, with fever, headache, neck stiffness and lymphocytic CSF, self-limited.
simple: Mild infection of the brain coverings by a virus, causing headache and fever.

name: Viral spinal infections
formal: Viral infections of the spinal cord or nerve roots, such as poliovirus, herpes zoster or West Nile, causing myelitis.
simple: Viral infections of the spinal cord causing weakness or numbness.

name: Virus-associated vasculitis
formal: Cerebral vasculitis triggered by viral infection such as VZV, causing stroke or aneurysm.
simple: Inflammation of brain blood vessels caused by a virus, leading to strokes.

name: Vision neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis
formal: Juvenile neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis (Batten disease) with progressive visual failure, seizures, dementia and ataxia.
simple: An inherited childhood disease with progressive vision loss, seizures and loss of skills.

name: Visual agnosia
formal: Inability to recognise objects visually despite intact vision, due to lesions in occipitotemporal cortex.
simple: Seeing but not being able to recognise objects, caused by damage in the visual part of the brain.

name: Visual simultanagnosia
formal: Component of Balint syndrome: inability to perceive more than one object at a time, from bilateral parieto-occipital lesions.
simple: Being able to see only one object at a time, unable to take in a whole scene.

name: Visuospatial agnosia
formal: Inability to appreciate spatial relationships and locate objects, from right parietal lesions.
simple: Trouble judging where things are in space.

name: Vitamin A deficiency
formal: Nutritional deficiency causing night blindness, xerophthalmia and, in neurological settings, raised intracranial pressure in infants and impaired mucosal immunity; seen in malabsorption and malnutrition.
simple: Not getting enough vitamin A, which can lead to night blindness, dry eyes and increased infection risk.
more: Serum retinol confirms it; replacement with vitamin A supplements is effective early, but corneal damage can be permanent.

name: Vitamin B12 deficiency
formal: Deficiency causing subacute combined degeneration, megaloblastic anaemia, neuropathy and cognitive impairment.
simple: Low vitamin B12 causing numbness, balance problems, memory trouble and anaemia.

name: Vitamin E deficiency
formal: Deficiency of vitamin E causing spinocerebellar ataxia, neuropathy and retinopathy.
simple: Low vitamin E causing poor balance and nerve damage.
more: Check serum alpha-tocopherol with the lipid ratio; abetalipoproteinaemia and cholestatic malabsorption must be excluded, while AVED has TTPA mutations. Treat with high-dose oral vitamin E, which can halt progression.

name: VLCAD deficiency
formal: Very-long-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency (ACADVL) with cardiomyopathy in infants, or rhabdomyolysis with exertional myalgia in adolescents.
simple: An inherited fat-burning defect causing muscle pain or heart weakness, especially during fasting or exercise.
more: Acylcarnitine and gene testing; avoid fasting, a low-fat diet with medium-chain triglycerides, and triheptanoin.

name: Vocal tics
formal: Involuntary vocalisations as part of Tourette syndrome, ranging from simple sounds to words.
simple: Repeated sounds or words made involuntarily.

name: Vogt–Koyanagi–Harada disease
formal: Autoimmune panuveitis with meningoencephalitis, poliosis, vitiligo and hearing loss, in pigmented populations.
simple: An immune disease causing eye inflammation, headache, hearing loss and patchy loss of skin or hair colour.

name: Von Economo’s disease
formal: Encephalitis lethargica, epidemic 1916-1927, with sleep disturbance, oculogyric crisis, parkinsonism and psychiatric features.
simple: A rare epidemic brain illness causing excessive sleepiness and later parkinsonism.

name: Von Hippel–Lindau (VHL) disease
formal: Autosomal dominant VHL mutation with retinal and CNS haemangioblastomas, renal cell carcinoma and phaeochromocytoma.
simple: An inherited condition causing tumours in the brain, eyes, kidneys and adrenal glands.
aN: vhl | von hippel lindau disease

name: Von Hippel–Lindau disease
formal: Autosomal dominant VHL mutation with retinal and CNS haemangioblastomas, renal cell carcinoma and phaeochromocytoma.
simple: An inherited condition causing tumours in the brain, eyes, kidneys and adrenal glands.

name: Walker-Warburg syndrome
formal: Severe congenital muscular dystrophy with cobblestone lissencephaly, hydrocephalus, cerebellar malformation and eye anomalies, due to defective alpha-dystroglycan glycosylation (POMT1, POMT2, FKTN and others).
simple: The most severe inherited muscle and brain malformation syndrome of newborns, with floppiness, brain and eye abnormalities.
more: Very high CK; autosomal recessive with prenatal diagnosis possible. Treatment is supportive and most affected infants die in the first years of life.

name: Wall-eyed bilateral internuclear ophthalmoplegia
formal: WEBINO: bilateral internuclear ophthalmoplegia with exotropia, from midbrain lesions affecting the medial longitudinal fasciculus.
simple: Both eyes drift outward and cannot turn inward, from damage in the brainstem.

name: Welander distal myopathy
formal: Late-onset autosomal dominant distal myopathy beginning in the hands, especially finger and wrist extensors, linked to a TIA1 variant; mainly reported in Sweden and Finland.
simple: An inherited muscle disease in older adults that starts with weak hands and fingers and slowly spreads.
more: CK is normal or mildly raised and biopsy shows rimmed vacuoles. There is no specific treatment; progression is slow and lifespan is normal.

name: Werdnig–Hoffman disease
formal: Infantile-onset spinal muscular atrophy type 1 (SMN1 deletion) with hypotonia and early respiratory failure.
simple: A severe inherited muscle wasting disease in babies.
more: Diagnosis by homozygous SMN1 deletion with one or two SMN2 copies; EMG shows denervation and fasciculations. Untreated, death occurs by two years; nusinersen, onasemnogene and risdiplam have changed survival, and early treatment is vital.

name: Wernicke syndrome
formal: Acute thiamine deficiency encephalopathy with the triad of confusion, ophthalmoplegia and ataxia, associated with alcoholism, malnutrition and hyperemesis; MRI shows periventricular lesions and mammillary body change.
simple: A brain emergency from lack of vitamin B1 that causes confusion, eye movement problems and unsteady walking.
more: Treat immediately with high-dose intravenous thiamine before glucose to prevent Korsakoff syndrome. Early treatment can fully reverse features.

name: Wernicke’s aphasia
formal: Fluent aphasia from left posterior superior temporal lesion, with impaired comprehension and paraphasic speech.
simple: Speech that sounds fluent but makes little sense, with poor understanding.

name: Wernicke’s encephalopathy
formal: Thiamine deficiency causing the triad of confusion, ophthalmoplegia and ataxia, often in alcohol misuse, treated with parenteral thiamine.
simple: A brain emergency from low vitamin B1 causing confusion, abnormal eye movements and unsteady walking.
more: MRI may show mammillary body and periaqueductal T2 hyperintensity; diagnose clinically, and thiamine should be given before glucose. Treat with high-dose IV thiamine, 500 mg three times daily; untreated, it progresses to Korsakoff syndrome and death.

feat: Confusion, ophthalmoplegia/nystagmus, gait ataxia (full triad uncommon)
Risk: alcohol, hyperemesis, bariatric surgery, malnutrition, refeeding
Untreated progresses to Korsakoff amnesia with confabulation
inv: Clinical — treat on suspicion
MRI: medial thalamic, mammillary body, periaqueductal T2/DWI change

case.story: Brought in confused and unsteady after a week of vomiting.
case.exam: Disoriented, horizontal nystagmus and bilateral abduction weakness, wide-based gait.
case.tests: MRI: symmetric medial thalamic and mammillary body FLAIR change.
case.q: Why give thiamine before glucose?
case.a: Glucose metabolism consumes thiamine and can precipitate or worsen Wernicke encephalopathy.

files.chapter: Chapter 26 Toxic, Metabolic and Physical Insults to the Nervous System
8 The Localization of Lesions Affecting the Ocular Motor System
11. NEUROPATHIES ASSOCIATED WITH VITAMIN AND ESSENTIAL MINERAL DEFICIENCIES AND MALABSORPTION

ddx.pt: Asterixis, liver failure, high ammonia
Sudden onset in a vascular territory (e.g. artery of Percheron mimics)
Ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, areflexia without confusion; GQ1b

aN: wernicke encephalopathy | thiamine deficiency | wernicke korsakoff | we

det.patho: Thiamine (vitamin B1) is a cofactor for enzymes of glucose metabolism; body stores last only a few weeks. When thiamine is depleted, energy failure and oxidative injury hit regions of high metabolic demand around the third ventricle, aqueduct and fourth ventricle — the medial thalami, mammillary bodies, periaqueductal grey, oculomotor and vestibular nuclei and cerebellar vermis. Alcohol use disorder is the classic setting, but hyperemesis, bariatric surgery, cancer, dialysis, starvation and refeeding are increasingly recognised.
det.clinical: The full triad of confusion, eye movement abnormalities and gait ataxia is present in only a minority; many patients show just one or two elements or only altered mental state. Eye findings include nystagmus, lateral rectus palsy, conjugate gaze palsy and, rarely, pupillary change. Hypothermia, hypotension and coma occur in severe cases. If untreated, patients develop Korsakoff syndrome, with profound anterograde and retrograde amnesia and confabulation, which may be permanent.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical; the Caine criteria (two of dietary deficiency, eye signs, cerebellar dysfunction, and altered mental state or memory impairment) improve sensitivity in people with alcohol use disorder. MRI showing symmetric T2/FLAIR or DWI change in the medial thalami, mammillary bodies and periaqueductal region supports it but a normal scan does not exclude it. Blood thiamine (or transketolase) levels can be drawn but treatment must not wait for the result. Exclude hypoglycaemia, hepatic encephalopathy, intoxication, posterior circulation stroke and Miller Fisher syndrome.
det.treatment: Give high-dose parenteral thiamine immediately — commonly 500 mg IV three times daily for several days, then lower doses — before or together with glucose. Correct magnesium, which is needed for thiamine-dependent enzymes. Give prophylactic parenteral thiamine to at-risk patients (alcohol withdrawal, hyperemesis, refeeding). After the acute phase, continue oral thiamine, nutritional support and alcohol treatment.
det.prognosis: Eye signs often improve within hours to days and ataxia over weeks, but memory deficits frequently persist; untreated, mortality is substantial.
pearls: Treat on suspicion: thiamine is cheap and safe, missed WE is devastating.
Low magnesium can make thiamine therapy ineffective.
Think of WE after bariatric surgery or hyperemesis, not only in alcohol use.

name: West syndrome
formal: Epileptic encephalopathy in infancy with infantile spasms, developmental regression and hypsarrhythmia on EEG.
simple: A serious infant epilepsy with clusters of spasms and developmental regression.
more: EEG shows hypsarrhythmia; MRI and metabolic and genetic work-up should be done urgently (tuberous sclerosis, ARX, CDKL5). First-line treatment is ACTH, prednisolone or vigabatrin, especially in tuberous sclerosis.

tempoNote: Spasms come in clusters, especially on waking; onset usually 3–12 months, with developmental plateau or regression over weeks
feat: Brief symmetric flexion or extension spasms of neck, trunk and limbs lasting about a second, repeated in clusters
Clusters typically appear just after waking and may be mistaken for colic or startle
Loss of social smile, visual attention or motor milestones once spasms begin
Underlying cause often evident: tuberous sclerosis, hypoxic–ischaemic injury, malformation, Down syndrome or a genetic variant

Genetic testing (epilepsy panel/exome, chromosomal microarray) and metabolic screen when MRI is unrevealing

case.who: 6-month-old boy brought to a provincial hospital in Surin
case.story: For two weeks he has 'startles' in runs of 10–20 each morning after waking, crying between jerks. He has stopped smiling and no longer follows faces.
case.exam: Poor visual fixation, reduced axial tone; three hypopigmented oval patches on the back under ultraviolet light.
case.tests: Sleep EEG: hypsarrhythmia; a recorded cluster shows each spasm with diffuse voltage attenuation. MRI: cortical tubers and subependymal nodules.
case.q: What is the syndrome and which first-line drug is particularly favoured given the cause?
case.a: Infantile epileptic spasms syndrome (West syndrome) due to tuberous sclerosis complex; vigabatrin is the preferred first treatment in TSC.

det.patho: Epileptic spasms are an age-dependent response of the immature brain to many different insults, structural, genetic, metabolic or unknown. Abnormal interaction between cortex and brainstem with a stress-hormone (CRH) component is proposed, which may explain why corticosteroids and ACTH help. Incidence is roughly 1 in 2,000–4,000 live births.
det.clinical: The 2022 ILAE term is infantile epileptic spasms syndrome (IESS), which covers spasms starting between 1 and 24 months with or without full hypsarrhythmia; West syndrome is the classic triad of spasms, hypsarrhythmia and regression. Spasms are often misread as colic, reflux or Moro responses, delaying care. Asymmetric spasms or associated focal seizures suggest a focal structural lesion. Some infants have no prior delay and a normal MRI, which carries a better outlook.
det.diagnosis: Video-EEG that captures a cluster is the key test; a normal awake EEG does not exclude it, so record sleep and the waking period. Search for a cause with MRI, skin examination, ophthalmology, genetic testing and metabolic studies (including a trial of pyridoxine in selected infants). Recognising IESS is a paediatric neurology emergency because the time to effective treatment influences development.
det.treatment: First-line options are high-dose oral prednisolone or ACTH, or vigabatrin; vigabatrin is preferred in tuberous sclerosis, and combined hormone plus vigabatrin gives faster cessation in some trials. Response is judged within about two weeks by stopping of spasms and resolution of hypsarrhythmia. Hormonal therapy needs blood pressure, glucose and infection monitoring; vigabatrin carries a risk of peripheral visual field loss and reversible MRI signal change. Second-line choices include ketogenic diet, topiramate or other agents, and epilepsy surgery for a resectable lesion.
det.prognosis: Most children have lasting developmental impairment and many go on to other seizure types, including Lennox–Gastaut syndrome; outlook is best with no identified cause and rapid response.
pearls: Clusters on waking plus loss of smile in an infant = IESS until proven otherwise.
Ask parents to film events — video often makes the diagnosis.
Tuberous sclerosis with spasms: vigabatrin first.

name: Whipple’s disease
formal: Tropheryma whipplei infection with arthralgia, diarrhoea and CNS involvement including oculomasticatory myorhythmia.
simple: A rare bacterial infection of the gut that can affect the brain, causing memory loss and eye movement problems.
more: Diagnosis by PAS-positive macrophages on small bowel biopsy and PCR for the organism in blood, CSF or tissue. Treat with ceftriaxone for 2 weeks then long-term co-trimoxazole for a year; relapse in the CNS is possible.

name: Wilson’s disease

simple: An inherited disorder where copper builds up in the liver and brain, causing tremor and mood changes.

ddx.pt: Chorea, family history, normal copper studies
No liver disease or KF rings; genetic parkinsonism

aN: wilson disease | hepatolenticular degeneration

det.patho: Biallelic mutations in ATP7B impair copper incorporation into caeruloplasmin and its excretion into bile, so copper builds up in the liver and spills into the blood, brain, cornea and kidneys. Free copper drives oxidative injury, especially in the putamen, thalamus and brainstem. It is autosomal recessive with a prevalence near 1 in 30,000.
det.clinical: Hepatic presentations (asymptomatic transaminase rise, chronic hepatitis, cirrhosis or acute liver failure with haemolysis) dominate in childhood, whereas neurological or psychiatric presentations usually start in the teens to 30s. Neurological forms include a coarse proximal 'wing-beating' tremor, dystonia with a fixed open-mouth smile, parkinsonism, ataxia, dysarthria and drooling. Psychiatric changes — mood disorder, impulsivity, falling school performance or psychosis — may precede motor signs. Kayser–Fleischer rings are present in about 95% of neurological cases but are often absent in purely hepatic disease.
det.diagnosis: Combine clinical signs with copper studies: low caeruloplasmin (below about 0.1 g/L is strongly suggestive), raised 24-hour urinary copper, and slit-lamp examination for KF rings. The Leipzig score integrates these with liver copper content and ATP7B genotyping. MRI often shows symmetric T2 change in the putamen, thalamus and brainstem. Pitfalls: caeruloplasmin can be falsely normal during inflammation and low in heterozygotes, protein loss or malnutrition. Screen all first-degree relatives.
det.treatment: Lifelong decoppering therapy is required: chelators (D-penicillamine or trientine) for symptomatic disease, and zinc salts (which block intestinal copper absorption) for maintenance or presymptomatic cases. Introduce chelators gradually, because neurological worsening can occur early in treatment, especially with penicillamine. Avoid copper-rich foods such as shellfish, nuts, chocolate and liver early on. Monitor urinary copper, blood count and renal function; liver transplantation is curative for fulminant failure or decompensated cirrhosis.
det.prognosis: With early, adherent treatment survival approaches normal and many neurological signs improve over 1–3 years; stopping therapy can be fatal.
pearls: Any unexplained movement disorder or liver disease before age 40 deserves copper studies.
Neurological Wilson disease without KF rings is unusual — look with a slit lamp, not just a penlight.
Early paradoxical worsening on chelation is a known hazard; start low and titrate.
det.thd: Wilson's disease เป็นโรคพันธุกรรมยีนด้อยจากยีน ATP7B ทำให้ขับทองแดงทางน้ำดีไม่ได้ ทองแดงจึงสะสมในตับ สมอง และกระจกตา อาการทางสมองพบในวัยรุ่นถึงผู้ใหญ่ตอนต้น เช่น สั่นแบบกระพือปีก dystonia พูดไม่ชัด และพฤติกรรมเปลี่ยน มักมี Kayser–Fleischer ring การวินิจฉัยใช้ caeruloplasmin ต่ำ ทองแดงในปัสสาวะ 24 ชั่วโมงสูง ร่วมกับตรวจตาและยีน รักษาตลอดชีวิตด้วย chelator หรือ zinc ถ้ารักษาเร็วผลดีมาก

name: Wilson’s disesae
formal: Autosomal recessive ATP7B mutation causing copper accumulation, with hepatic disease, Kayser-Fleischer rings, tremor, dystonia and psychiatric symptoms.
simple: An inherited disorder where copper builds up in the liver and brain, causing tremor and mood changes.

name: Woodhouse Sakati syndrome
formal: Autosomal recessive disorder with hypogonadism, alopecia, diabetes, intellectual disability and extrapyramidal features.
simple: A rare inherited disease causing hormonal problems, hair loss and movement problems.

name: Writer’s and craft cramps
formal: Task-specific focal dystonia triggered by particular activities such as writing or craft work.
simple: Hand cramps and twisting that appear when doing a particular activity such as writing.

name: Writer’s cramp
formal: Task-specific focal hand dystonia with cramping during writing.
simple: Hand cramping that occurs only while writing.

name: Writing tremor
formal: Task-specific tremor occurring during writing, a variant of essential tremor.
simple: Hand shaking that occurs when writing.

name: X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy
formal: X-linked ABCD1 peroxisomal disorder with very long chain fatty acid accumulation, cerebral demyelination, adrenal insufficiency or adrenomyeloneuropathy.
simple: An inherited disease affecting the brain wiring and adrenal glands, mostly in males.

name: X-linked ataxia syndromes
formal: Group of hereditary ataxias with X-linked inheritance, including fragile X tremor ataxia syndrome.
simple: Inherited balance disorders passed through the X chromosome.

name: X-linked CMT disease
formal: Charcot-Marie-Tooth neuropathy from GJB1 (connexin 32) variants, with intermediate conduction velocities, male-predominant distal weakness and milder disease in female carriers.
simple: An inherited nerve disease passed on the X chromosome that causes weak, wasted feet and hands, usually worse in men.
more: Diagnosis by nerve conduction and GJB1 testing; transient central nervous system episodes can occur. Treatment is supportive with orthoses, physiotherapy and surgery for deformity.

name: X-linked dystonia-parkinsonism (Lubag)
formal: Lubag: X-linked dystonia-parkinsonism in Filipino men, TAF1 haplotype, with focal dystonia progressing to parkinsonism.
simple: An inherited movement disorder in men of Filipino descent causing dystonia then parkinsonism.
aN: lubag | x linked dystonia parkinsonism

name: X-linked myopathy with excessive autophagy (XMEA)
formal: X-linked vacuolar myopathy from VMA21 variants causing slowly progressive proximal weakness in boys, with autophagic vacuoles and sparing of cardiac muscle.
simple: An inherited muscle disease in boys causing slowly worsening weakness in the hips and thighs.
more: CK is mild to moderately raised; biopsy shows autophagic vacuoles with sarcolemmal features. Treatment is supportive, and many remain ambulant into adulthood.
nN: x linked myopathy with excessive autophagy xmea
aN: xmea | x linked myopathy with excessive autophagy

name: Xp21 dystrophies
formal: Dystrophinopathies (Duchenne and Becker) arising from DMD gene on Xp21, with progressive proximal weakness and cardiomyopathy.
simple: Inherited muscle wasting diseases, mostly boys, from changes in the dystrophin gene.

name: Yellow star thistle poisoning in horses
formal: Equine nigropallidal encephalomalacia from ingestion of Centaurea solstitialis, causing necrosis of globus pallidus and substantia nigra with dystonia, dysphagia and abnormal chewing; a veterinary toxic parkinsonism model.
simple: A poisoning of horses from eating a weed that damages deep brain areas, causing stiff face muscles and trouble eating.
nN: yellow star thistle poisoning in horses

name: Zebra body myopathy
formal: Rare congenital or early-onset myopathy with distinctive zebra-striped subsarcolemmal inclusions on electron microscopy, with proximal weakness and hypotonia; genetics heterogeneous, ACTA1 linked in some.
simple: A rare muscle disease in which muscle samples under the electron microscope show zebra-like stripes, causing weakness.
more: Diagnosis relies on biopsy ultrastructure and gene testing. Care is supportive including respiratory monitoring; course varies from mild to severe.

name: Zinc deficiency
formal: Deficiency that can cause neuropathy, myelopathy or, via copper deficiency, ataxia; excess zinc causes copper deficiency myeloneuropathy.
simple: Low zinc can contribute to nerve and taste problems.

name: Zoster-associated encephalitis
formal: Encephalitis complicating VZV reactivation, with headache, fever, confusion and vasculopathy, mostly in immunosuppressed patients.
simple: Brain infection after shingles virus reactivates, causing confusion and fever.

name: Α-synucleinopathy
formal: Group of neurodegenerative diseases with pathological aggregates of alpha-synuclein, including Parkinson disease, dementia with Lewy bodies and multiple system atrophy.
simple: A group of brain diseases caused by build-up of an abnormal protein called alpha-synuclein.
more: Diagnosis is clinical with biomarkers such as DaT scan and skin or CSF seed assays. Treatment is symptomatic and disease-modifying therapy remains under study.

name: Anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis
formal: Autoimmune encephalitis driven by IgG that binds the GluN1 portion of the NMDA receptor, producing psychiatric symptoms, seizures, orofacial dyskinesia, decreased consciousness and autonomic instability; associated with ovarian teratoma in young women.
simple: An immune attack on brain receptors, often in young women, that starts with strange behaviour or psychosis and progresses to seizures, abnormal movements and reduced consciousness; it is treatable.
th: สมองอักเสบจากภูมิต้านทานต่อตัวรับ NMDA — เริ่มด้วยพฤติกรรมแปลก ประสาทหลอน แล้วชัก ปากขยับเอง ซึมลง พบร่วมกับเนื้องอกรังไข่
feat: Prodromal fever/headache, then psychosis, agitation, insomnia
Seizures, orofacial and limb dyskinesia, catatonia
Reduced consciousness, central hypoventilation, autonomic instability
Ovarian teratoma in young women
inv: CSF NMDAR antibodies (more sensitive than serum); CSF pleocytosis
EEG: extreme delta brush
Pelvic ultrasound/MRI for teratoma

case.story: After a flu-like illness she became paranoid and sleepless and was admitted to psychiatry; then had a seizure and grimacing mouth movements.
case.exam: Fluctuating consciousness, orofacial dyskinesia, labile BP and pulse.
case.tests: CSF WBC 30 (lymphocytes), NMDAR antibody positive; pelvic MRI: ovarian teratoma.
case.q: What are the first treatment steps?
case.a: Tumour removal plus initial immune treatment — steroids with IVIG and/or plasma exchange; rituximab/cyclophosphamide if no response.

ddx.pt: Fever, temporal necrosis on MRI, HSV PCR positive
Rigidity and fever after antipsychotic, high CK, no CSF inflammation

aN: anti nmdar encephalitis | nmda encephalitis | nmdar | autoimmune encephalitis nmda

det.patho: IgG antibodies to the GluN1 subunit cross-link NMDA receptors and cause their internalisation, reducing glutamatergic signalling without much neuronal death, which explains the potential for full recovery. Triggers include ovarian teratomas containing neural tissue and prior HSV encephalitis; many cases have no identifiable trigger. Among autoimmune encephalitides it ranks among the commonest, mainly in children and young women.
det.clinical: A viral-like prodrome is followed by psychiatric symptoms — anxiety, insomnia, agitation, bizarre behaviour, psychosis or catatonia — and then by memory loss, speech reduction, seizures and abnormal movements, especially orofacial and limb dyskinesias. Later stages bring decreased consciousness, autonomic instability (tachy- or bradycardia, labile BP, hyperthermia) and central hypoventilation needing ventilation. Children more often present with seizures or movement disorders; men less often have a tumour. Many patients are first admitted to psychiatry.
det.diagnosis: Test for GluN1 IgG in CSF, which is more sensitive and specific than serum testing (serum can be falsely positive or negative). CSF often shows mild lymphocytosis and oligoclonal bands; MRI is normal in most or shows non-specific FLAIR change. EEG commonly shows diffuse slowing, and the extreme delta brush pattern is characteristic in severe cases. Search for a teratoma with pelvic ultrasound and MRI in women, and consider testicular imaging in men. The Graus criteria allow probable diagnosis and early treatment before antibody results.
det.treatment: First-line immunotherapy is high-dose IV methylprednisolone with IVIG (total 2 g/kg, split across 2–5 days) and/or plasma exchange, combined with prompt removal of any tumour. If there is no clear improvement in about two weeks, escalate to rituximab and/or cyclophosphamide; refractory cases may receive other agents within specialist care. Supportive ICU care for dysautonomia, hypoventilation and seizures is often prolonged. Antipsychotics can worsen dyskinesia and mimic neuroleptic malignant syndrome — use them cautiously.
det.prognosis: About 80% of patients achieve good functional recovery, though it may take 1–2 years; relapses occur in around 10–15%, less often after tumour removal and second-line therapy.
pearls: A young woman with new psychosis plus seizures, dyskinesia or dysautonomia needs an LP and NMDAR antibodies.
Test CSF, not only serum.
Recovery is slow; long ICU stays are not a reason to stop aggressive treatment.
det.thd: Anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis เป็นสมองอักเสบจากภูมิต้านทานต่อ GluN1 ของตัวรับ NMDA พบในวัยรุ่นและหญิงสาว อาจสัมพันธ์กับ ovarian teratoma หรือเกิดตามหลัง HSE อาการเริ่มด้วยไข้คล้ายหวัด แล้วมีพฤติกรรมแปลก โรคจิต นอนไม่หลับ ต่อด้วยชัก ปากและแขนขาขยับเอง ซึมลง ความดันชีพจรแปรปรวน วินิจฉัยด้วยแอนติบอดีในน้ำไขสันหลัง EEG อาจเห็น extreme delta brush รักษาด้วยการตัดเนื้องอกร่วมกับ steroid, IVIG หรือ plasma exchange ถ้าไม่ดีขึ้นให้ rituximab หรือ cyclophosphamide ส่วนใหญ่ฟื้นตัวดีแต่ใช้เวลานาน

name: Spinal cord compression
formal: Compression of the spinal cord by extrinsic lesions — metastatic tumour, disc or spondylosis, epidural abscess or haematoma — producing back pain, myelopathic weakness, a sensory level and sphincter dysfunction; a neurosurgical emergency.
simple: Something (often cancer, a slipped disc or an abscess) presses on the spinal cord, causing back pain, leg weakness, numbness from a certain level downwards and bladder trouble; it needs urgent treatment.
th: ไขสันหลังถูกกดทับ — ปวดหลัง ขาอ่อนแรง ชาจากระดับหนึ่งลงไป ปัสสาวะผิดปกติ เป็นภาวะฉุกเฉิน

UMN weakness below the level, sensory level, sphincter disturbance
Root pain/LMN signs at the level of compression
Red flags: cancer history, fever/IV drug use, anticoagulation
inv: Urgent MRI whole spine
Dexamethasone for malignant compression; cultures for abscess

case.exam: Tender T9 spine, legs 4/5, sensory level T10, extensor plantars.
case.tests: MRI: T9 vertebral metastasis with epidural extension.
case.q: What are the immediate management steps?
case.a: High-dose dexamethasone and urgent oncological/neurosurgical review for decompression and/or radiotherapy.

ddx.pt: Intrinsic cord inflammation without compression
Areflexia without sensory level
LMN pattern, saddle anaesthesia, areflexia

aN: cord compression | mscc | metastatic spinal cord compression | compressive myelopathy | epidural abscess | cervical spondylotic myelopathy

det.patho: Extrinsic pressure compromises cord tissue directly and through venous congestion and ischaemia, producing oedema and eventually infarction if not relieved. Malignant compression arises mostly from vertebral body metastases (breast, lung, prostate, kidney, myeloma, lymphoma) and is most common in the thoracic spine. Other causes include degenerative cervical myelopathy, disc herniation, epidural abscess (diabetes, IV drug use, bacteraemia, spinal procedures), epidural haematoma (anticoagulation) and trauma.
det.clinical: Back or neck pain usually comes first, often worse at night, lying flat or with coughing, and may radiate in a band (radicular pain). Weakness, numbness below a level, gait ataxia and later urinary retention and constipation follow; once a patient is non-ambulant, recovery is much less likely. Cervical spondylotic myelopathy evolves slowly with clumsy hands, Hoffmann sign and spastic gait. Fever and raised inflammatory markers suggest abscess; sudden onset on anticoagulation suggests haematoma.
det.diagnosis: Obtain MRI of the whole spine as an emergency (within 24 hours, sooner if neurological deficit), because multiple levels are often involved. Use CT myelography if MRI is contraindicated. Investigate the cause: blood cultures and inflammatory markers for abscess, coagulation studies for haematoma, and staging or biopsy when malignancy is new. Examine sensory level and perineal sensation, and measure post-void residual volume.
det.treatment: For malignant compression give dexamethasone (commonly 16 mg/day in divided doses with gastric protection) and arrange urgent oncology and spine surgery review; decompressive surgery followed by radiotherapy benefits selected patients with good prognosis, while radiotherapy alone suits others. Epidural abscess needs IV antibiotics and usually surgical drainage; haematoma needs reversal of anticoagulation and evacuation. Degenerative myelopathy with progressive deficit is treated by surgical decompression. Pain control, bladder care, VTE prophylaxis and rehabilitation are integral.
det.prognosis: Functional outcome mirrors the neurological state at treatment: most patients walking at diagnosis remain ambulant, whereas few paraplegic patients regain walking.
pearls: New back pain in a patient with cancer deserves early MRI before weakness develops.
Image the whole spine — skip lesions are common in metastatic disease.
Fever plus back pain plus neurological signs = epidural abscess until proven otherwise.
det.thd: ไขสันหลังถูกกดทับเป็นภาวะฉุกเฉิน สาเหตุสำคัญคือมะเร็งแพร่กระจายไปกระดูกสันหลัง หมอนรองกระดูก กระดูกเสื่อม ฝีหรือเลือดออกในช่อง epidural อาการมักเริ่มด้วยปวดหลังตอนกลางคืนหรือนอนราบ แล้วขาอ่อนแรง ชาจากระดับหนึ่งลงไป ปัสสาวะไม่ออก ต้องทำ MRI ทั้งแนวกระดูกสันหลังโดยเร็ว ถ้าเป็นจากมะเร็งให้ dexamethasone และปรึกษาศัลยกรรมกับรังสีรักษาทันที ฝีต้องให้ยาปฏิชีวนะและระบายหนอง ผลการรักษาขึ้นกับว่ายังเดินได้หรือไม่ตอนเริ่มรักษา

name: Migraine with aura
formal: Migraine in which attacks are preceded or accompanied by fully reversible focal neurological symptoms — usually visual, sometimes sensory or speech — that develop gradually and spread over at least 5 minutes and last up to an hour.
simple: Migraine with warning symptoms such as zigzag lights or spreading tingling that build up slowly over minutes before or during the headache, then go away completely.
th: ไมเกรนที่มีอาการนำ — เห็นแสงหยัก ๆ หรือชาลามช้า ๆ 5–60 นาที แล้วตามด้วยปวดศีรษะ
feat: Positive phenomena (scintillations, tingling) that march slowly, then negative after-effects
Successive aura symptoms occur one after another, not all at once
Headache usually follows within 60 minutes
inv: Clinical; image if aura is atypical (sudden, motor, prolonged, first after 50)

case.story: A shimmering zigzag crescent grew from the centre of her vision toward the right over 20 minutes; as it faded, tingling crept from her right fingers to her lips, then a throbbing left headache with nausea began.
case.exam: Normal neurological examination and fundi between attacks.
case.tests: None needed; she has had four similar episodes since her teens.
case.q: Which feature of the timing argues most strongly against a TIA?
case.a: The gradual spread of symptoms over minutes, with one symptom following another — ischaemia causes deficits that are maximal at onset.

ddx.pt: Sudden negative symptoms that reach maximum at once
Faster spread (seconds), brief, may have motor jerking
Older patient, spreading episodes from cortical siderosis

aN: classic migraine | migraine aura | visual aura | scintillating scotoma | fortification spectra

det.patho: Aura is caused by cortical spreading depolarisation, a slowly propagating wave of neuronal and glial depolarisation (about 3 mm per minute) followed by suppressed activity; this explains the gradual march of symptoms across the visual field or body. The wave can activate meningeal trigeminal afferents, and release of CGRP and other neuropeptides in the trigeminovascular system generates the headache, sensitising central pathways. Familial hemiplegic migraine shows the same process driven by ion-channel or pump mutations (CACNA1A, ATP1A2, SCN1A). Migraine with aura roughly doubles ischaemic stroke risk, an effect amplified by smoking and oestrogen-containing contraceptives and linked in part to PFO and endothelial factors.
det.clinical: Visual aura is most common — a scintillating zigzag or scotoma expanding across the visual field over minutes — followed by sensory aura (tingling spreading up the hand to the face and tongue) and less often speech disturbance. Each symptom lasts 5–60 minutes and symptoms occur in succession rather than all at once. Headache usually follows within an hour but aura may occur alone, especially in older people (late-life migraine accompaniments). Hemiplegic migraine (motor aura, sometimes with confusion or coma) and migraine with brainstem aura (vertigo, dysarthria, diplopia, ataxia) are distinct subtypes. Complications include persistent aura without infarction lasting over a week and migrainous infarction, where an attack's usual aura persists and imaging shows an infarct in the matching area.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical using ICHD-3: at least two attacks with fully reversible visual, sensory or speech aura, plus at least three of six features — gradual spread over 5 minutes or more, two or more symptoms in succession, each lasting 5–60 minutes, at least one unilateral, at least one positive, and headache accompanying or following within an hour. Red flags requiring imaging and vascular work-up include first aura after 50, sudden onset, motor or prolonged aura, aura always on the same side, or a changing pattern. Distinguish from TIA (sudden, negative, simultaneous symptoms), focal seizures (faster spread, brief, often with automatisms), amyloid spells in the elderly, and RCVS or dissection when headache is severe. EEG is not routinely needed; genetic testing is reserved for familial hemiplegic forms.
det.treatment: Acute treatment uses NSAIDs or paracetamol with an antiemetic, with triptans taken at headache onset rather than during aura; gepants and lasmiditan are alternatives when vascular disease makes triptans unsuitable, and triptans are traditionally avoided in hemiplegic and brainstem aura. Preventive options include propranolol, amitriptyline, topiramate, flunarizine (widely used in Thailand), candesartan, valproate (not in women who may conceive), CGRP monoclonal antibodies, gepants for prevention and, for chronic migraine, botulinum toxin. Combined hormonal contraception should be avoided in women with aura; progestogen-only methods are acceptable. Address smoking, BP and lipids, and avoid medication overuse (simple analgesics on 15 or more days, triptans on 10 or more days a month). PFO closure for migraine alone is not recommended outside trials.
det.prognosis: Attacks often lessen with age, and isolated aura without headache becomes more frequent later in life; absolute stroke risk remains low in young women without other risk factors.
pearls: Positive phenomena that spread slowly = aura; sudden negative deficits = TIA.
Combined oral contraceptives are contraindicated in migraine with aura.
Persistent aura beyond an hour needs imaging for migrainous infarction.
A first aura after age 50 is a diagnosis of exclusion — image the brain and vessels first.

name: Hypoglycaemia
formal: Low blood glucose causing adrenergic symptoms and neuroglycopenia — confusion, seizures, coma or focal deficits that can mimic stroke; reversible with prompt glucose.
simple: Very low blood sugar, which can cause sweating, confusion, fits or even stroke-like weakness; it gets better quickly with sugar.
th: น้ำตาลในเลือดต่ำ — สับสน ชัก หมดสติ หรืออ่อนแรงครึ่งซีกคล้าย stroke แก้ด้วยกลูโคส

Focal deficit that resolves with glucose
Insulin, sulphonylurea, alcohol, liver failure, insulinoma
inv: Capillary glucose in every acute neurological presentation

case.who: 74-year-old man on insulin and a sulphonylurea
case.story: Found confused and weak on the left side at 6 a.m.; he skipped dinner the night before.
case.exam: Sweaty, GCS 13, left arm and leg 3/5, extensor left plantar.
case.tests: Capillary glucose 1.9 mmol/L; deficit resolves within 15 minutes of IV dextrose. CT brain normal.
case.q: Why must glucose be checked before any stroke reperfusion decision?
case.a: Hypoglycaemia can mimic a focal stroke exactly and is corrected in minutes; treating it as stroke would be harmful.

aN: hypoglycemia | low blood sugar | neuroglycopenia

det.patho: The brain depends almost entirely on glucose; when blood glucose falls (usually below about 3.0 mmol/L or 54 mg/dL) adrenergic counter-regulation produces warning symptoms, and further falls cause neuroglycopenia. Most cases occur in people with diabetes on insulin or sulfonylureas; other causes are alcohol, liver or renal failure, sepsis, adrenal insufficiency and insulinoma. Repeated episodes blunt the warning response (impaired awareness).
det.clinical: Autonomic symptoms — sweating, tremor, palpitations, hunger, anxiety — precede confusion, odd behaviour, slurred speech, seizures and coma. Focal deficits, including hemiparesis that resolves with glucose, can closely mimic stroke. Elderly patients and those on beta-blockers may have no warning. Prolonged severe hypoglycaemia can cause permanent damage to the hippocampus, basal ganglia and cortex.
det.diagnosis: Check capillary glucose immediately in any acute neurological presentation and confirm with a laboratory sample. Whipple's triad — symptoms, low glucose, relief with glucose — supports the diagnosis in non-diabetic patients. In unexplained cases, draw insulin, C-peptide, proinsulin, beta-hydroxybutyrate and a sulfonylurea screen during the episode. MRI after severe events may show DWI changes in cortex, hippocampi or internal capsule, sometimes reversible.
det.treatment: Give oral glucose if the patient is alert and can swallow; otherwise IV dextrose (for example 10% dextrose 150–200 mL or 50% dextrose 50 mL) or IM glucagon. Give thiamine first in malnourished or alcohol-dependent patients. Sulfonylurea-related hypoglycaemia can recur for many hours, so observe and consider octreotide. Review diabetes medications and educate on prevention.
det.prognosis: Rapid correction usually leads to full recovery; prolonged coma carries a risk of lasting cognitive impairment.
pearls: No stroke code should proceed without a glucose result.
Sulfonylurea hypoglycaemia is prolonged — admit and monitor.
Thiamine before or with glucose in at-risk patients prevents Wernicke encephalopathy.
det.thd: น้ำตาลในเลือดต่ำ (ประมาณ <3.0 mmol/L หรือ 54 mg/dL) ทำให้สมองขาดพลังงาน เริ่มจากใจสั่น เหงื่อออก มือสั่น หิว แล้วสับสน ชัก หมดสติ และอาจอ่อนแรงครึ่งซีกคล้าย stroke สาเหตุพบบ่อยคือยาเบาหวาน เช่น insulin และ sulfonylurea ต้องเจาะน้ำตาลปลายนิ้วในผู้ป่วยระบบประสาทเฉียบพลันทุกราย รักษาด้วยกลูโคสทางปากหรือ dextrose ทางหลอดเลือด ให้ thiamine ในผู้ที่ดื่มสุราหรือขาดอาหาร และเฝ้าระวังนานในรายที่เกิดจาก sulfonylurea

Adrenal crisis — give hydrocortisone

case.story: Sudden severe frontal headache while watching television, then vomiting and blurred vision.
case.exam: Bitemporal field loss, right ptosis with a dilated pupil and limited adduction, BP 88/50.
case.tests: MRI: haemorrhagic sellar mass extending into the right cavernous sinus; random cortisol low; sodium 128 mmol/L.
case.q: What must be given before anything else?
case.a: Intravenous hydrocortisone for acute adrenal insufficiency; then urgent neurosurgical and endocrine review.

Chapter 48: Headache attributed to arteritis, cerebral venous thrombosis,

aN: apoplexy | pituitary hemorrhage

det.patho: Sudden haemorrhage or infarction within a pituitary adenoma — often previously undiagnosed — causes rapid expansion of the sellar contents. Pressure spreads upward to the chiasm and laterally into the cavernous sinuses, while destruction of normal gland causes acute hypopituitarism. Precipitants include anticoagulation, surgery, pituitary stimulation tests, pregnancy, dopamine agonists and hypertension.
det.clinical: Abrupt severe headache, often thunderclap, with nausea and vomiting is typical. Visual loss (bitemporal field defects or reduced acuity) and ophthalmoplegia from III, IV or VI palsies follow; the third nerve is most often affected. Meningism and reduced consciousness may occur from blood in the subarachnoid space. Acute ACTH deficiency causes hypotension, hyponatraemia and collapse, which can be fatal if missed.
det.diagnosis: MRI of the pituitary is the investigation of choice, showing a sellar mass with haemorrhage; CT may miss it. Take blood for cortisol, thyroid function, prolactin, gonadotrophins, electrolytes and glucose, but do not delay steroid treatment for results. Formal visual acuity and fields guide management. SAH, CVT, meningitis and basilar artery thrombosis are the main mimics.
det.treatment: Give IV hydrocortisone (100 mg bolus then ongoing replacement) promptly to all suspected cases, along with fluid resuscitation. Management is shared between neurosurgery, endocrinology and ophthalmology. Patients with severe or deteriorating visual loss or reduced consciousness usually undergo early transsphenoidal decompression; milder cases may be managed conservatively with close monitoring. Long-term hormone replacement is frequently needed.
det.prognosis: Ophthalmoplegia usually recovers; visual field outcome depends on severity and duration of compression, and many patients need lifelong hormone therapy.
pearls: Thunderclap headache + ophthalmoplegia + visual loss = image the sella.
Give hydrocortisone before any test results return.
CT can look normal; MRI is needed.
det.thd: เลือดออกหรือขาดเลือดเฉียบพลันในเนื้องอกต่อมใต้สมอง ทำให้ก้อนขยายเร็ว กด optic chiasm และ cavernous sinus อาการคือปวดศีรษะรุนแรงทันที ตามัว ลานสายตาผิดปกติ และเห็นภาพซ้อนจากเส้นประสาท III, IV, VI อ่อนแรง ร่วมกับขาด cortisol เฉียบพลันซึ่งอันตรายถึงชีวิต วินิจฉัยด้วย MRI ต่อมใต้สมอง ต้องให้ hydrocortisone ทางหลอดเลือดทันที แล้วพิจารณาผ่าตัดผ่านทางจมูกถ้าการมองเห็นแย่ลง

formal: Trigeminal autonomic cephalalgia with frequent short attacks (2–30 minutes, many per day) of strictly unilateral orbital pain with ipsilateral autonomic features, completely responsive to indomethacin.
simple: Many short daily attacks of severe one-sided eye pain with a watery eye or runny nose, which stop completely with the drug indomethacin.
th: ปวดรอบตาข้างเดียวเป็นช่วงสั้น ๆ หลายครั้งต่อวัน ร่วมกับน้ำตาน้ำมูกไหล หายได้ด้วย indomethacin
feat: Attacks 2–30 min, often >5 per day
Absolute response to indomethacin
inv: MRI with pituitary views

case.exam: Normal between attacks.

files.chapter: Chapter 35: Cluster headache and other trigeminal autonomic

ddx.pt: Longer attacks (15–180 min), fewer per day, no indomethacin response
Seconds-long shocks with triggers

aN: chronic paroxysmal hemicrania | cph | episodic paroxysmal hemicrania

det.patho: Paroxysmal hemicrania (PH) is one of the trigeminal autonomic cephalalgias: nociceptive traffic in the trigeminal system reflexly switches on cranial parasympathetic outflow, so one-sided pain arrives together with eye and nose autonomic signs. Functional imaging shows activity in the posterior hypothalamic region, much as in cluster headache, yet why indomethacin abolishes PH so completely remains unexplained. Older pooled series suggested a female excess (around 2–3 to 1), but more recent prospective cohorts find the sexes roughly equally affected, unlike the clear male excess of cluster headache; most patients first develop attacks in their thirties or forties, although cases from childhood to the ninth decade are described. During attacks CGRP and VIP rise in the cranial venous blood and normalise with indomethacin, and the hypothalamic activation seen in the untreated state is absent once indomethacin has made the patient pain-free. The chronic form, with no remission or remissions shorter than three months, is seen more often than the episodic form. Secondary PH has been linked to pituitary and other parasellar tumours, vascular malformations and posterior fossa lesions.
det.clinical: Attacks are severe and strictly one-sided, usually always on the same side (although up to about 15% have attacks on either side), centred on the orbit, temple or forehead, last roughly 2–30 minutes and come more than five times a day for over half of the active period, including at night. Ipsilateral tearing, conjunctival redness, nasal blockage or discharge, lid swelling, forehead sweating, ptosis or miosis accompany the pain, and many patients become agitated during the attack. A minority of attacks are set off mechanically by bending, turning the head or pressing over the upper neck. Between attacks there is usually no pain or only a mild ache; a continuous one-sided background headache points instead to hemicrania continua. Photophobia or nausea can appear and do not exclude the diagnosis.
det.diagnosis: ICHD-3 asks for at least 20 attacks of typical duration and frequency with at least one ipsilateral autonomic feature or restlessness, and for complete prevention by therapeutic doses of indomethacin. A practical oral trial begins at 25 mg three times daily and is stepped up every few days to 50 mg and then 75 mg three times daily, judging the effect over about 1–2 weeks; where an injectable indomethacin test is available it gives a quicker answer. A partial response usually means the dose was too low or the diagnosis is different. Every patient needs MRI brain with pituitary views, with pituitary hormone tests when imaging or history raises concern. The key mimics are cluster headache (longer and fewer attacks, male excess, no indomethacin effect), SUNCT/SUNA (stabs of seconds with cutaneous triggers), hemicrania continua and trigeminal neuralgia.
det.treatment: Indomethacin is the drug of choice; once attacks are abolished, step down to the smallest dose that keeps the patient free (often 25–100 mg/day) and co-prescribe a proton pump inhibitor. Review renal function, blood pressure and gastrointestinal symptoms at intervals, particularly in older people. For indomethacin intolerance, partly effective options include COX-2 inhibitors such as celecoxib or etoricoxib (mindful of cardiovascular risk), piroxicam, topiramate (helping roughly two in five in pooled reports) and verapamil (less often), with isolated reports of hypothalamic or occipital nerve stimulation in refractory cases; sumatriptan, oxygen and occipital or supraorbital nerve blocks rarely help, in contrast to cluster headache. In episodic PH the drug can be withdrawn when a bout is expected to finish and restarted at relapse. Any secondary cause found on imaging should be treated directly.
det.prognosis: PH is benign and usually fully controlled by indomethacin; the long-term concerns are drug toxicity and the need for maintenance therapy in the chronic form, although some patients enter lasting remission.
pearls: Many short, one-sided attacks a day with autonomic signs, especially in a woman, should make you think PH before cluster.
The indomethacin response is part of the definition; a failed full-dose trial calls for rethinking the diagnosis.
Image every patient — pituitary and parasellar lesions can produce an indomethacin-responsive PH picture.
Always cover indomethacin with gastric protection and check renal function.
Absent autonomic signs (about one patient in ten) should not stop an indomethacin trial when the attack pattern fits.
Oxygen and triptans that rescue cluster attacks do little in PH — failure of both is another hint to try indomethacin.
det.thd: Paroxysmal hemicrania เป็นปวดศีรษะกลุ่ม trigeminal autonomic cephalalgia พบได้ทั้งหญิงและชายในสัดส่วนใกล้เคียงกัน (ต่างจาก cluster ที่พบในชายมากกว่า) ปวดรุนแรงรอบตาหรือขมับข้างเดียวครั้งละประมาณ 2–30 นาที เป็นมากกว่าวันละ 5 ครั้ง ร่วมกับน้ำตาไหล ตาแดง คัดจมูก หนังตาตกข้างเดียวกัน ลักษณะที่ใช้วินิจฉัยคือหายสนิทเมื่อได้ indomethacin ขนาดเพียงพอ (ไต่ขนาดถึง 75 mg วันละ 3 ครั้ง) ทุกรายควรทำ MRI ดูต่อมใต้สมองและบริเวณ parasellar เพื่อหาสาเหตุแฝง เมื่อคุมได้ให้ลดเหลือขนาดต่ำสุดที่ได้ผลร่วมกับยาป้องกันกระเพาะ และติดตามการทำงานของไต ถ้าทนยาไม่ได้อาจใช้ celecoxib, topiramate หรือ verapamil (oxygen, triptan และการฉีดยาชาที่เส้นประสาท occipital มักไม่ได้ผล)

name: Syncope
formal: Transient loss of consciousness due to global cerebral hypoperfusion, that starts abruptly, lasts briefly and resolves fully by itself; reflex (vasovagal), orthostatic or cardiac in origin.
simple: A faint: brief loss of consciousness because not enough blood reaches the brain, followed by quick full recovery.
th: เป็นลมหมดสติชั่วคราวจากเลือดไปเลี้ยงสมองไม่พอ ฟื้นเร็วและสมบูรณ์
feat: Prodrome of light-headedness, sweating, greying vision; triggers like standing, pain, micturition
Brief myoclonic jerks can occur (convulsive syncope) but recovery is quick
Exertional or supine syncope suggests a cardiac cause
inv: ECG; lying/standing BP; echo or rhythm monitoring if cardiac features

case.story: During a blood draw she felt hot, nauseated and grey at the edges of vision, then slumped; bystanders saw a few jerks of the arms for 5 seconds.
case.exam: Fully alert within a minute; normal examination; ECG normal.
case.tests: Lying/standing BP normal.
case.q: Do the jerks make this an epileptic seizure?
case.a: No — brief myoclonic jerks are common in reflex syncope; the trigger, prodrome and quick full recovery point to syncope.

files.chapter: 27 Fits, faints, funny turns, and falls in the differential diagnosis of the dizzy patient
Section II: Epidemiology, Etiology, and Diagnosis

ddx.pt: Aura, automatisms, prolonged post-ictal confusion
Long events with eyes closed, fluctuating movements

aN: faint | vasovagal syncope | reflex syncope | convulsive syncope | cardiac syncope

det.patho: Transient global cerebral hypoperfusion — systolic pressure falling to roughly 50–60 mmHg for several seconds — causes loss of consciousness and tone. Reflex (vasovagal, situational, carotid sinus) syncope arises from inappropriate vasodilatation and/or bradycardia; orthostatic syncope reflects autonomic failure, hypovolaemia or drugs; cardiac syncope results from arrhythmia or structural heart disease and carries the worst prognosis.
det.clinical: Reflex syncope typically follows prolonged standing, pain, emotion, micturition or coughing, with a prodrome of warmth, nausea, sweating and fading vision. Loss of consciousness lasts seconds to under a minute, with pallor and rapid reorientation. Brief irregular jerks occur in many fainters and are often mistaken for seizure. Syncope during exertion, while supine, with palpitations or a family history of sudden death suggests a cardiac cause.
det.diagnosis: A detailed eyewitness history plus examination, lying and standing BP and a 12-lead ECG resolve most cases. High-risk ECG features include conduction block, long or short QT, Brugada pattern, pre-excitation and ischaemia. Further tests are chosen by suspicion: echocardiography, ambulatory or implantable loop monitoring, tilt-table testing and carotid sinus massage. EEG and brain imaging are not routinely helpful. Features against syncope include prolonged post-ictal confusion, lateral tongue biting and head turning.
det.treatment: Reflex syncope is managed with explanation, trigger avoidance, hydration, counter-pressure manoeuvres and, rarely, medication or pacing for cardioinhibitory forms. Orthostatic hypotension responds to stopping offending drugs, fluids and salt, compression garments, and midodrine or fludrocortisone. Cardiac syncope requires treating the underlying arrhythmia or structural disease, including pacemakers or ICDs.
det.prognosis: Reflex syncope is benign apart from injury; cardiac syncope carries a substantially increased mortality.
pearls: Jerks during a faint do not mean epilepsy — ask about prodrome and recovery speed.
Exertional syncope is cardiac until proven otherwise.
Every patient with transient loss of consciousness needs an ECG.
det.thd: Syncope คือหมดสติชั่วคราวจากเลือดไปเลี้ยงสมองไม่พอ ฟื้นเร็วและสมบูรณ์ แบ่งเป็น reflex (vasovagal) จากความดันต่ำตามท่า และจากหัวใจซึ่งอันตรายที่สุด มักมีอาการนำ เช่น หน้ามืด เหงื่อออก คลื่นไส้ อาจมีกระตุกสั้น ๆ ได้แต่ฟื้นไว ไม่สับสนนาน การวินิจฉัยอาศัยประวัติจากผู้เห็นเหตุการณ์ วัดความดันท่านอนและยืน และ ECG ทุกราย ถ้าเป็นลมขณะออกแรงหรือขณะนอนให้นึกถึงสาเหตุจากหัวใจ

name: Leptomeningeal metastases
formal: Spread of cancer cells to the leptomeninges and CSF, producing multifocal deficits — cranial neuropathies, radiculopathies, headache, hydrocephalus and encephalopathy.
simple: Cancer that has spread to the fluid and linings around the brain and spinal cord, causing several nerve problems at once.
th: มะเร็งกระจายไปที่เยื่อหุ้มสมองและน้ำไขสันหลัง — เส้นประสาทสมองและรากประสาทเสียหลายตำแหน่ง
feat: Multiple cranial nerve palsies and radicular pain/weakness at different levels
Breast, lung, melanoma and haematological cancers
inv: MRI brain and spine with contrast: leptomeningeal enhancement
Large-volume CSF cytology (repeat if negative)

case.story: Over 3 weeks: headache, double vision, numb chin on the right and pain radiating down the left leg.
case.exam: Left sixth nerve palsy, right mental nerve sensory loss, absent left ankle jerk.
case.tests: MRI: linear enhancement of the cauda equina roots and basal meninges; CSF protein high, glucose low, malignant cells on the second sample.
case.q: Why is a single negative CSF cytology not reassuring?
case.a: Sensitivity of one sample is limited; repeated large-volume samples are often needed.

files.chapter: Chapter 50: Headache attributed to non-vascular intracranial disorder

aN: carcinomatous meningitis | leptomeningeal carcinomatosis | neoplastic meningitis

det.patho: Cancer cells reach the leptomeninges mostly through the blood (via choroid plexus or meningeal vessels), but also by direct spread from dural, subdural or parenchymal deposits, by creeping along nerve sheaths, or by spillage during resection of posterior fossa metastases; once in the CSF they drift and settle over the brain surface, cranial nerves, cord and roots. It complicates roughly 3–8% of cancers, with breast cancer the commonest solid primary, followed by lung cancer (small cell, and EGFR- or ALK-driven adenocarcinoma) and melanoma; leukaemias and lymphomas seed the meninges readily, and in a small minority the meningeal disease is the first sign of cancer. Tumour coating the arachnoid villi or basal cisterns impairs CSF absorption, giving communicating hydrocephalus in about one in ten.
det.clinical: Early complaints are often vague — nausea, vomiting, fatigue, intermittent confusion or an odd new headache — before signs appear at several separate levels of the neuraxis: multiple cranial nerve palsies (diplopia, facial weakness, sensorineural deafness, numb chin), patchy radicular pain and numbness, asymmetric lower motor neuron leg weakness and sphincter disturbance from cauda equina involvement. Raised pressure can cause papilloedema, seizures and plateau waves with transient loss of awareness, while frank meningism is unusual. The tempo is weeks, typically in someone with advanced, often progressing systemic cancer. Any cancer patient with unexplained, progressive multifocal neurology and an unremarkable brain scan deserves a deliberate search for this diagnosis.
det.diagnosis: Obtain gadolinium MRI of the whole brain and spine before LP, because puncture itself can produce meningeal enhancement; look for linear or nodular enhancement of sulci, cerebellar folia, brainstem surface ('sugar coating'), cranial nerves and cauda equina roots, which is seen in roughly 70% (CT is far less sensitive). CSF is nearly always abnormal — raised pressure and protein, low glucose ratio, lymphocytes — and malignant cells on cytology confirm the diagnosis; send at least 10 mL to the lab promptly, since one sample detects around two-thirds and three samples about 90%. Flow cytometry helps in haematological cancers, and CSF circulating tumour cell counts or tumour DNA sequencing increase sensitivity and can reveal targetable mutations. EANO–ESMO criteria separate cytology-proven from probable or possible disease using clinical and MRI findings; infection (TB, fungi), sarcoidosis, ICI meningitis and post-procedural enhancement are the main mimics.
det.treatment: Care is palliative and tailored to performance status, systemic disease control and tumour biology. Focal radiotherapy to bulky or symptomatic sites (posterior fossa, cauda equina) is the mainstay; proton craniospinal irradiation improved survival in a phase II trial for selected breast and lung cancer patients, whereas photon craniospinal treatment is limited by marrow toxicity. CNS-penetrant systemic agents are increasingly preferred — for example osimertinib for EGFR-mutant lung cancer, newer ALK inhibitors, HER2-directed drugs and immunotherapy in melanoma — while intrathecal methotrexate, cytarabine or thiotepa (or intrathecal trastuzumab in HER2-positive breast cancer) via an Ommaya reservoir or LP has a debated survival benefit and is useless with blocked CSF flow. Treat hydrocephalus with shunting, give steroids, analgesia and seizure control as needed, and involve palliative care early.
det.prognosis: Median survival is typically 2–6 months; breast cancer, haematological malignancy and tumours with an effective targeted drug fare better, whereas poor performance status, encephalopathy and melanoma or lung primaries without a target do worst.
pearls: Several cranial nerve and root deficits at different levels in a cancer patient = leptomeningeal disease until shown otherwise.
Scan the whole neuraxis before the LP, then send large-volume CSF for cytology and repeat up to three times.
A numb chin or new unilateral deafness in someone with known cancer is a red flag.
Ask oncology about actionable mutations — targeted drugs now change survival for some patients.
