det.patho: The basilar artery can be occluded by in-situ atherothrombosis (usually mid or proximal segment), by emboli from the heart or vertebral arteries (usually lodging at the tip), or by dissection. Rostral occlusion threatens the midbrain, thalami and posterior cerebral artery territories; mid-basilar disease affects the pons and may cause locked-in syndrome. Collateral flow via the posterior communicating arteries largely determines tissue survival.
det.clinical: Presentation ranges from sudden coma to a fluctuating, stepwise course with vertigo, dysarthria, diplopia and hemiparesis that may later switch sides. Bilateral signs, eye-movement and pupillary abnormalities and reduced consciousness are the main clues. Top of the basilar embolism produces behavioural change, hypersomnolence, vivid visual hallucinations, amnesia and bilateral visual loss with relatively little motor weakness. Because early symptoms such as dizziness can be vague, the diagnosis is often delayed.
det.diagnosis: Keep a low threshold for urgent CTA in any patient with unexplained coma, bilateral signs or a fluctuating brainstem syndrome. A hyperdense basilar sign on plain CT is helpful when present. Grade ischaemic extent (pc-ASPECTS, pons-midbrain index) and collaterals to guide decisions. Distinguish from seizures, metabolic encephalopathy and drug intoxication early.
det.treatment: Endovascular thrombectomy combined with IV thrombolysis when eligible is now standard for basilar occlusion, with randomised evidence of benefit within about 24 hours of onset in patients without extensive established infarction. Intracranial stenting or angioplasty may be needed for underlying atherosclerotic stenosis. Protect the airway, monitor in a stroke or intensive care unit, and watch for hydrocephalus or cerebellar swelling. Secondary prevention depends on the cause (anticoagulation for AF, intensive medical therapy for atheroma).
det.prognosis: Without recanalisation most patients die or remain severely disabled; with successful thrombectomy roughly 40–45% achieve independence.
pearls: Coma + abnormal eye movements = image the basilar artery now.
A stuttering 'vertigo' that keeps returning may be a basilar prodrome.
Locked-in patients are awake: test vertical eye movement and blinking.
det.thd: Basilar artery occlusion คือการอุดตันของหลอดเลือดแดงหลักที่เลี้ยงก้านสมอง ผู้ป่วยอาจซึมหรือโคม่า กลอกตาผิดปกติ พูดไม่ชัด อ่อนแรงทั้งสองข้าง ถ้าลิ่มเลือดอุดที่ปลาย (top of the basilar) จะมีอาการง่วงซึม เห็นภาพหลอน ความจำเสีย และตาบอดจากสมองส่วน occipital ต้องทำ CTA ด่วนและรักษาด้วย thrombectomy ร่วมกับ thrombolysis หากไม่รักษาอัตราตายสูงมาก

name: Cerebral amyloid angiopathy-related inflammation (CAA-ri)
formal: Autoimmune inflammatory response to vascular beta-amyloid in cerebral amyloid angiopathy, including perivascular inflammation and amyloid-beta-related angiitis, causing subacute cognitive decline, headache, seizures and focal deficits with asymmetric confluent white matter oedema and lobar microbleeds; it often responds to immunosuppression.
simple: An immune reaction against amyloid deposits in brain blood vessels that causes confusion, headaches or seizures with swelling on the scan, and often improves with steroids.
th: การอักเสบต่อ amyloid ในผนังหลอดเลือดสมองของผู้สูงอายุ — ความคิดถดถอยเร็ว ปวดหัว ชัก อ่อนแรง MRI เห็นสมองบวม (white matter) ไม่สมมาตรร่วมกับ microbleed จำนวนมาก ตอบสนองดีต่อ steroid
tempoNote: Develops over days to weeks; relapses may follow tapering of immunosuppression
feat: Patient usually over 60 with subacute confusion, behavioural change or rapid cognitive decline
Headache, focal seizures and focal neurological deficits
Asymmetric patchy or confluent T2/FLAIR hyperintensity extending to the subcortical white matter
Multiple cortical-subcortical microbleeds or cortical superficial siderosis on SWI
Strong association with APOE ε4 homozygosity; resembles ARIA seen with anti-amyloid antibodies
inv: MRI with SWI/GRE: oedema plus lobar microbleeds/siderosis meets the 2016 criteria for probable CAA-ri
CSF: mildly raised protein and cells; anti-amyloid-beta autoantibodies when available
APOE genotyping (supportive)
Brain/leptomeningeal biopsy when imaging is atypical or response to treatment is poor

case.story: Three weeks of headache and confusion; his wife says he gets lost at home and has had two episodes of right arm jerking.
case.exam: Disoriented, mild right hemianopia and right pronator drift; afebrile.
case.tests: MRI: asymmetric left parieto-occipital white matter FLAIR hyperintensity with mild mass effect; SWI: over 40 lobar microbleeds and focal cortical siderosis; CSF protein 70 mg/dL, 4 cells; APOE ε4/ε4.
case.q: What is the likely diagnosis and first-line treatment?
case.a: Probable CAA-related inflammation; high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone followed by an oral steroid taper, with repeat MRI to confirm resolution of oedema.

det.patho: In some people with cerebral amyloid angiopathy, the immune system reacts against amyloid-beta deposited in cortical and leptomeningeal vessel walls. This causes either perivascular inflammation without vessel wall destruction or a granulomatous, transmural angiitis (ABRA). Anti-amyloid-beta antibodies in CSF rise during active disease. The mechanism mirrors amyloid-related imaging abnormalities (ARIA) caused by anti-amyloid monoclonal antibodies such as lecanemab and donanemab.
det.clinical: Typical patients are in their 60s–70s and present over days to weeks with cognitive or behavioural decline, headache, seizures and focal deficits such as hemianopia or aphasia. Patients may appear to have a tumour or encephalitis. Untreated, it can progress to coma, and relapses occur in a substantial minority even after initial improvement.
det.diagnosis: Clinico-radiological criteria allow a diagnosis of probable CAA-ri without biopsy: age at least 40, a compatible clinical syndrome, asymmetric white matter hyperintensity reaching the subcortical region, and haemorrhagic markers of CAA, after excluding neoplasm, infection and other causes. SWI is essential as the microbleed pattern drives the diagnosis. CSF helps exclude infection and lymphoma. Biopsy is reserved for atypical features or poor treatment response.
det.treatment: Glucocorticoids are first line, typically intravenous methylprednisolone pulses then a slow oral taper over months. Steroid-sparing agents (cyclophosphamide, mycophenolate, azathioprine or methotrexate) are used for relapse or steroid dependence. Treat seizures with antiseizure medication, avoid antithrombotics where possible because of bleeding risk, and regard later anti-amyloid antibody therapy as relatively contraindicated.
det.prognosis: Most patients improve clinically and radiologically with steroids, but relapse occurs in roughly a third to a half and later lobar haemorrhage or dementia is common.
pearls: Asymmetric white matter oedema + many lobar microbleeds in an older person = CAA-ri until proved otherwise.
It is the spontaneous version of ARIA.
Repeat MRI to confirm resolution and monitor for relapse during steroid taper.
det.thd: CAA-ri คือภาวะที่ระบบภูมิคุ้มกันอักเสบต่อ amyloid ที่สะสมในผนังหลอดเลือดสมองของผู้สูงอายุ ผู้ป่วยมีอาการสับสน ความจำถดถอยเร็ว ปวดศีรษะ ชัก หรืออ่อนแรงในเวลาไม่กี่สัปดาห์ MRI พบสมองบวมในเนื้อขาวแบบไม่สมมาตรร่วมกับ microbleed จำนวนมาก เป็นภาวะคล้าย ARIA จากยารักษาอัลไซเมอร์ รักษาด้วย steroid ขนาดสูงซึ่งได้ผลดี แต่กลับเป็นซ้ำได้

name: Patent foramen ovale (PFO)-associated stroke
formal: Ischaemic stroke attributed to paradoxical embolism (or in-situ thrombus) through a patent foramen ovale in a patient, usually under 60, with an otherwise cryptogenic embolic-appearing infarct; risk is graded with the RoPE score and PASCAL classification, and percutaneous closure reduces recurrence in selected patients.
simple: A stroke caused when a clot from the veins slips through a small hole between the upper chambers of the heart and travels to the brain; closing the hole can prevent another stroke in suitable young patients.
th: stroke ในคนอายุน้อยที่หาสาเหตุอื่นไม่พบ และมีรูรั่วผนังกั้นห้องบนของหัวใจ — ลิ่มเลือดจากหลอดเลือดดำผ่านรูไปสมอง (paradoxical embolism) ประเมินด้วย RoPE/PASCAL และพิจารณาปิดรู PFO
tempoNote: Sudden embolic event, sometimes after Valsalva-type straining, coughing or a long journey
feat: Age usually 18–60 with no hypertension, diabetes or smoking (high RoPE score)
Superficial cortical or single embolic-looking infarct, often in posterior circulation
Onset during Valsalva (lifting, straining, coughing) or with concurrent DVT/PE
Larger shunt or atrial septal aneurysm increases the likelihood that the PFO is causal
inv: Transthoracic or transoesophageal echo with agitated saline bubble study (TOE shows shunt size and septal aneurysm)
Transcranial Doppler bubble study: sensitive screen for right-to-left shunt
Exclude other causes: vessel imaging, prolonged cardiac rhythm monitoring for AF, thrombophilia screen when indicated
Leg vein Doppler if venous thrombosis is suspected

case.story: While lifting heavy cement bags he suddenly could not find words and his right hand became clumsy. Non-smoker, no hypertension or diabetes.
case.exam: Mild expressive aphasia and right hand weakness.
case.tests: MRI: single cortical infarct in the left MCA branch territory; CTA normal; 7-day Holter normal; TOE bubble study: large right-to-left shunt across a PFO with atrial septal aneurysm. RoPE score 8.
case.q: What secondary prevention is recommended?
case.a: PFO-associated stroke with high-risk anatomy and high RoPE (PASCAL 'probable') — percutaneous PFO closure plus antiplatelet therapy is recommended over medical therapy alone.

det.patho: The foramen ovale fails to seal after birth in about a quarter of adults, leaving a flap-valve channel between the atria. When right atrial pressure transiently exceeds left (Valsalva, coughing, pulmonary embolism) venous thrombus can cross into the systemic circulation. Thrombus may also form within the tunnel itself, and atrial septal aneurysm adds risk. Because PFO is so common, many PFOs found after stroke are incidental.
det.clinical: The typical patient is a young or middle-aged adult with an embolic stroke without vascular risk factors or another identifiable cause. Infarcts are often cortical, cerebellar or occipital rather than lacunar. Some patients report onset during straining or have concurrent DVT or pulmonary embolism. Recurrence risk with medical therapy is low but meaningful over a young person's lifetime.
det.diagnosis: First exclude other mechanisms: large-artery disease, dissection, AF (prolonged monitoring), small vessel disease and other cardiac sources. Demonstrate a right-to-left shunt with bubble contrast echocardiography or transcranial Doppler, and characterise shunt size and septal anatomy with TOE. Use the RoPE score (likelihood the PFO is causal) and the PASCAL classification, which combines RoPE with high-risk anatomy, to decide on closure.
det.treatment: Acute stroke is treated in the usual way. For patients aged roughly 18–60 with a PFO-associated non-lacunar stroke and a 'probable' or 'highly probable' PASCAL class, percutaneous device closure plus antiplatelet therapy lowers recurrent stroke compared with antiplatelet therapy alone (CLOSE, RESPECT, REDUCE). Closure carries a small risk of procedural AF, mostly transient. Anticoagulation is indicated if there is concomitant venous thromboembolism or a thrombophilia; otherwise antiplatelet therapy is used when closure is not chosen.
det.prognosis: After closure the annual recurrence risk is very low (well under 1% per year); outcomes after the index stroke are generally good.
pearls: Prove there is no better explanation before blaming the PFO.
High RoPE score + large shunt or septal aneurysm = strongest case for closure.
Stroke during heavy lifting or with a DVT strongly hints at paradoxical embolism.
det.thd: PFO-associated stroke คือ stroke ที่เกิดจากลิ่มเลือดในหลอดเลือดดำผ่านรูรั่วระหว่างหัวใจห้องบนขวาและซ้าย (patent foramen ovale) ขึ้นไปอุดหลอดเลือดสมอง มักพบในคนอายุน้อยที่ไม่มีปัจจัยเสี่ยงอื่น ต้องตัดสาเหตุอื่นออกก่อน ตรวจพบรูรั่วด้วย echocardiography หรือ TCD แบบ bubble study ใช้ RoPE score และ PASCAL ประเมิน หากเหมาะสม การปิดรูผ่านสายสวนร่วมกับยาต้านเกล็ดเลือดช่วยลดการเป็นซ้ำ

name: Cortical superficial siderosis
formal: Linear haemosiderin deposition along the cortical sulci over the cerebral convexities, seen on blood-sensitive MRI, that results from previous convexity subarachnoid haemorrhage; most commonly a marker of cerebral amyloid angiopathy, it predicts transient focal neurological episodes and future lobar haemorrhage, and differs from infratentorial (classical) superficial siderosis.
simple: Old blood staining on the surface of the brain seen on MRI, usually from fragile amyloid-damaged vessels, which warns of future brain bleeds and can cause brief 'spells' of tingling or weakness.
th: คราบ haemosiderin ตามร่องผิวสมองด้านบน (convexity) เห็นใน SWI — มักเป็นเครื่องหมายของ CAA ทำให้มี 'amyloid spells' ชาหรืออ่อนแรงลามเป็นช่วงสั้น ๆ และเสี่ยงเลือดออกในสมองสูง ควรหลีกเลี่ยงยาต้านลิ่มเลือด
tempoNote: A lasting MRI marker; spells (TFNEs) last minutes and recur in stereotyped fashion
feat: Often found in older patients with cognitive impairment or after a lobar haemorrhage
Transient focal neurological episodes: spreading tingling, numbness or weakness over minutes, sometimes visual or speech symptoms
Disseminated (more than 3 sulci) siderosis carries the highest bleeding risk
Distinct from infratentorial siderosis, which causes deafness and ataxia
inv: MRI SWI/GRE: curvilinear low signal following cortical gyri, plus lobar microbleeds
CT in the acute phase: small sulcal hyperdensity of convexity SAH
Apply the Boston criteria 2.0 for CAA (cSS counts as a haemorrhagic marker)
In younger patients, look for RCVS, PRES, vasculitis or venous thrombosis as the source

case.story: Three episodes in a month of tingling that marches from the left fingers up to the face over a few minutes and then clears. GP started aspirin for presumed TIA.
case.exam: Normal neurological examination between spells; MoCA 23/30.
case.tests: CT: tiny right central sulcus hyperdensity; MRI SWI: siderosis over several right frontoparietal sulci and 15 lobar microbleeds; no DWI lesion.
case.q: What are these spells and what change should be made to treatment?

det.patho: Small bleeds from fragile, amyloid-laden leptomeningeal vessels leak blood into the convexity sulci, and haemosiderin left behind stains the cortical surface. Repeated convexity bleeding and spreading depolarisation in the underlying cortex probably explain transient focal symptoms. Other causes of convexity bleeding include RCVS, PRES, cortical vein thrombosis, vasculitis and trauma.
det.clinical: Many cases are discovered on MRI done for dementia or a prior lobar haemorrhage. Transient focal neurological episodes are characteristic: brief, recurrent, often positive and spreading sensory or motor symptoms that can mimic TIA, migraine aura or focal seizures. The siderosis itself does not cause hearing loss or ataxia, unlike classical infratentorial siderosis from chronic dural leaks.
det.diagnosis: Use SWI or GRE MRI to identify linear cortical low signal and classify it as focal (up to three sulci) or disseminated. In older adults, combine with lobar microbleeds and haemorrhages to apply the Boston 2.0 criteria for CAA. In younger patients or atypical cases, investigate other causes of convexity SAH with vessel and venous imaging. Distinguish TFNEs from TIA because the management differs.
det.treatment: There is no treatment that removes the haemosiderin; management focuses on preventing haemorrhage. Control blood pressure tightly, avoid antiplatelets and anticoagulants unless there is a compelling indication, and consider left atrial appendage occlusion instead of anticoagulation in AF. TFNEs may respond to antiseizure or migraine-preventive drugs. Avoid anti-amyloid antibody therapy in patients with extensive siderosis because of ARIA and bleeding risk.
det.prognosis: Disseminated siderosis predicts a high risk of first or recurrent lobar haemorrhage (around a quarter within a few years in some cohorts).
pearls: Spreading tingling that marches over minutes in an older person: check SWI before starting aspirin.
cSS is one of the strongest predictors of future ICH in CAA.
Supratentorial convexity siderosis is not the same disease as infratentorial superficial siderosis.
det.thd: Cortical superficial siderosis คือคราบเหล็กจากเลือดเก่าตามร่องผิวสมองด้านบน มองเห็นใน MRI แบบ SWI ส่วนใหญ่เกิดจาก cerebral amyloid angiopathy ในผู้สูงอายุ ผู้ป่วยอาจมีอาการชาหรืออ่อนแรงลามเป็นช่วงสั้น ๆ ซ้ำ ๆ ที่เรียกว่า amyloid spells ซึ่งต้องแยกจาก TIA เพราะภาวะนี้เสี่ยงเลือดออกในสมองสูง ควรควบคุมความดันและหลีกเลี่ยงยาต้านเกล็ดเลือดหรือยาละลายลิ่มเลือดหากไม่จำเป็น

name: Amyloid-related imaging abnormalities (ARIA)
formal: MRI changes that appear during anti-amyloid monoclonal antibody therapy for Alzheimer disease, comprising vasogenic oedema or sulcal effusion (ARIA-E) and haemosiderin deposition as microhaemorrhages or superficial siderosis (ARIA-H).
simple: Brain swelling or tiny bleeds seen on MRI in some people treated with new anti-amyloid drugs for Alzheimer disease.

feat: Occurs on anti-amyloid antibodies, mostly in the first 3–6 doses; many cases are found only on scheduled safety MRI
Symptoms when present: headache, confusion, visual change, unsteadiness, nausea; rarely seizures, status epilepticus or focal deficits

det.patho: Antibodies that bind aggregated amyloid-beta clear parenchymal plaques, and the mobilised amyloid moves toward the perivascular drainage pathways while antibodies also engage amyloid already lodged in vessel walls (cerebral amyloid angiopathy). The resulting vascular inflammation and loss of wall integrity let fluid leak into tissue or sulci (ARIA-E) and blood products escape (ARIA-H). The process mirrors spontaneous CAA-related inflammation, in which autoantibodies against amyloid produce the same picture. Antibody isotype, epitope and dose shape the risk, and APOE e4 carriers, who carry heavier vascular amyloid, are most susceptible. Because the vessel-wall amyloid of CAA is the substrate, markers of advanced CAA (multiple lobar microbleeds, cortical superficial siderosis, previous lobar haemorrhage) and poorly controlled blood pressure raise the risk of both ARIA and treatment-related intracerebral haemorrhage, and the same fragile vessels explain why thrombolytics and anticoagulants are so hazardous during therapy.
det.clinical: Most episodes are silent and appear only on protocol MRI, typically early in treatment. Symptomatic cases present with headache, confusion, behavioural change, visual disturbance, dizziness or gait difficulty, and a minority become serious with seizures, status epilepticus, focal deficits or coma; deaths have been reported, mostly with severe ARIA or after thrombolysis or anticoagulation. ARIA-E often resolves within a few months, whereas microbleeds and siderosis persist. Recurrence is possible after rechallenge, and the risk of new ARIA-E falls considerably after the first six months of dosing. Because treated patients are of stroke age, ARIA and acute ischaemic stroke can look identical at the bedside — and the two occasionally coexist, with small infarcts seen alongside moderate or severe ARIA. A falling cognitive score or any new focal or global symptom in a treated patient should be regarded as ARIA until MRI says otherwise.
det.diagnosis: MRI is the test: FLAIR shows ARIA-E as swollen hyperintense cortex and white matter or sulcal effusion without diffusion restriction, and SWI or GRE shows ARIA-H as new microbleeds or curvilinear superficial siderosis. Compare against the baseline scan on the same protocol; SWI detects more microbleeds than GRE, so changing sequence can mimic new lesions. Severity is graded radiologically (extent of oedema; mild about 4 or fewer new microbleeds and a single siderosis focus, moderate 5–9 and two foci, severe 10 or more or wider siderosis) and combined with clinical severity. Before lecanemab, the appropriate use recommendations exclude people with more than 4 microbleeds, any area of superficial siderosis, existing vasogenic oedema, a previous haemorrhage over 10 mm, more than 2 lacunes or any infarct in a major vascular territory, severe white matter disease (Fazekas 3), features of CAA-related inflammation, stroke or TIA in the past 12 months, any seizure history, a bleeding disorder or current anticoagulation; ARIA-E itself is graded radiographically as mild (single site under 5 cm), moderate (5–10 cm or more than one site each under 10 cm) or severe (over 10 cm with gyral swelling and sulcal effacement). When a treated patient arrives with new oedema on emergency CT, the differential is ARIA-E, acute infarct, PRES, encephalitis and tumour: ARIA-E favours occipital and temporal more than frontal lobes, ignores arterial territories and usually does not restrict on DWI, so urgent MRI should be obtained readily.
det.treatment: Under the lecanemab AUR, radiographically mild ARIA without symptoms allows dosing to continue with monthly MRI until ARIA-E resolves and ARIA-H stabilises; mild ARIA with any symptoms, or moderate ARIA, means suspending infusions until resolution, after which restarting is a shared decision; severe radiographic ARIA or severe (incapacitating) symptoms means stopping. The AUR also advises permanent discontinuation after any macrohaemorrhage, new superficial siderosis, more than 10 new microbleeds since starting, more than two ARIA episodes, or a new need for anticoagulation. Serious symptomatic ARIA is managed in hospital with early high-dose corticosteroids (for example IV methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 5 days followed by an oral taper over several weeks), seizure monitoring and treatment, and supportive care; any intracerebral haemorrhage follows standard ICH care. For suspected stroke in a treated patient (2026 AHA ARIA Summit consensus): activate the stroke pathway as usual, but generally withhold IV thrombolysis when MRI cannot exclude ARIA or shows it — consider it without MRI only in selected severe deficits after specialist discussion — and send patients with a large vessel occlusion straight to thrombectomy without bridging lysis, keeping procedural antithrombotics to a minimum. Long-term anticoagulation is advised against during therapy; for atrial fibrillation, left atrial appendage occlusion or a pause in treatment may be weighed, venous thromboembolism anticoagulation is ideally completed before starting, aspirin alone is reasonable, dual antiplatelet therapy calls for caution or a temporary pause, and prophylactic-dose heparin is probably safe. Control blood pressure, give patients an alert card, flag treatment in the medical record, and report ARIA on every MRI with a structured template.
det.prognosis: ARIA-E usually resolves radiologically within weeks to a few months, and most patients recover fully; ARIA-H is permanent, and a small proportion of serious cases cause lasting deficits or death.
pearls: APOE e4 homozygotes have the highest ARIA rates (ARIA-E about 33% on lecanemab versus about 5% in non-carriers, symptomatic about 9% versus 1–2%) — genotype before treatment and counsel accordingly.
In a patient on lecanemab or donanemab, new confusion or a stroke-like event is ARIA until proven otherwise — get MRI before thrombolysis.
No diffusion restriction separates ARIA-E from infarction; the FLAIR change often hugs the sulci.
Patient on anti-amyloid therapy with a large vessel occlusion: go directly to thrombectomy and skip bridging IV lysis.

name: ADCY5-related dyskinesia (ADCY5-RD)
formal: Genetic hyperkinetic movement disorder caused by gain-of-function variants in ADCY5, which raise striatal cAMP; it presents in infancy or childhood with chorea, dystonia and myoclonus that characteristically flare in paroxysms around sleep, with normal EEG and MRI.
simple: A gene change makes a movement-control enzyme overactive, so a child has jerky, twisting movements that come in strong bursts, often when falling asleep or waking, while thinking stays normal.

Violent paroxysmal bursts at sleep onset (N1–N2), in REM, at sleep–wake transitions or on waking

case.story: Since infancy he has fidgety jerky limbs; most nights, minutes after falling asleep, he wakes in a storm of flinging and twisting movements lasting up to an hour. Laughing with friends sets off brief attacks. Three antiseizure drugs did nothing.
case.exam: Generalized chorea with dystonic posturing of the hands, low axial tone, twitching around the eyes and mouth, normal speech content and school performance.
case.tests: Overnight video-EEG captures 4 episodes with no electrographic change; MRI brain normal; exome: de novo ADCY5 c.1252C>T (p.R418W).
case.q: Which simple treatment should be tried first, and what should happen to his antiseizure drugs?
case.a: An adenosine A2A antagonist — usually caffeine (or theophylline/istradefylline) — which lowers striatal cAMP; the ineffective antiseizure drugs can be tapered. Clonazepam is an option and pallidal DBS is reserved for refractory cases or dyskinetic storms.

det.patho: ADCY5 encodes adenylyl cyclase 5, the enzyme that makes most of the cAMP in striatal medium spiny neurons; its activity is pushed up by adenosine A2A receptors (via Golf) and held down by dopamine D2 receptors (via Gi/o), so it sits at the crossroads of indirect-pathway signalling. Most heterozygous missense variants are gain-of-function, raising striatal cAMP and destabilising basal ganglia output, which is why A2A blockers such as caffeine damp the abnormal drive. Inheritance is usually autosomal dominant, but de novo variants are common, somatic mosaicism is relatively frequent (and tends to give milder, purely paroxysmal disease), and a handful of families carry biallelic, probably loss-of-function variants with a more severe picture. Variant position shapes the phenotype: the recurrent p.R418W/Q hot spot in the catalytic C1a domain gives early, severe disease with nocturnal attacks and axial hypotonia, C1b changes such as p.A726T tend to be milder, and membrane-domain variants have been linked to spastic paraparesis. The original 2001 family was reported under the name FDFM, a label that predates discovery of the gene.
det.clinical: Onset is usually between 1 and 4 years (range from early infancy to about 10 years), sometimes preceded by neonatal hypotonia, poor feeding or an exaggerated startle. The core is a mixed permanent hyperkinetic disorder — chorea that worsens with action, dystonia, myoclonus and sometimes tremor — on which paroxysmal bursts are superimposed; in the largest series about nine in ten had both. The signature is nocturnal attacks lasting up to about 30 minutes that arise at drowsiness or, especially, on morning or night-time awakenings and stop the child getting back to sleep, while daytime attacks follow emotion, stress, fatigue, illness or heat, with preserved awareness and no postictal state. Perioral and periorbital twitches, axial hypotonia with delayed milestones (sometimes a 'frog-like' crawl or gait), and dysarthria in roughly two-thirds are typical; less common features include vertical saccade initiation failure, episodes mimicking alternating hemiplegia, pyramidal signs, attention problems, anxiety or OCD in children and depression or psychosis in adults. Intellect is usually normal or mildly affected, except in recessive cases.
det.diagnosis: Think of it in a child labelled dyskinetic cerebral palsy, 'sleep-related hypermotor epilepsy' or unexplained chorea, particularly when attacks cluster at sleep–wake transitions and the face twitches. Video-EEG or polysomnography shows the episodes arise from wakefulness or arousal without an ictal correlate, and brain MRI and metabolic tests are typically normal. Confirm with ADCY5 sequencing, usually within a hyperkinetic movement-disorder panel or exome; a mild phenotype or negative standard test should prompt deeper sequencing or allele-specific PCR for mosaicism. Because a few families also had heart muscle disease (dilated cardiomyopathy) or an underactive thyroid, an echocardiogram and thyroid function tests are sensible at diagnosis. Differentials include NKX2-1 benign hereditary chorea, GNAO1 and PDE10A disorders, myoclonus-dystonia and alternating hemiplegia of childhood.
det.treatment: Evidence is limited to case series, but caffeine is the most consistently helpful first step: in a survey of 30 patients nearly nine in ten reported at least a 40% reduction in hyperkinetic movements, with gains in sleep, gait, speech and mood; theophylline (including slow-release preparations) and the selective A2A antagonist istradefylline are alternatives. Benzodiazepines — clonazepam, clobazam or diazepam — are the usual second option, especially for nocturnal paroxysms, and propranolol may ease chorea. Tetrabenazine, trihexyphenidyl, acetazolamide and levodopa help some patients but worsen others, so trial one drug at a time and stop ineffective antiseizure drugs. Bilateral GPi deep brain stimulation can reduce both permanent and paroxysmal movements and has been used as a rescue for dyskinetic storms, but benefit is partial, less than in DYT-TOR1A dystonia, and may fade.
det.prognosis: The disorder is largely non-progressive and life expectancy appears normal, although data are sparse. Chorea and ballistic bursts often lessen in adolescence with a shift toward dystonia and myoclonus; some adults improve, others have more frequent attacks or later spasticity, and complete remission is rare.
pearls: Paroxysmal dyskinesia that erupts on waking or at sleep onset, with a normal EEG and facial twitching: test ADCY5.
Ask about coffee — caffeine is cheap, often effective and is now the usual first trial.
A mild, purely paroxysmal case with a negative routine test may be mosaic: ask the lab for deep sequencing.
Check an echocardiogram and thyroid function; cardiomyopathy and hypothyroidism have been reported in some families.

det.patho: Brief focal ischaemia of brain, retina or cord that resolves before infarction develops; the modern definition is tissue-based, so a DWI lesion makes it a minor stroke whatever the duration (about a third of classic TIAs show one). Mechanisms mirror ischaemic stroke: artery-to-artery embolism from carotid or intracranial plaque, cardioembolism (AF, PFO in the young), small vessel disease and low-flow states distal to a tight stenosis. Platelet-rich emboli that fragment quickly explain why symptoms clear, but the same unstable source can produce a lasting stroke within hours. TIA is therefore best seen as a medical emergency signalling imminent risk, not a benign event.
det.clinical: Most episodes last minutes and begin suddenly with negative symptoms: weakness, numbness, loss of speech or monocular vision loss (amaurosis fugax, often described as a shade coming down). Repeated stereotyped events, especially limb-shaking, suggest critical carotid stenosis with haemodynamic failure, while recurrent stuttering face-arm-leg weakness points to a capsular warning syndrome from a single perforator. Posterior circulation TIAs are harder to recognise: combinations of vertigo, diplopia, dysarthria, ataxia or bilateral visual loss count, whereas isolated dizziness, syncope, confusion or amnesia are rarely TIA. Crescendo TIAs signal an unstable lesion and need same-day assessment. Stroke risk after TIA is front-loaded, about half of it falling within the first 48 hours.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis rests on the history, ideally from a witness, because examination is usually normal by the time the patient is seen. Every patient needs urgent brain MRI with DWI, vessel imaging of the neck and ideally intracranial arteries (duplex, CTA or MRA), ECG with prolonged rhythm monitoring, glucose, lipids and HbA1c. ABCD2 and similar scores discriminate poorly: low scores still miss AF and symptomatic carotid stenosis, so current guidance favours seeing every suspected TIA in a specialist clinic within 24 hours rather than triaging by score. Imaging findings (DWI lesion, large-artery stenosis or occlusion) predict early stroke better than clinical scores. Exclude migraine aura, focal seizures, hypoglycaemia, syncope, transient global amnesia and amyloid spells, which should not receive antithrombotic loading by reflex.
det.treatment: Start antithrombotic treatment immediately: for high-risk non-cardioembolic TIA or minor stroke, give aspirin plus clopidogrel (loading dose) within 24 hours and continue for about 21 days, then a single agent; recent trials support starting up to 72 hours in atherosclerotic events, and ticagrelor plus aspirin is an option for CYP2C19 loss-of-function carriers. Anticoagulate with a DOAC if AF is found. Add a high-intensity statin, BP control, diabetes management, exercise and smoking cessation. Symptomatic 50–99% carotid stenosis should be revascularised, preferably within 2 weeks, with endarterectomy favoured in older patients and stenting an alternative in selected younger ones. PFO closure is considered for patients aged 60 or under whose embolic event remains otherwise unexplained.
det.prognosis: With rapid specialist assessment and treatment the early stroke risk falls by most of its magnitude; without it, roughly one in ten patients have a stroke within 3 months.
pearls: Duration does not define TIA; a DWI lesion upgrades it to minor stroke.
Amaurosis fugax is a carotid TIA — image the neck vessels urgently.
Limb-shaking TIA mimics seizure but reflects severe carotid stenosis.
A low ABCD2 score does not make a TIA safe; imaging and rhythm findings matter more.

det.patho: Clot in the dural sinuses or cortical veins impedes venous outflow, raising venous and intracranial pressure and reducing CSF absorption at the arachnoid granulations; local congestion produces vasogenic and cytotoxic oedema, venous infarcts and haemorrhage that respect no arterial territory. Most patients have at least one prothrombotic trigger — pregnancy and puerperium, oestrogen-containing contraception, inherited or acquired thrombophilia (including antiphospholipid syndrome), cancer, dehydration, infection of the ear, sinuses or face, head injury, or vaccine-induced thrombotic thrombocytopenia (anti-PF4 antibodies). Young women are affected about three times as often as men. The superior sagittal and transverse sinuses are most often involved, and partial spontaneous recanalisation is common.
det.clinical: Headache is present in about nine in ten, usually building over days, sometimes thunderclap or presenting as isolated intracranial hypertension with papilloedema and sixth nerve palsy. Other presentations are focal or generalised seizures (more frequent than in arterial stroke), focal deficits that may be bilateral or alternate, aphasia with left transverse sinus involvement, and encephalopathy. Deep venous system thrombosis causes bithalamic or basal ganglia lesions with drowsiness, memory loss or coma. Cavernous sinus thrombosis, usually septic, gives proptosis, chemosis and painful ophthalmoplegia. The picture often fluctuates, and isolated cortical vein thrombosis can mimic a TIA or produce convexity SAH.
det.diagnosis: MR venography or CT venography shows absent flow or a filling defect; MRI with SWI/T2* displays thrombus in sinuses and cortical veins and is the best test for isolated cortical vein clot. Plain CT may show a dense sinus or cord sign, and contrast CT the empty delta sign, but is often normal. Pitfalls include hypoplastic or atretic transverse sinuses and large arachnoid granulations, which mimic thrombus on venography. D-dimer can be normal, especially with isolated headache or late presentation, so it cannot exclude CVT. Look for the cause: full blood count (falling platelets suggest VITT or heparin-induced thrombocytopenia), infection, malignancy, antiphospholipid antibodies, and other thrombophilia tests timed sensibly.
det.treatment: Anticoagulate promptly with low-molecular-weight or unfractionated heparin even when haemorrhage is present, because stopping clot propagation is what lowers venous pressure. After the acute phase switch to oral anticoagulation for 3–12 months: dabigatran and other DOACs performed similarly to warfarin with less bleeding in trials and observational cohorts, whereas antiphospholipid syndrome still calls for warfarin; continue long-term after recurrent thrombosis or with severe thrombophilia. Treat seizures with antiseizure drugs (no routine prophylaxis), manage raised pressure and threatened vision, treat infection, and stop oestrogen; corticosteroids are unhelpful. Endovascular thrombectomy did not improve outcome in a randomised trial and is reserved for deterioration despite adequate anticoagulation, while decompressive craniectomy can be life-saving for large mass lesions with herniation. VITT needs non-heparin anticoagulation (argatroban, fondaparinux or a DOAC), IVIG, and avoidance of platelet transfusion.
det.prognosis: Most patients recover fully or with minor deficits; poor outcome is linked to coma, deep venous involvement, haemorrhage, malignancy and CNS infection. Headache, fatigue and mood problems often persist, and later pregnancy is generally allowed with LMWH prophylaxis.
pearls: Haemorrhage is not a contraindication to heparin in CVT.
Always exclude CVT before labelling raised pressure as IIH.
Bilateral parasagittal haemorrhagic lesions = think superior sagittal sinus thrombosis.
A normal D-dimer does not exclude CVT, and a low platelet count should prompt testing for VITT or HIT.
det.thd: ลิ่มเลือดอุดหลอดเลือดดำหรือ dural sinus ในสมอง ทำให้ความดันในกะโหลกสูง สมองบวม และอาจมีเลือดออกแบบ venous infarct ที่ไม่ตรงกับ territory หลอดเลือดแดง พบบ่อยในหญิงอายุน้อย ตั้งครรภ์ หลังคลอด หรือกินยาคุม อาการคือปวดศีรษะที่ค่อย ๆ แย่ลง ชัก อ่อนแรง และ papilloedema วินิจฉัยด้วย MRV หรือ CTV (D-dimer ปกติก็ยังเป็นได้) การรักษาคือให้ heparin ทันทีแม้มีเลือดออก แล้วต่อด้วย warfarin หรือ DOAC 3–12 เดือน (ใช้ warfarin ใน antiphospholipid syndrome) การทำ thrombectomy สงวนไว้เมื่ออาการแย่ลงแม้ได้ยาเต็มที่

name: Cervical artery dissection
formal: Tear in the wall of the carotid or vertebral artery producing an intramural haematoma, local pain and pressure signs, and thromboembolic stroke; a leading cause of stroke in young adults.
simple: A tear inside a neck artery that can cause neck pain or headache and a stroke, often after minor neck strain or trauma.
th: ผนังหลอดเลือดแดงที่คอฉีกขาด — ปวดคอ/ศีรษะข้างเดียว อาจมี Horner และ stroke ในคนอายุน้อย
feat: Unilateral neck, face or occipital pain preceding ischaemic symptoms
Painful partial Horner syndrome (carotid) or posterior circulation stroke (vertebral)
Lower cranial nerve palsies or pulsatile tinnitus may occur
inv: CTA or MRA of the neck; MRI fat-suppressed T1 shows crescent intramural haematoma

case.story: Left-sided neck pain after a chiropractic adjustment, then 2 days later clumsy speech and right hand weakness.
case.exam: Left ptosis and miosis without anhidrosis of the face, mild expressive dysphasia, right hand weakness.
case.tests: MRI: small left MCA infarcts; neck MRI: crescent of intramural blood in the left ICA.
case.q: Explain the Horner syndrome.
case.a: Sympathetic fibres travel on the internal carotid wall; the dissection injures them (third-order neuron), sparing facial sweating fibres that follow the external carotid.

Chapter 49: Headache attributed to carotid or vertebral artery pain

ddx.pt: Atherosclerotic/cardioembolic stroke lacks preceding neck pain and Horner
Recurrent stereotyped aura; no vessel wall haematoma
Recurrent thunderclap headaches; multifocal intracranial narrowing

aN: carotid dissection | vertebral dissection | cervical artery dissection | cad | arterial dissection

det.patho: An intimal tear or rupture of the vasa vasorum creates an intramural haematoma that may narrow the lumen, expand outward as a pseudoaneurysm, or seed emboli — embolism rather than low flow is the commonest route to stroke. Triggers range from obvious trauma to trivial neck movements such as sport, coughing or manipulation; connective tissue disorders (vascular Ehlers–Danlos, Marfan), fibromuscular dysplasia, migraine and recent infection are associated, suggesting an underlying arterial wall weakness. It accounts for up to a quarter of ischaemic strokes under 50. Extracranial segments of the ICA and vertebral artery (V3 at C1–C2) are typical sites, whereas intracranial dissection, more frequent in Asian patients, can rupture and cause SAH.
det.clinical: Carotid dissection classically combines ipsilateral head, face or neck pain, a partial Horner syndrome (ptosis and miosis without anhidrosis) and later hemispheric or retinal ischaemia; lower cranial nerve palsies (especially XII), pulsatile tinnitus and altered taste may appear. Vertebral dissection presents with posterior neck or occipital pain followed by lateral medullary, cerebellar or other posterior circulation stroke, and occasionally cervical root symptoms or cord infarction. Pain may precede ischaemia by hours to days, giving a window for prevention. Some cases are bilateral or multivessel, which should prompt a search for a connective tissue disorder. Intracranial dissection may present instead with thunderclap headache and SAH.
det.diagnosis: CTA or contrast MRA shows a tapering stenosis, flame-shaped occlusion, string sign, pseudoaneurysm, double lumen or intimal flap. Fat-saturated T1 MRI of the neck shows the crescent of intramural haematoma, though it may only become bright after the first few days as methaemoglobin forms, so early scans can look falsely reassuring. Ultrasound can miss distal ICA and vertebral lesions. DSA is reserved for unclear cases or endovascular planning. Consider fibromuscular dysplasia and inherited connective tissue disease in recurrent or multivessel cases, and image the intracranial vessels to detect intracranial extension.
det.treatment: Acute ischaemic stroke from extracranial dissection is treated with IV thrombolysis and thrombectomy under the usual criteria. For secondary prevention, randomised trials and meta-analyses found antiplatelet therapy and anticoagulation broadly similar: anticoagulation may prevent slightly more early ischaemic events at the cost of more bleeding, so the choice is individualised — anticoagulation is favoured for occlusion, intraluminal thrombus or recurrent events on antiplatelets, and antiplatelets for large infarcts, intracranial extension or bleeding risk. Short-term dual antiplatelet therapy is used by some centres but is not trial-proven. Treat for 3–6 months, re-image, then usually continue a single antiplatelet if the artery remains abnormal. Stenting is reserved for recurrent ischaemia despite medical therapy or an enlarging symptomatic pseudoaneurysm; advise against neck manipulation and heavy straining while healing.
det.prognosis: Most dissections heal or recanalise within months, recurrence is uncommon (a few percent, mostly in the first year), and outcome is set mainly by the initial stroke; pseudoaneurysms rarely cause later problems.
pearls: Neck pain + Horner + stroke in a young adult = carotid dissection.
The Horner is postganglionic, so facial sweating is largely preserved.
Vertebral dissection is a common cause of lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome in the young.
Intracranial dissection can bleed into the subarachnoid space, so be cautious with antithrombotics there.
det.thd: ผนังหลอดเลือดแดง carotid หรือ vertebral ที่คอฉีกขาดจนเกิดเลือดคั่งในผนัง ทำให้หลอดเลือดตีบหรือเกิดลิ่มเลือดหลุดไปอุดสมอง เป็นสาเหตุสำคัญของ stroke ในคนอายุน้อยกว่า 50 ปี อาการคือปวดคอหรือศีรษะข้างเดียว ร่วมกับ Horner syndrome บางส่วน แล้วตามด้วยอาการ stroke วินิจฉัยด้วย CTA/MRA และ MRI คอแบบ fat-saturated T1 ให้ยาละลายลิ่มเลือดหรือ thrombectomy ได้ตามเกณฑ์ปกติ ป้องกันซ้ำด้วย antiplatelet หรือ anticoagulant ซึ่งได้ผลใกล้เคียงกัน เลือกตามลักษณะผู้ป่วย นาน 3–6 เดือนแล้วตรวจซ้ำ ส่วน dissection ในกะโหลกอาจทำให้เลือดออกใต้เยื่อหุ้มสมองได้

name: Chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy
formal: A dose-related, mostly length-dependent sensory (sometimes motor or autonomic) neuropathy caused by neurotoxic anticancer drugs such as platinum agents, taxanes, vinca alkaloids, bortezomib and thalidomide.
simple: Nerve damage from cancer medicines that causes numbness, tingling or pain, usually starting in the fingers and toes.
th: ปลายประสาทอักเสบจากยาเคมีบำบัด — ชา เจ็บแปลบ ปลายมือปลายเท้า ขึ้นกับขนาดยาสะสม
tempoNote: Develops over weeks to months of treatment; platinum damage may keep worsening for months after stopping (coasting)
feat: Symmetric stocking-glove numbness, tingling or burning that tracks cumulative dose
Oxaliplatin: cold-triggered acute paraesthesia of hands and mouth, jaw or throat tightness within hours of infusion
Cisplatin: pure sensory neuronopathy with loss of proprioception and ataxia
Vincristine: sensorimotor with foot drop, cramps, constipation, jaw pain; worse with CMT
Bortezomib/taxanes: painful small-fibre symptoms; possible autonomic features
inv: Clinical grading (e.g. CTCAE) at each cycle; quantitative sensory exam
NCS: reduced sensory amplitudes (axonal) — confirms and grades, but is not needed in typical cases
Exclude other causes: glucose/HbA1c, B12, thyroid, paraprotein, tumour infiltration or paraneoplastic disease

case.who: 58-year-old man with colon cancer on FOLFOX
case.story: Each infusion leaves his fingers tingling when he touches cold water; after 8 cycles numbness persists and he drops coins and buttons.
case.exam: Reduced vibration and joint position at toes and fingers, absent ankle jerks, positive Romberg; power normal.
case.tests: NCS: low sural and radial sensory amplitudes with normal motor responses; HbA1c and B12 normal.
case.q: What should the oncology team consider now?
case.a: Dose reduction, delay or stopping oxaliplatin, since persistent functional neuropathy usually outweighs further benefit; duloxetine can be tried for pain. Warn that symptoms may worsen for a few months after stopping.

read.where: Chapter 14 Medication-Related Neuropathy (Peripheral neuropathies associated with chemotherapeutic agents)

det.patho: Most agents injure the dorsal root ganglion or distal axon. Platinum drugs accumulate in dorsal root ganglion neurons and damage DNA, giving a neuronopathy; taxanes and vinca alkaloids disturb microtubules and axonal transport; bortezomib affects proteasome function and mitochondria. Oxaliplatin's acute cold-induced symptoms reflect a transient sodium-channel effect on peripheral nerve excitability. The dorsal root ganglion lies outside an effective blood–nerve barrier, which is why platinum compounds produce a non-length-dependent ganglionopathy rather than a purely distal axonopathy. Thalidomide and lenalidomide, epothilones (ixabepilone), eribulin, brentuximab vedotin and immune checkpoint inhibitors widen the list; checkpoint inhibitors act through autoimmunity rather than dose-dependent toxicity.
det.clinical: Sensory symptoms dominate and start distally, with risk increasing with cumulative dose, dose intensity, pre-existing neuropathy, diabetes and alcohol; combinations such as carboplatin with paclitaxel are especially toxic. Vincristine adds motor weakness (wrist and toe extensors), cranial nerve palsies and autonomic constipation or even ileus, and can be devastating in undiagnosed CMT1A. Cisplatin gives a sensory ganglionopathy with loss of joint position sense, sensory ataxia and sometimes Lhermitte's sign, usually beyond about 300 mg/m² cumulative, and both cisplatin and oxaliplatin may show 'coasting' — progression for 2–6 months after the last dose. Oxaliplatin causes cold-provoked acute dysaesthesia of the hands, mouth and throat in most patients, settling within days of each infusion; paclitaxel can cause acute aching or myalgia days after infusion; bortezomib neuropathy (roughly 35–45% of treated patients) is often painful and autonomic, with postural hypotension. Ototoxicity accompanies cisplatin, and CIPN is increasingly recognised as a lasting late effect in cancer survivors.
det.diagnosis: Diagnosis is clinical: a typical pattern arising during exposure to a known neurotoxic agent, graded at each cycle with a standard scale (e.g. CTCAE) and, ideally, a baseline examination before the first dose. NCS shows axonal sensory loss, with absent sensory potentials in a non-length-dependent fashion after platinum, and helps when the picture is atypical; small-fibre CIPN (common with taxanes and bortezomib) can have normal NCS and needs skin biopsy if confirmation matters. Rapid, asymmetric, motor-predominant or proximal deficits suggest something else, such as GBS/CIDP triggered during treatment (including checkpoint-inhibitor neuropathies), tumour infiltration or neurolymphomatosis, leptomeningeal disease or paraneoplastic syndromes. Always exclude coexisting diabetes, B12 deficiency, hypothyroidism and a paraprotein, especially in myeloma.
det.treatment: The only proven preventive approach is modifying the dose or schedule — dose reduction, delay, stop-and-go oxaliplatin schedules or switching agents in discussion with oncology. Avoid cold during oxaliplatin infusion, and give bortezomib subcutaneously and weekly rather than intravenously twice weekly, which clearly lowers neuropathy rates. Vitamins, antioxidants, calcium–magnesium infusions and growth factors have not prevented CIPN; limb cooling or compression during taxane infusion is under study with mixed results and is not standard. For established painful CIPN, duloxetine has the best evidence; gabapentinoids, tricyclics and topical agents are used with weaker support. Physiotherapy, balance training, fall prevention and foot care are important.
det.prognosis: Taxane, bortezomib and vinca alkaloid neuropathy often improve over months (vincristine recovery can take up to two years); platinum neuronopathy and high-dose thalidomide neuropathy may be partly permanent, and a sizeable minority of taxane-treated patients keep residual distal symptoms.
pearls: Ask about family foot deformity before vincristine — CMT1A carriers can develop severe weakness.
Platinum neuropathy can worsen after the drug stops; do not mistake coasting for a new disease.
Duloxetine is the only agent with good trial support for painful CIPN.
Subcutaneous weekly bortezomib is much less neurotoxic than the twice-weekly intravenous route.
det.thd: CIPN เป็นปลายประสาทเสื่อมจากยาเคมีบำบัด เช่น platinum, taxane, vincristine, bortezomib และ thalidomide อาการชาหรือเจ็บแปลบเริ่มที่ปลายนิ้วมือนิ้วเท้า และรุนแรงขึ้นตามขนาดยาสะสม oxaliplatin ทำให้ชาเมื่อโดนความเย็นหลังให้ยา cisplatin ทำลาย dorsal root ganglion จึงเดินเซและอาจแย่ลงต่อหลังหยุดยา (coasting) vincristine ทำให้อ่อนแรง ท้องผูก และรุนแรงมากในผู้ที่เป็น CMT การวินิจฉัยอาศัยประวัติเป็นหลัก ควรตัดสาเหตุอื่น และถ้าอ่อนแรงเร็วหรือไม่สมมาตรต้องนึกถึง GBS/CIDP หรือมะเร็งลุกลามเส้นประสาท การรักษาสำคัญคือปรับขนาดหรือหยุดยา ให้ bortezomib แบบฉีดใต้ผิวหนัง และใช้ duloxetine สำหรับอาการปวด

Long-standing diabetes; no relation to chemotherapy cycles

name: Pyridoxine (vitamin B6) toxicity neuropathy
formal: A sensory neuropathy or ganglionopathy caused by chronic high intake of pyridoxine, usually from supplements, producing distal or widespread numbness and sensory ataxia that improves after withdrawal.
simple: Too much vitamin B6 from pills can damage sensory nerves and cause numbness and unsteady walking.
th: ปลายประสาทรับความรู้สึกเสียจากกินวิตามินบี 6 ขนาดสูงนาน ๆ — ชาและเดินเซ หยุดวิตามินแล้วมักดีขึ้น
tempoNote: Weeks to years depending on dose; very large doses cause rapid ganglionopathy
feat: Numbness and tingling in feet and hands, sometimes face or trunk
Loss of vibration and position sense with sensory ataxia and Romberg sign
Strength preserved; reflexes reduced or lost
History of B6-containing supplements, multivitamins, energy drinks or 'neuro' vitamin combinations
Lhermitte-like or burning symptoms in some
inv: Plasma pyridoxal-5-phosphate (often markedly raised)
NCS: reduced or absent sensory amplitudes with normal motor studies
Exclude B12 deficiency, paraneoplastic and Sjögren ganglionopathy, diabetes

case.story: For 18 months has taken a vitamin B1-B6-B12 tablet three times daily for hand numbness, plus a separate B6 supplement; now her feet feel wooden and she sways in the shower.
case.exam: Reduced vibration and absent joint-position at toes, Romberg positive, absent ankle jerks, normal power.
case.tests: PLP 380 nmol/L (high); NCS shows low sural and median sensory amplitudes; B12 and HbA1c normal.
case.q: What is the management?
case.a: Stop all B6-containing products and recheck PLP; most improve over months. Review every supplement label — combination B-vitamin tablets are a common hidden source.

det.patho: Excess pyridoxine is toxic to dorsal root ganglion neurons, which lack a protective blood–nerve barrier. Very high doses (grams per day) cause an acute neuronopathy, while chronic intake of a few hundred milligrams daily, and sometimes much lower amounts over years, causes a length-dependent sensory axonopathy. Individual susceptibility varies.
det.clinical: Symptoms are purely sensory: distal numbness, paraesthesia, unsteady gait and clumsy hands. In severe cases sensory loss affects the face and trunk. Motor power is normal, which is an important clue. Many patients take B6 for carpal tunnel, premenstrual symptoms or 'nerve health', sometimes several products together.
det.diagnosis: Ask directly about vitamins, energy drinks and over-the-counter combinations, as patients rarely volunteer them. Raised plasma PLP with a sensory axonal pattern on NCS supports the diagnosis. Rule out other ganglionopathies (Sjögren, anti-Hu, cisplatin) and B12 deficiency before attributing symptoms to B6.
det.treatment: Withdraw all sources of pyridoxine; no antidote exists. Provide balance and gait training, and symptomatic treatment for painful paraesthesia. Repeat PLP to confirm falling levels.
det.prognosis: Most improve over months after withdrawal, sometimes after a short worsening; severe neuronopathy may leave residual ataxia.
pearls: Ironically, B6 taken for neuropathy may be the cause of the neuropathy.
Pure sensory with normal strength: always take a supplement history.
Combination B1-B6-B12 tablets are widely used in Thailand; count the total daily B6.
det.thd: การกินวิตามินบี 6 ขนาดสูงเป็นเวลานานทำลายเซลล์ประสาทรับความรู้สึกใน dorsal root ganglion ทำให้ชาปลายมือปลายเท้าและเดินเซ แต่กำลังกล้ามเนื้อปกติ ตรวจพบระดับ PLP ในเลือดสูงและ NCS เป็น sensory neuropathy การรักษาคือหยุดวิตามินบี 6 ทุกแหล่ง รวมถึงวิตามินบีรวม ส่วนใหญ่อาการดีขึ้นในหลายเดือน

name: HIV-associated distal sensory polyneuropathy
formal: A length-dependent, predominantly small-fibre axonal sensory neuropathy occurring in people with HIV, caused by the infection itself and historically by neurotoxic nucleoside antiretrovirals.
simple: Nerve damage in people with HIV that causes painful burning or numb feet.
th: ปลายประสาทรับความรู้สึกเสียในผู้ติดเชื้อ HIV — ปวดแสบชาที่เท้าทั้งสองข้าง พบบ่อยที่สุดในกลุ่มโรคประสาทจาก HIV
tempoNote: Slowly progressive over months to years; antiretroviral toxic forms appeared weeks to months after starting the drug
feat: Symmetric burning, aching or electric pain in the soles and toes
Allodynia; patients avoid shoes or bedsheets touching the feet
Reduced pinprick and temperature distally, reduced or absent ankle jerks
Little or no weakness
Risk factors: older age, height, low nadir CD4, past stavudine/didanosine exposure, diabetes
inv: Clinical diagnosis; NCS may be normal (small fibre) or show low sural amplitudes
Skin biopsy for intraepidermal nerve fibre density if NCS normal
Screen for other causes: glucose/HbA1c, B12, syphilis serology, TSH, alcohol, isoniazid without B6

case.who: 46-year-old man living with HIV for 15 years
case.story: Took a stavudine-based regimen early on; now on TDF/3TC/DTG with suppressed virus. Both feet burn at night and feel like walking on hot sand.
case.exam: Reduced pinprick to ankles, vibration slightly reduced at toes, absent ankle jerks, normal strength.
case.tests: HbA1c 5.6%, B12 normal, VDRL non-reactive; NCS normal; skin biopsy shows reduced epidermal nerve fibre density.
case.q: Which neuropathic pain treatment has trial support in HIV neuropathy?
case.a: Evidence is weak overall; topical capsaicin 8% and smoked cannabis showed benefit in trials, while amitriptyline, gabapentin and pregabalin performed no better than placebo in several studies — though they are still often tried.

Chapter 9 Infectious and granulomatous neuropathies: HIV-related peripheral neuropathies
Chapter 8 Neurological illnesses involved in HIV and HTLV infections (peripheral nerves)
Chapter 23 Neuropathies Associated With HIV Infection and Antiretroviral Therapy
Chapter 12 Polyneuropathies (12.5.1 Human Immunodeficiency Virus-1 Neuropathy)

det.patho: HIV hardly ever infects neurons or Schwann cells; instead, infected and activated macrophages gather in the dorsal root ganglia and nerves, and shed viral proteins (gp120, Tat) and inflammatory cytokines that injure sensory neurons and their mitochondria, producing a length-dependent dying-back of the longest, thinnest axons with secondary demyelination. The older 'd-drug' nucleoside analogues — stavudine, didanosine and zalcitabine — added a dose-dependent toxic neuropathy through inhibition of mitochondrial DNA polymerase-gamma. Before effective ART about a third of patients had it clinically and sural nerve pathology was almost universal at autopsy; with modern regimens new cases are fewer, but prevalence stays substantial because people live longer. Today older age, greater height, diabetes, raised triglycerides, alcohol and past d-drug exposure predict it more than CD4 count or viral load.
det.clinical: Patients describe burning, aching, tingling or 'walking on hot sand' feet, often worse at night, with allodynia to socks and bedclothes; the hands are involved only late. Examination shows reduced pin and temperature sensation in a stocking pattern, mildly reduced vibration, absent or reduced ankle jerks and, at most, weakness of intrinsic foot muscles. Toxic neuropathy from d-drugs tends to start abruptly within months of exposure, is more painful, and may keep worsening for 1–2 months after the drug is stopped ('coasting'). Prominent weakness, asymmetry, cranial nerve involvement or rapid progression point elsewhere: HIV-associated GBS or CIDP, mononeuritis multiplex (including CMV-related), CMV lumbosacral polyradiculopathy, diffuse infiltrative lymphocytosis syndrome or lymphomatous infiltration. The stage of infection helps: GBS- or CIDP-like neuropathies cluster around seroconversion and the otherwise silent early phase, vasculitic mononeuritis multiplex in early symptomatic disease, and distal sensory neuropathy and autonomic neuropathy later. In treated cohorts roughly half of patients have signs of DSP on examination, and a substantial minority report moderate-to-severe pain that limits walking and sleep.
det.diagnosis: The diagnosis is clinical: typical symptoms plus distal sensory signs and depressed ankle reflexes in a person with HIV, after other causes are excluded. Nerve conduction studies may be normal (pure small-fibre disease) or show reduced sural amplitudes; skin biopsy for intraepidermal nerve fibre density and quantitative sensory or sudomotor tests confirm small-fibre loss when NCS are normal. Screen for diabetes, B12 deficiency, thyroid disease, syphilis, hepatitis C, alcohol, and neurotoxic drugs — isoniazid without pyridoxine, dapsone, thalidomide, vinca alkaloids and other chemotherapy. Reserve CSF, MRI of roots or nerve biopsy for atypical, weak or asymmetric presentations. HIV-DSP is therefore a diagnosis of exclusion; vitamin D is often low in people with HIV and is worth checking, and hepatitis C co-infection and substance use add their own neuropathic risk.
det.treatment: Keep the virus suppressed, withdraw any remaining d-drug and give pyridoxine with isoniazid; there is no proven disease-modifying therapy. Pain treatment draws on general neuropathic-pain practice, but HIV trials are discouraging: amitriptyline and gabapentinoids often failed against placebo, small studies favour gabapentin and lamotrigine, and the high-concentration (8%) capsaicin patch has the most consistent trial support, while low-strength capsaicin creams did not help. A pragmatic plan is a topical agent (8% capsaicin patch or lidocaine) plus a trial of duloxetine, a gabapentinoid or a tricyclic, checking interactions with ART and stopping what does not help; avoid escalating opioids. Foot care, glycaemic control, alcohol reduction, sleep and mood support all matter.
det.prognosis: Usually chronic and persistent; pain may plateau or ease over years, but lost small fibres seldom regenerate, and d-drug neuropathy may improve partly after drug withdrawal.
pearls: Always ask about isoniazid without pyridoxine in HIV patients treated for TB.
Weakness, asymmetry or rapid spread is not HIV-DSP — look for CIDP, mononeuritis multiplex or CMV polyradiculopathy.
Normal nerve conduction does not exclude small-fibre neuropathy; skin biopsy does.
Symptoms that keep worsening for weeks after stopping stavudine reflect coasting, not a new process.
Match the neuropathy to the HIV stage: demyelinating GBS/CIDP early, vasculitic mononeuritis in early symptomatic disease, DSP later.
det.thd: HIV-DSP เป็นโรคปลายประสาทที่พบบ่อยที่สุดในผู้ติดเชื้อ HIV เกิดจาก macrophage และโปรตีนของไวรัสทำลายเซลล์ประสาทรับความรู้สึก ร่วมกับพิษจากยาต้านไวรัสรุ่นเก่า (stavudine, didanosine) ปัจจัยเสี่ยงปัจจุบันคืออายุมาก ตัวสูง เบาหวาน และสุรา ผู้ป่วยปวดแสบร้อนและชาที่ฝ่าเท้าสองข้าง reflex ข้อเท้าลดลง แต่กำลังกล้ามเนื้อปกติ วินิจฉัยทางคลินิก ถ้า NCS ปกติอาจยืนยันด้วย skin biopsy และต้องตัดเบาหวาน ขาด B12 ซิฟิลิส และยา เช่น isoniazid ที่ไม่ได้ให้ B6 ถ้ามีอ่อนแรงหรือไม่สมมาตรต้องหาสาเหตุอื่น การรักษาคือคุมไวรัส หยุดยาที่เป็นพิษ และรักษาอาการปวดด้วย capsaicin 8% patch หรือยา neuropathic pain ซึ่งได้ผลจำกัด
